From Zawiercie — the denunciation says — Frommer moved to Sosnowiec, where he follows the same ways“..
It was signed on that [?] by a number of Sosnowiec Jews.
On the strength of the denunciation two secret agents [?] came to the local beit midrash in Koziegłowy to question the locals [?] about the „blackmail deeds“ of Rabbi Frommer..
It goes without saying that such a shameful denunciation against such a world-class genius as Rabbi Frommer has aroused bitterness in Sosnowiec, especially since some of the signatories declare categorically that they had no idea what their signatures were taken for and that they were deceived in an ugly manner...
In connection with this the Rabbinical Council held an urgent meeting yesterday, at which it was resolved to come out with a protest, to call a mass meeting, etc.
— Jewish Sosnowiec must not remain indifferent at a time when one sees that intriguers want by every possible means to sow hatred and quarrels among the Jewish citizens.
Bloody events between police and workers. Bread or work — a clash. — Dozens wounded

On Tuesday a bloody clash took place here between the unemployed and the police. The result: 3 workers were seriously and several dozen lightly wounded.
The course of events was as follows:
Already from 9 o'clock in the morning masses of unemployed gathered in front of the magistrate [town hall], demanding relief for the holidays.
At 11 o'clock the number of unemployed reached 8 thousand persons.
A delegation went to the town president Hilger; the latter had a telephone conversation with the voivode, who promised that the relief payments could only be given the next day, Wednesday.
When the delegation came back with this answer, the crowd was not satisfied and began singing „Czerwony Sztandar“ [„The Red Flag“].
At that moment a larger detachment of mounted police arrived, which was met by the crowd with stones, bricks, etc. The police dispersed the gathered crowd by force, and on the spot 3 workers were seriously wounded; the ambulance [pogotowie] of the Health Insurance Fund took them to hospital.
The lightly wounded received medical help on the spot.
At the same time a delegation went to the district starosta, demanding that the term of the relief payments be extended.
The starosta promised to deal with the request properly.
A bandit attack. — 4000 zł. robbed.

Four masked bandits broke into the property owner Skotnicz [?] in Grabaszyn [?] and, threatening with revolvers, robbed him of 4 thousand zł. The victim reported the attack to the police in Kazimierz, which arrested 1 bandit an hour later.
Under interrogation the bandit „told tales out of cheder“ [gave the game away], thanks to which the others who took part in the attack were arrested.
Another 3,245 zł. was found on those arrested.
Not „a foot for a foot“, only 1 month in prison.

At the railway station in Myszków the following case happened a few weeks ago: while a railway official was busy uncoupling a wagon of a goods train, the conductor gave a signal to the engine driver for the train to leave. As soon as [?] the train moved from its place, the official fell under the wheels, which cut off his right foot.
This week the conductor stood before the local district court, which sentenced him to a month in prison.
On building a post-office building.

The Post and Telegraph Directorate has informed the local magistrate [town council] that the Ministry of Posts is inclined to give the town a loan for the purpose of building a post-office building in Sosnowiec.
General Meeting of the “Bank Kupiecki”.

Next Monday, Isru Chag of Passover, the annual general meeting of the “Bank Kupiecki” [Merchants’ Bank] will take place at the “Hotel Polski”. The agenda is a very important one, and it is a duty upon all members to come to the meeting.

A fire broke out at the railway station in Strzemieszyce. Part of the station building burned down. The damage amounts to about 15 thousand zł.

The local Revisionist organisation is holding next Sunday, at the close of the holiday, a large Eretz-Israel ball with various attractions.
The ball takes place in the halls of the Merchants’ and Industrialists’ Association on Kahalska [?] Street.

To Collect a Tallit.
The beit-midrash gabbai Alter Zajdler asks us to announce that he found with a young man a new tallit which had been stolen in the beit midrash. The injured party should contact him.

Suicide Attempt by a Woman.
In Łazy a young woman threw herself under the train. Luckily she was rescued; she received only a few wounds.
The reason for the suicide [attempt] is an unsuccessful operation by a local midwife.
—o—
Distinguished Theatre Guests in Zagłębie.
On the second days of the holiday the well-known artists [?] founders of artists’ troupes, Zygmunt Turkow and Jonas Turkow, with their ensembles, are giving guest performances in Będzin and Sosnowiec.
Tonight Zygmunt Turkow is performing in Będzin, at the “Corso” theatre; “The Thought”, the famous tragedy by Andreyev, is being played.
The same performance will be given on Saturday evening in the Sosnowiec Municipal Theatre.
— Tonight Jonas Turkow and his ensemble are playing in the Sosnowiec Municipal Theatre “The Reason”, which was translated into Yiddish for the first time by Mr. Turkow. The same performance will be given on Saturday evening in Będzin at the “Corso”.
Dąbrowa — A “Herzliya” Founded.

On the initiative of the Będzin “Herzliya”, a branch of the organisation has been founded here too. It soon succeeded in recruiting a larger number of Dąbrowa school youth, who promptly joined the work under the guidance of the members of the Będzin “Herzliya”. The Zionist Organisation in Dąbrowa also helped with this, handing over the Zionist premises to the young organisation. The founding of the “Herzliya” is an important development; through the organisation the Dąbrowa school youth is being drawn into Zionist life.

Postponing all taxes and spreading them into instalments

[Zagłębie — taxes; local news.]
The chambers of commerce have approached the Minister of Finance with a memorandum demanding the following concessions regarding the payment of taxes:
1) To split the half of the income tax that must now be paid into two instalments, the first payable on 1 May and the second in August, without penalty or interest.
2) To pay the balance of the assessed turnover tax for the year 1929 in 4 instalments: 15 June, 15 July, 15 August and 15 September, without penalty or interest, and
3) To postpone the deadline of the first advance payment („zaliczka“) on the turnover tax for 1930 to 15 July, without penalty or interest.
The chambers of commerce have also sent these postulates to the Ministry of Commerce with a request to support the demands.
Inspection of cabs.
The Magistrat (city council) draws attention to the fact that an inspection of the condition of the cabs (droshkies) will take place soon. The owners must make sure that the cabs are fitted out according to the regulations, so as to avoid fines.
Keren Hayesod campaign in Zawiercie.
In connection with the campaign for Keren Hayesod in Zawiercie, Mr. Israel Ritov, a member of the Council of the Jewish Agency, stayed there. He held several meetings there, among others a youth meeting in the premises of the „Mizrachi“ cheder. Before a hall packed full of young people the speaker spoke about the present situation in Eretz Israel after the recent events and about the necessity of creating large funds for the further development of the country.
The second meeting took place in the „Apollo“ cinema before a large audience. Mr. Ritov lectured on „Zionism and its opponents“, in which the speaker brought various proofs that all our opponents are coming over to Zionism.
The guest also held a meeting at WIZO with the participation of a large number of women, to whom the speaker spoke about the task of the Jewish woman, both[?] for the Eretz Israel movement and for the work of Keren Hayesod.
A farewell evening in honour of Mr. Ritov took place in the hall of the „Bank Kpolruszelczy“[?] [probably Bank Spółdzielczy, the cooperative bank], attended by the notables („pnei“) of Zawiercie.
The response of the Jewish population was a warm one: despite the difficult material situation prevailing in Zawiercie, the number of declarants (pledgers) has grown considerably. M. A. Z.

The voivodeship office has received a circular from the Ministry of the Interior concerning apprentices and their relation to military service.
The circular explains that apprentices working in artisans' workshops, industrial enterprises or commercial enterprises must attach to their application for deferment a certificate from the board of the relevant artisans' guild; these certificates are issued by the Chamber of Crafts or by the Chamber of Commerce and Industry.

Letters to the Editor.

[Letters to the editor — kehilla; turnover tax; the Aleksander Hasidim in Sosnowiec.]
I.
Dear Mr. Editor!
In your paper no. 16 of 18 April 1930 the vice-president of the kehilla council, Mr. Frenkel, addressed us in an open letter, making a series of unfounded reproaches against us; we consider it necessary to give the following explanations:
1) We, as the kehilla board, could not at all consider Mr. Frenkel's resignation as vice-president of the kehilla council, because it is not within our competence to accept or reject resignations of council members. We therefore forwarded the letter of resignation to the kehilla council, which at its meeting of 2 April this year resolved to send copies of the letters of resignation of the council members Frenkel, Rechnic and Szejn to the starostwo, the voivodeship and the ministry, together with a declaration which Mr. Goldsztajn had submitted at an earlier meeting. The declaration states: "Taking into account that the term of the last council of the Jewish kehilla has already ended, and taking into account that some members of the council as well as of the board have resigned, not wishing to bear the responsibility for the activity in the Jewish gmina, we declare that the council and the board in their present composition are not entitled to draw up a budget for the Jewish kehilla. They must dissolve and a new one must be elected in their place."
To this the local starosta replied that the resignations should not be accepted, in the absence of extraordinary circumstances that would justify the resignation of a kehilla council member.
2) As to the manner in which the kehilla council draws up budgets — of what size and with how many members present — we can give no explanation; that is the business of the kehilla council itself.
3) Unfortunately, Mr. Frenkel, we cannot bear the consequences of not replying to your resignation. Your letter was not correctly addressed, and our task was to direct it to the correct address. This we did.—
Thanking you, Mr. Editor, for the space you grant us, we remain
respectfully
Vice-chairman M. Y. Prawer.
II.
Esteemed Mr. Editor!
Kindly allow me to publish the following letter in your esteemed paper, for which I thank you in advance.
Esteemed members of the assessment commission for the turnover tax!
At a time when almost the entire Jewish merchant class has been ruined by the incorrect assessment, year after year, of the turnover tax — which has provoked in the commercial world, Jewish and Christian alike, a storm of desperate protests — the right moment has, I believe, come to demand of you, "Jewish public workers", as members of the tax commission — that is, you who helped to assess the tax [podatek] — that you be so kind as to give the Jewish population a little account of your deeds and answer the following questions:
1) How could you accept that in the crisis year 1929 [?], in which Jews became poor people and their whole existence was ruined, it should be agreed [?] that they made larger turnovers, and that they be taxed with a much higher podatek than in previous years?
2) Did you check the documents which the "Urząd Skarbowy" [tax office] holds on each taxpayer and which are supposed to justify the assessment?
3) If you had no power to prevent the high tax assessment — which I strongly doubt — why did you not enter your "votum separatum" in the minutes, which might perhaps have been of use in the appeals? Or else, having no choice, why did you not leave the meeting demonstratively as a protest?
I ask you, very esteemed gentlemen, kindly to answer all the questions clearly, so that I shall not be forced to write about this again, with more details.
Respectfully
Y. Gelbart.

The Bloody Friday in Zawiercie

3 Killed and 30 Wounded.
On Friday regrettable events occurred here — clashes between the unemployed and the police, which ended in bloodshed. 3 persons were killed and 30 wounded, several of them seriously.
The indirect cause of the unrest was that the municipality had not paid the unemployed any relief.
From the very morning a very tense mood was felt among the unemployed, because the municipality had not paid out the relief for the holiday. Until 3 in the afternoon the crowd of unemployed milled about the street in great agitation. Seeing that it was already 4 o'clock and the municipal cash office was still closed, a crowd of 2000 persons went to the municipal building. At once a hail of stones poured down and the windows of the municipality began to shatter one after another. Several officials, men and women, were injured by the stones that fell into the municipal rooms.
Afterwards a larger group of unemployed forced their way into the municipal offices, breaking open the bolted doors and demolishing the interior furnishings. All the tables and all the chairs were smashed; the cabinets with books and files were thrown out and trampled, or thrown out into the street; the telephone connections were torn out, the typewriters smashed. In short, everything was reduced to a heap of ruins.
Meanwhile a detachment of police arrived and called on the crowd to disperse. The demonstrators then began pelting the police with stones. Several policemen were wounded in the head. When, even after a third call to disperse, the crowd would still not calm down, the police fired a volley into the air. Then the demonstrators threw themselves at the police with knives. Some also began shooting with revolvers, and one policeman was wounded.
The situation became extremely critical. The police fired into the crowd, and several persons in the crowd staggered. This served as a signal for the crowd to throw itself at the police. From all sides a hail of stones began to rain down on the police, and revolver shots were heard, coming from hiding places behind the houses. The revolver shots hit police and crowd alike. At last the police succeeded in dispersing the demonstrators. 6 policemen were seriously wounded; the remaining policemen, together with those who came later to help, fought the demonstrators, and the shooting went on, with short interruptions, until 8 in the evening.
In the shooting 30-year-old Meir Krakowski, a chance passer-by, was tragically killed; he was struck by a bullet in the heart and fell dead on the spot.
Besides him, two more workers from the crowd were killed, and 30 demonstrators were wounded.
After the demonstration 26 persons were arrested.
On the seventh day of Passover the body of the tragically killed Krakowski was examined[?] (the word „gepalmest“ is unclear), and the prosecutor's office established that the bullet had come from the crowd. On Sunday he was brought to Jewish burial.
Krakowski was a very quiet man, a native of Pilica; he earned his living as a boot-upper stitcher.
— — —
Of those arrested, 11 were kept in custody and the rest were released. This week the municipality began to employ the unemployed; 700 workers are already employed. The situation in the town is calm.
Planned activity — Responsible public work or frivolous pastimes. The need for unity

(Responsible public work or frivolous pastimes. The need for unity)
Here we learn nothing, we gain nothing and we lose nothing; we do not even take the trouble to think through what merits the good sides have and what drawbacks the bad ones. People are somehow indifferent to everything, apathetically disposed, and no one cares about the public losses that arise from all this, from which the community suffers continually.
What does the Będzin self-government apparatus look like? How are things with our city fathers? How do they feel in their roles? What do they do for the community, for the city? In other towns people envy us: after all, they say, you have brought in half Jews; surely you can run affairs to your best advantage, to the best advantage of the town's citizens.
But here, stand up and confirm that the first half is true — we have indeed brought half Jews into our self-government. But the second half, that we can carry through everything in the world to our advantage, is not true. Well, go and tell people that it is a fantasy, a utopia — rarely will anyone believe you.
One can believe in this harmony only as long as one does not look at what the activity looks like; but as soon as one looks at how the sessions are run, in what manner people take part in them, a completely different opinion is formed, and then one sees how pale everything is in relation to living reality.
While it is a matter of getting the seats, they promise you everything in the world, the very "plate from heaven"; but hardly have the seats been set up — oh, then everything is forgotten, they even forget what responsibility they took upon themselves. First of all, they do not come to the sessions, and if they do come once in a while, they are not at all interested in what is at issue, and of course in such a case one cannot bring great benefit to society. As a result of all this the activity has become petty, worthless, so that one can never know how this or that proposal will turn out. Every time, therefore, we run into sensations, into surprises; phrase-mongering [?] and caricatures emerge. And with the present activity this is no wonder, since some of our representatives regard self-government as a kind of toy [?], a sport, so that they come there to amuse themselves when they are in good spirits, when they feel in a good mood, cheered up. One can therefore imagine what such administrative activity can look like, how fruitful it can be and what benefit it can bring to society.
And when people come to amuse themselves, or even to spite one another, it stands to reason that if one pulls to the left, the other must pull precisely to the right; if one says yes, the other must say no — without any awareness whatsoever. The whole "awareness" consists only in this: that it must be done differently.
It goes without saying that the Jewish population loses a great deal through such a cat-and-mouse politics. People then lose their balance, and the greatest follies and errors are committed, so that more than once one cannot raise one's eyes for shame. But they reckon with nothing and no one when they stage their "attractions." Many disgraces are to be recorded to their account on the one hand, and on the other they are utterly incapable of performing any fruitful activity for the good of their voters.
Well, all year long there is "boxing" among one's own and strangers, and harm is done to the community in every possible way; but now it is time to draw up the budget, and it is horrifying to think in what manner they will approach this great undertaking. After all, the budget amounts to a sum of 2 million złoty. So in what way can this difficult matter be resolved for the good of the Jewish population, when there is no unity, when so much fragmentation reigns in our ranks? It is simply unheard of that public representatives should abandon so much Jewish money in these hard times!
It is, after all, understandable that our antisemites will take advantage of the favourable moment and see to it that the obligations are thrown onto Jewish shoulders. On the other hand, when it is a matter of a subsidy for our sake [?], they will do everything in the world to make sure we do not get it.
Do our councillors really not stop to consider this crucial point? Will they here too, on the budget question, carry on [?] with fragmentation, tripping each other up? Will the city fathers be able, with a clear conscience, to help, directly or indirectly, to squander Jewish money?
If there is no unification in the Jewish camp, it is out of the question that the Jewish population should not suffer defeat here at every turn. With the best will in the world Jewish money will be squandered, because, first, the quorum is rarely made up, so that we do not get the number of votes needed to pass a proposal favourable to us; and second, when they do come, they are so raw in the questions under discussion, they find their way about so poorly, that unwittingly they come to fail on all questions.
It would of course be quite different if planned, systematic work were introduced, where every question would first be considered well and diligently [?], so that on coming into the city council every councillor would be clear about what is at issue; and of course after such preparation one's position crystallizes and one knows which line to follow.
We know that there are also "wise men" who do not let themselves be harnessed to the wagon, who need no one's explanations, and with whom it may perhaps be hard to get along; it is quite possible that they will not want to cooperate at all with those who wish to unite and carry out planned work for the good of the Jewish citizens. In that case one will have to give up on them and do what one can, what is feasible; then at least it will be known that good will was shown, and that with so many and so many [people] it proved possible to carry out a united activity for the interests of the city.
Now the active councillors must see to creating a united front, so that the budget may be approached with full awareness. From now on the councillors must not find themselves in such a fragmented state as hitherto, if they intend to achieve something for the citizens in general and for the Jewish ones in particular.
R. Let.

Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings and remarks on this week's portion (Shemini)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings and remarks on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and edited by Y. P.
Parashat Shemini.
—o—
A) — "Take thee a young calf" (9:2)
The evil inclination has its own various back ways [?]. To a tzaddik it will of course not propose a sin — he would only shake himself free of it. So what does it do? It takes the sin, wraps it in a mantle of holiness and disguises it outright as a mitzvah. Well, a pious Jew is after all eager to do a mitzvah... In just this way he, the Evil One, lures even tzaddikim into his net.
Hasidic books.
*
The Rebbe of Błędów once ran about his house as if he were chasing someone to catch him; he runs like this and then stops at the Holy Ark and claps his hands together as if to say: lost, he slipped out of my hands..
The Hasidim ask him what happened here, and he tells them: I saw the Evil One in my house. I chased him and wanted to catch him, but he hid in the Torah, inside the Holy Ark (an allusion to the so-called "Torah-true" Jews) — and there, there I can do nothing more..
B) — "This is the thing which ye shall do, and the glory of the Lord shall appear unto you" (9:6)
That is how things go in our world: when a leader does something, however crooked and bad it may be, he is given honour for it. His slightest foolishness is held to be a glorious [?] deed. But Moses said: no — "this is the thing which ye shall do": if you truly do something for your God, or your people, then — "the glory of the Lord shall appear unto you": then he will earn the true honour.
Meleches Machshoves.
C) — "And Moses and Aaron went into the tent of meeting, and came out, and blessed the people" (9:23)
When a great man wants "to bless the people" — to lead the people and be a blessing to it — he must go "into the tent of meeting" (in Hebrew mo'ed means: time): he must fit himself [?] to the problems of the time, to the questions of the day; then he will be a blessing to his people and will understand how to lead it.
After the Ohev Yisrael [R. Abraham Joshua Heschel of Apt].
D) — "Drink no wine nor strong drink" (10:9)
The well-known gaon R. Abele [?] of Vilna was a very kind man. To every guest who came to him for a letter of recommendation, he gave one. Once he gave such a letter to an irresponsible person. The man got drunk, rolled [?] about in the gutters and in this way lost the letter, which people found and handed over to the gaon. The guest, sobering up, saw that he no longer had the letter, and ran quickly to the gaon for a second letter. When the gaon would not give it to him, he begged for mercy: "I have two daughters to marry off" — to which the gaon said:
— Now I understand why people say "drunk as Lot". Why don't they say "drunk as Noah"? Noah too was a drunkard, and an earlier one than Lot. But about Noah there is no question why he got drunk: he had already married off all his children and planted himself a vineyard — as the Torah says — so he could allow himself to get drunk; but Lot, who still had two grown daughters, had no business getting drunk...
E) — "Diligently inquired" (10:16)
"The law of the Lord is perfect" — God's Torah is entirely whole. After so many homilies and commentaries on it, it is still untouched; no one has yet [?] come near its deep essence.
Rabbi Israel Baal Shem Tov.
F) "Moses diligently inquired, and, behold, it was burnt" (ibid.)
The Torah is for some an elixir of life and for others a deadly poison. And the scholar too must possess the two opposite qualities: sometimes to heal and soothe, and sometimes to burn and [illegible word]. Yes, the latter is absolutely necessary for a leader too, for a Moses. The serpent of brass had the same quality; of it the Torah tells that whoever looked "unto the serpent of brass, lived". This is what a Moses must possess: "and, behold, it was burnt" — to be like the fiery serpent, sometimes to burn out what is bad.
Degel Machaneh Ephraim [R. Moses Hayyim Ephraim of Sudylkiv].
G) "Every raven after its kind" (11:15)
The Gemara (end of Chullin 63) says: "If you find a white raven, you will find a virtuous woman." What is the meaning of this allegorical saying?
The Talmudists [?] count as good Jewish qualities: bashful — modest, merciful, doers of kindness, and "guchim" [sic] to be enticed, i.e. of firm character. The last two are not found among women: they do not like to do kindness, and as for character, they are after all the weakest — "women are light-minded". The raven too has two signs of purity and two signs of impurity. Hence the comparison between raven and woman: both have two signs of purity, and the weakness is a symbol of impurity; therefore "if you find a white raven, you will find a virtuous woman."
Lev Aryeh, Chullin.
H) "And the stork" (11:19)
Rashi says: why is the bird called chasidah? Because it behaves kindly (chasidus) toward its companions. Now one asks: why does this bird belong among the unclean birds?
— Because it does kindness only with its own companions, and not with strangers..
Rabbi Yitzchakl of Warka.
I) "And every earthen vessel... ye shall break it" (11:33)
For an earthen vessel the only purification is to break it. "Earthenware vessels — their breaking is their purification." And man too is likened to an earthen vessel (both come from the earth), and his purification too can come only through a broken heart, through a broken and refined spirit.
The holy Ari.
———
Avot, chapter one.
"Moses received the Torah from Sinai" (1).
Moses was the humblest of all men. When God made him a messenger to Pharaoh he wanted to avoid it, would by no means become a leader — so why did he accept the Torah so easily? Why did he not try to fend off the honour as before? That is what the Tanna asks: "Moses received the Torah"? Why did Moses accept the Torah so easily?
The answer is: "from Sinai". Moses saw that the Torah was being given on Sinai — the lowest mountain in the world, and he learned from this that just as the mountain on which the Torah was to be given is the lowest, so too the man through whom the Torah is to be given must be the lowliest; and who else — Moses our teacher thought — is as lowly as I?
Kedushat Levi [R. Levi Yitzchak of Berdichev].
K) "And on deeds of kindness" (2)
The Gemara says that gemilut chasadim (deeds of kindness) is greater than charity, because with a loan of kindness — if someone borrows a hundred gulden and repays, the second time he receives a loan of two hundred, the third time more, and so on. With charity, by contrast, if someone gives a person alms and that person comes a second time, he gives him less, and each time less and less; therefore a deed of kindness is greater than charity.
Sichat Chullin.
L) "Aaron loved peace and pursued peace" (12)
Aaron was a pursuer of peace in Jewish families; he made peace between husband and wife thanks to his kindness and tact. Therefore he was so beloved that after his death it is written "and all the house of Israel wept for him", whereas for Moses only "and all the children of Israel wept for him" is mentioned — only the sons of Israel, but for Aaron the women too.
Sifra.
The Curtain Has Risen

(On the denunciations concerning the rabbinate affair in Sosnowiec)
Well, the curtain has risen, the actors have appeared on the stage and each is playing the role that suits him best.
But the spectacle is ugly and the roles are bad to the point of being unbearable — it is understood that we mean here to discuss the rabbinate question in Sosnowiec. Ever since the rabbinate affair arose among us, various combinations have been hatched, some very unpleasant scenes have been played out, and various illegal deeds have been done over the heads of the Jewish citizens of Sosnowiec. But everything was crude and brutal, coarse and insolent, and — the main thing — nobody remained satisfied; everyone felt wronged.
Of course it is very hard to manage in such a situation, when one has to satisfy everybody, when one has to bring to a town a mara de-atra [chief rabbi] who would be worthy of occupying the rabbinical chair; and the question became even worse because the kehilla representatives, in whose hands the bringing of a rabbi lay, did not handle the question honestly and sincerely; they did not take account of the fact that they had to bring a rabbi for the town of Sosnowiec. They went down various slippery paths, and the "responsibility" [probably meant: irresponsibility] and lawlessness exceeded every limit. Every group had its candidate, every party — its rabbi; none of them wanted to look reality in the eye; each was only out to smuggle in its own candidate, no matter whether by legal or illegal means.
But in the end all these unlovely means apparently became distasteful, and people began to think how to reach an agreement so that the matter would come to a conclusion. It even came to a certain agreement between several sides, which united, and this combination had a right to exist, and so it could be expected that peace and tranquillity would reign in the town.
And so it indeed was: it turned out that the question was solved, and the Jews of Sosnowiec are satisfied with the agreements reached between the sides. And why fool ourselves — the ordinary everyday Jew, the Jew who knows nothing of tricks and combinations, of squabbles[?] and intrigues, the Jew who has in mind his livelihood and living in peace and unity — he remained satisfied.
But there are also other Jews, those who are only waiting for quarrels, those who cannot live when things are calm and quiet — and now they strive [obscure word, "dos shtek"?] to kindle a fire; they stage[?] denunciations and quarrels. And when a fire is lit and the fire blazes — to our shame — they come alive like fish in water. They schemed so long, crawled so long through underground ways, dug so long and crawled like worms, like the lowest creature, until they forgot what and whom it is all about, and they lit the fire with such force that it should flare up and bring shame and humiliation not only in our own eyes but also in the eyes of the authorities, in government circles.
Do they think they will achieve anything with the false denunciations? Will they accomplish anything by taking a gaon and a God-fearing man, a man who does not know how to play politics or stir up quarrels, and writing about him that he came to extort money from the population of Sosnowiec? Can one with a clear conscience say such things about a man who is crystal-pure? About a man who does not know how to say one thing and think another? How dare one say of such a ben Torah, who does not know how to get involved in intrigues, that he came to Sosnowiec to stir up quarrels? Do the quarrel-mongers think that with the help of secret agents and detectives they will drive the man out of Sosnowiec? Do they think that with the help of signatures for their ugly deeds, tricked out of ignorant, naive people, they will clear the way to sow hatred and enmity between one Jew and another? Between one part of the Jewish population and the other?
Will Jewish Sosnowiec not reject with disgust and contempt all these shameful means? Will any decent Jew want to set off on such slippery paths, which bring into our ranks so much hatred and enmity that one forgets where in the world one is? And if we go down such paths, if we sully ourselves — what kind of face will we have then in the eyes of the authorities? What opinion can the outside world have of our great men at a time when, from the Jewish camp itself, sand is thrown in their eyes, and nothing at all stops people from presenting the intrigues more "politely"[?], so that they tear, agitate and arouse as much hatred and bitterness as possible? Can one watch all this ugliness with indifference, pass over it all with an ice-cold numbness, and give the impression that one sees nothing, feels nothing, as if it were not about us?
Even denunciations and intrigues and false interpretations must, after all, have a limit; one must know how far to go, how high to strike; and on the other hand one must also remember on whom one wants to throw mud, which man one wants to "crown" with the title "harmful element", "undesirable person".
We know very well that the intriguers stop at nothing to carry out their orgies; we know perfectly well that speaking then to their hearts, to their conscience, is just like throwing peas at the wall in the hope they will stick. But they, the small handful, strive to attract as many ignorant elements as possible, to persuade as many naive Jews as possible that these crooked "neytike"[?] ways are the most balanced and correct, the most just and the finest. Thus they want to create a split, thus they strive to use all crooked, clumsy and illegal ways — and they want to persuade the masses that this is the straight path, the way of truth and righteousness, justice and vindication.
And these naive ones, the ignorant elements, who can be persuaded of anything in the world, are found among us at every step, in all ranks and strata of our camp. And to them it must be said: do not let anyone persuade you that black is white, that night is day; have the courage to look reality in the eye. Do not be a blind tool in another's hands; do not let others make of you what they want to make of you.
You must not forget that you need not be dependent on anyone. After all, you are people with your own mind and an independent way of thinking, and you can find your own bearings and know what is beautiful and what is ugly, what is truth and what is falsehood.
We must not allow that, in this present bitter and difficult time for Jews, a fire of hatred and enmity should flare up in our own camp, and that we should spend all our energy and strength on it. To help go down such paths would mean bringing deadly poison onto our life's path; and therefore, therefore the deceitful deeds that irresponsible intriguers want to introduce into the Sosnowiec Jewish kehilla must be rejected with disgust and contempt.
A Parnas [kehilla board member].

Across the Great Beautiful World. XIII) The Egyptian Treasures in the Paris World Museum, the "Louvre".

[Feuilleton — travel impressions; series "Across the Great Beautiful World", part XIII.] By L. Szpigelman [the paper's editor]. (From my travel notebook)
8.*)
As we go up to the first floor, where thousands upon thousands of large and small objects and vessels of bronze, clay, stone, iron [?] and gold from various Egyptian pyramids are displayed, there is also also a large statue made of amber marble, which is transparent as a mirror. This is the figure of our hero Ramesses the Second, under whom, according to the historical accounts [?], the Jews were enslaved in Egypt, and in whose time the Jews were forced to build Pithom and Raamses.
Under the rule of this Pharaoh, king of Egypt, the Jews spent a full 67 years. Linked with him is the so-called "New Empire", which begins sixteen hundred years before Christ. In the time of Ramesses the Second Egypt was brought to a high cultural level.
Also displayed here are statues from Egyptian times dating from the second century after Christ. Here we already see the work of the Romans, who tried in many details to imitate Egyptian art, but which no longer has the distinctiveness and style of Egypt.
From the temple of Ramesses the Second we see here several blue-enamelled vases of earth dried in the sun. Further on we see many sarcophagi, coffins of that kind — of granite of various colours and of "pistn" wood [?; probably shittim/acacia wood] that is mentioned in the Chumash [Pentateuch], carved outside and inside with hieroglyphic pictures. There is such a sarcophagus here of Ramesses the 3rd.
Then there is a kind of tombstone similar to our present-day "crystalline" [?] stones, with various coloured ornaments and hieroglyphic drawings. This is the tombstone of Seti the 1st, which represents the god-king in the other world with the goddess Hathor.
Besides this we see a great many different original stones in the most varied colours and styles, with all sorts of hieroglyphic drawings, and one must be a great expert both in the stones [?] and in the drawings to understand the meaning of all this and to know from which century they come and how they were used. True, there are inscriptions beside them with explanations, but it is impossible to understand and grasp everything according to our perception and understanding.
———
Very interesting is a huge stone slab with various astronomical drawings. It is a whole epoch of Egyptian religious life. The work comes from their priest-astronomers. It is an exact plan of the heavenly worlds, the stars and the signs of the zodiac, in which all the peoples of that time believed.
Here we see the Egyptian god Apis [printed "Hapus"], in the form of an ox; it is made of stone in natural size. The Egyptians greatly worshipped him, building him special temples which were adorned with gold and other precious things; to him they prayed and offered sacrifices...
It is possible that the Golden Calf, which the Jews made later, was also an imitation of the ceremonies they had watched among the Egyptians.
The second god, standing beside the god Apis, is called the god Bes — a small stone ugliness, a real sight [?]. Almost the same kind of god we meet in the Louvre among the Indian idol-worshippers — Quetzalcoatl [printed "Ketsikatl"] is his name. Both are the same ugly things, and truly only God alone can know what they needed such gods for.
Spending several hours in the Egyptian hall, one gets the impression that we have been thrown back over a span of 6–7 thousand years. One can hardly believe that the people who are here together with the treasures are older by so many thousands of years. And contemplating all this, on the one hand we swell with pride [?], because mankind had so much understanding and collected these priceless treasures that no money in the world can buy; and on the other hand our spirits fall when we see what antiquities are in foreign hands, at a time when we have so strong a connection to them and our history is so closely bound up with them.
When we come to the Egyptian treasures that date from the times when the Jews were enslaved in Egypt, one ought to take the Chumash in hand and study them together; then it seems as though we were living in that period and had lived through it, experienced it ourselves.
In any case we see countless treasures from Egyptian times in the Louvre, so that this convinces us that the Orient was tremendously developed in those times, when Europe was still a wilderness. Contemplating the art of those times one sees plainly that the Oriental peoples, despite [lit. "with"] their humiliation [?] and enslavement, stood at a tremendously high level. So we now admire those great times in which technology and art held so honourable a place.
Not for nothing do people come from the whole world to view and admire the Louvre Museum, which has drawn to itself the most remarkable ancient treasures from the most primeval times, such as the world [elsewhere] does not possess.
Artists, philosophers, historians, poets come there, and each one perceives the historical remains differently; each forms his own notion according to his outlook, according to his perception. All of them study, according to their understanding and common sense, that interesting period which is for us a tremendous riddle.
At any time one thus meets, in other departments as well as in the Egyptian "corner", young students and professors who are occupied with the whole sharpness of their minds over every little stone and every little jug and sphinx — from what times they come and in what place they were at that time.
The ordinary flesh-and-blood person, the average man who has an understanding of historical treasures, can have no notion what priceless treasures are found in the Egyptian corner alone of the Louvre Museum. Evidently France knew what to acquire — and this is speaking only of the Egyptian corner alone in the great Louvre Museum.
* * *
There remain countless undescribed large and small figures, statues, various objects of Egyptian everyday life, which [?] give a splendid and faithful picture of those periods and epochs; but who is able to see and record them all at once? I have barely managed to depict in very brief strokes the tremendous treasure, the colossal cultural values gathered [?] in in the Egyptian corner of the Louvre Museum.
It is quite possible that we shall yet have occasion to depict other art and cultural treasures of the priceless Louvre Museum.
But one thing must be established: the strongest impression on the Jewish visitor is made by the little Egyptian corner, so enriched with interesting ancient treasures that are still engraved in our memory from childhood years, when the rebbe [cheder teacher] drilled the Chumash into us.

A Good Beginning.

[Będzin — education; Talmud Torah.] (The present changes in the Będzin Talmud Torah. — On the way to putting things in order. The introduction of secular subjects — let it not remain a mere beginning.)
For the success and the possibility of development of a public philanthropic or cultural institution, three important conditions are above all essential. Namely: 1) topicality, usefulness and purposefulness of the institution concerned; — 2) proper understanding and interest of the masses in the idea of the institution, and above all: broadly generous [?] masses; — and 3) able, energetic and h o n e s t leaders. These are the "three things", the three elementary laws, without which a broadly developed [?] public institution is not possible.
If, in line with this stated [?] premise, we examine the causes of the bad situation and disorder that have prevailed until now in the Będzin Talmud Torah, we come to the conclusion that the blame lies only in the lack of the third foundation mentioned, namely: the absence of capable, h o n e s t managers. It is this last that has caused the chaos and the simply shameful state of affairs until now. For there can be no talk here of a lack of usefulness, nor of a lack of understanding on the part of the people. Philanthropy is in the blood of this people, "merciful sons of the merciful", and [?] above everything it holds a house of Torah for poor children. It is the first and most important institution of the People of the Book. And it is obliged to it by the Torah, by law. The laws of Talmud Torah occupy a special place in the "Shulchan Aruch"; thus the duty to maintain an institution where poor children learn Torah is engraved in the people's consciousness. From the oldest times the first task of a kehilla was to found and maintain a Talmud Torah — "the study of Torah outweighs them all". It stood higher even than the kindest [?] philanthropic societies. It is also out of the question to see the blame in a stingy hand of the masses. Whatever, whatever you may reproach our Będzin with — such a charitable, broadly generous town you will have to search far for in Poland. People give a great deal for the [golden] calf, but also a great deal for the Tabernacle. True, at the present moment the material situation of our town is critical, but we are speaking of a period that began more than ten years ago.
And here we come to the only cause: the lack of suitable managers. It must be said that with the passing of the unforgettable rabbi, Rabbi Yissachar Dov of blessed memory, who held the Talmud Torah under his supervision — and how much effort he devoted, displaying [?] his expert abilities and most faithful [?] guidance for the good of the Talmud Torah — with his passing began the decline of this so [?] important popular institution, which under him had stood at an incomparable level. Having lost proper leadership, the decline began first of all in the pedagogical sense: nobody takes an interest in how the children are taught or whether they are taught at all in the Talmud Torah. The masses lose confidence, and its standing [?] falls from day to day. At the top stand people who not only lack the slightest qualifications to run an educational institution, but do not even possess the slightest confidence of the population. On the contrary, the latter still grumble about them, believing that the leaders draw personal profit from the institution; and it goes without saying that under such circumstances there can be no talk of proper activity.
There were indeed, during the two decades, moments of upswing, when it seemed that now the Talmud Torah was being led out of its swamp; but the swamp was too deep, and too many were interested in the existence of the swamp, for two or three sincere individuals to be able to drag it out.
And so we have looked on at the ruin of such an important institution, seen how our poor children grow up as utter ignoramuses, and nobody cares, nobody is pained by it. Our "notables" have more important things to do than to care for the children from "under the hill".
Incidentally, the two or three "heads" — each [?] in a different period — blocked the door so widely that there was no room for an honest worker who did not want to work with the rulers themselves, with the "shtelekh" [?] and whatever they are called there. They were afraid of competition. And again, as for someone who would take the uninvited leaders by the collar and show them that [?] side door — that much courage is no longer to be found in our Będzin. So years went by, years of destruction.
And now we see symptoms of a putting in order of the situation. The conscience of the Jews of Będzin has somehow suddenly woken up, been shaken. Many causes have led to a larger number of communal activists taking over the management of the Talmud Torah, and the former "heads" have been pushed somewhat into the shade. And when one shows just some activity — there is, after all, a rewarding field here, a broad field. And as a result of the enthusiastic [?] activity we have already achieved that a broad programme of secular subjects has been introduced in the Talmud Torah, so that it is being turned into a public elementary school ["powszechna" school]. And this, we believe, will bring increased attendance by pupils. For because secular subjects were not taught, many children attended the public schools, and only about two hours were left them to go to the Talmud Torah.
What remains to be done is that the beginning should have a proper continuation.
First of all, to secure the normal material budget, so that the melamdim [teachers] do not have to go hungry and run around to householders with kehilla ("gmina") receipts — that is neither nice nor right. A special committee must collect the money and pay the melamdim. We believe that with proper activity it is quite easy to secure the budget, and a special finance committee should be founded headed by Mr M. Danger [?], since the latter has proved himself capable in this field.
What still leaves much to be desired and done is the field of education. Here the old chaos still reigns, and a thorough reorganisation must take place. A special pedagogical commission, possessing the relevant qualifications, must be founded to take the education in the Talmud Torah under its supervision.
— "Take heed of the children of the poor, for from them Torah will go forth"!
From the Austrian Exhibition in Katowice.

[Katowice — art; exhibition.] The exhibition contains a series of works from the most famous works of [sic] the most famous Austrian painters, among them such Jewish celebrities as Georg Merkel, Kaufmann and others.
Great credit for the exhibition belongs to the famous Viennese Jewish art historian Dr Otto Schneid, who is its organiser.
Only rarely can one see such an exhibition, not only in Katowice but even in Vienna, because Dr Schneid specially selected the most modern and most interesting painters that Austria possesses.
When I speak of celebrities, I do not mean the so-called art connoisseurs who travel to Vienna to amuse themselves [?] and bring home as gifts kitschy flower pieces and tasteless landscapes, with which the Viennese market is flooded especially for foreign visitors.
The exhibition shows us a series of serious painters and graphic artists who are known not only to the general Parisian and Viennese public, but especially also to the connoisseur public.
Here one is dealing with artists who, as I feel, do not paint in order to sell, but sell in order to be able to paint. These are artists who do not want to be recognised by the average eye, which seeks in a picture the likeness of its outward, vulgar "I", copied in paint [?] by a skilful hand that they call a master.
This is an exhibition through which the personality of each exhibitor and his state of soul is revealed [?] by means of the subtle colours that lie hidden deep in universal human and universal cosmic nature, conveyed through the artist's temperament in such a way that it calls one to think, to love or to hate all the contrasts that are harmful to social progress.
The art exhibition is a great gain for the artistic part of Katowice as well as for Zagłębie.
I would advise every art lover to visit the exhibition, which remains open until the 30th of this month, daily from 10 to 6 in the afternoon.
Moshe Apelboim.
Spring

[Poetry.]
Spring,
dear one, beloved,
tell me, what is
this "storm" [?] with you —
you look to me [?]
half frozen,
you are hoarse
and you breathe heavily.

I remember,
years ago
your coming
brought joy.
Every twig,
turning green,
awoke with joy
from its sleep.

Birds would
sing songs of praise
when your breath
touched them,
and a choir
of bird-tenors
was called forth [?]
by your breath.

But now,
dear Spring,
you come like
who-knows-who,
you drag yourself along
on those paws of yours
slowly, shuffling
and heavily.

You have become
a cripple, brother,
something
has happened to you.
I still remember
that time
when you were still
green.

God, how fast
the years run!
It seems
not long ago at all
your coming used to
be a holiday,
be a time
of joy and happiness.

Once you were
a spring
as a spring
ought to be:
you used to greet [us]
with your breath,
like a good
old wine.

Evidently you have
grown old,
you come wrapped
in furs,
and your red
little nose, poor thing,
shows that you
have caught a bad cold.

You have
spent your spring, brother,
you have squandered
your world,
so now you crawl
like a frog,
wrapped in rain
and cold.

Yes, we are
[used?] to troubles.
Spring, brother, ah [?],
I am cold.
Which devil
has cursed
me and you
to grow old!

A. L. Wolfson.
He Lived to See Revenge...

[Humoresque.] By Ypsilon.

When Yankl Trask went up to heaven, he went straight into the night club there to take a look at the dancing couples.
When he entered the heavenly night club, he was simply dazzled by the wonderful, radiant beauties he saw there. So many young girls and women with enchanting angel-faces he had never seen on earth.
And the most beautiful of all was one — a slender, rounded blonde with big, sky-blue eyes, a small red cherry mouth, a white, finely cut [?] little face and two strings of dazzling-white teeth.
Yankl Trask did not even dare take a good look at this rare beauty. How should he, Yankl Trask, the insurance-policy agent, get to such a heavenly princess, around whom all the heavenly grandees buzz like flies around a flame?
But how astonished Yankl was when the blonde beauty left the whole circle of great men standing around her, came straight up to him, to Yankl Trask, and said sweetly:
"Hello, Yankl, don't you recognise me? I'm your wife, Sarah Trask!"
Yankl stood there as if thunderstruck. He rubbed his eyes to see whether he was not fainting. This heavenly, glorious, divine beauty — she is his wife, his Sarah? She is that old, ugly, [coarse?], quarrelsome Jewess whom he hated so terribly that he even had to die to get rid of her, because he had no other way out?
Yankl gazed with rapture at his brand-new Sarah and could not believe his own eyes.
"You... you are Sarah?" he cried out, and even burst into sobs from great joy and surprise.
"Yes. I am your lawful wife Sarah," whispered [?] the blonde beauty, and her cherry mouth smiled charmingly and her little teeth sparkled like the most precious pearls.
"My gold, my crown, my soul, my Sarahle!" Yankl Trask cried out passionately, and wanted to take the angelic figure in his arms and press her to his heart [printed: "Mark", marrow].
But the blonde beauty, with a flying twirl, spun out of his outstretched arms and went back into the circle of great heavenly personages.
The heavenly orchestra struck up a "jazz".. King David played first fiddle, the Levites blew on their trumpets and saxophones, Miriam the Prophetess beat her drum, and Sarah Trask, the new, young, dazzling and alluring blonde, began to dance with the men. She danced the "shimmy" and the "fox-trot" and the "Charleston" and the "jazz". Every moment she flew [?] into the arms of another man. She danced with King Solomon, with the handsome Prince Absalom, with Don Juan and with Rudolph Valentino. And every man glided [?] with her and tossed her about, lifted her above his head, pressed her to his chest and playfully kissed her on the neck or behind the ear.
Yankl Trask stood with blazing eyes, bursting with jealousy. He groaned, panted, bit his lips, clenched his fists, until he could bear it no longer and began to shout:
"Halt! Stop! [Drunkards?]! Scoundrels! Let go of my Sarah! She is my wife!"
But everyone laughed at him and frolicked even harder with the blonde beauty.
Yankl Trask was beside himself, and when he saw Rudolph Valentino holding Sarah in his arms and pressing his lips to her earlobe, Yankl threw himself at him like an enraged ox and wanted to tear him to pieces.
But at that moment Samson the Strong grabbed Yankl by the scruff of the neck, as a ritual slaughterer [?] grabs a duck, and hurled him through the door out into the street.
From the terrible throw Yankl woke up from his sleep and saw that he was lying at home in bed, and next to him lay his old, former Sarah, snoring — she who is neither blonde nor young. But thank God! Here she lies, not far from him, and she is not dancing with King Solomon and with Rudolph Valentino...
From the Passover Days

[Będzin, Sosnowiec and Dąbrowa — feuilleton: the Passover holiday.] A stroll, by Ben Amotz.

... Passover in the year 5690 had a great "production" [?]. There has not been such an abundance of "culture" for a long time. Almost every society or association prepared something in honour of Passover. All eight days were as if on a "golden chain", woven with lectures, theatre, jubilees and other delicacies.
The beginning was made by Poalei Zion in Będzin with the
collective lecture.
Comrade Yehuda Preger declared that he believes with perfect faith that redemption will be brought only by Poalei Zion, which is united with the Ts. S. [Tseirei Zion–Socialists]. Preger's speech was delivered in such an enthusiastic tone that the auditorium began to acquire faith...
Along came Comrade Weinstein, smashed Preger's credo and "opposition" [?], saying that every Jew must be "al ha-mishmar" — stand on guard and wait until the Messiah comes. But the proprietor of "Kursa", A. Kaufman, apparently did not have confidence in Weinstein's credo, and said:
— "Children, enough — you've played long enough"...
* * *
The dramatic society "Muze" [Muse] delighted us for the holiday with a
grandiose performance
in two towns, in Dąbrowa and in Będzin. We wanted to devote a few lines to the "grandiose performances", but "the power has been taken from us". We received a warning: — "If you don't sing praises and hymns to us, we will curse everything the world stands on"...
The warning "frightened" us, for one must beware of people who are "above reason".. and in the best case
— keep silent..
* * *
Tuesday bubbled over with plays. In Strzemieszyce "Bar Kokhba" stormed the stage, in Dąbrowa the Hakhnasat Kallah society "sold Joseph" [i.e. staged "The Sale of Joseph"], and (to make the distinction) in the Sosnowiec municipal theatre there played..
the "Habima".
A mighty power has the Habima: it draws to itself even such "Zhidkes" [assimilated little Jews] as already stand with one foot on the threshold of the church — and yet "Artyści z Palestyny" [the artists from Palestine] one has to see.
The public was deceived. Not by the acting, but because instead of "Keter David" [The Crown of David] the Habima staged "The Treasure", a comedy by Sholem Aleichem.
The content of the comedy is weak. But when Habima artists play the roles, the public laughs heartily, even those of whom the verse says: "ha-mukeh be-ivrato" [a punning pseudo-verse: "those smitten in their Hebrew"].. because the Habima management also sees to it that the spectators have an idea of the content of the play; for that purpose the content of the play is printed in Yiddish in the form of librettos, and during the intermissions the public reads the "Teitsh-Chumash" [the translated Pentateuch] with great pleasure...
The true spiritual delight, which will long, long remain in memory, the Habima provided in Katowice, staging "Keter David" by Ydars [?].
Although the performance began only at 11 o'clock at night, the theatre was packed full. The ovations for the world-famous artists were stormy; especially after the last act the enthusiastic public would not let the artists leave the stage.
It is also interesting to note that the impresario of the Habima was the "T.U.R." [the PPS-affiliated Workers' University Society]; apparently the gentlemen of the P.P.S. know that — "Jak bieda, to do Żyda" [when in trouble, go to the Jew]...
* * *
As we stressed at the beginning, every institution showed during the holidays that it is "alive". If not with theatre, one discharged the duty with
"flower days" [street collections with flowers].
In Będzin we had no fewer than 3 "flower days", among them two "hidden ones": a) for the benefit of the "Yavneh" library and b) the "Culture Fund".
Concerning the "flower days" we received a series of inquiries from our readers, who "really want to know": 1) whether the "Yavneh" library exists at the Jewish gymnasium, and 2) whether the left-wing parties already recognise philanthropy?..
* * *
"Sinai" in Będzin has, thank God, reached the age of 2 years and in honour of this celebrated a jubilee. Once people celebrated 25-year jubilees, later — 15-year ones, but when "life grows shorter" it is a great joy when an organisation has had the strength to last 2 years..
— Through this jubilee democracy scored a great "victory". The opinion that young men make kiddush over "shpener" [?] has gone bankrupt. The time has come when the youth will make kiddush over wine and the bearded Jews over shpener"..
We say this regarding the
jubilee of "Sinai".
A child of the Będzin Tseirei Mizrachi — a successful "child"; if only the "father" were like that... Taking part in the jubilee was the member of the Central Committee Elimelech Beifeld of Warsaw, who delivered a lecture rich in content in a lyrical tone.
Later Mr. Beifeld "regretted" having come to the jubilee. He heard a moralising speech from the young Kurtz, who, in a truly revolutionary manner, attacked as it deserved the board of trustees (curatorium) of the local Mizrachi school, and afterwards "went off" to Warsaw..
The public listened to Kurtz's speech with open mouths and thought:
— "These youngsters will drive us out"...
* * *
The Sosnowiec "Herzliya" arranged a
festive academy
in honour of the 5-year existence of the Jerusalem University. The academy began very "punctually" — it was late no less than about 3 hours...
But it was worth it: after a series of greetings Dr. Chameides [?], the Katowice rabbi, delivered a lecture which won great applause; after the speech of Magister Polakiewicz [?] came the concert part, which was performed with success by: a choir, S. Ziskind (violin), Prof. Z. Rozman (piano). Solos were sung by the Misses Fischer, Ginzberg, Plesner (recitation).
Very successful was the staging of Frischmann's "Bishvil ha-Mashiach" [For the Sake of the Messiah] [?].
* * *
On the second days [of the holiday] we had distinguished artists — the
Turkow brothers
Zygmunt and Jonas, both founders of artists' troupes (Zygmunt of the "VYKT" and Jonas of the "VGIT" [?]), gave several guest performances. The 2 gifted brothers do not play together: when Zygmunt played in Będzin, Jonas played in Sosnowiec, and vice versa.
Zygmunt's repertoire: "Shabtai Zvi" and "The Thought". Jonas's — "The Cause".
The performances unfortunately did not have the proper success. The cause of this was the "esteemed public" of the gallery, which had "naturalised" itself in the front rows and, as always, rolled with laughter at the most tragic moments..
Well, what else? When one sees crazy grimaces in the street, doesn't one laugh? So in the "theatre" [?] one must certainly laugh..
* * *
No small surprise for Jewish Sosnowiec was the news from the Koziegłowy "dozors" [kehilla board members] that in the high windows [i.e. in the offices of the authorities] there lies a base
denunciation against Rabbi Frommer,
that he is a blackmailer, a swindler, etc. etc..
When one informs on a Mizrachi rabbi — cry the Jews of Sosnowiec — one can explain it. That it is a party fight — a well-known matter. That Agudah and Mizrachi do not live in peace. But to denounce a rabbi who is as far from party quarrels as the east is from the west, to denounce a Jew who has only one task — to swim in the sea of the Torah — woe to the eyes that see such things...
* * *
On the last day of Passover Rabbi Hager "conquered" the "Daytshn" [modern, German-style Jews]. More precisely, not the "Daytshn" but their hearts. Before Yizkor Rabbi Hager delivered a short sermon and a "miracle" happened: the "cold" Daytsh hearts were stirred up and rivers of tears began to flow.
— A real parting of the Red Sea...
* * *
The Sosnowiec Revisionists accompanied the holiday with timbrels and dances. After a precise "revision" that the holiday had passed according to law and custom [?], they arranged in the halls of the big "kupcy" [merchants]
a Land-of-Israel ball.
The organisers did not mean the Haggadah but the kneydlekh, and therefore "revised" [?] the pockets: if a matzah was found — "to nie" [then no] in here; quarrels [?] were not lacking...
And people also enjoyed themselves in the best way, Jewishly; even the "solo dance" of Ral [?] Kirschenbaum had "a thousand flavours".
There was also an election — not for "beauty", but for the most beautiful Jewish type. Recognised as such was Miss Minia Roza.
At six o'clock in the morning the Revisionist youth in Sosnowiec "sang"
— "Chasal siddur Pesach" [the Passover order is concluded]...
"Thy Destroyers and They That Made Thee Waste..."

(On the question of the eviction of the Jewish Women's Gymnasium.)
In connection with the threat that the Jewish Women's Gymnasium is to be evicted, we turned to a person who stands at the head of the school, asking him to explain the whole matter to us.
And here is what emerges.
The landlord, Mr. Grinbojm, fifteen years ago, when apartments stood empty, had many apartments to let in his house, but there were no takers — when he learned that a Jewish school was being founded in Sosnowiec, he approached the founder and made her sweet promises, if only she would rent the premises. At that time there were much better and more suitable premises; nevertheless Mr. Grinbojm succeeded in getting the school into his house. A few years later, when the housing market had become quite different, Mr. Grinbojm's attitude to the school in his house also became quite different. Mr. G.'s "nerves" suddenly could not bear that there should be a school in his house; it began with petty chicanery, but that did not bother anyone. But a moment came when the further existence of the school became dependent on Mr. Grinbojm: the point was that the school authorities demanded that the school's premises be enlarged, [for] only on that condition could the school obtain state rights. The school's supervisory board approached Mr. Grinbojm with the proposal that, for a certain sum of money, he give his consent to enlarging the school's premises in his house. Mr. Grinbojm would not hear of it; the reason was that at the time the supervisory board had not wanted to give him a larger increase, and they rented a few rooms in a house adjoining Mr. Grinbojm's house.
Then they asked Mr. Grinbojm to permit a passage to be made to the new premises. Mr. Grinbojm declared that he would agree on condition that he receive a 50 percent increase on the rent. Although the demand was unjust, and although the school's financial situation did not permit it, the supervisory board undertook to give him a 25 percent increase. Mr. Grinbojm did not agree to that.
The negotiations went on, and meanwhile the passage was made. It was expected that sooner or later a positive result would be reached with Mr. G.
For Mr. Grinbojm the moment was just what he wished: the hour [?] had struck for him to take revenge (!) on the school, and he promptly went to court against the school; with the help of two non-Jewish lawyers he managed to obtain the eviction.
Some time later the school obtained state rights, the financial situation improved, and the supervisory board wanted to give him a 50 percent increase. But Mr. G. rejected this and demanded 12,000 złoty to withdraw from the lawsuit. It goes without saying that the gymnasium could not raise such a sum.
Mr. Grinbojm was also lucky in the Court of Appeal in Warsaw, where the judgment of the first instance was upheld for him.
Having won the case in the second instance, he will not receive any delegation; he lets no one approach him to talk with him about the matter. He has decided to evict the school, which was created with so much Jewish toil and sweat.
The Jewish public in Sosnowiec — says the head of the school — must take a stand on this so painful matter.

Sosnowiec — General Meeting of the "Merchants' Bank"

[Sosnowiec — banks & institutions.] On Monday the annual general meeting of the "Bank Kupiecki" [Merchants' Bank] in Sosnowiec took place in the hall of the "Hotel Polski".
The meeting aroused considerable [?] interest among the members. The large hall was full. The interest was — as later turned out — not for the sake of Heaven, but only on account of [?] a so-called opposition that had formed around the bank. The atmosphere was charged [?], but it was no more than a "storm in a glass of water".
The chair is handed to Mr. Kabak. Invited to the presidium are Messrs.: Advocate Kowalski, Shlomo Warman and Secretary Y. Kramałowski.
Before the start of the meeting Mr. B. Ferens [?] takes the floor and demands that the following point be added to the agenda: why Mr. Dudkiewicz was expelled as a member of the supervisory board. Mr. F. invokes the demand of the Auditing Union [Związek Rewizyjny] that the Dudkiewicz affair be dealt with at an extraordinary meeting.
Over this proposal a discussion begins which turns into personal abuse; a terrible uproar breaks out and the presidium withdraws for consultation.
After a pause of about an hour the presidium returns with the decision:
Since the demand of the Auditing Union concerning the Dudkiewicz affair arrived late, the matter cannot be considered at this meeting; instead an extraordinary meeting is to be called specially on this matter.
Tempers calm down and the agenda is taken up. After the reading of the last minutes and of the report of the Auditing Union, the chairman of the management board, Mr. G. Abramczyk, delivers the report on the past year.
The report shows that the total turnover in 1929 amounted to 163 313 277. In the course of the year the bank granted discounts and advances to 4387 persons; collections amounted to more than 16 million zł. Profit — nearly 22 thousand zł.
Mr. Abramczyk, who also gives a historical survey of the founding of the bank and its existence up to now, stresses that with such huge turnovers the profit ought to have been much larger, but the management is aware that the bank, as a cooperative institution, should not chase after profits but rather ease the situation of the merchant class.
After the report a discussion takes place, of a personal character.
The budget of nearly 80 thousand zł. is adopted. It is decided that the credit for a member may amount to up to 15 thousand zł., and that the bank has the right to take on obligations up to 1 million zł.
At the request of those assembled no elections were held; instead the same persons as before were re-confirmed by acclamation. The only change: in place of Mr. Dudkiewicz, Mr. S. Warman came in.

"Declarations" for income tax

[Economy — taxes.] The deadline for filing the declarations (zeznania) ends on 1 May. — Important information for taxpayers.
The deadline for filing "declarations" for income tax for the year 1929 ends on 1 May. These "declarations" must be filed at the tax offices where the taxpayer concerned resides.
These obligations are very important for the taxpayer concerned. Filling out the form improperly can cause him great harm.
The obligation to file "declarations" applies to all merchants, industrialists and craftsmen, except taxpayers of the 4th trade category and the 8th industry category.
There is a principle that income not greater than 1400 zł. a year is not subject to tax, and no "declarations" need be filed for it. All other taxpayers and citizens, however, must file "declarations", fill them out clearly and precisely, and send the declaration to the tax office in person or by registered post.
In the "declaration" one must first of all state one's first name and surname and place of residence. For this purpose forms are obtained free of charge at the tax office. At the same time, on the second side, in the second column, one must state the amount of income earned and note from what kind of source (whether from a commercial enterprise, from real estate, etc.) the income came.
One must also state the exact number of family members, i.e. how many persons the taxpayer concerned must support, and the age of each one separately. One must remember that for every minor child supported by the taxpayer a certain amount of tax is remitted [?].
Any misfortunes in the family that occurred during the year must also be stated precisely, such as illnesses due to which the shop was closed, or other calamities. It is very important to state all this, because the tax authority must take all of it into account when assessing the taxes. It is also very important to attach to the "declaration" any prescription, doctor's certificate and the like. If extraordinary events occurred in the family, these too must be stated.
The "declarations" must be signed. At the same time one must calculate, on the basis of the table on the last page of the declaration sheet, how much the tax may amount to, and pay half of it by 1 May, since otherwise the sum concerned may be regarded as overdue and distraint may be carried out for it.

Tragic accident at a match in Częstochowa.
[Częstochowa — accident.] On Monday a storm with heavy thunder and lightning passed over Częstochowa. A lightning bolt struck the telephone wires at the "Warta" sports ground, where a match was taking place at that very time.
The result was terrible. Through the torn wires one person from the public was killed on the spot and 20 persons were taken away.
—o—
A celebratory shot caused damage of 70,000 zł.
[Poland — fire.] Not far from Ojców [?] several young Christians were celebrating the holiday and fired shots "na wiwat" [in celebration]. It was enough that one bullet entered a grain barn, and in the blink of an eye the whole barn stood in flames. The fire spread to the surrounding peasant cottages and a terrible blaze broke out.
The firemen who arrived from the whole surrounding area finally contained the fire. Burnt down were 6 cottages, 7 barns with grain and also livestock. The damage amounts to about 30 thousand zł.

We Must Build!

(On the „Keren Hayesod“ campaign in Zagłębie.)
Zionism is now going through, without doubt, a hard period. But we ourselves have exaggerated these difficulties quite a bit[?]. We must see the situation in its true light and not fall into any hysteria and panic.
In Eretz Israel itself, despite the bad impression of the report of the commission of inquiry, the mood is cheerful. The shaken economic life has already fully stabilised, the boycott is disappearing; the possibilities of absorbing Jewish labour in the colonies are growing; a movement for house-building in the towns is beginning; preparations are already being made to restore the points that were destroyed during the events, and — last but not least — preparations are already under way to settle 1000 new families on the land of the Keren Kayemet.
The political situation is admittedly not entirely clear; the majority of the commission of inquiry — except for its member Harry Snell — has thrown a thick log under our feet, yet we know well that in the leading circles of the English Labour Party, which now governs in England, we are regarded with outspoken sympathy, and that this sympathy will also pour out into concrete deeds for the building of the Jewish home in Eretz Israel.
With the Arabs relations are naturally strained. And it is precisely here that our calm and self-control are needed, and nothing is so apt to calm both ourselves and the opponent as — work.
Instead of spending our energy, scarce as it is anyway, on debates and squabbles, project-making, compromise-seeking and politicking, let us all together forge a mighty, gigantic instrument for the very upbuilding of the country.
We have a reserve of a hundred thousand dunams of land that we can settle at once; we have possibilities of buying new hundreds of thousands of dunams of land; just as if to spite the pessimism of whole Jewish circles and the enraged attack on Zionism — by others, there are now enormous possibilities for immediate land purchase.
We now have a favourable situation for expanding the towns, and also for surrounding them with suburbs, above all with workers' quarters.
The importance of Totzeret Haaretz (Eretz-Israel produce) is growing in the Diaspora countries, and this opens great sales possibilities for Eretz-Israel industry and agriculture, and thereby, naturally, the absorptive capacity of the country is increased.
And all this must be exploited with the greatest speed!
Our budget must be secured, which contains such main items as aliyah, colonisation, labour, industry, town-building, education, health services, etc.
We must build, create, lay brick upon brick and conquer[?] position after position. We must confront our enemies with a „fait accompli“, and before a fait accompli one feels awe, respect; all of history is full of examples of it.
And building, our practical work, is our best policy, the surest road to peace, the most effective means of protection and security.
Our misfortune is that instead of building we do not stop talking, splitting hairs, philosophising and twiddling our thumbs.
Nothing has ever yet been done with words.
In the beginning — He created.
First comes creation.
We stand before a serious, very serious examination of history; we are running a dangerous race against time. And it depends on us that we join[?] with full impetus as partners in the work of Creation in the upbuilding of our land. We must — build!
Y. Ritov.
