The Poet of Industry

[Literature — criticism; Będzin — a native poet.]
In the monthly of the Jewish university students entitled "Trybuna Akademicka", the writer Mr. Shneiderman [S. L. Shneiderman] published the following essay on the young Polish proletarian poet Stanisław Wygodzki (son of I-Iche [?] Wygodzki, Będzin), who has already made a name for himself in the world of poetry.
We find it fitting to acquaint our readers of this section [?] with the abridged essay on the young talent Wygodzki.
The Editors.

Stanisław Wygodzki — that is the name of a young Polish poet — a Jew, who is far from the cheap and tasteless antics that are so characteristic even of the greater part of the Jewish-Polish poets.
I am speaking here exclusively of the youngest generation, which groups itself around the journals "Kwadryga", "Głos Literacki" and others. These are the "neo-poets" — "neo-classicists [?]", "neo-romantics" and above all: neo-Catholics. Such as the Słobodniks, the Bibrowskis [?] and many others, who still want to hide their noses behind the curtains of pious Catholic verse and are more papal than the Pope himself.
You see how the frightened young Jewish fellows would literally like to run out of their Jewish skin, and so they perform various tragic antics that are simply disgusting.
Stanisław Wygodzki is the only one among the Jewish-Polish poets who is not ashamed of his Jewishness and of his Jewish language. Wygodzki is also the most original and most sincere poet in the youngest group, which consists for the most part of Jews.
Wygodzki is a social poet; in his poems there is the ethical tremor of a person who feels the pain of the insulted and the oppressed.
Wygodzki is under the influence of the Polish proletarian group of poets and chiefly of Broniewski, from whom he took over the strong revolutionary pathos.
Wygodzki has, however, taken his own independent stride, in that he has condensed his word and verse and has not surrendered to any lyrical diffuseness [?] and sentimentality. In his poems one feels a strong intellect and social responsibility.
His strongest motifs are: prison and industry. And even in his mood-poems one feels the grinding [?] of wheels and the spattering of steel:

"In screeching [?], heavy groaning travel
trains without cease,
people from west and east drenched with
deathly [?] light,
at railway stations mothers lament, fathers
are heavily saddened,
and from the signal-whistle steel spatters
into the face."

Wygodzki is distinctive and interesting in his industrial motifs. Wygodzki was born in a region of labour — Zagłębie. From his earliest youth he absorbed into himself the rhythm of labour, the rawness of the toil-worn [?] towns of Zagłębie, and his poems are therefore also so raw, so steel-hard, and from them streams the darkness of the coal pits and the clangour [?] of the smelting works.
Alien to him are the stillness and dreaminess of life, alien to him are the gloomy people who have no desires:

"I do not speak to those who have no desire,
if you have desires — I will tear you along at once,
I have already considered everything in thought,
I call in the night, which is cracked [?] by the winds [?]."

Wygodzki is the poet of content, and with him the form grows out of the content.
He does not play at carved and chiselled verses; every word is a necessity for him, it is hammered out and full of kernel.
Wygodzki is socially disciplined and resolute; he does not waver and does not hang in the air, his position is a clear one, his world-view a crystallised one — he is the poet of social justice.
Wygodzki's poetry is not the poetry of the cult of labour that has lately been produced by the fascist hangers-on and social graphomaniacs. His poetry is the poetry of struggle, the poetry of battle, of the merciless battle between the two worlds: capital and labour.
In his poems Wygodzki makes no use of any external effects, of any decorative motifs, which always cheapen and flatten the content; he is direct and sparing of expression. In his poems one feels a certain restraint, a certain unsaidness; the words are chopped off, broken off, like lumps of coal.
In his latest poem "Ciphers" [Numbers] (in "Miesięcznik Literacki") Wygodzki brings out the tragedy of the great masses of nameless people, who like dead ciphers are struck out and entered again in the books of offices and factories. In this poem, as in all of Wygodzki's poems, there comes to expression the revolt of the masses, the deep suffering of the oppressed.
Wygodzki's poems are often complicated and already quite close to incomprehensibility, which is a consequence of his economy of words.
Wygodzki is in a state of development, of constant ascent and purification, which will consequently also bring more clarity to his poetic creation.
S. L. Shneiderman.
Gotthold Ephraim Lessing — Death

[Literature — poetry in translation.]
Gotthold Ephraim Lessing.
Death.

Brother, could you believe it:
yesterday, as I was eating grapes,
I was sitting then all alone —
suddenly Death comes in to me.

He had drawn his sharp knife,
my fear — growing ever greater:
"Flee quickly, you servant of Bacchus,
quickly, quickly, for I slaughter..."

"Dear Death," I beg with tears,
"how could I stand against you?
See, here lie grapes for you,
I beg you, go away from me!"

With a smile he sits himself down,
grabs a bunch by its end,
eats and smiles with flashing eyes;
I bowed my head in fear..

Joyfully I believe myself freed
when he has laid aside his sword.
"Fool! For your little glass of wine
you believe," he says, "you'll be set free?"

"Death," I beg, "I would gladly
be a physician on this earth, you hear;
let me go, I promise you
that I will take pains for the sick."

"Good, if that is how it shall be, you may live,"
he says, "only be devoted to me:
live until you are sated with kisses,
weary of drinking and befuddled..."

Ah, how beautiful that sounds in the ears!
Death, you have given me new birth;
this very glass full of the juice of wine —
Death, to good brotherhood!

Forever, then, must I live,
forever! by the wine beside me;
forever shall love and wine be mine,
forever shall they stay with me.

Translated for the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" by Yosef Perlberger.
Great Poets and Their Family Life

[Literature — biographical essay.]
Great Poets
and Their Family Life
Percy Shelley and Harriet Westbrook

The great poets, the singers of human joys and sorrows, those who penetrate the depths of the human soul, who perceive the tragic life-struggles [?] of man and feel the divine height of his love and happiness — how did they themselves live through their own happiness in love, or — misfortune? Were they in such moments poets too, feeling souls, or simple human egoists?

This cannot be answered by a general rule. Take the well-known English poet Shelley, the close friend of Byron. Shelley has been honoured with a few biographers, and all of them tell of the family tragedy of the great poet and his wife Harriet, with whom Shelley fell in love and with whom — the restaurateur's daughter — he went off to a corner far from the world, in order to enjoy their happiness in love alone. The exotic Shelley, however, quickly cooled off and left his beloved soon after the wedding. Why? — All the biographers assert that the fault lay with Harriet, that because of a certain [?] superficiality of hers she became estranged from her husband. Recently the American critic Leslie Hotson discovered in an English court archive a series of interesting letters from Shelley to his wife, and these very letters throw an entirely different light on the matter. How did the letters come to be in a court archive? — Soon after Harriet's suicide Shelley sued his father-in-law and demanded that he be given custody of the orphans left behind. The father-in-law submitted the said letters to the court as proof of Shelley's direct guilt in his wife's suicide. From the letters one can see that after a short life together a great abyss opened between the brilliant poet and his not very intelligent wife. And besides, he soon became acquainted with Mary Godwin, the daughter of the well-known theorist of a new moral doctrine. He writes about himself: "I am united with a person who suits my nature and my aspirations so aptly that it grants [?] us a firm and eternal friendship."

But he did not come and say to his Harriet: you have nothing more to do with me, we are divorced, go. He demanded of her something more terrible: that she calmly bear his new union with Mary and even rejoice in his new happiness.. And when his [?] brutal demand is not fulfilled, he grows angry with her and writes: "How foolish I was to have demanded of you such generosity and nobility"! And "instead of enjoying the new surroundings, which would have given you the most fulfilled [?] virtue, you show yourself so shallow and low". Then he proposes to her that "they unite in a new form of friendship that would know no stereotyped limits and be without prejudice". The simple, human Harriet, however, could not go along with such a poetically capricious life, and ended it with suicide.

Great spirits do not always feel the sufferings and feelings of those nearest to them.

Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings and remarks on this week's portion (Emor)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings and remarks on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and edited by Y. L.
Parashat Emor.
—o—
A) "Speak unto the priests, the sons of Aaron" (21:1).
Usually kohanim and tzaddikim consider themselves great — no small thing: chosen ones of God! That is why God ordered Moses, before he would speak with the kohanim about their holiness, first to tell them: you have nothing to boast about in your priesthood, for "the sons of Aaron" — because your father was a kohen, you too are kohanim.
Kedushat Levi.
* * *
Some communal leaders (parnassim) of a small town came to Rabbi Shmuel Mohilever to consult him. Since a "little bird" [a pampered scion of a pedigreed family], descended from a great rabbinic house, was laying claim to the rabbinical seat of their town, but it was not known whether he could study. Said R' Shmuel to them: the Gemara says, "If the rabbi is like an angel of the Lord of Hosts, they shall seek Torah from his mouth." If a rabbi comes and says of himself that he is "like an angel of the Lord" — that he is a tzaddik, an angel, a "little bird" — then "they shall seek Torah from his mouth": just see whether he knows Torah too. A son of holy men he is indeed, and precisely for that reason, leaning on the merit of his ancestors, it is rare that such a person should really find it necessary to toil over Torah
—o—
B) "There shall none be defiled for the dead among his people" (ibid.).
Even of "amcha," of the common folk, of the dregs of society, you shall not single out any soul, any Jew, and say that because of his coarseness he is not within the community of Israel — all are Jews.
Likkutei Maharal.
—o—
C) "That they separate themselves from the holy things of the children of Israel" (21:2 — so printed; actually 22:2).
There are such "holy men" who persuade themselves that they are God's sanctifiers, that with their piety they "make the Almighty a people" [?], that were it not for them God would have no devotees at all... Of them the verse says: "veyinazru" — one should keep apart from such "holy men."
Mahara of Kaszenik [?].
—o—
D) "When a bullock, or a sheep, or a goat, is brought forth" (22:27).
A Jew says: let it be from an ox, let it be from a sheep, let it be from a goat — as long as "it is brought forth," as long as some little profit comes of it.
Folk saying.
—o—
E) "But I will be hallowed among the children of Israel" (22:32).
The Gemara derives from this verse: "an individual does not say the Kedusha." An individual may be as pious and holy for himself as he likes, but as long as he is not active "among the children of Israel," among the people and for the people, his piety is worth nothing.
Yalkut HaDrush.
—o—
F) "Thou shalt leave them for the poor, and for the stranger" (23:22).
Usually "commandments require intent" — a mitzvah must be done with intent, with full awareness. And which mitzvah is fulfilled only when one does it without intent, when one does it unawares, and if one does intend it, one does not fulfil the mitzvah at all?
Precisely the mitzvah spoken of in this verse, namely: shikhḥa, the forgotten sheaf. The whole ritual of this mitzvah consists, after all, in forgetting ears of grain in the field — in doing it without intent.
Beit HaMidrash Ḥadash.
—o—
G) "If a man cause a blemish in his neighbour — as he hath done, so shall it be done to him" (24:19).
Whoever finds only blemishes and faults in his fellow is himself nothing but a blemished man.
Melekhet Maḥshavot.
* * *
There is a musical instrument called "nevel." The Gemara says it is called "nevel" because with its playing it puts all the other instruments to shame, so beautifully does it play; and "naval" in Hebrew also means vile, and because it disgraces (menavel) others, it is itself called nevel. The question arises: because of its splendid playing others are put to shame — so why does it deserve such a name?
— Yes: whoever shames others, however splendid he himself may be, is nonetheless base; whoever disgraces others is himself a scoundrel (naval).
The Rim of Gur.
—o—
Avot, chapter four.
A) "When thou eatest the labour of thine hands" (mishna 1).
Happy is he who eats from the toil of his hands, the fruit of his hands' labour, of his physical work; woe to him who eats from the toil of his thought, of his intellectual work — woe to him...
R' M[endel] of Kotsk.
—o—
B) "The hope of man is the worm" (mishna 4).
"Rimmah" means worms, and as is well known, silk fabric is produced from a kind of worm. That is what Rabbi says: "the hope of man is the worm" — expensive silk garments and all kinds of finery are the whole hope and the whole life of some people.
Magen Avot.
—o—
C) "Against thy will thou livest, and against thy will thou diest" (mishna 29).
The Dubno Maggid was once a guest of the Vilna Gaon. In conversation the Gaon asked about the mishna mentioned above: the Tanna enumerates that against our will we are born, against our will we live, against our will we die, and against our will we must give an account for our deeds. The question arises: if we are born against our will and live against our will, why then are we obliged to give an account? One is responsible only for deeds done of one's own free will, not when one is coerced.
The Gaon answered: very well, we are born by force, live unwillingly — but when the minutes of death approach, do we not fight death with every means, do we not want to save ourselves with all our strength? That is surely a sign that life is pleasing to us after all; and if "against thy will thou diest," then indeed "against thy will thou art destined to give an account."
If "against thy will thou diest," if you have no desire to die, that is proof that life too was pleasing to you — and if so, pay up your account.
Yesodei HaIkkarim.

What Is Heard in Zagłębie?

What is heard in Zagłębie? Friday, 18 Iyar 5690. — Piątek 16 maja 1930 [Friday, 16 May 1930].
Będzin
—o—
New members of the kehilla board.
As reported[?], the following members pass automatically into the kehilla board: in place of Mr. Fürstenberg — Parnas[?] Goldsztajn; in place of Mr. Chinadzki — Abraham Limer; in place of E. Fajnski — S. Schönwald; in place of Y. Najmark — P. L. Buchheitz[?].
„Excuse me, sir, only those of Catholic descent may buy land in Poland“.

The local Jewish merchant Mr. P. read in a certain newspaper an advertisement of the „Bank Ludowy“ in Biała, which is selling plots of farmland at various stated prices.
Mr. P. went to the bank, where a clerk showed him the parcellation plan and informed him about the prices.
When Mr. P. wanted to pay a deposit („a conto“) for a certain plot, the clerk explained to him that it was not necessary. There is time, he said; come in a few days and pay the whole sum.
But when Mr. P. came a few days later to complete the deal, the clerk told him: „Excuse me, the squire who is parcelling out the plots of land has drawn our attention to the fact that we should sell only to those of the Catholic faith“...
A Sequestrator Sentenced to a Year in Prison

A great sensation was caused by the arrest of the sequestrator [tax-distraint officer] of the local tax office, Uchnast[?], who, while performing his office as sequestrator, committed various embezzlements. Besides causing the tax office a loss of 2,146 zł., the sequestrator took „a conto“ payments from taxpayers, to whom he gave false receipts.
For this Uchnast stood trial before the Sosnowiec District Court, which, after hearing a number of Będzin merchants, sentenced him to a year in prison and the loss of all civil rights.
Fairs to Be Held Twice a Week

At the request of the „Merchants' Association“, the local municipal administration has decided that the fairs on the market square on Modrzejowska[?] Street shall be held twice a week, on Monday and Wednesday.
The proposal was on the agenda of the city council.
Examination Board for Apprentice Candidates

An examination board has been opened at the municipal vocational schools by the School Curatorium.
Candidates for journeyman status who are admitted by statute to the journeyman examination must submit certificates showing that they have completed a three-class vocational school. Detailed information is given in Będzin[?] from 7 to 9 in the evening at the premises of „Piast“, and in Sosnowiec at Wawel 18.
The examinations will take place on the 22nd, 23rd, 24th and 25th of this month.
Because of a Letter-Carrier's „Competence“ a Jewish Merchant Is Suspected...

The local merchant and house-owner Abraham Zylberberg carried out a certain transaction at the office of the notary Rakowski in Sosnowiec.
This week the notary summoned Mr. Z. by postcard to come to him. But the letter-carrier could not „orient himself“ where Rybna Street in Będzin is, and the postcard was sent back to Sosnowiec with the remark that „the addressee cannot be found in Będzin“...
When the notary got the card back, he came to suspect that he was dealing with a swindler and informed the police about it.
On the strength of this intervention the local police took Mr. Z. in for questioning, and only then did the „secret“ affair become clear...
Mr. Z. has lodged a complaint with the local postmaster.
Another Passenger on the Kehilla's Old Nag...

This week a meeting of the kehilla „board“ took place. At the meeting, at which it was decided to increase the number of shochtim [ritual slaughterers], the question was also raised of granting a pension to the rabbinate secretary...
The First Pro-Palestine Workers' Congress

On the initiative of the Poale Zion Ratteger[?] in Będzin, a conference of representatives of social and professional institutions took place this week in connection with the Pro-Palestine Workers' Congress on 3 July in Warsaw.
At the conference the questions on the congress agenda were broadly discussed. In workers' circles the congress has aroused an understandable[?] interest. Up to today more than 500 election cards have been sold.
The workers of Zagłębie will be represented at the congress by a larger delegation.
In connection with the congress, the Będzin Pro-Palestine Workers' Committee is organising this Sabbath at 3 p.m.[?] („g. m.“) a meeting in the courtyard at Modrzejowska 61, with the participation of the well-known speaker and labour activist Mietek (Chaim Brand) from Łódź.
An Association of Office Workers

[Będzin — clerks and trade associations.]
The difficult economic situation, the uncertain tomorrow and the reductions [cuts and dismissals] have forced the local office employees to think about their own fate.
On the initiative of a group of bank employees, a general organizing meeting was called a few weeks ago.
The meeting took place in the hall of the local City Council, before an audience of over a hundred office workers.
A committee of 7 persons was elected, entrusted with the legalization [official registration] of the association and the preparation of the general meeting.
“Hakoach” Founds a Swimming Section

[Będzin — sport.]
The board of “Hakoach” [the Jewish sports club of Będzin] has adopted a resolution to found a swimming section. The founding meeting takes place today, Friday, in the evening.
A Flag-Day Sale

[Będzin — charity; followed by a short item: sport.]
Next Wednesday a sale of emblems [badges sold for a public cause] will take place in the town [Będzin]. The proceeds go to the “Malbish Arumim” society [clothing the poor].
—o—
On the Excursion of the Będzin “Hakoach” to Bielitz [Bielsko]
In connection with the excursion to Bielitz on Sunday, 18 May, the assembly point for all participants, including motorcyclists and cyclists, has been fixed for Sunday at half past 4 in the morning at the club's own premises. Tickets for all members and guests who have registered will be handed out on Saturday from 2 to 8 in the evening at the club's own premises.
Sosnowiec — The Kehilla Board's Reply to the Starosta on the Rabbinate Question

[Sosnowiec — rabbinate, kehilla.]
The local starosta [district head], Mr. Mandryszewski [?], approached the kehilla board with a proposal to nominate Rabbi Frommer as temporary rabbi.
In this connection the kehilla board held a meeting, at which it was unanimously resolved to reply to the starosta as follows: 1) only the kehilla board has the right to decide on such matters; 2) Rabbi Frommer is also a member of the Rabbinical Council, with which the entire Jewish population is very satisfied; and 3) the official rabbinical functions are, after all, performed by Rabbi Schwarz.
Official Notice Concerning the Previous Rabbinical Elections

[Sosnowiec — rabbinate, kehilla.]
This week the gmina [Jewish community] received an official notice that the rabbinical elections of 1927 have been annulled by the State Tribunal [probably the Supreme Administrative Tribunal] and that new elections will take place.
Meeting of the Bank for Artisans and Small Traders

[Sosnowiec — banks and cooperatives, artisans.]
In the hall of the “Hotel Polski” the annual general meeting of the members of the Artisans' and Small Traders' Bank took place on Sunday evening.
Dr. Hercman opens the meeting and hands the chair to Mr. S. Lewkowicz. The latter invites to the presidium Messrs. Abraham Opatowski, Jurkiewicz, and as secretary — Kromołowski.
The report of the board and council is given by the chairmen Fürstenberg and Hercman, who stress that, apart from the general economic crisis, the bank also suffered heavily from the elements who exploited the institution in internal party quarrels; but the harmful element has been removed and the bank is working on a normal line.
The balance sheet is read by Mr. Buksbaum. In the course of 1929 the bank discounted bills of exchange for 79 thousand zł., loans 20,840 zł.; there are over eight hundred members; deposits 45,197 zł., shares 42,847 zł., profit 595 zł. and 73 groszy.
After the reports a discussion took place, and the management was granted an absolutorium [discharge].
The budget of 36 thousand zł. was approved.
For the elections the compromise list was proposed, put forward by the president of the Artisans' Association, Mr. Opatowski, and the list was adopted by acclamation.
The board now includes, besides the previous members, also: Ch. Binkowski, “Degt.” [?] Rotsztajn, J. Fiks.
The council: Advocate A. Kon, Julian Rotenberg, J. Grinfeld, Ch. Gawriłowicz.
From the Mutual Credit Society

[Sosnowiec — banks and cooperatives.]
The credit institution “A. G.” [?] “Wzajemny Kredyt” [Mutual Credit], which was founded 7 months ago, held its first meeting last Sunday, attended by about 60 members.
The chairman of the board, Mr. Zendel, opens the meeting and hands the chair to Mr. Józef Majtlis. In the presidium: Izydor [?] Baruchowski, P. Słomnicki, and as secretary Rotman Tobiasz.
Mr. Zendel gives the general report, in which he points out that although the bank was founded in a very hard time, it is developing very well and occupies a respectable place.
The bank manager, Mr. Rudawer, reports that in the course of its 7-month existence the bank had a turnover of 14 million zł.; it discounted bills of exchange for 180 thousand zł.; deposits amount to 100 thousand zł.
Having heard the report, those assembled express their thanks to Mr. Rudawer for his achievements.
The budget of 43,640 zł. is adopted. The elections brought no change whatsoever.
After 25 Years She Repents and Wants to Convert Back to Judaism

[Sosnowiec — kehilla, religion.]
An elderly woman came to the gmina [Jewish community] and told: “I am,” she says, “an apostate; I converted 25 years ago. My husband has been dead for several years, and I make my living by washing laundry; and since I know that I will not live much longer, I want to become a Jew again and die as a Jewish woman.”
The Rabbinical Council referred the apostate to the Kraków rabbinate.
Deputy A. Hartglas in Sosnowiec.

[Sosnowiec — Zionism; lecture.] On the initiative of the Zionist youth organization named after Theodor Herzl in Sosnowiec, the former president of the Jewish Club [Koło Żydowskie, the Jewish caucus in the Sejm], Deputy A. Hartglas [Apolinary Hartglas], will deliver a lecture on Sunday the 25th of this month in the Sosnowiec Municipal Theatre, at half past 8 in the evening.
His coming has aroused due interest.
He Fancied Riding "Na Gapę"...

[Sosnowiec — miscellany; chess; free-loan fund.] Last Sunday a tram ticket inspector had the "editor" of the Będzin "Tsaytung" brought into the police commissariat; he was detained because he had ridden from Będzin to Sosnowiec "na gapę" [Polish slang: without a ticket].
The inspector demanded of him a fine of 2 zł. for 4 tickets. The "editor" refused to pay.
—o—
From the Sosnowiec Chess Club
Last Sunday the club played its last cup match in its group, against "Yazot" [?], over which it won a victory with a score of 5½ pts. to ½ pt.
The final will take place on the 25th of this month in Bielitz [Bielsko] against the very strong local club.
—o—
From the G"Ch Fund.
At the last meeting of the local Gemilut Chesed (interest-free loan) fund a series of loans was approved to a total of 17 thousand zł.
Dąbrowa — A Stormy Session of the Town Council.

[Dąbrowa — town council.] The last session of the local town council in Dąbrowa [Dąbrowa Górnicza], which lasted until 2 at night, was a very stormy one, like a Sejm session. Councillors threw themselves into fighting and swore at each other as in a tavern.
At the beginning of the stormy session President [mayor] Madejski [?] came forward with a motion that his statement be read in connection with the article in "Głos Zagłębia", in which the present municipal administration [magistrat] is insulted.
The PPS [Polish Socialist Party] members were against the motion, arguing that the town council does not have the task of rehabilitating Dr. Madejski.
Over this a heated discussion developed, which then took on a sharp character. During an exchange of views between Councillors Czepłak [?] and Szarym [?], the latter cried out:
— Shut up, you dog's blood! I'll tear you apart...
Czepłak then grabbed an ashtray and threw it at Szarym. Other councillors did the same, and a terrible scandal broke out in the hall. The president then moved to remove Czepłak from the session hall, and at the same time he also interrupted the session.
After a 2-hour pause the session was reopened.
The chairman holds to his first motion regarding Czepłak, and by a majority of votes Czepłak is excluded from the session.
The PPS then demand that Szarym, too, be excluded like Czepłak. When the motion fails, the PPS leave the session singing "Czerwony Sztandar" ["The Red Flag"]. The gallery sings "Pierwsza Brygada" ["The First Brigade", the Piłsudski Legions' song].
When it grows quiet, several motions are adopted, among them the agreement with the gasworks in Königshütte [Chorzów].

Protest Meeting against the Decree on Immigration to Eretz Israel

On Tuesday evening a meeting took place at the „Mizrachi“ school in Sosnowiec, attended by representatives of all the national and political parties.
The meeting heard a report on the latest decree against immigration to Eretz Israel.
It was resolved to organise a large protest meeting. The meeting will take place next Sunday morning at the Municipal Theatre. Speeches will be given by Rabbi Hager (Mizrachi), Dr. Melodysta (Zionists), Ganzreich (Poalei Zion), Klarman (Revisionist) and Milsztajn („Hitachdut“).

An Air Disaster in Katowice

In connection with the Aviation Week proclaimed in the country, a ceremony took place yesterday, Thursday, at the airfield in Katowice, attended by representatives of the authorities, the local self-government, organisations and school youth.
During the ceremony a large number of aeroplanes flew around the field and the pilots performed various stunts.
During one such stunt an aeroplane crashed; aboard it, besides the pilot, were also two gymnasium pupils from Katowice.
The result: the pilot was seriously injured, the pupils — lightly.

Hard to Build, Easy to Destroy... (On the Liquidation Decision of the Dąbrowa 'Bank Ludowy')

[Dąbrowa — people's bank; letter to the editor.] Esteemed Editors!
Having attended [?] the last meeting of the "Bank Ludowy" [People's Bank] and listened to the sad reports on the activity of the new management so far, I ask you to allow me to speak out on this question in the columns of your esteemed newspaper, in case the present leaders might yet realise that an institution such as the "Bank Ludowy" must not be liquidated.
In the month of April 1929 a management board and a council, which had practical experience in banking behind them, were elected by acclamation at a general meeting of the bank. Soon after the meeting there came "to the floor" persons who have only a slight connection with public work and who, apart from their "protégés", also "worked over" the street with all kinds of lies about the newly elected board and council. The upshot was that the board as well as the council, bearing full responsibility for this useful [?] institution, laid down their mandates, and new elections were called.
At the new general meeting, because of the suspicions that had been cast that "things are not in order at the bank", a commission [printed "ka-mutye"] was elected, which over 3 months audited the bank's activity and found that the bank had even made a profit of 700 zł.
After the audit another meeting was held, at which a board [printed "meeting"] was elected from the "heads of the bench", the very notables of the town, of whom it was confidently expected that these gentlemen would raise the bank back to its proper level.
But, as it turns out, from words to deeds is a long way. The prominent gentlemen of the board and council, instead of working actively for the good of the bank, installed [?] their own relatives in posts and left the bank to God's mercy...
The consequences of such fine "management" are as follows: a few weeks ago the leaders discovered that there was a deficit of 4 thousand zł. in the till. Instead of the board finding remedies, they wanted to smear the loss onto the members. When that did not succeed, the board again kept quiet and waited until the deficit should double — the deficit already amounts to 8 thousand zł.
Only the figures "opened" the eyes of the above-mentioned gentlemen, who decided that the bank, which has existed for a number of years already, should be liquidated...
— Gentlemen members of the board and council! Consider what you are about to do; remember the saying of our Sages, "even if a sharp sword rests on a man's neck, let him not despair of mercy"; if only your good will is there, the institution, which was created with blood and sweat, can surely be saved...
— Perhaps He will have mercy!..
A member of the bank.
Careful with Radio Sets — When Leaving for a Summer Residence

[Radio — practical advice.] Every radio subscriber who goes away to a summer residence has the right to take his radio set there with him for a short time. There is no need to report this at the post office.
In the town flat, however, the radio installation must for that period be secured in such a way that it cannot be used under any circumstances.
The outside aerial, which is located outside the house (in front of the window or on the balcony), must be connected to the ground.
Persons going away to summer residences must without fail "earth" the aerial and fit it with lightning arresters; if not, the house is in danger.
When one comes home from the summer residence, the same must again be done with the aerial at the summer residence.

[Sosnowiec — youth movements.] Already at 4 o'clock at dawn the strains of the Shomer hymn were heard — "Arise! Shomrim, do not slumber" — waking the Shomrim from sleep for their traditional Lag ba-Omer outing.
At exactly half past 5 more than 100 Shomrim marched in closed ranks, to the strains of the Shomer orchestra, to "Wilhelmsthal". In the course of the day various lectures and sports exercises took place. The match between "Hashomer Hatzair" and "Sosnowiec" ended in a 7:1 victory for "Hashomer Hatzair".
In the evening, around the "medura" — a Land-of-Israel campfire — there was talk about the significance of Lag ba-Omer and the situation in the Zionist and Shomer movement.
At about 10 in the evening the Shomrim marched in exemplary order through Dekerta, Modrzejowska and 3 Maja streets to their premises. In Dekerta Street the onlookers greeted the young Shomrim with loud applause and cries of "hurrah". In front of the premises the procession was dismissed.

[Będzin — education and culture; elementary schools.]
On the initiative of elementary schools no. 4 and 8 in Będzin, a "fantastic performance" in the form of a charade in 3 acts with a prologue and an epilogue, written by Mrs. P. Sznajderman, was staged at the "Corso" by a number of pupils of the aforementioned schools.
The content: lost children in the house of a stepmother who is very bad to them, to the children; then the spectators are shown a kingdom that thinks only of creating friendship and good for children, and the ending is, as in all plays, that the children find their mother again.
The "play" is also spiced with dances, theatrical effects, spotlights — no worse than with real stage actors.
The authoress deals with a very important problem — for can there be a more important question than providing for poor children so that they too do not live in worse conditions than rich children? — but the plot is put together[?] and arranged in a very pale form; the good impression is created only by the stage effects, especially in the third act, which was richly staged, and the rhythmic dances of the young pupils gave real pleasure.

The Assessment Commissions Are Being Abolished

[Taxes — Poland; tax reform.]
The project of unifying the tax organisation is being prepared at a fast pace; a law on it will appear very soon.
First of all the law provides for the abolition of the assessment commissions. At the same time each appeals commission will become the sole body in which the civic element is represented; the appeals commissions will be divided into small sub-commissions for each branch separately, with the participation of persons well versed in the corresponding fields of trade and industry. It should be noted that this concept was put forward in his time by Prof. Kemmerer.
Further, the ordinance introduces a system of paying taxes in monthly instalments. Each instalment is to amount to 1/12 of the tax that was paid in the previous tax year. In connection with this principle certain complications arise in cases where the income or the turnover has grown or shrunk in the new tax year.
As regards the publicity of the procedure, it is envisaged that publicity is to remain only for income and property tax. As regards the turnover tax, no publicity is to be recognised.
The ordinance provides that within 3 years an additional tax may be assessed for the past period. Within 10 years the tax authority has the right to claim[?] an overdue tax. If the overdue debt is secured by a mortgage, legal prescription occurs after 30 years.

Small Remarks on Big Matters

[Zagłębie — opinion column; livelihoods, municipal affairs, railways.]
When one does not stand on guard.
Last week a conference took place at the Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce, at which the new draft of the Ministry of the Interior was considered, which provides for new regulations on meat processing.
Only Christian butchers from Będzin and Sosnowiec — the paper tells us — took part in the conference. As for the Jews — although they too had been invited, not one of them came.
We happen not to be familiar with the new regulations; we do not know what they are; but the matter surely ought to have concerned those affected, they surely ought to have taken an interest in the question: this is their trade after all, and every trifle may mean a great loss for them and a disruption of their trade — so how can one make light of matters that touch on livelihood? In our time making a living is as hard as the parting of the Red Sea. Later, as soon as changes for the worse come about for Jews which make their trade harder, they will then — perhaps when it is already too late — begin to shout and to rage, and they will have complaints against this one and that one for having allowed undesirable things to happen; and then they will above all forget that the representatives did not look after their own at the time when they should have stood on guard and remembered that they must defend themselves, th[at] they must protect what is due to them.
This very fact characterises our negligence, our indifference to the most important matters concerning professional interests. We ourselves oversleep just when one needs to be awake; we ourselves will not put a hand into cold water, regardless of the fact that it concerns the continuation of economic interests.
Let those concerned remember not to throw onto anyone else what they bring upon themselves through their criminal indifference. Let people remember that an apathetic attitude means not only negligence — it also means ruining oneself, having no say over one's own affairs, which play such a great role in our present period.
What about the gates?
To this day the question of the [courtyard and house] gates has not been regulated in any town of Zagłębie. All one knows is[?] that the gates are locked, that one has to ring, and that whoever rings must be let in. On the other hand the caretakers ("stróże"), or as one must call them nowadays, "dozorcy", do whatever pleases them and whatever they want: they shut the gate whenever they like, and when one wants to get in, in many places it happens that one cannot; as soon as the gate is locked it is locked indeed, and if you come later you may as well go and spend the night in a hotel; in other places there is no bell at all, so that there you have no recourse whatsoever. Elsewhere, where one can indeed be let in, there is no [fixed] price[?]: one takes from you whatever you give him, and another has set himself his tariff of half a gulden, and will not accept anything less; it goes without saying that you have no other choice and must meet his demand, no matter how many times you need to go in and out during the evening; and so[?] such a caretaker is already interested in locking the gate as early as possible, so that he may have larger earnings — after all he has a material interest in an evening bringing him as many half-guldens as possible.
All this shows how far our local self-governments limp behind, how much disorder prevails, that they have not yet bothered[?] to regulate even such a trifle. First of all, why are the gates not closed at a regular time everywhere, instead of one street or one house being locked at ten o'clock and another at eleven? And if it is locked, why should there not be a bell everywhere, and why should the caretaker not sit at the gate until such-and-such an hour, as is the custom in the bigger cities? Then, why should there not be a uniform price, so that one knows that it is a tariff and that the gate must be opened? After all, many tenants are afraid to come into and go out of the houses after the hour. Is it fitting that one should find oneself somewhere out under the "ḥarei ḥoshekh"[?]?
It would therefore be high time for the question to be settled once and for all in all the towns of Zagłębie, so that it be published at what time the gates must be locked and how much one must pay for being let in, both early in the night and in the middle of the night; there should also be a bell, and the caretaker should be obliged to open the gate at any time.
Seen with our own eyes...
A week ago, on Thursday — it was in Będzin, on 15 May — when some members of the editorial staff had agreed among themselves to go to the railway station to see how an express train (kurier) would pass through without stopping, on arriving there we saw that we were not the only privileged ones: other curious people like us were already there, waiting impatiently to see the express train. Everyone was curious to see whether it could really be that a train would pass our station without stopping. Somehow nobody believed such a thing, and therefore so many people came to see what was impossible to believe; but what had been impossible to believe became a reality, a fact, a living phenomenon that now already occurs in our everyday life. With our own eyes we had the opportunity to establish that the fast trains run past the town exactly as if a booth stood there in an open field... It does not even bother them in the least that from time immemorial they were used to stopping here. When it comes down to it, Będzin no longer exists even as a station — as a town, there is no point even talking about it!
But we need not think ourselves so grand[?]: although Dąbrowa and Zawiercie are smaller towns than Będzin, younger in years, they too were given a surprise — for instance, in the other towns too not all trains stop: the one that stops in Zawiercie does not stop in Dąbrowa, and the one that stops in Dąbrowa no longer stops further on in Zawiercie; but at least they were given something, whereas we in Będzin have been reduced to nothing altogether.
Neither we nor anyone else believed that the sensation could become reality, that it could actually happen that a train should pass Będzin without stopping, and that is why we wanted to see it with our own eyes.
Będzin has begun "to knock on doors" (kołatać — to petition) over the matter, and it is characteristic that from the Railway Directorate in Warsaw an answer arrived that the president of the Directorate is in Madrid and one must wait until he returns from his long journey[?].
Upon my life, all this is comical; and if the president is away travelling, must things therefore stay as they are? He surely leaves a deputy, and if the deputy is unable to do anything, there is surely a Ministry of Railways! Upon my life, it is a farce; all this looks like a comedy.
— When it comes down to it, saying that it [Będzin] is going backwards is surely out of the question!
R. Let.
With the "Hakoach" excursion to Bielitz.

Reported by Ben Amotz.
The "World Union" "Maccabi" in Bielitz [Bielsko], in accordance with the resolution of the last "Maccabi" convention, organised a Lag ba-Omer celebration combined with a competition in gymnastic exercises.
Invited to the competition were: "Maccabi" (Sosnowiec), "Hakoach" (Będzin), "Maccabi" (Olkusz) and others.
The Sosnowiec "Maccabi" approached the competition in a practical way: only the first men's group travelled [?], accompanied by the chairman Herszowicz [?]; it passed the test, took the first prize and – off [?] home.
Quite differently did the Będzin "Hakoach" behave. "With thunder and lightning", with noise and clamour, the club set out to the Lag ba-Omer celebration – after all, it is "Hakoach"! A club that within a short time has risen to greatness, wealth and honour – no mere Jewish luck...
"Hakoach" "mobilised" all its forces, called to service (the work of mouth and song...) all age-groups; even the "meteraners" [?] and the veterans left "hoe and pick" and placed themselves under the "Hakoach" banner...
The departure
was imposing. At dawn the stones of the streets began to tremble from the noisy motorcycles. The commanders simply flew on them like spirits. From all sides of the town larger and smaller "soldiers" marched to the assembly point at Kołłątaja 45; from minute to minute the camp grew (may they multiply). Half-asleep mothers and fathers also came to the departure and watched with proud, beaming faces how their children, wearing blue-and-white caps, were lively and merry.
"Remember, Malkele – a mother begs her little daughter – don't go into the 'Gypsies' forest'. More than once it has happened that Gypsies have kidnapped Jewish children..."
Close by the wall stands a couple who came to see off their son. "When I – he says – went to cheder, when Lag ba-Omer came the rebbe gave every pupil a bagel and an egg. Then we went off behind the shtetl, and there the shkotsim [gentile boys] met us with stones and..."
The signal of the command calls to board the cars, and we, some three hundred Hakoach members of both sexes, [with] our own [?] orchestra, drive to the competition.
"Berl with the fiddle"...
You surely know the folk song "Berl with the fiddle, Shmerl with the bass". The same motif can be applied here too: we left Będzin in eight cars and arrived in Bielitz with five... After all, for thousands of years we have been crowned with the title "ama pezize" [a hasty people]... We never have time, we hurry, run, chase, and we never know what you are running for like that, Reb Shakhne...
Instead of keeping one "glue" the whole way, staying closed up one with the other, they scattered completely, and the cars whose "innards", the entrails, were not in order said "nie pojadę" [Polish: "I won't go"].
And when a stubborn chauffeur wanted to "force" his "little horse" to run uphill, the little horse made a "retreat" and freed itself of its passengers... It was a miracle that together with the passengers there was the banner, and the "power" of the banner – a Jewish banner after all, won in struggle with blood and tears – protected against serious mishaps, and to spite [?] our enemies almost all came out safely without any mishap...
"Hospitality"...
The German "Yehudim" are very friendly people, only not towards the "Polish Jews". Indeed, what worth do we, little Polish Jews, have compared with a "people of nothing but doctors"... How do we "dumb folk" [?] come to "top-hat heads"...
The reception by the Bielitz "World-Unionists" was a very "grandiose" one. Apparently it was too little for the shrunken Bielitz "in-laws" that such dressed-up guests came to them with their own orchestra, who lit up the locals and gave everybody great pleasure...
But "Hakoach" did not know that the local "Maccabi" would grant it a yasher koach. Rather, the good impression that "Hakoach" left on Sunday will long, long remain in the memory of the Bielitzers...
The first appearance
started from the assembly point at the railway station. In closed ranks, with the orchestra under P. Barenblat's command, the "Hakoach" groups marched to the gymnastics hall where the gymnastics competition took place.
In front of the gymnastics building the Bielitz "in-laws" were already standing, and they declared that the Będzin people had missed the fixed deadline and could not be admitted to the competition.
Despite the intervention of Dr. Rechtman the decision was not changed – "es geht ja nicht" [German: "it just isn't possible"], and that's that. Inside [?], in the splendid gymnastics hall, the gymnasts Banszykowski, Cukerman and Plesner were already there from before; they performed various fine exercises, while around them stood the commission, just like at a draft board... and judged... The verdict came out only at dusk. So: the Sosnowiec "Maccabi", famous for its men's group, received the first prize (Trajster), Będzin (Banszykowski) the second prize. The latter shows with facts that the commission robbed him of several points... "With an honest commission – shouts Banszykowski – I would certainly have received the first prize."
Generosity and politeness the Bielitz "Maccabi" did not show [?].
In the Gypsies' forest.
This "article" they granted us wholeheartedly and in full measure. They also took care that in this forest – which is town property, received as a gift from a prince – no couples should "get lost"... For the Yekke has a sharp nose [?]: he instantly sniffed out that the Będzin youth was eager to "assimilate" with the little Bielitz Germans...
From the pleasant and healthy mountain air the crowd got a real appetite and began to enjoy itself, but in the midst of it a report came from the gymnasts who had lost their way that the car had overturned on the road. The news "tore off" the music, and a heavy mood weighed on the heart.
The mood, however, changed a little later. After commander Banszykowski came back with the report that luckily nothing had happened, they proceeded to the main business – the Lag ba-Omer celebration.
On the open field.
All around, mountains and forest. A splendid natural panorama. The "Hakoach" banner flutters, the orchestra plays the Polish and the Jewish anthems, and Dr. Rechtman speaks about the importance of physical development among Jews, which plays a great role, and concludes: Long live "Hakoach"!
Then the crowd marches to another spot, where speeches are made from a platform: Dr. Machna [?] and Engineer Waksberg [?]. The former greets "Hakoach" and the latter speaks about the significance of Lag ba-Omer for the revival of Eretz Israel.
The orchestra answers with "Hatikvah", and with that the "festive programme" – which the "Yehudim" did not stop mentioning the whole day – is concluded.
On the whole the excursion was not a success. "Hakoach's" luck [sic] was in the sky but not on earth. The sun shone splendidly, caressing like a tender mother her children; but precisely "between man and his fellow", the atmosphere, the living together, the collective spirit and especially the organisation were lacking from the very beginning to the very end.
We would commit a "moral crime" if we did not mention the cyclist Plawner. If all Jews flew on bicycles the way Plawger does, "we would long since have been in Palestine"... Plawger is an aeroplane on the ground: he doesn't ride, he flies...
On a Normal Path.

(Destructive financial institutions and flourishing real deeds.)

It has now become such a fashion: like a person, like a society, like a minyan — as soon as a few people gather together, a bank is founded there at once. And so it is no wonder that the banking business has become so petty and has reached a [—] of rare irresponsibility.

Formerly, as we know, a bank was such[?] a thing that people took pride in; everything possible was done so that the institution would stand at the proper level and enjoy a good reputation in the street, and that is precisely why these institutions were always spoken of with so much respect and with reverence. People knew that this undertaking was taken up by persons with a sense of responsibility and understanding; people without competence did not dare to touch banking — they knew it was not within their competence and therefore kept away from it. Thanks to that the banks had their naturalness, their true lustre and splendour.

But the years have passed — not so many in number as they have taken us far from ourselves, from our notions; it seems as if a span of decades had gone by, and in that short time, in those few years, so much change has set in, so much irresponsibility, beyond understanding, beyond grasping with our [sm]all[?] human mind.

A year ago we watched how in Będzin one of the finest and oldest banks in Poland went off the rails — a bank that had developed so brilliantly and become popular among all strata of the population; and despite all that, despite its having had such good years, the seven lean cows swallowed the seven fat ones, and no trace of them could be seen...

It is truly a wonder how one can fall so far at a time when there were almost only good times; but the answer is quite simple. Politics, „shmor li ve-eshmor lekha“ (“you look after me and I'll look after you”) — and with that the hard question is answered. It drifted like a ship without a rudder...

Now we have again attended a general meeting of our Sosnowiec bank, which belongs to the artisans and small traders. It too was led astray; this institution too left its straight line; there too politics took the seat of honour and brought in so much destructive spirit that it became impossible to continue the work. Now the bank is back on its normal path and there are chances that the institution will regain its true face, and then[?] we shall know that we have a people's bank, which will be able to serve and advance the interests of those who need such a bank, of those who are in need of such an institution.

The Sosnowiec Artisans' and Small Traders' Bank numbers 800 members; that, of course, means a public financial institution in its full strength. An institution with such a number of members around it has the right to want to exist, and indeed must exist, and it can indeed do a great deal for its members.

And therefore, therefore every means must be used to raise the institution to the proper level so that it can serve the interests of its members. We know very well in what a difficult situation the popular masses in Poland find themselves today. No one doubts the bitter present, when the whole country is living through enormously hard times; from all this one can understand how hard it is at such a time for the average artisan or small trader to live, who have nothing to lean on. And if their financial institution does not concern itself with them, if the bank's management does not concern itself with their situation, if they do not come to the aid of these oppressed and helpless people — without a bank, who can help them, and to whom can they turn at all for financial help? Who knows them and who cares about them, to whom will they go and where will they have access?

The formula must be adopted once and for all that an artisans' and small traders' bank must concern itself exclusively with its members, for whom the institution was created and to whom it belongs — that is what matters, that is what must be kept well in mind on every occasion.

Then the institution must be raised to its proper height; the work must be done carefully, with love and devotion; the leaders of the institution must regard their activity as an ideal. No intrigues, self-interest or egoistic politics may be allowed, for that is the dangerous microbe: as soon as they force their way in, the whole public activity becomes a heap of ruins (tel olam); that is the deadly poison that stifles and crushes useful popular work.

Therefore the destructive element, which quite often likes to slip in unnoticed into every corner of our public activity, must not be allowed.

Sosnowiec needs, and can have, a sound bank for the above-mentioned members; therefore the leaders of the institution must use all possible means so that the life and interests of these common people are concentrated around the bank.

At the same time the truth must be told: we are still far from having conscious artisans and small traders in the full sense of the word, and that is the reason why what ought to exist and live is so often destroyed. „Es iz rekht“ — it takes only Berl coming to Shmerl with an intrigue against this or that public figure, against this or that institution, and the other accepts it as good coin — and here the digging begins, until the intriguers bring about what they are after.

Of course, when one deals with conscious, intelligent people, they do not believe at once; they investigate and get to the truth; whereas naive, unaware Jews can be talked into anything in the world, and here the dangerous web[?] begins to be woven that saws everything off at the root. These dangerous intriguers must be shunned by Jewish society, for they sow hatred and enmity over every trifle, because they are not seated in the place they want to occupy. With them self-interest, intrigues, quarrels and squabbles stand above everything in the world. There are such as cannot manage without it, who without intrigues feel like a fish on dry land.

Let the conscious, the mature, the intelligent see to it that the dangerous microbe does not slip into the healthy public sphere, which can bring immeasurable benefit to the popular masses through normal and healthy activity.
Dr. Papuri.
