Chaotic Activity. / (Self-government work as a system. — If only a change would come about.)

[Opinion — the city council and the budget.] We thought that the situation would change after all; we were sure that clarity and restraint would set in in the municipal self-government on the part of our Jewish councillors. We were almost sure that at last people would realise that local economic activity is not some ball that one throws wherever one likes and does with whatever one likes. Others perhaps not, but they know perfectly well that the present management simply disrupts the life of the citizen and often even brings it to the point of ridicule and farce.
At every session they talk among themselves, take nothing and no one into account, and when the neighbours look on, they of course derive pleasure from it; and that every moment is exploited and does us harm is self-evident. This they surely see, our representatives, at every step, and yet they play dumb about it, as if they had not caused it.
It is unheard of: somehow they forget where they stand in the world; they think that the population must put up with their whims. It often gives the impression that each of them makes his own "mistakes" [?] for himself, for his private affairs. They do not take account at all of the fact that they are emissaries of the people and that they must adapt themselves to those who sent them there. Our present-day people's emissaries have two cardinal faults: first, they do not want to adapt to the needs of the voters, and second, they have no sense for it at all; it seems to them that everything within their competence is their private affair, in which nobody has any business meddling, and they are sure that they can do everything or nothing on their own authority and that nobody has any say over them. That is why the situation is not favourable; that is why things are not improving.
Nevertheless, we thought that when it came to the budget question people would become more conscious, more refined, more restrained; we could never have imagined that all at once they would be standing at the very same starting point and would not take a single step further in the interest of the public.
Somehow people treat the most important matters coldly and apathetically altogether. When was the budget ever treated with such indifference as is happening now? After all, the whole of one's attention should have been given to the budget question. It is known perfectly well that the largest revenues come out of Jewish pockets — so why doesn't one stand on guard? Why isn't every item properly defended separately? Why does one only look to settle scores and throw [?] pins at one another, so that responsibility for the community is turned into disgusting private intrigues, and it becomes simply repulsive to listen to such things and to witness [?] all this.
Once, among councillors in general and ours in particular, one saw more restraint and responsibility, more sanctity and reverence, and therefore every problem was approached with exact [?] calculation and conviction, with composure and reverence. Gradually, gradually, however, all this has vanished, and the real public problem has lost its true colour beyond recognition.
Often one can spend the time quite pleasantly being at the sessions and listening to the most varied dialogues and "urgent motions". All would be well, if it did not come at the expense of the public, if unnecessary expenditures were not made, which one could have done without in the present time of crisis.
Had one approached public activity with more composure and sincerity, one would first of all have stopped to reduce the excessive budget. Why shouldn't public money be spared at a time when the people are stinting themselves in private life? If each of us must stint himself more in his private expenses, then surely one must see to it that he also pays lower taxes; that is surely a self-evident thing, that is surely not hard for every councillor individually to understand.
It is no longer a secret that we are living in an enormously critical time, when life is becoming steadily harder — so why should the "city fathers" not stop to consider such a serious phenomenon and help ease the conditions in which the citizens live?
Of course some of the non-Jewish and left-wing councillors want to make the budget as large as possible, because they know that we have to give, whereas they are the first to take. The larger the budget is, the larger the needs they will have.
One must look reality in the eye in order to arrive at the conviction that there is no point in drawing up excessively high budgets that afterwards cannot be carried out.
Also wrong is the reckoning by which one accepts every tax, however high it may be, merely on the grounds that the representative will obtain a subsidy for an institution of his party; that surely means selling the birthright for a pot of lentils. Such subsidies cost the population too dearly and therefore must not be allowed.
With the subsidies there is altogether an unheard-of lawlessness: the institution that has a hand [?] in the dish, or that belongs to a party which has its representatives on the city council — such a one [?] will be subsidised no matter what; whereas however necessary an institution may be, if it has no representatives of its own on the city council it will not be subsidised. That is surely unheard of.
We could still understand that private institutions should not be subsidised; but public philanthropic institutions ought to be properly subsidised — not merely pro forma, as they say, just to shut their mouths, but really with adequate sums, so that they know they are being helped and their means of existence made easier.
As for our leftists, who quite often do harm when it comes to Jewish "bourgeois" demands and always want to be more papal than the Pope — they too could learn something from their Christian comrades.
In general it is high time to pay more attention to having the activity in the city council arranged differently by our councillors. Somewhat better relations ought to begin among them; a comradely rapprochement is called for between one group and the other, between one representative and the next.
After all, one can come closer; after all, one can reach an understanding, especially when this will bring much, much benefit both to the Jewish population in general and to economic activity in particular.
Under present conditions it is very hard to work for the public; it does not look good in front of the Christian colleagues and it is not seemly for ourselves either, not to mention that one suffers at every step.
Perhaps a rapprochement, a change for the better, will come about after all? Upon my life, it is high time.
R. Let.
A Stowaway... — How they want to smuggle a shochet into Będzin

[Będzin — ritual slaughter and kashrut, Ger Hasidim; letter of protest.] How they want to smuggle a shochet [ritual slaughterer] into Będzin.
As is the way of the world, when the post of a religious functionary falls vacant in a kehilla, a competition is announced for the post in question, and from the candidates who apply the most suitable one is chosen. With us in Ger [the Ger Hasidim], however, it is understood that the candidate was not created for the kehilla, but the kehilla exists only so that it should provide a livelihood for "one of ours". So what does it matter whether the post is vacant, whether a better man is needed or not, when an ish-shlomenu ["one of our people"] needs a livelihood? I mean it really — what does it matter?..
There is among us a young fellow ["yungermantshikl"] who is good for nothing else but slaughtering cattle, and he is still hardly skilled, without practice, without anything; and after all, it is not a question of some little village but of such an ir va'em be-Yisrael [a "mother city in Israel"] as Będzin — oh, how can one entrust such an enormous responsibility — as kashrut is for a religious Jew — to such a young fellow? — But what's the use of all this nonsense, kashrut, responsibility and the like, when one of the anshei shlomenu needs a livelihood! Be grateful to him — our young fellow — that it did not occur to him to become... a rabbi. Believe me, on my word of honour, that too would have been a lost cause... lost as in Brody ["farfaln vi in Brod"]. Don't you remember that exclamation of a Ger Hasid, who is already in the World of Truth: "If we — (the Ger Hasidim) — want it, even a priest will be a rabbi"... Believe me, in this at least he told no lie at all...
But brains they do have. They brought the plan out into the open and saw that it aroused a little anger among the Hasidic public; enough people are grumbling about the Będzin shechita as it is, and now to do such a thing in broad daylight — so they resorted to the old Ger method: to smuggle him in. With us! In Ger that is always how things are done... A few butchers were bribed (mit a dlid[?] leyen... — "with a [?] loan"), and the young fellow was taken on at the slaughterhouse [?] just like that, "to watch a little"; for the time being, so to speak, he [—] ["er shiebur[?] zem[?]"]. Just let him crawl in... And "for the time being" they gave him the first beast, to see what he can do. Imagine: at his very first "debut" he managed straightaway to make the beast treyf. But let us admit the truth: alive it did not remain... Perhaps, perhaps at the Resurrection of the Dead it will rise and ask "lama" [why] it was slaughtered; and in town there goes about a gang of cattle that let themselves be led by a couple of youngsters... People have even already caught on to the "blind passenger" [stowaway] whom they want to smuggle aboard the kehilla Zeppelin; but don't worry, our little shochet has already come to terms with the town's cattle. By kittel and tallis I swear to you that if it has been written down in the Ger shtibl — it's a lost cause, nothing will help you...
But what about kashrut, gentlemen?
Is it then in order to entrust to such a young fellow, who is certainly not "a man of knowledge who knows how to take care" (Rema, Laws of Shechita, 1:5), the shechita of such a town as Będzin?
We want to know: what does our rabbinate say to this?
Ish-Hasid.
Flower Days. (Not a feuilleton)

[Będzin — social feuilleton, street collections ("flower days").] (Not a feuilleton).
For months one waits for spring. Winter, together with his charming in-law, autumn, drags on and on like the Jewish exile. And spring passes so quickly that one doesn't manage to enjoy it at all. And when spring comes, it brings us, together with the warm sun and fragrant flowers, also... flower days [street-collection days on which a pin-flower is given for a donation].
There is no day on which you are not met with the collection box ["pushke"]. To list everything that is being collected for is beyond our strength. It is easier to list what is not being collected for... We do not want here to censure the organisers of these events ["imprezes", Polish imprezy]: when one is drowning one grabs at a straw. But still it is not good when every blessed morning some madame, or a young lady, or a couple of schoolchildren block your way and stick a pin right into your heart.
Something ought to be done about the flower days: if the world had more understanding for radical solutions of problems, I would propose settling the flower days in the same way as they intend to settle the turnover tax for small shopkeepers — a "ryczałt" [a fixed lump sum]. The collection-day season has a certain number of days; the size of the coins one is usually [?] accustomed to throw into the boxes is known to all who count the bit of copper and nickel after a hard day's toil ["harevanye"]; it would be a plan for everyone to bring in at once the few gulden he gives out every summer on little flowers; the societies, which already chase after us with their "days", should divide it among themselves, and one would be able to walk down a street in peace.
A "ryczałt" for the payers of the flower tax — that might succeed in freeing us from this legacy of the war: unfortunately the world always goes along the line of least resistance, and of course it is easier to go out with the box and collect the few gulden than to carry out the plan I propose. I shall therefore make another proposal, somewhat less radical, which should, if not eradicate [?] the plague, at least soften it a little.
There is great trouble with the flower days in that one doesn't know when they take place. There was once a time when a flower day used to be announced in advance. Now they have probably realised that the expense is a pity.
And this involves a great many inconveniences. True, as experience teaches us, one may expect a flower every day God gives; but just as a gravely ill man only hopes that the Angel of Death will forget about him, so it seems to us that perhaps today the misfortune will pass us by; but just as if to spite you, you are met with the big collection box — and you haven't a grosz! Let it not happen, as it does happen, that a Będzin Jew goes out into the street early in the morning and simply hasn't even the 10 groszy with which one can get rid of a collector. But if one knew beforehand, one would find some way or other.
Further, there is another point. Flower and flower are not alike. There are flower days on which you give a larger coin, whether you can or not. So one really ought to know beforehand who and who the collectors are, so that one need not stop and talk about what is being collected for today.
I would therefore propose to all our esteemed societies that they announce their flower days in advance; then one will know where one stands in the world and what coin one must warm in one's pocket before setting out into the street: a copper one, a nickel one, or even a silver one...
It will not even be too great a consolation for the Będzin public — the public would gladly be rid altogether of the flower nuisance ["blimlekh-tsutshepenish"] — and perhaps it was not worth dwelling on it at such length; but to speak one's heart out a little — that too is something.
Me.
Będzin Zionists and "Mizrachi" "protest" against the aliyah decree

[Będzin — Zionism, Mizrachi, protest against the restriction of immigration.] The chairman of the Będzin "Mizrachi" woke up from his deep sleep and heard that all the national groupings in Będzin (apart from the Zionists, Bundists and Communists) are organising protest meetings against the English government, which has restricted immigration to Eretz Israel. In great haste the chairman of the "Mizrachi" polished his pince-nez ["binaklen"], took the telephone receiver in his hand and telephoned the premises of the organisation:
— We must protest!
And when the "Rebbe" commands — it was indeed made known through screaming posters all over town that the "Mizrachi" is organising a protest meeting with the participation of Rabbi Hager of Sosnowiec.
The meeting was supposed to take place on Sunday, the eve of Shavuot, in the morning. But the chairman, as it turns out, regretted the whole business. What for — he thought to himself — must one protest, make a racket [?]; that is a matter for others, but not for the "loyal" Mizrachists in Będzin, and he
— called the meeting off..
What Was Heard, What Was Seen.

[Będzin and district — weekly feuilleton.] Noted down [?] by Ben Amotz.

A word in season...
The order of the day of the Sosnowiec Jewish kehilla is — the matter of rabbis.
In the street, in the shop, while eating and going to bed, people talk, debate and prophesy about the matter.
Besides in the street, the talk is also widely discussed in the shtiblekh and even in the synagogue.
But Sosnowiec has a gabbai, a very practical one. He recognises no modern fashions whatsoever. What belongs to the street and what to people..
And when he sees that in the synagogue the worshippers are talking about the rabbinate question, he lets out a shout:
— "A disgrace and a shame, that in a holy place people should talk about rabbis!"..

A victim of the economy...
Into the editorial room creeps an elderly Jew, his black beard shot through with whitish patches. He stands still like a statue, and his lip moves as if he were speaking..
— What do you wish, Reb Yid?
— For 32 years I have been carrying. The Magistrat [town council], nothing to be done, Rosh Chodesh a few groszy..
— But tell us, what do you want from us?
— "I want — I was told [?] to come in here, to have something written in the paper, that I am a water-carrier in Będzin, I have been carrying water for 32 years, every day I earned 4—5 gulden [złoty], and we lived; but today the Magistrat has put water into every house, so I have nothing to do, nobody needs me any more — so I want you to write about it".
— And what do you make a living from?
— I have already become like everyone.. I have lived 60 years and today I must hold out my hand for alms...
We sent the victim of the economy to the PPS [Polish Socialist Party]: let him enrol with them as a member, then their councillors will take care of him.. Other councillors (not all) are unfortunately powerless; they do not sing "Czerwony Sztandar" ["The Red Flag"] and do not have the power to see to it that a Jew who fell victim to the water-supply system should not have to collect alms..

"We are guilty of everything"...
— Is this the editorial office?
— What does the lady wish?
— Such a matter — she begins — should long ago have been taken up in the "Zaglembier".. Będzin is after all a Jewish community of several thousand Jewish families without a rabbi — and how are the town taxpayers [?] treated?
— But excuse us, what connection does the matter have with the editorial office?
— Just hear me out, sir.. Why shouldn't a town like this have a moreh hora'ah [rabbinic decisor] on duty from the morning? I — she says — am not one of those "modern" [?] women who are ashamed to ask a she'eilah [ritual question], but it is unheard of that one should have to run around for several hours from one to the next until one finds a moreh hora'ah at home... Is the task of the rabbinate only to officiate during the hours of din-Torah [rabbinic court cases]?
We heard out the complaint and promised what we do...

"Reb Yaakov pays"...
Have you ever been at a celebration in Będzin? For example at a tena'im [engagement], a wedding and the like? Probably yes; but perhaps there are some who have not yet seen the scene — so for them I have the honour of presenting in miniature at least one act of our "kehilla film".
When you enter the home of the host of the celebration, you see in the courtyard or on the stairs certain types in human shape milling about.
At that moment it does not occur to you that these figures are lying in wait for you, more precisely for your pockets. But it doesn't take long and the "veil" is lifted. The door bursts open and people of various ages push in, each holding a slip of paper in his hand and hurrying to the head table [?], in order to grab a plate...
Your "right hand" has begun to move... Done with "Malbish Arumim" [Clothing the Naked], along comes the Talmud Torah, "Hachnasat Kallah" [Dowering Brides], "Menachem Avelim" [Comforting Mourners], "Zokef Kefufim" [Raising the Bowed], and after that a row of hands... hands of shammashim, little hands of "German" cantors, one goes out, the next comes in.. Reb Yankele is "busy": he came to the celebration, and the "bees" give him no peace; he must — they say — "pay" for the roll [bułka] too..
Right next to me sits a Jew from Łódź; he watches the "charity campaign" and then asks:
— The Będzin kehilla, which has a budget of a quarter of a million złoty, permits such ugly beggary? Such lawlessness you don't see in any town or shtetl! Phooey!..
— Perhaps you have an answer to the question?..

My proposal...
— Are you going to the "Cegiel"?
— No, I'm going to the "Aspena" [?].
For Będziners, for the "locals", such a question is nothing strange. Each of us knows that this dialogue refers to the "górki" [hills] that we possess, thank God: an "Aspena" and a "Cegiel" [from cegielnia — brickworks].
In my "conception" the names are not fitting: the "Cegiel" ought to be titled "Aspena", because whoever wants to enjoy that "quiet corner" must open his purse and pay 15 groszy for every living creature...
But that is not what we are after now; it stays the old way again, and we — that is, I, the wife, the children, the mother-in-law and as a "supplement" a "wózek" [pram]... clamber up to the "heights" and then down into the "Cegiel's paradise". Arriving there one "forgets" for a while that we are in smoke-blackened Będzin. We can't believe ourselves that the avenues, the rustle of the trees, the "romantic" walking paths are on our coal soil.
But one thing is missing there — a "kawiarnia" [café], and the wife of a "radny" [town councillor] indeed draws attention to it and appeals to me that we should alert our Magistrat, so that a café with "dancing" be set up on the "Cegiel górka", so that visitors need not drag along parcels of food.
— A very sensible thing; but [?] why indeed shouldn't our Magistrat, which cares so much that the citizens should have "fun", set up a buffet for the "Cegiel" visitors?
I add an amendment to the proposal. Let a few benches also be put up there for the masses from Podzamcze street, so that they need not drag parcels of bedding along with them..

This against that.
And when the festival of Shavuot drew near, the merchants' associations held meetings; at the meetings it was said that one should run to the authorities, so that the authorities take into account that according to the rules of hygiene, health and above all — to take in a few gulden for a livelihood — the shops be allowed to be open for a few hours on Sunday, the eve of Shavuot.
The authority heard out the just request, nodded as a sign of consent and advised submitting the same request also to a second, stronger authority.
The second authority also heard out the request and
— also nodded...
The "sound" of that nodding carried through all the Jewish homes, and the women's faces shone with joy.
— Really very good; a mere trifle — three days! And in such heat? The authority surely has pity on its sheep and takes care that they shouldn't stuff themselves with food that isn't fresh...
Sunday morning — a disappointment! The "guard" is stronger than on the Sundays of the whole year. "Eyes" stare, search, rummage in order to catch smuggled baskets with a bit of greens [?], pieces of meat and perhaps even a few loaves of bread...
— We rejoiced in vain — whisper the frightened women — and we thought... Oh, Master of the Universe, when will the "evil decrees" finally be annulled?
—
A day earlier, i.e. before the Sabbath, the well-known antisemite "Reb" Mach, editor of "Do Czynu" ["To Action"], came to Dąbrowa. It is not enough for him that he poisons the air in his own place [?], in Upper Silesia — he wants to poison the Zagłębie air too with his venomous speeches against Jews, against Jewish merchants, against the citizens who fill the coffers at the tax offices.
The Dąbrowa Jews took fright, and they too ran to the authority — to the very same authority from which the Będzin Jews had requested free permission to shop for the holiday.
But Mach's speeches against Jews are surely not as "serious" as the desecration of Sunday, and — "Mach's mouth they did let open".
In truth this is very "logical": for if Mach's agitation against Jews has its effect, the Jews will in any case not need to ask to be allowed a few hours to trade, to supply themselves with fresh products — after all, the one depends automatically on the other.
— This against that...
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings and remarks on this week's portion (Naso)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings and remarks on this week's portion.
Collected and adapted by Y. L.
Parashat Naso
—o—
a) "By their fathers' houses, by their families" (4:22[?]).
In the previous portion, in counting the sons of Kohath, the verse puts it: "by their families, by their fathers' houses" (see Numbers 4:2), whereas here, with the sons of Gershon, it is written the other way round: "by their fathers' houses, by their families" —
Because the sons of Kohath possessed not only lineage; they themselves were also important people — there was Moses, there was Aaron. Therefore with them "by their fathers' houses" is mentioned later, since ancestral lineage stood in second place for them, a side matter; whereas the sons of Gershon had nothing to boast of but lineage, "their fathers' houses" — therefore with them it is mentioned in first place...
And indeed it was to the sons of Kohath that the Holy of Holies was entrusted, and the Torah mentions them before the sons of Gershon, although Gershon was older than Kohath. —
Machazeh Avraham.
* * *
A certain rabbi of distinguished lineage was bandying words with the well-known scholar and gaon Rabbi Moshe Chefetz; the other reproached him with not being of distinguished descent. Rabbi Moshe said to him:
The verse says: "each one head of his fathers' house." What matters is only the one who begins to found[?] a fathers' house, a lineage. And you see: with you your parents' lineage runs out, and with me a lineage begins... and what more[?]
Peninim Yekarim.
* * *
The Ostrowiec Rebbe, of blessed memory, came from an ordinary family. Once he was sitting in the company of Galician rabbis, most of whom were "grandsons" [scions of dynasties]. The company wanted to needle him, and each began repeating Torah teachings of his grandfathers, until it came to the Ostrowiec Rebbe's turn, and he immediately spoke up sarcastically:
My grandfather was a baker, you know, and he used to say that fresh baking is better than old, pedigreed and mouldy baking..
—o—
b) "And commit a trespass against him" (5:12).
"U-ma'alah" — if his wife betrays him, it is a sign[?] — "bo ma'al", [the fault is] in him, because he is no better either; most likely he is the same sort as she... "A man is provided only according to his deeds."
Be'er Mayim Chayim.
* * *
The Rabbi of Brody's wife complained to him: just see how low we women are in your eyes, that even a wretched wagon-driver praises God "for not having made me a woman." —
He answers her: — Everyone praises only in accordance with his obligation...
Sichat Chulin.
—o—
c) "If any man's wife go aside" (ibid.).
"Sateh" in Hebrew also means to turn away, to go off. And that is indeed the trait of restless[?] women: always running about, never at home..
Rabbi Chaim of Czernowitz.
* * *
The Gemara says that the people of the West [the Land of Israel] used to ask a young man after his wedding: "Matza or motze?" — because about women there are two verses. One: "Whoso findeth (matza) a wife findeth a good thing"; the other: "And I find (motze) more bitter than death the woman." So they ask him which woman, from which verse, he has come upon...
The question has a further sense: with a good woman it is "matza" (past tense) — he found her once (in the Talmud taking a wife is likened to recovering a lost object, the "one of his ribs"..) and that is enough. With a bad woman, on the other hand, it is "motze" (present tense): he must always look for her and find her, because she is always running away from him.... Afikei Yehuda.
—o—
d) "But the former days shall be void" (6:12).
A bitter lot is his, the pious Nazirite: he has already counted twenty-nine days, and one more day and he would have been free — suddenly a relative of his dies, he must defile himself and start counting thirty days afresh. — And why is no such case of sudden death written of a priest — a priest too is enjoined against impurity?—
Because a priest is a wise man, such things do not befall him; whereas the Nazirite is only a pious man who wants to play the saint — and all the misfortunes befall the pious man...
Rabbi Baruch Stimshiner[?].
—o—
e) "The Lord bless thee — the Lord make His face shine upon thee" (6:24, 25).
The Midrash says: "'Bless thee' — with money": may God bless you with money; "'make shine' — with Torah", with Torah, because the Torah is called light: "For the commandment is a lamp and the Torah is light." The question arises: why first bless with wealth and only afterwards with Torah?
Because the rich, who support Torah scholars with their money, take precedence over the scholars themselves. Zebulun comes before Issachar, and therefore the Midrash says on "and keep thee — from the evil inclination": for if the evil inclination lets the wealthy give money for Torah purposes, "bless thee" will come before "make shine"... Beit Shmuel Acharon.
—o—
f) "Nahshon the son of Amminadab" (7:12).
With all the princes without exception the title "prince" is mentioned: "Nethanel the son of Zuar, prince of Issachar", "prince of the children of Zebulun, Eliab the son of Helon", etc.; but with Nahshon the title prince is not mentioned at all.
— Because the self-sacrificing Nahshon, the first of all the tribes to leap heroically into the sea, the most heroic of them all, did not feel in himself at all that he was a prince. Nifla'ot Chadashot.
—o—
Avot, Chapter One.
"On three things the world stands: on the Torah, on the service, and on deeds of lovingkindness" (Mishnah 2).
The Noda BiYehuda [R. Yechezkel Landau, rabbi of Prague] once rebuked the Jews of Prague for giving little charity and doing no acts of kindness. When his words had little effect, he once closed the yeshiva, stopped teaching and went out into the town among the merchants. Everyone is astonished and asks: Rabbi, what is this?
— Have you ever seen a table — he answers — that stands on three legs? If one leg breaks, you prop it up with something and it stands. But if the second leg breaks too, no propping will help any more; you must break off the third leg as well, and then the table will be level. The world is a table standing on three legs: Torah, service, lovingkindness. With the destruction of the Temple one leg was broken: the service. That leg was propped up with a substitute: prayer ("service — this is prayer"). Now, when you break the second leg — lovingkindness — as well, the world-table will surely topple; so I must break off the third leg — Torah — as well, and then the table will be level..
—o—
b) "Let thy house be open wide, and let the poor be members of thy household, and do not talk much with the woman" (Mishnah 5).
The Mishnah means: "do not talk much with the woman" — do not ask your wife whether "the poor shall be members of your household," whether you should bring a guest home, because she won't let you. When there is "do not talk much," there will be "your house open wide"... Sichat Chulin.

Delegation to the President of the Railway Directorate concerning the express trains

This week a delegation consisting of President Michał and the vice-president of the Chamber of Commerce, Mr. Mirowski, called on the President of the Railway Directorate in Warsaw; they conferred with him and handed him a memorandum about the fact that the express (courier) trains do not stop at the local stations.
The President declared that a great injustice had indeed been committed by abolishing the express trains in such a town as Będzin, and he promised to put the mistake right in the nearest future.
A city council resolution annulled

In 1927 the local city council adopted a resolution that there must be no timber yards (składy) in the town. The resolution was later also approved by the voivode.
In spite of this, the deputy mayor, Mr. Rubinlicht, on behalf of the "Merchants' Association", turned to the voivode with a memorandum pointing out how illogical the above-mentioned resolution is.
The voivode sent the matter on to the Ministry of the Interior, which this week informed the Magistrat that the resolution is annulled.
Tuesday — third reading of the budget
As we are informed, a city council meeting will take place next Tuesday, at which the budget for 1930/31 will be determined in the third reading.
Tragic death of a child

In Zagórze a tragic accident occurred which cost the life of a child, a Christian boy aged 16 months.
The child went out of the house and sat down right by the railway (kolejka) line. At that moment a locomotive passed and the child was crushed.
Craftsmen's registration

The Starostwo calls on all craftsmen, members of guilds, and also owners of craft workshops, to report as soon as possible at the Starostwo (room 24) in order to make statements (zeznania) concerning the receipt of the craftsmen's registration certificates from the Chamber of Crafts in Kielce.
Those reporting must have: a craftsman's card, a diploma, and also a proper trade licence (patent).
When it comes to monetary law...

In the local Agudah bank, as is well known, all banking operations are carried out "according to the law" [of the Torah]. Without a heter iska, it goes without saying, not a single transaction is made.
But the bank was "active" in the very best manner this past Shavuot. The sum due on the bills of exchange was indeed taken in by a shikse [a gentile girl], but in a pinch a clerk also did something...
From the "HaShachar" library

Under the chairmanship of Mr. Grojer, the general meeting of the "HaShachar" library took place in its own premises. Mr. Rafael Liwer gives reports on the treasury and the library, and then discussions follow; then the following board is elected: A. Grojer, Rafael Liwer, M. Z. Grossman, Jakub Muszyński, J. Blum, J. Fridman, M. Herszlikowicz.
Stormy outbursts by the unemployed

In front of the premises where the office for distributing relief to the unemployed is located, several hundred workers gathered and, under the influence of agitators, began to storm the office.
The police who arrived, and who were received by the crowd with stones, dispersed the demonstrators.
Lecture by Dr. Nunberg

[Będzin — lecture.] This evening, Saturday night (motzei Shabbat), Dr. Nunberg will give a lecture to the members of "Tse'irei Mishmorei ha-Kholim" (Young Guardians of the Sick) on the subject "The role of the Mishmar (guard) in nursing the sick".
He wanted to do a good deed — and got his "reward for walking"

[Sosnowiec — an evicted old woman.] On Thursday evening Yekhezkel Chmielnicki, finding himself by the house at Kołłątaja 10, saw the old woman N—r lying on the stairs; she had been "evicted" by her own son and grandchildren.
Chmielnicki went into the flat of Mr. Sencer and from there telephoned the police station (komisariat) about the case; police were sent from there, who intervened and saw to it that the old woman was taken back into her son's flat.
When Mr. Chmielnicki came out of the house he received his "sekhar halikhe" (reward for the walk): the N. sons attacked him and "honoured" him in full measure..
The "epilogue" will be played out in court.
—o—
The waterworks — in two months.
[Sosnowiec — water supply.] A conference was held in recent days with the participation of President Wilner and the management of the waterworks. At the conference the director of the waterworks declared that filtered water will be available in two months.
Short of money for expenses, they carried out an attack

[Sosnowiec — district court.] This week the local district court heard the trial of two 16-year-old young Christians, pupils of the state gymnasium in Wilno (Vilna), who several months ago carried out an attack on a woman teacher from Zawiercie.
The indictment against the attackers is as follows:
Between Strzemieszyce and Ząbkowice, a young man entered the second-class compartment in which the teacher Frysztak [?] of Zawiercie was sitting alone, and sat down too.
At Ząbkowice station the teacher wanted to change to the train going to Zawiercie. But at the moment she approached the exit she received a heavy blow to the head. The teacher did not lose consciousness, put up fierce resistance and tore an iron hammer out of the attacker's hands.
The attacker, seeing that the "experiment" had not succeeded, jumped off the train.
The alerted police at once searched the train, and a young man without a ticket was arrested.
Under interrogation the detainee admitted that the attack had been carried out by his companion, who had fled to Kraków.
It did not take long before the second "bird" was caught, and this week both stood before the local district court.
The accused stated that they had earlier taken 650 złoty from their parents in Wilno and had gone off to "have a good time" in the world.
Their first visit was to Warsaw, then to Zagłębie and Upper Silesia, and since they no longer had money for the journey back to Wilno, they planned to carry out an attack on the train.
The court took into account the circumstances of the attack and sentenced each to six months in prison.
Public appearance of the poet Moshe Stavsky

[Sosnowiec — literary evening.] This Saturday at 8:30 in the evening, the popular Jewish poet Moshe Stavsky from Eretz Israel will read his best works in Yiddish at the "Sala Angielski", Warszawska 22 (in the house of Mr. Priwer [?]).
The interest the poet has aroused in town assures the evening of great success.
Besides the poet's recitations, there will be living pictures (tableaux vivants) of the life of the halutzim in Eretz Israel, singing and declamations performed by the members of "Hashomer Hatzair".
"The whole world is going under"... So says President Wilner

[Sosnowiec — city council.] At the Saturday session of the local city council the new municipal budget for 1930 was on the agenda. Before the matter is taken up, President Wilner delivers an exposé in which he describes the situation of the whole country and of Sosnowiec in particular. It will not be long — says the president — before industry comes to a standstill, trade dies out and the sequestrators (bailiffs) are left without work..
From the Chamber of Commerce

[Sosnowiec — Chamber of Commerce.] We have been asked to announce that the Chamber of Commerce is already accepting applications for importing foreign goods for the 3rd quarter of 1930.
The deadline for submitting the applications expires on the 17th of this month.
The Chamber of Commerce reminds at the same time that applications for the 3rd quarter submitted after the above-mentioned deadline will be considered only if a quota (contingent) reserve remains.
Official announcement on the decision of the State Tribunal

[Sosnowiec — rabbinical elections.] The chairman of the kehilla council has received the verdict of the State Tribunal concerning the rabbinical elections in our town.
The main reason for which the elections were annulled is the monetary agreement between certain parties.
A protest meeting

[Sosnowiec — protest meeting.] On the night after Shavuot a grand protest meeting was held in the courtyard of Mr. Abramczyk, Modrzejowska [?] Street, organised by the committee of the League for Labour Palestine in Sosnowiec. Speeches were given by: Gancwajch, Goldberg, Chlebowicki, Kaner and Kerner. Sharp resolutions were adopted concerning the Colonial Office, and a greeting was sent to the workers of Eretz Israel.
The protest resolution was sent to Geneva immediately after the meeting.
—o—
When the power fails...
[Sosnowiec — power cut.] On Tuesday at about 10 o'clock in the morning the electric power was cut off on the entire tram line. The interruption lasted half an hour.
—o—
A Balfour campaign.
[Sosnowiec — Keren Kayemet.] The local Keren Kayemet (JNF) committee is undertaking a campaign to inscribe Balfour in the "Golden Book".
Dąbrowa — A Lecture by the Editor of “Do Czynu”

[Dąbrowa — antisemitism.] Last Saturday the well-known Jew-hater Man, editor of the antisemitic gutter sheet “Do Czynu”, was here and gave a lecture on “The Jewish Flood in Poland”.
Because such a lecture could have provoked serious consequences for the local Jewish population, the town councillors Messrs. Stuszegowski, Rechnic and Puterka went to the starosta, Mr. Baksa, and drew his attention to the fact that such a lecture was undesirable.
The starosta declared that he had not known about the lecture. “I will order,” he said, “that a reinforced police guard be posted, but I can promise you that no more such meetings will be held in the Będzin district.”
At the same time the delegation raised the request that shops selling basic necessities be allowed to be open every Sunday for 2 hours in the morning.
To this the starosta replied that permitting shops to open on Sunday is against the Sunday-rest law.
—o—
Unemployed Rob a Jewish Shop.
On Friday a crowd of unemployed gathered in front of the magistrate, demanding relief. From there the workers fell upon the shop of Abrahamcze Bajtner, where they plundered several dozen loaves of bread and seized the day’s takings, amounting to some twenty-odd złoty.
The main culprits have been arrested.
Obtained a “Discount”..

[Dąbrowa — Zionism; town council.] The committee of the local Zionist Organization applied to the town council with the request that the Zionist premises be exempted from the housing tax.
Thanks to the advocacy of Councillor Rechnic on the budget committee and of the PPS councillors at the plenary session of the town council, the motion was adopted.
—o—
A Cat — a Glutton and a Drunkard.
On Sunday evening the cat of the A—k family sniffed out the place where the freshly baked cheesecake for Shavuot was kept, and while the household was sound asleep the cat ate up the cheesecake...
At the break of dawn, when they saw what the “glutton and drunkard” had done, the house went dark before their eyes, and in revenge they gave the gobbler a thorough “removal” and threw her out half-dead into the street.
This was seen by some Christian young men, who reported it to the society for the prevention of cruelty to animals (“Tza’ar Ba’alei Chayim”), and a police report was drawn up against the beaters.
Strzemieszyce — A Protest Meeting

[Strzemieszyce — Zionism; immigration.] On Wednesday the local Zionist Organization held, in the “Iluzjon” cinema hall, a grand protest meeting against the latest restriction on immigration to Eretz Israel for the pioneering (halutz) youth.
The meeting was opened by the chairman of the Zionist Organization, Mr. Dov Glikstein, and the chair was handed over to Dr. Eliezer Chazanowicz. Messrs. Klarman and Pilc appeared with successful speeches. Afterwards an appropriate protest resolution was adopted unanimously by the large assembled audience.
—o—
An Accident.
On Thursday a cyclist ran over twelve-year-old Shmuel Federman and broke his leg,

Budget of the town of Będzin — adopted in the third reading

[Będzin — municipality; budget.] At Wednesday's session of the Będzin town council, chaired by vice-president [?] Sz. Fürstenberg, the dubious [?] municipal budget was adopted in the third reading.
The motions: 1) of councillor Lewin, that the Jewish Benevolent Association and the tenants' (lokatorzy) association should each receive up to 1000 zł for the benefit of evicted [?] families; 2) of Dr Rechtman, that the „Talmud Torah“ should receive a subsidy of 500 zł; 3) of councillor Ehrlich, that the Jewish heders should be subsidised with 10,000 zł — were adopted.
For the subsidy to the Jewish heders the clause was inserted that only those heders may receive it in which secular studies have been introduced according to the curriculum of the public elementary schools.
When the balanced [?] budget was being settled, President Michel had the wish to „bless“ the population with the investment tax.
The arguments of councillor Gitler, however, convinced [the council] that the merchants are already gasping enough under the burden of taxes, and the motion for an investment tax was rejected.
—o—
Report of the general meeting of the Będzin Artisans' Association
[Będzin — artisans.] In the presence of about 350 members the chairman, Mr Grossman, opens the meeting, and after passing on greetings to all members from Mr Goldstein [?], who is now staying in Köln am Rhein (Cologne), he informs the meeting of the agenda.
On item 1, the illegal workshops, a discussion develops in which a large number of members take part. The speakers describe the situation of the artisans, who fall victim to competition from the illegal workshops: apprentices who have worked a short time with a master set up [?] their own workshops and there undermine the livelihood of the older artisans.
As a result of the discussion the board is called upon to take energetic steps to regulate this painful [?] question.
Item 2: the director of the Artisans' Association, Mr Kleinman, reads out a circular from the Starostwo (district office) stating that, in order to create a register of artisans for the Chamber of Crafts, all artisans are called upon to register.
After a discussion in which Hofman, Kleinman, Frajlich and Blachowicz [?] take part, it is decided to send a delegation of the guild elders to the Starostwo, so that the registration should take place through the guilds.
Item 3: the new project for increasing [?] the revenues of the Chamber of Crafts is read out [?]. According to the project every artisan will have to pay: 25 zł a year per workshop, 12 zł a year per journeyman, 6 zł a year per apprentice.
On the motion of Mr Klejman [sic; probably Kleinman] it is decided to send the Chamber of Crafts a protest resolution against burdening the poor artisan with new taxes.
Regarding tax matters the following is announced:
1) On the basis of a ruling of the Supreme Court the Ministry of Finance has issued a circular stating that artisans who employ only one assistant are exempt from buying trade licences (patents).
2) Master-owners of workshops are not counted in the number of employed workers.
3) Artisans who produce articles of prime necessity pay only 1% of turnover.
After several important regulations were read out, the meeting is closed.
Examinations for artisans and journeymen

[Sosnowiec — artisans.] In connection with the fact that the examinations for masters and journeymen are due to begin in the next few days, a conference will take place next Sunday, the 15th of this month, at the Sosnowiec Artisans' Association, at which very important questions concerning the „examination decree“ will be discussed.
—o—
The kehilla receives the nominations of the new members of the Będzin kehilla board
[Będzin — kehilla.] Yesterday afternoon the Będzin kehilla board received notice from the Starostwo (district office) that Messrs Abraham Liwer, Lejbisz Buchwajc [?], Hersz Goldsztajn and Majer Szenwald are nominated as members of the kehilla board in Będzin.
—o—
Great protest demonstrations of Zagłębie Jewry against the immigration decree
[Będzin and Sosnowiec — Palestine; aliyah.] Jewish Będzin and Sosnowiec yesterday evening expressed their deepest anger against the British power, which has stopped the immigration (aliyah) of the halutzim to Eretz Israel.
In Będzin the demonstration formed in the courtyard of the Szajn brothers. The large courtyard was full of all strata of the Jewish population, besides the organisations „Hashomer“, „Betar“, „HaPaCh“ [?], „Gordonia“, Poale Zion, „Tzeirei Mizrachi“ and „Poalei Emunei Israel“ with their banners at their head.
All Jewish shops were closed at 6 o'clock.
In the name of the united committee Mr Hofer [?] opens the meeting. Speeches against the immigration decree are delivered by: Abraham Liwer, Józef Lew (Lado [?]) and Pilc (Mizrachi).
The mass procession marched to the synagogue, where Cantor Żutowicz [?] recited „El Male Rahamim“ for the martyrs of Eretz Israel and sang a chapter of Psalms.
—o—
June and July — only 1 percent
[Sosnowiec — municipality; taxes.] The Sosnowiec town administration has decided that on overdue (zaległe) municipal taxes paid in June and July a penalty of only 1 percent will be charged.
After that deadline the percentage will be raised.

The Knife in the Back of Our Last Hope

[Article — protest against Britain (restriction of immigration).]
(In connection with yesterday's protest demonstrations.)
Beneath the great, noisy, tumultuous space of the world, from end to end, over all our most distant dispersions, there rolls a wretched, wild and wrathful[?] cry of protest — the cry of the most tormented, most afflicted people, against whom a sword has been raised over its last, only hope. A cry against human wickedness, the brutality of nations and the falseness of rulers.
Since most ancient times we have been reproached with being enemies of mankind, and that this is why we shut ourselves up behind ghetto walls — because we hate the world, because we go about the world with torches in order to subjugate it.
Yes, we have not the slightest trust in the world. But this mistrust, this disbelief in the world's honesty and justice does not spring from our own essential being, but because no one as much as we has come face to face with human hypocrisy, with human thirst [for blood]. On our back the ugliest human instincts have been played out; with eyes flooded with blood we have seen the beast in man.
And what is taking place at the present terrible moment, if not an act of the worst human cruelty and baseness?
For thousands of years we lived shut up within ourselves, huddled[?] in our own narrow domain, cherishing our messianic dreams. In the deepest silence we nurtured them; we did not want to carry them out into the world, because we knew that we would be met with nothing but mockery and shame. We knew that the weak one still has no one to turn to for help and support. Thousands of years flowed by, and quietly, modestly we cherished our dream of redemption. But then a time came when the edifice of the world [printed "veltbgin"] was shaken, and we thought that with it the world's conscience had awakened. In our naivety we believed that the nations wished to atone for their thousand-year guilt, that Great Britain truly wished to take upon itself the mission of honour; and, like people starved for the least act of justice from the world, we threw ourselves body and soul into the arms of the [?"bigl"] sympathizing people, and delivered to it the whole abundance of faith we had stored up. And like a blind lover we overlooked — more correctly, pretended to overlook — the symptoms of betrayal beneath us. We did not want to see them, because it is too terrible, too horrifying for such a starved, blind faith to become convinced once again of the world's base falseness. But the most cruel of the cruel has come. The hand into which we entrusted so much devotion and faith has plunged a knife into our last and only hope; the life-blood spurts hot and sharp over the foreheads of the treacherous hangmen, and the hangman — our "friend" of yesterday — stands and mocks cynically, perfidiously[?], and will not let the knife out. And one is still cynical enough to console and cheer up the stabbed one while the knife is stuck in and the blood spurts.
All, all the nations of the world have our bloodstains on their conscience. Countless thousands of Jewish souls split the Ukrainian heavens. Thousands upon thousands of Jews breathed out their last breath on the Spanish pyres and autos-da-fé. There is not an ell of earth that does not cover Jewish blood. But Great Britain is committing the most terrible pogrom in Jewish history, the greatest and cruellest, because it is a pogrom on the whole Jewish people at once, a pogrom on the Jewish soul, a pogrom on the last hope of Israel.
We are used to keeping silent when the pogrom sword hangs over our necks. Quietly, with sealed lips, we perished for the sanctification of the Name. But now we cry out so loudly, now we protest so mightily, because we feel that now the thousand-year struggle of Israel with its fate is coming to its end. We have been sinking and sinking for thousands of years, and lo, we saw a plank of rescue and grabbed hold of it. And now we are brutally pushed off it. We know that if, God forbid, we lose now, we are eternally lost, doomed. The last act of the great tragedy is taking place: Israel and its fate — shall we remain the vanquished? Shall we perish for good? Is it possible? — Great God[?]!
To whom do we protest? To whom do we cry? Do we demand justice of the world? Do we cry to the conscience of Great Britain? No, and a thousand times no! Reflect on Israel's path through life and you will see that the world has no conscience, there is no justice, there is no righteousness among the nations — none!
Our martyrs, when they perished under the hand of the world's cruelty, did not bear on their lips the call "Shim'u amim", "Hear, ye nations!" — as martyrs of other peoples appealed to the conscience of the world. Our martyrs, rather, cried "Shema Yisrael!" — "Hear, O Israel!" We knew that the nations would not hear us, that it is in vain to cry to them; it was to Israel, to ourselves, that we cried. And now too we do not protest to the conscienceless world — that would have been a profanation [printed "farshverung", an abjuration/oath] — but we cry loud and bitter:
— Shema Yisrael!
A. Safir.

Tragic death of 2 young people.
In Oświęcim on Sunday evening the following terrible tragedy occurred: the journeyman baker Abraham Jedur [?] of Katowice fell in love with 21-year-old Chaja Brauger [?], daughter of the well-known Oświęcim merchant Szymon Brauger.
The father, on learning of the love, declared that as long as he lived he would not allow his son-in-law to be a journeyman baker. On Sunday evening, when the enamoured Abraham wanted to see his bride, the girl's parents would not let him into the house.
This affected young Abraham so much that he went straight to the railway station and threw himself under a train, which crushed him.
When his beloved Chaja learned of it, she drank a large dose of acid ["essence"] and died on the way to hospital.
The funeral of the loving couple, whom cold death united, took place on Tuesday.

International swindler punished.
In 1928 the firm Blum & Reichel of Katowice sent [?] a certain firm in Lagren [?] 4 wagons of eggs for 75 thousand zł. The sum was placed as a letter of credit at the German Bank in Katowice.
Some time later a person presented himself at the German Bank, introducing himself as a delegate of the firm Blum & Reichel, and by means of various forged documents he had the above-mentioned sum paid out to him.
The firm later reported the swindle to the police, which opened an investigation, and suspicion fell on a certain Glicksman.
The accused stood this week before the Katowice district court, which sentenced Glicksman to 2 years in prison.

District Conference of "Hitachdut" in Będzin

[Będzin — Zionism; workers' parties.]
To the Zagłębie district conference of the Zionist labour party "Hitachdut", which took place on Monday in Będzin, came over 30 delegates from 10 towns and 150 guests from the surrounding region.
The conference is opened by Mr. Motek Haspel with a Hebrew speech, in which he discusses the worst hour in Zionism. The speaker protests most sharply against the immigration decree and calls on the delegates to rally around the national banner of liberation of working Eretz Israel.
After the opening speech a presidium is elected, which includes Messrs. Dr. Rechtman, Szpajzer (Będzin), Fiszel, Igtraligater [?] (Sosnowiec), Strauss (Częstochowa) and Rapaport (Pilica).
The general secretary of "Hitachdut" in Congress Poland, Mr. Josef Lewi (Łódź), then lectures on the subject "The state of Zionism at the present moment". In a fine 3-hour lecture the speaker illuminates the development from the sad August events up to the latest "passpil" [?] decree, the closing of the gates [?] to halutzim; the speaker strongly censures the "minimalists" of "Brit Shalom" and the "maximalists" of "Brit Trumpeldor", who have tendencies dangerous to the upbuilding of Eretz Israel. Despite all the decrees and difficulties — Mr. Lewi concludes his interesting and learned lecture — we say: aloh na'aleh ["we shall surely go up"].
At the second, afternoon session the member of the central committee of "Hitachdut" Mr. Gedalyahu Geller [?] (Kvutzat Tzrifin [?], Eretz Israel) lectures on the economic conquests of the Jewish Eretz-Israeli worker, "HeHalutz", hachshara, aliyah and youth problems. The third lecture, by Mr. Lewi, is devoted to the state of "Hitachdut" in the whole world and particularly in Poland.
At the third and last session a lively discussion develops over the lectures given. Messrs. Lewi and Geller reply to the discussants. Then various resolutions are adopted unanimously, among them a protest resolution against the English government because of the immigration decree and a protest resolution against "Brit Trumpeldor" because of their irresponsible deeds in Kfar Saba.
With "Hatikvah" the district conference is closed.

Economic Obligations (Summer in Zagłębie and in the Country. — How Can Life in Town Be Made Easier?) / From the Keren Kayemet, Sosnowiec

[Zagłębie — municipality, city services and summer living conditions; article. Followed by a news item: Sosnowiec — Keren Kayemet.]
It is summer, it is hot, it fries and it roasts, and the air in town is stifling to the point of being unbearable.
Summer is a delight in the country: there the sun caresses so that it is a pleasure, and the shade cools people and breathes into them a fresh spirit of life and courage for the future. Exactly the opposite is the same thing in town: here the sun is a hell, it bakes and scorches and one cannot hide from it, because there is no cool place where one could rest; there are no trees under which one could stretch out [?] and rest, and where a refreshing little breeze might come and stroke the body and the exhausted bones.
It is therefore no wonder at all that people emigrate out of the town into the country as soon as summer comes. Above all from our hot and stifling Zagłębie: the big people, never mind, but also the middling ones, those who have just enough to get through the day somehow and are not tied economically and financially to the town, run away from it, avoid it, so that at first glance it seems that all of Zagłębie is in the villages. That, however, is far from the case. In town remain all those who have no other choice; there remain those who are tied to their little shops and workshops in town and cannot tear themselves away from them even for a single minute.
And today, after all, is not like the old days: the human machine is weaker, more sensitive. Humanity is sick and broken and cannot endure what our old grandfathers endured. Incidentally, the town air was once not as polluted as today; there were not so many factories from whose chimneys so much smoke billowed [?]; motor traffic did not exist at all, and so the air was not so stifling.
After all, we now live in a completely different period; the whole environment is different, harder, and this has acted on humanity powerfully and with lightning speed; moreover, the whole round of life has become harder, and duties have grown enormously greater and more responsible.
That is why in the modern and civilised countries the fashion of building garden cities was born long ago, i.e. towns that lie within gardens; on all sides one sees trees, gardens, plantings, everything is wrapped in greenery, and one can barely make out the houses and streets. Life in such towns is very comfortable, the air is good, nature is cleaner, and at the same time one is at home and enjoys the attractive life of the town.
Here in Poland too the town has begun to take on a different look; here too one tries to introduce as much greenery as possible, as much shade and as many trees and flowers as possible, but unfortunately it is done so clumsily, so unaesthetically, so ill-planned, that it is often disgusting to the point of losing one's patience.
First of all, nobody is ever in a hurry; apparently one is never late for anything.
How long has there been talk in Będzin about a park, how long has there been talk that the "Górka" should be accessible to everyone! But it has gone no further than talk; people talk from year to year, from summer to summer, and leave it at that — there is still no garden, and no park is to be seen either.
True, some order has been brought to the Górka; it looks more respectable, and here we have the best proof of what can be achieved when there is good will. But what is the result? Access to it is only for a select few, because firstly one must pay every time one enters, and secondly it is too small. Of course it could be enlarged considerably by adding the open "Górka". That, however, is a very complicated matter, and who knows whether it could have been managed. But freeing the entrance is surely possible: let the magistrat [municipality] rent for the summer the one and only park we possess, so that entry is free to everyone who wants to rest.
Surely a municipal self-government may have some kind of duty toward its citizens at a time when the citizens have so many obligations toward the town. At least this much can be done, and then it will know that it has given something to its citizens who remain in town the whole summer. What it would pay for renting [the park] from the Polish "Dobroczynność" [the charity society] it could recover from the income that an elegantly furnished milk bar (milk hall) would bring in.
Once one administers a town, one must after all take into account the citizens who stay at home the whole summer. One must therefore see to making their life easier — which, incidentally, can be done to a very large extent with good will.
And one more thing: no effort at all is made to repair things; one barely starts doing something and nothing gets finished. Take Będzin, where a monument to the Unknown Soldier is being made on 3 May Square. Work has been going on there like this for the second year now — or rather, no work is going on, and the place has been fenced off like this for half a year now, since nothing is being done. One asks: why does it stand like this, neither here nor there? Could it not have been finished long ago, so that the square would not be in such disorder and in such a dusty state? And in general the square there always looks unheard-of disorderly: always dust and sand and stones. When one undertakes something one must not forget that this is in town. Let it be done in one-two! It does, after all, spoil the town's order and aesthetics.
The same goes for the pavements and the cobbled roadways. Everything is constantly rebuilt and re-cobbled, and so we always have pits and holes in almost all the streets of the town, and nobody hurries to put all this in order either, so that this too raises dust and brings various quarters of the town into disorder.
Now, when it rains, Modrzejowska [?] Street is flooded, and on Małachowskiego Street, opposite 3 May Square, one has to cross the water in boats. Can this be left like this? Why does it stay like this from year to year?
Why is it that if a house owner does not observe the proper regulations he is punished at once, whereas nobody is held responsible for the public disorders, especially when they cause harm to the citizens? It disrupts communications, the tram traffic is held up from time to time, and it obstructs the passage of the citizens.
If a house owner is responsible for not complying with the proper regulations, then surely one must be even more responsible for not maintaining proper order in the streets.
One must after all finally come to the conviction that the streets must be beautified and improved and the town must be in a hygienic condition.
For all this one must start taking proper care right now.
R. Les.
