Our Panorama

[Zagłębie — weekly feuilleton.] By Ben Amotz.

(Shavuot happenings. — An old society with new quarrels. — Blessings turn into curses. — Possession prevails. — Benches with magnetic powers. — May a maid[?] sleep where people pray?)

Even if "all the rivers turned to ink", it would still "be too little" to describe the "happenings" of the past Shavuot. I swear to you by my kittel and tallit that the "League of Nations", which holds its assemblies in Geneva, surely never receives such "heart-rending reports" from the little states that live by its grace.
Reports that do not "qualify" to be counted in the first rank — for example, that a kehilla president is squeamish about gelila [the honour of rolling the Torah scroll] and, when he is honoured with it, says:
— "Giv paiade"[?]... or the story of how the mikveh money was confiscated — these we will mention only for form's sake, so that such "lofty matters" are not forgotten. Important are only the happenings that are "adorned" with blows, police and the like.
We shall make the "poczatek" [Polish początek — the beginning] with the Będzin Chevra Nos'ei [the pallbearers' society]. A society — an old one; the top place is its due. In the society a split has occurred: the camp of the "nos'im" [bearers] has split apart and is divided into two camps, into two groups. Each group has its own chairman and also — a beer-tavern, where the plans of internal policy are worked out...
Over a glass of drink, plans are worked out for how to seize the amud [prayer-leader's lectern] early in the morning, so that by the time the "hostile" camp arrives there will be no "trace" left of prayer in general and... of Kiddush in particular.
And when both "forces" meet, the blow-up comes — it "carries everyone into the air", just like real bearers...
There are also "neutral" ones among them, those who cannot drink much and long for rest, for peace. They, the neutrals, come to the editorial office with a request that we "react", so that in this society, which has such a "rich past" and is one of the first "chishe"[?] societies, no quarrels should occur, and that the same should happen as with Jacob, when all the stones became one stone — and here all the members of the society should "receive one heart"
— a heart of peace...
———
In the Sosnowiec beit midrash a fire has flared up because of — guess what?
— Because of blessings... literally: the worshippers of the beit midrash will not allow R' Leibishl to say the blessings aloud.
For ten years now R' Leibishl has been saying the blessings every day, and the congregation answered Amen after him.
But Satan, out of great sorrow, acted as accuser and worked deeds so that R' Leibishl's blessings, which "awakened" the gates of mercy, should be said in a whisper, quietly, so that they would no longer have the power they have had until now..
And Satan prevailed. A "heavenly voice" went out that R' Leibishl is on England's side... he is hatching secret plans with the blessings.. therefore he must say the blessings quietly, so that nobody hears and nobody answers Amen...
But R' Leibishl, the holder of the established right [chazaka], will, God forbid, not have his mouth shut. "Let heads fly," he says, "I will not stop saying the blessings aloud."
Both sides are "gnashing their teeth" and refuse to accept even the compromise that the gabbai proposed, namely that "the blessings be said at another table". In short, the air in the Sosnowiec beit midrash smells of gunpowder
— all because of the blessings...
———
The "krastfirentsye"[?] [apparently a mocking distortion of "conference"] from Strzemieszyce tells us about "the troubles of suffering" that the members there have from the cooperative bank. In the bank there are — so they say — little benches with a tremendous[?] magnetic force: hardly does someone sit down on such a bench than he can no longer be torn away from it.
How great this magnetic force is — [?] to render word for word the further part of the "krasfirentsye", which we crown as the "Strzemieszyce poem".
So then, the "poet" has the floor!
"As soon as the possessed[?] caught the scent,
They grabbed the benches straight away,
At the elections made a scandal,
They came with rubber truncheons and sticks,
To give everyone a sniff on the nose,
On the 13th of May this came to pass,
The shoemaker sat sprawled on the president's chair,
With the two council members at his side,
In the pockets — in one, bottles,
Printed ballot slips in the bags,
The members began to protest,
The elected ones with weapons began to rule,
At once they grabbed each other by head and neck,
And everything turned into one heap,
There arose one great outcry,
And the police were called,
The police stood on guard.
And the chairman did a 'vayivrach' [took to flight]...
The ruler called the vote,
And only the board with their relatives voted,
And the members were left under the 'oybes'[?],
The rulers won with the carters,
They will indeed keep driving the horses on,
Because for them this has great value."
Thus far — here the horses stop, and from the wagon climbs down the "poet", who declaims[?] that "the whole world should learn of the May upheaval in... Strzemieszyce".
———
In the "happenings" in Dańdówka carters also take part, only without rhyme...
In the holy community of Dańdówka the artisans together with the carters organised a minyan at one of their fellows' homes, and they prayed "as God commanded".
The "idyll" did not last long. One carter wanted to "drive" faster, the artisans shouted "Back!" — one word led to another, they started to "box", and the owner of the minyan-room had his say:
— Stop! Enough praying! Out!
And when the artisans came to pray, they saw how the premises had suddenly been turned into a "hotel"... (our correspondent swears by his wife and children that in[?] one bed a "sakher"[?] was sleeping...)
The indignant worshippers came with a policeman, who declared that "there is no such law that would not permit a 'sakher' to sleep where people pray"...
So the congregation brought, as the deciding authority, the senior przodownik [police sergeant], who made a search of the bed and found lying there the owner of the apartment.
— What is this? — asks the przodownik.
— I'm sick, panie przodowniku [Mr Sergeant]!
— No, your lordship — the worshippers shouted — he is not sick, and the proof: he is sleeping in his trousers...
— Panowie [Gentlemen]! — As a przodownik I know of no such ustawa [law] that one may not sleep in trousers; I can't help at all...
When the artisans saw that with the "button"[?] [the policeman] they would achieve nothing, they, as true artisans, took to "physical work". In the blink of an eye the bed with the sick man in his trousers was standing in the street.
The "sick man" raised the alarm for help, and a real war broke out.
The end was that "the 'sick' shoemaker in his trousers came out the victor"...
Ben Amotz.
The Voice of the Fortress

[Palestine — Mandate policy; protest article on the halting of immigration.]
Shabtai Weiss (Jerusalem)
We, the Jewish Yishuv in Eretz Israel, are likened in these days to a besieged fortress — „none went out and none came in“. English policy has hung locks on the gates of Eretz Israel, has stopped the stream of aliyah. And from the fortress, the last fortress of the Jewish people, the Masada of today's generation, the mighty voice of the Jewish Yishuv now resounds — resounds in silence. From Dan to Beersheba the Jewish Yishuv has stopped its work and gives protesting expression to its bitterness and its protest against the closing of aliyah. From the extreme-right „Agudath Israel“, which announced in special proclamations that it joins the Yishuv's „Shabbaton“, to the left-wing „Poalei Zion“ — all, all circles of Jewish Eretz Israel have today, as if at the signal of a magic wand, cast aside their work and business with a festive religious sanctity, in order to express their grief and anger at the decree of the English Colonial Office.
And the police representatives of Albion, who now shine with their numerous presence in every corner of the city, are witnesses to the grandiose double phenomenon — that we were born here in this land, and what we signify here for this land: in this land we were born a PEOPLE, and we are the breath of life of this land. And the representatives of Albion probably also hear the mighty voice that resounds out of the silence of the Jewish Yishuv: no weapon formed against us shall prosper!
*
For more than twelve years, from General Bols to Governor Storrs, and from the latter to Luke, English policy held the Balfour Declaration on the scales. For more than twelve years English policy played, with its solemn undertaking to build the Jewish home in Eretz Israel — which received an international stamp and was signed by 52 states — a devil's game of „balance“. At first they spoke of „balance“ in a supposed half-voice and with modest bashfulness. „Of course we must and want to help build the Jewish home“ — English policy stammered to us then, „but you are hot-blooded and we are slowish, unhurried; „go slowly“ — that is our way“. And when years had passed, in the course of which one could, even with English slowness, have managed to do something for the realisation of the Jewish home — they adopted a new method; they began to speak openly about „balance“. „Of course we must and want to help build the Jewish home — but... we surely cannot provoke the Arabs“. And so year in, year out they hurled us in the sling of „balance“. When bloody attacks were made on us by an organised hand — „wait, we are sending a commission of inquiry“, the Janus-mouth of English policy told us then. The commission of inquiry — that was our „success“ after the massacres in Hebron and Safed. The commission of inquiry comes back to London with a report in which falsehood competes with hypocrisy — MacDonald makes a statement in Parliament, on the third of April, that the international obligation will be carried out. The negotiations with the Arab delegation were broken off — so the Jewish aliyah must be closed. And here comes the „statement“ of the English Colonial Office, which brings the whole matter into a third stage: an end is made of the „balance“, the scale is allowed to tip entirely to the Arab side, and all means begin to be mobilised to protect the Arabs from the „danger“ that threatens them from the rain of capital and energy and enterprise and modern working methods which Jews have brought to this land — aliyah is closed; a special envoy is sent, who is to strive [?] to find a supposedly scientific, objective seal of approval for the plans of assault that were prepared against Jewish aliyah and against Jewish land purchase in Eretz Israel.
*
There is no bad without some good, and we ought to be satisfied with the brutal faithlessness on which English policy has finally resolved. We ought to be grateful to the English Colonial Office, which in its latest „statement“ has given us an „Ariadne's thread“ that leads us with sure steps through the tangle of its Palestine policy. This „statement“ of Lord Passfield speaks in plain language: we did not give the Balfour Declaration for the sake of the Jews' pretty eyes, but because we were engaged in a hard war and wanted to win over all factors that could help us to our victory; we then needed the help of America, where the Jews have a certain influence — and we gave them a Balfour Declaration. Now, after twelve years, we have already forgotten the war and its consequences — and we now stand in another war, which is called India. There the Jews have no influence, whereas the Arabs can be useful to us there — and so we turn the shaft [i.e. we change direction].
From this sharp, brutal turn in English policy we must draw the proper conclusions. We too must put an end to the policy of hesitation and wavering, covering up [?] and hushing up, that we have pursued in recent years. The Shabbaton of the Jewish Yishuv in Eretz Israel must be the signal for a mighty political opposition, which we must now conduct with vigour in every country where there is but a Jewish community.
We must raise a cry of woe against the policy of falsehood and robbery that they want to apply against us. And this weapon of ours has more than once already proven sharp and effective. Under a concentrated attack of the Jewish people in all the lands of its dispersion and from all the positions it holds in finance, trade, science, the press and politics — the decrees with which England wants to strangle the building of the Jewish home in Eretz Israel will have to fall.
And the second way — the uninterrupted strengthening of the work of construction, which is now in the very midst of its development. If England has closed aliyah — long live the intensified aliyah, which forces its way into Eretz Israel by all sorts of roads and byways. If England now plans an assault on Jewish land purchase — let all the forces of the people be strained to redeem the land on a scale that we have not been able to until now.
Only a few weeks ago we drew up in Eretz Israel a ten-year balance, and established the tremendous victory of our work — despite all disturbances and stumblings. In the first 40 years of our colonisation work (from the eighties of the past century to the year 1920) we created 23 colonies in the land; in the last ten years we created 80 new colonies. In the first forty years we redeemed 11 thousand dunams of land each year; in the last ten years we redeemed 76 thousand dunams of land each year. And this growth of our work, this strengthening of its foundations, makes possible an even greater absorption of immigrants in the coming years. This we must now exploit with impetus and fervour. That is the command of the latest decree, and that is the memento of the decrees that still hang in the air. It is a time of trouble for Jacob — and out of it he shall be saved!
24 Iyar 5690 — the day of the protest Shabbaton.
I'm a Free Bird.

(Monologue of a Jew who has been freed from wife-exile.)
Gentlemen, Jews, why are you sleeping? Let's be lively! Dance along with me, rejoice in my joy — for when one rejoices at other people's celebrations, one lives to see celebrations of one's own.
Happy is an exiled people that, after years of oppression, is freed from its conquerors. Happier still is a man who, after years of enslavement, is freed from wife-exile; and now here I stand before you — the eternal slave, the eternal martyr — freed, redeemed, independent, and together with all the freed and redeemed I proclaim:
Long live freedom!
Down with enslavement!
Long live independence!
Down with wife-exile!
What, you know nothing of my joy? You don't know what luck has befallen me? Luck has befallen me that comes only once a year — my wife is already on the other side of the rogatka [the city toll-gate].
And perhaps you think she went off somewhere to a dacha behind the stove[?], to Bystra or to Rajcza, so that every Monday and Thursday she could come to Będzin to give me a "niespodzianka" [surprise] and catch me "na gorącym uczynku" [red-handed]? This time she went far — to Ciechocinek she went; the doctors determined[?] that this year my wife "konieczne" [absolutely] must have — mud...
And what won't one do for a wife; for one's own wife even mud is not too dear...
Learning that my wife needs mud, I spoke up to her: Yenteshi, my crown, maybe you'd rather go abroad? Foreign passports are cheap. Rather than crawl into some Polish mud, better crawl into German mud; German mud is, after all, not Polish — German mud has quite another taste; you remember, after all, that the German baked bread out of mud.. True, Poland has enough mud too: money is mud, all Jewish livelihoods have turned to mud, the Sejm is held on a par with mud, the Sanacja too has sunk into mud. Yes, Poland really has enough mud too; nevertheless I would like, I say, for you to sink rather into German mud — German mud has quite another taste...
So I said to her, but what I meant was something else entirely. What I meant was that she should be as far away as possible — that she be in Germany and I in Będzin; then I'd feel "pewniejszy" [safer], I wouldn't have to have any palpitations.. that I could "skorzystać" [take advantage] of my wife's absence as God commanded, that my soul wouldn't leave me in fright at every ring at the door, that I wouldn't have to be ready to hide the "contraband" in the cupboard..
She really would have gone abroad, but the trouble is that she is a strong supporter of home production. Since the campaign for home production began she has become a fierce "patriotka". Whatever smells of abroad is treyf. She no longer uses Turkish pepper, she doesn't rub herself with French turpentine, she doesn't drink Wiener Trank [a laxative tea] or Karlsbad salt. She doesn't eat Swiss cheese, doesn't drink Chinese tea or Hungarian wine, she no longer catches the Spanish flu, she doesn't wear shoes with American toes. Everything that smells of abroad is treyf. Of the only two foreign articles she still keeps, they are: American dollars, and the German sublokator [subtenant], may his name be blotted out.
And precisely because of her patriotism for home production she boycotted the German mud and crawled into Polish mud, into home-grown Polish mud.
Now my wife is already, in good luck, in Ciechocinek, the residence of salt, mud and flirtation. And I? May all Jewish men have such a bright life. Only now do I know that I am a free bird, now I celebrate the true "Season of our Freedom", only now have I felt the taste of an exiled people suddenly freed from its conquerors.
Oh, listen, what a life I'm having now! May all the children of Israel — I mean all Jewish menfolk — have the same. Only now have I "odświeżył" [refreshed] my years. In the morning I lie "spokojnie" [peacefully] in bed and nobody goes over my "moshn"[?]. Oh, listen, what a nasty [habit?] the wives have, rummaging in the husband's pockets: searching, she searches for money, and finding, she finds something else altogether... And woe and alas to you if the wife finds in your "schowanka" [hiding place] such things for which you can give no excuse... But now I sleep soundly and fear no pocket inspection.
At 12 noon I get up and put on royal garments. Why not — it's a kind of holiday for me in the middle of the week, so why shouldn't I put on the finest and best. Every day I go out in freshly pressed trousers, in the new "broyge"[?] [brown?] shoes, in a freshly pressed shirt, with a genuine necktie, with a white embroidered handkerchief in my jacket [marynarka] pocket, in one hand a [?] walking-stick, and over the other arm my coat. A hat I don't wear at all — like a "yold" [a dandified simpleton].
Every morning freshly shaved smooth, so my lady neighbour won't be "put off" [razić]. Every day I douse myself with eau de Cologne and spray myself with perfume. On top of that I stick a red flower in my lapel, and off I go to the "Górka".
When I go out into the street in such a "strut", I forget that I have a wife who is a patriot of home production. I forget for the moment that my Yentl is bathing in mud; I also forget that this happiness is only "tymczasowe" [temporary], that when all is said and done, in a few weeks I'll be the shlimazl again, the harnessed donkey — I don't want to think about such terrible thoughts at all. Now I am free, now I am independent, now I am a cavalier with a rose in my lapel and I laugh at the world..
On the "Górka" I sit down on a bench, twirl my stick and cast glances at the girls, just like in those bachelor days. The girls throw back an "oczko" [a wink] — and there follows a mutual exchange of glances.
Oh, Jews, listen, what luck this is — may it be said of all Jewish children, I mean all Jewish men whose wives bathe in mud!..
At midday I go to a restaurant, sit down at a little table, order whatever my heart desires; the waiter doesn't tell me he has no appetite for food, that it stabs him so in the "boki" [sides]. I hear no crying, no "spasms", I don't hear the maids being scolded, the food doesn't stick in my throat, I chew with all my molars, just like in those golden bachelor years.
In the evening I pop over to Katowice. The weather is fine and there is still someone to go with — I pop into the "Monopol", pick myself a "wygodne" [comfortable] spot. We sit [?] and chat about politics, this and that. Oh, Jews, listen, what luck this is — may it be said of all Jewish men whose wives bathe in mud...
In the evening — I mean at dawn — I come home; the house is empty, my wife's bed stands, poor thing, orphaned, not a rustle is heard. I walk into the bedroom with firm steps, humming a hit tune to myself — not as when my wife is at home, on tiptoe. I don't hear the old refrain: So, you're here already? Where have you been lying in damned miseries till daybreak? I'm supposed to lie at home while you roam about whole nights? Who? What? Yesterday's days [i.e. nothing of the kind] — nobody curses, nobody scolds, nobody makes scenes, nobody plays me any night-symphonies. I go where I want, I eat what I want, I come home when and with whom I want. I stroll about musing on the best and the finest — I'm a free bird.
Oh, Jews, listen, what luck this is — may it be said of all Jewish men whose wives bathe in mud!..

Miniatures

[Literature — prose miniatures; literary supplement.] By Yosef Elszade [?].
I.
Beggars..
Now and then you condescend, from on high, to toss them crumbs of pitying glances — them, the creatures cursed by God and spat upon[?] by you, whose lot has fallen to the most terrible calling in life: to stretch out a withered hand to people and beg meagre scraps of bread and dried-out crusts, to stand ready with open mouths to snatch the morsel that you, the sated, spit out, and to lick their lips over it. Ah, how their lost, resigned figure disgusts you, their frozen gaze. You shake your heads over them: people fallen so low, stripped of the last feeling of shame, emptied[?] of the last drop of honour. In the shamelessly outstretched beggar's hand you see an insult to the remnant of the divine image that still nests, in remnants, in the wrinkled folds of their blackened[?] faces. You are sickened by them, your human dignity feels offended by them, and in their presence you suddenly perceive yourselves as higher and more human and begin to feel respect for yourselves.
But tell me, all of you, you knights of honour, just tell me: are you not all beggars yourselves, with hands forever outstretched for the favour of those richer and mightier? — Yes, your outstretched beggar's hand does not go begging[?] in public, is not shown plainly to everyone. Stealthily, cleverly, cunningly you do it. With anyone in whose mouth you see just a piece of bread or in whose hand a bit of honour, and you cannot tear it from him, you sidle up to him on all fours, fawn on him, lick him like dogs, bow and bend before him, shamelessly kiss the hems of his clothes — so long as, so long as he deigns to toss you a scrap of honour, just a bone for your doggish snout, so that you may have the gnawed[?] bone to chew.
So why does the beggar's outstretched hand disgust you so, when all of you do the very same thing, only uglier still, still more insulting to the divine image in you — because to the hateful game of doggish flattery and human falseness is added mouse-like cowardice, cunning concealment, the pretence that you are proud, dignified people, that you are faithful servants of the arch-idol[?].—
A thousand times dearer to me is the hand that dares to stretch itself out openly, in broad daylight, and humbly beg, than the hand that does the very same thing behind one's back, cunningly, so as not to be noticed by others or by itself..
You are all like common beggars, only more disgusting, because more cowardly[?], more hidden, and because your hand reaches not only for a scrap of bread to quiet a hungry stomach, but also for a crumb of honour to satisfy greed..
II.
In the Back Alley.
One day you pass, deep in the night, through a back alley. At a corner a woman's figure steals out towards you from the thick veil of darkness. Over her head and shoulders she has thrown a woollen shawl to hide the shame. Her whole body is frozen in a dead, motionless shadow. Only her heavy feet, in big laced shoes and flesh-coloured stockings, knock into the night. She, the creature driven out by the night, fixes on you a pair of dull, stagnant eyes like frozen fish-heads in a dirty standing puddle; she meets you with an insolent harlot's wink, and a shudder[?] runs through you. You want to spit in her face, in the face of the black night and of the whole dark world. It shocks you, you are sickened by this scum lying before you so [—?], so shameless, selling her body for a few groszy. Her brazenly painted[?] face, her sharp-resigned[?] gaze soil your refined, decent feelings, and with quick steps you hurry home, home to your chaste wife or innocent beloved, you throw yourselves into her arms to shield yourselves from the world's insolence, its ugliness...
But tell me, all of you, you knights of decency, just tell me: in what way is your chaste bedroom purer and more conscientious[?] than the back alley? Does she — your one and only — not throw herself into your arms, does she not sell you her body for a cheap [—], admittedly not for a few groszy to buy a loaf of bread, but for a base instinct and indeed sometimes for a costly ornament, for a silk dress... Or is it, because it happens more hidden, under the fig-leaf of false shame, less ugly, less disgusting?
Ah, she is your one and only — her lips whisper it in your ear every moment. But had fate not happened to bring you together with her, would she not have been the one and only of another, and whispered the same into his ear?.. She has in you a good protector; it does not pay her to exchange her one and only. That unfortunate, lonely creature of the back alley must do it — every moment have another 'one and only'.
Why then contempt and hatred for that one, who takes part in the same game of body-trade, only less disgustingly, because less hidden, less falsified.. — is not covered-up disgustingness uglier still?..
Great Writers in Their Family Life

II.
F. M. Dostoevsky, Apollinaria Suslova and Anna Grigorievna
When we read the works of the great Russian writer F. M. Dostoevsky we are refreshed[?] by the bright, luminous rays that stream from some of his heroes, but soon we are horrified[?] by the dread and naked terror that strike from his other heroes. No one like him has managed to bring out so vividly human dread and terror; yet among the dark, frightful heroes with whom his works are filled, there steal in splendid[?] ideal types who light up the darkened horizon — mostly of the female sex. And we know, after all, that whatever the poet creates is to a smaller or larger degree the reflection of his own life. It is therefore interesting to get to know the prototypes of Dunya (Raskolnikov's sister in "Crime and Punishment") and Katerina Ivanovna (in "The Brothers Karamazov") and other similar figures.
This ideal, luminous figure, who awakened Dostoevsky's most ideal feelings, is Apollinaria Suslova. He met her when he was already forty years old, the husband of a sickly, dying wife, and he himself was also a sufferer, a broken man, just returned from Siberia. Suslova was still young and charming then, and between this mismatched pair a hot love was bound[?]. But it did not last long. About a year later (1863) she leaves for Paris, and he was to follow her, and from there both were to travel to Italy. Meanwhile she meets a young and frivolous Spanish doctor and falls passionately in love with him. For him it is a light[?] and passing Parisian "romance", and for her — a hot, burning, deep love. She writes at once to Dostoevsky that there is no longer any point in his coming to Paris. But he does not receive the letter and comes at once. Learning what has happened, he falls at her feet and cries out: "Ah, I knew that I would lose you!" He questions her about her lover and says: "Surely a younger and handsomer one, but you will never find a heart like mine"...
After a short time the Spanish doctor abandons her in a coarse manner, and she reunites[?] with Dostoevsky and both leave for Italy. In her diary she then describes him as ideal and warm-hearted. But soon the love for the Spanish doctor reawakens in her, and this, together with Dostoevsky's jealousy, turns the days of their being together into hellish torments. After six weeks she goes back to Paris and Dostoevsky — to Russia. On the way he stops in Hamburg, where he gambles away his last pennies at roulette. He writes Suslova a desperate letter. She pawns her watch and sends him 150 gulden. Some time later she returns to Petersburg. Dostoevsky tries to win her back, but she will not listen. He says to her: I know, after all, that if you marry, you will leave your husband within three days... "With you, people are either infinitely[?] brilliant or at once scoundrels and base"...
In her diary she then records: "I simply hate him; he caused me so much grief at a time when it was possible to be without grief and suffering."
He then marries Anna Grigorievna; she is devoted to him and endures all the caprices of her nervous and epileptic husband. She loves him dearly, but he cares little about her. She tells, for instance, of one summer: he, Dostoevsky, acquires for himself with effort an expensive[?] fine suit and does not care at all that she has nothing to wear. She also records — in her personal diary — how she was once badly insulted in his presence and he did not react to it at all.
These two vital and luminous women lit up Dostoevsky's clouded life.
X.
Echoes

"Serious" and ironizing arguments against Hebrew in the Diaspora.
It would not be at all paradoxical if to the question: where is the greatest and most zealous opposition to a Hebrew revival in our dispersions? — we were to answer: "In Eretz Israel". We shall not now enter into the tangle of the causes and the development of such a stance among our Palestinian spokesmen. But the proven[?] fact must be stated that the sharpest arrows into our poor, tottering, barely-holding-on Hebrew organism are sent to us precisely from our "spiritual centre". True, an inexplicable riddle, but unfortunately a sad truth.
Until now the opposition expressed itself in disdain and irony. Every attempt at Hebrew creation in the Diaspora was accompanied there by [?] unclean[?] mockery and scorn. They cynically sneered at our poverty, and even important and very great writers such as M. Ben-Eliezer and others did so. The appearance of a Hebrew organ in the Diaspora found its echo in the Palestinian literary (especially the literary) press only in a regular sarcastic feuilleton, in which they cynically dismissed[?] the ridiculousness of our poverty and degeneration.
A last characteristic example:
A group of Hebraist activists in Vienna undertook a campaign for a Hebrew revival. It is truly astonishing what this group managed to accomplish in a relatively short time — simply out of nothing they created it themselves, supported by no one, isolated even from the Zionist organizations: a group of workers succeeded in organizing six hundred and fifty Hebrew-speaking members, in convening a Hebrew conference (which took place during Hol ha-Moed Passover with great success) and in creating a Hebrew monthly organ, "Devarenu". And all this was done on abandoned, empty ground. Should such a thing not have aroused the greatest enthusiasm in Eretz Israel? It turns out, however, that apart from a mocking feuilleton in "Ketuvim" (issue 175) about the poverty of "Devarenu", not a peep was heard about the whole large-scale campaign. True, the first issue of "Devarenu" is perhaps not so successful, but the people do say that "poverty is no disgrace". And is it so morally decent to mock the rags and holey clothes of a poor brother? No — a sincerely faithful brother takes off his own clothes to cover his brother's naked shame, but to stand and laugh along with the chorus of enemies at a brother's nakedness is not ethical at all.
One may boldly say that many attempts to create a Hebrew tribune in the Diaspora came to nothing[?] because of those cynical mockeries. Eretz Israel is regarded as the most competent authority for approval or rejection of Hebrew creative work, and since no word of encouragement was found there, only barbs and mockery, the desire passed and people lost heart.
Now there has been added to the mocking negative arguments yet another, "worst" argument. The famous Palestinian poet and public figure Natan Bistritzky has come out, first in "Moznayim" (issue 31) and now in "Haynt" (no. 129), with an article in which he tries to "prove" that a Hebrew revival in the Diaspora is simply a danger, since, as no full Hebrew revival is possible in the Diaspora, a superficial Hebraization may lead to a Hebrew assimilation, which is much more dangerous than ordinary assimilation, because with its poverty it will disappoint our youth.
That the foundations of modern Hebrew literature were laid precisely in the Diaspora surely needs no proof. And where are the ruins that "Hebrew assimilation" has wrought? Again: also. From there, from the land of pioneers, one is to hear an argument: "A full Hebrew revival is impossible"? Have they not seen there how many impossible things have become possible? From there, too, they preach lack of faith?
We do not now intend to polemicize with the arguments of the esteemed poet; we only wish to point to the paradoxical curiosity of the "spiritual centre", from which we believed we would draw our spiritual nourishment, draw encouragement and desire for Hebrew creation and activity — and we receive from it the most brutal rejection — a sad paradox.
I Myself Am a Song

ZANGEN (Ears of Grain)
Literary supplement
N. Szterenberg
I Myself Am a Song.
(From the book "Bagínen" [Dawn]).
I myself am a song.
Every song sings and rings within me.
With the quiet, pent-up joy of a pure, deep soul,
And like a ship laden full of gold on the distant sea —
Fate carries me, richly laden, in harness [?]
With quiet steps across a dewy field at dawn!
With a morning song spun of gold.
And the forest sings, the field prays,
And the whole great, beautiful world
Rises within me in quiet song.
I myself am a song.
When the day spills [?] light on all the distant roads,
Song bursts out of me with praise to meet it,
And then everything sings: the world around me,
And then I wish to be silent and hear only the mute one
That murmurs deep within me like a quiet spring of water from a mountain,
And sings, and rings within me, in my soul:
I — my gentle, pure song.
Warsaw, 1930.
"Pan-Europe"...

[Opinion — international politics; peace and disarmament.] By Szymon Rotenberg.
The messiah of the idea is Count Coudenhove-Kalergi, son of the Hungarian Count Coudenhove and a Japanese woman.
It is quite possible that the thought of the United States of Europe was born in the Count's brain after he realised that he himself was, after all, the product of a miniature union of peoples. If a peaceful life together could come about between his father, the Hungarian count, and his mother, the Japanese woman, where the distance and the differences are so colossal, then why should one not be able to make such an experiment on a larger scale, in Europe itself, where the peoples lie almost pressed together and where the antagonisms do not seem to be so sharp.
And he did indeed decide to create the Pan-European movement, which found a handful of followers in intellectual circles, and nobody took it seriously.
For who takes dreamers seriously? They are, after all, the most innocent people in the world. Has dreaming ever done anyone harm? Who cares if people sit in an attic room or in a palace (mostly they sit in attic rooms) and dream of beautiful, ideal worlds and see "fata morganas" in the desert of everyday reality.
If dreamers are harmless, the apostles, however, become dangerous — those who want to apply the dreamers' ideas to their political combinations. Therefore, when such a professional politician as the French Foreign Minister Aristide Briand comes along and starts talking about Pan-Europe and sends out memoranda to all European states, including even Russia, which Kalergi had excluded, something must be very wrong with the peace of nations.
That this is so was shown to us by the fiasco of the London Naval Conference, where instead of disarming a mad race began between France and Italy in building warships. Why, the English delegate at the Naval Conference, Snowden, said after one stormy session that one more such conference and a war will break out. At the same time as Briand sent out his memorandum, which was supposed to be the overture to the great symphony called "Pan-Europe", Mussolini delivered a speech in Florence to his Blackshirts, containing such sweet "pacifist" sentences as: "Pan-Europe is indeed a fine thing, but finer still are rifles, machine guns and cannons" and "unarmed prophets must always perish". A fine accompaniment to Briand's peace prelude! Nothing to say. And to prove that with him this is no mere rhetoric, the "Duce" assured that very shortly 20 new warships will be launched in Italian waters.
What a practical idyll of peace — almost "the wolf shall dwell with the lamb"!
Even more strongly than before the war, militarism now reigns in the whole world; the youth continue to be educated in the fascist spirit, and military heroism is constantly cultivated among the youth, who did not go through the World War and did not feel the horror of the fratricidal slaughter. In them one can quite easily implant the lust for war and educate them as blind tools for the various chauvinists.
We still remember quite well how people were glorified who distinguished themselves by having learned the craft of killing well. During the world slaughter they mobilised not only tens of millions of people in order, in the course of a few years, to set up across the whole world a butcher's shop of human flesh, but at the same time they also mobilised science, art, literature and even the clergy, who before every battle consecrated with holy water both the cannons and the "material" for them — the soldiers transformed into automatons and deprived of will.
They were persuaded that by killing the enemy one does a good deed not only for the fatherland but for all mankind, because the enemy is a barbarian, an obstacle to the development of civilisation.
The very same means — one must know — were used by each side separately, and each persuaded itself that it was in the right, that it was the one attacked and innocent.
Writers and poets sang the heroism of dancing into the arms of death with a song on one's lips and at the same time, in the last leap into the grave, still managing to murder a human being. For many of the God-blessed poets the most beautiful picture their imagination could paint was a heroic soldier holding the enemy's head impaled on a pike.
Reality far surpassed the poets' imagination, and for breaking a record in murdering people one was awarded as a distinction a cross — the symbol that recalls the love of man, the teaching "if one gives you a slap on the right cheek, turn your left".
Still more terrible, still more cruel, still more barbaric will the future war be: it will be a murderous [?], lightning-fast annihilation of all living creatures with the help of poison gases, microbes and death rays, which are nowadays being developed in the laboratories of the whole world; and the various pseudo-peace manoeuvres are nothing more than a means of diverting the attention of the masses, of blinding their eyes so that they should not see the destructive [—] that is being prepared for them. Therefore the cruel war depictions of Barbusse [?], Remarque and Sherriff come out pale, far inferior in the writers' imagination to the cruel reality that the diplomacy and [printed: in] various military castes are preparing for us.
Peace among nations! It is the dream of every honest and sincerely thinking person, but it is not the various peace and disarmament conferences that will bring it, because one comes to the negotiations, a priori, with bad intentions and with mutual suspicion.
One must know that the danger of war does not lie in whether the ships and cannons are larger or smaller, in quality as well as in quantity, for even the largest cannon is harmless [print apparently: "harmful"] when one does not fire it, when there is no lust for murder; and if one wants to kill, one can do it with a simple piece of wood too — people already waged wars among themselves in the most ancient times and with the most primitive means.
[—] more important than physical disarmament is moral and psychological disarmament, for all deeds a person commits are the product of earlier preparation in our subconscious, and according to the newest psychological research (Émile Coué) the subconscious can be steered in such a way that one would simply be incapable of committing any criminal act.
Peace among nations will come when it succeeds in creating and cultivating a mass psychosis — not of murder, but of a heroism of creation; when one will teach [printed: "instead of teaching"] that human happiness lies not in wars, not in the struggle of man against man, whom one artificially makes into enemies, but in the struggle against the common enemy of all mankind — against the obstacles of raw nature, which have always been the greatest hindrances to human progress, to human development.

Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings and remarks on this week's portion (Beha'alotecha)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings and remarks on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and edited by Y. L.
Parashat: Beha'alotecha
—o—
A) "And Aaron did so" (8:3)
Rashi says on this verse: "To tell the praise of Aaron, that he did not deviate." All the commentators ask: is it a fine praise for Aaron that he did not act otherwise than God had commanded?! Quite a feat...
— "That he did not change" means that he himself was not changed: although he was entrusted with so great a service as the kindling of the menorah, and thereby reached the highest rung of the priesthood, he nevertheless remained the same approachable, simple Aaron, the same humble man who mixed with people as before. That is the praise.
Rabbi Meir of Przemyślany (Premishlaner).
• • •
In the portion of Korah there is a midrash: "The wisdom of women builds her house" — this refers to the wife of On ben Pelet, because she said to her husband: what for should you carry on a quarrel! If Aaron is High Priest, you are his disciple; if Korah becomes High Priest, you will be his disciple too — so what difference does it make to you? — One asks: what tremendous wisdom does the midrash see in her words? —
This is what she said to her husband: You want to depose Moses and Aaron from leadership because, in your opinion, they put on airs a little, while Korah is more at home[?] with the common people. But that is only before he sits on the "chair". Afterwards, when he is already leader, he will be just as puffed up as Moses is today, in your opinion, and then he too will not want to exchange a word with you... Today you are Aaron's disciple, a hanger-on, and tomorrow you will be Korah's hanger-on — so what is the difference?...
Rabbi Mendel of Warka (Vorker).
B) "Stand still, and I will hear" (9:8)
When the unclean men asked Moses "Wherefore are we kept back?", why should we not celebrate[?] Passover?, Moses told them to wait, and he went to ask of God. Whereas when the daughters of Zelophehad asked him: "Wherefore should be done away?", "why should we have no share of inheritance?" — then "Moses brought their cause before the Lord". He did not tell them to wait as he did here with the unclean men, because with the daughters of Zelophehad — with women — he did not want to carry on a conversation... "Do not converse much with a woman"...
Rabbi Tzvi Hirsch of Liszka (Liskover).
C) "Then Moses heard the people weep throughout their families" (11:10)
The midrash says about this that the elders wept "because forbidden unions were prohibited to them", because marriage with close relatives had been forbidden — and why was it precisely the elders who wept?—
Usually, when an old father or mother was left alone without a home and wanted to go to one of the children — if it was to a son, he says: "Father, I would gladly take you in, but your daughter-in-law, my wife, is a shrew and she will embitter my life because of you. Here you will spill[?] on her and there you will spit — in short, I cannot." He comes to a daughter, and she says: "Daddy dear, with all my heart I would like to have you in my home, but my husband, your son-in-law, the villain, will torment me and eat me alive. Can I disturb my domestic peace because of you?" — But had brothers and sisters been allowed to marry each other, they would have had to take in an old father or mother and would have had no excuse.. And so, when the old people heard of the prohibition of marriage between brothers and sisters, they began to weep...
"Velfs-vertl"[?] (a saying of Velvel's[?]).
• • •
A Hasid came to the author of "Tiferet Shlomo" to seek advice about a match proposed for his son with the only daughter of a rich man. He did not tell him to make the match, for the following reason: in old age, when a man has many children, sometimes he spends the night with one child and sometimes with another. But when one has only an only daughter, he will always be at the daughter's, and "an old man in the house is a snare in the house"..
Ohel Shlomo.
D) "And it came to pass, when the ark set forward" (11:35 [sic])
It is a custom, when the Torah scroll is taken out, after saying "Vayehi binsoa", to kiss the Torah. Once the Malbim came to a German synagogue and saw how the Orthodox worshippers kissed the Torah by way of their hands, because it is not "hygienic" to kiss with the mouth. He said to them: you really are topsy-turvy people — charity you give with your mouth alone, and the Torah you kiss with your hands; why should you not kiss the Torah with your mouth and give charity with your hand?..
E) "And he said: My lord Moses, forbid them (kela'em)" (11:28)
Joshua did not mean to destroy them in the plain sense of the word; he only said to Moses: do you want to be rid of them? — hand them the management of the community's needs, and of themselves they will become a heap of ruins, they will perish by themselves...
Sanhedrin 17a (also quoted in Rashi).
F) "Now the man Moses was very meek" (12:3)
On the word "meek" (anav) Rashi explains: "lowly and patient (savlan)"; savlan here means: tolerant — he bears with and tolerates other people's views and opinions...
Nifla'ot Hadashot.
—o—
Avot, Chapter Two.
A) "Whatever is an honour to him who does it and brings him honour from men" (Mishnah 1)
If you want to know whether what you do is good, see whether it "brings him honour from men" — whether, if another person did it, you too would find nothing at all to reproach him with.. For most people do not tolerate in another what they themselves do and see no fault in it..
Midrash Shmuel.
B) "Excellent is the study of Torah together with worldly occupation (derekh eretz)" (Mishnah 2)
Even if one is a scholar and can study well, nevertheless it is good that one should also be a person of derekh eretz... mixing with people, being "one who deals with all the world"..
Rabbi Shlomo Halevi.
C) "In a place where there are no men, strive to be a man" (Mishnah 6)
If you want to be a man, if you want to practise piety, see that it be "in a place where there are no men" — when people do not see...
Arvei Nahal.
D) "And know what to answer an unbeliever (apikoros)" (Mishnah 19)
What does "and know" (you should already know) mean? Why does the Tanna not say outright what one should answer the unbeliever, but only the expression "and know"? — The Tanna means here that you should answer the unbeliever with the second verse of the Song of Songs.. and because it is not respectable to set this out openly in the Mishnah, the Tanna expresses it in the word "and know" — "take the hint"..
Rabbi Gershon Henekh of Radzyń (Radziner).
E) "Be careful with the authorities (reshut)" (Mishnah 3).
The Hida, in his commentary "Hasdei Avot", interprets the word reshut as the rich (because money is power), and of the rich the Tanna says "they befriend a man only for their own needs".. "they appear as friends when it is to their benefit, but do not stand by a man in his hour of need"...

A Swindling “Meshulach” Cons People out of Money for the Radzymin Yeshiva

[Sosnowiec — fraud.] A certain Wolf Glazman claimed to hold credentials and receipt books from the Radzymin yeshiva and came to Zagłębie and Upper Silesia to collect money for the yeshiva “Torchot Chaim” [so printed].
In every town and shtetl the “meshulach” [charity emissary] had the help of certain people who want to support a yeshiva, and when that did not work out for him, he hired assistants who helped him collect money for a proper fee.
The “meshulach” made his first “guest tours” in Katowice, Königshütte [Chorzów] and other towns in Upper Silesia, where the “business” went very well. From Upper Silesia Reb Wolf came to Zagłębie, where he set to work.
For the collection he engaged 2 young men from Będzin, who agreed (“became settled”) to receive 25 percent of the collected sum.
The young men from Będzin, seeing that the public was giving money and that the “business” was not difficult at all, demanded a raise: they asked for half and half, i.e. a full 50 percent of the income.
The “meshulach” Reb Wolf did not want to concede the raise, and all 3, i.e. Reb Wolf and the assistant “meshulachim”, went to Rabbi Hager to hold a din Torah [rabbinical arbitration].
The claims of both sides aroused suspicion in Rabbi Hager; in particular he was struck by the claim of the “meshulach”, who shouted: “How can I give 50 percent when I myself get no more than 50 percent from the Radzymin Rebbe!”...
Because of this suspicion Rabbi Hager demanded that the “meshulach” show the receipt books and all his official documents as a meshulach, and also bring the collected money.
Having no choice, the “meshulach” handed over the following 2 receipt books: 1) “Orphanage under the supervision of the Radzymin Rebbe, may he live long and well, Amen” and 2) the yeshiva “Torchot Chaim” under the supervision of the Radzymin Rebbe, may he live long and well, Amen.
To Rabbi Hager's question why he carried receipt books in 2 versions, the “meshulach” explained as follows: “When I come to the ‘Deitschen’ [modern, Westernized Jews] I ask them for the orphanage, because the Deitschen do not want to give to a yeshiva, and among Hasidic Jews I collect for the benefit of the yeshiva”...
After this explanation Rabbi Hager, having taken the money, the receipt books and the “meshulach's” credentials, declared that he would not return them until he received word from Warsaw about the whole collection campaign.
The persons tried to react, but seeing the firm resistance on the part of the rabbi, they left.
The next morning the “meshulach” came to the rabbi, this time without his assistants, and demanded back the money with the documents, declaring that he had already come to terms with his partners.
When the rabbi refused him, he began to pretend to be a nervous wreck and threatened that if he did not get his documents back he would throw himself down from the fourth floor.
After many interventions by our “merciful ones”, the rabbi gave him [money] for a ticket to Warsaw and sent him away.
On leaving, the “meshulach” begged that the rabbi not pass the facts on to the newspaper, because he was sure that his honesty would soon become clear...
Last Monday the rabbi received a letter from the president of the Warsaw kehilla, Mr. Farbstein, informing him that the Radzymin Rebbe declares that no meshulachim have been sent out from his yeshiva for 2 years now, and that this Wolf Glazman is not known to anyone as a meshulach.

Thursday — General Meeting of the "Moshav Zkeinim" Members in Sosnowiec

[Sosnowiec — community and welfare; local news.] The magnificent building for a "Moshav Zkeinim" (old-age home) in Sosnowiec is nearing completion. The board is therefore convening a general meeting, to be held next Thursday, the 19th of this month, at 11 a.m., in the hall of the "Kupcy" (merchants' association) on Kowalska [?] Street.
It is superfluous to stress once again the importance of the institution for Jewish Sosnowiec, and it remains to be hoped that all members to whom the existence of the "Moshav Zkeinim" is dear will come to the meeting and help bring it to the desired goal.
—o—
[Będzin — municipal services.] At the height of the season the "Będzin bath" is being closed.
Renovation is being carried out at the municipal bathhouse from Monday on; because of this the establishment will not be operating.
—o—
[Zagłębie — education.] The Minister of Education in Zagłębie.
Accompanied by the Kraków school curator Kupczyński and the inspector (wizytator) Antonowicz, the Minister of Education Czerwiński came to Dąbrowa [Górnicza], where he acquainted himself with the activity of the local mining (górnicza) school.
Afterwards the minister left for Katowice.
—o—
[Sosnowiec — courts; labour.] The "Alkusz" events before the district court
On the 27th of this month the trial will take place at the Sosnowiec district court of the workers who on 9 April ("Kwiecień") of this year demolished the "vagung" [?; perhaps the weighing scale, or a misprint for "voynung" — the residence] and also took "captive" the director of the "Alkusz" aluminium factory.
Twenty-four workers, men and women, will sit in the dock.
—o—
[Upper Silesia — economy and trade.] Conference of paper merchants and manufacturers.
On Wednesday a conference was held at the Hotel "Savoy" in Katowice with the participation of manufacturers and merchants of the stationery trade in Poland and Upper Silesia.
The aim of the conference was to standardise prices and combat harmful competition.
After the lecture part a board was elected. Its seat will be in Katowice.
—o—
[Strzemieszyce — youth movements.] A "Betar" founded.
On Sunday a "Betar" branch (ken) was founded in Strzemieszyce. At the founding a fairly large number of members signed up at once. It is characteristic to note that in the course of the last 2 months no fewer than 5 institutions have been founded here (may they multiply...).
—o—
[Strzemieszyce — fires.] Fires.
On Friday and Saturday a great many fires broke out in Strzemieszyce, in which several buildings and barns went up in smoke.

For calling someone a „moser“ — a 20 zł. fine.

Last Friday the Będzin court heard the case against Mr. Yekl Gutman, who was charged with having shouted „moser!“ [informer] at his rich brother Mr. Natan Aharon Gutman of Dąbrowa, because the latter had brought the police into the courtyard at 3-go Maja [Street] 11, and in passing the police drew up reports on several tenants.
The interpreter of the district court, Mr. Lejbowicz[?], was called as an expert and explained the meaning of the expression „moser“.
After hearing the witnesses — the caretakers of the building, who supported the charge — the judge fined Mr. Gutman 20 zł.

„Jeszcze Polska“ is kosher and „Hatikvah“ is treyf...
On Monday Mr. Zajdner[?] of Dąbrowa celebrated a siyum ha-sefer [completion of a Torah scroll]. The scroll was escorted in a procession into the synagogue, where the appropriate celebration took place.
At the end the orchestra played the Polish anthem and then began to play „Hatikvah“, but at the sounds of the Jewish anthem the „hot-headed“ Agudah men flew into a rage and disrupted the playing of „Hatikvah“.
Horrifying suicide of 2 Christian schoolgirls in Zawiercie.

The 18-year-old Irena Mitles[?], a pupil of the 3rd class, committed suicide by throwing herself under a moving train. The suicide happened in the following circumstances. Coming to school on Saturday, where she learned that she had not been promoted to the 4th class, instead of going home she walked along the railway line in the direction of Łazy and on the way threw herself under a moving train, which crushed her.
A second suicide, of a pupil of the same school: the 18-year-old Helena Domagała[?] of the 2nd class, also for the same reason, hanged herself in the forest near Włodowice.
The two suicides made a very heavy impression in the local pupils' circles.
Festive housewarming in Zawiercie.

At last, after several years of existence, the „Linat ha-Tsedek“ society has succeeded in renting premises of its own from Mr. Zalmen Winiarski[?]. On Shabbat Parshat Shelach the society celebrated its „housewarming“. Taking part were the local rabbi, the moreh hora'ah Sternfeld[?], kehilla officials, the Chevra Kadisha and many of the local notables. Very impressive was the reception in honour of the rabbi, who delivered a fine address. He pointed out the importance of the institution in our town, which supplies the sick with various medical appliances, and called on those assembled to fulfil their sacred pledges to the institution. Then greetings were given by city councillor Mr. Yitzchak Aharon Szwarc, the society's chairman Mr. Yitzchak Krajcer, and vice-chairman Mr. Yisroel Grinblat. Then, over a glass of drink, the company spent several hours.

Jewish artisans will receive loans.
Yesterday, Thursday, Messrs. Menashe Sztern and Z. Gancwajch, on behalf of the Jewish artisans of Zagłębie, intervened with the director of the „Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego“ in Katowice, Mr. Mitnik, concerning long-term credits for the Jewish artisans of the Będzin powiat.
The delegation pointed to the difficult economic situation of Zagłębie's Jewish artisan class and recalled the injustice done to the Jewish artisans in 1928 when the first long-term state loan for artisans was distributed.
Director Mitnik declared to the delegation that he will never tolerate any national or racial distinction among the artisans of the Polish Republic; he holds that every craftsman has the full right to benefit from the credits, and he pointed out that the entire sum (300.000) for individual financing is in the hands of the Będzin „Powiat. Komun. Kasa Oszczędn.“ [County Communal Savings Bank], and the final decision with the Będzin Starostwo.
Since the Będzin starosta Mr. Baksa[?] also has a positive attitude to the question and promised to meet the wish of the Jewish craftsmen as far as possible — the matter of the loans (which will be granted in the first days of July) will be settled in the best possible way.

What Every Craftsman and Journeyman Must Know

In the previous issue of our paper we already pointed out briefly the duty of all Jewish craftsmen who do not wish to lose the right to work independently and to employ apprentices: not to overlook the present responsible moment for Jewish small industry in general, and to present themselves en masse for the craftsmen's and journeymen's examinations, which have already begun in the territory of the Kielce voivodeship in accordance with the regulations of the Kielce Chamber of Crafts.
Before we proceed to examine in more detail the most important points of the regulations of the examination commissions for journeymen and masters — for those who on the day the Polish guild law came into force did not hold, and still do not hold, the title of journeyman or master — it will be worth dwelling on the new industrial (guild) law itself, which appeared under the decree of the President of the State of 7 June 1927.
The said decree imposed the same rights and obligations on all guilds in the Polish Republic. Since 15 December 1927 compulsory guild membership no longer exists, and consequently the guilds must either liquidate themselves or, within the following half-year, adopt and submit for approval new statutes conforming to the provisions of the above-mentioned decree; that is, they may create such bodies whose task is to maintain contact among the members and to safeguard and raise professional prestige.
In place of the liquidated guilds, Chambers of Crafts were founded with the aim of permanently defending the interests of craftsmen. The Chambers of Crafts are organs of the economic self-government of the crafts, which is envisaged as a component of the general economic self-government in Art. 68 of the Constitution of 21 March 1921, and they are laid down in the provisions of the above-mentioned decree (of 7/6 1927).
The Chambers of Crafts fulfil the following tasks: they cooperate with the state industrial authority in supporting and fostering the development of the crafts, provide information, etc.; they consider and submit to the industrial authority appropriate wishes and resolutions concerning craftsmen's interests, and every year render an account of the state of the craft trades; they regulate apprenticeship matters on the basis of the binding regulations, set up examination commissions for journeymen and masters, etc.
The members of the Chamber of Crafts are elected for 6 years; every 3 years, on 31 December, half of the elected members retire.
There are 17 (seventeen) such Chambers of Crafts in Poland. Zagłębie belongs to the Kielce Chamber of Crafts, which officially began its activity on 3 March of this year.
The Chamber of Crafts is supposed to consist of 24 members, under a voluntary agreement — 12 Christians and 12 Jews. Because Zagłębie did not take part in the elections, though it was entitled to 4 seats (2 Christians and 2 Jews), the Kielce Chamber of Crafts consists of only 20 members, half Christians and half Jews.
———
The title “Master” combined with the name of the trade concerned may be borne only by one who has passed a master's examination before a special examination commission appointed by the Chamber of Crafts, or at a crafts school, a master school or another institution specially suited by its character and composition to that purpose. By contrast, craftsmen who on the basis of the regulations valid until now have already obtained the right to the title “Master” etc. — in a word, those craftsmen who hold diplomas issued before 15 December 1927 — are no longer subject to new examinations, retain this title and have the right to bear the name “Master” combined with the name of the trade concerned.
All craftsmen who do not hold the master's title (have no diplomas) must appear before the examination commission, for which the Chamber of Crafts has drawn up a special examination that provides especially favourable concessions for older craftsmen who have already been running independent craft workshops for more than 8 years, and for external journeyman candidates.
Whoever does not obtain a diploma by 15 December of this year will lose the right to employ apprentices. An inspection (lustration) of workshops will begin, and then a considerable number of workshops of undiplomaed masters will surely be closed.
With all the provisions of the said regulations — what every craftsman and journeyman must [know] when presenting himself for the examination, the examination material for journeymen, and the manner of regulating the question of apprentices — [we shall deal] in the following articles.
A. Gancwajg.

Letters to the Editor.

[Będzin — small trade and the market; letters to the editor.]
I.
Esteemed Mr. Editor,
As the section of Upper Silesian traders within the Merchants' Association in Będzin, we request space for the following letter in your esteemed newspaper, for which we thank you in advance.
Reading in the „Zaglembier Tsaytung“ of last Friday about a proposal in the Będzin town council not to admit outside craftsmen and petty traders to the Będzin trading market, we ask the honourable proposer and[?] also the Jewish councillors whether they are aware that such measures are not permitted, simply because no one can be prevented from earning his piece of bread.
Let the honourable proposer know that we Upper Silesian traders have had enough to endure in Upper Silesia from a certain Jew-baiter, Sila[?]; there at least the incitement against us Jews came from a non-Jew, not one of our own; but that a Jew — and a community board member and craftsman at that — should permit himself such a thing, one can only say: „Woe to the ears that hear such things.“
How did you not take account of the fact that with the above proposal you are ruining several hundred Jewish souls, exposing them to total ruin and to beggars' bread? Your argument that the outsiders compete with the locals is quite unfounded — on the contrary: competition makes business, and it is precisely because of the competition, thanks to the incoming petty traders and craftsmen, that the outside customer comes, who at the same time brings „pryon“ [so printed; probably „pidyon“ — takings] to the local merchant.
We agree with our esteemed president of the Merchants' Association, Mr. Rubinlicht, that the question should be removed entirely from the agenda. And to you, Mr. Proposer, we advise withdrawing the proposal.
With respect,
The Board of the Trade Section in Upper Silesia.

In Old Age (More on the “Old-Age Home.” — The Coldness Must Disappear, a Warm Attitude Must Take Its Place)

[Sosnowiec — community; charity; opinion.] Jewish Sosnowiec has finally set up a “Moshav Zekenim [old-age] home” for Jews who have nowhere to be in their old age.
Certainly this is a fine and useful deed; certainly the Jewish population of Sosnowiec owes a debt to the town as long as the institution does not begin its activity; certainly it is self-evident that a town must take care that the old people should have somewhere to rest their bones in their old age — the old people who worked honestly and decently as long as they had the strength, and now have no resting place where they can live out their few remaining years.
For some time now we have been hearing that the building is complete and finished; all that remains is the final fitting-out, for which 30 thousand zł. are nevertheless needed. For this purpose a meeting was convened, in which the rich local Jews took part, and at this very meeting the 30 thousand zł. were discussed — how to obtain them; and it is characteristic that the rich Jews decided to take a loan for the above sum at the “Bank Gosp. Krajowego” [Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego, the National Economy Bank].
Say what you will, you may take offence, you can say that it is easier to criticise than to create realities, you may say whatever you would [like] — and still it is incomprehensible to you. How could these Jews decide among themselves to take a loan for the above sum? What role does 30 thousand zł. play in such a Jewish community as Sosnowiec? How many rich Jews does one need in order to collect these 30 thousand zł.? There are, after all, still enough well-to-do Jews who have not yet put their hand in their pocket for the institution. So one ought to have visited them [?] — they could, after all, have given, and the sum would have been put together from these very people.
It is, after all, a disgrace to come into a bank to take 30 thousand zł. for a public institution. What impression can that make in the bank? With what eye does one look upon such activity, upon such concern? It is incomprehensible how rich Jews could bring themselves to have the question solved in such a way.
We do know Sosnowiec, and we know that there are Jews who until now have given nothing at all to the above institution, and however bad things may be with them, the said sum could have been obtained. And one more thing: if one did not want to hurt oneself, if one did not want to be intensively active, one could at any rate have obtained the sum as an interest-free loan from a few individual rich Jews, for whom lending such a sum without interest is one of the easiest things. One is therefore forced to conclude one of two things: either the board is not in contact with all strata of the rich Jewish population, or it does not know how and in what way to speak with them.
Had it been otherwise, had the board known how to draw in all the rich Jews, the 30 thousand zł. could have been raised quite easily and quickly.
Jewish Sosnowiec is, after all, not so penniless [?] that such a sum could not quite certainly be raised. But if the shortcoming here really is that the takers [?] or the givers [?] do not behave as they should, that they do not know in what way to interest one another in the idea — then this is a great shortcoming, which must be corrected in good time. From the very beginning one must react properly to such a cold attitude, if one does not want to have afterwards various unwanted complications, which may in future blunt the continuing organisational work.
It is absolutely not nice that because of such a ridiculous sum, which could without doubt have been raised in the town — let alone borrowed without interest, certainly and surely — there had to be so much debating, and in the end such [sums] were taken from a bank at interest. This does not befit Jewish and philanthropic Sosnowiec. It is also not nice towards the initiators of the idea, who have already given so much strength in order to bring the institution into being.
We know that there are many rich Jews who give nothing at all to such causes. And these Jews are left in peace — they are not bothered, they are not visited. But this is far from in order. One must not tolerate such unheard-of deeds, because everyone who can in any way help to build such a necessary institution is obliged to lend a hand; one must not pass such Jews by, they must not be missing from the list for the one reason alone that they think more of taking than of giving...
In addition one must also bear in mind that from the moment the institution opens its gates to the old people it will already need a budget, and from whom will it have to be collected if not from the well-to-do Jewish population?
It comes down, then, to this: the “Old-Age Home” is to be opened for those for whom it was built, and therefore it is indeed important to get used in good time to the thought that a sizeable budget will have to be created, which willy-nilly will have to be taken from the town. And in that case one must not take offence when things are not as they should be, when someone does not understand how to receive the representatives of the “Old-Age Home” kindly.
One must already prepare for the necessary work. One must already begin collecting monthly pledges, so that by the time the home is opened a certain sum will have accumulated, which will serve to purchase the necessary preparations.
The others [?] who stand at a distance, those whom one must approach by clever means — just as one lures a child into the heder with sweets — they must be told that the building brings benefit to everyone equally: both to the one who gives, who sacrifices himself for the idea, and to the one who spits from a distance and imagines that it is a matter for those who give their strength.
A Moshav Zekenim is a home for all elderly people who have already worked out their years and have nowhere to be looked after in their last years.
It seems that such an institution should be equally close and equally dear to everyone.
Dr. Papuri [?].

Jews, We Are Still in Trouble!..

It was in those years when in Russia people were fighting for Jewish equal rights.
At that time the newspaper "HaZman" used to print in every issue, in large letters on the front page, the line:
"The Jews of Russia still have no equal rights!"
"The Russian Jews still have no equal rights!"
— Jews, that is, are still lying nine ells deep in the earth [Yiddish idiom: deep in trouble]!..
— Jews are still forbidden to set foot on the holy soil of Moscow!
— Jewish children still cannot get into a Russian university!..
And since then a good many years have gone by. Many waters and many fires have passed over the whole world.
And it seemed that the world had been purged by the fires, made kosher and fit for Passover; that the waters had washed away all impurities and filth.
So it did seem, — but it has not even begun.
The world has remained the same as it was, and perhaps even worse.
And the Jews have remained in the same troubles as before, and perhaps even greater ones.
And I would propose that our Jewish press all over the world should do exactly as "HaZman" once did: it should print every day, in large letters on the front page:
— "Jews, we are still in great trouble!..."
Here, there and everywhere, and all over the globe.
Ah, but there is a question: what will it help us, and what will come of it for us?
The answer is: and what good do all the various protests do us, which we protest every Monday and Thursday against every trouble-that-should-not-befall-us?
Hardly a single week goes by without our having to call protest meetings, each time against another injustice committed against us.
Our old father Jacob left us a precious inheritance, the Jewish luck: that we should never know a single good day.
You surely remember: "Jacob wished to dwell in peace" — Jacob wanted to sit quietly a little, and every time a brand-new trouble fell upon him.
And from then on we carry Jacob's inheritance around with us, his luck, and nowhere are we let rest a single minute — always a new trouble.
And what other choice do we have?
Fight with the world — we cannot, we have no strength for that.
And even if we could, we would not do it either; we do not believe in fighting.
So the only thing left for us to do is to protest.
To protest as sharply as possible and as often as possible.
And the merit of protesting is that, if protests cannot always help, they certainly cannot do harm; we have nothing to lose[?]. Worse than worst it cannot be.
Take, for example, the story with England in the Land of Israel.
She gave us a Balfour Declaration, she promised us mountains of gold. We on our side did the best that could possibly be done. Hundreds of thousands of fresh, educated, self-sacrificing Jews have come into the Land of Israel since the Balfour Declaration. The Jewish people has invested tens of millions of dollars in the desolate land. We have founded dozens of colonies on the worst soil, the most abandoned and neglected for hundreds of years. We made a blossoming Garden of Eden out of a desert. Both England gained a great deal from us, and the lazy Arabs too. They took a great deal from us, and gave us nothing, — except good hard blows and [?] from time to time...
And they keep on promising us, and then, when we need workers in the Land of Israel — it is precisely the Labour government that comes and forgets all the promises, and shuts the gates to Jewish pioneers, at a time when others, non-Jews, are precisely let in.
And that is supposedly called socialist justice. Not letting people into their own land!
England's pity for the Jewish people is like that well-known "parnas-chodesh" [the kehilla's warden of the month] who used to collect the taxes from the Jews in Russia. And when a poor man could not pay, they would take his household things and sell them.
Once a parnas-chodesh came with the "strazhnik" [policeman] to a poor, destitute Jew to collect the tax debt.
The poor man tells him his situation: his wife lies sick, the children go about naked, barefoot and hungry, everything in the house has already been pawned and eaten up, and nothing is left but the one pillow on which the sick woman lies.
The parnas-chodesh listens to this story, shakes his head and sighs:
— Oy, oy, oy, truly God have pity on you, Reb Feivish, oy, oy, oy!
The Jew sees that the parnas-chodesh pities him, so he tells him more and more.
— Oy, stop it, Reb Feivish! — says the parnas-chodesh — I cannot bear the pity, I have a weak heart, stop already, enough!
And in the meantime he says to the strazhnik:
— "Tem chasom beri podushku, Ivan"! [Russian: meanwhile take the pillow, Ivan] — meaning, meanwhile pull the pillow out from under the woman!
He does indeed have pity, but meanwhile he takes away the last pillow.
England does indeed pity us, she knows the Jewish situation and her heart is sorely torn for the "People of the Bible", but nevertheless — "beri podushku", she takes away more than she gives us!..
And so it is in all the other countries of the world too: almost without exception, they remind us that we are "Jews".
So what other choice do we have but to protest against all the injustices of all the states against us? If it does not help much, it does not harm either.
And therefore I say that if protests do no harm, perhaps my proposal will indeed help a little too.
We must remind our Jews themselves:
— Jews, we are still in trouble!
And when all Jews remember this constantly, some good will come out of unity.
The trouble is that most Jews forget, or want to forget.
And if the whole Jewish people remembered and knew its situation, it could surely help itself better than its best friend, even England..
— Yes, my dear Jews, we are still in great trouble!
Pini Ba'al Lashon.
