Where Is the Logic? (When the tasks are not understood. — The result of immaturity.)

The Będzin city council last week considered the question of preventing craftsmen from the Kielce region from bringing their handmade wares to the market in Będzin.
Had we not known who raised the question — that the initiative came from the representatives of the Jewish artisans — we would surely have been certain that this was a fresh little flower of the antisemites; we could not have imagined it otherwise, the idea would not otherwise have occurred to us, our logical understanding could not otherwise have grasped it.
After all, the antisemites constantly devise schemes and stratagems for creating as many restrictions and difficulties as possible, and it goes without saying that it is the Jew who is meant, though it is never said aloud, though it is done so cleverly that one should not know whom is meant and what one is aiming at. But we already know from practice that every addition, every new phenomenon is for us a stumbling block, a point of obstruction from which one cannot free oneself so quickly.
And therefore it is simply astonishing how Jewish councillors, and our own members besides, could have had the nerve [?] to demand restrictions against their fellows from other towns. When one starts to take stock, it gives the impression that they were not fully conscious, that they did not account to themselves for their demands; otherwise they could not have brought themselves to have restrictions introduced against their colleagues, with the initiative coming precisely from their own camp.
People always spoke of a large Poland, and our popular representatives pointed out that for Jews a large Poland is particularly desirable, so that the great percentage of Jews should not need to concentrate in compact masses but should have the possibility of moving freely and widely across all of great Poland. Yet people come from our own camp, our own flesh and blood, and demand nothing less than restrictions, another Pale of Settlement [czerta osiadłości], in which it would be laid down: here you may not go and there you may not stand.
Who does not remember what troubles the Russian Jews suffered because of the Jewish restrictions, because they could not move freely across great Russia? How much effort, work and sacrifice our brethren in Russia invested to have the "temporary" restrictions abolished, and how happy the Russian Jews would have been had they succeeded in this before the war — it would have counted as one of the most important events in Jewish life.
And here come people, Jewish artisans, and plead with the self-government [the municipality] to introduce restrictions against their fellows from other towns. Is it not comic? Is it not ridiculous? Is it not tragic? Such an attitude is simply incomprehensible. How do people dare to come before the public with such ill-considered steps, which can bring so many foreseeable damages? How do they not reckon that, if the intended resolution is adopted and Będzin shuts its gates to imports, what damage this can do in general? It follows that every town should imitate the Będzin "feat" [?], if it is so brilliant, and then it means that one must shut oneself up in a kind of ghetto: every town must produce its goods only in the quantity the little town itself needs. Need one even imagine what ruin that would be for the smaller towns? We know, after all, that everywhere there are dozens of little towns that live thanks to the large town around them, and as soon as the large town ceases to exist for them, it follows that the craftsmen will have to sew themselves beggars' sacks and go begging through the land; otherwise no livelihood remains to them.
And if so, what complaints do we have against the Upper Silesian antisemites when they want that our bones should not come there? It all comes to the same thing: if you are right, then they are certainly and doubly right.
Upon my life, such conduct is neither nice nor decent, neither tactful nor understandable. Perhaps for you here it would indeed have been a salvation, but in the social sense one must not be egoistic and think only of oneself at a time when for the community it is a great harm.
We understand perfectly well that the demands did not arise out of contentment; we know that this is a matter of livelihood and, as the saying goes, need breaks iron. But everything must have a limit, everything must have a measure.
We know, and we have said it more than once, that not wanting [?] to earn is a curse; it is just as dangerous as it was dangerous in those times when the public engaged in profiteering [?] and every hour brought a different price.
Yet it does not follow from this that, because someone does not want or does not need to earn, such dangerous methods must be adopted, methods that are neither ethical nor healthy, neither decent nor fine on our part.
It happens more than once that private businesses collapse because of certain disruptions, and remedies are found for them that could radically heal the dangerous wounds undermining the business; but the remedies are too drastic, and so one does not use them. And that is said when private matters are concerned, in which nobody else has any say; all the more so when it concerns society, public opinion — there one must surely, doubly surely, be sensitive and tactful.
Nobody doubts that one must earn, but at the same time one must not forget that throughout the whole world there exists freedom of competition, and everyone may make his own reckoning and calculation. Insofar as others are more competitive and the local artisan or small trader suffers loss on that account, one must think up a remedy with a calm mind — and that can ultimately be solved.
After all, nobody is so well united and concentrated as the artisans, who have their branches everywhere; they can unite on a party basis and arrive at some kind of settlement.
It is surely too drastic and dangerous to stand before a self-government body with the demand to shut the town's gates to people who bring in their products from other towns, justifying it only by the fact that the articles are too cheap.
Have you ever heard such an idea? The population might well answer that it ought to receive a certain gratuity for it, since the citizens are, after all, precisely out to buy as cheaply as possible.
Can one, in the twentieth century, shut oneself and others behind Chinese walls and say: here we must wait until a customer comes to us, and there we must sell our wares, and we may not move from the spot?
Where, then, is the logic and the decency? Where is the understanding of the time we live in?
R. Let.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings and remarks on this week's portion (Korach)

[Oneg Shabbat — words of Torah on the weekly portion.] Torah sayings and remarks on today's portion.
Collected and edited by Y. L.
Parshat Korach
a) "Now Korah took" (16:1).
Rashi asks: "Korah, who was a clever man — what did he see to commit this folly?" — People ask about this: how does Rashi conclude that Korah was a wise man? The Midrash says: "Korah was a great sage."
The answer is: about Korah the verse "He who trusts in his riches shall fall into evil" is expounded. So he was a very rich man — and if so, then he was automatically a wise man too. — Folk saying.
* * *
"Happy is he that maketh wise the poor [maskil el dal]" (Psalms) — it is only the poor man who needs to be made wise. But surely he needs bread, not wisdom! Rather: when one helps the poor man and he becomes rich, he automatically becomes clever too.
That is why the Men of the Great Assembly instituted for wayfarers the prayer "Havinenu" ("give us understanding"), because travellers on foot are, after all, poor (the rich ride), and so they pray for understanding, cleverness — meaning: money, for "in the shadow of wisdom is the shadow of money" [Eccl. 7:12]. — Imrot Tehorot.
b) "The son of Izhar, the son of Kohath, the son of Levi" (ibid.).
With Korah and his helpers Dathan, Abiram and On, the verse lists their pedigree exactly — so-and-so and so-and-so's son, grandson — because for the makers of strife this is the only protective cloak: pedigree. In themselves they are nothing — Korah, "bald" (bare). — Zot Zikaron.
c) "Called to the assembly, men of renown" (16:2).
One who is truly a great man does not need anyone to advertise him; his greatness advertises itself. By contrast there are "men of renown" of the sort — advertised "geniuses" and "tzaddikim" — whose experienced hangers-on see to making them a name. — The difference between the two is like that between the Sabbath and a festival. "The Sabbath is fixed and established": the Sabbath is holy in itself, whereas a festival must first be sanctified by a rabbinical court (see Rosh Hashanah 25); without the court's sanctification a festival is nothing. — These partners of Korah were "men of renown" of that kind, advertised "great men" who are "called to the assembly [mo'ed]": like a mo'ed, a festival, which is sanctified only by a court — and without another's sanctification it is nothing... — Imrei Shefer.
d) "And they gathered themselves together against Moses and Aaron" (16:3).
Why did rabbis in former times have to suffer bitter troubles and the torments of hell from the common mob — all manner of persecution and oppression — whereas today it is much quieter in this respect? —
The hatred of coarse people for a rabbi stemmed from the natural hatred of an ignoramus for a scholar (see Pesachim 49); and since the ignoramuses were not, after all, judges of who is truly a scholar, so as to persecute him, they chose the rabbi as the target of their hatred, for he was surely a scholar. That was once. Today, however, when rabbis are appointed who are far from being scholars, the mob has nothing against them, and so the rule that a rabbi is a scholar and must be persecuted no longer holds... From this even the rabbis who are scholars now profit... — Gahalei Devash.
* * *
Long ago every village Jew (yishuvnik) took a scholar as a son-in-law and provided him with [?] (reading of the phrase doubtful). It was worth giving him room and board just to get [?] a man of Torah. Today, however, the village Jews have grown wiser, and to save money a whole town takes on a rabbi — a kind of "town son-in-law" on board — and keeps [?] him in partnership... It works out much cheaper... — "Farn altn varker" [?].
* * *
A rabbi was once asked: What's new in your town?
"Well — not good. Peace."
"If there's peace, it's not good? On the contrary!"
"Listen: when there is a dispute I have at least one side. A small side or a big one, but one side is for me. Whereas when there is peace I have nobody; they forget entirely that I need to eat too..." — From the mouth of the people.
e) "Wherefore then lift ye up yourselves" (16:13, as printed).
Rashi says about this: Korah's company argued thus: if you have taken the kingship for yourself, you should not have given your brother the priesthood — for kingship, a kingdom, is given only to one who comes from a fallen family, so that he should not grow too proud. Of Saul's kingdom it is said that it fell for this reason, because no blemish whatsoever was found in his family. "No one is appointed leader over the community unless a basket of reptiles hangs behind him." This is what they argued: if your brother is a priest, then your family must be pure, without any blemish — so how can you be king? — Yeriot Shlomo.
f) "I have not taken one ass from them, neither have I hurt one of them."
For the rabbinate of Prague the "Noda Bi-Yehuda" [R. Yechezkel Landau] and R. Zerach Eidlitz were candidates. The scholars backed the latter, and the common people only the "Noda Bi-Yehuda". When the Noda Bi-Yehuda was elected, his opponents came over to him, and he indeed drew the scholars close. A tailor [?], one who had worked hard for the "Noda Bi-Yehuda", asked him: Rabbi, your enemies you draw so close — and us, who made you rabbi, not?
The Noda Bi-Yehuda answered him thus: usually, when a government changes, the first thing the new ruler does is to replace the officials — he dismisses his enemies, and seats his friends in the chairs, though they are not fit for it, in order to strengthen his power. Moses our teacher, however, acted differently: "I have not taken one ass from them" — I did not raise a single donkey-head among them to a high post, even though he is my supporter; and "neither have I hurt one of them" — on the other hand "one of them", a man of worth, I did not harm [?] because he was my opponent.
With me too a donkey remains a donkey, and an important man — important, not measured by the way they behaved towards me. — Olat Chodesh.
Avot, Chapter Four.
a) "Engage little in business and occupy yourself with Torah, and be lowly of spirit before every man."
If you are one who occupies himself with Torah — trading little and sitting in the study house learning — you will automatically be lowly of spirit, because you will be humbled in people's eyes, they will laugh at you... For "they are wise to do evil": he who does evil and is a wicked man is in people's eyes a sage; whereas "to do good" — he who does good and sits over the Torah — of him they say "they know not": he knows nothing... — Lami Torah [?].

1915 — Be strong and of good courage! — 1930
Special supplement, dedicated to the 15th anniversary of the Będzin "Hakoach".

By Szymon Fürstenberg.

To write today about the need for sport and gymnastics, as a means of physical development in general and for the youth in particular — seems, I think, as superfluous as proving the necessity of using water every day to wash one's face and hands. The understanding of physical development through sporting exercises — which, incidentally, is already today a compulsory[?] subject in the school curriculum — is already so widespread today that only an extremely backward person can still deny this branch of education.

But when we speak of physical education within Jewish society, the situation is not so brilliant. Whereas among the nations of the world the sport movement has embraced all circles without exception, a rather large part of the Jewish population unfortunately regards the movement with complete indifference, and often even with hostility. No one cares at all that Jewish youth, who mostly spend the whole day in cramped and often not at all clean or hygienic dwellings, need physical development, strong muscles and a hardening of the body, which can only be achieved by taking part in various games in the open air; people here will not, or cannot, understand that sport and gymnastics also have, besides this, an important economic significance for our youth. —
Będzin is no exception in this respect.

The new economic conditions of Polish Jewry force a large part of the population to take up hard physical labour, for which the first condition is a strong and resilient organism. And here I can state, as an industrialist, that only[?] a person who is trained in physical work can work precisely and productively and earn a corresponding wage. Such training and endurance at work are found only among people who have engaged in sport and gymnastics. —

Wishing the Będzin gymnastics and sports association "Hakoach", on its 15th jubilee, a brilliant further path of development, and expressing my admiration for its results to date, I permit myself at the same time to point to the most important task that the present jubilarian has yet to fulfil. I mean acquiring a sports ground of its own and building a gymnastics hall of its own. I am of course aware that these tasks exceed the material resources of "Hakoach"; but will Będzin, with such a compact Jewish population, refuse its financial help to realise the plan? I don't believe so. One need only interest the Będzin public, draw it in, and convince it of the necessity of expanding the sports home that already exists here.

That is the urgent and serious task of the Będzin "Hakoach".
Problems of Modern Education.

Dr. R. Rechtman.
[Sport — Będzin, 15th anniversary of "Hakoach"; essay on education.]
The problem of human education already has its own history within the whole complex of problems that together make up general culture.
Parallel to the development of culture, the concept of education also develops; new aspirations and ideals are created.
Whereas only a few decades ago the aim of education was to ease the struggle for existence for the young, today the aim of education is to create the ideal human type, who should take over science and all the experience of the older generation and, on that basis, create new values more quickly and easily. And although the concept of human education has not yet finally crystallised, there already exist basic principles recognised by almost all cultured nations; the most important of them are: the harmonious development of the physical and mental powers of the young, the elevation of human ethics, the changing of character by removing all kinds of harmful instincts such as hatred, revenge and the like, and the development of all social feelings — in order to create the type of the friend of mankind (homo socius).
All these aspirations of a purely materialistic nature should, in the opinion of the practitioners, create the best material living conditions for the ideal human type.
Although practical life — the real educational systems, which every country and government creates as a tool for its own ends — stands for the most part in open contradiction to the above-mentioned principles, it is nevertheless known that progress leads to their realisation and that some of them are already partly being realised. Such is the case with the principle of the harmonious development of the mental and physical powers of the young: the truth that without physical education the mental development of the young is almost impossible has today no opponent at all; that is precisely why the gymnastic and sport associations have grown so strongly and form a mighty organisation in all countries.
That is why the name "Hakoach" or "Maccabi" is today a symbol of physical strength, mental development and strong organisation.
Shimon Rotenberg — Body and Spirit.

[Sport — Będzin, 15th anniversary of "Hakoach"; essay.]
One must truly admire the daring of the few young people who, 15 years ago, had the courage to take upon themselves the initiative of founding in Będzin the gymnastics and sport association "Hakoach".
The growing-up youth thinks that in those days, on the Jewish street, people looked upon practising sport as naturally as they do today, when even the older generation already understands something of the significance of sport and its usefulness for health.
There was a time when among Jews, especially in Poland, sport was regarded as acrobats' tricks, as some non-Jewish occupation not at all fitting for decent young men. After all, the symbol of an honest[?], refined young man, with whom mothers felt blessed, was a pale, thin young man with the look of "Rabbi Zadok's dried fig".
It was still the time when Torah was the best merchandise and physical culture was looked upon with disdain and even contempt, and a healthy, broad-shouldered young man was regarded as a "Greek" with only a very slight connection to Jewishness.
It is no wonder that this negative view of sport was so deeply rooted in the psyche of the Jewish masses, for in the course of generations, chained by the spirit of history, always exposed to the "mercies" of the mob, the Jew became so dejected, so degraded in his human dignity, that his sense for physical culture simply atrophied. He realised that any physical resistance was useless and that by force he would be unable to get through his life among the various nations, among whom he forms a proportion of one to a hundred. The Jew therefore had to find another way out — how to slip through and stay on the surface of life, and not go under in the sea of the nations that hate him.
Therefore, searching for means not to be crushed by "the hands of Esau", we neglected the body and developed the brain, which we forced to invent the most varied unnatural combinations — how to smuggle ourselves through life and save ourselves from destruction. We brought our brain to such a level that we became wonderful mental acrobats, but at the same time we became physically crippled and turned into shadows of human beings, with a kind of illusory, sickly, strange[?], daring life.
Thanks are therefore due to the founders and leaders of "Hakoach" for their lofty and difficult task — to cultivate sport in Jewish society and thereby contribute to the regeneration of the Jewish race, which had already almost found itself on the threshold of complete physical degeneration.
One thing, however, must be remembered: sport must on no account be brought to the level of senseless competition, made into a fetish, a kind of new "idolatry", as is the case with boxing and football, where thousands of spectators fall into a crazed ecstasy and the crowd divides into hostile camps, and very often it even comes to bloodshed.
Sport has a right to exist only as long as it serves its purpose, i.e. when its task is to make the body healthy and resistant to the bad influences of nature.
But we must on no account repeat the mistake we made with brain-gymnastics, when we neglected the body for the sake of the brain; perhaps we thereby gained a somewhat heavier brain, but in return the body withered. Care must therefore be taken that in sport our whole attention is not devoted to the feet, thereby causing the neglect of the brain. The golden mean must be found that will lead to a harmony of body and spirit. Only then is there a guarantee that we shall succeed in raising a healthy, life-loving generation, which will surely have to wage a heroic struggle for its existence, and which will have to carry, in the hopeless black night that seems to cover all mankind, the torches of light and freedom, in order to show mankind new, brighter and better ways.
Long Live Jewish Sport!

[Będzin — sport; feuilleton for the 15th anniversary of “Hakoach”.] (Chatter for the 15th anniversary jubilee)

The old Torah's worth nothing, friend,
No one will pay its price,
A Torah counts today, my friend,
If you kick in four goals...

A good smash, a good crack,
My friend, if you can deliver,
Then you're sure of success,
Then you make a fine living...

Gone, gentlemen, are the years of old!..

Oh, once!... Once! Once — tell me — a young man was called a prodigy, a genius, if he knew some 500 folios of Gemara by heart, or at the very least all six orders of the Mishnah; later, when the Haskalah arose — if one knew all of Pisarev, with Belinsky, Pushkin, Lermontov, with Goethe and Schiller... Today, for our many sins, whom do we call a hero? The one who can give the ball a good shot so that it lands straight into the “bramka” [the goal]... Do you hear? A hero, so to speak [?]!.. And once someone does score a goal — so what? A trifle! And the brains one needs for that, the strong grasp, the brilliant memory?...

Sprasln [?], brother dear. You won't remake the world! We live today in such a time that all wisdom lies in the hands...

A good smash... a good crack... Yes, yes, my friend. How well off the people of Israel would be if it could smash... England would reckon with us quite differently, and we would not have to go begging for another few hundred certificates for our halutzim, and we would now be spared protesting.

Protesting!... Ah, why not? What harm can it do? On the contrary.., only the paper protest would have the proper effect if the little paper were accompanied by at least a tiny free supplement of a couple of little forty-two-centimetre howitzers, two or three little tanks and three little barrels of the newest, modern poison gases..

You see, that would work better than Weizmann's best, most successful speech at the Geneva assembly...

It appears that the blessing with which Isaac blessed Esau — “By thy sword shalt thou live” — was in fact the true blessing...

That the American boxer Dempsey has had more success in life than Shakespeare, you surely know. A mediocre circus athlete [?] earns a bigger fee than a well-known poet — that is the world we have today.

Yes, against what am I saying this? Against the fact that in today's cultured twentieth century only the hands count.

Until now we have had the “voice of Jacob”, and that is not in fashion now; well, never mind, we shall now learn to adopt Esau's fashion...

Therefore I say: blessed and beatified [?] be the Będzin “Hakoach”, which is forging for us a generation of strong, healthy Jews with muscles of steel and mighty chests.

I have just been in Bielitz [?] [Bielsko] at the congress of Jewish sports associations.

What shall I tell you, gentlemen — it was impressive; my heart swelled with pride watching how our brethren, the children of Israel, do gymnastics, and now — their marching in a ceremonial march.

Their running did not even impress me: I know that Jews are used to running... But marching! With discipline, in step on the left foot.. at the proper distance, to the sounds of an orchestra — that, you see, was a surprise for me.. And one must admit that they do it magnificently; it seems to me that Hindenburg himself, if he saw the marchers, would have his Junker heart swell with pride — even though these are Jews...

And now — you should have treated yourselves to a look at our maidens, the daughters of Zion, as they marched in the ranks and shot.. not with the ball but with their eyes. I tell you, gentlemen, that I, a sedate [?] man, already a father of children, no evil eye — would you believe it or not? — could not tear my judging [?] eyes away.

Yes, thus grow the true grandchildren of Bar Kokhba. And let us indeed wish them with the genuine Jewish blessing:
Hazak ve-ematz! [Be strong and of good courage!]
Strong! Courageous! Strong!
Ah, sharp the muscle and the fist,
Einstein's spirit, Herculean strength —
together, after all, it gives a firm hold [?]!..
Kaligraf.
1913–1930. (A Bundle of Memories)

[Będzin — sport; "Hakoach", memoirs.] By Yaakov Erlich [Jakub Erlich].
Actually we already have behind us today not 15 but 17 years of "Hakoach" work in Będzin, for as early as 1913 the idea was born among a group of us pupils to found a Jewish gymnastics society (Turnverein) in our town. In the summer of 1913 we are already realising our wish, and we meet in the garden at "Kardan's", where we carry out various gymnastic exercises on the primitive apparatus that we had procured for ourselves with our modest funds. The Tsarist authorities regard our activity with suspicion and hatred, as they do any public organisation in general; we therefore hold our lessons "conspiratorially". For that reason, too, we could not admit any women to our circle, although many of them also wanted to take part in the gymnastic exercises. —
Our development work makes no halting[?] progress, so that already a few months later, in February 1914, several of us, together with the writer of these lines, take part in the first Jewish gymnastics festival (Turnfest) in Łódź.
At that festival our performances were very highly rated, and we travel home from Łódź with an ecstatic urge to widen the field of our activity and to draw the whole of Jewish youth into our physical-education work.
With what joy, I remember, we received the first bars [parallel bars] from Kielce[?] in April 1914. We carried the bars on our shoulders from the railway station to "Kardan's"; with religious fervour we marched with them through the town, proud that we already owned our own first apparatus, like other people. We carry on the work with enthusiasm, but it can no longer be conducted in secret, and we look for ways to become legal. Our statutes, which were signed by Messrs. Dr. Wasercwajg, President Rubinlicht, Szlama Gutman and the recently deceased Mr. Izydor Sercaush[?], were rejected by the Governor of Piotrków. Only thanks to the help of Mr. R. of Piotrków and a few "red papers" [i.e. banknotes, a bribe] are we legalised by the Russian authorities on 7 May 1914. —
In 1913 we had held the first founding meeting in the "Kardan" garden, where the name of the society — "Hakoach" — was also decided. The official founding meeting, however, takes place only on 12 June 1914 in the "Harmonia" hall, chaired by Dr. Wasercwajg, with a large attendance of Będzin's Jewish youth. —
The first legitimate board, however, was not destined to enjoy a long life. In August 1914 the world slaughter [the World War] already begins, and the general depression that then gripped Jewish public life did not spare "Hakoach" either.
After the partial normalisation in connection with the "newly created situation" brought about by the war, the most brilliant period of our "Hakoach" work in Będzin begins. The years 1915/16/17 undoubtedly belong to our golden epoch of colossal and fruitful activity.
In the autumn of 1915 we rent our present premises from Mr. Zmigród, from which, however, we had little joy, for within a short time [—] [—] [—] [—] [—] [—] a horde of German secret agents [—] our premises and sealed the premises on us. The activity is thereby naturally interrupted, and a new "legalisation series" begins, which cost us a good deal of trouble and effort at the time.
Just then the society for Hebrew culture "Ivria" is founded, and we persuade its initiators to include[?] in their statutes the right to conduct physical-education work among Jewish youth, so that we could continue our development under the cloak of "Ivria". For quite a long time we indeed figured specifically as the "Hakoach" section of the "Ivria" society. —
Because of administrative disputes, and mainly because of "Ivria's" condition that all "Hakoach" members must learn Hebrew, we again begin the efforts to become independent. Both the German district (Kreis) administration and the Governor-General for Poland, von Kries, refused by any means to legalise us.
Only thanks to the intervention of the "Zionist Federation for Germany" with the government in Berlin do we receive — the first in Poland — permission to found "Hakoach".
At that time we succeeded in popularising the idea of physical education among Będzin's Jewish youth to an enormous extent. Whole hordes of pale little faces and hunched backs came to us, in order to get back the sparkle in their eyes and strengthened muscles. Our work also yielded fruitful results. Thus, e.g., at the Częstochowa competition in 1916 our members received 6–7 diplomas. And the splendid review of our ranks at Vika-vitz[?] on 15/7 1917, at the unveiling of the flag, first truly showed us the greatness of our work. Hundreds of members and girls became more vigorous and more full of the joy of life thanks to their physical development. When we saw the shining eyes of the young, healthy throng, we received our reward for our long years of trouble and effort. Their joie de vivre was our wage, for we too had a large share in it.
In 1916/17 we also ran courses in hygiene and anatomy, which were conducted by Messrs. Dr. Weinzieher, Dr. Wasercwajg and Dr. Rechtschaft[?]. We also obtained at that time from the German school inspector the introduction of compulsory gymnastics in the schools and heders, to which we delegated our instructors. I remember how I taught the children of the "Talmud Torah", and with what grateful looks the little ones rewarded me after every lesson (the present board, too, should give this some thought).
At the end of 1917, beginning of 1918, we begin preparations for the great all-Polish competition of the Jewish gymnastics societies. But suddenly, like a bolt from the blue, comes the news: "the Lwów pogrom". Bitterness and disappointment reign among Jewish youth; we no longer think about the competition and inform the Jewish population that "for reasons beyond our control" the competition is cancelled.
Along with this, a degeneration sets in within the society. Members leave for the Land of Israel, some go to serve in the army, a standstill reigns in the movement. The special situation of the Jews in the country at that time does not permit the continuation of our work. This state of affairs lasts until 1922. Later, too, up to the most recent time, "Hakoach" confines itself solely to the sport of football.
Me personally — who wants to see in "Hakoach" the all-round physical training cauldron, from which the young person should emerge armed with healthy muscles and a strong organism, fit[?] for the hard struggle of life awaiting him in today's stubborn, merciless reality — the merely one-sided physical education of football, of "star-ism" and favouritism could not satisfy. I therefore withdrew in 1922 from the active ranks of the society.
Those who came after me shall tell how it was later.
The Aims and Tasks of the “Maccabi” Movement

Dr. Ewin[?] Mechner (Pilica [?])
(Dedicated to the 15th jubilee of the Będzin Jewish Gymnastics and Sports Association “Hakoach”.)
The world union “Maccabi” is the federation of all national gymnastics and sports associations, from all countries; its main task is the physical revival of the Jewish popular masses.
For the welfare of the Jewish people and of the Jewish land, which demands a healthy and strong generation.
We Jewish sportsmen must contribute to the revival of the Jewish people.
In the revival movement we have taken upon ourselves a very difficult task, and that is the physical education of the Jewish people.
Already 30 years ago we came to the conviction that, simultaneously with the cultural and spiritual revival, the physical one must also come. This difficult task was taken on by the Jewish gymnastics and sports associations, which put into their programme: to raise a healthy Jewish generation.
The will to physical strengthening and to the national education of the Jewish people is the driving force in the “Maccabi” movement.
The world union “Maccabi” strives for our gymnastics associations to be the standard-bearers of the revival of the Jewish people, as the associations of all other nations are.
The task that the “Maccabi” union has set itself is not only to train gymnasts, or to pursue other sports for the sake of self-gratification; it has a great educational significance. For us the gymnastic apparatus is not merely a mechanical tool, and the practice of gymnastics [not merely] a world-view, but both [?] together are a means of education.
The times are past when one had to prove that we Jews are not incapable of taking part in sports exercises; nor is it appropriate nowadays to make propaganda for founding sports associations merely for their own [?] sake.
We take pride in the fact that our movement is one whose roots have already struck deep and wide. Alongside the gymnastics lessons and other sports games, we want at the same time to acquaint our members with the great history of their people and with their own language, and in this way we want to educate our youth, physically and spiritually, and to make of them people of strength and energy.
Whoever wants to take part in the education of the Jewish youth, whoever believes in the future of the Jewish people and wants to work for this beautiful idea, must join the ranks of the world union “Maccabi”.
A Look Back...

(Pictures from the past.)
In a small garden behind the town a few young people stand carrying out the orders of their leader. Quietly he commands: “Ready! Right turn! Forward march!”
Suddenly a comrade comes running: “Sh! and no further [?], quietly — a strażnik [policeman] is coming!”
Barely 2–3 minutes pass, and not a trace is left of the gymnastics lesson!
That is how the first Hakoach members — Erlich, Klajman, Lederman, Pasternak, Winer and others — began building “Hakoach”, in the garden by the “Kordan” [?], in the year 1913.
* * *
The whole town is “boiling”, astir... Here they come! Now the orchestra can be heard; the first cyclists ride up in blue-and-white caps.
The streets are full of people. All the balconies decorated and overflowing with friends of Hakoach [?].
“Gymnast, brother, firm and strong”... the song rings out from afar; the voice grows ever stronger...
Yes, our “Hakoach” is marching...
One, two, three, four — they march; “Bravo!” cries the crowd with enthusiasm.
Long live “Hakoach”!
The Hakoach excursion of 1917 left unforgettable days behind it.
* * *
Lemberg, Kielce, Płock and Jabłonna [?].
It is quiet in “Hakoach”: the people's militia needs [?] the premises.
The beloved apparatus fall through the windows.
With bowed heads the gymnast brothers pass by.
But we comrades are strong enough;
Interventions [?], endless efforts — and the Hakoach member is once again doing gymnastics in his premises.
The hard days of 1919 are gone.
* * *
In closed ranks they march, the gymnast sisters and gymnast brothers, in their costumes, through the streets of the town.
— What holiday is it? an old Jew asks himself.
— It is the 10th jubilee of “Hakoach”...
Behind several dozen notables [?] of the town, headed by Dr. Weinzieher, the association marches to its own “boisko” [sports ground], where hundreds of guests are already waiting impatiently.
Once more the town has lived through a “great day”.
* * *
Already the second generation attends the association...
Gymnastics is popular by now; it has penetrated almost everywhere: into schools, into various organisations.
Who today cannot command, or teach gymnastics?
Every child already knows what a handstand [?] is, or a “Reck” [horizontal bar], a “goal” or a “bramkarz [?]”; cyclists, swimmers — as many as you like;
medals, prizes, “genrades” [?] and the like — a respectable [?] total..!
R.
Programme of the 15th anniversary of the Jewish Gymnastics and Sports Association „Hakoach“, Będzin

The 15th anniversary of Będzin's „Hakoach“, which falls this Friday, Saturday and Sunday, promises to be an imposing demonstration of Jewish sport in Zagłębie.
After lengthy requests and interventions, the Railway Ministry has agreed to grant the participants a 50 per cent railway reduction on the return journey from Będzin. Special certificates will be issued by Będzin's „Hakoach“.
The great sports festival has aroused strong interest. The „Maccabi“ associations of Lemberg (Lwów), Kraków, Cieszyn, Bielitz (Bielsko), Dziedzice, Chrzanów, Sosnowiec, Königshütte, Częstochowa, Olkusz, Dąbrowa, „Chieruszów“[?] and others have announced their participation. A number of over 300 participants, apart from delegates and guests. Also represented will be delegates of the presidium of the World Union [of Maccabi], „Maccabi“ Berlin, Warsaw, Kraków, Bielitz.
Because of the large number of participants the board of „Hakoach“ has endeavoured to enlarge the sports ground. For this reason a special grandstand has also been erected.
The programme of the celebration is as follows:
○ Today, Friday the 27th of June, in the afternoon, visits will be paid to the Polish zinc-sheet industry in Będzin, the filters of the waterworks and the technical installations of the municipal electricity works.
○ Saturday the 28th: at 3 p.m. handball match between „Maccabi“ Bielitz — „Maccabi“ Königshütte; 3.30 p.m. football match between „Wisła“ Kraków — „Hakoach“ Będzin, 1st „League“. 9 p.m. torchlight procession through the streets. Assembly point: Sobieskiego street. The march passes through the streets: Sobieskiego, Kołłątaja, Małachowskiego, Piłsudskiego, „Magroshever“[?] [probably Modrzejowska], to the station and back. 10.30 p.m. a festive academy, including a concert part performed by the „Hakoach“ orchestra.
○ Sunday the 29th: 6 a.m. reveille signals performed by the „Hakoach“ orchestra; 7 a.m. competition: gymnastic exercises, light athletics (on our own sports ground), from 10—12 a.m. general rehearsal with the participation of all associations; from 10—12 a cycle race, 40 kilometres. Taking part: „Hasmonea“ (Lemberg), the „Maccabi“ associations of Warsaw, Piotrków, Sosnowiec, Kielce, Kraków, „Bar Kochba“ (Warsaw), „Hakoach“ (Radomsko), „Warta“ (Częstochowa), „Bar Kochba“ (Łódź). Assembly point: 9 a.m. on the „Hakoach“ ground; departure: Kościuszki — „Gawa“[?], via Małobądz, Czeladź, Grodziec, Wojkowice Komorne as far as the Szarlej bridge and back. 2 cups have been donated: the Polish zinc-sheet factory „S. Fürstenberg“ and Dir. Natan Gutman. Valuable objects have been donated by the firms: Gutman and Lichtenstein (Katowice) and „Esper“ (Katowice). From 10 to 12 a relay race. Assembly point 9 a.m. on the „Hakoach“ ground. At 2 p.m. the delegations and associations assemble with their banners on Sobieskiego street. 2.15 p.m. march-out with our own orchestra through the streets Kołłątaja, Małachowskiego, Kościuszki to our own sports ground. 3 p.m. general gymnastics festival. Free exercises performed by all participants (500 persons), special displays by the „Maccabi“ associations of Bielitz, Chrzanów, Sosnowiec, Cieszyn and „Hakoach“ (Będzin), gymnastics on the horizontal bar, parallel bars, horse; the musical part performed by the „Hakoach“ orchestra. 5.30 p.m. football match between „Ruch“ (Hajduki) — „Hakoach“ (Będzin), 1st League. 10 p.m. a reception (raut) in the „Góra Zamkowa“ hall for delegates and invited guests.
What's Heard in Zagłębie? — Będzin — The First Group of Schoolchildren off to the Summer Colony

[Będzin — municipality, children.] This year the girls go first.
This year's summer colony at the Magistrat (town council) has been reorganised as follows: in enrolling the children who qualify to go to the summer colony, the decision rests only with the doctors, officials of the Magistrat, and not, as until now, with the committee.
On Monday evening, under the chairmanship of Vice-President Mr. Rubinlicht, the first meeting of the committee, teachers and others took place.
At the meeting it was decided, at the request of the heads of the girls' schools, that this year the girls from the public (powszechne) schools go first.
The first group, numbering 240 children, leaves for Sławków next Tuesday, 1 July (lipiec).
Each child pays 5 zł. for travel expenses.
In addition, it was decided to admit to the summer colony a certain number of children from outside the schools for a minimal fee.
The second group, of boys, will probably go only on 30 July.
Kehilla Delegates to Lublin

[Będzin — kehilla.] At the opening of the "Yeshivat Chachmei Lublin" the Będzin kehilla was represented by the dozór (board) members Elazar Bżykowski and Abraham Liwer.
Mr. Bżykowski had even proposed that he alone should go, since Mr. Abraham Liwer had only recently been a delegate at the congress of kehillot; but after all, there is no such thing as a poor kehilla — so 2 delegates went...
As in the Old "Good Times"...

[Będzin — education, Agudah.] We know that the "Agudah" is a modern party, just like everyone else. On the other hand, in the "Agudah" cheder the old methods of the former "khurim" [sic; probably cheders] are still in use.
Now we are told that on Tuesday a melamed of that cheder took revenge on his guilty pupil and tried to throw him by force into a dark cellar.
The struggling boy fought with his last strength and finally tore himself out of his tormentor's hands.
A Bus Disaster beyond Siewierz

[Będzin area — accident.] Several passengers, among them 2 Jews, seriously injured.
On Monday morning a disaster befell the bus running on the Chmielnik—Będzin line. The bus was completely smashed, and the passengers, among whom were 2 Jews, were injured.
The victims are being treated in the local hospital.
The Rabbinate Does Not Permit "Hakoach" to Hold a Prayer in the Synagogue

[Będzin — rabbinate, sport.] In honour of the 15th anniversary of the local Jewish gymnastics society "Hakoach", the committee applied several times to the rabbinate, and especially to the Rabbi, for permission to hold in the synagogue, on Saturday night (motsei Shabbat), a prayer and a memorial service (hazkarah) for the deceased members.
The Rabbi, despite the fact that the gmina (community board) did give permission, turned the request down.
Distinctions for Pupils of Bojarska's School

[Będzin — education.] This year the 8 pupils of the commercial school under the direction of Maria Bojarska passed their examinations with good distinctions.
The names of the pupils are:
Z. Binsztok, L. Fiszer, E. Fiszer, G. Gliksman, G. Heller, C. Meryn, S. Pasterman (Sosnowiec) and M. Patasz.
In addition, the pupils won the following good places in the stenography competitions:
At the Chamber of Commerce in Königshütte [Królewska Huta] (2nd and 3rd place).
At the Stenography Society of the Silesian Voivodeship (1st place) and at the Economic Commercial School in Katowice (3rd place).
Don't Leave Your Flats Unguarded

[Będzin — theft.] On Saturday afternoon a young Jewish couple on the Grobla went out for a walk, leaving their flat locked. A short time later the couple had a visitor, who suddenly saw that the couple's flat was open and that a "craftsman" was moving about inside.
At the visitor's alarm the thief vanished.
General Meeting of "Hachnasat Kallah"

[Będzin — charity, societies.] On Thursday, under the chairmanship of Mr. Yechiel Zojberman, the annual general meeting of the "Hachnasat Kallah" (dowering of brides) society took place. On the presidium were: Mrs. Chawa Unger and Noach Ojazd [?].
The report on the activity to date was given by Mr. Sendyszew. It turns out that in the course of the year the institution gave out subsidies to 38 brides in a sum of 1380 zł. In the treasury there are 999 zł. and 33 groszy.
Then the following board was elected: Ch. B. Goldblum, Mrs. Ch. Unger, Noach Ojazd, H. Sztajnkeler, Mrs. S. Salcberg, Ch. Wekselman, Mrs. A. Rajzman, A. Strucel [?], Mrs. T. Fiszer.
Deputies: J. Rajzman, Ch. A. Zylberman, J. L. Jeruszi [?], Ch. Zojberman, M. C. Zygdorf.
On the audit committee: J. Zojberman, Mrs. Landau, Ch. Pozmantier.
On Tuesday the “Poradnik” will start operating.

The “Merchants’ Association” announces that the department called “Poradnik [Adviser] Bookkeeping”, where guidance and advice will be given to merchants on how to keep commercial books and the like, will begin operating as early as Tuesday the 1st [of July 1930].
People are “throwing away” the kehilla seats...

Mr. Meir Szenwald, who had been nominated by the Starostwo [district administration] as a member of the kehilla board, has handed in a letter in which he resigns from the office.
The same was also done by the nominee to the kehilla council, Mr. Chaim Dawid Rudzin.
The kehilla “needs” to increase the number of rabbinic deciders.

There is no one to rule on a ritual question.
Moshe Sonnenschein, a poultry dealer, needed on Friday morning to ask a ritual question (shayle) about a goose. So he — as he tells it — wandered from one moyre-hoyroe [rabbinic decider] to the next, and everywhere he got the answer:
— “Not at home, go elsewhere”..
The running around went on like this for several hours. In the end he could not get through to any moyre-hoyroe, and the goose thereby became treyf...
Sonnenschein turned with the complaint to the kehilla board, which promised to settle the matter.
A big fire averted.
On Wednesday before dawn a fire broke out in the house at Kołłątaja [Street] 20, at the home of Mr. Gelk [?]. Fortunately the fire was noticed in time, and thanks to that a big fire was averted.
General meeting of office employees.

On Sunday the general meeting of the Będzin office employees took place. Despite the hot summer day, the local “proletariat in white cuffs” turned up to the meeting in masses. It is indeed to be regretted that the older generation of office workers was so sparsely represented.
In the presence of about 100 persons, councilman Fajner opens the meeting and proposes to elect a chairman; Mr. Zarachs is elected, who invites Miss Glik and Mr. Hercyger as assessors and Mr. Gelbard as secretary.
The report, delivered by Mr. Braner, is taken note of by those assembled, and the meeting proceeds to its most important task — approving the statute. A discussion develops around the individual points, in which a number of speakers take part; finally, at around midnight, the statute is adopted with the votes of all present against 3.
Elected to the board were: Zarachs, Wygadzki, Tenenbaum, Frajlich, Braner, Fajner, Rechnic, Hercyger and Kozłowski.
On Thursday the first constituent meeting of the board took place. Since Mr. Zarachs laid down his mandate, Mr. Strachlik entered the board in his place.
The presidium consists of Mr. Fajner (chairman), Frajlich (vice), Tenenbaum (secretary) and Mr. Rechnic (treasurer).
At the last meeting it was decided to send declarations to all offices and to call on all office workers to enrol as members of the association.
Sosnowiec — the kehilla council “sweats” at home...

On Sunday a meeting of the kehilla council was supposed to take place; on the agenda were several kehilla questions to be considered. But the meeting did not come about, because the vice-president himself also stayed at home.
Meeting of Zionists.

In its own premises a general meeting of the Zionist organisation took place on Thursday.
Mr. Wajgreb opens the meeting and recalls the [memory?; printed “tsviye”] of the late Abraham Podliszewski, who is honoured by those assembled by rising.
The chair is handed to Mr. Engineer Mangel, with Messrs. Jasny and Buszecki as assessors.
The report on the activities is given by Mr. Wajgreb, on the treasury — by Mr. Gitler; it turns out that there is a deficit of 13 hundred złoty.
After the discussions, which bore a party character, confidence is expressed in the board.
The new board comprises: Wajgryb, Rozman, Tages [?], Gitler, Klarman, Feldman, Mrs. Langer, Ojazer [?], Glidman, Jasny, Kramałowski. Deputies: Ankielewicz, Buszecki, Triger and Abramczyk.
A woman and her child run over.

On Tuesday morning at Modrzejowska [Street] 15 a droshky ran over a woman and her child. Both were taken to the municipal outpatient clinic, where the doctor established that the child is “seriously injured, while the mother was only bruised.
Plenary Session of the Chamber of Commerce.

On Thursday, the 3rd of July (lipiec), in the afternoon, the 5th plenary session of the local Chamber of Commerce will take place; among other things, the agenda includes the question of erecting a building of its own for the Chamber of Commerce.
“Vita” No Longer Comes to Sosnowiec.

The price commission at the local magistrate [municipality] included the Kraków bread “Vita” in the price set for wholemeal rye (razowy) bread. The police saw to it that consumers should not pay more for the “Vita” bread than for ordinary wholemeal rye bread. Because of this, the firm in Kraków has stopped sending the “healthy” bread “Vita” here.
From the Keren Kayemet.

The Flower Day, which was to have taken place on Tuesday the 24th of this month, has for a certain reason been postponed to Thursday, the 3rd of July.
—o—
The “Birds” Have Been Sent Back to Their “Nests”.
The local police have arrested the international thieves Fridlig and Kastenbaum, who had already been wanted for a long time for various thefts.
Fridlig was sent home to Lemberg [Lwów] and Kastenbaum to Warsaw.
—o—
If You Have “Cash”, You Must Guard It...
From the flat of A. Gajman [?] on Kołłątaja Street, 18 hundred zł were stolen.
Dąbrowa — Celebration in Honour of the Opening of the Lublin Yeshiva.

On Tuesday evening the local committee for the Yeshivat Chachmei Lublin held a celebration in the synagogue in honour of the opening of the Lublin yeshiva.
Before a large audience, the parnas L. Szczepanowski [?] and M. Ch. Ajzenman spoke on current affairs and called for support of the yeshiva.
On behalf of the “Tzeirei Emunei [Israel]”, Grignraz [?] and Fuks spoke; the choir sang “Mizmor Shir Chanukat [ha-Bayit]”, and at the end the young men danced, singing “Ve-taher libenu”.
—o—
The “Activity” of the Local Kehilla Leaders.
As has already been reported in the paper, a young Jewish woman has lost her mind, and she causes great troubles to those around her.
The local “Women’s Association” took an interest in the unfortunate Jewish woman, as did people with compassionate hearts, who took it upon themselves to create a fund to send her away to a mental institution.
Naturally, the so-called “Rescue Committee” turned first of all for support to the kehilla leaders, whose task, after all, is to support such cases of need [?]; but the kehilla leaders gave the same answer as the “democratic magistrate” [municipality]: — “We have no fund for such matters.”
The tactics of the kehilla leaders have outraged a great number of kehilla taxpayers, who ask themselves: “Is this case not as important as travelling to the congress of kehillot in Warsaw?”
For everything, even for things truly unnecessary, there is money; but when one has to rescue a respectable Jewish woman — there is no fund of a paltry 100 zł...
—o—
Summer Colonies of “Hashomer Hatzair”.
As every year, the local “Hashomer Hatzair” is organising summer colonies for its members. Up to 50 people in 2 groups will take part in this year’s colony, which will take place in Kotowice (near Żarki). The first group of 25 people leaves already on the 2nd of July. In order to have funds for the colony, the leadership has proclaimed the 1st of July “Shomer Day”.
On that day a Flower Day and a forfeit lottery will be held. We believe that the Dąbrowa public will appreciate this valuable organisation and support the campaign.
—o—
Nowaczyński Is Honoured with Rotten Eggs.
The local Endeks brought down from Warsaw the well-known antisemite Nowaczyński, who gave a lecture here on the subject “Gases over Warsaw”.
In the middle of the lecture a shower of “fresh” eggs poured onto the platform, which chased the lecturer off the platform.

A Great Fire in Sarnów. 30 Houses, 12 Barns Gone up in Smoke.

[Będzin district — fire.] On Tuesday morning a fire broke out in the village of Sarnów which, because it quickly engulfed the surrounding village buildings and barns, was only put out in the evening — despite the great rescue effort of hundreds of firemen under the command of the Będzin police commandant and the starost Baksa.
30 houses and 12 barns went up in smoke. The damage is very great. For the most part working people have suffered. As the firemen report, 2 children also perished in the fire.
Letters to the Editors

[Będzin and Sosnowiec — letters to the editors: the tenants' union and the water question; charity; the Zionist Organisation.]
I.
Esteemed Editors!
I ask you to print the following letter, for which I thank you in advance.
In no. 25 of your esteemed paper, in the article entitled "Short-sightedness in every field", the Tenants' Union is attacked, among other things, in connection with the water question. As chairman of this institution I consider it my duty to point out to Mr. R. Les that: 1) he is unfortunately not versed in the water question, because he probably did not hear, or did not want to hear, my statement in the city council on the water question concerning the tenants who pay rent together with the water; and 2) the author ought first to have acquainted himself with the decree of the President of the Republic, which says:
Do opłat za wodę i za kanały w domach znajdujących się w miastach względnie w części miast, które gminnych urządzeń wodociągowych i kanalizacyjnych w dniu wejścia w życie ustawy, nieposiadały, skoro domy takie zostałe połączone z wodociągiem gminnym albo kanałami gminnem
["For charges for water and sewerage in houses situated in towns or parts of towns which on the day the law came into force did not possess municipal water-supply and sewerage installations, if such houses have been connected to the municipal water mains or municipal sewers"]
According to this decree, or in other words this harsh edict, one must indeed be "short-sighted" not to see that the town, which in 1924 still had no water mains, does not benefit from art. 7 of the tenants' protection law, in which it is said that when [the rent] reaches 75 percent of the pre-war rent, the tenant stops paying for water. Only the Sejm can change the law. But one swallow does not make a summer, and articles that stir up the public can in no way improve the situation. This is not the way, Mr. R. Les. The Tenants' Union has done much for its members and also for all tenants, very quietly, modestly — without unfeasible undertakings and without unfounded alarms. The Union will never come out with demagogy; that we leave to Mr. R. Les.
Respectfully,
M. Lewin,
Chairman of the Tenants' Union in Będzin.
II.
Esteemed Mr. Editor!
Allow me to print the following lines in your esteemed paper, for which I express my best thanks.
Next Tuesday, 12 Tammuz, is my 60th birthday. Instead of holding a banquet I pledge 100 zł. to the following institutions: the free-loan (Gemilut Hasadim) fund, "Malbish Arumim", the Talmud Torah, Beit Lechem, the orphanage, Hachnasat Kalla, Hachnasat Orchim, Ezrat Menachem Avelim, Linat Hacholim and the Dobroczynność [charity society] — 10 zł. to each institution.
I believe that in the present hard, critical time in which we Jews find ourselves, everyone ought, according to his means, to support every institution.
Respectfully,
Eliezer Brzykowski.
III.
Most esteemed Mr. Editor!
Reading in the last issue of your esteemed paper that I have been elected to the board of the local Zionist Organisation, I have the honour to declare publicly that because of my state of health I unfortunately cannot accept the mandate. Thank you, Mr. Editor.

What Is Happening in Upper Silesia?

[Upper Silesia — politics and unemployment.]
The Sejm session called off.
On Tuesday the 1st of this month a session of the Upper Silesian Sejm was to take place in Katowice. By a decree of the President of the Republic the Sejm session was called off.
Deputy Korfanty gets slapped.
On Saturday night, when Deputy Korfanty entered the "Savoy" hotel in Katowice, Dr. Kijowski[?] of Brzezin[?] approached him and asked whether he had the pleasure of speaking with Korfanty. When Korfanty declared: "That is I", Dr. Kijowski gave him a fiery slap and at the same time introduced himself, saying: "This is for my wife".
The reason for the slap is that at the session of the Upper Silesian Sejm Korfanty insulted the wife of Dr. Kijowski, who is also a deputy.
Demonstration of the unemployed.
In Königshütte [Chorzów] a demonstration of the unemployed took place with the participation of Sejm deputy Wieczorek; under the slogan "We want bread and work" the crowd marched to the municipal offices. There the police forced them to disperse.

How Będzin's Hakoach Celebrated Its 15th Jubilee

[Sport — Będzin; 15th jubilee of Hakoach.]
On 27, 28 and 29 June, Hakoach in Będzin celebrated in grandiose fashion the 15th jubilee of its existence.
In honour of the jubilee, gymnasts, delegates and guests came not only from Zagłębie but also from Dziedzice, Bielitz (Bielsko), Cieszyn, Königshütte (Chorzów), Chrzanów, Warsaw, Olkusz, Zawiercie and elsewhere. The largest gymnastic groups came with their banners. Particularly outstanding in this respect were the gymnasts from Königshütte, who drew attention by marching like real military men.
The guests were lodged in comfortable premises specially prepared in the public schools (in "Piast"). In general the organisers saw to it that the visitors from outside were properly received.
In the course of Friday the delegates and guests, together with representatives of the [municipal] administration, visited Fürstenberg's zinc factory, the filters of the waterworks, the municipal power station and the "Paryż" coal mine.
For the jubilee Hakoach engaged first-class football teams from Kraków and Hajduki, with which Hakoach held matches (report on the matches in the sports section).
The sports festival opened on Saturday night [after the Sabbath] with
A Torchlight Procession
through the town. On Sobieskiego Street, where the participants had gathered, hundreds of people stand waiting for the "great event". Headed by the Hakoach orchestra, the torchlight procession marched through Kołłątaja, Małachowskiego, Piłsudskiego, Modrzejowska[?] and back to the Hakoach premises.
That same evening a festive
Academy
for delegates and invited guests took place in the "Corso"[?].
The academy was opened by Dr. Rechtman, who handed the chair to Dr. Weinzieher. Invited to the presidium were: Vice-President [of the town] Rubinlicht, councillors Goldfeld and Lewin, Dr. Wasserzweig and Dr. Rechtszaft.
After the chairman's short introduction come the greetings. On behalf of the municipal administration — Mr. Rubinlicht, who declared that the subsidy Hakoach receives from the Magistrate does not correspond to what it deserves, and he promised that in future the Magistrate would help Hakoach obtain suitable premises for its needs.
Alderman (ławnik) Mr. Goldsztajn also stressed the same point in his greeting. After Dr. Rechtszaft's greeting, Dr. Rechtman delivered the closing words and also read a greeting from the Maccabi World Union.
Then various sports items were performed by Hakoach (women's group), the Chrzanów sports club (a beautiful dance by the women's group), and finally a splendid item in the courtyard performed by the guests from Cieszyn.
The concert part was performed by the club's own orchestra under the direction of Mr. P. Barenblat.
The main and most festive programme took place on Sunday. It began with a competition in exercises, light athletics, a bicycle race, etc., on the Hakoach sports ground, with the participation of all Hakoach groups and gymnasts from elsewhere.
At 2 p.m. the
Parade Through the Town
was formed. The procession formed up on Sobieskiego Street. Each group came with its banner, and the festive mood grew from minute to minute.
At the head marched the Hakoach orchestra, then the commandant Jakub Ehrlich, representatives of the municipal administration, Vice-President Rubinlicht, Alderman Goldsztajn, Dr. Rechtszaft, the Hakoach board, delegates of the Zionist Organisation in the persons of Abraham Hampel, Nute Landger, Baruch Brasa[?], Meir Zimmerknopf, press representatives, the seniors' group, guests from Cieszyn, Bielitz, Wieruszów[?], Chrzanów, Königshütte, Sosnowiec, Zawiercie, Olkusz and Będzin.
The grandiose procession, which marched through the streets Kołłątaja, Małachowskiego and Kościuszki to the sports ground, made a very good impression and aroused enthusiasm among the thousands of Jewish onlookers.
Before the entrance to the sports ground there took place
A March-Past.
The orchestra plays, and the "Jewish military" marches past with strict discipline, saluting the fluttering blue-and-white banners.
On the sports ground there are thousands of people from all strata of the Jewish population. The orchestra, "quartered" on a special stand, gives the signal, and the chief "in-laws" [i.e. the stars of the day] — the hundreds of young men and girls, male and female gymnasts — appear on the field, and under the command of Icchak Bażykowski[?] there begin
The General Free Exercises,
which went off very well. A strong impression was made by the round dance performed by the 4th women's group and the 5th men's group of Będzin Hakoach.
After the various exercises on the parallel bars, horizontal bar, vaulting horse, etc., the match between "Ruch" (Hajduki) and Hakoach (Będzin) takes place.
The result of the match is 9:3 in favour of "Ruch", but considering that the guests are one of the league teams, and the weakening of Hakoach in Saturday's match against "Wisła" (Kraków), the defeat is understandable.
In the evening a
Reception [raut]
was held for guests and delegates in the hall on the "Góra Zamkowa" [Castle Hill].
But because of the terrible heat the public had no desire to come to the reception; the "panie" [ladies] in particular were very much afraid that their "teisters"[?] [dresses?] would suffer "from the heat"... and they stayed sitting at home.
That evening the chief judge Jakub Ehrlich announced the results of the competitions held in the course of Sunday.
The results are: in the men's nonathlon (1st grade) first place was taken by Treister (Maccabi Sosnowiec), 2nd Plessner (Hakoach Będzin), 3rd place Zuckerman (Hakoach Będzin).

Women's octathlon, 2nd grade: 1st place Miss Kszyszywa[?] (Hakoach Będzin), 2nd Miss Joker (Maccabi Bielitz), 3rd Miss Zylberberg (Hakoach Będzin).

Who Will Get a Master's Diploma? II.

II.
Every regulation — even one of a general character — if it affects only certain parts of the people, is from the outset called a "decree" (gzeyre) among us, and only when one begins to get used to the new system and to adapt to its provisions does yesterday's "decree" become such a clear, understandable and natural phenomenon — unless quite uninvited benefactors take pains to crawl[?] into the minutiae of every single provision and to dig out of it [—][?], whose real aim is nothing but to bring contradictions, headaches and needless costs to the circles concerned.
We say[?] this with regard to the guild law. An uproar, a tumult arose in the Jewish artisans' camp as soon as the well-known ordinance of the President of the State appeared, which regulates and lays down precisely and in detail the paths of development of the artisan class.
The most grateful element was it — this very artisan element, submissive by nature, large and backward, on whose shoulders all sorts of political tricks were carried out.
But one thing must be established: it is not the fault of today's generation of artisans that it cannot write, cannot read, and is in general a person to whom all kinds of cultural achievements are enormously remote and whose comprehension is terribly limited.
Insofar as the Russian Tsarist regime was simply bloodily interested in letting all the millions of kustars (artisans) and peasants "wander in the darkness", permitting no reforms whatsoever in the field of schooling and being utterly opposed to any kind of attempt to raise their cultural and economic condition — things were absolutely no better in our homely, small-town "kingdom" either. As the Christians did, so did the Jews: if our bigwigs, the monthly parnassim and all sorts of other communal benefactors did show a bit of kindness to the children of the "tailors and shoemakers", it was a poor, neglected Talmud Torah that fell far short of the most elementary educational requirements. And when the boy had a pair of healthy hands, the little "khevre-man" was harnessed, in his earliest years, into the heavy collar of the artisan's yoke.
It is therefore no wonder at all that the overwhelming majority of Jewish artisans regard the new guild law as an evil decree that has stuck to them like a hump to the back — the decree demands the ability to write, read, geography, natural science and the like, which are as foreign to the average artisan as shatnez is to a pious Jew.
But this "decree", apart from its harmful side, also has a considerable amount of sense[?], and first and foremost the merit that it tears open[?] the rusted eyes of the Jewish artisan and leads him out onto the broad road of social, organisational and cultural work. The guild law is thus one of the most favourable positive phenomena in the life of Jewish crafts and small industry, and only future generations will be able properly to appreciate its practical value. The state compulsory school up to the age of 14 on the one hand, and the binding guild regulations on the other, will produce a conscious, culturally well-developed and technically well-prepared[?] generation of Jewish artisans.
And I will allow myself to say that it is therefore perhaps worth sacrificing the grief and pain of a considerable part of the Jewish artisans who, as said — through no fault of their own, God forbid — feel hit by the new guild law, so that in the near future we may gather the fruits of our own sowing: our children and grandchildren, to whom our darkened exile life will sound like an unbelievable legend of a past so near and yet so far.
On the law itself and its paragraphs — in the next article.
Matriculation Certificates — and What Next?

In many Jewish families there is now joy and gladness: the children have received their matura, but the joy will not last long; soon the sad question will awaken in the homes: what next? And the lamentable and painful worries will come[?].
When one tries to draw a parallel between the former and the present life of our youth in these parts, a picture emerges: life, with all its comforts, is a fine salon, which however has in front of it a whole row of locked antechambers.
The former Tsarist power hung a lock already on the very first door: Jewish children were hardly admitted even to the lowest classes of the gymnasia. Naturally, one was thus spared thinking about the further course.
A second heavy lock hung on the door of the universities, where the percentage was smaller still. But whoever had already broken through the first locks went freely into the palace of life.
Today the locks of the antechambers have become much looser. If the way into the state elementary and secondary schools is still not quite free for our children, we have our own schools with full state rights, with matriculation rights.
Harder already is access to the university — precisely because the number of Jewish graduates of the secondary school is very large, a kind of over-production is created which is hard to place[?]. Into the most useful and practical faculties, such as medicine and law, it is quite hard for a Jewish school-leaver to break in. Thousands of Jewish young people must indeed set out for the university cities abroad to fulfil the "way of the Torah" — living on bread and water, under the most tragic conditions — just to taste[?] of the tree of knowledge.
A large part of the youth must therefore remain halfway, unable to reach the last door of life's salon. They form a class of a lumpen-intelligentsia, if one may put it so, torn away from practical life, not having reached intellectual life, and in the end turned into a poor sort of malcontents.
And those who have already broken through all the locks and have entered life, crowned with the diploma of science, meet the hardest obstacles only on the threshold of life: life does not take them in, their path is strewn with prickly thorns. Only after passing through all the corridors do they see themselves as outcasts, estranged, and often it vexes them why[?] they ever set out on this hard, impassable road.
That is how all the illusions about good careers look — like a mirage, like a dream; what is the use of being let into the corridor, if one is not admitted to the salon!
The matura thus belongs to that sort of papers which we obtained under the democratic order and which in reality have scant significance.
K.

On the initiative of the culture commission of the Jewish artisans' association in Sosnowiec, a fairly large meeting took place on Sunday with the aim of founding a branch of the "Shul-Kult" school association.

There has not been such a drought for 116 years as this year.
The astronomical observatory in Kraków, which has kept weather statistics for Poland since 1782, establishes that since 1814 no such drought has been recorded[?] as in this June (czerwiec).
In the course of those 116 years it happened only once that 14 days of heat prevailed in succession in June.

Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings and remarks on this week's portion (Chukat)

[Oneg Shabbat — weekly Torah portion.] Torah sayings and remarks on this week's portion. Collected and edited by Y. L.
Parshat Chukat
a) "This is the law: when a man dies in a tent" (19:14).
The Torah is like that great man who lies in his grave in an "ohel" [tomb-tent]. While he lived, nobody listened to him, nobody followed his ways; only after his death is he on everyone's lips: "What a pity, a great man has gone."
The Torah scroll, too, is embraced[?] and kissed when it is rolled up and closed. People kiss it because it stands in the Holy Ark and bothers nobody.. — Ateret Yeshuah.
* * *
The Sanz [Nowy Sącz] Rabbi once watched how the congregation kissed the Torah scroll as the cantor carried it back into the Holy Ark, and remarked: You love the Torah too much, it seems to me; you love it when it is closed. — Heard.
b) "These are the waters of Meribah" (20:13).
The letters of "mi" stand for: mamon [wealth], yikhus [pedigree]. These two classes — the men of wealth, the magnates, and the men of pedigree — are the ones who sow quarrels and strife among Jews. — Or Pnei Moshe.
c) "Aaron shall be gathered unto his people" (20:24).
Nachmanides asks why such a punishment befell the Jews that immediately after Aaron's death Amalek came to make war on them. What were they guilty of?
— Because they had been told beforehand, "Aaron shall be gathered unto his people," so they knew that Aaron was going to die, yet they did nothing about it. They did not pray, did not try to save him. Only when he had already died — "and all the house of Israel wept for him" — did they begin to mourn him. While there was still time, nothing was done. — Yaarot Dvash.
d) "That Aaron was dead" (20:29).
In a Sabbath table hymn we say: "They delay going out and hasten to come in" (they linger in leaving the Sabbath and hurry into it). Everyone asks: why does the hymn put the end of the Sabbath before its beginning? First should come "hasten to come in" and then "delay going out".
When the hymn speaks of lingering and hurrying, it means the tosefet Shabbat — the few extra minutes we add to the Sabbath at its beginning and its end. This is because we cannot pin down[?] the exact minute of sunset. In the wilderness, by contrast, when the pillar of cloud accompanied the Jews by day and the pillar of fire by night, they did not need to keep the tosefet Shabbat, for they knew that when the pillars changed places, exactly then it was night. After Aaron's death the escort of the pillars continued in Moses' merit (Tractate Taanit 9). Moses died on the Sabbath. It follows that the first time Jews had to keep the tosefet Shabbat was at Sabbath dusk, because on Friday at dusk the change of the clouds still showed the exact hour; only when Moses died and the clouds departed did one need to require an addition to the Sabbath, and that first happened on a Sabbath at dusk. Therefore first "delay going out" and only then "hasten to come in"... ve-r"l. — R' Pinchas of Korets [Korzec].
e) "And the Canaanite, the king of Arad, heard" (21:20 [as printed; should be 21:1]).
Rashi says that the Amalekites deliberately changed their language and began to speak Canaanite, so that the Jews would think they were real Canaanites and would pray to God that the Canaanites be defeated — and in this way they would deceive the Jews. Meanwhile the Jews recognised them by their clothing.
And why did they not change their clothing too, to deceive the Jews?
Had the Amalekites dressed as Canaanites as well, they would indeed have become real Canaanites. — Or Yesharim.
* * *
See: by speaking a foreign language one is not yet as assimilated as by not dressing like a Jew. The Amalekites themselves preferred to speak a foreign language rather than dress in foreign attire. — Rabbi Yechezkel of Kuzmir [Kazimierz Dolny].
* * *
The Midrash (Shemot [Rabbah]) says of Moses: "He is a Hebrew and his clothing is Egyptian." So Moses, too, went about in Egyptian dress.
But Jethro had formerly been a heathen priest and lived among idol-worshippers; he would have been afraid to take a Jewish son-in-law, and so it was his good fortune that Moses dressed like an Egyptian, so that the neighbours would not notice him.
But this gives no licence in ordinary cases. — Ohel Yitzchak.
f) "And from the wilderness, Mattanah [a gift]" (21:18).
The Gemara says of this: the Torah is given precisely to those who make themselves ownerless like a wilderness; to them the Torah gives itself[?] as a gift.
Rabbi Bunem of Pshischa [Przysucha] said of this: I do indeed love the one who renounces himself, but I hate the one who renounces others..
g) "We have shot at them; Heshbon is perished" (21:30).
These lofty ones, those who hold themselves high — they lose all reckoning entirely; they do not know where they stand in the world. — Ilana de-Chayei.
