The Wall Speaks...

[Satirical feuilleton — Palestine, the Western Wall.] I was looking for a topic for a feuilleton and could not find one. So what does one do? A thought occurs to me: I will resolve to dream that I am in Jerusalem, a spectator at the hearing on the Western Wall now going on there.
I also resolve to dream that the chairman of the commission proposed sending for the Wall itself, to hear what it, the chief party concerned, has to say. Not two seconds passed and the Wall shuffled into the courthouse and stood before the judges' table, head held high, as always.
And then the questioning of the "witness" began:
Chairman: What is your name?
Wall: "Al-Buraq" is what they call me (all the Jews present in court exchange glances in surprise).
Chairman: Is that your real name?
Wall: No.
Chairman: Why then do you not give your real name?
Wall: Because for the truth one gets beaten.
Chairman: But do you know that before the court one must tell the truth?
Wall: I know.
Chairman: Why then do you not tell your real name?
Wall: Because I want those in power to win this dispute over me.
Jewish lawyer: This is terrible treason! (An uproar among the Jewish public in the courtroom. The chairman bangs his gavel and calls to order.)
Wall: The trouble with you humans is that you have made yourselves words and think everything already lies in them. What is treason? A word, that's all. We walls are not impressed by words...
Jewish lawyer: But surely you cannot deny that your "gar vosige" [?] claim is treason against the Jewish people.
Wall: I deny it.
Jewish lawyer: What then is your explanation of this?
Wall: My explanation is — I decline to make explanations.
Jewish lawyer: You say, then, that your name is "Al-Buraq"?
Wall: So I say.
Jewish lawyer: And you also admit that this is not your real name?
Wall: Everyone knows that.
Jewish lawyer: What then is your real name?
Wall: You know it.
Jewish lawyer: The Western Wall.
Wall: You have already said it.
Jewish lawyer: Then why do you like calling yourself "Al-Buraq"?
Wall: Because I myself do not consider myself so important that rivers of blood should be shed on my account. After all, I am no more than a wall.
Jewish lawyer: But you are holy.
Wall: There is nothing holier than a human life.
Jewish lawyer: Well, and what about Kiddush Hashem [martyrdom]? Have people not risen to the highest level by giving their lives in defence of holy things?
Wall: I am old enough, and I have heard this before more than once, but since until today nobody asked my opinion on the question, I kept as silent as a wall...
Jewish lawyer: What then is your opinion?
Wall: My opinion is that blood does not sanctify; blood stains and makes unclean.
Jewish lawyer: The blood of the "martyr" included?
Wall: The blood of the martyr lays an even heavier stain on the human species.
Jewish lawyer: Why?
Wall: Because the deed of shedding innocent blood is terribly unworthy.
Jewish lawyer: Surely the guilt must be thrown on the heads of the guilty, and not, as you would have it, make the victim responsible for the savage deed of the innocent [sic; probably "of the guilty"]?
Wall: We old ones have long since learned that potentially all people are alike. Everywhere and at all times the stronger is the one who strikes and the weaker is the one who is struck. Give the weak one power and he stops being a lamb — he becomes a wolf!
Jewish lawyer: What do you mean to say by that?
Wall: I mean to say that I was well off before the tears of millions of aching hearts soaked my stony being with the sorrow of the whole world; and today my heart weeps over the blindness and misguidedness of the pogromist no less than over the martyr's death of the pogrom victims. More than once I have begged God: put an end to me, topple me! But the answer from heaven is: "Your time has not yet come. There is still an element of stone in you that has not yet been soaked through by human tears. At the end of days you will become one great fiery pillar of tears, and then an order will go out from heaven and you will scatter into single sparks and fill the whole world with compassion and mercy. Then you will be dissolved — and the world redeemed"!...
A strong emotion is felt in the court; everyone is as if electrified; a long pause.
Jewish lawyer: What then do you think, holy Wall, should be the way out of our present dispute?
Wall: The more you tear at each other and fight over me, or over something else, the sooner I will reach my promised redemption through dissolution. But I have already soaked up too many human tears to be able to be as selfish as you humans are...
Arab lawyer: So it is your wish to be called "Al-Buraq"?
Wall: My wish is that every wicked holiness be left to sink in its own foolishness [?]. My advice is not to give the sanctimonious villain any chance to wrap himself in righteousness.
Jewish lawyer: I am beginning to understand you, holy Wall!...
Wall: That is all I meant to achieve by coming here. Now I am going back to my three-thousand-year silence.
The Wall slowly begins to shuffle out of the courtroom. Everyone sits dumbfounded. A holy silence reigns in the hall for some minutes; then the Arab lawyer takes the floor and — — — — — —
What happened next I do not know, because the typesetter ran out of the printing shop shouting "Material!", and I decided that for this time it would be enough dreaming...
Unwanted and Useful Institutions.

[Editorial — housing; tenants' associations.] (The economic associations bring no benefit whatsoever to the ruling "order".)
It is very bad when one does not find one's bearings in general, but it is even worse when one does not know when one does need to find one's bearings and when not, what is worth dwelling on and what is not.
Thus, for example, people here complained a great deal [?], all along, that we are not socially mature, that we do not know how to create and maintain institutions; the upshot of it all was that people began founding institutions and more institutions, one on top of the other, so that of every kind [—] there are duplicates. That one needs "little benches" [seats, posts] — that, after all, is out of the question; let heaven fall to earth, the plan of future progress must be carried out.
It goes without saying that such "double bookkeeping" brings nobody any benefit whatsoever. Yet if we consider all this calmly, we will become convinced that there are nevertheless some who do benefit — for example, first of all the chairman, then the collectors, the beadles, etc. So it turns out that income covers expenses, debit and credit balance out, and thereby one has satisfied every opinion; and whether this or that institution brings the public any benefit at all — that does not interest the whole rattling apparatus [?], as long as they have a place in which to practise politics, and that's that.
It must not be allowed, however, that in the present hard times institutions should be turned into toys from which only interested persons derive benefit, and for that reason burden [?] the community.
It is therefore high time that all institutions be subject to public control, and that the decision finally be reached that institutions which do not benefit the public be liquidated by it; on the other hand, those which bring benefit and can bring the public salvation, as soon as they receive due recognition, one must strive to raise to the proper level, so that they serve their members and bring benefit to the enlightened civic elements.
In today's hard times we must first of all pay great attention to the economic institutions, which already play, and can later play, an even greater role in our [?] economic field.
Take, for example, the tenants' associations ["lokatorzy"] here in Poland at the present moment: it seems that they are already half liquidated, and those still barely alive also have a minimal number of members. For who needs the association now, when the landlord charges rent according to the decree? And that is the reason they are dying off one by one, not understanding their civic tasks.
And let us imagine something else: suppose that the danger of raising rents has already become an accomplished fact — then the people will come and shout and clamour: what does this mean? Why on earth raise the rent for a dwelling at a time when such bitter and hard times have come upon us, when we do not see [?] a bare groschen before our eyes? So they will shout in the street and in the association, but nothing of substance will be done, for two reasons: first, because people remain indifferent to everything until someone comes to demand the increase; and second, because afterwards, even with the best will, nothing more can be done — simply because there will no longer be the proper number of members and institutions able to come forward in the name of the people and demand this and that.
As soon as one has to come and speak in the name of the people, one must surely have well-established "tenants' associations" that stand at the height of their tasks — and this, unfortunately, we do not have. If, on the other hand, these miniature "tenants' associations" were to come and speak, with their few dozen members, in the name of the people, that would mean making ourselves ridiculous, and in that case it is wiser not to come forward [?] at all — and then we will know that we do not possess this institution.
One can plainly see that they have set about raising rents with all their might, so that meanwhile people will talk and talk, and in the end the fantasy will become reality, and then no doctor in the world will help us any more.
It goes without saying that it would be quite different if we had well-established tenants' associations everywhere, in which all tenants were enrolled as members; then [?] these associations would have come forward before the decision was adopted, and the government would have seen that it was dealing with the citizens of the country, so that willy-nilly it would have had to reckon with them.
Let us therefore, in good time, while it is not yet too late, see to renewing the tenants' associations; let us see to it that all tenants are enrolled as members, and then, when the opportune moment comes, let us come with all our baggage [?] and speak and storm in the name of the people, in the name of the broad strata of the population.
Many of us think that this institution is superfluous, an element belonging to the past. Unfortunately, people who do not know life and do not know the laws of our time can think so; otherwise they would not think so, otherwise they would not reason so.
As long as the housing question is not solved, as long as the problem is of the first rank, so long must we have our institutions, which will protect us from every attack that may arise.
And one more thing: the tenants' associations must not merely exist as a means of protection against an attack; they must also reach the level of helping to solve the hard housing question, which not only is not being removed [?], but grows ever harder and harder.
Selekt.
The Dangers on the Road

Car accidents are by now a common phenomenon throughout the world, but here there is a difference: the car does not maim others, only its own passengers.
Among the causes, the main ones must be pointed out:
First of all, the wildness of the horses, which take fright at the steel beast and thereby disturb the normal course of the car.
Secondly, the narrowness and crookedness of the highways, because of which, at the slightest tilt, the car is liable to overturn.
Thirdly, the lack of training of the driver, who gets lost in thought, or sometimes even strikes up a conversation, and does not manage to see the danger in time so as to be able to steer the car over a wider area; instead he catches himself only at the last moment, gives the steering wheel a hasty turn and brings about the catastrophe.
So what is to be done about it?
The highways cannot be repaired so quickly; a lot of water will flow by before then:
The horses will probably get used to our civilisation in time, and that cause will disappear.
But the negligence and lack of discipline of the drivers must be combated with the utmost severity.
One can often see how the drivers chat away comfortably, although the well-known notice hangs over their heads; they behave like the Jews of old who used to urinate on the "No urinating" sign. On the road, where they have no supervision over them, they don't give a fig for any of the regulations and forget that a few dozen human lives are entrusted to their hands.
The moving car has brought a new way of life into our existence, one that the law has not yet noticed. The matter must be handled more strictly and firmly if we want motor transport to develop.
M. P.
Ephraim Fishel with the Bottle of Vishniak

[Humorous feuilleton — the end of the summer-cottage season; Będzin.]
Y. Oberzhanek.

All's well that ends well. The main thing is the end: if the sequestrator [tax bailiff] took and took from you, and the end is that you were left with nothing but your wife — now that is a good end...
If you were [?] a "słomiany wdowiec" [Polish: straw widower — a husband whose wife is away on holiday] for three months and your "Yidene" [wife] did not once catch you "na gorącym uczynku" [?] [Polish: red-handed] — that too is a good end.
The main thing is the end; if the end is good, all is good.
But what is the rule when the beginning was woeful and the end is even worse? When the end is not good, it is really "paskudne" [Polish: nasty].
I mean it with regard to the dacha [the summer cottage].
The beginning of summer is still somehow bearable: you fly from the town out to the village, on Sunday you fly from the village back into town, the days are big and the nights small, you are separated from your wife and your wife is separated from you — one gets through it.
But the worst is the "Ne'ilah" time — the last days, I mean. When the Ne'ilah days come, the short days and long nights, it begins to get boring. And [—] [?] all the more so for the "fair sex" — that need not be "[—]" [?]... Just as at the beginning of May they feel "duszno" [stuffy] and want to fly off to the "świeże powietrze" [fresh air], so, when they see the sheaves [?] of grain lying in the fields, they suddenly feel "smutne" [sad]. And what do they do next, when they feel "smutne", do you know? The more "musical" ones "zabawiają się" [amuse themselves] with poker, with mah-jongg or with "dushevigske" [?]; others "przepędzają" [while away] the long "smutne" evenings with gossip, and the more housewifely ones, the "skromne kobietki" [modest little women], think about something useful. And since mine, be it said, is hardly musical — that is to say: play she does — on my nerves, but cards — God forbid the mention — what does my "Yidene" do in the last dacha days? She makes preserves.
What does she put up? What all the "letniczki" [female summer guests] put up — vishniak [cherry liqueur]. It's heaven and earth and vishniak. Into whichever summer guest's place you walk, you see a "wystawa" [exhibition] of bottles, big bottles and smaller bottles and plain flasks, everything full of cherries and berries, and each one tries [?] to outdo the others. If one has put up only vishniak, the other must put up cherries with berries; if one has cherries with berries, the second puts up [—]-wine [?] with apple "sok" [juice].
It goes without saying that the biggest preserve-maker, with the biggest [—] [?] for cherries, berries and sugar, is my "Yidene". You surely think she puts up the vishniak for herself, that she has such a great sweet tooth? God forbid. She doesn't even put it in her mouth. So for whom does she make it? — For guests. Because in winter my "Yidene" makes a different celebration every week. One time it's an "urodziny" [birthday], one time she "zaprasza" [invites people] "na karty" [for cards], and one time just simply a "przyjęcie" [reception] — and for such a lot of celebrations you need such a lot of merchandise.
This week I come out to the summer lodgings, I take a look, and my eyes start swimming: bottles and flasks, big flasks and little flasks.
— What's all this, Miriam Rokhl? A whole laboratory you've got here.
— Don't you know? — she says, pleased with herself. — I've put up preserves.
— For whom did you put it up, and what did you put it up for, what good is it to you?
— What did you want then? — she let loose with her tongue. — Everybody will put up preserves and I'm going to sit with folded hands? They shouldn't live to see it!
And how is this bit of merchandise going to get to Będzin?
What do you mean, she says, how? And what are you for? Every week you'll take one bottle with you. What did you want, should I drag myself with the bottles?
Well, I know my Miriam Rokhl: when she says take [?] a bottle, no tricks will help. And last Sunday she indeed honoured me with the first "hakafah" [the first round, as with the Torah on Simchat Torah].
Well, the end I had I wouldn't wish on my worst enemy. You are surely also a "letnik" [summer guest], and surely your wife has also put up preserves, and if she has, she will surely also want to honour you with such a "hakafah" — so listen how [?] my end looks:
How I walked along, the "czemodan" [suitcase] in one hand and the bottle in the other — that I'll spare you. One thing I couldn't understand at all: why do people look at me as at some freak [?]? They look and smile — what happened? I take a look and everything goes dark before my eyes. My new light trousers are red as blood, as if I had just come out of the slaughterhouse. I turn the bottle to the right and to the left; the more I try to hide the bottle, the more it pours. I feel the blood rushing to my face. What does one do? Should I throw it away — what will my Miriam Rokhl do? She won't survive it; should I keep carrying it — how does one make a public laughing-stock of oneself?
What was the end? The end was that the bottle of vishniak, which my Miriam Rokhl had worked so hard and bitterly at for the guests, I gave away [—] [?], come what may.
You surely think I was now rid of it? You are mistaken. Here only the thick of it begins:
No sooner do I step out of the railway carriage than I feel a pair of strong hands on my shoulders, and before I manage to look round to see who has given me such a "sholem aleykhem", two fellows are already standing next to me, and one of them says to the other: "Nareszcie mamy tego ptaka" [Polish: Finally we've got that bird].
I go [—] [?]: who are these lads and what do they want from me?
"Dowód osobisty!" [identity card] one of them shouts at me. I start searching my pockets. Search today, search tomorrow — what Jew has a "dowód osobisty" right at hand? What, am I travelling across the border, that I need a passport?
I talk Turkish, I talk Greek [i.e., we don't understand each other], I shout: "Co się stało?" [?] [What happened?] and they shout: "[—]" [?] — on and on, at length and at breadth, until... until they invited me to the "[—]" [?], and only there did I find out what they were after: since they had been waiting at the railway for some dangerous bandit, and since they saw my light trousers with the fresh red stains, they were sure that I was indeed the wanted bandit.
When I heard what they were after, I began explaining to them: "Przecież to jest sok od mojej żony Mirjam Rachel" [But this is juice from my wife Miriam Rokhl]. "Proszę" [please], I said, "to jest prawdziwy wiśniowy sok" [this is genuine cherry juice].
Only after a long inquiry and investigation, after a precise analysis, was it established that this was not blood but vishniak, genuine vishniak, which my Miriam Rokhl had put up herself for the guests for the winter — and only then did I get out of their hands in peace.
So it was that, because of my Miriam Rokhl's vishniak, I buried myself in shame before people, and because of my Miriam Rokhl's bottle I became a bandit.
Now I have no vishniak and no trousers, and the worst of it is: what excuse am I to give my Miriam Rokhl?
Jews, I warn you: run away from wives who think about something useful. Let them rather play "poker" and "mah-jongg", let them rather gossip — as long as they don't put up any vishniak.
Jews, if your wives honour you with a bottle — run!
Between Our Own and Other People's Children

[Będzin — municipality and summer camps; impressions of a visit.]
(Impressions of a visit to the Christian and Jewish summer camps in Sławków.)
The presidium of the Będzin City Council invited us to take part in the city councillors' excursion to Sławków, to the non-Jewish and Jewish summer camps for schoolchildren.
The interest of the Jewish councillors was this time almost the same — as in the city council sessions. Why bother finding out where and how city money is spent? It is enough that at the vote one raises one's hand and is done with it; let Mr.[?] Anczyk worry about the rest..
The car is full of non-Jewish councillors. Of Jewish ones there is a "mezuman" [three, a quorum for grace] — Moshe Haspel[?], Efraim Kleinman and Mordechai Berish Rotenberg; they are the ones who were not frightened by the overcast sky and did go!
After a long walk between field and forest we reach the camp for Christian children. The school orchestra plays several marches in honour of the arrivals, the head of the camp, Ławik[?] Herczanik[?], extends a "sholem aleichem", and until the promised breakfast the guests have time to get acquainted with the camp buildings and other institutions maintained by the Będzin magistrate.
Here, for example, we visit the premises of the Christian "old-age home", which is joined to the long[?] building of the camp, and in small but clean little rooms we find the old men and women snuggled up one right next to the other. From the conversation we have with them we see that the old people are very content with their lot. They get meat 3 times a week, besides plenty of other food. Only one thing we lack, they tell us: we get[?] no tea at all from Monday to Sunday...
When I hear the great "longing" — how the old people crave a little tea — I am reminded of the complaints of the old people in our own "old-age home" at the "Linat haCholim". Our old people have quite different notions: they are not always satisfied with the meat they get day after day, they look for faults in the dishes, which are "not tasty". Never mind — a piece of fish every day for lunch and a few fried eggs for supper really must not be missing either..
The grounds around the camp are large, broad and very [?]. For the children (Christian, naturally) care has been taken that in unfavourable weather they eat in an enormous hall; the kitchen — a comfortable one, the storeroom — in a separate room, spacious; and then a large stretch of land surrounded by a splendid garden, just as it should be — a camp..
About the general regime we are informed by the camp director. Everything — he says — is run in the best order; the children get 5 meals a day (we can see it in their faces), and he does not spare words of praise for the Będzin city administration, which takes such care of the school youth.
From there we drive to the camp for Jewish children. The road (for driving) is atrocious, and the coachman, the "road expert", often reminds us to be careful and not to "take risks", as happened not long ago to the vice-president [deputy mayor]..
After a long trek through sand and mud we finally arrive at the right place. Already from afar we hear that we are approaching our brethren the Children of Israel; the voices and shouts from there testify that Jews are a lively people...
At the first reception one gets the impression of being at a rich wedding in a small shtetl. Jews have time, it is a festive[?] day; [—] there is a hubbub all over the camp [lit. "hack and pack and heyza" — doubtful reading], where people make themselves heard, and incidentally a "reinforcement" is brought into the kitchen.. And no wonder the cooks shout and get angry: the crowding is great, a buzzing as in a beehive, one comes in, the other goes out — after all[?], among Jews — a little boiled water, black coffee, and that's the life.
The orchestra (graduates of Public School No. 2) plays; the participants of the excursion arrive, together with the management and staff of the Christian camp. The latter felt "shame" and chagrin seeing what the reception looks like when one comes to Jewish leaders and to a Jewish camp. They lowered their heads in shame on hearing the greeting of a little "colonist". The greeting and the speech of the chairman Mr. Goldsztajn, who stressed the importance of spending time in the free, healthy air, and last but not least the gymnastic exercises, the recitation under the direction of Icchak Bauszykowski[?], a programme as it should be, even little Polish songs; the gentiles "got" respect and were not embarrassed to ask for "Hatikvah" to be played (our Agudah people would no doubt have fallen asleep...).
Under this good impression we go into the new building, which was completed 2 months ago. The rooms in which about 200 children sleep are large and airy, bright[?], with verandas[?] along their whole length, and from the building report we hear from Mr. Goldsztajn it can be seen that thanks to the goodwill and energy of the camp management and of [—] Mr. Dżybikowski[?] the building was put up within a very short time.
Then came the real thing, at which the non-Jewish councillors were truly carried away[?] with admiration and very nearly converted to Judaism.. A lunch had been prepared for the guests — genuine, tasty Jewish dishes, even chopped liver..
During the meal Goldsztajn read out the report of the summer camp, the children's development and so on; but who among those at the table paid attention to the report? The "distinguished"[?] Baczewski "did not allow" it..
In honour of the "appetite" the orchestra performed the newest revue[?] hits, which the company joined in, and the little ones on the veranda also snatched a little dance.
The children are very content; all the stories that were told are baseless. Care is taken not only of the body but also of the soul. The so-called "Torah-loyal", who "care" so much about Judaism, ought to come and take a lesson in how the cause of Judaism is safeguarded among the children. — Prayers are held — the storekeeper Mr. Abraham Balimowski[?] tells me — 3 times a day with a minyan; there is also a Torah scroll on the spot, and the kitchen? kosher le-mehadrin min ha-mehadrin. It is — he says — a vile act by the obscurantist fanatics[?] well known in Będzin, who allowed themselves to "write" that the camp does not keep kashrut...
———
We take leave of the cheerful little Moishes and Shloimes. We are better off — they shout after us — we stay here and you are going back to Będzin...
———
So as not to remain in anyone's debt, mention must also be made of the courtesy of the owner of the "Federal" car, who said "kol ditzrikh" — anyone who needs to should ride home; nobody was left in a fix.
Jakob Hirszson[?] (printed "הירשס—זאן").
From the Philological Section of the Yiddish Scientific Institute

[YIVO, Vilna — letter to the editor; language research.]
The Philological Section of YIVO [the Yiddish Scientific Institute] is now conducting an investigation into the grammatical gender of nouns in Yiddish. This work will not only help to regulate an important point of the Yiddish literary language, but will also make it possible to draw more general conclusions about the history of the Yiddish language and its dialects. But for the investigation to have the proper effect, as many Jewish communities as possible must be drawn into it. For this purpose a questionnaire has been worked out, which is sent to anyone interested and which is very easy to answer: one need not be a philologist for it; every educated person is able to do it and can in this way help to achieve an important scholarly goal.
We therefore ask the readers of your paper to respond and to request the questionnaires from the Philological Section. Correspondents are especially needed from the following[?] places: Siewierz, Zawiercie, Pilica, Wolbrom, Dąbrowa, Sławków, Sosnowiec, Olkusz, Miechów, Skała.
With great respect,
Philological Section of YIVO
Dr. M. Weinreich
Scientific Secretary
Vilna, August 1930.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings and remarks on today's portion — Parashat Re'eh

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings and remarks on today's Torah portion.
Collected and edited by Y. L.
Parashat Re'eh

a) "Behold, I set before you this day" (Deut. 11:26)
The verse begins by addressing a single person: "Re'eh" ("behold", singular), and at once passes to the plural: "before you" (lifneikhem). — For the Torah was indeed given to all as if to one; only we have made of it a "book of the many", a plural thing, because each person interprets it differently, each as he pleases...
From the Kotzker Rebbe [Kock].

b) "And when ye go over the Jordan... and He giveth you rest from all your enemies round about, so that ye dwell in safety" (Deut. 12:10)
The Gemara says that the terrible curse with which Jews were punished: "And the Lord shall give thee there a trembling heart" (God will give you an agitated, nervous heart) — that is, the specific [printed: "kpetsifish"] Jewish nervousness, which causes quarrels[?] and disputes — that this cruel curse was spoken only of Babylon, not of the Land of Israel; this proves that when Jews are in the Land of Israel the scattered, agitated Jewish spirit will be cooled and calmed.
So the Torah says: "And when ye go over the Jordan" — as soon as you cross the Jordan to come to the Land of Israel, "and He giveth you rest from all your enemies round about" — you will have rest from your external enemies around you, "so that ye dwell in safety" — you will live securely and calmly among yourselves as well, you will not quarrel among yourselves. Only the Land of Israel is capable of making Jewish life healthy.
Tiferet Yehonatan.
* * *
The Gemara says: why was the Second Temple destroyed? Because of baseless hatred; and that is precisely why the Jewish redemption can come only when baseless love prevails — love of one Jew for another without a "why" and without a [?]. Only thereby will[?] we be able to come to the Land of Israel.
From the Drobitsher Rebbe [Drohobycz?].

c) "Thy manservant, and thy maidservant, and the Levite — and thou shalt rejoice before the Lord thy God in all that thou puttest thine hand unto" (Deut. 12:18)
A person can rejoice only when he looks beneath himself, when he sees that there are people still more unfortunate than he; but not when he looks ahead of himself, when he looks at those richer and more fortunate than he. Look at your manservant, your maidservant and the Levite — they are poorer and more downtrodden than you — and then: "thou shalt rejoice in all that thou puttest thine hand unto", you will rejoice in what you have.
Rabbi Yonatan Eybeschütz.

[d)] "And shew thee a merciful heart, and have compassion upon thee" (Deut. 13:18)
In former times there was a custom that a shochet (ritual slaughterer) had to invite to his home all the passing travellers, give them food and drink and a place to sleep. The Rizhiner [Rebbe of Ruzhyn] explained the reason for this custom: a shochet, after all, has a trade whose character is cruelty, and therefore he must awaken in himself the quality of mercy, so that he is not infected by the essence of his calling. And therefore, after the law of the condemned city (ir ha-nidachat), which is in essence a far from merciful act — to take and destroy an entire city — and so that cruelty should not take root in the people, the Torah promises: "and shew thee mercy, and have compassion upon thee" — God will radiate feelings of mercy into you. After such an act as the condemned city, this is necessary.

e) "Ye are the children of the Lord your God" (Deut. 14:1)
Rabbi Meir says: either way (whether Jews behave well or badly) you are called children, as it is said: "they are foolish children" (Jeremiah 4:22), "children in whom is no faith" (printed "Yevamot 32:20" — read Deut. 32:20), "corrupt children" (Isaiah 1:4) — and yet you are always called "children", whatever you may be.
Tractate Kiddushin, 36.
* * *
The word "atem" ("ye") is expounded in another matter: "atem — even unwitting, atem — even wilful". Here too the meaning is: "ye are children" — you are children[?], even unwitting, even wilful... even the young people who are wilful sinners, who do things "to spite", are nevertheless Jews, God's children.
From Rabbi Yeshayele of Pshedborzh [Przedbórz].
* * *
"And in order[?] to distance[?] you from sin[?] I come to warn you that you should not split off[?] from people who abandon the Torah." "And this (— that we push away the freethinkers) is the cause of decline and degradation."
Rabbi Mendele of Vitebsk, in a letter.

f) "If there be among you a poor man" (Deut. 15:7)
Actually, according to the style of the language, it should read "ki yihyeh lekha evyon" ("if you have a poor man") and not "bekha" ("in you"). Originally the world was meant to be equal; everyone was meant to have equal wealth, but God took from one and gave it to the other, and so there are rich and poor. It follows, then, that the poor keep their wealth with the rich... That is the meaning of "if there be in you a poor man": the poor man has what is his with you... so give it back to him, it is his own[?]...
Ohel Yaakov.

g) "Thou shalt not shut thine hand" (ibid.)
Two Jews go collecting donations for a needful cause. They come to the door of a well-known rich man, but also a thoroughly[?] well-known "davar acher" [lit. "the other thing", euphemism for a pig — a nasty miser]. One says to the other: you'll see how[?] I will make the rich man stop being the master of the house here. —
— What do you mean, you'll make him stop being master of the house? — the other wonders.
— He'll unmake himself as master of the house, you'll see.
Coming to the door, they ring. The rich man comes out and, hearing for what purpose they have come, he says at once:
— The master of the house is not in now, I can't give anything, I'm only an employee...
— You see, — says one of the collectors to the other, — how he has made himself no longer master of the house.
From the mouth of the people.
* * *
A rabbi once came to a rich man, a miser, and asked him for a donation for a certain cause. The rich man says: I give charity only in secret; public charity — that I don't hold with.
The rabbi retorts: even a sin you commit in the innermost chambers, the whole town talks about it; and if you had ever given a groschen to charity in secret, the town would surely have heard about that too — and so far I have not heard of it...
Nahalei Devash.

h) "Thy poor brother" (Deut. 15:9)
King Solomon says: "a brother is born for adversity" (printed "Proverbs 28"). Meaning: "a brother for adversity" — such a one who would want to be a brother to someone who is in trouble — "is born" — such a person has yet to be born; meanwhile such a person is not yet to be found... Meanwhile, if someone finds himself in trouble, all his former friends distance themselves from him and he remains alone.
Binah le-Ittim.

i) "Poor man" (ibid.)
The word "evyon" (poor man) derives from the root ta'av — to long, because a poor man longs for everything...
Rashi.

j) "For because of this thing the Lord shall bless thee" (printed "15:11")
"Bi-glal ha-davar" — because of the speech (davar — dibbur), because of the soft and soothing words you speak to the poor man — God blesses you. For thus says the Gemara: he who gives charity is blessed with six blessings, and he who speaks soft words to him is blessed with a thousand (alef) blessings.
Eretz Hemdah.

Avot, Chapter Six.
"Bread with salt shalt thou eat, water by measure shalt thou drink... and if thou doest so, happy art thou in this world and it shall be well with thee in the world to come."
It is good only when you are rich and want to fulfil "bread with salt shalt thou eat" — when "and if thou doest so", when you do it voluntarily, not when God brings it about that you are forced to eat bread with salt...
Likkutei Maharam Schiff.
The Great Cry of Pain

[Upper Silesia — Jewish peddlers; letter to the editor.]
Of the peddlers trading in Upper Silesia [Górny Śląsk].
(A letter to the editors.)
One often reads in the Jewish press that „Farbstein and Hartglas have intervened", or „the peddler question in Upper Silesia has been fully solved", etc., etc. But all these favours have come to zero, for in sum none of our public figures in Warsaw does anything for its own sake; only when they are pressed do they say a few words where needed, and all the peddlers and traders of Upper Silesia remain in great danger of ruin, because the chicanery the administration employs against them, against the traders in Upper Silesia, was not applied even in Tsarist times with the famous „cherta" [?] [the Pale of Settlement].
Until 1928 a peddler who had taken out the so-called „itinerant trade licence" (Wandergewerbe) could trade throughout Upper Silesia, and no border pass was needed at all; only in 1928, with the appearance of the new Industrial Law, which says that itinerant trade requires a licence which everyone must obtain from his own starostwo [district office], did Katowice in 1929 stop issuing itinerant trade licences to people from Sosnowiec or Będzin; they did, however, need to have their licences endorsed (visaed) for trading in Upper Silesia, and this the voivode [provincial governor] refused to do, because in that same year the filthy gutter sheet „Do Czynu" [„To Action"] began to appear, which set itself the task of undermining Jewish trade in Upper Silesia. As his first scapegoat the „editor" took the Jewish peddler. The paper turned to the administration demanding that it give no one any visas. Besides this the antisemite also held meetings at which he called for killing every Jew who should merely enter a Christian's home wishing to sell a bit of merchandise; the same incitement is carried on to this very day. With Upper Silesian customers the antisemite achieved nothing, because the Christian customer in Upper Silesia knows well that from a Jew he buys cheaply; he did, however, succeed with the local authorities, and also with the voivode, who refused to stamp the licences for trade in Upper Silesia.
The peddlers and traders, seeing how great the danger was, united in order to repel together the bloodthirsty enemies who want to tear their very hard-earned piece of bread out of their mouths, and after great effort and hard work at the Ministry of the Interior, with the great help of „Gtw." [?], Deputy Wiślicki managed to obtain from the ministry a decision that the voivode must issue some of the permits.
What does the voivode do after being forced to issue the visas? He digs out an old German law dating from 1869. That law says that within 10 kilometres of the border one may not trade. Relying on this law, which incidentally has already been abolished in Germany itself, he applies it with the harshest means, and since there is no town or village that is not within 10 kilometres of the border, one may not travel anywhere, because as soon as one so much as steps out into a street near Katowice a report is drawn up at once and the „culprit" must then pay a fine of 20 to 50 złoty. One may hold the dearly paid patent and licence and also the hard-won visa — and still one may not trade.
All interventions about this have been fruitless. The voivode has even promised twice that he would see to it that the Mysłowice customs office issues all the border passes to those who received visas for trade in Upper Silesia; he even summoned a delegation of the associations concerned, and when the delegation, led by Vice-President Mr. Rubinlicht, presented itself to him a few weeks ago, he promised that after acquainting himself with the reports on the matter he would give us an answer. As an answer he sent us to the naczelnik [district head], who in turn sent us to the directorate in Mysłowice, and from the directorate we finally heard a clear answer: that they will issue them only then [?], when the Ministry of Finance forces them to.
Such are the decrees the poor peddlers endure, at the present time, when selling a piece of merchandise is like winning a victory in wartime.
And Jewish public opinion is silent. More than once we have turned through the press to our representatives, who make so many promises at election time, — to help us in our hard struggle for our honest, hard piece of bread; more than once we have pointed out to our representatives the poison that the filthy sheet „Do Czynu" is for the Jewish traders in Upper Silesia, and we know that a proper intervention on the part of our representatives would have helped. But our cries of pain go unheard; our cry is a voice crying in the wilderness.
Therefore we, the poorest of the poor, must help ourselves. It is necessary that every trader and peddler join his organisation, so that with united strength we may withstand the heavy blows still awaiting us, for already now the voivode has informed the delegation, so that they should know, that he is about to liquidate the trade in Upper Silesia: in the coming new year he will no longer issue the permit.
Therefore it will be necessary to keep intervening with the highest authority, and that can only be done with united forces, for only in unity is there strength, and if we are united we shall weaken and overcome the danger lurking for us from strong, black, dark forces.
Ch. Żelanke.
To the Jewish Academics Studying Abroad

[Warsaw — Jewish students abroad; announcement.]
The Central Executive Committee of the Union of Associations of Jewish Students from Poland studying abroad announces that the Academic Emigration Bureau in Warsaw, Elektoralna 8, flat 24, tel. 307-73, through its activity makes it easier for fellow academics to carry out the formalities connected with going abroad to study, directs those leaving to the most suitable and appropriate institutions of higher learning, to the cheapest academic centres, and recommends the fellows to the academic associations abroad, which will assist them in settling in.
The Academic Emigration Bureau combats the so-called information bureaus that have existed until now, which drove those concerned into very high and superfluous expenses, directed those leaving badly, and about which academics constantly had to complain in our academic bodies abroad as well as at the head office in Warsaw.
The Bureau accepts orders for translations of academic documents into foreign languages, [handles] admissions to foreign institutions of higher learning, arranges passports and visas, and issues international student cards (C.I.E.), which make it possible to enjoy various railway and visa reductions.
The Academic Emigration Bureau reminds that enrolments at foreign institutions of higher learning have already begun, and calls on all fellows concerned, in their own interest, to hurry in arranging their admissions.
At the same time the Bureau announces that, as in previous years, it arranges individual railway reductions and organises group departures to Belgium and France on the following dates: September: the 18th; October: the 9th, 15th, 20th, 25th, 28th, 30th; November: the 5th, 12th and 18th.
Written information on study conditions abroad is given upon receipt of the sum of 2 złoty.
Tragic Death of a Young Man from Olkusz in Dąbrowa. / Investigation of the Participants in the “Centrolew” Congress in Kraków / Doctor Punished for Immoral Acts / Orders by the Soviet Government.

Struck by a pole and killed.
Last Friday morning the 28-year-old Shlomo Hersh Fridman of Olkusz died in a tragic manner.
The tragic accident happened under the following circumstances:
Fridman was the co-owner and the fare collector of the bus that runs on the Olkusz—Sosnowiec line. Arriving in Dąbrowa, on Garuczowicz [?] Street, he noticed that part of the luggage was threatening to fall down. Therefore, while the bus was moving at full speed, he opened the door and leaned out to fix the luggage parcels. At that moment he received a heavy blow to the head from a telephone pole, from which Fridman suffered a brain concussion and was killed on the spot.
The tragically deceased was brought to Będzin, and after the necessary formalities had been completed he was taken on Sunday to Olkusz, where the burial took place the same day.
—o—
Investigation of the Participants in the “Centrolew” Congress in Kraków
The prosecutor of the District Court in Kraków, through the Sosnowiec police, has opened an investigation against 9 persons who took part in the “Centrolew” congress.
The 9 accused must answer a series of questions, among them: 1) which acquaintances took part in the congress, 2) which persons were the agitators, 3) whether there was an organizing committee, 4) who conducted what kind of agitation, 5) who made speeches, 6) what the content of the speeches was, 7) who drew up the resolutions, one or several persons, 8) in what way the resolutions were adopted, etc.
In this connection the accused, Messrs. Dobrowolski and Respawski [?], have issued an appeal to all who took part to register.
—o—
Doctor Punished for Immoral Acts
[Recently?] a great sensation was caused by the deed of Dr. Tehila [?] of Zawiercie, who lured a young girl into his apartment and raped her.
The child's parents brought charges against the doctor in court, and last Thursday the doctor stood trial; the court sentenced him to two and a half years of heavy imprisonment.
—o—
Orders by the Soviet Government.
The Soviet trade mission in Poland has placed orders with the machine factories in Polish Upper Silesia.
The first order, which is only of a trial character, amounts to 18 thousand dollars.
The purchased machines will be transported to Soviet Russia in the coming weeks.
A Good Friend. (From the Local Tales).

Beware of house-friends!
Every home, every married couple has its house-friend, but very few deserve this guest. For the great majority of house-friends it is healthier, for them and for everyone, if they are not let over the threshold.
Just such a fine [?] “przyjaciel domu” [house-friend] was Mr. Abraham K—l, a frequent visitor at a certain couple, Leib and Lea B—n, on Wari-Pienga [?] Street. Abraham, a childhood friend of the husband, became an even closer friend after the wedding, and it was not at all hard to see that the friendship was on account of the young, pretty wife his friend had married. The young wife Leahle, however, had scant sympathy for her husband's companion and received him in a friendly way only out of politeness. Abraham, though, sought all kinds of means to win the trust of his friend's wife; to this end he began writing letters to Ustroń, where the wife was spending the summer in a holiday lodging. In one such letter he informed her in deepest secrecy that her husband was betraying her, and that as his closest companion he even knew with whom and when. He also suggested to the wife that she come home to catch [?] her husband “red-handed”.
The young woman felt that these were no empty words; she indeed came suddenly to Będzin, knocked at her apartment and convinced herself that Abraham had not deceived her. Not wanting to cause a scandal, she kept silent, immediately left the apartment, went to the station and took the next train back to Ustroń!
The next day Abraham was already in Ustroń. Sure that with his little denunciation he had won the young wife's heart, he began persuading her that the only thing she had to do was to pay her husband back an eye for an eye — let her betray him too. Leahle agreed and assured him that it would happen. Abraham was certain from the start that by this she had him in mind — him, her “best” friend; so he did not stop criticizing her husband, who did not appreciate her and had the nerve to exchange her for such-and-such women. Leahle assured him that her revenge would be terrible.
The “best” friend spent three days in Ustroń waiting for the “revenge”. To his great disappointment he saw that Leahle was indeed preparing for revenge, but not with him — with some other young man unknown to him. Learning on which night it would happen, he telephoned his friend in Będzin and urged him to come to Ustroń at once: he would have the opportunity to see for himself how his wife was behaving. The husband left for Ustroń by the next train and, having waited for a late evening hour, went to his wife's lodging. Peeping through a crack in the shutter, he saw his wife sitting at the table with an unknown young man; they were drinking tea and carrying on very intimately. He waited a long time at the door until he could bear it no longer and knocked. His wife opened at once, introduced him to her friend, and all three sat down at the table. The new friend was somewhat at a loss and slipped away at the first opportunity. The couple remained alone. The husband had no clear proof that his wife had betrayed him; so on the one hand he was afraid to reproach her, and on the other he felt guilty enough to be able to have complaints against her [sic]. But the wife helped him out and openly explained that she had decided to take revenge on him and repay [?] him with the same sin he had committed against her. Whether she had already done it — that remains her secret.
For a long time the couple talked and argued; the husband swore by the holiest oaths that he would never betray her again; the wife — women are light-minded, as the saying goes — let herself be persuaded, and the rest was done by the fragrant summer night. And when the “house-friend” came the next morning to visit his friends, expecting that the couple was already ready for a divorce, he learned that his provocative tricks had been unmasked and that he was asked not to cross the threshold any more.

What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: There Are Many Takers, but Little to Give

[Head of the local page; Będzin — Loans for artisans.]
What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 28 Av 5690 — Piątek 22 sierpnia 1930 [Friday, 22 August 1930].)
Będzin
There are many takers, but little to give.
In connection with the planned loans for artisans in the Będzin powiat (county), we learn that the board of the Communal Savings Bank [Komunalna Kasa] in Będzin will shortly proceed to examine the lists of candidates.

—o—
Street Advertisements Must Have an Aesthetic Appearance.
A large part of the Jewish merchants in the Old Market are being harassed by the police on account of the street displays (wystawy), the so-called "shenklekh" (little cabinets).
The merchants therefore applied to the town board for permits for the "displays".
The matter was dealt with at Monday's meeting of the town board, which resolved that the street advertisements will be permitted if they are made aesthetically.
The same resolution also applies to the street advertisements of the local cinemas.
Parents, Avoid Fines

[Będzin — Education; compulsory schooling.]
We have been asked by the "Dozór Szkolny"[?] (school supervisory office) at the local Magistrate to bring the following to the attention of our readers:
Next Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday, i.e. on the 25th, 26th and 27th of this month, the children born in the years 1917, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22 and 1923 must be registered with the heads of the public (folk) schools.
In particular, the boys of the aforementioned age who study in unlicensed chadarim must be registered.
Parents who evade compulsory schooling will be punished with 5 days' arrest or 100 zł.
A New Member of the Kehilla Board

[Będzin — Kehilla.]
The newly nominated board member Mr. Meir Szenwald has resigned from the office. In his place R' Leybish Dymant (Mizrachi) is entering.
From the Second Floor onto the Pavement

[Będzin — Accident.]
Two-year-old Piasecki, sitting on the window-sill of the 2nd floor, lost his balance and fell down onto the pavement. The child's skull was fractured, and a few hours later he died.
Suicide by hanging.

In Małobądz, 28-year-old Więcławski hanged himself from the ceiling.
The cause of the suicide is an incurable illness.
A gang of swindlers arrested.

The police have arrested several swindlers who cheated a number of people in Zagłębie.
The swindle was carried out as follows: entering some home or other, they would ask whether the occupant did not own "dolarówki" [dollar-loan bonds] or other state securities.
When they were shown the dolarówki, they pretended to check the numbers and then declared that a prize had fallen on one of the numbers, and that once they were satisfied [paid], the holder would at once receive the sum won.
In this way they cheated a number of families in Zagłębie, until they fell into the hands of the police.
The swindlers are from Łódź.
From the Zionist-Revisionist movement.

Last Saturday a "question-box evening" took place before a packed hall, at which the following questions were discussed: 1) our attitude to the Congress for Labour Palestine [Eretz Israel], 2) the unity of the Histadrut ha-Ovdim [General Federation of Workers] in Palestine.
— This Saturday Mr. Y. Langfus will deliver in Będzin a report from the 4th World Conference in Prague.
— At the same time Mr. Kla"man [?] will deliver a report in the premises of the Zionist Organisation in Sosnowiec.
Revenge of a "deceived" girl.

On Sunday at midday, not far from the local railway station, the following scene was played out:
From Modrzejowska Street onto Małachowskiego Street ran, hurrying, the young man P., accompanied by his "kochanka" [lover] and her relatives, who demanded that he say "Harei at" [the Jewish betrothal formula]...
When Mr. P. rejected the proposal and started walking away, the "bride" treated him to a little sulphuric acid right into his right eye.
Hundreds of people witnessed the merry scene.
Out of laughter there came a...

On Sunday several young Christians in Gołonóg "amused themselves" with... blows. The amusement later took a serious turn: they came to blows, and one of them killed 24-year-old Lik with a plank.
The participants are in prison.
Shooting in the middle of the night.

On Saturday night at 12 o'clock the residents of Kołłątaja Street were woken by shooting in the street. It later turned out that a plain-clothes agent had fired at a gang of drunks who had thrown themselves upon him.
The caretaker of the house at Kołłątaja 40 was hit by several revolver bullets and was taken in a serious condition to hospital.
His parents stopped him marrying his sweetheart — he cut open his belly.

On Sunday the police were called to a would-be suicide who had cut open his belly with a knife.
The would-be suicide told the police that he is from Radomsko and has wanted for quite a long time to marry his "kochanka" [sweetheart], but his parents will not allow the match; on coming here to Będzin he suffered a nervous attack, which caused him to attempt suicide.
The dates for hearing the appeals.

On the 27th, 28th and 29th of this month the tax appeals concerning "umac" [?; probably the turnover tax] will be heard at the Izba [Treasury Chamber] in Kielce.
Those concerned must enable the local representative to be present at the sessions, at which Jewish livelihoods are being judged...
Died Suddenly

[Będzin — deaths.]
The 65-year-old Rajzl Cieszkowska, a resident of Zawale [?] Street, died suddenly. The cause was a strong epileptic attack.
— The 70-year-old Abraham Gasfrid [?], a resident of Małobądz, felt unwell on coming out of the “t-amtay” [?], and on entering his home he collapsed and died.
From the “Hitachdut”

[Będzin — Zionism, parties.]
In connection with the World Congress for Labouring Eretz Israel, a mass meeting takes place today, Friday, at which Messrs. Dr. Rechtman, Gerefler [?], Gertner and others will speak.
From today the regular lectures begin, which take place every Friday.
The next topics are the following: 1) the present situation in Zionism and the Balfour Declaration; 2) the juridical-political situation of Eretz Israel; 3) the mandate countries and the League of Nations.
From “Beit Lechem”

[Będzin — charity.]
The chairman of “Beit Lechem”, Mr. Balimowski, asks us to “wake up” the board members of the society, who sit with “folded” hands and do not come to the meetings at which the organisation of the relief campaign for the coming holidays must be considered.
We hold that Mr. Balimowski's complaints are justified, and that a board which takes the responsibility upon itself must be active and fulfil what lies within its competence.
Until 1 September the Concession of Paying 1½ Percent Tax Penalty Applies

[Będzin — taxes.]
The “Urząd Skarbowy” [tax office] has sent the Merchants' Association a notice in which it is stated that on 31 August the term for paying a one-and-a-half percent penalty on overdue [zaległe] tax debts expires, and from 1 September a 2 percent penalty will already be paid.
Sosnowiec — Large-Scale Abuses at the Local Customs House; Several Officials Already in Prison

[Sosnowiec — customs, crime.]
At the local customs house a series of abuses has been discovered, which were carried out systematically by officials of the office.
Several officials have been put in prison.
The damage suffered by the state treasury amounts to several hundred thousand zł.
The First Shipment of Eretz Israel Etrogim

[Sosnowiec — religion, Eretz Israel.]
This week Mr. Yehoshua Horowitz [?], delegate of the “Agudat ha-Etrog” in Jerusalem, stayed here with the aim of spreading the Eretz Israel etrogim, which grow on Jewish soil and are tended by Jewish hands.
Mr. Merowitz [?] concluded an agreement with the firm Zendel, which has undertaken to bring 300 etrogim of the best quality.
In connection with this a number of rabbis, headed by Rabbi Kook, have published an appeal that every Jew who buys an etrog should support only Jewish produce in Eretz Israel.
—o—
A Terrible Mistake by a Sick Woman
[Sosnowiec — tragedy.]
When misfortune is fated, it comes into the house.
Two weeks ago the 31-year-old Lea Rajnman fell ill with typhus. The course of the illness was not a bad one and was quite normal. The sick woman's mother, wishing her daughter to have proper care, moved her to her own flat at Mondoszewer [?] [perhaps Modrzejowska] 29.
On Thursday night, when the household had fallen asleep from tiredness, the patient, who at that moment had developed a high fever, got out of bed, went into the kitchen and drank a small bottle of vinegar essence.
All rescue measures were of no help, and the next morning the unfortunate woman died.
The case has aroused great grief and shock in our town.
—o—
A Child Is Killed Before Its Mother's Eyes
[Sosnowiec — accident.]
The 5-year-old Stanisława Hosława [?] wanted to cross the street to her mother, who was standing on the other side of the pavement. At that moment a car of the paper factory “Klucze” [?] drove past. The car ran over the child, who was killed before her mother's eyes.
—o—
He Grew Tired of Life
[Wojkowice — suicide.]
The 60-year-old Stanisław Chila [?] of Wojkowice tried to have his sick wife and daughter admitted to hospital, so that he could run the household. When his efforts achieved nothing, he cut the veins of his neck in order to commit suicide.
—o—
A Large Memorial Assembly
[Sosnowiec — Eretz Israel, commemoration.]
This Saturday night a large memorial assembly will take place in the municipal theatre on the first anniversary of the bloody events of 5689 [1929].
Speakers: Advocate [?] Baumeler [?] of Eretz Israel, Dr. Agisfeld [?] and others.
There will also be a large artistic part, including solo singing, recitations, a choir, pictures of life in Eretz Israel (among them a picture of the sad events) and more.
Zawiercie — Dedication of the “Brit Trumpeldor” Premises

[Zawiercie — Revisionist Zionism, Betar.]
Next Sunday the opening of the premises of “Brit Trumpeldor” takes place here, with the participation of the member of the Supreme Command Rozental, the chief commissioner of Keren Tel Hai Dr. Feldszuh, Ed. Hofman [?], Arch. [?] Zvi Banfeld [?], as well as Betar organisations of the Kielce voivodeship. At 2 in the afternoon a wreath will be laid on the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, there will be a general march through the town, and an entertainment in the town park with a very rich programme,
After 5 years the answer arrived..

Mendel Kornfeld, owner [of premises] on Browarna Street in Będzin, in the year 1925 submitted to the “Izba Skarbowa” [Treasury Chamber] in Kielce an appeal concerning turnover tax.
The “Izba” issued its decision on the appeal only on 30 April 1930. And until the answer reached the “patent” [i.e. the licence-holder], another 4 months went by, so that only this week did Mr. Kornfeld become clear whether he must pay the tax debt from the year 1925 or not..
Będzin will be on a par with everyone...
The cinema “Nowości” is being equipped for sound films. The first “talking” pictures are to be shown in the first half of the month of September.
On 14 September — political demonstrations.

On Tuesday the political commission of the Centrolew [the centre-left opposition bloc] in Warsaw held a meeting, at which it was decided that on the 14th of September demonstrations are to take place in a number of localities against Germany, which wants to tear away the “Danzig Corridor”.
On that day protest meetings are also to take place in Zagłębie.
—o—
He could not bear it..
At Mr. Gruszczyński’s, owner of a mill in Pilica, a sequestrator carried out a distraint. Gruszczyński took this to heart, and while lying in bed he suffered a heart attack.

Accident during a fire

In the night from Monday to Tuesday a fire broke out in Małobądz at a local owner’s [?].
While rescuing the ploughing machines, the peasant Giedrałowski [?] cut off his right hand.
—o—
A bloody brawl between a chauffeur and porters.
On Targowa Street in Sosnowiec a brawl broke out between a chauffeur from Upper Silesia and a group of Jewish porters. The brawl took on a most serious character and drew hundreds of people to the “battlefield”.
Only the police put an end to the brawl and led the “heroic” chauffeur off to the police station.

Campaign to reduce the tax on rail freight.

The Sosnowiec magistrate, with the consent of the city council, raised several months ago the tax on goods brought into Sosnowiec by rail.
The increase from 30 to 80 groszy per 100 kilos also applies to cheap foodstuffs, so that it quite often happens that the merchant has to pay more in tax than his entire profit amounts to...
The Small Traders' Association intervened several times with the city administration, which promised to reduce the tax, but everything stayed as it was.
It was therefore decided to send a delegation to the „Izba“ [the Chamber — probably the Treasury Chamber], where it will be demanded[?] that the unjust tax be set at its former level, i.e. 30 groszy per 100 kilos.
A representative of the Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce is also to take part in the delegation.
—o—
Large swindles at the „Strzemieszyce“ glassworks.
In Strzemieszyce there was a glassworks named „Strzemieszyce“. The owners of the works were Messrs. Surin and Drecki. A few months ago the glassworks passed to a new firm, „Teps“[?], and the former owners remained owing large sums, among them 150 thousand zł. to the State Monopoly, which had lent 200 thousand zł., the debt to be repaid in bottles.
Despite this, the original owners made use of the cheques of the old firm and in this way carried out further money transactions.
All the creditors, among them Baron[?] von Hagen[?] in Kraków, applied to the public prosecutor, who laid a „hand“ (an attachment) on the glassworks.

Mill owners want a higher price for flour.
In the premises of the Sosnowiec magistrate a conference took place with the participation of the price commission and the owners of the local mills, who demand that the commission raise the price of flour, arguing that wages keep rising and the products have become dearer[?].
After a lengthy discussion the proposal to raise [the price] was rejected.

"Two Neighbouring Towns"

(Chatter of a simple Jew.)
Having attended the Yizkor evenings in 2 neighbouring towns, I feel like drawing a parallel between the outward impressions of the evenings.
The first town, where the Yizkor evening was held on Thursday, we shall call "A"; the second town, where it took place on Saturday night, we shall call "B".
Both towns announced by posters the Yizkor evening for the benefit of the KKL (Jewish National Fund); both invited by telegram the speaker from Warsaw (incidentally[?] a citizen of the Land of Israel, in Poland by chance), who holds a high post in the KKL head office in the Land of Israel, a lawyer by profession and, on top of that, something "exotic" — the word is out that he is a Revisionist — God preserve us.
In both towns an "artistic" dessert was served after the speeches.
But my God, what a colossal difference between "comrades" and "comrades", between hospitality and tactlessness.
Town "A" awaits the invited guest; town "A" delegates the most respected Zionists to bring the guest into[?] the hall.
Town "B" does not wait for the guest invited by telegram; the academy is opened without him, and the "decorations" occupy the presidium..
Both towns formed presidiums: in town "A" the chairman of the Zionist Organisation and the guest, whereas whole[?] comrades do not want to "go up"[?] — what are decorations for?
Town "B": a presidium of the truest[?] deserving workers for the KKL, and all the comrades of[?] the guest do not want to "go up"[?] to receive the guest.
Both towns had speakers: town "A" — invited outsiders, heard out in absolute quiet; even the opposing youth is interested in hearing the "exotic" Zionist, a Revisionist leader (not a practical man[?]). His way of speaking on questions of land purchase is interesting.
Town "B" — also 6 speakers, local ones, speeches by everyday comrades and[?] the guest; an overtired audience makes noise, doors are banged, people run about, shouts: Chaim, Shmerl, Sala, Regina; even in the box sits a KKL activist with his sweetheart, talking and chatting, flirting to their heart's content. "Comrade, do turn round[?], you are disturbing, excuse me!"
For that I get laughed at: "You must be a Revisionist"... Now they sing "Hatikvah", then "Hatik-vah"[?], and a whistle is heard — apparently "Zionist" treyf, just like the concept of a Jewish State!
At the end a brawl, just like at..
In both towns, disputes in the KKL: town "A" debates principle; there is fear of "glui-chaim"[?].. Dr. Herzl of blessed memory is also a bit of a nuisance; perhaps a "pastifler"[?] or a "towarzysz" (comrade) of the PPS — these are "principles" (misprinted), God help us.
In town "B" also disputes, but — brr.. brr.. enough.. why wash [linen in public]? Why flog oneself publicly?
In town "A" the fathers say to the children: where are you going?
In town "B" the children say: Father! What have you done, I am ashamed..
Both towns have Zionist "premises", which cost tidy sums; but town "A" levied contributions on its members "after the good and after the [?]"; town "B" — what do you call that?..
In both towns prominent Zionists gather:
Town "A" always invites private persons with a friendly face, but town "B" always with "dessert" — people curse each other in the presence of guests, as in a tavern..
— 2 neighbouring towns..
A. Kanai.
Sports.

[Sports — football; match results.]
„Hakoach“ (Res.) — „Policja“ S.C. 2:2 (2:1)
Last Saturday the reserve team of „Hakoach“ held a friendly match with the strong „Policja“ [police] club. The latter came out with several reserve players and, despite its great ambition, did not manage to defeat the technically excellent „Hakoach“. In the first half the police club had a slight advantage and already in the 5th minute scored the first goal from an „eleven“ [penalty] through the right back. 15 minutes later the inside right shoots the second goal for „Policja“. Shortly before the break Szymek 4 shoots, with a splendid header, the first goal for „Hakoach“. After the change of ends „Hakoach“ takes over the initiative and the whole time has a strong superiority. Yet only 2 minutes before the end did Richter manage to score the equaliser. The best on the field: Rozen 11 [II] and Bożykowski of „Hakoach“ and the centre half of „Policja“. Referee: Mr. Chmiel.
—o—
„Hakoach“ — „Harta“ (Częst.) 1:1 (0:1)
At the same time that „Hakoach“ was on its outing to Olkusz, the first football team played a friendly match with „Harta“ in Częstochowa. People were sure of a certain victory for „Hakoach“, but the result was different. In the first half „Hakoach“ had the upper hand. Several chances are not used by the forwards; only in the 32nd minute does Gutman shoot a splendid free kick and „Hakoach“ leads 0:1. „Harta“ holds out excellently and, thanks to its backs Rapsztajn and Żewak[?], „Hakoach“ cannot shoot a single „goal“; but just before the end the ball goes through Przewoski[?] into the „Hakoach“ goal. Distinguished themselves: Bożykowski in goal, Jankielewicz 2, Szymek 2 and 3. Of „Harta“: the goalkeeper and the backs. Referee: Mr. Meyer.
—o—

What's New in Upper Silesia?

[Upper Silesia — short news items.]
Protest of the City Council against the German Government.
On Monday a session of the local city council took place in Katowice, which approved a series of economic points.
At the session Deputy Korfanty made an urgent motion to protest against the German government, which wants to curtail Poland's borders.
Before the vote on the motion the German councillors left the session.
—o—
Resignation of the German Consul?
The „Kölnische Zeitung“ reports that in the very near future the German consul-general in Katowice is to step down.
The consul is being appointed head of the personnel department in the Foreign Office.
—o—
An Unfortunate Accident.
In the Katowice brickworks a mass of earth broke loose and buried the 31-year-old worker Wieczechowski, who was killed on the spot.
—o—
Hurried to Her Death...
On Sunday evening the 39-year-old Krumpe[?] of Ligota got onto the train to Katowice. But the train had already moved off, and the passenger went[?] under the wheels..
—o—
The 14th — a Political Demonstration.
As our readers already know, the Centrolew (the [parliamentary] clubs that are in opposition to the present government) has decided that on the 14th [of September?] demonstrations are to take place in the larger centres of Poland.
Such a demonstration is also to take place in Katowice on that day.
In this connection the Christian Democratic [Chadecja] club in Katowice has issued an appeal calling for mass participation.
—o—
9 Miners between Life and Death.
On Monday at 12 noon a terrible catastrophe occurred at the „Hildebrandt“ coal mine. In the mine several pillars broke loose and buried 9 workers under them.
The rescue work is still going on, and according to the estimates there is no prospect of getting them out alive.
Dąbrowa

[Dąbrowa — crime; court.]
The Father Wanted to Marry — He Got a „Drashe Present“ [wedding gift] from His Children.
At 3-go Maja [Street] 38 lives the 68-year-old Kaspszyk together with his 3 grown-up children, 2 daughters and one son. Some years ago the old man became a widower, and he made up his mind to marry a second wife.
The children were against their father marrying, and because of this frequent quarrels broke out between them.
All of a sudden — it was on the 1st of March — the children found out that their father had already become a bridegroom and that the „ślub“ [wedding ceremony] was coming soon. At first they did not believe it, but seeing one day how the „bridegroom“ was dressing himself up „in vinegar and in honey“ [i.e. all spruced up], and that he was already getting ready for the „ślub“, the children tied his hands and feet to the bed..
At the „bridegroom's“ groans the neighbours came running and called the police, and the „bridegroom“ was untied.
This Monday the „devoted“ children stood before the district court in Sosnowiec, which sentenced the children to 6 months in prison

While repairing a balcony on the second floor, the worker Moshe Wolfmut[?] fell onto the pavement. In a grave condition the unfortunate man was taken to hospital.

Meeting of the Unemployed.
On Sunday the P.P.S. [Polish Socialist Party] organised a meeting of the unemployed here. A speech was given by Mr. Cypiał[?] of Dąbrowa, who stressed that the crisis is due only to the Sanacja, which runs a bad economy.

Terrible Consequences of a Children's Game.
On Sunday 3 Christian boys were playing on the square of the local „targowisko“ [market place]; they laid the 5-year-old Skapiński down in a pit, put a cap over his face and, laughing, covered him with sand. When the children dug out their friend, he was already dead.
—o—
A Big Fire.
On Sunday at midday a fire broke out in the village of Puszydłówka[?], which spread quickly over the village. Dozens of houses and barns were burnt down. The damage is very great.
Theatre Notes.

[Sosnowiec — theatre; review.]
(From the revue theatre "Arlekin").

The revue theatre "Arlekin", already well known in Sosnowiec, has reopened after a break of almost 3 months. As its first programme it staged a revue entitled "The Bewitched Wood" [?], consisting of 15 more or less successful numbers.
In first place stands out the well-known singer Mrs. Perl-Poretska [?], who performs several atmospheric songs in her pleasant voice, for which she is rewarded with long applause. A great attraction of the revue is the ballet, headed by Miss Lisińska and Kasadinach [?], which performed stagings of oriental dances very beautifully and successfully. Very good, too, is Miss Wiceszerkiewicz [?], who strolls about the hall singing, "gabbaing" [?] the "grass widows" who are among the audience. The number is a great success.
The sketch "The Double Bookkeeper", performed by Messrs. Bashan [?] and Marski, turned out not badly. But why must the main heroes of the sketch be called precisely "Tsinamon" [?] and "Leyzer" and speak a mangled Polish? It seems [?] that a Polish revue cannot manage without Jewish "shmontses" [cheap jokes].
That the audience is to be served [?] "Jewish" jokes we see from the compère, who conducts his "conférence" with much humour and special Jewish "kawały" [jokes]...
The programme is complemented by the excellent orchestra under the direction of Mr. Bajgelman–Abramowski.
The only thing that can be criticised is the decorative side, which is somewhat lame. On the whole the first programme is a very successful one.

A Letter to the Editor.
[Sosnowiec — hospital; letter to the editor.]
Dear Mr. Editor!
I ask you to print in your esteemed newspaper the following reply to Dr. Bigowski [?] of the Szelcer [?] hospital in Sosnowiec, to his explanations which were printed in your esteemed newspaper, number 32.
Although it is not pleasant for me to engage in polemics about a personally painful matter, I must reply, because you, Mr. Doctor, want to whitewash yourself and compromise my person.
1) It is not true, Mr. Doctor, that you only did [?] the "favour" for my child with the bandage; even on the days of "[?]" I was not let in to my child, for in the presence of witnesses the hospital staff would not let me in, saying: "P. doktór nie kazał wpószczić, bo pan jeszcze nie załatwił" [Polish: "The doctor ordered you not to be let in, because you have not settled yet"] — even though I had paid the hospital costs of 12 zł. a day in advance. Also, on the day before I went to the public prosecutor, I wanted to give you a proportionate sum, as is paid to other doctors, and you answered me that if I did not give you the demanded 800 zł. you would not release the child to me; and when the prosecutor inquired by telephone why my child was not being released, the staff answered: because I had not yet settled with you — whereupon the prosecutor ordered that the child be released to me at once. That simply means that you held my child as a pledge until I gave you as much as you, Doctor, wanted.
The proper fee for such an operation I am still ready to pay even now, and in addition — thank you.
Respectfully,
S. Suszek, Sosnowiec, Kowalska [?] 8.
