An Assault on the Jewish School.

(Can it be true that our conscience's feelings are to be trampled upon?)

We do not believe it, because it cannot be believed, one does not want to believe it, because it seems to be a thing of impossibility. We do not believe it, even though sensible persons came into the editorial office and assured us that the fact has already taken place and is already coming into force.

It is a matter of nothing more and nothing less than this: the Jewish general public schools (szkoły powszechne) in Sosnowiec have changed the order of instruction in such a way that, instead of studying six days a week as until now, there will be no more than five days of study a week, and the Jewish child will no longer be free from school only on the Sabbath day, as until now, but also on Sunday.

At first sight one might think that this outcry need not be an outcry at all; a simple, naive Jew without sophistication might ask: what is the noise about? What harm is there if the child also has Sunday as a holiday, so long as he can keep the Sabbath — and that is enough for him.

That is roughly how a simple Jew would think at the first moment; but as soon as one begins to analyse the matter, one must come to the conviction that it is not simple at all. For why, actually, was the reform made? What has made Sosnowiec suddenly different from all the other towns in Poland? Who in Jewish circles took the trouble to bring this change about? And since nobody raised the question, then for what purpose and for whose sake did the change come about? It is therefore self-evident that something is being aimed at by it, and that being so, we must not remain indifferent to the question.

We still cannot understand how the school inspector could allow himself this. One must remember well that these are the simplest, plain elementary schools for Jewish children, and since Jewish children study there, exclusively Jewish ones, and they have Jewish teachers — why should both the Jewish children and the Jewish teachers be freed here on Sunday?

If there is no special intention here, it is incomprehensible. The teachers — well, the teachers: they need not be watched, we need not worry about what they will do on that day; they are, after all, grown people. But the children — what will they do on Sundays? Who will look after them, and why should they be freed from lessons on that day?

It can only mean that the garment has a lining with a ground of a different colour. Who knows — perhaps once the teachers are freed on Sunday, they can in the near future be exchanged for Christian ones, and who knows, it may come so far that they will afterwards say that two days a week without lessons is really too much; and that being so, once there are Christian teachers, it is self-evident that it will be more convenient for them to exchange the Sabbath for Sunday.

Thus they will lead us step by step into the "cheder" [i.e. into the trap], and only then will it become clear to us why the present comedy was created; only then shall we learn that all the preparations were systematically, consciously calculated in advance, and then the picture will be revealed to us with all its colours and hues in its full size.

It is truly hard to believe that it should come to such a degree. Yet one must nevertheless not forget that here we are dealing with Jewish children from their earliest years, who must be brought up by Jewish educators in the spirit of the people — and that must nevertheless be reckoned with. The question of education is the most delicate matter in human life, and it is self-evident that the spirit of the child can be known only by an educator from the people to which the child belongs.

Should five-day instruction be introduced in the Sosnowiec public schools — which we find very hard to believe despite all the assurances from the most competent circles — it would be an unheard-of insult to our national feelings; it would mean a direct assault on the Jewish public schools; it would show us that we have no say in the upbringing of our people's children — and that is no trifle, it must not be taken lightly. We must already begin to carry out an energetic inquiry that will hold back the unbelievable decisions that would offend our feelings.

Jewish Sosnowiec must intervene in this question right now. It must confer with the school inspector and convince him that we cannot permit such an assault on the Jewish school and children.

We must tell him that for us Jews the upbringing of the child is everything in the world; the school is the child's home and the teacher is the spirit, the embodiment of the child; and from this standpoint we must have a say over the schools and the children whom we entrust to our educators, who bear responsibility for their deeds.

As it is, we do not have the school we would need to have; the present schools do not express the spirit of the people; the subjects are far from being according to our taste and needs; our languages are not taught there, the subjects our children need are not taught. The general (powszechne) schools are, after all, houses of education, institutions for all strata of the Jewish population, so they must be adapted to the needs of the people; and as if it were not enough that no attention is paid to this and that the children are in this way systematically cut off from the people, so that after the children leave school a kind of estrangement arises between them and us, between parents and children — they are still not content with the systematic opportunism[?] and want[?] to bring about an upheaval in the questions of the people's educational institutions. We must therefore not allow this assault to become reality.

Already now we must react[?] and find out[?] everything that is intended to be done with the schools to which we have entrusted our future.

Dr. Papuri.

On Creating Premises for a Hachnasat Orchim (Hostel for Poor Wayfarers) in Będzin

Będzin is a town that maintains a whole series of philanthropic institutions. But one institution is still missing which really ought to exist and is very necessary: namely, we have no „hachnasat orchim“ (hostel for wayfarers) where a stranger, a poor Jew, could spend the night instead of knocking about in attics and damp cellars.
The question of creating this necessary institution is already on the way to being realised. Some time ago Mr. Itshe Rozirowicz[?], who owns a house on Zawala[?] Street in Będzin, made over 5 rooms for the benefit of a „hachnasat orchim“, „oyf der grbn“[?] [unclear word]. Mr. S. Fürstenberg, on learning of the project to create such an institution, pledged 500 gulden [złoty].
Now the matter depends on the well-to-do part of the Jewish population; if the will is there, the „hachnasat orchim“ can be realised.
Elul in the Old Home (Pictures of the Little Shtetl of Former Times)

Only a few days have passed since the sad Three Weeks, from the Seventeenth of Tammuz to Tisha b'Av, and already in the shtetl one feels a kind of new gloom, a new sorrow and a deep seriousness; everyone's face is already clouded and mournful.
— The month of Elul is already coming — Elul is no small thing! — say a handful of Jews among themselves between Mincha and Maariv in the beit midrash — even a fish in the water trembles then!
And everyone really did tremble; you could see it on every face.
Here stands Yekl the butcher, a Jew who always used to make noise and bluster everywhere — in the beit midrash, in the street — cursing and insulting everyone, calling each person all sorts of nicknames; you look at him and simply don't recognise him. He is somehow so calm, quiet, almost gentle and soft as butter. He sits in a corner of the beit midrash in his place, holds a siddur or a book of Psalms and recites with humility and a weeping melody.
And even Shlomke the treyfnyak [eater of non-kosher food], a fellow who lies around day after day among the gentiles in the village and eats their butter and milk, is now quite a different person. He doesn't mix with the gentiles, hangs around the beit midrash all day and is happy when the shammes Ure-Hertse lets him put the candles into the hanging lamps.
— Elul! — he mutters as if to himself — no small thing, Elul is coming!
The coming of Elul made the greatest impression on the women of the shtetl. Like frightened little sheep they gather in circles, their kerchiefs (patshaylkes) pulled far down over their foreheads, their faces saddened[?], and they talk with sighs about the Day of Judgement, about the Days of Awe, and tremble with fear.
Here stands a group of shopkeepers' wives and market women. All year long they tear at and bite each other just like cats, and call each other everything under the sun. Now they talk among themselves like the very best of friends; no more quarrelling, no more cursing, and everyone is as quiet as little doves.
Even Tsipe Dvoyre, a shrew, a scold, a quarrelsome woman, a „cooking-spoon“ [busybody], who gets under everyone's skin, who knows what goes on in everyone's pot and spoon, whose mouth everyone fears like hell itself — even she is entirely different: she speaks humbly, meddles nowhere, runs every morning to the beit midrash to hear a Kedusha or a Barchu and is as quiet as a dove.
— Elul is coming soon — she whispers as she runs, her Korban Minchah [women's prayer book] under her arm — Elul is no game!
On Saturday evening the whole congregation gathers in the synagogue to hear the rabbi's sermon.
The rabbi reproves the congregation severely: he speaks about baseless hatred, slander and gossip, about begrudging one another, about sins between man and his fellow and between man and the Omnipresent — between man and man and between man and God. He speaks about Sabbath desecration, about Torah study, about prayer. He is angry that people talk during prayers and the Torah reading, and he concludes with a melancholy tune:
— The Day of Judgement is already coming, the day when everyone must give account before the Master of the Universe. But the Holy One is, as it were, good: He gives us time to mend our deeds, He gives us a whole month to repair what we have spoiled all year. Let each of you see to improving his ways; live well with one another, give charity, study, pray, hold your tongues, forgive everything to everyone, and the Blessed Name will forgive you too.
„Ashrei temimei derekh“ — Yossi the fisherman begins with the skarbove [traditional High Holiday] melody, and the congregation repeats after him with relish verse after verse. Everyone recites Psalms, young and old — even Berke the shoemaker and Khaimke the tailor, who always used to take advantage of the Sabbath twilight darkness in the beit midrash to throw wet, crumpled towels at the heads of the eastern-wall householders — even they now sit decently[?] and don't touch the towels hanging on the pillars of the bimah; this is no time for such things — it's Elul!
„Vehu rachum yechaper avon velo — o — yashchit“ — the town's mourner [leading the service] twirls the „velo“ to the Saturday-night tune, but this time with more devotion than ever. As if he were begging the Master of the Universe not to act by the measure of strict justice, and the whole congregation feels the intention and draws out the „velo yashchit“.
In the beit midrash dread reigns; it is dark all around, the sun has long since set, the edge of the sky in the west is red as blood, and the redness reminds everyone somehow of fires and other sad things that have happened in the shtetl since it was built. Everyone prays with broken hearts and promises in their hearts to be good and pious.
The strongest impression on the shtetl was made by the shofar. Mightily its voice bursts out through the windows of the beit midrash and echoes everywhere. Tru-oo-oo! The shofar resounds, the shofar calls, the shofar warns!
And quiet and calm it was in the shtetl the whole month of Elul. All the disputes about shochtim and about seats in the beit midrash vanished; enemies become good friends, and people make amends to one another with a pinch of snuff and a cigarette; quarrelsome women send each other some of the preserves they have just cooked. Cheder children who had not spoken to each other a whole year try to make up, and swear by a handshake and a tzitzit fringe to live in peace. Girls with boys[?] stop meeting secretly in the evenings behind the priest's orchard, and the women scold their daughters less. The shtetl's jesters, the habitual joke-tellers, stop making jokes and suddenly become serious. Jews sit mostly in the beit midrash, praying and studying.
And late at night there drift from the open windows of the beit midrash the voices of dozens of Jews who sit bent over the big yellowed Gemaras, Mishnayot and Ein Yaakovs, before the dim little flames of the tallow candles, and study with great diligence.
Elul is no small thing!
Dr. M. Katz.
The Peddlers' Question

(The antisemitic campaign around the matter. — What would we need to do in order to hold back the black clouds?)

Last week we read in our paper the „great cry of woe of the peddlers who trade in Upper Silesia“, and whoever paused after reading the article and took stock of everything the author, Mr. Zhlanke[?], told us, must have come to the conviction that the matters are serious: black clouds are being driven onto the small trader, already hunted and plagued as it is, to whom the bit of livelihood from peddling comes so hard and bitterly, with so much toil and torment, that with the best will and energy, with the most strenuous efforts, he squeezes his already weak strength out of himself until he earns his living.
But of all this our antisemites want to know nothing; the black crows do not want to be satisfied with that, and they strive with all their strength to provoke friction and hatred between those who bring the goods into the homes and their customers, who are satisfied with the trade.
And when even that did not help — when the working mass shook itself off in disgust from the antisemitic incitement, from the „da tshini[?]“ „ideals“ with their sermons about what the world stands on; when the „loyal“ citizens saw here the true aim of those who go about idle and empty and want to ride the old social mare, and like parasites want to suck the body and draw their livelihood from it — they shook off the unwanted guests and distanced themselves from them.
True, the antisemitic plantings were not entirely lost; here and there fruits of the antisemitic incitement appeared, but it would not have lasted long, because in the end the calm, quite simple inhabitant saw that what was meant here was nothing more than to oppress the Jew, without regard to where he can buy better and more conveniently; and therefore the customers did not listen to the talk of the bribed people and acted as was more convenient for them, as their common sense dictated.
When it was realised that these methods had gone bankrupt on all their fronts, it was decided to proceed by force: they would[?] search and rummage in the archives — perhaps they would manage to find some old restrictions or other against the Jews, and that would be the best and most consistent course, because in that case they would go with force and power, with the force of the law; and it is, after all, an old rule: he who seeks, finds. And indeed they dug up an old German law, not used since time immemorial, that within 10 kilometres of the border trading is forbidden. They seized upon it as upon a windfall[?], for with this argument one can operate[?] quite well, since in Upper Silesia everything is around the border. And precisely here lies the crux that endangers peddling in Upper Silesia.
The number of peddlers among us is quite considerable, and we must reckon with them so that it should not, God forbid, reach the level of a catastrophe, for in that case many, many Jews would be left without a livelihood, without a piece of bread. They would have nothing at all to get through the next day; and then the complications — they would drag new bankruptcies along with them. We must therefore see to it with all our strength to avert this terrible catastrophe, which can happen as soon as we remain indifferent to the dangerous situation.
Mr. Zhlanke[?] comes to the conclusion that one may not rely on anyone, that one must oneself see to tackling the solution of the question, because nothing came of all the salvations and consolations of our [Sejm] deputies. True, one can be in full agreement with the idea of „If I am not for myself, who will be for me“, because if we do not act for ourselves, others will certainly, certainly do nothing; here, however, in this case, one must stop and consider calmly: are these persecuted Upper Silesian Jews able to achieve by themselves what they need? Can they get through to the high windows they need to reach so that this very difficult question may be finally resolved in their favour? Do these Jews have the time and possibility for it? Can they arrange it themselves? We must look the truth in the eye; we must not fool ourselves here, because in that case we would suffer a complete defeat, which we must not allow.
Why should we fool ourselves, when we are firmly convinced that it is a matter of impossibility: people who live on a day's wage cannot undertake[?] to bring about the solution of such a difficult question, which will everywhere run into impossible difficulties. To work out a free path for the peddlers one must have enough time and a special understanding of this matter; otherwise it would mean carrying out an intervention merely for form's sake. Moreover, people from the ranks of the peddlers will by no means have the possibility of reaching the personalities who must be approached and with whom the conferences must be continued constantly.
In any case one must not imagine that it is so easy to overcome the difficulty. One sees clearly and plainly that by force they want to tear the morsel from the mouths of people who work so hard to keep up their possibility of existence, which they earn with so many difficulties and so much bitterness.
The peddlers' question is a matter that should concern the whole Jewish Zagłębie, because indirectly it touches every Jewish citizen.
We must therefore see to it that the most important personalities take an interest in the question — ones who are, specifically, in contact with our deputies; otherwise it will not be possible to overcome the difficulties and to obtain a free path for the peddlers in Upper Silesia.
Had we sound economic institutions, we would say that they should take this into their charge and that it should be conducted under their direction; unfortunately, however, we have so little trust in them that they would do no more than neglect so important a matter. True, among decent people such institutions would handle such a matter, but we cannot allow ourselves to stake a question of first-class importance.
And therefore the most fitting plan would be for a special commission to be created for this purpose, which would deal intensively with this important affair.
In such a commission we would need lawyers and economists who would understand how to approach[?] this so important question.
R. Let.
Interviews with High-Placed English and Arab Personalities (Reported by Rabbi Yaakov)

[Satire — Palestine; British policy.]
With MacDonald.
— Mr. Minister, what is the sense of your government having withdrawn the certificates?
— Oh, that is only a temporary measure; the Balfour Declaration, on the other hand, remains forever unshaken, and it cannot be withdrawn...
— True, Mr. Minister, but how is it possible to create the Jewish national home, according to the letter of the Mandate, without the party concerned itself, i.e. without Jews?
— Ah [?], certainly, the creation of the Jewish national home is our most sacred duty! Of course one cannot provoke the Arabs by letting [?] too many Jews into the country, but accept my most precise assurance that the foundations of the Mandate remain iron-firm...
— But, Mr. Minister, there is talk of restricting land sales and other such rumours; so [?] how is it possible to build the Jewish home without land, simply in the air?
— Mister, that is only a temporary measure to protect the poorest fellahin. But I assure you that the English government will never renounce its most sacred and agreeable duty of safeguarding the foundations of the Mandate...
— But, with all due respect [lit. "may you be healthy to me"], how can a Labour government shut the gates of Eretz Israel to Jewish halutz workers?
— Oh yes, Mister, England has no intention whatsoever of giving up the Mandate, and she will continue to conduct her policy in accordance with the terms of the Mandate and with the Balfour Declaration. You may tell all Jews that they can sleep peacefully...
With the chairman of the Arab delegation.
— You are surely satisfied with the latest ordinances of the British government?
— What are you saying? The British government is handing over huge tracts of land to the Keren Kayemet and driving out the native fellahin; so [?] how can we be satisfied?
— But the withholding of the certificates is surely a proof of goodwill [?] towards your delegation?
— Aha, all in all the delegation went away with nothing, and the English government would on no account give in and take anything off the terms of the Mandate..
— And what do you think, Effendi, about a peaceful coexistence between Jews and Arabs?..
— Of course a peaceful coexistence of the two Semitic peoples is necessary. But the English, may their name be blotted out, give the Jews the highest posts in the Palestine administration, the whole budget [?] is spent on Jewish purposes, all the workers at the Haifa [?] port are Jews, and of the Jewish murderers only one was punished with death, while of the peaceful Arab population no fewer than twenty-five were sentenced — can there then be any talk of peace?..
What I Heard, What I Saw (Reported by Ben Amotz)

[Sosnowiec, Będzin — local feuilleton.]
1.
A new "disease".
There is nothing new under the sun — so says Ecclesiastes. Along came the Jewish "proletarians" of Sosnowiec and discovered something that truly contradicts King Solomon's words. This news will no doubt cause an "upheaval" in the medical world; the greatest scholars will take up the question, and I am "sure" that the new discovery will win more fame than Einstein's theory.
— You are curious? Then listen.
In all times, up to the present generations, it was known that mankind suffers from the "patented" diseases, for example: kidneys, heart, lungs, ears, nose and the like. Every human organ has its doctor who specialises in it. But these methods [?] were valid once; in the present time, when it is [?] possible for important novelties to be discovered in all fields, a new disease has been discovered in Sosnowiec
— a "proletarian disease".
And whoever of you strolls through the streets of Sosnowiec has probably seen a posted death notice (klepsydra) in which it was announced that "So-and-so son of So-and-so died of the proletarian disease".
Henceforth [?] the "old diseases of former times" cease to exist today; there will be no more than 2 diseases in life
— a bourgeois one and a proletarian one...
The supplicatory prayers (tkhines) will also undergo a change. Instead of praying "that we be guarded and protected from all manner of illnesses, God save us", people will pray: may it be Thy will that my prayer be accepted, not to fall ill with the proletarian disease...
2.
The same Yente, only differently veiled..
Sosnowiec is counted among the towns of the first rank: there are shops in the European style, an educated youth, a theatre, doctors [?]; even suicides happen in Sosnowiec no less than in Warsaw, Łódź, etc.
To what does this apply, when was it said? To external matters; but the inner Jewish life, or better said kehilla life, is very well suited to the Chełm tales [printed "Chlemer"] of old...
For years people have been saying that the town synagogue must be repainted; it is surely a disgrace for a kehilla to possess such a shabby, half-ruined holy place.
They talked so long until the kehilla said:
— We will hear and we will do! [an inversion of "we will do and we will hear"]
— Enough preaching already, we are setting to work.
And indeed scaffolding (rusztowania) was put up, the painters cleaned their brushes, and.. (here comes a pause, because the same scaffolding was put up in the Old Sosnowiec synagogue, and since the gabbaim of the synagogue in Old Sosnowiec are busy with "politics", the scaffolding was put up in the open field...)
3.
"Half wild beast, half cattle"...
The same matter again. An embarrassing one, a tragicomic one, more comic than tragic. They take a cantor with a name, at whom everyone — Hasid and ordinary Jew alike — "melts" with sweetness, and toss him like a ball between treif and kosher. It is unheard of on the whole globe — a Hasidic Jew shouts at me — that a cantor should be declared kosher on Sabbath, become "treif" again on Thursday evening, and be kosher again on Friday at noon..
And the cantor, listening to the complaints of the naive Jew, says:
— "Woe and alas to my years that I find myself in such a fix. They drain my blood every day; I think to myself: what am I, and who am I? — 'half wild beast, half cattle'; yes, woe to my years, that...
The cantor's words suddenly break off like strings during playing, and another Jew, a Radomsko Hasid, tries to console him:
— Don't fret, cantor — the Jew says to him — we Będzin people are used to it; it often happens that on the Sabbath during prayers the shammes proclaims a ban on the cholent bakers, and on Sunday morning [printed "gri" for "fri"] the cholent bakers are kosher again...
4.
Courtesy comes first..
At a Yizkor evening.
Not in Będzin but in Sosnowiec, in the town where everything is available except one thing:
— a soul — more precisely, a tiny drop of decency among the youthful part...
He speaks, Advocate [?] Bugeld [?], about the cruel massacres that took place in Eretz Israel in the month of Av 5689. His words — like lightning during a storm [?] — as he describes the Arab attack on Hulda, which together with the Herzl Forest was destroyed and burned; Jewish heroes [?] fertilised the soil with their holy blood. And...
— In the hall there is whispering [?]; from afar come shrill voices, cynical laughter and, regrettably — a whistle... A large share in this belongs to the organisers, who allowed the front boxes (loges) to be filled with "hooray-boys".. who turned the mournful Yizkor evening into
— a "hinky-pinky" [?] evening..
5.
"Wise men", take heed..
Before us lies a homely proclamation (kol koreh) in which people are called upon not to read the afternoon papers.
We do not suspect the authors of the appeal of bad intentions; we believe in their honesty. But — "this is not the way"! The proclamations will not improve the situation; on the contrary (let it stay between us), the more bans, the more curiosity; it is, after all, a well-known thing that
— "stolen waters are sweet"...
When the young man or the girl learns that a ban has been issued on this or that newspaper, which feeds its readers titillating stories, he will "break down gates" in order [?] to get the paper, with which he will settle down in the innermost rooms and swallow every word...
It is better — in my opinion — not to interfere; let the readers "drink" full cups of the filth that the sheets spread; he will drink so long until he becomes sick of it, and only then will he shake himself free of the "cultural fare".
What Must We Do — For the Jewish Children of the "Powszechne" Schools?

We stand on the eve of the new school year, and once again the question lodges in the minds of thousands of Jewish parents: — where shall we send our children? The question is a very painful one, and every father and mother, without exception, approach it with the necessary[?] deliberation.
But today's economic situation does not allow Jewish parents to permit themselves[?] to dwell long on questions of education. The yoke of earning a living makes one forget the sorrow and pain of the aforementioned[?] problems, and the upshot is that difficult questions are not thrashed out and are not brought to their proper, real implementation.
And so, year in, year out, the ranks grow of parents who deal with their children's school question in such a way that wherever the door of a school opens easily, that is where the children are pushed in.
It is a fact that the number of Jewish children in the "powszechne" [state elementary] schools in Zagłębie has grown several times over during the last 3 years, and the trend for the future is stronger still. There are, God forbid, no assimilationist intentions in this. But meanwhile a new generation is growing up with a new face, and, consciously or unconsciously, a youth is slipping out of our hands.
What are our "patented" communal workers doing about it? Is anyone thinking about it?
The existing communal and private schools are too much occupied with themselves. When the eve of the school year comes, they fire off all their gunpowder at the head of the opponent, but nobody lifts a finger for that "unknown soldier"[?] who becomes an outright[?] deserter[?] and slips away from the front — and that is a crying injustice.
In Western Europe and America a remedy has been devised for the children of the public schools, or whatever they are called there: alongside the civic schools — public schools and the like — they have added[?] afternoon schools, especially for Jewish studies (in America a whole network of Talmud Torahs). How much has been rescued there by this we do not know; about America, however, we do know that to this day 10 per cent of the Jewish children study in Talmud Torahs — 60,000 out of a total of 600,000. Here, where national pressure bears down harder, the number of Jewish children who would attend afternoon Jewish study would be much larger.
But here nobody is thinking about it yet, although the situation is becoming analogous to that in America and Western Europe. It is a question of the coming decade, and there will grow up among us a youth without Torah and without knowledge.
What will Polish Jewry then pride itself on?
Will we in future, too, be able to show America and Europe that, if materially we are often dependent on them, we stand ten heads higher in the spiritual respect?
And not only towards the outside — it is a question of preserving our existence from within.
In today's bitter economic situation we are not in a position to open cheap[?] schools for Jewish children. We are not waging any war[?], and if only we could preserve the surviving remnant that we possess from better times.
But something must be done: independent Jewish cultural activists must set about at once organising, in Będzin and in Sosnowiec, evening courses with Jewish studies for the Jewish pupils of the powszechne schools. The initiative here belongs to the kehilla, and in our opinion the parties have little here on which to spread out their agitation. The programme can be as innocuous as possible.
As for the financial means, they can be quite limited here. The question of premises (the hardest in school economics) does not arise at all. For this purpose all the school buildings stand open, where lessons take place, as usual, in the morning. The teaching staff can also easily be found, especially considering that enough unemployed teaching forces are wandering about among us.
One way or another, the question is topical and must be placed on the agenda, at the public table of all our activists to whom the fate of the growing Jewish generation is dear. If we live in a time when a national upswing and renaissance on a larger scale is impossible, then at least let what can still be saved be saved!
Zelig Amiel.
The Peddler Problem in Upper Silesia

[Upper Silesia — economy; peddlers.] (A reply to Mr. Zielonka of Sosnowiec)
In your article entitled "The great cry of woe of the peddlers in Upper Silesia" you reproach our communal activists for doing nothing about the new decree against the peddlers — the so-called "border pass permit".
It is true that this is an unheard-of chicanery against several hundred families who earn their living from peddling. It is evident that with this decree the aim was, in general, to do away at one stroke [lit. "to make"] with the few hundred trade licences and permits that had been issued after all the interventions with the authoritative quarters.
But whether all the effort and exertion is worth it — and about the whole peddler question in general — I will state my doubts in the columns of your esteemed paper; first of all, though, a few figures:
Two years ago, i.e. before the peddlers were organised in associations, the peddlers were to be found in 5 towns. First place was held by Oświęcim with about 600 peddlers, for the most part people who had a "chazakah" (established right) from Austrian times to peddle across the border in "Germany"; then Katowice with about 100 peddlers; later, after the union with the whole of Poland, there came to Upper Silesia [people from] Zagłębie and [?] immigrant Polish Jews. All in all, the number of Jewish peddlers can be reckoned at up to 1000 men.
They peddled all kinds of articles, from a necktie to [?] ("esnharg"); everything was given to the worker on instalments. The worker earned well, so he paid his instalments punctually, and thus the peddlers multiplied like mushrooms after rain. A whole army of girl peddlers came into being, and when a girl went home for a holiday to her native shtetl in Eastern Galicia decently dressed [?], then right after the festival (isru chag) several dozen more families arrived and threw themselves into the same trade. It became a "new America": for a cellar or attic room in Katowice or Königshütte [Królewska Huta, now Chorzów] people paid [?] ("san-frion"); Oświęcim was overflowing with strangers, "not of the [?]" ("hapishe"); whoever after a year had a few hundred gulden [złoty] became a full-fledged wholesaler (hurtownik). It is estimated that Oświęcim alone had 200 "wholesalers". Łódź had already supplied them with packets of goods; anyone who had a finger signed. Thus one could see how with every train from Oświęcim several hundred peddlers arrived, until... until the inevitable collapse came.
If the economic crisis made itself felt throughout Poland, here in the peddling trade it took on a catastrophic character; blow after blow rained down on the poor peddler's head.
All at once a large part of the clientele, i.e. the mine and smelter workers, became unemployed and consequently had nothing with which to pay their countless debts. Besides this trouble there also came the Jew-hater Mr. Horymach [?] with his hate [?] sheet "Do Czynu", which is backed by a group of antisemitic merchants. The sheet waged a hooligan pogrom agitation, so that it simply became dangerous for a Jew to go out to the village to collect a few gulden.
But the greatest blow for the peddler was the sudden withdrawal of his credit; for as long as he still supplied the worker with all his needs, the latter still had an obligation to pay something off; but the moment the credit was cut off, the customer had a ready and justified excuse: since you don't supply me with fresh goods, I must buy for cash myself, so I cannot pay any old debts. And then the well-known "bewitched wheel" (vicious circle) arose: the peddler did not collect, so he did not pay the wholesaler; the latter in turn could not redeem the protested bills; Łódź stopped giving packets, and bankruptcy came along the whole line and dragged everyone down without exception.
As said, credit suddenly ceased; only one thing grew stronger — the harassment and chicanery. 75 percent fell victim to the troubles enumerated above, and for the small number who remained the licence decree began.
Every year the peddler used to receive his licence 3 months before the New Year; since 1929 the reduction began. For months people ran around with intercessions; at long last Oświęcim received [licences] for 200 persons in the 4th month, Zagłębie — in the 5th month, and Katowice — in the 6th month. Altogether the number of Jewish licences reached up to 400.
The "lucky ones" thought they would now have peace — unfortunately they were mistaken: someone dug up an old, mouldy law that peddling is forbidden within 10 kilometres of the border, and since all of Upper Silesia is close to the border, the licence is consequently worth nothing at all. The peddler goes about with his bit of merchandise like a smuggler; every day a police report, which costs 20 zł.
Now I ask you, esteemed comrade Zielonka: is it worth exerting oneself so much for peddling? Is there a lower livelihood, [?] speaking, than hawking in Poland? Don't you know yet that this "trade" is condemned to go under? Why, the voivode declared it to our Sejm [?] deputy Mr. Hartglas: that he will endeavour every year to issue fewer licences, until it stops altogether.
True, we are a stiff-necked people and also somewhat organised, but don't forget, Mr. Zielonka, that beside us stand powerful merchants' organisations and economic associations, which see in the peddler (rightly or wrongly) a competitor to their existence, and in the "higher spheres" they are reckoned with more than our poor associations; when they bang on the table they are heard more than our poor intercessions.
You will surely ask: what, then, are the 400 families who live from peddling to do in such hard times? I will answer you: firstly, this is no livelihood; it was good once, when goods were being thrown around. Secondly: here I come to a crux and a deeper problem — the "Menachem Mendel" must be restructured and made into a productive element. How? — partial emigration, creating cooperatives on sound foundations, training them as artisans, etc.
True, from saying to doing is a long way, but a beginning must be made some time, and precisely through our associations, for as a productive element there is still room in Upper Silesia for thousands of Jewish families. In any case, it cannot go on as it has until now; servile intercession and lamenting "Eicha" will create nothing positive; entirely different livelihoods must be created for the peddler of today.
Dawid Ehrlich,
President of the Small Traders' Association in Katowice.
We Are Going Forward.

Dedicated to the Elul campaign for the "Keren Kayemet" [Jewish National Fund].
(From our Eretz Israel correspondent.)

Do not weep and do not lament
and do not bow your head
in such days.
Go on your way.

And the day went by and the night came. A quiet one, a dark one. Jerusalem was torn into quarters, into streets, into pieces of streets. People spoke quietly, stole along the walls:
— Quiet?
— Quiet!
They say: in our area there is plenty of self-defence.
— Yes, there is. And a very long line runs[?] there; after all, we already border on the field, on the suspicious valley.
The suspicious valley stretches along several quarters, and opposite, on[?] the hill on the far side of the valley, a few little houses lie[?] scattered, suspicious, dark, without[?] a sign of life. In the darkness they sit — the Arabs — straining all their senses, listening whether the Jews are not coming up against them.
In the faint, mystically quiet starlight a row of black silhouettes moves out of the last alley. Unhurried, with heavy steps, they file like a single[?] row down into the valley. Not a word, not a human voice; only the creaking of the heavy heels is heard.
The children are asleep. The father and the mother sit awake; from time to time he goes out, catches a rustle, meets the neighbour:
— Quiet?
— Quiet!
The mother, the tender young mother, covers with hidden love the "little chicks"[?], smiling in their sleep, and steals a glance into her husband's eyes. She, the Jewish daughter, feels that there, in the hospitals, in the mortuaries, lie now in rows people bloodied by knife stabs, with glazed, staring eyes. She feels that the struggle has begun, the struggle is going on, and no one may think of himself, not even of the little "chicks". The struggle is for the greatest vital interest of the people and for a just cause that has been cradled[?] since the prophets and since the bloody uprisings of two thousand years ago.
A rifle cracks, a second, a third, and soon the single shots pass into a lively shooting. It is strangely light on the soul. No fear, no dread — all feel and acknowledge that without birth pangs so great a thing is not born. Without sacrifices no people can conquer its free, dignified existence. These rifle shots, if they are unavoidable, must be overcome...
* * *
So people reckoned, so they felt, because no one knew what net of treachery, hatred and human insolence[?] they — the English officials — had prepared for the Jews in their last hope in this land. People did not know that human beings, Englishmen, proud "Albionites"[?], could be so cynical. People did not know that history repeats itself so, in every detail; that the age-old "Come, let us deal wisely" [Exodus 1:10], with all its bloody means, is still accessible in our times to the nature, spirit and morals of a high culture.
It is unbelievable, but a fact is a fact. Slowly, for years, the net was woven. Thread after thread, step after step, a step here, a step in London, until the net reached the necessary length and breadth, until it had enveloped the whole matter, and then the executioners began to draw it tight.
It is unbelievable, yet it is so clear that one can picture it in details, in figures: how the criminal idea was born, how it was raised, warmed up and was meant to be carried out in life. A step in Eretz Israel and a step in London. In Eretz Israel — through cynical national insult, through poison, hatred and blood. Literally blood, through lost human lives. There in London — through the high-political game of diplomatic cunning[?] and lies.
But we are here: we live, we hope[?] and we act. One can destroy a house, two, three, ten, but thousands of houses will not be destroyed. [Barn?], colonies, towns, factories and 170,000 Jews can no longer be uprooted.
We are here and we shall go on along the same road: to peace we shall answer with peace, and to hatred we shall answer with hatred, and we shall come into the land more and more, and we shall build and create. No one will stop this process any more.

Do not weep and do not lament
and do not bow your head
in such days.
Go on your way!

P[?]. Eiger.
Solemn Yizkor Academies in Będzin and in Sosnowiec

Last Thursday, on the first anniversary of last year's events in the Land of Israel, the local Keren Kayemet committee organised a solemn Yizkor academy in the „Nowości" theatre. Before a packed hall and in a serious mood the academy is opened with the Polish and the Jewish anthems played by the orchestra of „Hakoach"; then the chairman of the academy, the trustee of the Ts.S.[?], Mr. G. Landner, gives the opening speech in Hebrew. He dwells on last year's events in the Land of Israel, which shook the whole world; all of world Jewry united and raised its mighty voice of protest against the English mandatory power, and especially against the Palestine administration, which did not manage to suppress the attacks of the incited Arab murderers who wanted to destroy the whole Jewish Yishuv, built up with so much sweat and blood. But our halutzim in the Land of Israel were not frightened, and a mighty voice was heard: „That which cometh into your mind shall not be at all." And here the speaker switches to Yiddish and says: even now there still stand before our eyes the holy innocent souls of Safed and Hebron and the heroic Maccabean figures of Hulda, Talpiot, Jerusalem, Haifa, and we must honour their memory. At these words the orchestra plays a funeral march and the entire audience rises from their seats and remains standing throughout the funeral march; and the spilled Jewish blood, which still cries „O earth, cover not my blood", will be a new blood-covenant of the Jewish people with its land, the Land of Israel — and he ends with the words „No weeping, no mourning — onward to act, onward to work."
Then the chairman gives the floor to the guest from the Land of Israel, our townsman, the president of Hadar HaCarmel, Mr. Yehuda Shneur, who delivers an impressive speech in warm, heartfelt Hebrew. He declares that the Jews of the Land of Israel were not at all frightened by the events, and turns to the Jews of the Diaspora: do not be discouraged, do not be downcast; it is a mistake to think that a pogrom took place in the Land of Israel. No! There was no pogrom there in the sense people are used to in the Diaspora countries, only a struggle between two peoples, and we are proud of this struggle; and we also know that this is not the last struggle, but we take up the struggle and we are sure of our victory, because justice is on our side. The audience, it seems, understood his beautiful Hebrew and rewarded him with resounding applause. Then the floor goes to the delegate of the Jerusalem directorate of the Keren Kayemet LeIsrael, the lawyer Mr. Banefeld[?], who delivers a masterly rhetorical speech, and the whole audience was as if electrified. With the greatest suspense the audience listens to his long expositions, and he carries away the whole audience with his enthusiastic speech, such as Będzin has not heard for a long time. The speaker develops the whole present grave Zionist problem and the deeply practical answers we must give at this moment. The first is — land: the more land is in our possession, the more secure our positions will be. Second — people: the more people we can bring into the Land of Israel, the sooner we will reach our goal of a Jewish state. Third — arms: we must be prepared so that, should such attacks, God forbid, recur, we will be sufficiently protected. We do not want to use arms offensively, to attack anyone; we are not murderers, but if anyone disturbs our work of building we will have to defend ourselves, even with arms in hand. Fourth — capital: a country cannot be built on sentiment alone; both private and national capital must be drawn in. Fifth — sacrifices: no country has yet been built without sacrifices, and the Jewish people too must bring various sacrifices, sacrifices of money and also human sacrifices; and it lies in Jewish national ambition to fulfil the task we have taken upon ourselves, so that the world cannot say of us that we are a people of bankrupts. — Amid thunderous applause the speaker ended his lecture, which left a strong impression, and the audience could not calm down for a long time; then the chairman declared a 10-minute break.
In the second part Miss Zaks recited the poem by the well-known Palestinian writer Moshe Stavsky „To my sister, Be'er Tuvia", translated into Yiddish. Very fine, too, was the tableau vivant depicting the struggle in the Land of Israel and the work of building.
A strong impression was made by the successful flying advertisement with the inscription: „If you will it, it is no legend."
With the singing of „Hatikvah" the chairman closed the academy.
———
In Sosnowiec the Yizkor evening took place in the „Municipal Theatre". Interest was very great, especially among the nationalist youth. Unfortunately, however, the evening did not leave the slightest impression. This was thanks to the disregard on the part of the „esteemed public", which had come to the theatre to amuse itself and had no patience to listen to speeches on the topics of the day.
The evening is opened by Mr. Y. S. Weinreb, who recalls in warm words the heroes and martyrs, whom Mr. W. compares to the „Ten Martyrs".
Then the Polish and the Jewish anthems are „played", and speeches are given by Messrs. Dr. Anisfeld (in Hebrew), Klarman, Kahn, Gancwajch and finally the lawyer Banefeld[?], who gives a longer speech. The audience, however, has no „time" to listen, thanks to which chaos breaks out in the hall.
After the reading of the appropriate resolutions „Hatikvah" and „Teḥezaknah" are sung, and with that the first part ends.
In the second part Mr. Sheynerman very successfully performed a recitation „The Messiah", too. The tableau vivant „The Smithy" (Kuźnia), performed by „Hashomer", came off very well; the latter also sang several songs.
Towards the end a sharp incident broke out between the Trumpeldor people and the „Hatikvah" singers. The incident unfortunately led to the police having something to do...
Friendly Reception of Polish Doctors in Karlsbad

(Communications from the Karlsbad spa administration for the „Zaglembier Tsaytung".)
On Sunday the 17th of this month 23 Polish doctors, who are making a study tour through Central Europe, arrived in Karlsbad. At the railway station the excursionists were warmly welcomed by the spa director Mr. Rudolf Nitschner, and the guests were taken to the hotel in specially prepared carriages.
The next morning the guests visited the town of Karlsbad and the bath establishment, where the bath inspector Dr. Müller gives the necessary explanations.
On behalf of the town of Karlsbad the guests are welcomed by the deputy mayor Prof. Becker, who expresses the hope that the good relations between Poland and Karlsbad will be renewed.
On behalf of the doctors Dr. Halman of Łódź replies, stressing that Karlsbad with its famous springs has made a name for itself throughout the world as a first-rank spa.
The excursionists also visited the Sprudel springs and all the facilities, where Eng. Mr. Zörkendörfer gave the appropriate information.
On Wednesday the guests left, greatly satisfied, for Joachimsthal.

Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings and remarks on this week's portion (Shoftim)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings and remarks on today's portion.
Collected and edited by Y. L.
Parashat Shoftim
—o—
a) "Judges and officers shalt thou make thee" (Deut. 16:18)
In Tractate Megillah (13) it is told that when Haman offered Ahasuerus ten thousand talents of silver as the price for destroying the Jews, Ahasuerus objected, arguing: "Ith beinayhu rabbanan" (there are, after all, rabbis among them). What did Ahasuerus mean by that?
This is what Ahasuerus meant to Haman: You want to give me ten thousand hundredweight of silver to kill off the Jews — but there are among them people who want to become rabbis, and from just one such person, for confirming him as rabbi, I can get as big an "apotiki" [a pledge, i.e. a sum] as you are offering me for all the Jews.. Zera Derekh ha-Shelishi [as printed; probably "Zera Berakh Shelishi"].
* * *
Someone once asked a failed rabbinical candidate who had not found favour with "the lord, the squire", while another man, a competitor of his, had "precisely" found favour in his eyes — they asked him why the squire had not liked him: was it because he knew little learning?
"I am indeed," answers the rabbi, "versed in the whole Talmud, down to every last dot, but in 'Nekudot ha-Kesef' (such a book — hinting at: silver dots, kligers[?]..) I am, it seems, little versed. The rule[?] also demanded that I be well versed in 'Kesef Mishneh' [lit. 'double money']..." From the mouth of the people.
* * *
One of the virtues a rabbi must possess is: hatred of gain — to hate money. Today's rabbis do possess this virtue, for to become a rabbi they pay out[?] so much money... Siftei Hakhamim.
—o—
b) "In all thy gates" (ibid.)
The author of "Terumat ha-Kri" was first rabbi of Sulisz[?] and later became rabbi of a bigger town: Sighet. He was asked why he had moved to a bigger town, where one is busier and cannot devote oneself so much to the study of Torah.
He answered: the Gemara says that whoever becomes a rabbi, a leader, is forgiven all his sins. Well, one who has few sins — a small-town rabbinate is enough for him. But one who has great and many sins must become rabbi of a big city, so that his great sins may be forgiven.
Asifat Geonim.
—o—
c) "Judges and officers shalt thou make thee.. and they shall judge the people with righteous judgment" (ibid.)
If there are many judges, many rabbis in one town, there will be "and they shall judge the people with righteous judgment": there will be honest judgments, because one rabbi will keep watch and spy on the other.. Divrei Shaul.
—o—
d) "Thou shalt not wrest judgment" (16:19).
Do not say: this one is my relative, so I will make him rabbi; that one is a handsome man, so I will make him rabbi; this one is rich, or that one is a poor man and therefore needs a rabbinical post; or that one knows various languages, so I will appoint him rabbi — "Thou shalt not wrest judgment"! Sifrei in[?] Midrash.
* * *
A Masorah of three "ve-nishma"s:
1) Na'aseh ve-nishma ["we will do and we will hear"].
2) Ve-nishma kolo be-vo'o el ha-kodesh ["and his sound shall be heard when he goes into the holy place"].
3) [printed "6)"] Ve-nishma pitgam ha-melekh ["and the king's decree shall be heard"].
Once, when they sought to engage a rabbi, they only saw to it that he be great in Torah and in deeds. First "na'aseh" — whether he is honest and pious, and after that "nishma" — whether he is a speaker and one will sometimes hear a fine sermon from him; that was a side matter.
Later they paid more attention to the rabbi being a good speaker — "and his sound shall be heard when he goes into the holy place": that in the synagogue he should let himself be heard...
Today a rabbi must also know "goyish" [the gentiles' language]: "and the king's decree shall be heard" — he must also be able to deliver a fine sermon in a secular language.
Yalkut Peninim.
—o—
e) "Justice, justice shalt thou follow" (17:5 [as printed; should be 16:20])
It is commonly held that the end justifies the means: if the aim is only justice, one may attain it even by dishonest means. Says the Torah: "Justice, justice shalt thou follow" — to attain justice, use only means that are themselves just. With justice attain justice. From the Rebbe R' Bunem [of Przysucha].
—o—
f) "If there arise a matter too hard for thee in judgment, between blood and blood, between plea and plea, and between stroke and stroke, matters of controversy within thy gates" (17:8).
The Midrash tells: the fish once came with a complaint to the Master of the Universe: why have You forbidden the blood of all kinds of cattle and beasts, while only our blood is ownerless and permitted to everyone? Why for all kinds of beasts and cattle must one seek[?] a halef [slaughtering knife] without a nick in order to slaughter, and there are regulations as to how and when one may slaughter, whereas us fish one may slaughter freely and lawlessly, without a halef, without a shochet? —
God answers: because among you one swallows the other — that is why you are so ownerless.
We Jews also ask: "between blood and blood" — why is our blood so free for all; "between plea and plea" — for us no law exists, anyone may do with us whatever he wants, against justice and law, and no one will punish him for it.
God answers us: because of "matters of controversy within thy gates" — because we are always quarrelling with one another...
Sefer Derushei.
—o—
g) "And it shall be, when he sitteth upon the throne of his kingdom" (17:18)
Let the king, the leader, always conduct himself as finely and well as "when he sitteth upon the throne of his kingdom" — as at the very moment[?] when he sat down on the royal throne; let him always be as good and pious as at the beginning of his "rule". Zikhron Yitzhak.
—o—
Avot, chapter one.
"Loving peace and pursuing peace, loving one's fellow creatures" (Mishnah 12)
Peace is an old hater of mankind, for the Midrash tells that when God was about to create the world and took counsel with Peace, it answered: do not create it, the world, for it is nothing but quarrels.
Says the Tanna: "loving peace" — love Peace. But since Peace is a hater of men, you be "loving one's fellow creatures" — love people. In this one thing do not go along with Peace; be a "pursuer of peace" — be against it in this one thing. Petah Einayim.
What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: Tragic Death of a 2-Year-Old Child

[Head of the local page; Będzin — Accident.]
What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 5 Elul 5690 — Piątek 29 sierpnia 1930 [Friday, 29 August 1930].)
Będzin
Tragic death of a 2-year-old child.
In the building of the local Talmud Torah lives the trader Abraham Gottfried. The latter owns a "budka" (stall) on the market squares on Modrzejowska [?] Street.
On Tuesday Gottfried and his wife went off to their trade, leaving a 2-year-old little boy under the supervision of a Jewish servant girl, whom Mrs. G. had told to bathe the child.
The servant carried out the order of her "mistress" [?] and sat the young soul in a kettle of hot water.
Naturally the child began to jump from the pain, but the "clever" servant, thinking that the child was afraid of water, forcibly sat him down in the boiling water... and the whole little body became as if half-cooked.
All efforts to save the child's life were unfortunately of no avail, and the next day the unfortunate little Jewish child died.

A Swindler Cheats Money out of Poor Jews

[Będzin — Fraud.]
An unknown young man, well [?] and elegantly dressed, is "touring" the town, swindling poor Jews and taking from them their scraped-together pennies.
He carries out the swindle in this way. The young man calls over a poor man and explains to him that he has to give away 1 złoty as a vow; therefore the poor man should give him 9 złoty, and he will go up to his room and bring out a 10-złoty banknote. At the same time he tells him that together with the 10 zł. he will also present him with a garment. The poor man has no suspicion that a swindler is speaking to him and hands him 9 złoty...
As we are informed, the young fellow has already cheated several poor people in this way.
A Young Man Who "Eats" Needles and Nails...

[Będzin — Miscellany.]
The 19-year-old passementerie-maker has managed to carry out experiments in swallowing needles and nails. The last experiment, which he performed this week, did not succeed for him, and for this reckless step he will have to undergo an operation.
Many Sick People on the Sabbath Day

[Będzin — Health.]
Last Sabbath dozens of Jewish families in our town suddenly fell seriously ill. The doctors who were called established that the cause of the illness is the eating of fowl that is not fresh, especially that which is brought from distant places.
From the Zionist-Revisionist Movement

[Będzin — Revisionist Zionism.]
Last Sabbath D. Ganfeld [?] from Eretz Israel, a member of the Revisionist world party council, visited [?] and lectured on the following questions: 1) the situation in the Keren Kayemet policy, 2) the founding of the "Histadrut ha-Ovdim ha-Le'umiyim" (National Workers' Federation), 3) the independent political actions of the Revisionist Union with regard to the Zionist Executive, 4) the prospects of the Revisionists at the coming Congress, and 5) the attitude to the "Haganah" [?], which is now sanctioned by the English authorities.
In a 2-hour lecture the speaker illuminated all the questions comprehensively and logically, and held the large auditorium in the greatest suspense.
With long-lasting applause and the singing of "Hatikvah" the lecture was concluded.
———
On Sabbath, 6 September (września), the discussion on the resolutions of the World Conference in Prague will take place.
The Building Campaign in Będzin

[Będzin — Construction.]
This week the construction of the 8 houses for the officials of the insurance office in Königshütte (Królewska Huta) has already begun. The construction has been undertaken by engineer G. Weinzieher.
—o—
[Będzin — Post.]
To the address of the "Merchants' Association".
Many merchants complain that at the local post office it is not clearly indicated where one can send registered letters. It happens quite often that only after losing a good deal of time does one find out that registered letters are not accepted at that window.
Scandalous Deeds of the Kehilla Administration against Cantor Żupowicz

[Będzin — kehilla, cantorate.]
For several weeks now a sharp conflict has been going on between the kehilla leaders and the town cantor Mr. Żupowicz. Thanks to base intrigues, the fabrications of irresponsible persons, Mr. Żupowicz has been thrown from right to left and from left to right. It turned out that on Thursday he became “unfit” (pasul) and on Friday afternoon — kosher again.
Mr. Żupowicz, wishing to put an end to the slanders and lies being spread about his person, demanded a din Torah before the local rabbinate, which should establish once and for all the actual truth.
The rabbinate accepted the proposal, and the din Torah was to take place on Wednesday, but a day earlier the rabbinate withdrew from the din Torah, with the story that “the rabbinate wishes to be impartial in this matter”.
Because of this both “sides”, the “opponents” and the supporters of Mr. Żupowicz, came to an agreement — to engage rabbis from the neighbouring towns to settle the matter.
But in this, too, the tendency of those who want, without any factual grounds, to push Cantor Żupowicz out of his position in Będzin came clearly to light.
Without any prior agreement the gmina [kehilla] brought here on Wednesday evening the rabbi of Zawiercie, and the supporters of Żupowicz, who had decided to bring here the rabbi of Königshütte [Chorzów], Rabbi R' Yosele Blumenfeld, were left powerless, because Rabbi Blumenfeld, not knowing of any fixed date when to come to Będzin, was in Kraków that day.
As we are informed, it was decided that the din Torah should be postponed to next Sunday.
— As long as people say that our kehilla leaders are not capable[?]...

[Będzin — crime.]
While cleaning the latrine pit in house no. 10 on Zawodzie Street, a dead infant, a baby girl, was found. The police are conducting an investigation.

From the League for Labour Palestine
[Będzin — Zionism, labour movement.]
On Saturday the general meeting of the “League for Labour Palestine” took place. Mr. M. Oppenheim was elected chairman. From the report given by Mr. Liwer it emerges that 300 members have been registered so far.
Mr. Shmuel Liwer gives a treasurer's report. In the course of 5 months a sum of 12 hundred zł. was sent to the Central Committee.
After that Mr. S. Gutman gives a substantive[?] lecture on the forthcoming Jewish World Congress for Labour Palestine in Berlin.
Elected to the new board were: Dr. Rechtman, Aharon Hampel[?], Moshe Gutman, S. Rozenberg, Y. A. Liwer, Kokotek[?] and Grojer. Audit committee: Cukierkandl and Gertler.
Will There Be No Lessons on Sunday in the “Jewish” Public Schools? — A Fresh Injustice against Hundreds of Jewish Children

[Sosnowiec — education.]
In the course of the week various versions circulated that for the new school year “reforms” would be introduced in the Jewish public (powszechne) schools. One of the reforms is to be that on Sunday no lessons will take place in the said schools, and that the lesson time for boys will be from 2 in the afternoon until 8 in the evening.
Although the report comes from an authoritative source, one cannot believe that such an injustice should be done by the local[?] school authority against hundreds of Jewish children.
A Proselyte Receives Support from the Kehilla

[Sosnowiec — kehilla, conversion.]
Several weeks ago a young, healthy Christian from Sielec got the “urge” to become a Jew. When he came with this proposal to Rabbi Schwarz, the latter tried to influence the young Christian to give up his proposal, since the “business” doesn't pay...
But the present proselyte was not deterred and declared that he must become a Jew, he has an urge for it and he must realise it.
The rabbinate sent him to Kraków, where he was converted, and last week he came back here, already a Jew, with the name Avraham Gierbal[?].
The proselyte, in whom the rabbinate takes an interest, has received material support from the gmina [kehilla] and he diligently studies Jewish laws.
The Number of Pupils in the Jewish Girls' Gymnasium Has Grown Considerably

[Sosnowiec — education.]
As we are informed, at the beginning of the current school year the number of girl pupils enrolled in the local Jewish girls' gymnasium grew considerably. This is a gratifying phenomenon. That Jewish parents have finally come to the conviction that Jewish children must study in Jewish schools, in the schools where, together with the necessary secular subjects, they also receive a large measure of Jewish learning, Jewish history and the like.
Slaughter Levy on Treif Reduced — 2 zł. on Treif, 8 zł. Kosher...

[Sosnowiec — kehilla, shechita.]
When drawing up the kehilla budget for 1930, the kehilla administration raised the slaughter levy according to the following prices: for a calf from 3 to 3.50 zł.; a cow from 5 to 8 zł. The increase was approved by the authorities.
The butchers, seeing that the increase harms them[?], began a counter-campaign to have the increase withdrawn; above all the butchers protested that when they slaughter an animal that turns out treif they must also pay the 8 zł. per head, as for a kosher one.
Last Sunday, during a session of the kehilla administration, a delegation of the butchers presented itself and categorically demanded that for animals slaughtered and found treif the levy should be no more than 2 zł. per head.
The administration gave in to the demand and decided that the price of 8 zł. continues to apply to kosher, and treif should cost only 2 zł.
The slaughter levy for calves is again as before, only 3 zł.
—o—
On the Abuses at the Customs Office
[Sosnowiec[?] — customs, corruption.]
In connection with the abuses discovered at the local customs office, several auditors[?] came here from Warsaw, and in checking the activity of the office it became clear that the abuses had begun as early as 1926.
False accounts were also discovered, through which the state treasury suffered considerable monetary losses.
The further investigation is under way; it is expected that new arrests will take place in the coming days.
—o—
Coal Is to Become Dearer
[Economy — coal, export.]
As reported, the price of coal is about to be raised by 10 per cent or even more. The coal dealers explain the increase by saying that the wholesalers or the mine owners have reduced the discount, and therefore they themselves must raise prices.
This increase, however, has a deeper cause, connected with export policy. As is known, the export of coal is forced by the mine owners and by the state. The state facilitates export by a low duty. Polish coal competes chiefly in the Scandinavian countries; the competition costs us very dearly, because the English will stop at nothing to win back the markets they lost during the great coal strike of 1926. The competition causes Polish coal to be sold there for next to nothing: while in the autumn of last year a ton of coal (1000 kilo) cost 15 English shillings in Danzig, it now costs only 10 shillings; out of this the seller must pay for transport and he is left with only 5—6 shillings per ton, i.e. less than he pays for getting the coal out of the pit. Export is therefore possible only when the mine owner recoups the loss on the coal he sells in the country itself.
This is the same policy that is pursued with the export of sugar: the cheaper Polish sugar is sold abroad, the dearer it costs in Poland.
—o—

An Audit of the Tax-Wronged Merchants
Some time ago the board of the Sosnowiec Small Traders' Association submitted to the "Urząd Skarbowy" (Treasury/Revenue Office) in Sosnowiec a list of the small traders who had been badly wronged [?] in the assessment of the turnover tax for 1929.
On the basis of an understanding with the decisive factors, it was decided to audit the "businesses" of those wronged, in order to ascertain their actual material situation.
The audit will be carried out by a special commission, which will include 1 representative of the Small Traders' Association, 1 representative of the Chamber of Commerce, 1 from the "Urząd" (office), and the head (naczelnik) of the office.
The audit, as we are informed, is to take place already in the course of next week.
—o—
A Competition and... Politics
The board of the Będzin Jewish kehilla published a competition for the post of a shochet-mumche (certified ritual slaughterer). And, as we are informed, shochtim-mumchim came here wishing to take over the "vacant" post, but they were told that "it is not yet topical; for the time being they can go home"...
—o—
Sports Impressions from the Olkusz "Maccabi"
(W-ski) On Sunday the Olkusz "Maccabi" organised an outing in the Leszno [?] forest.
The sports [?] associations of Będzin, Sosnowiec, Königshütte (Królewska Huta) and Chrzanów took part in the outing; already from the morning one could notice in the streets of the town that some holiday was taking place.
At 2 o'clock there was a parade (défilé) through the town, which turned out very impressive, and the public marched into the forest, where several sports items were performed by the Sosnowiec "Maccabi" and the Będzin "Hakoach".
Then a match took place between "Maccabi" (Sosnowiec) and "Chesta" [?] Olkusz; the match ended in a 2:1 victory for "Chesta" [?]. The whole time the "Hakoach" orchestra played. At the end the orchestra, under the direction of Mr. Borenblat [?], performed several concert pieces, which were very warmly received by the Jewish public.
In the evening there was a reception (raut), at which the guests enjoyed themselves quite nicely.
—o—
Vodka, Knives and Wounded
The residents of Kościuszki Street in Będzin witnessed the bloody scenes that played out in the street in the night from Saturday to Sunday. One of the brawlers (awanturniki) [?] was so badly wounded that reviving him took a good hour.
—o—
Under the Wheels of a Car
On Dębowa [?] Street in Sosnowiec Mr. Matuszewski was run over by a car. The injured man was taken to the hospital of the Sick Fund (Kasa Chorych).
—o—
Two Brother-Cains...
In the open field at Środula two brothers met and began to fight. During the brawl both fell into a pit and broke arms and legs.
—o—
Before the Wedding and After the Wedding...
In Sosnowiec the number of suicides is growing. There is hardly a day that passes without a suicide.
In the course of Monday two suicides occurred. The 25-year-old Sojówna [?] of Czysta Street poisoned herself with vinegar essence; the cause of the first suicide is a romantic one. The disappointed woman had quarrelled with her husband [?].
—o—

The presidium together with the committee has set about reorganising the work as well as the collections on rational foundations.

Success of the Summer Colonies for Jewish Schoolchildren in Sławków

From the management of this year's summer colonies of the Będzin Magistrate for the Jewish children of the public schools in Będzin we have received the following report:
During the month of lipiec [July] there were 275 girls at the colony, who gained 589 kilos and 20 deca in weight.
In the month of sierpień [August] there were 289 boys, who gained 594 kilos and 30 deca.
The girls were recruited from: public school no. 4 — 114, from school 8 — 104, from the ochronka [kindergarten] — 14, "Beys Yaakov" — 4, Bojarski's school — 4, working girls — 5.
The boys from: school no. 2 — 159, Talmud Torah — 41, "Agudah" — 29, "Mizrachi" — 15, "Yavneh" — 8, Megeri's[?] ochronka — 30, working boys — 7.
———
On Friday, 29 sierpień [August], the colony operation was wound up. The writer of these lines, spending that day at the colony, found the departing boys sad; they did not like parting from life in nature, and leaving the colony they marched like "deportees to Siberia".
On the way to the station Mrs. Wajcenberg, ławnik [magistrate member] Goldsztajn, Icze Wajcuberg[?] and S. Lewkowicz gave the boys various sweets and chocolate.
At the station the stationmaster declared that there had been a "mistake" and that the specially ordered carriage for the children would not be provided.
The news sharpened[?] the serious mood of the children even more, but a "miracle" happened and all got onto the train.
The whole way from Sławków to Będzin the children's singing could be heard from the carriages.
In Będzin all the children went into the courtyard of "Piast", where ławnik Goldsztajn took leave of the children; the children answered with cheers in honour of the city administration and in honour of the President of the State.
After singing a "hymn" in honour of the city council the children scattered home.
A Few Words on the Cantorate Question

(A letter to the editors).
If there were still some of the Jewish population here in Będzin who did not yet know of the great achievements and the "self-sacrificing" work of our kehilla administrators for the benefit of the Będzin Jewish public, they had the opportunity to convince themselves of it last Sunday.
As is known, we have a cantorate question. Not a question of engaging a cantor, for a cantor — and a capable one at that — we have in Będzin; but our "kehilla administrators", relying on the talk[?] of a few ringleaders of thugs[?], have cooked up a mess that will remain a stain of shame on our kehilla. The situation became quite serious and the cantor's admirers demanded firmly that the matter be settled by a beth din. The Będzin rabbinate declined, advising that the matter be handed to an outside beth din. And so it was: a beth din of the following 3 rabbis was brought here: Rabbi Frommer, Rabbi Blumenfeld (Königshütte) and Rabbi Yehoshua Tojc[?] (Zawiercie). It took place in the hall of the Jewish kehilla last Sunday, 6 August. The kehilla hall was packed with almost all strata of the Będzin Jewish population.
To the beth din's question, who are the claimants? two claimants then come forward, one on the cantor's side and one against the cantor. The rabbinate, quickly grasping the situation, turns to the claimant against the cantor with the words: if 10 worshippers of the synagogue do not present themselves as opponents, the din Torah [—] cannot take place. Hearing this, the claimant begins to shout: "Opponents, come here and sign up!" But of all those "zealous for the Lord of Hosts" there were no more than 3 opponents (read: three).
One cannot imagine the great indignation that prevailed[?] against our so-called kehilla administrators, who trample[?] on a congregation of Jews. It is also astonishing that our three-member Będzin rabbinate allows a dispute to flare up in a town without any basis. It is enough to point to a responsum of R. Yosef, the rabbi of Posen, son-in-law of the Noda BiYehuda of blessed memory, who says explicitly: "better to set up an idol in the sanctuary than that disputes multiply in Israel"...
Ben Dovid.
Artisans in Sosnowiec and Vicinity!

Communiqué of the Central Jewish Artisans' Union, Sosnowiec branch.
As we have learned, the Chamber of Crafts of the Kielce voivodeship has approached the local voivode concerning carrying out an inspection of the artisans' workshops, whether they hold artisan cards; and the local authority has ordered an inspection, commanding that the workshops of artisans who do not hold artisan cards be closed.
In connection with this, recently, right after the holidays, at a session of the Kielce Chamber of Crafts, a resolution was adopted on the question of penalising those artisans who do not conclude agreements with their apprentices in accordance with the Industrial Law and do not register them with the Chamber of Crafts. It was also resolved to apply to the Government Commissioner in Warsaw, enclosing[?] the ordinances of other voivodes on this matter, so that he too, following their example, should carry out an inspection of all artisans' workshops, and the workshops that hold no artisan cards should be closed, while those that do hold artisan cards and are [...]
... non-certified masters lose, after 15 December of this year, the right to keep juveniles under 18 years of age, and against those who do not comply the full severity of the law will be applied: a fine of up to 1000 zł. or 2 weeks' arrest.
The said resolutions were adopted against the will of our representatives, Dep. Rosner and J. Glazer, who also spoke out against the proposals and even lodged a veto against them.
We therefore consider it necessary to warn all Jewish craftsmen in Sosnowiec and in the provinces: those who have no craftsman's cards should obtain them as quickly as possible, and those who keep apprentices should conclude agreements with them, which must be registered with the Kielce Chamber of Crafts.
Information on examinations for masters and journeymen, as well as on obtaining craftsman's cards, is given by the secretariat of the Craftsmen's Association in Sosnowiec, Maruawa[?] 9.
The Board of the Craftsmen's Association in Sosnowiec.
What's New in Upper Silesia?

Demonstrations in Katowice.
On Sunday a huge demonstration took place in Katowice against the speech of the German minister Treviranus about shrinking Poland's borders.
A speech was given at the Theatre Square and the procession moved toward the street where the German consulate is located.
On the way the procession was stopped by a police patrol, so the route of the march was changed and the demonstration went off through side streets, but everywhere they were stopped by the police.
On Opolska Street patriotic songs were sung and the demonstration was dispersed.
—o—
They Fought Like Real Sportsmen.
On Sunday the society „Friends[?] of Sport“ held an entertainment evening. At the party a brawl broke out among the guests, who treated one another to bottles, stones and the like.
At the alarm the police arrived, and they too were greeted with the same „welcome“. Then the police used their weapons, and only thus, afterwards, was the brawl put down.
One of the guests was taken to hospital in a serious condition.
—o—
The Price of Coal Will Not Be Raised.
We are asked by an authoritative source to correct the report in our paper that from the 1st of this month the price of coal will be raised; it does not entirely correspond to reality.
It is true that the special discount the merchants received during the summer has been withdrawn since the 1st of this month, but this has nothing to do with raising the price of coal. Given the present state of the coal market it is almost out of the question that coal will become dearer.
