Concern for the Folk School

(Neglect in the field of children's education. Who should be concerned with it?)
What we did not believe has been confirmed; what we doubted has become a fact of life. All of a sudden a new concept has been created in Sosnowiec, which consists in this: that the Jewish children shall not attend the folk schools [public elementary schools] on altogether 3 days of the week, i.e. Friday, Saturday and Sunday.
What sense is there in such a change? Why such sudden disregard? Was the consent of the Jewish population asked for these reforms? Does the question not concern the parents who send their children there? Why such an upheaval? It would be interesting to know from whom this arbitrary rule comes. Who is in a position to rule so dictatorially over the Jewish children of the people? Where has it ever been heard that one may act like this, just like that, as one pleases? It would be interesting to know how this concept was created, who raised the question, and whom it bothered that the Jewish children attended their schools on Friday and Sunday?
After all, the schools were created exclusively for Jewish children — so who has the right to decide about them without the consent of the community? This is an unheard-of phenomenon in our poor life.
After all, there are parents' committees at the folk schools — so how did they react to these acts of coercion? This is unheard-of neglect in the field of pedagogy and education. For which parents can bear that their children should regularly be free from school 3 days a week? What will the children do on such 3 days at home? Where will the parents put them? Under whose supervision will they be in the 2nd half of the week? In that time they will surely forget what they learned in the first half of the week.
And besides all this, the question of education is one of the most sensitive and delicate problems in our life, so that the smallest change can play an important role — and who can understand the physiognomy of our children better than we ourselves? Who can know better than we under what conditions our children of the people are brought up? How the development of our children proceeds?
And it is characteristic that, as hard as it is for parents to raise their children, so lightly are they tossed about, as if they were ownerless.
And indeed, who must care about them and who must concern himself with them? Who cares under what conditions and in what manner the children of the broad masses are brought up, what they learn and when they learn? Now one hears that Hebrew will no longer be taught there either — so the question arises what and when they will learn, and who are the teachers to whom the Jewish children are entrusted?
Were we a people with [proper] people at the same time, we would have needed to concern ourselves with all this, regardless of whether our own children study there or simply Jewish children, who must be equally dear and precious to us.
But apparently it is known that for us these are matters of the second rank, which one does not care about much, and therefore they dared to violate the rights of our children; otherwise such injustices would not have been heard of, otherwise they would have had to reckon with us as with our children — and therefore only we can be blamed for the injustices being committed against our folk schools. There they know very well that over something that does not concern livelihood or quarrels, nobody here will tear himself apart; they apparently know that for little children who belong to cellar and attic dwellings nobody will lift a finger [lit. put his hand into cold water] — and if that is so, we are excellent indeed. Otherwise a storm should have been raised; the question should have been dealt with at least no less than, let us say, the first quarrel that comes along, where people quite often even stake their lives just to fulfil their own ambition. How much courage and energy and strength and money would be spent here if it were a matter of removing someone from a chair and seating another on the same chair? That would have been an affair with which a whole town of people would busy itself; whereas when it concerns the fate of children's education — who would bother with such trifles, which are not worth talking about...
And outsiders know this; outsiders know that for us everything in the world is preferable to concerning ourselves with the children of the people. Had they known that we respect and value the future generation, that we want to make human beings and Jews of our children, they would not have permitted themselves to do what they have now accomplished.
Among other peoples one would have reacted properly to such unheard-of deeds; one would have shown those who allow themselves to make a toy of our children's education that they are not entitled to barter away our holiest ideals for small change.
And be that as it may, we must not tolerate the unheard-of injustice done to us thereby, which shows us that we have no say over the fate of our children. We must prove to the irresponsible people that our children are dear and precious to us and that only we have the say over them, and nobody else.
If we have Jewish schools intended for Jewish children, the lessons there must take place as they did until now and as they do everywhere.
There are parents' committees, whom we hold responsible for tolerating the unheard-of injustices. Whoever else may have, but they should not have dared to allow others, who do not know the spirit and character of our children, to rule over them in an impermissible manner.
All as one we must show understanding for the education of our children of the people; we must not let the rights we have had until now be trampled. We must prove that we are the masters of the fate of our future generation and that we have the right to decide how they shall be brought up, so that they may be of use both to their own interests and to the interests of the people to which they belong.
Dr. Papuri.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings and remarks on this week's portion (Ki Tavo)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings and remarks on this week's portion.
Collected and adapted by Y. L.
Parashat Ki Tavo
—o—
a) "And the Egyptians dealt ill with us, and afflicted us, and laid upon us hard bondage" (26:6)
The tactic of the Egyptians was like that of all antisemites of all generations. Seeing that the Jews still had some money — "vayare'u otanu ha-mitzrim": they began to befriend the Jews (re'ut — friendship), supposedly gave them equal rights. In return for what? — "vay'anunu", as the author of the Haggadah explains: "vay'anunu — as it is said: and they set over them taskmasters [lit. officers of taxes]". That was Jewish equal rights: paying taxes, building Pithom and Raamses. The "equal rights", that bit of friendship, made us into poor people — "vay'anunu" (aniyim — the poor).
Dvarim Nehmadim.
—o—
b) "And our toil" (26:7)
The author of the Haggadah explains: "'And our toil' — these are the children", because all of a person's toil, effort and torment is for his children.
The Holy Jew [of Przysucha] once said: You ask a man, for whom do you work so hard? What is all this needed for, and all the torment? He answers: for myself I really would not "tear the world apart" so much, but one has to — for the children.
His child, as soon as it grows up, likewise throws itself at once into the hustle and bustle of life, forgets everything spiritual, and only toils [?] and chases about. Ask such a one: what is it needed for? — his answer too will be: for the children.
"I would really like to see," said the Holy Jew, "the real child for whom everyone torments himself."
—o—
c) "And with extreme burning" [u-va-harhur] (28:21 [as printed; the verse is 28:22])
What kind of plague is "harhur" in the Rebuke?
— The letters har-har stand for: hatzi rav, hatzi rebbe — half a rabbi, half a rebbe: these are the rabbis who also play the Hasidic rebbe. That is a plague for a town — such a rabbi.
Folk saying.
—o—
d) "Because thou servedst not the Lord thy God with joyfulness and with gladness of heart" (28:47)
Not enough that "thou servedst not the Lord", that you sinned and blasphemed God — you were also "joyful and glad of heart" about it, you even rejoiced in it... That is why such a harsh rebuke is upon you: because you sinned out of spite.
Alshikh.
* * *
The Łódź rabbi, R. Eliyahu Meisel, once came on a visit to a Łódź magnate to ask him for a donation. The magnate, who was a freethinker, is sitting right at his midday meal, bareheaded, eating forbidden foods. The rabbi bows and wishes him "bon appétit" [a gutn apetit].
The magnate speaks up: "I know, Rabbi, that you are honest through and through and show favour to no one — so how can you wish me 'bon appétit' when you see that I am eating meat with milk? May one be false out of politeness?"
"Heaven forbid," answers the rabbi, "I am not false at all. I wish you with all my heart a 'good appetite', for without a good appetite you would have eaten meat with milk purely to spite God [le-hakhis]; this way, however, with a good appetite, it is merely out of appetite [le-te'avon] — and le-te'avon is a much lighter sin than le-hakhis..."
—o—
e) "Then the Lord will make thy plagues wonderful" (28:59)
Nahmanides remarks that the Rebuke in parashat Behukotai was said about the destruction of the First Temple, and the one in this portion — about the destruction of the Second Temple. The first was said in the plural, and it touched upon the national catastrophe: "And I will make your cities waste, and bring your sanctuaries unto desolation, and I will bring the land into desolation"; but the second rebuke was said entirely in the singular, because in the Second Temple period gratuitous hatred prevailed, and because of it the Temple was destroyed; and when hatred reigns among a people, a national catastrophe no longer touches anyone — let the land be destroyed, as long as "there is peace upon my soul". And therefore they were punished [?] with individual misfortunes: "The Lord will smite thee with madness, and blindness, and astonishment of heart." O.H. [Or ha-Hayyim?]
The sin of the First Temple was still a curable one: "if then their uncircumcised heart be humbled, then they shall accept the punishment of their iniquity" — so the Torah concludes; it believes that the people will in the end come to its senses. Whereas the Rebuke of the Second Temple ends: "Then the Lord will make thy plagues wonderful — until thou be destroyed": there is no rescue from the plague of gratuitous hatred.
El Ami.
—o—
f) "Also every plague which is not written in the book of this law" (28:61)
People also repeat a homily which is quoted in all the respected books of homiletics: "'Every plague which is not written' — that is the death of the righteous." R. Isaiah Pick, who was the greatest expert in Talmudic literature, was asked where this homily is to be found. He answered: That itself is a "plague which is not written", for in truth the homily is not written anywhere.
* * *
R. Yosef Shaul Nathansohn once came to the funeral of a prominent personage. The deceased was also eulogized by another rabbi, who read the eulogy out from a sheet of paper. R. Yosef Shaul remarked: "The rabbi evidently does not regard the deceased as a righteous man, for it is said: 'A plague which is not written — that is the death of the righteous', and with this eulogist it is, after all, a written plague (a plague set down in writing)..."
—o—
g) "And thy life shall hang in doubt before thee" (28:66)
The folk interprets the curse thus: his children all emigrate away from him, he remains all alone, and only the children's photographs hang in his home. "Ve-hayu hayekha" — your life, the children — "teluim lekha mi-neged" — hang opposite you on the wall — their pictures; but they themselves are far away.
—o—
Avot, chapters three and four.
a) "He who walks by the way and studies, and interrupts his study and says: How fine is this tree, how fine is this ploughed field — Scripture accounts it to him as if he were guilty of his life" (3:7)
"He who walks by the way" — he who is already on a path, but — "and interrupts": he breaks it off, he lets himself go down a false path; because of [?] — "his study": because of the bit of learning that he knows, and he says of himself "how fine is this tree, how fine is this field" — just look what a fine Jew I am — he is "guilty of his life", he is worth nothing.
By [?] the Maggid of Mezritch.
* * *
"Shogeh [printed: shogat] u-foresh more than all of them."
The worst of all is he who is "shogeh u-foresh": he who studies and spreads himself out [?] (shows off) with his learning...
By [?] Rabbi Moshe of Kobrin.
—o—
b) "Who is wise? — He who learns from every man. Who is rich? — He who rejoices in his portion" (4:1)
Ben Zoma separates the wise man from the rich man. The rich man whose wealth consists only in his great "fortune" [?] — "he rejoices in his portion". But the truly rich man, who owns gold and silver — about him one need not ask separately "who is wise", because such a rich man is in any case wise as well...
Rishpei Keshet.
By [?] Rabbi Shaul of Frankfurt.
—o—
c) "Whoever neglects the Torah in wealth will in the end neglect it in poverty"
Whoever is rich — the world is already accustomed to stick on him the epithet "lamdan" (scholar) as well. A magnate is taken for a talmid hakham too — that's just how it is. So the Mishnah says: "Whoever neglects the Torah in wealth" — he who is rich and, thanks to his prestige, passes [?] for a ben Torah, while in truth he neglects it, learns nothing and knows nothing — there is no other remedy but "to neglect it in poverty": let him become a poor man; and as soon as he becomes poor, the people will at once take from him the title of talmid hakham too...
Eli-Zayit.

Who has time for them? — What we really ought to concern ourselves with here, and what not

(What we really ought to concern ourselves with here, and what not.)
It has become a custom among us that the schoolchildren visit the town synagogue after they finish the school season, and a second time when lessons begin.
We remember that after the end of the school year the teachers of all the schools gathered together with the children in the Będzin synagogue, and they thought that our spiritual leaders would have something to say to them; but unfortunately none of them saw any need to bother with the little children — who knows, who has a head for that, whom do such "trifles" interest? The children together with the teachers then waited and waited, and when they could not wait for anyone they got up and left the synagogue.
The teachers went away embittered and voiced their anger to the writer of these lines. We then dwelt on the incident in a short notice and drew attention to the improper conduct.
Now that the school year has begun, the same children with the teachers again came into the synagogue, and this time too they were left there helpless: there was no one to receive them, and they had to make do as best they could.
It goes without saying that such tactics are vexing and make no good impression, neither on the children nor on the teachers.
But the question arises: why should such disorder reign? Why should a rabbinate and a Jewish kehilla board remain so indifferent to our own children? [And yet?] at times they have complaints against the Jews that the parents, who are themselves harried and plagued, do not bring up their children as they should — while they, whose duty it is to stand on guard and see to it that every movement is sound, are not interested at all in the whole question; so what claims can they have against others?
Among all peoples and in all countries it is an accepted rule that everything is for the future; to it one gives the dearest and best, the most beautiful and beloved. The child is the future, and the future is surely the apple of one's eye.
Very well, one might have thought that all is fine and good, that there is nothing to object to, and that therefore our spiritual leaders need not concern themselves with the children — so, at any rate, one could have thought. But what if the lessons in the public (folk) schools are far from satisfactory? One must not forget that the children have been torn away from the cheder and thus get nothing of sacred studies; a few years will pass and the children will leave the schools as utter ignoramuses (amei ha-aretz). In this case one surely, most surely, ought to have used every opportunity to say a few warm words to them, which would give them courage and strength to keep the whole Jew within themselves.
For the children in the public schools draw so little nourishment from the old Jewish stock, they are torn away there from everything that smacks of Jewishness, of folk tradition — and in this case someone surely ought to have been found to say a few words to them at least at the end and at the beginning of the school year, when they already come into the synagogue; perhaps they would then have heard such words as would influence them on their path to the future.
Must we really tell those concerned [?] that the children must not be left without any supervision? Does it not pain every conscious Jew when he sees in what manner the children are brought up in the government public schools? And if ordinary, busy Jews see and feel this, why should our spiritual representatives, the rabbinates and the kehilla boards, not see it?
Why, then, should one have to say of them that they are busy with disgusting affairs which lead to shame and degradation?
A cantor had to be spied upon — whether he walks on his head or on his feet — and witnesses had to be sought to confirm what Shmerl or Berl had seen. For this purpose a rabbinical court (beit din) was brought here, even from other towns; our rabbinate did not want to undertake so hard a piece of work. The interest grew from day to day, from hour to hour, so that it paid to hold the trial in one of the largest halls, as if the gmina (municipality) would take in a pile [?] of money for tickets...
As long as we think that our leaders cannot arouse any interest in themselves.
Is it any wonder, then, that they take no interest in the children of the people, when they have so much work on their hands, when they are so very busy with trials concerning grown-up people, who must be closely watched? One surely cannot demand of people that they be everywhere and meddle in everything?!
Say what you will — it is disgusting, it is ugly to talk about what our Jewish society busies itself with today. Would we ever have imagined that people would degrade themselves so, that they would keep sliding further and further down slippery paths? Would we ever have conceived that such disgusting affairs would ever be taken seriously and would reach such a level — among those who are supposed to be entrusted [printed: "deceived"] with guarding our holiest ideals?
What is going on here in the 20th century? Where are we going and what are we seeing? Even when one lets oneself go downhill, there must surely be a limit.
Is it any wonder, then, that the respect (derekh eretz) and reverence that ought to exist are gone, once people make themselves ridiculous in the eyes of the Jewish public? Do they really think one can throw sand into the eyes of the public and not feel it on one's own shoulders?
They are busy with more important matters — with espionage and with trials — so that even with the best will there is no time to bother with the little youngsters, the urchins.
Who knows — who has time for them, who has patience for them, who has a head for them?
R. Les.
HaMelech ha-Yoshev... (The King Who Sits...)

[Feuilleton — politics; Poland.] (A little feuilleton)

You surely know how it is with us during the Days of Awe.

With an enthusiastic storm, at the top of his voice, as with an alarm and a din, the cantor begins:
— "Ha-ha-ha-HaMelech!" ["The King!"]

The cantor then sets about stirring everyone up, so that the walls simply tremble and it seems the world will turn upside down — until one finally lives to get past the "HaMelech"...

And after another short pause, another moment of silence, the storm subsides, and slowly, calmly, the cantor begins again with supplications: oy-oy-oy "Yoshev" ["Who sits (on the throne)"]...

So it is every time the "HaMelech" goes by... there is a commotion, and one is given to understand, as it were, that one must not forget in whose presence, in whose power one stands.

And then there really hovers in the air "u-mal'akhim yeichafezun" ["and the angels hasten"]: everyone is seized by fear and trembling, as before an important event hanging over everybody's head.. until people calm down.

Malkhuta de-ar'a ke-malkhuta di-rki'a [the kingdom on earth is like the kingdom of heaven]. Just so, and not otherwise, did the first "prologue" of the drama take place during the May events [?] four years ago [the May 1926 coup], when there was heard [?] — a stormy "HaMelech" and an ordinary, still-small-voice "Yoshev"...

It is the same now, as the "prologue" of the "drama" begun four years ago is already playing...; the beginning is the "HaMelech" with a storm of dissolving the Sejm and Senate, and perhaps also changing the constitution, so that life in the country should be "sanated" [?] [a pun on the Sanacja] and it should be — "hand over mouth" [?] — one government and a firm hand should conduct the initiative and the affairs of the entire life of the state.
But the days of noise and storm are already over.

Life goes on along its old-fashioned way, and time spins and makes its usual webs, spoiling and making...

The whole world now has a negative attitude toward the old and dull parliamentary life, as though it were the sole cause and chief culprit of the economic crisis now reigning in the whole civilized world. Let us hope that by changing the constitution and concentrating power in the sole hands of the creator and father [?] of reborn Poland [Piłsudski], the economic conditions in the country will also be improved.
Ah, how good it is for one who hopes!..
Let us hope, for new times — new winds!...

R' Eliyahu.
End of Summer...

End of summer.
Something is turning chilly [?], gloomy; soon, soon the last bird will fly away and take its songs along with it.
And sad will remain the forest and the field, and sad will remain the garden and the orchard.
With the bird's last song the last leaf will also fall from the tree.
And the black crow will appear with its dark cries.
And the white little frost will appear — the herald [?] of winter.
The white Selichot-frost, which dresses the worn-out grasses and the roofs and the dry branches in white clothes — in shrouds.
And from the Jewish windows pour the sounds of cantorial records: each cantor with his pizmon, with his nusach, with his "woe".
The end of summer comes, and from every Jewish window you hear cantors weeping.
One shouts and weeps: "The soul is Yours and the body is Yours"; a second laments in a wailing voice: "Cast us not off in old age"; and a third weeps and sobs with a broken heart: "Man's origin is dust and his end is dust".. We come from the earth and return to the earth.
A fine future for us...
And all the gloomy melodies, which remind you that your life is not worth more than a penny, that now you are here and now you are there, in "the other world" — they blend together into "one weeping choir", and you yourself grow gloomy too..
And unwillingly you remember your old home, your shtetl, where your cradle stood..
And all the years you have lived through are wiped away as if they had never been; you see yourself as a little boy at your father's in a poor little house.
At home the season of Selichot arrives.
The cold little winds blow so angrily, so without mercy — these are the Elul winds, which cast gloom, fear.
No joyful tidings do they announce, these little winds.
Here, here Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur are drawing near, three dreadful days.
It seems that poverty, your want, gave you no chance at all to sin; you had a dry piece of bread, and yet — and yet it seems to you that you have sinned... And here comes the Day of Judgement, the day when God will judge you.
I remember:
I am no more than 16 years old; we live in an old, tumbledown little house. The house stands in an old garden. The house and the garden are not my father's; they belong to a gentile. I watch the leaves falling down; they leave their home, their tree, their trunk.
And the leaves turn yellow and red and full of holes.
Sick leaves.
It is the end of summer — winter is coming.. So it was a year ago, so it is this year, so it will be a year later, millions of years later.
Is that the purpose? Where will it lead? Ah, how gloomy it becomes!..
And with every leaf that falls from a tree goes a sigh from my father, as if he were mourning their fall, their death, their ruin...
I wonder: where does such a weak little father get such deep, strong sighs? One would need a world of strength to sigh so much!
And since he is already busy sighing for the leaves, he sighs a little for himself too:
Winter is coming, there are no warm clothes, no whole shoes, no firewood, no shoes — nothing.
Who will help?
God.
He helps the rich, the great magnates; them He helps, although they already have enough for themselves, for children and grandchildren.
They, the magnates, have fine, warm hearts, big businesses, many thousands, fine clothes, healthy wives and children — them God helps; but the poor, who have nothing with which to get through a day, to them God gives only the strength to pray a great deal, to fast fasts, to be flogged with malkot on the eve of Yom Kippur — and to sigh.
And my father is one of the greatest sighers in the shtetl.
A genius in his field!
He deliberately gets up every day two hours earlier, so that he can sigh more.
Other poor people come to him to learn the craft.
I remember further:
It is a few days before Rosh Hashanah. I stand under the window of our cantor, Reb Tzadok; I listen to his prayers as he rehearses them with his "keymsherlekh" [?].
Half a shtetl of Jews stand under the window and gape..
No small thing, such a singer; such a weeper! He pulls the very soul out of you with his singing, ay-ay-ay!..
Do you hear, Reb Chaim, a "who by hunger", a "who by thirst", a "who by the sword"? It goes into every limb.. That's what you call a cantor!... There aren't many such Tzadoks!
And Jews who think they have voices pick up the cantor's prayers; the little winds grow curious, they too come flying, take the prayers upon their wings and fly away with them far, far off..
And the little leaves that still cling to the trees seem to be listening, too, to the cantor's singing.
I come back into the house. The same gloom, the same want, the same sigh.
Father paces back and forth across the room, the old skullcap on his head, his beard dishevelled, tangled [?], his sidelocks curled. He is pale, distracted, hands behind his back, and — he just sighs...
And so, as good mother sits and looks at father, and there is nothing to do — she neither cooks, nor bakes, nor tidies the room — she helps father sigh.
We children see that mother is sighing too, so we help them out as well — a choir of sighers!
As you say: "If sighing, then let it be a proper sigh!"..
And not only my father and my mother and we children sigh like this — all the poor people of the shtetl sigh: sighing is our music, our song...
We are born with the sigh and we die with a sigh.
Yes, all Jews sigh: except the few rich, the magnates.
No more and no less — my father is the king of all sighers, the conductor.
And again I look outside and I see great clouds drifting. Who knows where they are drifting?
And now the last bird flies away, and now the last red leaf will come down from the tree, and now night falls and the cold little winds come to us under the window, take up our sighs and carry them far, far away, together with the old cantor's weeping prayers.
— — — — — —
Of these old, old pictures I am reminded when the end of summer comes...
B. K.
A Painful Question

[Education — Będzin; opinion piece.]
Mr. Zelig Emiel [?] did very well to raise, in the columns of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung", the very, very painful question of the Jewish, properly Jewish-minded [?] education of our children in the "powszechne" schools [Polish state elementary schools]. It has long been high time to take up this matter. After all, what is at stake here is the moral and spiritual future of the truly broad Jewish popular masses, who are brought up in the said schools almost without the slightest connection with the Jewish people, with its sufferings and dreams, its strivings and hopes.
From year to year the number of Jewish children attending the "powszechne" schools grows. Formerly these were mostly girls, about whose Jewish education our parents care least of all; but in recent years the number of boys educated in these schools has also grown enormously. These schools are already now the main educational institution of our growing generation, and what will be in a few years' time is easy to imagine. And the danger lurks that, before we can look around, a generation will grow up before our eyes with whom we will be utterly unable to talk, who will have no understanding of our sufferings and worries, of our aspirations and strivings.
True, Jewish society must fight unceasingly and consistently, with the help of all the means at its disposal, to have a sufficient number of public schools adapted to our needs opened everywhere for Jewish children; but until this just struggle is played out (and who knows how it will end) much water will yet flow away, and meanwhile the hard question already stands before us now in all its sharpness, demanding an absolutely prompt and decisive answer: what are we to do so that our children, who are being educated by the tens of thousands in the "powszechne" schools, do not become estranged from us and are not torn away from our glorious national culture?
The trouble also grows from year to year because the Jewish teachers (who, in their overwhelming majority, are themselves far removed from our national interests) are being pushed out of these schools more and more, and from year to year more and more Christian teachers are appointed [?] to them.
The instruction in "religion", given in these schools for one or two hours a week in the Polish language, has almost no significance at all.
In the last school year the teaching of the Hebrew language was even introduced for Jewish children in the Będzin "powszechne" schools. But no more than one hour a week was allotted to this subject. Practice has shown and confirmed what could easily have been foreseen: that this subject would yield such paltry results that they are not even worth talking about. Considering that the Jewish school divisions are so overcrowded that one class often numbers sixty-odd children, and that the lesson in school can in no way last longer than 50 minutes, it does not come to even 1 minute of Hebrew per child per week.
And the Jewish parties, with their fossilised doctrines, think only of founding, with public money, party schools exactly tailored to their world-outlook, and do nothing to paralyse the destructive influence of the "powszechne" schools on our youth.
The Zionists too, who are more capable than others of reckoning with the real needs of the Jewish popular masses, they too must unfortunately beat their breasts with "al chet" for the grave sin they have committed by looking on indifferently at the situation that arose and not dipping a single finger in cold water to do something in this respect.
True, three times already a solemn resolution was adopted among the Zionists in Będzin to open a "Tarbut" school in our town, and special committees were created with the mission of carrying out this task, but each time it ended with just that.
But even if it had come to realising this resolution, which involves quite large expenses, one would have saved from national-cultural ruin a hundred or two hundred children. That, however, would not have solved the question of the Jewish education of the thousands of children who would have had to go on remaining in the "powszechne" schools. And this question can be solved without great financial efforts (in any case considerably smaller than founding a new school) only in the way that Mr. Z. Emiel rightly pointed out in his article.
We must follow the path taken by our brethren in the countries where the public schools already have a longer tradition behind them: in America and in other countries, and in Poland and Galicia, the question has been solved by creating afternoon schools where the children study only Jewish subjects. Every day the child spends two hours in such a school, that is, 10 hours a week. The child studies at the school for 7–8 years. It goes without saying that, spending a few hours day after day throughout the years of childhood in a purely national environment, the child comes out of there with quite a large measure of Jewish knowledge (Hebrew, Tanakh, Jewish history, old and new literature), with a strong national consciousness and with a firm, lifelong attachment to Jewish culture.
A sacred duty lies upon our cultural workers to set about, immediately, the carrying out of this sacred task. The "Tarbut" activists have a splendid opportunity to accomplish something for which they will earn a heartfelt "yasher koach" from public opinion.
Azbsh"n.
How Can We Be Helped?

A conversation with Germany's greatest economic politician. Specially for the "Zaglembier Tsaytung". By Z. Haber.
The Leipzig autumn fair, which has just closed, was held at a very difficult economic time. The distress in almost all the countries of the whole world is so great that on all sides means and ways are being sought at least to ease the distress. At such an important place as the Leipzig fair, which is the largest market in the whole world, there is the possibility of talking things over with all the greatest personalities of the world economy and of finding out what measures can be taken at least to reduce the crisis, which has no equal in the whole economic history of all times.
Your correspondent had the opportunity to speak with the director of the Leipzig Fair Office, Mr. Paul Voss [?], Germany's greatest economic politician, and asked him:
— What must happen in order to be rid of this crisis in a short time?
Director Voss answered:
First of all it is necessary that the war debts and all war obligations throughout the whole world should disappear.
Further, it is very important that the tariff walls be torn down, and that the banks of the whole world carry on proper, systematic work, so that capital on the international market will be more stable and more balanced.
Of course it is very important that the various trade agreements which have been concluded should actually be carried out, their obligations [sic]. For example, the Polish-German trade agreement has still not been ratified by the two states. This agreement would bring Poland great relief, because Polish agriculture could sell its products more easily, and German industry could also export a large part of its output. That would bring stabilization to the Polish and also to the German market.
Further, it would be necessary for both countries to show their good will here and to find the golden mean that is needed, so that the agreement does not remain merely a scrap of paper.
The Polish and the German press ought now to show by every means how important the agreement is and how necessary it is that no politics be mixed into the trade agreement, neither from the one side nor from the other.
Through the crisis in America all the European countries have been hit as well. Not only the crash on the stock exchange and the fall of prices of all raw materials created the bad economic situation there; the high tariff walls also did their part in making the situation even worse. On top of that, because of the severe heat of recent times the grain of all America has been burnt and the farms too have been badly damaged.
American tariff policy is today the most harmful, not only for America itself but also for all the European countries. Were it not for the tariff difficulties, it would be possible not only to bring all kinds of European goods in there, but also to move the great American financiers to take part with their capital in the European economy, and that would be the greatest revival of the international market.
But as long as the tariff walls in the world are not abolished, one cannot count on the world economic situation improving.
Leipzig, September 1930.
Once, in My Shtetl

(For the First Selichot)
By D. Lerman.

"Rise for Selichot! Rise for the service of the Creator!" calls Yankev the shammes into the dark night. A cool Elul breeze catches up [?], like a "radio station", his creaking [?], hoarse call and spreads [?] it over the whole sleeping shtetl, over the whole empty dark void that reaches as far as the smeared, darkened void.

Somewhere far away, high up in a small patch of clear sky, a star looks straight down on the dark, sinful earth. It looks like a spy, like a heavenly spy, as if it wished to search out and inquire what is going on there in the sinful world, and what he is doing there, in the innermost chambers, behind locked doors and windows — the chosen of creation, the crown of God's world, the sinful Jew.

"Rise for Selichot! Rise for the service of the Creator!" the shammes clamours louder, as if he wished to warn the sinful world to be on its guard, for a spy is watching, a spy spies on everything and reports everything to the Heavenly Household, to the Supreme Authority; therefore one must abandon the life of the moment, the follies of this world, and return to "Our Father in Heaven" with one's whole heart; He will have mercy on His sinful little Jews and forgive them their great sins, and He will not withdraw His mercies from our brethren the Children of Israel henceforth, just as until now.

A thin, fiery strip of light suddenly breaks through a pair of chained shutters, and right after it another and another, already so many that they cannot be counted. They pour into the dark void above the black, mute earth, as though they were taking [?] signals from the dark, sleepy houses to the shammes, so that he may know that people are awake and he may rest easy — they know what they have to do.

The fiery strips, the signals, go out one after another; black figures move through the streets like night-time ghosts. They stride in a kind of muffled [?], dreadful silence straight to the beit midrash.

Like a lighthouse in a sea of darkness stands the old beit midrash. The old beit midrash is too narrow to hold so much light within itself, and so it must, as if unwillingly, let whole rivers of light out through the windows into the street, where the darkness has sprawled and spread out as if at home, as though it had already taken up permanent residence here forever.

From time to time, from minute to minute, the door of the beit midrash opens, and a piece of light tears itself out to greet in friendship the one who opens the beit midrash door, and instantly, together with the one entering, it turns back and is swallowed up in its source, in the great holy light that fills the beit midrash.

Fuller and fuller grows the beit midrash with broken, battered Jewish bodies, with dark, careworn faces, with frightened, wide-open, faint [?] eyes, like those who stand before a criminal court, like those who know that they are the guilty ones — only they still have one hope, in the great King, the King of Kings: He is good, the Master of Mercy, He waits [?].. He forgives.. But the heart is afraid: who knows! No small thing — so many sins! And there stands the dark night, hard and stubborn, beside the windows of the beit midrash, and lurks and lurks.

"Yitgadal v'yitkadash shmei rabba" bursts out of the mouth of Reb Yechiel the cantor with such force that the light trembles, that eyes see what cannot be seen: a great Yitgadal soars through the luminous void, through a world-void, through world-space. There is no darkness — light, light in all the worlds; hearts grow stronger, firmer, more believing; faces grow happier, more festive; eyes — more shining [?], more hopeful; and lips whisper quietly with great devotion: "Amen, yehei shmei rabba."

People are uplifted — quite ordinary, everyday, average people — to a high level, to open-heartedness, to innocence; all at once they all make a single reckoning of the soul, truly, without any ulterior motives: "Yours, O Lord, is righteousness, and ours is shame of face" — You, God, are just, and we must be ashamed; and so we are all of equal lineage, there must be no hatred, there must be no envy. They all set out on one and the same road — some with quicker steps, some with restrained ones — but all as one go along the same road on which Reb Yechiel, the shliach tzibbur, strides ahead, with fervour, with ardour. They throw off materiality, coarseness, earthliness, and pass over into a world of pure spirituality, refinement, holiness and cleanness; into a world in which there exists no vexation, no hatred, no envy, only pure love from small to great. They forget entirely where in the world they are. They forget entirely that the darkness stands hard and stubborn beside the windows, and lurks and lurks.

Day swallows the darkness, day stands close by the windows of the beit midrash, day wakes people from their dreams.

Good-natured Jews return from the beit midrash. They greet the day with a contented smile on their lips. It seems they have no gall at all; it seems the evil inclination has cast them off — you may do to them whatever you like, they will not become angry. They return — one to his little shop of the whole year's weekdays, one with a pack on his shoulders, as always, into the village, and one simply into the house, for he has always been a stay-at-home, a man of the house — but all with a thought of repentance: that the way they have lived until now is no good, "this is not the way", this is not the road; one must turn in another direction, onto another road; one must become good and pious.
The Siyum ha-Sefer in Königshütte, Celebrated with Full Parade

[Königshütte — community.] Last Sunday Jewish Königshütte (today Chorzów) celebrated the festivity of a siyum ha-sefer [completion of a Torah scroll].
Since the Jewish community in Königshütte has existed, no Torah scroll has been written there to this day in which almost the entire Jewish population would take part.
Torah scrolls are, thank God, not lacking in Königshütte, but the scrolls were bought: as soon as the "Yahudim" [mocking name for the German Jews] had the opportunity to buy a scroll now and then, they did not refuse it. One scroll is even present in the German synagogue, which a Jew from Leipzig, a certain Goldstein, donated as a gift.
And when the Jewish community began to grow, and political and economic Jewish organisations arose in the place, the "Mizrachi" took the initiative to write a Torah scroll.
Everyone took part in the campaign; from the richest to the poorest Jew, everyone contributed to the cause and could hardly wait impatiently for the day when the first scroll would be brought into the local synagogue.
Great preparations were made for the celebration, as for a wedding of the rich and wealthy. Hundreds of invitations were sent out to Zagłębie and beyond; they brought in the well-known badchan [wedding jester] Mr. Israel Weintraub and his son, and an "orchestra" all the way from Sosnowiec (they did indeed play at the Sosnowiec market..), and the chief in-law, the local rabbinical judge (moreh tzedek) Rabbi Blumenfeld, invited his bosom friend, the rabbi of Tomaszów [?], Rabbi Brodt, who did indeed take part in the celebration and gave spiritual delight with his speech.
Already from the morning one could see in Königshütte that a Jewish celebration was being prepared with great pomp [?], with every arriving guest [?]; in the streets one meets the Königshütte Jews dressed up in holiday clothes, their faces beaming with pride over the privilege of having managed to "Judaize" the place, which used to recall a temple, a Rabbiner, an Oberkantor and a minyan of "Jewish" top hats..
In Rabbi Blumenfeld's apartment is the gathering point of the "groom's side"; around the tables served with refreshments sit Jews in Sabbath clothes, some listening to the Torah witticisms that "pour" like precious stones from the mouths of the learned rabbis Brodt and Blumenfeld, while the "practical ones" are busy with the cakes and drinks..
The crush grows bigger, people come to greet, everyone comes, the top-hat Jews too. The dispute that reigned between several circles has been liquidated; the greatest opponents, the [?] representatives, drink and wish each other "l'chaim".. and "assimilate" with the Polish Jews. Yes, the Polish Jews have already penetrated deeply into all branches of Jewish communal life; even "punctuality" is by now a "Polish" one...
At last the awaited messengers arrive and announce:
— It is time to drive to the wedding hall, for the "bride", the Torah princess, is already waiting for her representatives...
The community hall, where the writing of the letters takes place, is soaked in human sweat; the crush is so enormous that getting to the table smacks of mortal danger.
Everyone who writes a letter is announced by the badchan Weintraub; music plays "Stechfengiu" [?], as in the good old days..
The writing of letters lasts until 10 in the evening, and they begin to prepare for the parade, to bring the new scroll into the magnificent synagogue.
The new scroll, accompanied by several scrolls, is carried with song under a wedding canopy into the magnificent synagogue. One is simply astonished to see the splendid synagogues, community offices and other community buildings, built by small Jewish communities. Upon my life, it would only be fair for our community representatives to become acquainted with what decent people call — communal activity...
Before the Holy Ark stand several rabbis and town notables, and after the singing of "Mah Tovu" and "Vayehi Binsoa" by Cantor Kohn and his choir, and after the hakafot [processions] in the manner of Simchat Torah, the Rabbiner Dr. Kalberg [?] delivers a very fine sermon; he speaks about the great significance of writing a Torah scroll and ends with a call that the frictions and disputes should cease, and that the peace just concluded in the Königshütte community should be lasting.
"Boże, coś Polskę" and "Hatikvah" are played, and with this the ceremonial part ends.
The crowd of guests then goes up to the community's meeting hall, where the material part takes place; but the moreh tzedek Blumenfeld does not let anyone near the "set table" until the Haggadah has been said..
The head table is occupied by Rabbi Brodt, Rabbi Dr. Kalberg, Rabbi Dr. Panzelson [?], Rabbi Blumenfeld, the Wolbrom Rebbe and delegates from Zagłębie and Upper Silesia.
On behalf of the committee Mr. Weigrib [?] greets the guests, and the chairmanship of the banquet is handed to Rabbi Blumenfeld. The latter greets the participants, the rabbis, and above all Rabbi Brodt, who — he says — sacrifices himself for the Jewish people, works for the preservation of Judaism and for the revival of the Jewish nation.
The floor is given to Rabbi Brodt, who delivers a masterly speech about Jews and Jewishness; with tremendous pathos he speaks about the spiritual decline that prevails in the modern Jewish family.
The speech made an extraordinary impression and the eminent rabbi was showered [?] with stormy ovations.
Very finely speaks next Rabbi Dr. Panelman [?]; he dwells on the phenomenon that the Jews who immigrated from the small shtetls — as soon as they set foot on Upper Silesian soil — became "modern and civilised"...
The speeches are summed up by Rabbi Blumenfeld and they turn to the material part, to the eating and drinking, which was prepared very lavishly.
During the rich feast the Będzin cantor Mr. Żupowicz [?], at the rabbis' request, sang "Habet mi-Shamayim u-Re'eh" and "Elohai Neshamah". The vocal numbers met with great applause.
Then a varied "repertoire" is performed. The badchan Weintraub and son perform several comic numbers, among them very banal ones; Mr. Granek sings "Dos Pintele" [?], Mr. Rubin imitates the sermon of the Białystok Maggid, the orchestra "bangs out" the "Dybbuk", and it seems that any moment now they will dance the mitzvah dance..
The company does a little dance, and when the grey dawn begins to seep inside, the celebration comes to an end.
Yaakov Hirsch's Son.
The Bailiff in the Role of a Matchmaker

[Katowice — slice of life.] The Katowice merchant G. owed a Warsaw firm twelve hundred złoty on bills of exchange, which he let go to protest.
Being unable to pay the debt, a settlement was reached at 50 per cent, and G. wrote out new bills for that sum. At the same time, for security's sake, the Warsaw firm also kept the first bills.
But even this did not help: G. let the second bills go to protest as well, and the owner of the Warsaw firm sent his son here to Katowice to collect the debt through the courts.
But when the young gentleman [?] from Warsaw came to collect the debt with a komornik [court bailiff], he took a strong liking to G.'s daughter, and the bailiff no longer had anything to [do] [—]
Now the roles have been reversed:
The Warsaw in-law is hitting the ceiling — he forgives the several hundred złoty, as long as they leave his son alone, who could have had [?] a rich match, and here the "Ślązaks" [Silesians] have actually "put a spell on him".
G., on the other hand, argues that although he is a poor man, he is ready to pay the debt at once, as long as the in-law does not interfere and does not make him a laughing-stock before people.
And the young man, for his part, does not want to talk about money at all. For him the right thing is to go to the wedding canopy soon, and by the look of it, he will get his way.
So it will turn out that the bailiff, instead of an enforcement fee, will still have to take a matchmaker's fee..

Sosnowiec — The Shochtim Resolve to Wage a Struggle Against the Kehilla Leaders

[Sosnowiec — kehilla; ritual slaughter.]
The local shochtim [ritual slaughterers] have addressed a letter to the kehilla leaders in which they announce that if by the 15th of this month the shochtim's pensions are not guaranteed according to the earlier agreement, the shochtim will start a struggle against the kehilla.
The first step in this struggle will be that the shochtim will slaughter on their own account and will not hand over the slaughter tickets of the gmina [community].
Sosnowiec — The New School Decree Is in Force

[Sosnowiec — education.]
The unexpected decree for the new school year, because of which hundreds of children wander about idle on Sunday, has already come into force: on Sunday there are no more lessons in the local “powszechne” [public elementary] schools; but the Jewish parents have this time, too, remained indifferent and do not react to the attack [?] perpetrated against their children.
Yesterday evening a meeting of the school guardians [opiekunowie] was convened. What was decided at the meeting had not yet been communicated to us by the time this issue went to press.
Sosnowiec — The Bakery Journeymen's Strike Is Over

[Sosnowiec — labour; education.]
On Tuesday a conference on the strike of the bakery journeymen took place at the labour inspector's.
The conference did not produce the desired result, but the bakery journeymen agreed to return to work on condition that in 2 weeks' time a conference will take place at which the wage is to be raised.
—o—
The commercial courses will take place as before.
For the new school year the city administration wanted to introduce that the evening commercial courses at the magistrate [city hall] should take place also on Friday and Saturday. Thanks to the intervention of councillor Mr. Rotsztajn [?] the “reform” was withdrawn, and the courses will take place as before on Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday.
Sosnowiec — Conference of Artisans' Representatives

[Sosnowiec — artisans; taxes.]
On Sunday a conference took place in the premises of the Artisans' Association with the participation of representatives of the artisans' organisations in Zagłębie.
The conference discussed a number of current questions, and it was resolved: 1) to create a supreme council, to which each organisation delegates 2 representatives; the supreme council shall act on all artisans' questions in the name of all the artisans in Zagłębie; and 2) to start a campaign so that the artisans have their own representatives on the local main tax-assessment commission and also in the “Izba Skarbowa” [Treasury Chamber] in Kielce.
Sosnowiec — Wedding of a Convert

[Sosnowiec — religious life.]
In the polish [vestibule] of the synagogue the wedding of the convert from Czeladź, who converted to Judaism a few weeks ago, took place this Monday.
The bride is from Sosnowiec.
Sosnowiec — Small Traders and Artisans to Be Exempted from the Road Tax

[Sosnowiec — municipality; taxes.]
At a meeting of the budget commission the statute of the “podatek drogowy” [road tax] for the year 1931 was dealt with. A member of the commission, councillor Dr. Rotsztajn [?], put forward a proposal that small traders and artisans be exempted from this tax.
The proposal was adopted by the commission.
Sosnowiec — Zionist Life in Sosnowiec

[Sosnowiec — Zionism; culture.]
The culture commission of the Zionist Organisation in Sosnowiec has vigorously set about intensive activity. Almost every Sabbath there are lectures and members' talks on various Zionist and cultural topics.
A choir has been formed under the direction of Mr. Sangal [?], and a drama circle under the leadership of the local amateur [?] Mr. A. Krawiec; next week the Hebrew evening [?] courses resume, which were temporarily interrupted because of the summer holidays; so far over 60 pupils, boys and girls, have already enrolled.
To honour the memory of the late president of the Zionist Organisation, Dr. Abraham Perlman of blessed memory, the festive opening of the library named after him will take place shortly.
— This Sabbath afternoon a members' talk on the subject “From Herzl to Weizmann” will be held in the organisation's own premises.
Unsuccessful Communist demonstrations

On Sunday the Communists tried to hold meetings in several places, but everywhere the police intervened and dispersed those assembled. In several places the Communists managed to hang out red flags. 11 persons were arrested.
A chase after thieves

On Sunday thieves broke through a wall[?] of Mr. Reinberg's drapery (manufaktura) shop in Ząbkowice and took goods worth several thousand złoty.
With the loot the thieves boarded a goods train going in the direction of Zawiercie. On the way, when the thieves noticed that they were being pursued by the railway officials, they jumped off the train and started running toward the Łazy forest.
The officials chased them, and the thieves, seeing that they were in danger, threw away the stolen goods and vanished.
—o—
When the power fails...
On Tuesday evening the tram running to Sosnowiec came to a halt on Żeromskiego street. The cause was that the electric current had been cut off.
After an interruption of 15 minutes traffic resumed.
—o—
A lawyer holds office hours at the Artisans' Association.
In order to spare the members from being exploited by lawyers, the board has engaged the lawyer Mr. Zylbiger[?], who holds office hours twice a week in the premises of the Artisans' Association, where he handles various legal matters at reduced rates.
—o—
Under the wheels of a car.
On Małachowskiego street Mrs. Kalaruszypczyk[?] fell under the wheels of a car; the woman was seriously injured.
—o—
The city budget approved.
The city budget has been approved by the voivode. The budget was defended by the deputy chairman of the city council, Dr. Sawelek[?], and Mr. Sulikowski.
—o—
From "Herzliya".
Under the chairmanship of Mr. Czarny the annual general meeting of "Herzliya" took place. Chairman Buszecki[?] presents a report on the past year, which is accepted with satisfaction.
After the reports the board is granted the absolutorium (discharge).
Elected to the new board were: Czarny (chairman), Miss Proskurowska (vice-chair), Miss Glmerge[?] (secretary), Buchbinder (treasurer), Zylberberg, Abramowicz, Trajman, Rozuson[?], Cwajgenbaum and Cukerman. Audit committee: Tegner[?], Śmietana, Plesner, Hamburger and Lubelska. Comrades' court[?]: Buszecki, Śmietana and Miss Sztajnfeld[?].
—o—
Car accident.
On Wednesday evening a young woman from Upper Silesia, who had come here to buy goods, was run over by a car on Magruszew[?] street.
Both of the woman's legs were broken. The unfortunate woman was taken to hospital in a serious condition.
Dąbrowa — A theft

A theft was committed in the apartment of Berl Szwarcbaum. The police energetically set about the investigation and uncovered the theft [i.e. the stolen goods]. At the same time the thief was also arrested; he is a well-known "Tsel Malke".
—o—
Arrested.
At the request of the prosecutor's office, the local resident M. Farasal[?] was arrested in Katowice; he is accused of committing a series of embezzlements at Katowice firms to the amount of 14 thousand złoty.
Olkusz — From the city council

On Monday evening a session of the city council took place, devoted to the elections to the Sejm and Senate. Election commissions were elected, altogether 9 members and 9 deputies. Of the Jews, 4 members and 4 deputies were (elected): A. Taluch[?], A. Muszkablat, M. Kerner, Ch. Czarniecki, K. Wajslfisz, K. Żeryker[?] and B. Framojer[?].
A. B.
Not a Single Jewish Representative on the Main Electoral Commission

[Będzin — City Council; Elections.]
The "unity" among the Jewish councillors.
On Wednesday a session of the Będzin city council was held. At the session our councillors once again practised among themselves the system of "not me, not you", and in the main electoral commission the Jewish population will not have a single representative.
The session was chaired by the council chairman Mr. Fürstenberg. The main item on the agenda was: to elect 2 members and 2 deputies to the main electoral commission for the coming Sejm elections.
As members, the candidacies of chairman Mr. Fürstenberg, the mayor Mr. Michel and Dr. Borolicki (B.B. [?]) were put forward. The vote, which took place amid the greatest tension, gave the following result:
Elected with 14 votes were Messrs. Michel and Fürstenberg (Dr. Borolicki received 13 votes).
In the election of the deputies "unity" reigned among the Jewish councillors. The Jewish side's candidates were Messrs. Dr. Rechtman and vice-chairman Mr. Ehrlich. But when the votes were cast the Jewish votes split, as always, and both Jewish candidates were defeated. In their place were elected Łaźnik [?], Hetmańczyk and Kiszyński...
As we are informed, Director Fürstenberg intends not to accept the post of member of the electoral commission, because the Jewish population of Będzin, which put through 16 councillors, does not have a single Jewish representative in the main commission...
—o—
[Sosnowiec — City Council.]
Sosnowiec city council allocates 20,000 zł. for the election campaign.
At Tuesday's session of the Sosnowiec city council, before proceeding to the agenda, an interpellation is tabled by councillors Dr. Liberman and Hamburger concerning the fact that the magistrate has raised the levy on foodstuffs brought in by rail.
The mayor declared that an answer to the interpellation would be given at the next session.
Then, on the proposal of the council presidium, the candidates for the 34 electoral districts were approved, and 20 thousand zł. were allocated to cover the expenses of the elections to the Sejm and Senate.
—o—
[Będzin — Charity.]
Support the holiday campaign for the "Orphans' Home".
The management of the Będzin orphans' homes has decided that, as every year, the children shall spend the holidays together and not be scattered [?] and dispersed at strangers' tables. For this purpose donations will be collected next week by the collector of the Będzin charity society.
It is to be hoped that this time too nobody will hold back from this important cause, and will help ensure that the orphans have a joyful holiday.
—o—
[Sosnowiec — A True Story.]
The dead father "worked" on the groom to marry his first bride.
A year ago Miss G. from the shtetl W. signed betrothal terms (tnoim) with Mr. D. from Z. The wedding date was set for the past Sabbath after Shavuot. For various reasons the wedding was postponed to Shabbat Nachamu; on the bride's side the proper wedding preparations were made.
Two weeks before the wedding date the bride's father received word from an outside source that the groom claims ch-ta [?], that he has no wish at all to marry. The bride's father, though he doubted that the groom would refuse the match a few days before the wedding, travelled to Z. to his groom — but how surprised he was to hear from the groom plainly that:
— "New demands"... If — I am not given — he declared — an additional dowry and [?] 2 thousand zł., I will not go to the chuppah...
Naturally the in-law was shaken by the surprising news and rejected the groom's demand. The bride too declared categorically that she wanted to hear no more of him; the upshot was that the bride and groom came to Sosnowiec, where they obtained a release (ptorin) at the rabbinate.
A short time passed [?], when the former groom's late father came to him in a dream and threatened him with the words: "If you do not marry the first bride, whom you have so shamed, you will die"...
The threat affected the groom so strongly that with tears in his eyes he pleaded with his uncles and aunts to take steps [?] so that the first match would come into force again...
At first the bride would not hear of it, but when people pressed her and begged her earnestly, she agreed to marry her first intended. Two weeks ago the wedding was celebrated with great honour; the couple now lives in Sosnowiec, where they lead a happy life.

[Notice — rabbinical court, ruling on a synagogue cantor; Będzin / Sosnowiec.]
[P. 8, right column, lower part, below the pills ad; original in Hebrew]
With God's help. Sosnowiec, Thursday (of the week of) Ki Tetze 5690 [4 September 1930].
Sitting as a bench of three together, we judged the dispute that arose between certain
people of the community of Będzin and the cantor of the synagogue there, Mr. Ozer
Menachem Żubowicz [?], concerning the bad reputation of the said cantor. After receiving
the testimony [?] under the rule „if he does not tell, he shall bear his iniquity“ (Lev. 5:1), and after investigation [?], since we did not
have sufficient testimony to disqualify him, the ruling went forth from us, the undersigned court:
a) That he is not to be removed from his post.
b) However, he has no claim that the great rabbi, head of the court of Będzin, may he live long, should give
him a share of the „RaChaSh“ [unclear abbreviation — apparently the wedding fee] (but he himself may ask the host of the wedding for „RaChaSh“).
Nor has he any claim to any new income that he did not have before, unless
with the consent of the community, with the head of the rabbinical court, may he live long, at its head.
c) We hereby decree with all possible severity that the said cantor shall not join
the witnesses of the marriage ceremony (kiddushin) at any wedding (and we have a hidden reason; in all towns
this should be instituted, that the cantor not be among the kiddushin witnesses, but since this case came
before us concerning the cantor of Będzin, we hereby express our opinion). We also
appeal to the people of the town to wish with all their might to uphold this without change, and this
is binding.
d) That he shall appease the great rabbi, head of the court of Będzin, may he live long, and take upon himself
not to speak again any word that is not respectful, and from this day on he shall be
submissive and obedient to his authority, with due honour, as is customary in all the dispersions of Israel.
e) That he shall take upon himself „the obligations of a chaver“ before the Będzin court, that from this day
on there shall be no murmuring and no bad rumour about him, and he shall guard his mouth
from ugly language, as in „woe to the prayer leader who wants his words accepted in Heaven
on behalf of the congregation“, as the Alshich wrote on the verse „and his sound shall be heard when he goes into the holy place“ (Ex. 28:35).
In witness whereof we have signed on the day stated above. Aryeh Tzvi Frommer, head of the court of
Koziegłowy, now head of the court here in Sosnowiec. Yehoshua Zysman, dayan and moreh tzedek
of Zawiercie. Yosef Baruch Blumenfeld, son of Rabbi Sh. Y., may he live long,
dayan and moreh tzedek here in Królewska Huta.

3 New School Buildings Opened in Zagłębie — 2 in Będzin, 1 in Dąbrowa

[Zagłębie — education, Będzin and Dąbrowa.]
On Sunday the 14th of this month Zagłębie was enriched by three new school buildings, built by the municipalities of Będzin and Dąbrowa with the help of government loans.
Taking part in the ceremony were the starost Baksa[?], the school curator of Kraków Mr. Kupczyński, the visitor (school inspector-general) Drewsiński[?], the school inspector Kuźniak, Major Kożegowski[?], town councillors and a large number of the pupils' parents.
In Dąbrowa the ceremony opens with a speech by Mayor (President) Madejski; then the delegates speak, and with the playing of “The First Brigade” [the Legions' song] the festive act is concluded.
Instead of a banquet the town administration assigned 15 hundred zł. Of this sum the church (kościół) receives 750 zł., and 750 zł. is to lay out a school garden.
———
In Będzin the ceremony took place with more splendour, but for sheer joy one “trifle” was forgotten — organization. With the chief in-laws from outside one still concerned oneself[?], whereas the “home folk” had no “resting place” and “assimilated” with the whole crowd [printed “geyendik” — walking/standing?].
First the school for Christian children was opened. When the representatives of the municipal and school authorities arrive, they are greeted by Mayor (President) Michał. The school orchestra plays the Polish anthem, then comes the ceremonial part. After the religious part has been performed, the priest delivers a speech in which he calls on the schoolchildren to grow up good Catholics and loyal citizens.
Then greetings were given by: the representative of the voivode, the school curator, the starost, the school inspector, the alderman (ławnik) Wszebrowski[?], and finally a pupil.
———
The building for the Jewish children is on Krakowska Street. To the ceremony came [ʿa"h?] a large number of Jewish parents, who took great pleasure in seeing the splendid rooms and hygienic facilities for their children.
The opening speech is delivered by Deputy Mayor Mr. Rubiglicht [so printed; probably Rubinlicht]. The school orchestra together with a choir plays “Jeszcze Polska”, then the representatives of the authorities speak (the same as at the opening of the school for Christian children), and finally the headmaster (kierownik) Mr. Rapaport, who points out the great importance of the school building for the school youth, which had been knocking about in cramped, unhygienic premises.
A fine greeting is given by the pupil Szwajcer, who presents a bouquet of flowers to Mayor Michał. The choir sings a school anthem, and afterwards the large Jewish public views the fine, large rooms.
———
Finally, a few words:
The rabbinate and the Jewish kehilla were also invited to the ceremony. The Rabbi, may he live long, came accompanied by the kehilla president Mr. Prawer[?], but at the beginning of the programme Mr. Prawer left and left the Rabbi without a proper escort.
A second question is: if the Rabbi, may he live long, intended [printed “bre'a” for “bede'a”] not to say a few words at the festive occasion of the Jewish children, then why did he have to be present?
What's Happening in Upper Silesia?

[Upper Silesia — news.] Session of the Upper Silesian Sejm.
Under the chairmanship of the Sejm Marshal, Mr. Wolny [Konstanty Wolny], a session of the Upper Silesian (Silesian) Sejm took place in Katowice on Tuesday.
As the first item, the Voivode's proposal was adopted that every year a sum of 250 thousand zł. be set aside in advance in the Sejm budget for the benefit of the Polish navy.
The PPS [Polish Socialist Party] deputies spoke out against the proposal.
The proposal was sent on to the budget committee.
After that a series of statutes was adopted.
—o—
A united Polish front.
On Tuesday a meeting of the Polish intelligentsia of Upper Silesia took place in Katowice.
The meeting resolved that for the coming Sejm elections a union of all Polish groupings should be created.
—o—
Terrible death of a motorcyclist.
On Monday afternoon the policeman Rydzewski was crossing the railway line between Załęże and Katowice on a motorcycle. At that moment a freight train passed by, which killed the policeman on the spot.
—o—
Run over by cars.
On Saturday in Królewska Huta [Königshütte, today Chorzów] five-year-old Maria Szymałowa[?] and eight-year-old Lenert[?] were run over by cars; the boy's condition is dangerous.
—o—
A protest meeting.
In one of the largest halls in Katowice a protest meeting took place, organised by the PPS and the German worker-socialists.
After the speeches a protest resolution was adopted against the arrests of the deputies.
—o—
Murdered her husband with an axe.
On Tuesday night a resident of Rudnik Piekar[?] (near Tarnowitz [Tarnowskie Góry]), A. Szatan[?], came home drunk and began to quarrel with his wife and son. From words they passed to deeds, and a bloody war broke out within the family. The mother and her son fought against husband and father.
When Szatan was already lying unconscious, the woman split his head open with a sharp axe.
The murderess has been arrested.
Zawiercie Has "Crowned" a King

[Zawiercie — monarchists; elections.] An election meeting of the monarchists.
Last Sunday the monarchists in Zawiercie organised a district congress in the "Stella" cinema.
Also present at the congress were the priest Stepieha[?] and Ćwiąkowski of Warsaw, who opened the congress with a speech in which he pointed out that salvation will come when Poland has a king.
During the speeches the "king" came out onto the stage, dressed up with a paper crown, and said the following:
"I, Zygmunt the First, King of Poland — bread and land I will not give you, because I have none; therefore I want to give you the heavens"...
The "king" was then carried out on the hands of the enthusiastic audience...
It's Not the Haggadah They Mean, but the Dumplings...

[Agudath Israel — press; satire.] Reading the "Agudah" organ is a great mitzvah.
On a command from "above", the "Tze'irei Emunei [Yisrael]" (Agudah youth) called a meeting at which speeches were made against the newspapers that feed[?] their readers with trashy sensations.
Every honest person will admit that the 10-groszy rags stand[?] at a very low level as regards their content; but as we know, the protest-makers are out for nothing more than to spread their own organ — it's not the Haggadah they mean but the dumplings. The resolution at the meeting was in fact that one should read only their own organ.
But they are not satisfied with the resolution: well-known Agudah activists go from house to house like brokers [telling people] that whoever subscribes to the Agudah organ fulfils a great mitzvah, no smaller than one of the 613 commandments...
(An authentic fact)
A Letter to the Editor

[Będzin — city council; letter to the editor.] Dear Mr. Editor!
I ask you to give room in your esteemed newspaper to the following lines:
In the previous issue of the "Z. Ts." [Zaglembier Tsaytung] there appeared a report on the elections in the Będzin city council of members to the main electoral commission.
Since[?] the report was presented tendentiously, I consider it my duty to state that on behalf of the Jewish councillors only 1 candidate and 1 deputy were put forward; the second deputy was put forward quietly, with the sole intention of drawing off 2–3 Jewish votes in order to make possible... the election of a non-Jewish member of the city council, without whom the present ruling majority would immediately fall apart.
History repeated itself with the election of the ławnicy [lay members of the municipal board]: then too the politicians had one candidate against two, in order to elect... a third, who was more important for creating a majority in the city council.
Again the same politicians won, and again the Jewish community suffered.
After this defeat the second soon came: the Sanacja quickly "took revenge" on the Jewish population for the failure of its candidate Dr. Barlicki[?] in the city-council elections, and of the total number of 15 chairmen of the "agmracja"[?] commissions confirmed barely 1 (one) Jew!
The politicians of the present city council may well rejoice: thanks to the outcome of the elections they have secured their positions for long months and will be able to go on turning their "public" work into a source of wealth, while at the same time pretending to regret that there is no "unity" among the Jewish councillors (who also want to have an opinion and do not let themselves be led... by the nose).
But the term of the city council is drawing to an end, and then, when they render an account, we will remind them of: the ławnicy elections, the Old Market, the halls, the evening courses, the investment and water taxes, and also... the last elections.
Respectfully,
Dr. R. Rechtman.
