[Będzin — kehilla; the kehilla budget; article.]
(In what manner are the budgets of our kehilla leaders approved?)
[—] [?], it is impossible to understand, it is in no way [?] possible to imagine what kind of [—] [?] is going on here.
What does it mean to belittle like this the representatives of an entire Jewish kehilla? Has such a thing ever been heard of?!
It concerns the budget that the administration of the Będzin Jewish kehilla drew up.
The government favoured us with Jewish self-governing bodies which took on such a shape that we did not get what we needed to get, and we are not satisfied with this created representation, which came out as nothing but a caricature, bringing not a few bitter drops into our communal [turmoil] [?]. But that does not mean that from the outside, towards the outside world, one may mock them; be that as it may, the elected representatives are after all our representatives, and if we have no joy of them, that is our affair, our internal matters.
Well, it is already an old rule, and we have more than once expressed our bitterness that, apart from drawing up the budget for the current year, our kind-hearted representatives do nothing, and as soon as they have dispatched this bit of work they can go on resting until the Master of the Universe grants health and life a year hence.
Of course, such a kind of "activity" is null and obsolete and we cannot agree with it; but still we know that there it goes on "on tables and on benches" until they agree among themselves to whom and how much "Sabbath fruit" to hand out — to this trend and that institution, to this association and that party; and when they have already haggled well, when they have come to terms among themselves however it came out, and the budget is sent off for approval — along comes the authority and turns everything upside down.
And this upheaval is galling, because the changes [?] hurt every one of us, for here we see a kind of provocation against us, and that our hard-earned money becomes free for anyone to grab.
Most of the subsidies for the local institutions, except the Agudah ones, were struck out completely. The question therefore arises: who is to help the local institutions exist if not our kehilla representation? On the other hand, the subsidies of the Agudah institutions, both local and non-local, were not struck out. It turns out, then, that local institutions need not interest our kehilla representatives, whereas we must support [outside?] party institutions which are not located in our town and drum everywhere with their charity boxes ("pishkes").
Can such tactics be understood? Can such conduct be understood? Is this not provocation [?]? Is this not playing on the nerves of our popular interests? What can one call this unheard-of injustice? What does it mean to mock everything that is worked out by our kehilla representatives?
If one has no confidence in them because one [does] not reckon with them, then what does one need them for, and why does one demand of them the drawing-up of budgets? In that case one could have understood it if the kehilla representations had been dissolved and the local authority had itself drawn up the proper budgets; at worst they would have taken a "żydek" ["little Jew"] to help, and the question would have been "solved" in the best possible way. But it is neither this nor that: one neither [—] [?] the kehilla representations, nor values them for what they were called to do.
That is what cannot be understood, that is what remains unanswered.
We did not, after all, elect our representatives so that they should be tossed once to the right and once to the left. One must nevertheless not forget that when one insults the Jewish representatives or does not reckon with them, it is exactly as if one did not reckon with all those who sent them there, and in that case the entire Jewish population as such finds itself insulted and hurt.
Such treatment of representatives of the most diverse strata of the population means mocking a town full of people, means not reckoning with them and with their interests. Such conduct is an insult; to treat an entire representation like that means to give it a slap in the face that makes one blush with shame.
Interesting, in any case, is the attitude of our kehilla representatives both regarding the insult to themselves and to the entire Jewish community.
We would have understood if certain changes had been made in the budget, as sometimes happens; we would have understood even if it had been changed completely — provided that this had taken place in the presence of those who drew up the budget, and the changes had been justified. But when it is done in the absence of the authors and without any justification, it means belittling a public work which ought to have been reckoned with under any circumstances whatsoever; and if this is not done, if money taken from the pocket of the entire Jewish population is not reckoned with, then the representatives who were called to collect the money must come and ask why we and they deserve to be treated so insultingly.
An individual, when he is insulted, retains the choice whether to reckon with the insult or not; that is his own affair, his own business. It is quite different, however, as soon as it takes on a public character: a community must be reckoned with, and therefore it is interesting to know in what manner our kehilla representatives react to the shameful slap in the face they received at the last drawing-up of the budget.
Selekt.
A Few Words

[Będzin — City Council; polemic.] To the "Responsible" Public Workers
By Vice-President L. Rubinlicht.
In connection with Councillor Rechtman's letter in the "Zagl. Tsayt." I consider it my duty to give some explanations to the Jewish population of Będzin, which went to the city-council elections with self-sacrifice and in great numbers and got as many as 16 councillors into the city council.
Soon after the city-council elections a Jewish opposition of 3 Jewish councillors was formed: one who said he was worthy of being a ławnik [member of the municipal executive board] and was not elected ławnik; the second had to "amanisirn" [?] his opinion in a municipal enterprise and did not succeed; and a third is in the opposition for the sake of opposition.
It is also unpleasant for me to polemicise with the "article writer" of the local Agudah sheet (an ignoramus in municipal affairs), who writes that "the Jewish representatives in the city council and in the magistrate neglect one field after another and abandon one Jewish position after another".
I will not answer the accusations, for the Jewish population of Będzin knows well enough the activity of a large number of Jewish councillors and magistrate members, who conquer with blood and sweat one field after another and one Jewish position after another, because they bear [lit. "represent"] the great responsibility they have taken upon themselves; bearing the title of councillor or magistrate member, they can point to many positive things for the Jewish population of Będzin, because the entire upkeep of "Linat ha-Holim" (10,000 zł. a year), the "Moshav Zkenim" [old-age home] (16,000), the orphanage (28.000), subsidies for building the orphanage in the last 2 years 74 000 zł., for "Yavne" 7.000; a colony [summer camp] for Jewish children was bought in Sławków for 50 thousand zł.; a practical [vocational] school building was put up especially for Jewish children for 400,000 zł. In the Będzin magistrate there now work Jewish doctors, secretaries, clerks; in the municipal electricity works the vice-director is a Jew, a Jewish cashier, 2 Jewish collectors; up to 8 Jewish officials are employed at the summer colonies; altogether up to 20 Jewish officials are employed in the Będzin magistrate. Besides that, last summer Jewish workers were taken on for municipal work. In the last year a water supply was installed here; the price of water is 50 gr. per metre [cubic metre] (at a time when in Częstochowa, Kielce, Radom a metre of water costs up to 1,50 zł.); poor tenants who live in cellar and attic rooms are entirely exempt from paying for water.
This is only a small part of the positive work of the municipal Jewish representatives in the Będzin city council.
Now a few words about the Jewish councillors who are in the opposition. They play their main role when elections come: hardly has the Jewish representation suffered a defeat than they rejoice and criticise in the press the "politicians" (so Councillor Rechtman calls the present Jewish leaders in the city council).
And for the present defeat in the elections to the main electoral commission we have our irresponsible public workers to thank. Two days before the city-council session the Jewish councillors were also summoned, in the name of the Jewish councillors' club, in order to discuss the question of Jewish candidates for the main electoral commission. Only a few councillors came to the meeting and the meeting did not take place. At the city-council session, on the other hand, a representative of the artisans put forward the candidacy of Mr. Fürstenberg and Dr. Rechtman. I succeeded in persuading the councillors of the P.P.S. and the Endeks to vote for Mr. Fürstenberg, but under no circumstances did they want to vote for Councillor Rechtman, and they voted for Councillor Ehrlich. Therefore the votes were split and the second Jewish candidate failed completely, whereas the allies of Councillor Rechtman (B.B. [BBWR]) had promised to vote for him — and voted for Councillor Kusenki [?] (B.B.), who unfortunately got through as deputy to the Jewish member Mr. Fürstenberg on the main electoral commission.
How does our only Jewish member, Mr. Fürstenberg, fulfil his duties on the main electoral commission? So far 4 sessions have taken place. Mr. Fürstenberg did not come to the first, most important session, and he was "represented" by Mr. Kusiński, who saw to it that out of 15 electoral districts only in 1 district is the chairman a Jew, and all the Jewish candidates proposed by the Będzin and Sosnowiec magistrates were thanks to this rejected.
You, Councillor Dr. Rechtman, write that the city council's term is drawing to an end. That is indeed good, because when we hand our offices over into the hands of our voters, the active representatives in the city council and in the magistrate will be able to point with pride to the fruits of their untiring work, and you, as one of the opposition, will unfortunately not be able to show that.
“Only Not on Paper”

[Zagłębie — artisans and guilds; a reply.]
(A reply to Mr. L. Sh.)
In issue no. 39 of the „Zaglembier Tsaytung“, under the above-mentioned heading, the esteemed editor Mr. L. Sh. devoted a longer article to the situation of the Jewish artisans' movement in general, and in particular to the latest step of the Sosnowiec artisans' organisation — its initiative to create a supreme council of all the Jewish guilds in Zagłębie.
Allow me at the very outset to stress with particular satisfaction the fact that from the columns of the Jewish press a sincere voice is heard on the painful question of the Jewish artisan — the question of the legitimate representation of the artisans' organisation as such.
The Central Union of Jewish Artisans in Poland counts only about 15 years of official organisational existence. It is therefore no great wonder at all that to this very day we meet, here and there, in smaller or larger towns, various self-appointed benefactors, „fine Jews“, who are out „exclusively“ for the good of the poor wretched artisan, who lives [in] want and penury, and who push [?] themselves forward by force to be his only representatives...
Incomparably sadder, however, is the case when within the artisans' ranks themselves there are such elements who do not use their mandates for the improvement of the socio-economic interests of the broad Jewish artisan masses — not to mention that literally nothing at all has been done in the field of cultural and educational work.
But the situation changed radically with the establishment of the guilds. A considerable part of the organisational work passed automatically into the leading guild bodies, and probably — in parallel with the development of the guilds — the artisans' organisation as such will in time be pushed down [?] to a second rank.
And therefore, when the slogan was put forward by the Sosnowiec Artisans' Association to found a supreme council of all the Jewish guilds in Zagłębie, we were first and foremost keen to create that legitimate body of the entire artisans' movement in the territory of the Będzin district (powiat), which, besides representative work, should care above all for the cultural and educational side of the artisan masses and prepare [?] the Jewish artisan for the situation into which he is being brought by the compulsory guild law.
As a non-political economic institution representing about 3000 Jewish artisans in Zagłębie, the said supreme council will without any doubt become in time the actual regulator of Jewish craftsmanship — not to mention what it can achieve in the official government offices in pursuing interests of a general character.
„Only not on paper“ — that is what it is all about. Only a serious approach to the matter on the part of all the existing artisans' organisations in Zagłębie will be able to realise this very important project. A proper secretariat apparatus must be set up, and all the necessary means created, together with the proper persons who will be fit to conduct this very important work. The supreme council must give the proper impetus to each Jewish guild separately towards joint work. The supreme council must stand on guard and be the direct intermediary between the Kielce Chamber of Crafts and the Jewish artisans (this is especially important for us because Zagłębie is not represented in the Chamber of Crafts).
But all this is well and good. The question of „only not on paper“ nevertheless remains the one open wound, which depends to a great extent on understanding [?], devotion and, above all, a sense of responsibility on the part of the leading persons who stand at the head of the individual local organisations.
I wish to hope that the ardent call of Mr. L. Sh. will find the proper echo, and that from paper we shall pass on to deeds.
The floor belongs to the artisans' leaders in Zagłębie.
L. Pariser.
On the Cooperative Day celebrated on the 5th of this month — On the Day of the Cooperative Holiday

[Cooperatives — article; Cooperative Day.]
By former Sejm deputy Dr. H. Rosmarin [Henryk Rosmarin], chairman of the "General Union of Cooperatives" in Lwów (Lemberg).
Every holiday, and especially the holiday of a movement, serves as a day of "soul-searching" (cheshbon hanefesh). On this day of rest from the everyday work of the movement we try to draw up a kind of balance sheet: to see by how many steps [?] we have advanced on the road to our ideal, and from the victories already won we draw new strength to endure the hard daily work of struggles, efforts and exertions which make up the road to the realisation of the ideal.
If we want to draw up an honest account of the cooperative movement in the Jewish street in Poland, we must say that although it has recently taken a significant step forward, it is still in its period of development; today we are still far from being able to state that in the Jewish street, too, there exists for the so useful cooperative movement the understanding it enjoys in many civilised countries, where it has become a popular movement in the broadest sense of the term. Now is not the time to dwell in detail on the causes that brought this about and still bring it about to this day. We must, however, state that thanks to the educational work, which is carried on without pause, the cooperative movement has nevertheless grown stronger. Cooperatives are steadily being added; the number of people who understand the cooperative ideal and strive to realise it in everyday life is growing; in a word, the cooperative idea is growing — this protective idea for our abnormal life.
We must not forget in this connection that the largest percentage in our economic life is made up of the merchant class [?], whose hard struggle for existence today does not allow it to reflect calmly on its situation and to choose more suitable and easier forms of economic life. In government circles, which in general have shown [?] an interest in the cooperative movement in the country, recognising it as a sound and important factor in economic life, the same interest is unfortunately not shown in the Jewish part of the cooperative movement. At the very time when Polish cooperatives are being supported by the government more and more, no change whatsoever for the better can be seen in the attitude toward Jewish cooperatives — and this is precisely one of the main reasons why Jews are not represented in the cooperative movement as they should be in proportion to their share in economic life.
Despite all the difficulties standing in the way of the Jewish cooperative movement in Poland, we can nevertheless look to the future with faith and confidence. We rely with the fullest confidence on the healthy instinct of the Jewish people, that this instinct will bring it, too, onto the cooperative road, the surest and finest road in economic life. The Jewish people has shown more than once that it can overcome difficulties and not only equal others but serve as pioneer and model for all others. We also believe in the pioneering and exemplary activity of Jewish cooperatives.
On this holiday, however, we must not refrain from addressing the government and its institutions, and we want to tell them:
It is high time you began to look differently at Jewish economic life; it must not be treated as an isolated island. Since you, too, recognise that the conditions of Jewish economic life are abnormal — give the opportunity to create normal, healthy, secure conditions for that life; for if the remedy and the proper doctors to heal what is unhealthy in Jewish economic life are not found in time, the disease will spread through the whole economic body of the country. Our government, which shows a great and understanding attitude toward the cooperative movement, is called upon to show such an attitude toward the Jewish part of the movement in the country as well; the government is called upon to give proper support to Jewish cooperatives, which create the normal, so necessary conditions for Jewish economic life.
The Cooperative Movement on the Jewish Street

The "General Cooperative Union" (Allgemeiner Kooperativn-Farband) is the first Jewish cooperative union in Poland (founded in the year 1901). As such, the union did much to help the ideal of cooperation penetrate the Jewish street as well, where there had been almost no sense at all for so useful a movement. At first, however, the union limited its activity to Galicia alone; thanks to it, many cooperative enterprises arose there, which were the first Jewish cooperatives in Poland.
The work of the "General Cooperative Union" brought the desired results. In a relatively very short time the cooperative movement in Galicia developed considerably and was transformed into a first-rank factor in Jewish economic life. The development proceeded normally, with ever faster and surer steps, until the outbreak of the World War. The World War had a destructive effect on this important institution. A whole series of cooperatives went under, and together with this the union went through a severe crisis. The union did not manage to free itself from this severe crisis even several years after the war, during the uncertain inflation years.
In recent years, in connection with the stabilisation of economic life, the "General Cooperative Union" in Lwów (Lemberg) has been revived. The union was completely reorganised, and at its head stood the well-known economist and public figure, Deputy Dr. H. Rozmaryn [Henryk Rosmarin]. A new, energetic and enterprising era begins. The union grows considerably and no longer limits its activity to Galicia alone. Many cooperatives from Congress Poland, Volhynia and Polesie join it. The union's leadership, too, consists of cooperative representatives from all parts of free Poland.
The reorganised union, taking into account the enormously great importance of cooperation for Jewish economic life in Poland today, has devoted much attention to propaganda and educational work on the Jewish street. A special department for propaganda and educational work was founded at the union. The union publishes 2 cooperative journals, one in Polish under the name "Przegląd Spółdzielczy" and the other in Yiddish under the name "Der Kooperator". Both papers have been warmly received in cooperative circles and their circulation rises steadily.
A special publishing department was also created at the union, which supplies the union's members with all necessary printed matter and also publishes a cooperative people's library. Great success was enjoyed by the popular brochure entitled "What Is Cooperation" by the chairman of the State Cooperative Council, Mr. Janusz Kszypczyński[?], which appeared in the people's library. The activity of the publishing department is soon to be considerably strengthened.
Alongside the union's planned propaganda and educational activity, which is also expressed in the district cooperative conferences and popular meetings organised from time to time, the union comes to the aid of its affiliated cooperatives with cheap credit. In this respect much good is also being done by the union's Central Bank, headed by the well-known Jewish economics expert, former Senator Dr. F.[?] Rottenstreich, which is developing in a thoroughly satisfactory measure.
The popularity of the union and the confidence in it of the broad Jewish popular strata are growing literally from day to day. In the official cooperative circles of the country, too, the "General Cooperative Union" has won great recognition. Clear proof of this is the nomination of the union's chairman, Dr. H. Rozmaryn, as a member of the State Cooperative Council.
A General Bloc (A Little Feuilleton)

It is truly heaven-sent that Marshal Piłsudski dissolved the Sejm just before the Ten Days of Awe, when "even a fish in the water begins to tremble" and all Jews are ready to forget the wrongs "between man and his fellow".
Only at such a time could the idea of unity have been born among Jews — of a united Jewish front that would represent the Jewish manufacturer and worker, Hasid and Misnaged, Orthodox and freethinker, householder and neighbour, as the verse says: "and they shall all form one band"...
There is only one trouble: the elections themselves are set for the end of November, or rather — for the end of Marheshvan, when every Jew is not only long done with the "sealing" [of judgment], but even the "kvitl" in his pocket is long since crumpled.
And this endangers the whole business, because a Jew is ready to lie down on the bench [for the ritual lashes] only on the eve of "Y.K.", but after Yom Kippur he laughs off the whole forgiveness...
And therefore we must at least take care to tie up the general Jewish bloc in such a way that right after the holidays, in the very height of the election season, we should not, God forbid, meet with any mishap — that the knots should not burst.
So how does one do it? For that there is one piece of advice: don't tie everyone together, but each one separately.
For example:
Zionists — they have in their ranks all kinds: rich and poor, capitalists and workers, the pious and the free — one needs them all; the political Zionists and the practical ones, the "Poalei Zion" and the "Sorchim"[?], the Revisionists and the "Hitachdut" people — tie them together in one band and we already have a general electoral bloc.
Agudah — the same: the Hasidim of the various rebbes, the "Poalei Agudat Yisrael" with the "Tseirei Agudat Yisrael", those who ride to the rebbe in rubber-tyred carriages and those who go on foot with their shoes on their shoulders — tie them all together and you have a second Jewish electoral bloc.
The Folkspartei — small as it is, you still need a big rope to tie it up...
The Jewish socialists — that goes without saying[?]: you won't tie them with any rope, you need actual chains...
Take[?] the Jewish economic organizations — merchants, petty traders, craftsmen and artisans — here you surely have all the "ve-khol ma'aminim" to create a united bloc, and not just one bloc but several.
You will surely ask — what use are so many general blocs to us? The answer is: if one general bloc is good, then several are even better...
And by the way — you undertake to create the truly genuine general Jewish bloc out of all the general Jewish blocs? On the contrary — try it!
Onkelos.
From the Polish Stage

[Sosnowiec — theatre; review.]
("One Day Without Lying", a comedy in 3 acts by Montgomery, director W. Tański, staged at the Sosnowiec Municipal Theatre).
"Teatr Miejski" redivivus. It is with great satisfaction that one must note the fact that the Sosnowiec Municipal Theatre has become active again under the direction of artistic forces. After the various phases the theatre has gone through, after the epoch of a political regime over a purely cultural institution, which should not be an instrument of agitation for parties but a tribune of pure art, the time has come when the theatre has passed into the hands of the artist Tański, who will probably fulfil his duty as head of the only Polish theatre in Zagłębie.
The theatre's debut[?] was a very successful one. "The Faithful Beloved" drew a large audience.
"The Faithful Beloved" already showed that Director Tański is appearing here with good artists, who take their duty seriously and devote themselves to their roles.
In the second programme "One Day Without Lying" was given. The very title sounds paradoxical. Is there a single day on which not one untrue word is spoken. The author, Montgomery, consistently carries through his leading idea, that one cannot imagine any normal life without lies. The entire ideological weight of the comedy lies in the first act. In it the conflict between truth and life is tied. The other two acts are merely a means of carrying through the author's idea, which, however, already emerges quite unambiguously from the first act. Of four men only one "hero" is found, the likeable Bob, who has undertaken to speak nothing but the truth for 24 hours. But that too only for money. He actually carried it through, but the "victory" brought him to the ruin of the business, to insulting the guests, to various family quarrels, etc.
If, within the framework of present-day social conditions, one wants to keep oneself alive and have recognition, one must tell lies and [—][?]... shout[?]. That, then, is the canvas that runs through the comedy, which provokes laughter to the point of tears and brings out the sad social doctrine.
The whole comedy is permeated with materialism, and Bob does indeed undertake "to speak only the truth", but not so that truth should reign in life and drive out falsehood, but only because he will receive a large sum of money for it..
The attraction of the comedy rests on its topicality. For example, the role of Mr. Ralston, who shows us how a father of grown-up children kisses young girls in his office. In general the author Montgomery has presented here types of real businessmen. The flaw of this stage play is its excessive drawn-out-ness and a certain[?] repetition of the humorous moments.
The artists fulfilled their duty, playing — with small exceptions — irreproachably. Mr. Van Dusen (Tański) and the honest pastor (Kowalski) were rendered as Montgomery would surely have wished to see them; Mabel (Mrs. Tańska) played with humour; Gwen (Mrs. Gicowska[?]) presented herself charmingly. The pleasant Bob (Sarnecki), who tells the truth to "every friend", amuses the audience. The artists were showered with strong applause and the spectators left the theatre hall with satisfaction.
* * *
We also wished to remark at this point that this theatre should not limit itself only to Polish plays, for, bearing in mind that a large part of the visitors are Jewish, the theatre management should also bring onto the stage the dramatic works of Jewish authors. In this way the theatre will also fulfil its duty towards the Jewish population of Zagłębie.
A. Gertner.
Problems of Jewish Handicraft

By Eng. M. Belagoski [Bełagowski?].
Is Manual Work Being Pushed Out of Modern Industry?

In the present era, when industrial development and the rationalization of the factory economy have reached the highest stage, when the machine turns out finished mass-produced articles almost automatically, the opinion is very widespread that industry does not require trained, skilled workers. This supposedly corresponds to the character of modern production methods, which have carried the division of labour to its utmost limits, where every operation is broken down and divided into its simplest elements, which are performed directly by special machines, simple and complex.

This opinion, regardless of its being accepted by the broad public, is fundamentally wrong. Only people who have a scanty and blurred notion of the innermost processes of factory production can think that today's large factories have no need of skilled workers. In reality, it is precisely in these factories that a great shortage of skilled manpower is felt, and it is not for nothing that many modern factories maintain vocational schools at their own expense, in order to prepare the trained, skilled workers they absolutely need. The point is that the more industry mechanizes itself, the more complicated and ingenious the instrument, the device it uses, must be; and in order to create these complicated and ingenious instruments and devices, industry needs capable, intelligent, skilled workers.

What, in fact, does the basic difference between the production methods of modern industry and the handicraft of former times consist of? It consists in this: the craftsman used to create single, so to speak individual, articles, while the machine creates typical mass articles. The means of production of the craftsman of old consisted of simple tools: an axe, a hammer, an "ekber"[?] etc.; working by hand, he would very slowly shape each single object out of the raw material. The tinsmith, for example, would slowly and carefully beat the sheet metal with the hammer on the anvil, put the metal through all kinds of manipulations, until he had shaped the single individual object — let us say, a particular vessel. Working this way has no value today. The vessel would have cost too much. Such a vessel now costs so little in the shop that making it by hand does not pay in any way. And it is cheap now because it is now made not by hand but by a machine, which turns out quickly and, as said, almost automatically, not single, individual vessels but typical, uniform vessels in masses. But here lies the great mistake, when one thinks that since the machine turns out finished articles, the old mastery of the skilled worker is no longer needed at all. It is indeed true that for the direct manufacture of mass articles one needs no skilled workers. One simple, untrained worker can often tend several machines. Skilled work, however, is absolutely necessary — perhaps to an even greater extent and at a higher level than before — for another purpose, which cannot be done without at all.

Let us see: how does the machine produce these typical, uniform mass articles? It produces them with the help of moulds, models and templates. Once it possesses these moulds, models and templates, it creates almost "in their image and likeness" and casts out masses of these typical, uniform articles; but in order to create the moulds, models and templates themselves, the art and skill of a professional are required. If formerly a master made ingenious things with simple instruments, today one needs ingenious instruments to make even the very simplest things, and still more perfect instruments — to produce complicated articles.

These ingenious instruments, the moulds and models, are produced on special machines by workers who have gone through a practical school and are well qualified in the trade. An untrained worker cannot be entrusted with any work on this special machine: he may break a delicate mechanism or damage an expensive instrument. When a mould has been preliminarily worked on this machine, it is handed over to a master for final hand-finishing — first with the help of electric grinding devices and then with fine files.

Thanks to the special sense and the fine sensitivity of the skin on the fingertips, he feels out the slightest uneven spots and files them away with a special file and whetstone.

However strange it may sound at first glance, it is a fact that even in modern, thoroughly mechanized industry the last word still belongs to the unarmed but experienced hand of the master. Not everything there is turned into an automaton. There still remains quite a broad place for the manual art and intelligence of skilled workers. The master's art, which was once required to produce single, individual articles of use, is now applied to creating moulds and instruments. It has been proven, however — and this is the main point that interests us here — that today workers are needed to make instruments no fewer than were once needed to produce articles of use. This is explained, on the one hand, by the fact that needs in general have grown enormously and both the kinds and the quantity of objects produced have increased [printed "suzen"] colossally; on the other hand, the production of instruments and moulds is incomparably more difficult and complicated and therefore requires much more labour.

We therefore establish that even in our time, when the machine is achieving such enormous victories, there are branches of factory production where the intelligent and experienced worker cannot be replaced by an automaton. One of these branches is the metal-working industry — in the departments for producing moulds and instruments, which employ quite a large number of trained workers. This category of workers is very well paid. At Ford's the toolmakers are called "production aristocrats". Despite the great unemployment, the toolmaker finds plenty of work at the factory even now. It goes without saying that he must receive a good practical and also a certain theoretical preparation. He must be able to find his way easily in drawings and be able to draw himself.

For Jews this work is as if made to measure. It requires intelligence, it is not automatic, it gives nourishment to the intellect, it is a certain creative process, and above all — the trade ensures steady work, which is moreover well paid. It therefore seems to us that one of the most important tasks of our community in the field of the vocational training of our youth must be to prepare cadres of Jewish toolmakers.
Children of Famous Parents

It remains one of the great secrets of nature why famous parents, people with special abilities, do not pass on their name and their abilities to their children. Already among the prophets – who, after all, as people were blessed and endowed with all virtues, as it is said that the Shekhinah rests only on one who is wise, strong and rich – we do not find that their children inherited even one of those virtues. In general one hears nothing at all of the children, and if one does hear, as for instance in the case of Moses our Teacher, there is merely a supposition that people were so ashamed of the heir that the grandfather's name was deliberately altered. The grandson was a vagabond ("shlepper") who served whoever wanted him, and all for a piece of bread.
Torah and wisdom usually do not pass down by inheritance among the gentile nations either. It is known that the son of the great poet Wolfgang Goethe was something of a madman; things looked no better with Bismarck's children. It is just lucky that true geniuses do not marry and therefore have no children. If they had all left children behind them, we would now have half a world of idiots. This very fact is one of the arguments against the monarchist principle, against rule passing from father to son: almost all rulers who were significant personalities left behind them an heir who was an idiot, or simply a villain and a fool. This was seen in Russian history with Peter the Great and his heir, and it was also seen with the last German Kaiser, the grandson of Frederick the Great...
I know that there are enough facts that prove the opposite. There are families that can show a lineage of ten generations of rabbis. Likewise there are, to make the distinction, families that count more than ten generations of pastors. But regarding these facts one must agree with the opinion of the Talmud that if three generations in a row are men of Torah, it is already a presumption (chazakah) and the Torah remains rooted in the family; that is, one must distinguish between intelligent, capable people and people of genius. Intelligence can pass down by inheritance, provided the stock is a healthy one; but genius does not pass down by inheritance. On the contrary: if from an ordinary family – as for instance with the poet Goethe, who came from a family of shopkeepers – a child of genius breaks forth, it takes for itself the whole spiritual energy of the stock, and the later generations are inferior or even idiotic.
As we have already remarked, the problem of spiritual inheritance belongs to the great secrets of nature. Everything that has been said and written about it is no more than conjecture; no certain knowledge can be had in this field. But the problem is raised so often when we come across an heir of a great name who commits petty, foolish and criminal deeds. Thus we have now received news from Bordeaux, in France, that the only son of Theodor Herzl has committed suicide there. That Herzl was a great personality no one doubts. One therefore asks: how is it that his dear son turned out so badly that he constantly brought disgrace on us, and now forces us, with his unnatural death as well, to talk about him?
Herzl was undoubtedly a tragic figure. His sudden emergence from the depths of Viennese assimilation to Jewish nationalism and to Judaism was such a tremendous surprise that even the clever psychiatrist[?] Nordau doubted whether his friend was in his right mind. But even the clever Nordau later penetrated his friend's ideas and even became his follower; for his family, however, Herzl remained incomprehensible. Above all his wife, the inveterate Viennese society lady, who was proud of the great prize she had won – of having caught[?] for a husband the handsome, tall, elegant writer and speaker, a man destined to make the greatest career. And indeed he was on the right path: he is editor of the greatest, most influential newspaper, he goes to Paris as diplomatic correspondent, he writes books that are highly praised, writes plays that are staged – in a word, the little [?] woman with the blond hair is content, she is admired, her friends envy her, and she already dreams of decorations, of court balls where she will shine at the side of her great, handsome and famous husband.
Suddenly comes the great disappointment[?]. Her great husband suddenly becomes small; he makes himself small, he loses himself in nothing but empty fantasies, associates with vagabonds who speak some "jargon" there, who cannot even speak German, and ruins his career. Herzl's wife lived and died convinced that Zionism was her misfortune, that because of the "mad fantasy" her husband had made himself, her and the whole family unhappy, and that because of it he departed this world before his time. And she planted this hatred in the children as well.
After Herzl's death his friend and successor David Wolffsohn, who had no children, took little Hans to himself and strove to give him the best education. Wolffsohn, a Russian Jew living in Germany and rich enough, believed that he would succeed in bringing up Herzl's heir so that he would grow into the proud Jew who would bear with pride the name of the first leader. He sent him to the best schools, to the finest English colleges. But it helped little: the little boy was indeed called Herzl, but he remained a "Hans". In his little head, which was filled with images of the old imperial Austria, a fantasy was woven that he was a prince, like today's Otto of Habsburg, and that people were only waiting for him to come of age in order to seat him on the throne his father had left.
Meanwhile Wolffsohn died, the war came, the world was turned upside down, and the young prince stumbled about in the world where no one noticed him. Such little Hanses roll about in their millions and no one sees them. Since he had to make a living, connections were used and a good position was obtained for him. But the prince felt insulted and took revenge on the ungrateful Jewish people: he converted. But the conversion too did him little good. For a while the world remembered him, and not to his credit, and then he was forgotten again. He [—] wandered from one faith to another, but that was already an entirely futile effort – people did not even want to take notice[?] of it. Hans the apostate interested no one, and so he sank ever lower, until he has now put an end to his wild and damaged life.
Great personalities usually leave behind them small people. So it was once, and so it is today too. And Herzl was indeed the great personality, and his greatness is not diminished even by the shadow that little Hans casts upon him.
Sh. Y. S.
A Convert Comes to Synagogue...

A convert comes into the Sosnowiec synagogue
for the first time since his conversion;
Jews smile with pleasure into their little beards
and the youngsters prance about like young colts.

The idlers whisper in the corners
and eyes are already twinkling at each other:
"A real eager one for a piece of Leviathan,
this[?] is a bit of a young lad, a bridegroom."

The prayer leader takes his place before the lectern,
he (the convert) keeps getting up from his seat,
then suddenly sits down again just like that[?],
not knowing what the purpose is.

Communal prayer begins,
he leafs through the Yiddish-Polish prayer book,
young men[?] proudly point out to him:
"Right here, from 'Mah Tovu' is where one starts..."

And when they reach the blessing "who has not made me a gentile",
mouths[?] exchange glances, deliberately so.
He sways all the more piously,
to cover up[?] his own sorrow.

After the prayers he gets ready to go home;
the synagogue folk hold him back a while:
"Nu, nu, Reb Avraham, what's the rush[?],
[?], let's have a chat meanwhile."
He excuses himself with a pretext:
"As the gentiles[?] say... I have a bad headache today."
The Jews nod their beards in assent:
"Well, never mind, but don't be a stranger, you hear!"

A convert comes into the synagogue
for the first time since his conversion;
Jews smile with pleasure into their little beards
and the youngsters prance about like young colts.
Leyzer Shikman.
Sosnowiec, 5691.
I Would Have Taken a Stroll...

[Będzin — economy and taxes; feuilleton.] In the beginning, at the start, it was quiet; whispering prevailed, just among ourselves, just a murmur. That was the beginning of the roll down the mountain.
The Jewish press — be it said not to its discredit — treated it with disdain: a yawn, now and then perhaps an article just to discharge the obligation. But no one heard the echo of the deep groan of the old, collapsing tree on which the Jewish press sits and leans.
When the economic wounds began to fester harder and the pains grew greater, the tone rose. A cry burst out, indifference was lost, and the civic press was already reproducing public opinion.
Cries, however harsh and however strong they may be, and however beautifully worded[?] and composed, work only the first time; afterwards one grows used to them and they stop working. Our Talmud has already said: just as it is a mitzvah to say what will be heard, so it is a mitzvah not to speak when one does not want to listen.
When Deputy Grünbaum demonstrated our troubles and sufferings from the Sejm rostrum, the ministers sat in their boxes[?] and shook their heads: he exaggerates greatly, he makes an elephant out of a fly.
And when Deputy Farbstein spoke more calmly and proved with facts and figures that the Jewish citizens are dropping like flies, that we are already squeezed-out lemons, that we are going under and so a part of the state organism is being ruined — a minister gave him to understand that the tax machine must press on and run at a fast tempo, because revenue in a state budget is a sacred duty and stands above all troubles and torments, above even the ruin of the citizens.
The main thing — they did not believe us and do not believe us; a sign that more is being exacted[?] than was budgeted, which means one can still milk and milk.
We live in a democratic state. A delegation of petty traders leaves the ministerial cabinet, and representatives of the artisans come in. They talk over the oppressions and decrees against people who are rolling down the mountain — and one surely drives them into the abyss instead of strengthening them and holding them at the edge of the abyss.
After all the groans and talks, the directors stay with the ministers in their cabinets: they calculate, they total up the taxes that have flowed in, they pull out and put back the statistical tables — everything tallies exactly, everything stays as it was, nothing has been heard or seen.
It would really have been better worthwhile to ask our department directors and ministers: what did they hear and see while they travelled through the towns and little towns of the Republic — did they stroll through the streets and look into the shops and little shops?...
But here is the trouble: when a minister comes to a town he does not walk — he is led. Ahead of him goes "Righteousness shall go before him" [Psalm 85:14; misprinted "צרק"]: the reports, for example, are prepared, the finest apartments are reserved, breakfast is ready, and one rushes through the streets in a closed automobile.
I am a local patriot; first of all I care about Będzin. If a minister — no matter whether the Minister of Trade or the Minister of Labour — accepted my invitation and came to Będzin, I would not hold long conversations with him; on the contrary, I would be very, very laconic, I would use my fingers more than my mouth...
I would hold no conversations or discussions with him. I would raise my finger, point, and walk along Małachowskiego–Kołłątaja, stop several times, and [?] on the Old Market. A long pause. I keep silent and show him with my finger where several tombstones stand with the new inscription "Do wynajęcia" [Polish: "To let"]!
In the very centre of town, for generations, life bustled there; pillars they were — and now nailed shut, bolted, and on the front door — a slip "Do wynajęcia"!
But the ministers will not accept my invitation, so I will take no stroll, and everything will stay as it was, as though nothing at all had happened...
W. Albek.
Hosha'na!

[Reflections — Jewish politics; Sukkot and Hoshana Rabba.] Thoughts — by Y. G. Steinsapir.
It is a time of trouble for Jacob — a tumult on the Jewish street, a bacchanalia and a dance of demons; one brother does not recognise the other, and they tear from one another not only pieces of flesh but pieces of soul as well.
If until now people only talked about "two nations", it has now become a fact — even worse than in the era of Jeroboam son of Nebat, for then we split into two kingdoms, but one nation we nevertheless remained..
And the heart trembles: the day is gone and the night comes on — a long, rainy autumn night on the Jewish street!
Naked trees, torn-off branches, golden[?] leaves and flowers that not long ago were green and in bloom, roll about underfoot, and the wicked autumn wind scatters them in all directions — only yesterday they were joined together, and now they are wild strangers to one another..
The wind howls, the rain sobs, the lost leaves and flowers whisper:
Hosha'na!
* * *
Watchman, what of the night?
What can such a dark night bring us?
This question is on the lips of every one of us — of everyone who does not stand with both feet in this camp or that, on the right or the left, but feels himself a child of the eternal people, of the whole people, not of a split one...
True, the "fruit of the land" [as printed] is holy and dear to us: the etrog with the lulav — we pride ourselves on their pedigree, we have sentiments for them; but neither can we distance ourselves from the everyday "hoshanot" — from the simple twigs that grew up in masses on the banks of the swampy rivers...
All of them together are for us one festival — "the Season of our Rejoicing"!
And when people split apart, we stand in despair and cry:
Hosha'na!
* * *
Who are you two, from the left and from the right?
You are all Jews, after all, modern Jews, children of one father and mother, sons of a people that has been bleeding for generations for liberty, equality and fraternity, for eternal peace between man and his fellow. So why have you taken up knives and carried yourselves back into a primeval era — the era of Cain and Abel?...
No, you shall not slaughter each other — we will not let you!
Yes, we know the secret — you are both already old and weak, the legs beneath you are already giving way, so you want to spill each other's blood and raise an outcry over the fresh "ruins of Zion"..
But it will not help you at all!
We, the core of the people, the millions of Jews who are not stuck in your mire, will not go your ways..
Time is stronger than you — you did not create it, it created you! It brought you forth and it will destroy you!...
The same autumn winds that scatter all the withered leaves will scatter you too.
And after that a cold winter will come, and after the winter a new spring!
So why should you slaughter each other? Better bend quietly towards one another, listen well to one another, listen well to one another, listen well to how the winds howl — and you will catch in them the sounds of new songs — songs of the spring that is to come.
Bend.. bend...
Hosha'na!!!

In Honour of Sukkot

[Sukkot — Torah sayings and anecdotes for the festival.]
Torah sayings and anecdotes relating to Sukkot
Collected and styled by: Y. Y.

a) The four species of the lulav.
The Midrash compares the four species of the lulav to the four kinds of Jews that exist. The willow (aravah) has neither taste nor smell — it symbolises the simple folk [?] of the people, those without Torah and without deeds. The myrtle (hadas) has a smell but no taste — it represents those who do good and give charity, but without Torah, without knowledge. The lulav — the dates of the palm have taste but no smell — they are likened to the masters of Torah who have no good deeds in them. The etrog already has both taste and smell; it symbolises the perfect Jew. All of these must unite; all together they are one. To lose [them]? [?] — “it is impossible to destroy them”: one cannot pick out a people made only of the perfect.
* * *
And remarkably: all three — myrtle, willow and lulav — are bound tightly together, but the etrog, the fine Jews, can only be brought close to the people's bundle; to bind them tightly like the other three kinds — that, no... The etrog remains, after all, a pedigreed one apart.. Yalkut Margaliyot.

b) “The fruit of a goodly tree” — a tree whose wood and fruit taste the same (Sukkah 31).
Among other nations their whole glory is that later generations go further than their parents, that they progress, because the nations really do perfect themselves more and more. Their forefathers were, after all, ignorant. It was different with us Jews: our ancient generations stood on the highest spiritual level, on the greatest height of culture; they brought forth prophets from among themselves and created the Bible. We only wish that our whole generation would be such that “the taste of its wood and its fruit are equal” — that the fruit would have the same taste as the tree... Derashot el Ami.

c) “That all the peoples of the earth may know that the Lord is God, there is none else.”
R. Yehuda Leib Teomim, later the well-known rabbi of Brody, once as a young man [?] prayed in the synagogue on Sukkot, and, as the custom is, during the Hoshanot one circles the bimah with the lulavim in hand. No doubt the first to go round the bimah were the rich men, the ignoramuses, and him, the great Torah scholar, they left for the end. He then made the following sharp-witted remark:
Now I have been given the answer why, after circling the bimah during the Hoshanot, one calls out aloud “That all the peoples of the earth may know that the Lord is God, there is none else”: for the verse “Et the Lord your God you shall fear” is expounded in the Talmud to mean that the “et” includes Torah scholars — that before a Torah scholar one must show respect and fear as before God. So then, whoever has no fear of a Torah scholar finds the word “et” superfluous, and he might even come to the conclusion that the “et” includes another god. Therefore, going round the bimah, where the rich ignoramuses display their disrespectful attitude to the Torah scholars, one calls out: “That all the peoples of the earth may know — know ye, all you ignoramuses — that the Lord is God, there is none else — that there is no more than one God.” It follows, then, that the “et” includes Torah scholars — therefore, respect for them!...

d) When one shakes..
A Jew came to the Kutno rabbi, Rabbi Yehoshuale, to ask for advice, since he wanted to emigrate from home; he wanted to go and seek his fortune, although he did not lack a livelihood at home either — he simply craved more fortune. Rabbi Yehoshuale said to him: See, at “Please, O Lord, save us” (hoshia na) one shakes the lulav. At “hoshia na” — when one is in need and requires help, one must wander and seek a livelihood, although the tribulations, the wandering, are not the best thing. But at “Please, O Lord, grant us success” (hatzlicha na) the cantor no longer shakes — when it is a matter of success, of extra fortune, it is not worth going through the hard and shaken life of a wanderer.

e) The commandment of the sukkah.
See how great a commandment the sukkah is: one enters into the commandment even with one's boots on..
For [?] Rabbi Levi Yitzhak of Berdichev.

f) “In return for love they persecute me.”
On Sukkot seventy bullocks were offered for the welfare and peace of the seventy nations. Only on the last day, Shemini Atzeret, was an offering made for the Jews. We cared first for others and only afterwards for ourselves — and yet how they hate us.
Midrash Tanhuma.

g) The temporary dwelling.
After the “ingathering”, after the harvest has been brought home, when the granaries fill up and a man becomes firmer and surer of himself, he is told: go into the temporary dwelling; do not think that there is anything secure and permanent — everything is relative [?], temporary, passing... Mikra Kodesh.
* * *
Sukkot is called “the first for the reckoning of sins”, because, entering the temporary dwelling and feeling the insecurity of life, its transience, one makes a reckoning — then a soul-searching awakens in a person. Toldot.

h) Ushpizin.
Inviting the ushpizin on Sukkot means that one must then share with the poor and invite in the hungry (ushpizin — guests). See Bnei Yissaschar.
* * *
“These are the appointed seasons of the Lord which you shall proclaim.”
Only those are called “appointed seasons of the Lord” in which you call the poor to the table — “which you shall call”: when you call the hungry to eat with you... Noam Megadim.

i) An etrog and — a rabbi.
There was once a gaon, Rabbi Yaakov Kozlover [?], who on no account wanted to accept a rabbinical post. Various towns pleaded with him, but he would not listen. Once his wife began to persuade him to take the rabbinate of Brzeżany [?], which was being pressed on him; he said to her: Good, but first you must buy me, for the whole of Sukkot, an etrog, the choicest of the choice. And she indeed bought him a wonderfully beautiful etrog. Well, no doubt the whole town said the blessing over that etrog. On Hoshana Rabba he sent for his wife, showed her the etrog, which had become soiled from being used so much, and said to her:
“Just see how wonderfully beautiful this little etrog was before; but as soon as people took it into their hands, it became so soiled.”
“I too am now a respected, fine Jew; but if I become a rabbi and everyone will take hold of me and finger me — I shall look like this etrog does now”...
* * *
With an etrog (with a fine Jew) even a tiny blemish does harm... But, as is known, the blemishes come from the leaves growing next to it; so too the faults found in Torah scholars come from the “stabs” of Satan of those around them... R. Ch. Hirschsohn.
The Question of School and Education — Then and Now (How Are Our Children Being Raised?)

[Education — opinion.] Education!
This very word, education, is said so offhandedly, yet in truth it has great significance. We do not give ourselves any account at all of the significance of education. We all forget, one and all, that the problem of education is very, very sensitive, very, very modest [sic], and one must know how to deal with this question, how to act around it, how to take it into consideration, in what manner to handle it.
If the question of education was once a matter of weighty importance, now, in our times, it is one of the most important things in our life. Now, in the age of world progress, when everything is making enormous, gigantic strides that one can hardly catch up with or even see with one's eyes, and that leave a mighty imprint on the question of education; in an age of an open world, when the coming generation can, like any adult, easily reach every phenomenon harmful to it — one ought, of course, to devote more attention to pedagogy, more awareness, more professionalism, we would say.
Of course, today's system of education cannot be compared with the education of the past; true, the question is studied more, one engages [?] with it more systematically and intensively — and yet it is not what it ought to be, what it could have been.
It is just as with medicine: in our times there are more doctors, people take more interest in life, people doctor themselves [?] more — and yet there are more sick people. Medicine does advance with giant strides, but what comes of it? The diseases overtake medicine, because they advance with bigger strides. Pedagogy finds itself in roughly the same situation. True, there is more interest in the psychology of the child; this sensitive matter is considered very precisely and from all sides — but what comes of it? In our progressive times the child has more chances to overtake these researches by a long way, and can thus slip off the straight path at lightning speed.
Incidentally, pedagogy is more studied than carried out in life, and it would have been healthier if it were exactly the opposite.
We send our children to the schools in order to educate them, and the pedagogues say that the parents should educate them. In the past it was the reverse: back then, when the teacher or the rebbe did not know at all [?] how to deal with children, the whole burden was laid on them, and if the child did not grow up fit for God and for people, the educator was to blame. Moreover, one must not forget that in the past parents could [?] also devote themselves more to the children's upbringing, for two reasons: first, they knew that the educators were not competent and that they could not hand their children over entirely to the teachers' responsibility; and second, the times too were different: life was quieter and in altogether different circumstances, every little thing was calculated to the minute and second, every day and every year were as alike as two drops of water, no changes, no surprises occurred over the course of years. Our parents lived quietly and modestly like their parents, and the grandfathers like their grandfathers; so monotonous and uniform was their whole life, and that was the reason they had every opportunity to take a calm interest in their children's fate and to raise them as they had dreamed, as they had hoped and as they had wished.
We find ourselves in quite different conditions in the present period. Which of the parents has the possibility of taking upon himself the whole responsibility for education? Who can undertake to follow every glance, step and movement of his child? And therefore it was necessary that educational homes for children be set up, with which the pedagogues would concern themselves; but the latter do it to discharge a duty [?], in a routine, stereotyped way, and if the children do not submit to the prescribed discipline, the parents are told to educate their children themselves.
Nowadays parents have more understanding and sense of obligation for their children's education, but they are not in a position to educate them because of the circumstances in which they find themselves.
For we live today in such conditions that even with the best will the parents cannot occupy themselves intensively with the course of their children's education; citizens today are too agitated and too distracted to be able at the same time to afford being the educators of their children. Moreover, one must not forget that today, when everything is open and free to everyone, it is not easy to carry out the education of children.
And yet it must not be forgotten that we may not abandon children's education like this, for if we look with open eyes we will be able to establish that no movement whatever can be satisfied with children's education, beginning with the public [powszechne] schools and ending with the Yesodei ha-Torah chadarim: everywhere panic [?] and lawless self-rule reign, the lessons are not held as they should be, no one wants to submit to a definite regime, despotic rule exists on every front, nothing and no one is taken into account; let only, for instance, the money question [tuition] not be settled to the minute, and the children are immediately sent home without mercy.
And formerly, whenever the bein ha-zmanim [the break between terms] came, the simple parents of those days had one thing on their minds: what do we do with the children? How do we see to it that they are brought up as human beings and as Jews? No trifle was the bein ha-zmanim of old, as long as the children's fate had not been decided. All that time a father could do no business; everything centred on the decision about education — and that was at a time when there was still so little understanding of children's education.
Now, when one lives in other times, in a period of democracy and progress, when there are so many schools, chadarim and educators, everything is abandoned and demoralisation is gaining the upper hand. This can be stated quite boldly, with a light conscience and openheartedly.
And therefore, however hard our living conditions may be, in whatever critical situation we may find ourselves, we must once and for all take the fate of our children's education into our own hands. We may no longer leave this painful question abandoned, as it unfortunately is today.
Dr. Papuri [?].
Our Duty Toward the Young Generation

[Będzin — education; state schools.] In issue no. 38 of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" we read the encouraging news that the decree of "Shabbat sheni shel galuyot" for the schoolchildren ("tinokot shel beit rabban"), which had been introduced in the "powszechne" schools [state elementary schools] in Sosnowiec and was to be introduced any day in Będzin too, has been revoked. It must be stressed that great credit in this matter belongs to the "Zaglembier Tsaytung", which for weeks on end stirred up Jewish public opinion and energetically called on the decisive factors to apply suitable means to avert this harmful phenomenon. And Jewish public opinion, which gave its courageous expression in the columns of our paper, won a victory, and the new danger that threatened our children has been removed.
We would, however, commit a crime if we let Jewish society rest on its laurels after this victory. Incessantly we must awaken the attention of our parents, cultural workers and kehilla administrations to the danger of assimilation that threatens us in the very near future, when on the broad arena of public life there will appear the young [?] men and women who received their upbringing and education exclusively in the "powszechne" schools, which by their whole programme and essence are adapted e n t i r e l y to the spirit and needs of the Polish people.
The task of our national representation will be to win for our children by struggle a school that will, as far as possible, meet our demands, o u r needs.
That, however, is music of the future. Meanwhile great care must be taken that the generation already being brought up now in the "powszechne" schools should not, God forbid, be estranged from Jewishness, and should be bound to the Jewish people by strong spiritual threads.
As is known to us, the Zionist Organisation in Będzin intends [printed "bre'a"] to do something substantial in this field by opening an afternoon school devoted specially to Jewish studies, so that the pupils of the "powszechne" schools can receive there a proper Jewish education according to a broad programme.
The initiators of the new institution are to be wished the greatest success. The establishment of the new, highly useful and necessary institution and its development will, however, be possible only through proper moral and material support from parents, cultural workers and the representative Jewish personalities. That this sympathy and support will not be lacking — of that there can be no doubt.
Azbsh"n.
We Count

[Feuilleton — New Year; reflections.] Ch. Lazarson.
Counted off and turned over one more leaf. A new year — five thousand six hundred and ninety-one — has arrived.
There was a year that was counted 5690 — turned over, and it is no more.
These are all things everyone knows; one always says the same thing.
As you wish — so you may look at it.
Is it really the same thing?
Did it mean exactly the same thing to every single person when he thought or said so a year, two, five or ten years ago?
No, gentlemen, it is not so; it is a little different. People perhaps lose the keen sense to feel a thing when they use it many times. One counts constantly, and the counting no longer has the power to make the strong impression — but not all counting is alike.
There is a philosophy of the sort which, if you wish, can be told to you. When a man begins to understand how to count, he mostly no longer has any joy from counting. Every [printed "ye-das", apparently for "yedes"] turned-over leaf is a sealed chapter which one cannot catch back — and one would often like to catch it back.
We see so seldom, or never, children dealing with calendars in order to count the days and the years. It would seem, on the contrary, that they ought to be the real counters — the whole world is still before them, the whole future still lies ahead, as they say. And there is plenty for them to count and count. But it is not so. When they are very little they are rocked [?] until midday. And they have no understanding [?] at all of why they do it; and when they grow bigger they run around like wild merry foals [?], and it does not concern them whether today is yesterday or tomorrow is today, a year up, a year down — what difference does it make to them [?]. Children are not good counters; that is why one does not entrust them with money;
When a man begins to count, he is mostly already older and more serious. He begins to ponder where he stands in the world, and he begins to reckon, to count and to turn the leaves. And when he has come that far, his heart grows sad. The time when one could count and look fondly [?] at the distant open future — that time is gone and will not come back, even if it were promised the greatest happiness. And the time still ahead looks even more serious and gloomy; it grows autumnal [?] in the heart; the leaves of the calendar, just like the yellow withered leaves of the trees, have fallen and been trampled, destroyed and — gone.
For what is man's counting?
He counts time, you say. How can one count time? Does it have a measure or a number? Does it move, or does it stand still? It is very doubtful [lit. "forbidden"] whether any of us simple little people can give any answer to that; we do not know what time is, and we do not know how one should weigh or measure it. In the great infinity by which we are surrounded there is perhaps no such thing as time at all, and if there is — it is not known. This year is like a year ago, ten, a hundred and a thousand years ago. What is the difference? Infinity does not look at it the way the mortal tiny little man does, who — here he is, and soon — he himself does not know what he will look like or where he will come to a stop.
We weak and helpless ones have invented such a thing as a day, a week, a month, a year and so on. Short is our whole sojourn on the sinful earth; this shortness we have divided into smaller and larger parts, and we play and pay attention to the leaves and tear them off. One tears and tears until the whole calendar has been torn out.
For about half of the time one cannot and does not want to; for about half of the other half one does not like the hurrying [printed "dos aylen"; perhaps "dos tseyln" — the counting] — with every torn-off leaf there snaps, as they say, a string in the heart.
There have indeed been — perhaps they are still here today — people who strove to count on into eternity. It all depends on how one looks at the thing. If one wishes, one has before one no more than this present minute: what came before is gone and what comes later is not yet here. And if one wishes, one has before one thousands of years back and thousands of years ahead. It has no measure and no limit at all. One looks around on both sides and lives in all the past and coming years; the torn-off leaf does not wither, and the new one shines forth with rays of light and sunshine — it is good and warm.
We have heard it said that such people existed, perhaps they are still here — and without such people it would be sad, very sad in the world.
And for such people the world is a precious thing; they make on it a delightful pleasure trip and enjoy their travelling or strolling. They have divided the course of life into certain parts; at each part there is a station, and there one stops and the tickets are checked. The leaf for the stretch already travelled is torn off, and the leaf for the onward journey is stamped as valid. And so they travel merrily and gaily to the end of the journey; but the roads are always full of travellers. At one shore many are already nearly finished, and at the other shore people are only just beginning to walk and stroll. And an endless, unbroken chain thus stretches from eternity to eternity.
And we, the counters — all we have done is tear off the leaves of the ticket for what has been travelled and hand over for stamping the leaf for the onward way. Let us hope it has been well stamped.
And may 5691 [Tav-Resh-Tsadi-Alef] be a good, happy year.
A Sad Tally

[Kehillot — opinion; Będzin.] When modern Jewish kehillot founded on democratic principles were introduced in Poland, we Jews regarded this as the beginning of a new era and as a surrogate for national cultural autonomy, and we hoped that in time we ourselves would become the masters of our inner Jewish little world, and that the kehilla, as the representative institution of the Jewish population, would take care of, nurture and educate Jewish society towards new social and communal forms; that it would first of all reform the old, mouldy order, cleanse and make healthy the desolate atmosphere of Jewish kehilla life, then take under its wings the various existing Jewish institutions, and also strive to create new social, cultural and educational institutions — above all the last: to support and create educational institutions in which the coming generation would be raised as free, proud and national Jews. And a reason to believe that our supposition was correct was given to us by the fact that the central government created a special Jewish department at the Ministry of Education, with a Jewish head at the top, whose task was to deal with the Jewish affairs of the kehillot. This was without doubt a significant achievement and a giant step forward towards our goal — that we ourselves, and not a stranger as before, should administer our institutions; a stranger who does not know, does not feel and does not understand our interests. And although the head was not elected by the Jewish population but appointed, and moreover was not at all a man ideologically suited to the concepts of modern Jewish national life — on the contrary, practice showed us that he was more inclined to fulfil the demands of the clerical part of Jewry — one must nevertheless admit that, on the whole, he was loyal to Jewish cultural demands. And his activity over a number of years — when we consider the kehilla budgets in general and that of Będzin in particular — fully confirms the opinions we have expressed.
Unfortunately, however, our kehilla leaders have not grown up to their great and fine task and do not fulfil their duties with a proper sense of responsibility and with reverence, but regard the kehilla seat as a private little shop, where everyone can arrange himself as he pleases, and everything is run according to the system of "guard mine and I'll guard yours" — which is best confirmed by the swollen, clumsy kehilla budgets, in which we see that no care is taken of the public interest, but everyone looks after the interests of his own clique, and a bitter party struggle is waged along the whole front, and the end justifies the means. And so a certain Jewish party — or let us call the child by its proper name: the "Agudah" [Agudat Israel], which wants to uproot everything that smells of life and hope and wants by every means to fight and extinguish every ray of light and revival, thinking it could thus more easily[?] dominate the Jewish street and gain hegemony over the Jewish masses — also aimed its arrows at the Jewish referent, who did not fully identify with their opinion and position.
The Jewish referent was simply a stumbling block for them, knowing as they did that a Jew who knows Jewish life cannot allow the common interests to be bartered away for the ambitions of a certain clique; and that is why they fought and intrigued against the referent for so long, until the "victory": the Jewish referent capitulated and submitted his resignation, and his place is now taken by — of all people — a Christian; and this Christian must now be the final arbiter and the deciding factor in Jewish affairs. And we are already enjoying[?] the first fruits of what they planted, as we see from the approved budget that has just come back, which presents a sad picture to us.
But about this in a second article.
Y. Wygodzki.
The Festive Academy for Labour Palestine in Sosnowiec

[Sosnowiec — Zionism; Poale Zion.] On the 27th of last month, on the initiative of the Right "Poale Zion" in Sosnowiec, a festive academy was held in connection with the opening of the World Congress for Labour Palestine in Berlin.
Before a packed hall ("Hotel Polski") Mr. Y. Piekarski opens the academy with a short speech. He then gives the floor to Messrs. Asher Kleinberg and Leybl Kokotek (Będzin), who point to the importance of the first world workers' congress for Labour Palestine. In a long, inspiring speech the last speaker, Mr. Gancwajch (Abramek), then presents the history and development of the "Poale Zion" movement, the founding of the P.A.S.[?] and all the achievements of Labour Palestine up to the great historic moment of the convening by the Palestinian "Histadrut" of the first congress, in which representatives of the Jewish working class of the whole world are represented. The speaker settles accounts on this occasion with all the other workers' parties in the Jewish street and their attitude to Labour Palestine, and ends with the call that at today's congress in Berlin the strong word of proletarian Zionism must be heard loud and bold, and that instead of "It is good to die" a new slogan and song must be inscribed on our banner: "It is good to live for the homeland!" (Long applause.)
After it is resolved to send a telegram of greetings to the congress, the first official part of the academy is concluded.
In the second part, conducted by Mr. Berman, several workers' songs were performed (by the "Frayhayt" choir) and recitations by the Misses Tabakowska (Będzin) and Jakubowicz.
In an elevated mood and to the sounds of the "Poale Zion" "Oath" the academy is closed.

District Conference of the Zionist Revisionists of the Kielce Voivodeship in Sosnowiec
[Sosnowiec — Zionism; Revisionists.] From the Central Committee of the Revisionists we have received the following communiqué for publication:
To all branches of the Brit ha-Tzohar in the Kielce Voivodeship.
The last world conference of the Zionist Revisionists in Prague[?] has once again clearly demonstrated the strength that Revisionism represents[?], its steady growth and its growing influence.
In order to make proper use of this influence for the benefit of Zionism, the Central Board is proceeding to wide-ranging organisational work in Poland.
Among other things, the Central Board has resolved to hold a series of district conferences with the aim of organising the districts, carrying out a broad recruitment campaign and creating close contact for cooperation among all Revisionist groups in each district.
In this connection the Central Board, after a corresponding agreement with the majority of branches in the Kielce Voivodeship, has resolved to convene the first Kielce district conference of the Zionist Revisionists for Sunday, 12 October this year (the 4th day of Chol ha-Moed), in Sosnowiec.
Comrades! The moment is serious; questions of first-class importance stand on the agenda; in every Revisionist heart a series of problems and questions have accumulated that demand an answer.

W. P. Joseph Klarman
