The Visit to Heaven

[Feuilleton — a Hoshana Rabba fantasy.] By J. Weinsztajn.
(A fantasy)

A few days before Hoshana Rabba I packed my things, took an aeroplane and set off flying to heaven.
I flew all by myself, and on purpose [?], because I wanted everything I would see to remain a secret... But, as if to spite me, everyone found out about my heavenly visit...
How people found out, you will see later.
When I reached the border between heaven and earth, an angel stopped me:
— Where to?
— To heaven...
— Your documents?
I stood there, confused. Do you really need documents in heaven too?
I began to stammer: I... forgot them down below... I didn't know you needed them here...
— What are you carrying with you? the angel went on asking me...
— What would I carry? A pencil, a little notebook to write in and... a bit of a head.. nothing more...
— And you're not carrying any goods [?] with you?
— No, I haven't come here at all as a permanent resident... It's only a short visit... So why should I drag unnecessary baggage along?
— Your profession?
— I am a.. a... journalist...
The angel wrinkled his nose... I saw that I had failed and wanted to put the matter right.
— That is to say, Mr. Angel, I am no journalist, because I often write the truth, I am not dying of hunger, I pay my rent — so you can't count me as a real journalist...
— Well, all right.. I'll let you through, but on condition that you see, hear and keep silent...
— Yes, that I can do very well!..
The angel gave a flap of his right wing and at once there sprang up before me a second angel with very beautiful silver wings and clever eyes, just — lehavdil — like those of a wise man.
— Colleague, you must take this guest from down below to the Heavenly Court. He is a journalist and wants to be here for the announcing of the kvitlekh [notes of judgement] that are called out until Hoshana Rabba. Meanwhile show him our facilities.
All at once we were at the Garden of Eden.
I went in, and I became terribly bored. Not a living soul to be seen. A colossal garden, thousands of kilometres long, and a few hundred people wandering about in it.
I look for someone I know, one of our own — nobody.
— Not interesting, I say to the angel who was escorting me. Better take me to Gehinnom.
No sooner had I entered Gehinnom than I immediately felt better. At every step — an acquaintance, a "good brother".
And the crowd there has already settled in with comforts. However much you suffer of Gehinnom, you suffer; but after the 8 hours (there too an 8-hour working day has been introduced) it's a real paradise. People carouse, dance, sing songs, "hold songs" [sic], make speeches (there is no censorship there, because all censors are, after all, honest people and they don't end up in Gehinnom) and have a merry time.
Suddenly I heard a terrible shriek.
— What has happened? — I asked my angel, frightened.
— It's nothing. That's the old bachelors who have crowded together.. We have special departments for all sorts of categories of people, and among them there is also a category of old bachelors.
— What are they shouting about?
— They want to get into the Garden of Eden before their time, but they aren't allowed, and in protest they shout, squeal, cry "gevalt"...
— What's so bad for them here, then?
— They think that in the Garden of Eden they will find themselves beautiful brides...
We went on through the compartments of Gehinnom. I saw thousands of little rooms. It's quite impossible to describe them all, but still I will describe some of them to you.
In one little room I found a fat personage sitting with a pince-nez and a fine tailcoat. In his mouth he held a fine Havana cigar and was smoking.. But I saw no fingers on him at all.. only arms, hands, without fingers...
— What is this? I asked my angel for an explanation.
— This is a famous public figure; in all societies and organisations he was chairman or vice-chairman.. He was considered one of the most honest communal workers, but here, of course, everything is known, well, well..
— What do you mean — well?
— They merely chopped off his fingers, with which in the lower world he "took" public money... And now every day they take him here to meetings, he makes the finest speeches, gets heated, and when he reaches the height of his ecstasy, an angel suddenly runs up and raises his hands without fingers — and he falls silent...
— And who is the woman with the little mirror in one hand and the box of paint in the other?
— She used always to paint her face, the hair on her head, her lips... So she was punished: she has to go around here with her make-up kit [?] and be painted at the hands of Gehinnom...
— She has remained [?] such an old thing?
— No, down there she was a young thing; she painted and smeared [?] herself so much that one could think she was a young girl.
— And who is hiding over there in room number 15800?
— That is a rabbi.
— Are there rabbis here too?
— Of course! They don't want to leave this place at all.. However often they have been offered to move over to the Garden of Eden, they have no desire to.. They say that here they feel better... Here they can provide the world with the World to Come, but in the Garden of Eden whom would they provide for? So they sit here and cool off..
— But there's nothing so terrible here as people think — I said to the angel.
— It's like this only now, because you have come to visit us.. But if you had not come as a guest, we would have opened your eyes and you would then have seen something quite different...
Suddenly my angel vanished, and beside me I saw... my wife..
She stood there smiling..
— You were talking something in your sleep all the time about angels — what were you dreaming?
— I dreamt that I was in Gehinnom, and in the end I was even..
— With me, my dear.
— Yes, hm... with you, that is, yes, with you..
———
And because she was standing beside me, everyone found out about this story.

Oy, the Passport!

[Humorous feuilleton — Yom Kippur.] By Y. Oberżanek [?].
The tragedy of a "kest" son-in-law [a young husband boarding at his father-in-law's table] who this Yom Kippur fell victim to Satan, may his name be blotted out.

Perhaps you know what passports are needed for? For what earthly purpose must a person have a passport? Is it a law given at Sinai that a person must always carry around such a silly little booklet, which only embitters his life and at every opportunity reminds you how old you are, that you are getting closer to the "rogatka" [the toll-gate, i.e. the end]? And without the silly passport you wouldn't have known it? I ask you, Jews, what does one need a passport for?
For the female "sex" the passport is simply a disaster. Why carry an informer around with you? If a woman wants (and which woman doesn't?..) to shave off some ten years, the passport sticks in her throat like a bone...
How do you like this passport-calamity? You go to register — a passport; you go to take out marriage records — a passport; you go to report a child — a passport; you walk crooked in the street — always passport and passport. What more do you need: when you are already "stop!" [finished, dead] and you want to pack yourself off to the next world — you need a passport again. Passport and passport, passport in front and passport behind. I ask you, what does one need a passport for at all, what for!
Since when have I become such a sworn enemy of passports? Why am I so embittered against the passport system? Why shouldn't I be embittered — it's because of that passport of mine that I've become unhappy, because of my passport I have now lost my fat father-in-law, and what else? Because of the passport I am getting a divorce from my wife. Listen to the story:
As you know, I board "on kest" at my father-in-law's. My father-in-law bought himself a toy for the house, bought himself pedigree — a trifle: such an antique, such a ben-Torah; so I was indeed the table-ornament, the one who gave opinions, the little jewel of the house.
Now, my wife — she guarded me like the apple of her eye, she stuffed me and crammed me [?] like a fattening-goose, I became fatter than I was tall, I never put a hand into cold water, I ate and drank and lived like God in Odessa, I had no worries about a livelihood. Why should I worry — the father-in-law has a big head, let him worry! He wanted a toy son-in-law — let him sweat...
But as you say: even capons [?] become tiresome, and I too got fed up with my wife's pampering [?]. How long, really, can one stand like a fattening-goose in a cage? Why not take a look at what goes on in God's little world — enough of being a doll for my wife.
When I came out onto Główna [Main] Street, a world opened up before me. I saw that besides kest there are other pleasures in the world. I saw that besides the World to Come there is also a This World, and above all: I saw that besides my wife there are other women in the world, and decent ones at that, plump as olive oil, not such lemon-faced ones as my Jewess, women with life, with fire. A world, a new world, a beautiful, a free world was revealed to me.
In short, I decided to become "progressive". Little by little, little by little my kapote [jupica, long coat] grew shorter and my trousers longer, the little beard caught consumption, the sidelocks began to shrink, the soft collar became stiffer and stiffer, I wore my hat "na szpic" [at a tilt] — on the tip of my head, that is; I began washing with scented soap. On weekdays I swapped Nisan Silberberg's mikveh for the Central Baths in Katowice; from time to time I sneaked into a cinema to Leml Jannes [?; apparently Emil Jannings], Reb Liedtke [Harry Liedtke], Shepsl Chaplin [Charlie Chaplin]; I watched Mia May and "Paltsht Negliš" [?; perhaps Pola Negri] ride across the white screen. I became a frequent visitor at the Katowice opera, I began reading "Haintige Nayes", I didn't miss a single fat joke — I licked my lips as at my wife's fat cholent... I swallowed novels like brown cholent potatoes; I didn't miss a single football match. When it comes to being progressive — there's nothing more to say.
All this, of course, was in the street; in the street I was a complete "facet" [a regular guy], but at home, at the father-in-law's, I was still the same little kest-son-in-law, the same table-ornament; to my wife I was still the fattening-goose.
But as the saying goes: "The jug goes to the water so long until its handle breaks off" — and this Yom Kippur it really did break off with me; yes, you hear, it broke off with me: I came a cropper, an ugly cropper — gone the father-in-law, gone the wife, gone the fattening-goose, gone the kest; I'm about to divorce my wife, and all this because of my wife [sic].
It happened like this:
This Yom Kippur, as every year, I stood in the synagogue together with my father-in-law, beating my breast at "Al Chet" one after the other. My navel was knocking and my stomach was pulling, so that sparks flew before my eyes. Satan wasn't sleeping either, he kept buzzing [?] into my ear:
Fool that you are, you're some kind of progressive after all, why should you torture your body? You're beating your heart for "Al Chet" anyway; since you're already beating, give it one more blow. Listen to me, Satan wouldn't let go of me, laugh off those "zabobony" [superstitious] tales and go grab a bite somewhere.
At first I didn't want to listen to Satan. Feh, to go eating on the holy day — how does that look? But later I thought it over: perhaps he, Satan, is really right; after all I'm some kind of "progressive", after all I'm thick as thieves with Mia May and "Paltshe Negliuš" [?], after all I already wear a short kapote with long trousers — why should I torture myself, why? Fasting is a business for my father-in-law and my wife with her lemon face.
No sooner said than done. Between Musaf and Mincha I slipped out into the street and into the "Zacisze" [a restaurant] by a back door. I was sure that here I'd be the only Jew, for who would think of such an apostate's trick — on Yom Kippur after Musaf to pop down here for lunch?
So I thought, but it turned out quite differently: besides me there were more such "progressives" as I, they too had slipped out after Musaf to rub their teeth.
Never mind, I think to myself, it's lost anyway. So, as befits a progressive, I began knocking my knife on my plate, and it didn't [?] take long before I was working on a "wieprzowe" [pork dish] with all my molars. I ate, and before my eyes appeared my father-in-law in his kittel with the tallis over his head. While gnawing the bones of the "squealer" [the pig] I saw my wife in her lace blouse, standing in the women's gallery sniffing at her little bottle of "Herzstark" [heart drops]... I licked the plate clean and heard the cantor's oy... oy... oy... oy...
Having eaten [?], I went back to the synagogue. I took my place again, as if nothing had happened.
Coming home at nightfall, my wife pitied me: just look, Zeligl, what a face you have, what a serious [?] faster you are, why, you're dead as all the dead.
Yes, I sighed, I can't fast. You know what? I said to my wife, before the meal give me a clean glass of tea to rinse out my innards.
Yes, yes, the father-in-law added, he's a delicate young man, give him something to drink on an empty stomach.
In my heart I thought: if you only knew that there's a "squealer" in my innards!
Everything really would have gone off fine, if not for the passport. You may well hear what a bitter end I came to, and how the "squealer" fell out on me head-first:
Next day I come home from the street. In the house it's dark. The father-in-law runs about the house wailing like the best of prayer-leaders. My wife lies on the sofa with a bandaged head, groaning, and as soon as I step over the threshold the father-in-law falls on me with his fists and wants to trample me:
Out of my house, you sheygets! Get [?] out of my house this minute, you sinner, you eater of treyf! I barely got out of the house alive. Sparks flew before my eyes, I couldn't understand how they knew it, who had told them the story?
Why make a long story of it — you want to know how they found out — because of my passport: when, in the restaurant, I took out my wallet to pay for lunch, I at the same moment forgot my passport on the table.
The goy from the restaurant, apparently a great fool, asked no questions and sent the passport by post to my father-in-law's home. That too wouldn't have been a great misfortune, but the goy added a friendly little letter, in which he describes how, when and on which day I forgot the passport, and that he is doing me a favour and sending me back the passport.
And so I became unhappy. I lost my fat father-in-law along with my kosher little wife, and all because of a passport.
I ask you, tell me, gentlemen, for what earthly purpose does one need passports?!..
The Tragic Sukkot in Łęczyca — A Page of History

[History — Łęczyca.] By Moshe Feinkind.
It happened in the year 1656.
Poland then stood between two fires. In the south-east Chmielnicki, with his murderous bands, with the Tatars and Ukrainians, attacked and laid Poland waste (1648—56), and from the north-west, in turn, the Swedes together with the Brandenburgers, led by Charles Gustav the Tenth and by the former Polish vice-chancellor Hieronim "Badziejowski" [sic; read Radziejowski], burst into Poland and devastated and ruined the country no less than those bands: they burned and roasted, robbed and destroyed, murdered and slaughtered the Polish as well as the Jewish population. At that time the so-called Confederation of Tyszowce was formed in Poland, at whose head stood the persecutor Stefan Czarniecki, the starosta of Piotrków, and within a short time he succeeded in freeing Poland from the Swedes and driving them out of the country.
But wherever he and his "confederates" set foot, the first victims were the Jews; he completed against the Jews what the despoiler [?] Chmielnicki had not managed to do in the towns and townlets. Accusing the Jews of supposed treason, the mob together with the "confederates" slaughtered entire Jewish communities, burned and plundered the Jews' goods and property, etc.
Among the great number of Jewish towns in Poland that were destroyed at that time was also Łęczyca, the so-called "mother-city in Israel."
On the eve of Yom Kippur the siege of the town by King Jan Kazimierz (died 1668) began. The Jews were gathered for "Kol Nidrei" in the newly built synagogue; outside the cannons thundered. The fire-blazing shells flew through the streets, and their whistling and howling accompanied the loud weeping of the worshippers. In the synagogue it suddenly became completely dark, all the candles went out [printed: "were abandoned"] at once, the roar and thunder of the cannons stopped; in the darkness of the night the Swedes abandoned the town, and Jan Kazimierz entered Łęczyca with his unruly and starving soldiers. They turned first to the Jews, robbed and destroyed whatever they could, and on the second day of Sukkot they set about butchering all the local Jewish inhabitants like sheep in an open field.
Three thousand Jews then perished by the Polish sword; the canals around Łęczyca were full of their blood.
The small Jewish children who by a miracle or by chance remained alive were then dragged by force into the churches, baptised there and handed over to the peasants as shepherds.
Almost all of Łęczyca went up in smoke; the new synagogue was burned together with six hundred Torah scrolls, and no trace and no survivor or remnant of the local Jews was left.
A Polish chronicler relates that the heart-rending cry of the murdered Jews in Łęczyca was so great that the Swedes, who were still barricaded in the old castle — whose ruin remains to this day — hearing the lamentation, decided to surrender to the Poles; but the same fate befell them as those wretched Jews. Jan Kazimierz himself actually wanted to spare the Jewish population of Łęczyca; he did not want to soil his royal hands with Jewish blood, but he was too weak to stand up to the rebellious soldiery, which was incited and inflamed by the local Christian population.
Having regained control of Poland and only then realising where this anarchy in the country was leading, the King issued at Częstochowa on 20 June [czerwiec] 1657 a "universal" [royal proclamation], by which he pardoned all Jews their supposed guilt and freed them from the accusation that they had stood on the side of the Swedes during the war with Poland, and also threatened everyone with severe punishment for murder and robbery. Only then did the population calm down, and they stopped robbing and murdering the Jews.
The Jews of Łęczyca also then received from Jan Kazimierz the privilege to go on living there and to rebuild the synagogue, which was not permitted to be bigger or higher than the previous synagogue.
From then on, to this day, on the first day of Hol ha-Moed Sukkot a memorial service is held in the great town synagogue in memory of the martyrs "who were killed, slaughtered and burned in fire." From a pinkas [communal record book] of the time of the Swedish war, an account of those tragic events of the year 5416 (1656) is read out, and a great number of names of those who perished for the sanctification of the Name — rabbis, communal leaders and the like — are mentioned, and the Hevra Kadisha holds a kiddush with honey cake and brandy.
There was also a large marble tablet with a Hebrew inscription, set into the town wall opposite the synagogue, on which the Jewish tragedy of Łęczyca in the critical year 1656, "in the days of the war of the Swedes", was inscribed. When the walls that once encircled the town were taken down in 1830—1834, this tablet was removed and was lost.
The only relic of that sorrowful time left in Łęczyca is the tall dark tower by the magistrate's building [town hall], built by Kazimierz the Second [sic], where the Jews used to be tortured and tormented with all kinds of cruel torments, unto death. The writer of these lines was held in this tower for some time in 1883, because of a parcel of foreign books that was found on him and that had not been passed by the censor.
From that time also comes the custom of the Tiefenbach family of Łęczyca of lighting in the synagogue during the Days of Awe, in memory of the holy souls of those martyrs who perished in that war, a large wax candle. [—] The candle weighs 18 times 18 lot. In the year 5660 [1899/1900] the Tiefenbach family did not light such a candle, and it is said that because of this a great misfortune and God's wrath came upon the town again: at Kol Nidrei someone shouted in the synagogue "Fire!", and because of that 33 women perished that night.
Since then that family has lit the wax memorial candle of 18 times 18 every year without fail. It burns all of Rosh Hashana, Yom Kippur and all of Sukkot in the synagogue.
Two Sukkahs.

[Feuilleton — a Hasidic tale for Sukkot.] By B. Tapuach.

It was the eve of Sukkot, already past midday. And the old man's (of blessed memory) sukkah was already ready for the holiday: the walls — hung with white tablecloths, with "shehecheyanu" fruits; the table — set, and the crowd was milling about the courtyard. Each was lost in his own thoughts. And suddenly the old man, of blessed memory, comes out, and one sees at once that something is not right: grief is on his face, his brow — deeply furrowed, and with it — a hidden fear.

The crowd gathers around. He, of blessed memory, is silent, and everyone is silent. He stands like that and looks somewhere far away; then he looks at the sky, over which dark clouds are tearing [?] in, climbing [?] up from the west and swallowing the sun. A little wind starts to blow, grows stronger and stronger, and all at once: he, of blessed memory, lets out a groan and commands:

— Jews! Make ready a sukkah!

They stand for a while and do not understand: the sukkah is standing ready, isn't it? But ask they do not ask: some dread seizes their hearts, and no one dares to ask.

And the old man, of blessed memory, is already growing angry:

— Fools! What are you standing there for? It's already past midday. Quickly, take boards and put up a sukkah! Move!

A commotion breaks out in the courtyard: people run, get tangled up, hurry; Jews carry boards together, young men nail them together — and not an hour passes before a new sukkah already stands at the other end of the courtyard, far from the spot where the earlier sukkah is.

The old man, of blessed memory, smiles:

— Let that sukkah stay as decorated as it is. In here — put a table, a couple of benches, just for tonight...

And he, of blessed memory, goes back into his private room to change for the holiday.

The crowd is greatly astonished. What can it mean? But what good does wondering do? They truly do not understand. Meanwhile — and an honoured guest arrives: in the courtyard appears Reb Eliyahu Mesever. Who was Reb Eliyahu Mesever? — Reb Eliyahu Mesever was a God-fearing man through and through, a great Hasid, a "silken" Jew, and one of the closest intimates of the old man, of blessed memory.

He had now arrived from the road. Having come on foot, he was very dusty: his boots white with sand, his clothes covered in dust [?], and sweat dripping [?] from his brow. On the way he had hurried greatly so as to arrive here for the holiday.

There is joy over him, great rejoicing. They stand around him, help him take the bundle off his shoulder. Reb Eliyahu hurries, washes up, catches his breath — he still wants to manage to greet [the Rebbe].

But just then the door of the old man's room swings open, and he, of blessed memory, steps over the threshold into the beit midrash. But instead of a greeting all one hears is:

— You shaygets, you! You sinner in Israel! What do you think you are doing? Eh?

Reb Eliyahu, white as chalk, listens, and his legs begin to tremble:

— I... a sinner?..

Tears choke his throat.

But he, of blessed memory, entirely without mercy:

— A sinner you are! A transgressor you have become!

The crowd stands aghast, and the old man, of blessed memory, commands:

— Go [?], go into the sukkah! Wait for me there! Don't you dare come out of there until I tell you.

And with his hand he points to the new sukkah.

With bowed head, on stumbling knees, Reb Eliyahu went out of the beit midrash..

* * *

The story behind it was this:

Reb Eliyahu Mesever was bound to the old man, of blessed memory, heart and soul. He had a custom: to spend all the holidays, from Rosh Hashanah until after Sukkot, with the old man, of blessed memory, for he simply could not live without him. This year, however, Satan had troubled him: before Rosh Hashanah — a few days before the holiday — a son of his died. Is there any choice? Shiva! From all the great troubles his wife fell ill, and until Yom Kippur she was in great danger. So again he had to stay at home. He was therefore [?] in great sorrow; he could not be consoled for his son, because he was far from his source. He had no rest, because his soul was strongly drawn to its root.

After Yom Kippur his wife was out of danger, and he wanted at least to get there for Sukkot, as his heart drew him. He had no money for expenses, so he made himself a bundle of his tallit and tefillin and set out on the road on foot.

So he walked by day and by night. Through distant fields and dark forests he was not afraid; nothing could be a stumbling block for him, for he knew: the road is long, time does not stand still, and so he must hurry.

On the eve of the holiday, in the morning, he arrives in a village, no longer far from the town where the old man, of blessed memory, is. He goes in to a Jew, a leaseholder [arendar], to wash, rest [?], taste something and continue on his way. Now he was no longer in such a hurry. He washes, says his prayers, has a bite to eat.

The leaseholder, for his part, was overjoyed with him: none other than God Himself had sent him this guest. In the village they had prepared everything: an etrog, a lulav — but what of it? They are one Jew short of a minyan. Drive into town for another Jew? Which Jew would want to leave home before the holiday?

But Reb Eliyahu smiles:

— No. He cannot stay and will not stay. He must not stay.

But the leaseholder smiles:

— You will stay all the same.

The other Jews of the village gather. And all with one voice: they will not let him go. He must stay here. They do not want a spoiled holiday.

And someone else wanted it too: was hoping for it very much.

It was the soul of a tzaddik who had once stumbled in his lifetime: for some reason he had spent Sukkot in a village and had not prayed with a congregation.

And as is well known: with a tzaddik even a small sin [?] is great...

So the soul of that tzaddik wandered about this world, roaming among the villages. And since the soul suffered greatly from this and wept great weeping, the Heavenly Court considered the matter, and it was agreed: the soul must wait until one of the old man's (of blessed memory) disciples keeps Sukkot here in the village, prays with a minyan and leads the prayers before the ark — then the soul will pray along and attain its tikkun [repair].

And here begins a story with the Adversary: will he allow it? He indeed goes to Reb Eliyahu and argues with him thus:

"Fool! You've tormented yourself so long, walked on foot, and now, when you are already so near the place where he dwells — you'll stay here in the village, you fool?"

"Ah — Reb Eliyahu argues back — are the Jews then to be left without a minyan? Don't they deserve pity too?"

But the Adversary argues again:

"You need consolation. Such a misfortune has befallen you — an only son... And consolation is not far... 'He', may he live, will console you. Rosh Hashanah is gone, Yom Kippur is past, and you were kept far away — and now, because of these ignoramuses, these village folk, you will stay here? How can it be? All year long they make do without a minyan — so why do they need one precisely now? They won't bring down the Messiah anyway, and greeting one's Rebbe — is that a trifle?"

And his love for the Rebbe blinded his eyes, and — no! He will not stay.

No pleading helped; his mind was set: he cannot, by no means, and he will not stay.

Meanwhile it had become past midday. Driving to town and back was no longer possible — and besides, deep sands.

And when Reb Eliyahu left, the soul burst into bitter sobbing. With such a wail and with so much grief that the weeping reached up to the Throne of Glory.

And then a decree was decreed...

But the old man, of blessed memory, sensed it..

* * *

Meanwhile night had fallen, and the old man, of blessed memory, sits at the table in the new sukkah. The congregation stands around, pressed shoulder to shoulder, all are silent and all brows are furrowed; the holiness of the festival has descended, but the fear does not cease.

Reb Eliyahu sits in a corner, deeply downcast; he reflects on his deeds and contemplates repentance; his heart melts within him.

And outside the wind grew stronger. It tears at the sechach, the walls tremble, the candles go out, and all at once a mighty crash is heard and rain begins to pour down with force, with a storm.

And the old man, of blessed memory, is silent. He does not say the ushpizin, he does not make kiddush. He sits sunk in thought, and one can plainly sense that he is waiting for something. The rain pours, and all at once a terrible thunderclap rolled through the darkness. A ball of fire struck into the empty sukkah and whirled around there several times, as if looking for someone, and finding no one, the piece of fire went out and [struck] [?] somewhere into a tree, which split in two...

Then the old man, of blessed memory, smiled. His face began to shine, and he stood up and called out:

— Sholem aleichem, Reb Eliyahu Mesever!

And the old man, of blessed memory, said:

— Mazel tov to you, Jew [printed "Yisro'"]! You are saved! You know: when today, in the daytime, you let yourself be led astray by the evil inclination, grew stubborn and would not stay in the village, you prevented the tikkun of a soul... That is as if you had killed the soul; therefore death was decreed upon you. But I guarded you against it, and the Destroyer was left the fool. You, with your thought of repentance, brought it about that no one should betray my stratagem to the Destroyer. Now we will both see to repairing the soul...

— — — — — — — —

The rain stopped. The sky began to clear, they went back into the real sukkah, and the old man, of blessed memory, began with joy and fervour to say the ushpizin...
Napoleon and the Young Polish Countess Walewska

[Historical feuilleton — Napoleon; by M. Osherowitch.]
In his stormy life, which shook the pillars of the whole world and drew to itself the attention of generations, Napoleon the First showed that, besides being a good military commander who could give the world an example without equal in history, he was also a human being with feelings, weaknesses and sentiments, and that everything human was not alien to him.
The same Napoleon who, with so much boldness and indeed with so much chutzpah, could say that he "doesn't give a pinch of snuff for the lives of a million people" — that same Napoleon was not always the man of steel and iron, and at times he showed so much softness, so much tenderness and so much weakness that it is hard to imagine that this was really he and not someone else.
And Napoleon the Great showed these weaknesses mostly in love.
He was not only a great military commander but also a great lover. Although as a commander he showed far more heroism and strategy than in the field of love..
He, one of the cleverest men in the world, could be deceived by the most foolish woman. And this was perhaps because into most of his love affairs he put the same seriousness as into war on the battlefields, and completely forgot the rule that one cannot always rely on a woman's seriousness...
Napoleon the leader of wars and Napoleon the conductor of love affairs are like two separate people who have nothing whatsoever to do with each other. The only similarity on this point lay precisely in this: just as he always wanted peace and was nevertheless forced to wage wars, so he always wanted to be faithful to his wife and was nevertheless driven to carry on love affairs with others..
It was the unfaithfulness of his first wife Josephine that brought him to later become a "Don Juan" in his own fashion and to begin carrying on love affairs with others.
Before, until he found out that Josephine had deceived him so vilely and basely, he took no interest in any other women and never even looked at them.
Napoleon had many love affairs, but only a few of them were truly great and beautiful.
Remembering[?] the historical fact that many crowned rulers in Europe paid too dearly for letting themselves be too much influenced by their mistresses, Napoleon was very careful with the women with whom he fell in love. Politically he never let them near him; he never allowed any of his mistresses to meddle in affairs of state.
But although in this respect he guarded himself so strongly against women, it nevertheless turned out that he partly lost his crown and his power over a woman. This, however, was not a mistress but his own wife — the second — Marie Louise, the daughter of the Austrian Emperor Francis.
The most distinguished place in Napoleon's loves is held, without doubt, by the Polish countess Maria Walewska.
Like most great loves in life, Napoleon's love for Maria Walewska also ended sadly. But that love remained one of the most beautiful chapters in the story of Napoleon's life. And it is a fact that of all the women Napoleon was close to, the charming Polish countess remained the most faithful and the most devoted to him, and she showed him her faithfulness and devotion not only when he was great, not only when he held in his hands the fate of nations and countries, but also when he had already fallen, when he had already lost both the crown and the power, and the hope as well.
Napoleon became acquainted with Maria Walewska in Warsaw in the year 1807. In Poland the hope of regaining national independence was then stronger than ever, and the greatest patriots of the oppressed country looked upon Napoleon, the conqueror of the world, as their Messiah, who would free them from the foreign yoke.
The great Polish aristocrats were interested in having the great Emperor of France see that they were ready to do anything in the world so that he would feel as good and as pleasant as possible in their country: they paid him great honour and gave for him the most beautiful, richest and finest balls.
Napoleon for his part did not lag behind in this respect; he too gave magnificent balls for the Polish aristocracy, in order thereby to win the Poles to his side and to make use of their eagerness for battle, which could be useful for his further war plans.

A—h. Praised be He who is above us that the matter of the sukkah came easily to me; for in these times, in today's severe crisis, you surely know how bitter and hard it is for such a down-and-out [?] as me to bring the holiday into the house — and therefore, you see, it was not hard for me to put up a sukkah, and a real gem of a sukkah at that. I had no hard work: I took a few boards from the Sejm, may it rest in peace, and made the walls out of them. Instead of skhakh I took the last speeches of "Zayrn" [?] and covered the roof with them — it is according to the law, it is "its shade exceeds its sun", nothing but shade...
My neighbour tells me that before I went to put up my sukkah I should have had the boards approved by the building-safety commission; it may happen — he says — that right in the middle of Kiddush people with brass buttons will walk in and say "no", that my sukkah poses a danger to the neighbouring tenants...
It may be that my neighbour is one who "foresees what is coming", but it does not bother me; the main thing is that I have a kosher sukkah, in which I shall sing hymns and praises that I am not sitting in "Zayrn's sukkah" — in Brisk [Brześć], I mean..
— Let us enjoy ourselves, it is after all the Season of our Rejoicing...

[“Der Kokh-lefl” — humour; poem.]
How is it
that one who has a heart
and human
feelings
can, because of
his good heart,
gamble away
his only luck?
I carry on myself
a great burden
and daily
it grows heavier:
my white rooster
demands of me
ever more “answers” [teshuvos]
more and more.
I have already
spent a whole treasure of money
on him,
just so that he be
content
and live
his life freely.
Now my yard
is full of life,
of voices
and of noise.
And he,
my red-capped one,
plays the sultan
in the harem.
For every hen
he has a word,
for every rooster —
a “kaske” [a knock?].
The hens fall
for his word
like little mice
into a trap.
He knows the game
that is called love;
he knows it
well and thoroughly.
And when he gets angry,
then he deals a slap —
the fellow
is touchy.
His eyes become
filled with blood.
His wings
he spreads wide;
he opens
his beak [?]
and full of murder
he crows.
The hens fall
suddenly silent
like nuns
who pray,
and without
any resistance
let their [?] rooster
tread them.
Scandals
are not lacking,
nor is there any lack
of obedience.
More than once I hear
how he shouts:
“I need you
for kapores” [idiom: I couldn’t care less about you].
And shouting,
he flies off to his
hen-coops
and shows
his wives
two great
giant figs [the mocking gesture].
The other day I put
a question to him:
“Reb Rooster,
where is justice?
True, you
play the sultan.
Well, is that fitting
for an emperor?”
“Why, you undermine
morality,
the sanctity
of the family;
why, you trample
with your feet
a holy
idyll.”
“Idyll-shmidyll! —
the rooster
cut short [?]
my speech —
put on your cloak [?]
of morality
of your grandmother’s
or grandfather’s.
“We live
as nature dictates,
we obey
its drives.
I am a child
of that tribe
which believes
in free love.”

A Sukkot Lecture for Women

[“Der Kokh-lefl” — humour; Sukkot.] (By radio).
My dear ladies!
You know, of course, that the men have a saying: “When you become a mensch, you will sit in the sukkah.” And a woman, that means, is no mensch, because, after all, she does not sit in the sukkah.
But you need not eat your hearts out, my dear ladies! For as soon as it starts to rain, the men scatter out of the sukkahs and run back into the houses, back to their wives.
Always like that: as soon as there is trouble, the husband comes back to the wife.
Nor does he want to sit in the sukkah hungry; he wants someone to hand him something, to bring him something. And who is to do it? Why, this very wife from whom he supposedly runs away into the sukkah.
No, no, my dear ladies! You have nothing to fear from male grandeur with its male high-handedness!
The man is a big shot in his own eyes only as long as he has a wife at his side. Then he can puff himself up and act big and play the wise guy and laugh at the women. But when he has no wife, his lordliness is over, and there is no one to sew a button on for him and cook him a pot.
And when the man celebrates his high-handedness and his humanity in the sukkah, he is thinking of the pot the wife is cooking for him.
No, no, my dear ladies! Don’t think that because the men sit in the sukkah they are already human beings.
Not all who sit in the sukkah are human beings, and not all who do not sit in the sukkah are not human beings.
One can be a human being and not sit in the sukkah, and one can be a non-human and sit in the sukkah.
A man can make a sukkah, but a sukkah cannot make human beings.
When someone is no mensch, the sukkah will not make a mensch of him.
I tell you just once, my dear ladies, that you should not eat your hearts out because you do not sit in the sukkah.
True, from the suffragist standpoint this is an affront; how so — the woman has no right at all to be a sukkah-sitter!
A market-sitter she may well be, but a sukkah-sitter — no!
That’s just how it is: when the man is no mensch and the wife supports him, then when Sukkot comes he is a complete mensch and sits in the sukkah!
Not everything, my dear ladies, can be measured with the suffragist yardstick [arshin], and you should also not look at the festival of Sukkot from the suffragist standpoint.
A great worry of yours, that the men enjoy the festival of Sukkot: after all, they must come to your mercy [laske] in the end anyway.
Yes, you can grant them, the men, the pleasure of sitting in the sukkah by themselves, without the women.
No harm done; one may sometimes part for a while: the world will not come to an end because of it.
What then? Always only be together, looking one another in the eyes, or even treading on one another’s corns [“hen’s eyes”]?
And therefore I tell you, my dear ladies, that you should leave the sukkah to the men, as it has always been, and not strain yourselves precisely to sit in the sukkah.
One thing, however, I want to tell you: you must not become beaten-off hoshanos.
Let the men not think that as soon as they take you into their hands, you must at once become beaten-off hoshanos.
I have already seen women of whom nothing more than twigs was left — you should know that, if you don’t know it.
Yes, let the man sit alone in the sukkah and let him remember that Adam, the first man, was also alone for a certain time; God took pity on him and gave him a wife.
That’s how it is, my dear ladies, and therefore you should not worry at all! Bm… zhzhzh…

Wonders of technology.
In the local Jewish mechanical laundry named "Kryształ" a novelty has now been introduced which until this very day does not yet exist anywhere in all of Poland.
The novelty consists in the owners having brought from abroad machines that clean and wash all kinds of clothing entirely without water. Dozens of people, especially school youth, seeing this, are amazed at the wonders of modern technology.
The same firm "Kryształ" is opening branches in all the towns of Zagłębie.
What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: Voters Check the Electoral Rolls (and other news)

[Head of the local page; Będzin — short news.]
What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Monday, 14 / 14 Tishrei 5691 — Poniedziałek 6 października 1930 [Monday, 6 October 1930].)
Będzin
Voters check the electoral rolls.
Until the 10th of this month (inclusive) is the period in which every person entitled to vote should go to his electoral district and check whether he is entered in the lists of voters for the Sejm and the Senate.
Anyone who is not properly registered must submit a declaration.
—o—
Scandal among the synagogue worshippers.
A group of synagogue worshippers did not pay for their "seats" in the synagogue because of the prices, which were too high for them. For this the kehilla board took revenge and published [the names of] the "recalcitrant" in a prominent place in the synagogue.
But the kehilla representatives were still not satisfied with that, and ordered the shammes to announce on Shabbat Shuva, after the Torah reading, those who had not paid for the "seats".
When the shammes began to read, a scandal broke out on the part of the offended worshippers, who in the end forced the shammes not to make the "decree" public.
—o—
A synagogue committee elected.
At the Tuesday meeting of the kehilla board a synagogue committee was elected, which comprises 10 synagogue worshippers and 3 kehilla representatives.
—o—
A 16-year-old girl throws herself under the tram.
On Friday at midday a young girl aged 16 threw herself under the tram going from Czeladź to Będzin, near the "Sibeuki"[?] [probably Syberka, a district of Będzin].
The motorman stopped the tram at once, but it was already too late to save the suicide; she was already dead and her whole body was badly mangled.
The elegantly dressed suicide, on whom no documents whatsoever were found, was taken to the mortuary of the local municipal hospital.
Only yesterday did the police establish that the suicide was a resident of Sosnowiec and that the cause of the tragic suicide was a quarrel with her parents.
—o—
A visit by architects.
On Saturday some 100 architects from all over Poland stayed here; they are making a tour of the largest centres in Poland. The excursionists, whose purpose is to become acquainted with the plans for regulating Polish towns, visited the new school buildings on Promyk[?] and Krakowska [streets] and acquainted themselves with the municipal plans worked out by architect Kamiński.
—o—
A "treasure" found in Czeladź.
While laying a telephone cable in Czeladź the workers came upon an underground tunnel.
The sensation at once spread quickly among the local inhabitants, among whom there are "knowers of secrets", who relate that the tunnel leads to the Będzin castle and that on that site "there is a room full of treasures of money".
—o—
The Będzin magistrate receives loans.
At a time when the neighbouring magistrates are being dissolved, the local magistrate has received the following long-term loans:
from the "Bank Gosp. Krajow." [Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego] 250 thousand zł., and from the Communal Bank 100 thousand zł.
The loans give a full guarantee that the local magistrate is not on the list of the "magistrates condemned to death".
—o—
Sale of badges for "Beit Lechem".
On Thursday, the first day of Chol ha-Moed, the society "Beit Lechem" is organising a sale of badges.
For the holidays "Beit Lechem" carried out a wide-ranging campaign: hundreds of needy families received the most necessary products, even meat and wine too. It is desirable that the badge sale be properly supported.
—o—
Annual general meeting of "Hakoach".
Because of the large number of members that "Hakoach" has today, the board has decided to convene the annual general meeting in the hall of the "Góra Zamkowa", which takes place on the first day of Sukkot at 2 p.m.
The meeting has aroused great interest in Jewish sports circles and promises to be very interesting.
Official Decision Concerning the Kehilla Chairman / Sosnowiec Jews, Check Whether You Are on the Voters' Lists

[Sosnowiec — kehilla and elections.]
Sosnowiec
Official decision concerning the kehilla chairman.
The starosta [district head] has officially announced that Mr. Y. S. Wajgreb [?] (perhaps Weinreb) is appointed chairman of the kehilla board, and in place of Mr. Wajgsztok [?] (perhaps Weinstock) Mr. L. Jungster becomes a member of the kehilla board.
—o—
Sosnowiec Jews, check whether you are on the voters' lists.
The Jewish representatives in the electoral offices complain that the interest of the Jewish population in the elections is very scant. Only a very small number come to the offices to find out whether they are properly entered in the voters' lists.
The time for checking is only until the 19th of this month.

[Sosnowiec and Zawiercie — municipal affairs; followed by eleven short news items.]
City councils and municipal boards dissolved
In Sosnowiec and Zawiercie.
On Tuesday the starosta Bakisa [?], in the name of the voivode, delivered a decree dissolving the local city council and municipal board.
The hitherto school inspector, Mr. Kuśniak, has been appointed temporary commissioner.
The dissolution of the city council took place in the following manner.
That same evening a session of the city council was to have taken place. The session had been set for 7 o'clock, but the councillors were late, so that at 9 o'clock there was still no quorum.
Before the session the starosta, accompanied by Mr. Kuśniak, went in to the city president and ordered him to telephone the chairman of the city council, Dr. Pawlek [?].
When Dr. Pawlek came, the starosta handed over the decree of the Minister of the Interior stating that the city council and also the municipal board are dissolved.
The last session is conducted by Mr. Pawlek, who passes on the sensational news.
At the end the PPS councillors sing the „Czerwony Sztandar“ [The Red Flag].
———
The same thing happened on Thursday morning in Zawiercie.
A delegate of the voivodeship came to the magistrate [town hall] and informed the president, Mr. Wasf [?], of a decree of the Minister of the Interior that the city council and municipal board are dissolved.
At the same time the vice-starosta, Mr. Langert [?], was appointed commissioner.
———
In the next few days a council is to be created in Sosnowiec by the voivode, which is to consist of a larger number of representatives of local society.
The unexpected events naturally made a strong impression in Zagłębie.
—o—
The Number of Protested Bills of Exchange in August 20 Percent Lower Than in July
In the month of August (sierpień) 4998 bills of exchange were protested in Sosnowiec for a sum of 981353 zł., in Będzin 3922 bills for a sum of 5149 70 zł., in Dąbrowa 1384 bills for 2406,53 zł., in Zawiercie 1448 bills for 1982 94 zł.
In comparison with the bills protested in the month of July (lipiec) it turns out that the number of bills in the Kielce voivodeship decreased by 20 percent in August.
—o—
One Must 'Envy' the People of Krzepice...
The Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce has expressed the opinion that the town of Krzepice should be classed in the 4th category [for taxation].
The opinion is justified by the fact that the Krzepice merchants are very impoverished.
—o—
A Terrible Act of Revenge by a Woman
She Doused Her Husband with Hydrochloric Acid
On Wednesday at the Sosnowiec District Court the following family tragedy [was heard — verb missing in print].
During court proceedings a Christian woman doused her husband with hydrochloric acid and blinded him in both eyes.
The woman declared that she had done it because her husband had abandoned her and her children and gone off to his mistress.
—o—
District Conference of the Zionist-Revisionists
On Sunday, the 12th of this month (the 4th day of Chol HaMoed Sukkot), a conference will take place in the local municipal theatre, in which delegates and guests from over 70 towns of the Kielce voivodeship will take part.
The conference will be opened with a festive academy with the participation of the members of the Central Committee, Messrs. the poet Dr. Yaakov Cahan, Dr. R. Feldszuh (Ben-Shem), Dr. D. Wdowiński [?], Dr. A. Lipman, Mgr. S. Gutkowski [?] and others.
On the day of the conference there will be a march of the Zawiercie, Będzin, Dąbrowa, Strzemieszyce and Sosnowiec „Brit Trumpeldor“ through the streets of Sosnowiec.
Lectures will be given by: the poet Yaakov Cahan — „The Hebrew Movement“, Dr. R. Feldszuh — „The Political Situation in Zionism“, Dr. A. Lipman — „Lwów, Prague, Berlin“, Dr. D. Wdowiński [?] — „The Way of Youth“, Mgr. S. Gutkowski [?] — „The Situation in Polish Zionism“.
———
Admission cards to the conference can be obtained at the secretariat of the Zionist org[anization].
—o—
Jabotinsky Is Coming to Sosnowiec
The local Revisionist organization has received Jabotinsky's consent to come to Sosnowiec for one lecture.
Jabotinsky's visit has been set for 15 December (grudzień) of this year.
In Sosnowiec he will lecture on the subject „England, the Arabs and the Jews“.
—o—
Now That Is a Devoted Landlord
A Christian Landlord Provides His Tenants with a Sukkah
The Christian house-owner at 3rd [?] May Street 7 [ul. 3 Maja] has, for the convenience of his Jewish tenants, put up a sukkah for them.
The Jewish tenants, however, are in doubt whether the sukkah is kosher, because the sukkah was built on the Sabbath.
—o—
Pledge Campaign for the Free-Loan Fund
Every year the board of the local Gemilut Chesed (free-loan) fund proclaims a pledge (nedarim) campaign, which lasts from Rosh Hashanah to Simchat Torah.
This year the campaign has been changed for various reasons, so that the pledge campaign will last only during „Zman Simchatenu“ [Sukkot].
Let every well-to-do person [?] who is called up to the Torah not forget to make a pledge for the benefit of the institution, which sustains hundreds of Jewish families.
—o—
A 14-Year-Old Girl Has Disappeared
The 14-year-old Perl Białogórska left her parents' apartment at Kołłątaja 8 several days ago, and as we write these lines the girl has still not returned.
—o—
The Suicide Has Died
As we have already reported, the 70-year-old mentally ill Rajzel Ratner [?] threw herself from the 2nd floor on the 2nd day of Rosh Hashanah.
On the Sabbath the woman died.
—o—
Do Not Leave Small Children Unsupervised
At Targowa 5 a 2-year-old Jewish child fell from the second floor. The child, who remained lying unconscious, was revived only after much effort. The accident ended luckily and the child only received a bad wound on the face.
—o—
Reduction of Officials at the Sickness Fund
At the head office and the local sickness fund (Kasa Chorych) a larger number of officials have recently been dismissed. The reduction applied above all to married women,
Zawiercie

On Sunday the first election rally, organised by the B.B. [BBWR — Non-Partisan Bloc for Cooperation with the Government], took place here. Dr. Gszegoski [?] of Sosnowiec delivered a speech in which he called on those assembled to support the action of Marshal Piłsudski, who has undertaken to heal [?] the life of the Polish state.
At the end "The First Brigade" was sung.

Meeting of the "Oyferat" (umbrella council?) of the artisans' organizations of the region.
Yesterday, Sunday afternoon, a meeting of the "Oyferat" took place in the premises of the Artisans' Association in Sosnowiec.
Taking part in the meeting were representatives from Będzin, Dąbrowa, Czeladź, Strzemieszyce, "Magurshov" [?] and others, who resolved that in all artisans' affairs the Oyferat shall act in the name of all artisans' organizations in Zagłębie.
A position on the coming Sejm elections was also adopted.
A detailed report in the next issue.

"Heart, Man and Dream."
On Wednesday, at the close of the first days of Sukkot, at 8 in the evening, Mr. A. Gan will give a lecture at the "Hotel Polski" on the subject "Heart, Man and Dream" (according to Freud's theory).
—o—
The "city fathers" of Jędrzejów arrested.
After an inspection was carried out, the following were arrested in Jędrzejów: the "local" mayor (burmistrz) Pczagewski [?], deputy mayor [?] Stróż Gondzik [?], and the councillors Szlomo Dudkiewicz, Naftali Horawiński [?], Wolny [?] and Kończewski.
The arrested men are accused of embezzlement at the local power station to the amount of 60 thousand złoty.
—o—
Sequestrator sentenced to a year in prison.
Last Saturday the sequestrator (bailiff) Hahn of Będzin (Małachowska 11) stood before the Sosnowiec district court, accused of appropriating a sum of 1,456 zł. that he had collected from taxpayers in Będzin.
The sequestrator was sentenced to a year in prison and loss of rights.
—o—
The interest in the Blue-White Evening in Strzemieszyce.
As was to be foreseen, the Blue-White Evening being organized by the Zionist Organization on Wednesday, 8 October (the close of the first days of Sukkot), has aroused enormous interest among the Zionist intelligentsia of Zagłębie, which is preparing for the evening. And judging by the great preparations of the organizing committee, which spares neither effort nor money, it is to be hoped that the evening will be a success and impressive.

A living child in the mortuary.
A year ago, the wife of a worker, a woman in difficult childbirth[?], was brought to the hospital of the sick fund (Kasa Chorych) in Sosnowiec. The woman was operated on, but after the operation she died, and the newborn child was alive.
When the deceased was taken to the mortuary, the staff carried the living child into that same room as well...
After some time a woman passing by happened to hear a crying voice coming from the mortuary; when the woman went in, she saw the crying child lying beside its dead mother.
She took the child, but a few hours later the child died too.
Over this case the police brought the midwife to court, and the district court in Sosnowiec sentenced the midwife to six months in prison.
This week the case came before the Court of Appeal in Warsaw, where the verdict of the first instance was overturned.

The son-in-law cries „Hoshana!“ and his father-in-law deals out „one and one“.
The Jewish residents of Małobądz[?], sitting in their sukkahs, had a story to tell: that of Mr. G., who is angry with his son-in-law H., who has a great urge[?] to talk and, by the way, tells everyone that his father-in-law cheated him and is not keeping the dowry promise.

A Sad Sum Total

[Będzin — Kehilla; opinion article, part 2.]
2.
That Jewish communal (kehilla) life is more than sad, that complete chaos reigns there, an absolute tohu va-vohu, that the kehilla does not fulfil even the most minimal and elementary of the tasks it is called to, that it creates nothing positive, nothing real, and that its activity cannot stand up to any criticism at all — of this there is no longer any doubt today. It is "a secret to all of Berdichev" [i.e. an open secret] that the Jewish communities are nothing more than nests for the "Agudah" [Agudat Israel] politicians and other black forces, where all kinds of machinations, combinations and intrigues are carried out at the expense of the Jewish masses, and instead of caring for the interests of the community as a whole, behind-the-scenes politics and various machinations and intrigues are conducted over ritual slaughterers, gabbaim, cantors, etc.
As an example of how little interest and understanding the Jewish community has for the most painful Jewish problems, even for religious interests, there is the sad fact that to this very day the Będzin Jewish community — which belongs among the largest Jewish communities in Poland — has shown no initiative whatsoever to create even one single Jewish elementary (folk) school, where the children would receive a Jewish national education and which would meet our demands in so important a field of our national life. The Będzin Jewish community does not see the sad process of assimilation of the coming Jewish generation, for unfortunately, because of the difficult economic situation in which the Jewish masses and the broad popular strata find themselves, they are forced to send their children to the [state] elementary schools, where they are brought up in a foreign culture and thereby become completely assimilated and consequently estranged from the Jewish people, from the Jewish spirit and from its religious and national values.
The question asks itself: who must care for Jewish education — the poor, ruined, spiritually and materially broken Jewish masses, or the Jewish community with the rabbinate at its head? It would seem there can be no two opinions that the duty lies first of all on the kehilla, the institution called upon to care for the Jewish public. I will not touch now on other questions which also belong to the tasks and competence of the kehilla and for which the kehilla has absolutely no understanding. This time I will content myself with the one single, so painful question of education, for which there is no excuse whatsoever, and I ask once again: why does the kehilla not show the slightest initiative in this matter? And why does nobody take an interest in the hundreds of Jewish children who are brought up in a foreign, assimilated spirit and atmosphere? With good will one could achieve a great deal in this field; one could engage at least one single good Jewish pedagogue who would concern himself with Jewish education; or perhaps the kehilla should call on the rabbinate to take an interest in this painful question — for, as is well known, the three moreh hora'ah [rabbinic decisors] figure in the kehilla's books as religion teachers, so they ought to fulfil their duty and care for Jewish education. This fact alone already shows clearly that the kehilla does not fulfil even the most minimal and elementary of its tasks.
And so the question arises: who is to blame for this? And why should a kehilla like Będzin, which operates with a budget of almost half a million, not fulfil its most elementary obligations toward society?
Here we must once again recall the opinion we expressed in the previous article, that a secret black hand is at work here, which is interested in using every means to reach its goal, which consists in gaining hegemony over the communities and then managing them in its own way. And that is also the secret of why this same secret hand — let us call it by its name, the "Agudah" — strove for a number of years to remove the Jewish desk officer (referent) at the Ministry of Education, so that his place would be taken by a Christian who would be more inclined toward their demands than the Jew. And that they made no mistake in their calculation and hit the right target is shown us by the latest approved Będzin kehilla budget, which has already been approved by the new Christian referent: in it all subsidies for cultural purposes were struck out, such as [?] for Jewish schools, libraries, artisans' courses, etc., whereas subsidies were approved for "Beit Yaakov", "Poalei Agudat Israel", Chachmei Lublin [yeshiva], "Chizuk HaDat", "Tze'irei Emunei Israel", etc., etc. And on top of that, as a gratification, they added another 15 thousand złoty for the mikveh, for the mikveh, which has been turned into a hell that cries "give, give!" without measure and without limit.
Comment is superfluous; let Jewish Będzin only reflect a little on this sad sum total and see the abyss into which the "Torah-true" "Agudah" is leading it.
Y. Wygodzki.

A Railway Disaster Beyond Częstochowa. 30 Wagons Smashed — Several Railwaymen Seriously Injured

[Railway accident — Herby–Częstochowa line.] On the Herby — Częstochowa railway line a great railway disaster occurred on Tuesday [7 October 1930] at 10 in the evening [?]. Owing to the carelessness of the station duty officer, one freight train ran into another.
The collision was so violent that both locomotives were smashed, 20 loaded wagons overturned and 10 wagons were destroyed.
In the disaster 5 railway employees were seriously injured and 12 lightly; they were taken to hospital in Tarnowitz [Tarnowskie Góry].
On the order of the prosecutor the railway duty officer was arrested.
Why Was the Sosnowiec City Council Dissolved?

[Sosnowiec — City council.] The former chairman of the city council, as well as the municipal administration, have received from the Voivodeship office the grounds on which the city council and the municipal administration were dissolved.
The Sosnowiec city council — so the grounds state — took no account at all of the real financial possibilities, did not even think of introducing any kind of economy, but set up an office staff that swallowed a sum of 1600,000 [sic] zł. from the budget, did not observe the regulations of the Minister of the Interior concerning control, so that the auditing committee has to this day not yet audited the budgets of the years 1927—28. The magistrat [municipal board] increased the sum of expenditure every year without reckoning with the budget's possibilities, and therefore ran into heavy debts.
President [mayor] Wilger [?] came to the city council with proposals for expenditure without having any cover for them in the budget. He also did not present to the city council any report on the magistrat's activity.
Because of such management the Minister of the Interior found it necessary to dissolve the magistrat and also the city council, and appointed Mr. Kuśniak [?] of Dąbrowa as commissioner.
An appeal against this decision may be lodged with the Supreme Administrative [state] Tribunal.
Theatre Notes. "Arlekin", "Pat, Pat Doypushka" [?]

[Theatre — "Arlekin" revue.] The "Arlekin" [Harlequin revue troupe] has shown itself to us with a new face. The number of artists has grown; it is only a loss for the theatre that Mr. Ma[—]ski has left. Friday's premiere had a rich programme which, true, was not especially successful as far as humour goes, but to make up for it the director introduced more serious and mood-making numbers into the programme. The sketch "Prince Sagin" was rendered by Mr. Lubitsch and Mrs. Karszówna [?] with great dramatic expression; Mrs. Wipszarkówna [?], who is a good talent, was poorly used, especially in the first part of the revue. The solo dances made a good impression. Mr. Szapski is somewhat too stiff on stage. On the whole the artists are [?] in a good school and under good direction.
Municipal Theatre

[Będzin — Theatre.] "The Charming Pensioner".
"The Charming Pensioner" is not a comedy that the author, Rapacki, wrote with only one idea before his eyes. The action of the characters is fitted into the frame of family life, through which there merely creep conversations and opinions of the author on theatre, film, sound film, and on the difference between the pre-war and the post-war population. For that very reason, however, the comedy offers great possibilities to the actors.
The family consists of one pensioner — the grandfather ("dziadek"); a second pensioner — the father; and[?] a daughter brought up "salon-style" by the Frenchwoman, who "murders" the Polish language well; and [—] a subtenant, a "young" and... third pensioner (the mother is in Karlsbad). The pre-war generation is represented by the grandfather (Mr. Komalski), who lived his way into his role and gave a good creation. Excellent was the acting of Mr. Sarnecki (his role makes up half of the comedy), who only now has shown his great dramatic talent. His outward figure, voice, deep declamation and naturalness come to expression in his acting. The acting of all the artists, and not the comedy itself, delighted the assembled audience.

[Sport — football.] Representative team of Königshütte — Representative team of Zagłębie 4:4 (2:2)

There were moments when one thought the home side would have to lose; the result was uncertain the whole time. The line-up of the Zagłębie team was changed this time.
