The Problem of the World Crisis. (How is it viewed in the world, and how is it treated here at home?)

[Article — economy; the world crisis and Poland.]
The whole country is writhing [?] in an enormous crisis. From all over the world come sad tidings; here and there one hears of stock-exchange crashes that deafen the financial circles; everywhere the general situation is hard to the point of being unbearable, everywhere hard times, gloomy days have arrived. World billionaires [?], manufacturers splendidly established for generations, are leaving the arena. Magnates who shook the world are ceasing to exist altogether. Dread falls upon the citizens of every country when they hear how everything is tottering, how unbelievable, legendary fortunes turn into soap bubbles; billionaires who ran [?] kingdoms and countries, magnates before whom ministers and presidents used to bow, stop at lightning speed to play any role whatsoever, and the world is shaken hearing what panics, what surprises are now taking place in various parts of the world.
Everywhere the causes of the grave situation are being sought, everywhere people want to find a solution to the hard problem; but the cause cannot be tracked down so quickly, and the crux is not so easily found. In the more civilized countries, in the states of higher culture, people look to the root; they want to come with sure steps to the place from which the crisis grows — the crisis that spreads its infectious poison with its wings over the whole world. In many countries professors and scholars and financiers and industrialists have also [?] been set to this, and they interpret and investigate in order to find those who could be put in the dock.
We see that some countries are trying to reduce taxes, applying [?] means so that citizens should understand the great virtue of saving, putting grosz to grosz; they are also helping to solve the serious question of building housing, which after so many war years has become a product of prime necessity. So [?] they are concerned with easing the citizens' living conditions.
It goes without saying that it is hard to answer whether this will solve the question, whether in this way salvation will come to suffering humanity; but of one thing people are sure — "I have toiled and found": that they will search so long until they find, will study and research and think seriously so long about what makes life hard, about what makes it unbearable to continue the course of life, until rescue is found and other forms of life are created.
The situation is much harder with us in Poland, even though the crisis here has not yet reached the level it has in other countries — and this is because here people believe in nothing; they do not believe that there is and can be a crisis, they do not believe that there are hard times and serious days. That is precisely where the trouble lies, and thanks to this very unbelief hard times must come and the situation must worsen.
Here one sees that the factories are stopping, that the chimneys are not smoking, that the workers are unemployed, that the artisans wander about without a scrap of work, that the big merchants stand yawning and sleeping in their ever-smaller shops — and still people do not believe it is so; on the contrary, not only do they not believe that things are bad, they hold that things are constantly getting better. One sees this palpably when it comes to assessing the citizens' earnings.
One knows, for example, how to assess from year to year that this or that firm had a larger turnover, that it earned more; the tax office [urząd skarbowy] has a perfectly simple proof that this is so: that in the last year more bills of exchange were sold than in the previous one. As [?] the bill could not be paid when the due date came and had to be rewritten for a later date, the exchange took place several times — this nobody knows, this nobody sees, this nobody wants to see, to this nobody even wants to give a thought. Naturally, such shutting of one's eyes to reality is harmful both to the citizens, who keep going under, and to the government, which in this way will have smaller revenues.
After all, it is known that from year to year the number of patents [trade licences] grows smaller, which is also not a good sign; one ought to have reacted properly to such an unfavourable phenomenon [?], one ought to have asked why this or that person no longer takes out a patent, what the reason is, what does he live on? But people take no interest in that, because they understand that these are fallen citizens, people without vital strength, from whom no more use can be had; and instead of taking an interest in them, instead of wanting [?] to come to their aid so that they do not become a burden on the country, people say otherwise: since there are now fewer merchants, fewer workshops, fewer factories, they surely do better business — so let them pay for themselves and for the fallen. In other words, it means: as long as you have strength, as long as you stand on your feet, work beyond your strength, pull the marrow out of your bones, take upon yourself all the overloaded tax obligations that make the citizen ill and do not let him breathe.
On the other hand, no opportunity is given to set back on their feet the great number of the fallen, who are constantly wasting away, and no thought is given to how those who exist — as they exist, by miracles [?] — might hold out on their already weak feet. Who is even talking about caring for a healthy existence, in which one could save up, grosz by grosz, a certain sum for the future, for when the citizen no longer has the strength to toil, neither for himself nor for others.
Even if there were no crisis in Poland, even if everything were in the best order, life would still keep getting harder, because the expenses, the obligations both toward the government and for household needs, are all growing at once.
If here, as in other countries, people tried to seek the causes — how they arose and in what way they could be removed — there would still be a way out; but as it is, when this interests nobody, when one sees [?] no crisis whatever in the country, when everything is good and fine and dandy and one allows oneself to tax the citizens with ever [?] larger sums — it means that one does not want to see reality, does not want to see the truth as it looks; so how can things get better, how can the situation improve for the citizens' benefit? And if things are generally bad, if the citizen in Poland is not well off, then the Jewish citizen is surely, most surely, not well off [printed: "גיט"], and his situation is no doubt becoming ever more serious and dangerous.
From all that has been said, only this can be summed up: that since the outbreak of the war the world has still not reached a normal stage; the wheels still do not fit into the gears [tryby], and this disturbs the normal course — a regular [?] inflow and outflow, as there must be in a regular [?], well-functioning tool. The difference is only that elsewhere people set about finding the causes of the danger, the reasons for the irregularity [?], thanks to which one can get onto the right road — while here in Poland people do not even want to begin to believe that not everything is in the best of health.
That is what is no good, that is what is not desirable, neither for the country nor for the citizens!
R. Let.
Napoleon and the Young Polish Countess Walewska (2)

[Serialized historical tale — Napoleon and Countess Maria Walewska; installment 2.]
M. Aszerowicz.

2.

One hand washed the other: both sides sought their own advantage [?], and since Napoleon then stood at the highest level of power and could abolish all thrones and create new ones, in Poland he was looked upon as a god.

Napoleon fell in love with the Polish countess at first sight. He met her at one of the magnificent balls given in his honour, and as soon as he caught sight of her his gaze became riveted to her, and the whole time he could no longer take his eyes off her.

She was a blonde, with beautiful blue eyes and very fine manners, and she was then altogether no more than 18 years old.

From the very first few words he exchanged with her he immediately sensed that she was not like the other women he had known [?]. She was different.

More than anything he was taken by her modesty, her quietness, for he had always held the opinion that the finest and most pleasing thing in a woman is — modesty...

Toward [other kinds of; doubtful word] women he had a different attitude: he could take them lightly and cast them off lightly. He never opened his heart to them, and he did not care whether they themselves had a heart or not...

Precisely the fact that the young Countess Maria Walewska did not throw herself in his way like the other ladies who swirled around him at the ball — precisely this greatly pleased Napoleon, and he at once decided that she was not only beautiful but also endearing. As he later put it, speaking about her with his brother Lucien, whom he held in very high regard: "She was," he said, "a most charming woman, an angel, and there can be no doubt at all that her soul was just as lovely as her face."

Although the Polish countess was still so young, she was already married and the mother of a child. Her husband, Count Anastazy [printed "Anastasius"], Colonna-Walewicz-Walewski [so printed], one of the most distinguished Polish aristocrats, was a good many years older than she; how great the age difference between the couple was can be imagined from the fact that the count's youngest grandchild was ten years older than the countess.

Between her and Napoleon, too, the difference in years was no small one: Napoleon was older than she by a full twenty years. But he was, after all, much younger than [her husband; word missing in print].

That night, after the ball, Napoleon was very restless. The whole time he did not stop thinking about the beautiful young countess with the blond hair and the blue eyes: it robbed him of his sleep, and in the morning, when he got up, his valet had a very hard job dressing him...

The emperor could not stay in one place; he was very nervous and kept pacing the room back and forth: the face of Countess Walewska hovered constantly before his eyes, she never left his mind the whole time, and when he saw and felt that it was really serious, he sent her a little letter.

"The whole time I looked only at you," he wrote in the letter. "I long to be alone with you. Send me an answer at once, so that the fire that burns me may be quelled."

He thought that as soon as she received the letter she would come to him at once... Are the most beautiful daughters of Poland not ready to throw themselves at his feet? Do they not show this readiness at every opportunity?.. Well, surely the young Countess Maria Walewska will come to him at once!..

But he was greatly mistaken. The young countess did not come; she did not even answer his letter.

To treat Napoleon so at that time one needed courage, a great deal of courage, and perhaps even more than that — genuine womanly dignity, which shows resistance when one feels that it is not a matter of a beautiful, noble love but of an ugly passion that is extinguished once it has been satisfied.

With the exception of a few individual cases, in Napoleon's attitude toward women there was first of all [?] passion, carnal lust; when he saw a beautiful woman he wanted her to be his, and he did whatever he could to get her. Her other virtues did not interest him. He simply had no time for that.

In this field Napoleon was by then already accustomed. The most beautiful women in the world did not refuse him, and it is very possible that toward Countess Walewska, too, he at first had no other feeling than passion: she had caught his fancy, so he wanted her to be his, and he did not care what would happen later.

Walewska sensed this clearly [?], and since she was a very refined, very modest and very dignified woman, not one of those women who let themselves be dazzled by momentary pleasure, she felt insulted by Napoleon's brazen approach, and that is why she did not even answer his letter.

So Napoleon put his pride aside [?] and wrote again.

His letters to the young Polish countess recall the ardour [?] that could be felt in the love letters he wrote to Josephine from the Italian front, before he learned that she had been unfaithful to him, that she had exchanged him for another who could not even reach up to his ankles.

It is true that in the letters to Josephine there was more fire, more burning, but this is explained by the fact that Napoleon was then younger and had not yet had so many disappointments in women.

Napoleon's second letter to Countess Walewska read as follows:

"Have I perhaps failed you in something? It seems to me it is the other way round; or perhaps nothing has remained of your first feeling for me? My passion for you grows ever greater; you have robbed me of my peace. Grant a little pleasure, a little happiness to the poor heart that so yearns to love you! Is it really so hard for you to answer me? You already owe me two answers."

In this short letter [?], too, one certainly does not sense the tone of the ruling emperor. Rather one senses in it the tone of a man truly in love, whose "poor heart" is pining for love.

And this was at a time when the whole world listened with bated breath to every word Napoleon uttered and watched every step he took, because every word of his, every step of his, could change the map of the world and turn the fate of nations and countries in another direction.

To the world — a mighty ruler; to himself — a human being with weaknesses, with a poor heart that longs for love.

And so, not only in individual cases — a mystery to those who came into close contact with him, after they had heard so many terrible things about him; a mystery riding on a horse, a riddle that cannot be explained.

Vanity of Vanities.

[Feuilleton — a reflection for the Sabbath of Sukkot; Ecclesiastes.] By A. Drazhner [A. Drażner?].

Vanity of vanities, said Koheleth, vanity of vanities, all is vanity.

Can you imagine anything even more empty and hollow than the emptiness ["pustota"] that Koheleth lamented?

A clever person may tell me that in our world there are nowadays things that are emptier still: they will point out to me the Jewish charity societies, the platforms of the politicians, the conferences, England's promises concerning the Land of Israel. One can point to more such things that are even emptier than Koheleth's "vanity of vanities", and nevertheless I still go about with the notion that the world is a very fine one, a decent one and, above all, a beautiful one. Its beauty enchants; for the sake of its beauty I would not want to grow old and would not want to die.

In Rückert [Friedrich Rückert, the German poet] there is a little tale like this:

A man was walking in the desert, starving and thirsty. He looks for a drop of water, a crumb of bread. His strength is running out. Suddenly he sees a wild beast. Fear seizes him, and in terror he runs to hide somewhere. From afar he sees a pit; he runs to it and begins to let himself down; but before he reached the bottom he saw a snake with its jaws open to swallow him, so he quickly grabbed hold of the little wild shrubs and wild grasses that had grown on the walls of the pit... He is tired, frightened to death, he barely has the strength to breathe, but he holds on with all his might to the grasses and shrubs, because on both sides death lies in wait for him: above, outside, the wild beast, and here, in the depth of the pit — the snake with its open jaws. So he hangs in the air... Suddenly he sees two mice come out of their holes beside the shrubs and grasses he is holding on to, and they begin to gnaw at the shrubs. He screams, he thrashes like a dying man in the last moment of his life, but the mice stand there indifferently and gnaw and gnaw... Any moment now, one more moment, and he will fall straight into the jaws of the terrible snake.

The unfortunate man despairs, gives up all hope and awaits with dreadful fear the last moment of his sad life. He looks around on all sides, and as he searches thus, almost without hope, for something to hold on to, the man sees a drop of honey on a leaf of the wild grasses... His face lit up with joy, and a sun of happiness rose in his heart. With all his strength he raised himself to the leaf and licked up the honey...

Vanity of vanities... Can there be anything more vain than the life of the man in the snake's pit? — But the drop of honey... one single drop of honey is, after all, so sweet!

Outside stands the bloodthirsty beast, inside — the venomous snake, the one feeble hold on life is being gnawed through by mice, death looks you straight in the face and shouts at you at the top of its voice: Man, O man, everything is nothing of nothings! You, you great nothing who turns worlds upside down, you hang on a gnawed-through straw — death stands with a sharp knife, ready to cut you off the straw — the man hears the voices, trembles before them in mortal dread, but... there, he has spotted a lick of honey, and he laughs at death, and his ear goes deaf [printed "toyt", dead — apparently a misprint for "toyb", deaf] to its shouting.

And why should we deny it: there is, thank God, enough of it in God's little world. One man finds the honey in the "seven wisdoms", at which Koheleth of all people laughs; another finds the honey in the vanities of this world, of which Koheleth has already had his fill, like a millionaire's little son; and a third — for him it is a small piece of bread and butter in the surroundings of his own home, in good health. Each one finds honey in things that for Koheleth are the greatest vanity.

I therefore think that instead of reciting Koheleth in the synagogues, it would be better to send speakers out to all the towns and townlets to show the public where it can find fine honey.

There will still be time to recite Koheleth. What is the hurry to recite Koheleth, eh? Here, people have been reciting Koheleth for so many years, and nevertheless there are very few fools who get frightened by the "vanity of vanities"; and precisely while they are reciting the "vanity of vanities" they already have it in mind that as soon as they finish reciting, they will run off to have a lick of a drop of honey somewhere...
Hakafot.

[Poetry — Simchat Torah; the hakafot in the beis medrash.] [The credit "by Shaul Tchernichovsky, Yiddish by Israel Lewin" stands at the top of the adjacent column, see 2.18.]

In the beis medrash a crush.
   A radiance [?], a press [?]!
And packed from wall to wall,
   the bimah is taken.
The din grows louder, it resounds,
young men push up against old,
   even the "mizrach" is crammed full [?].

Rivers of brilliance pour out,
   flooding every space:
from every electric lamp on the ceiling,
   from candles stuck in radishes.
A voice calls: Nu, cantor, sing!
And boys stand in a ring,
   ready to sing along.

They walk slowly, fine and splendid,
   their heads held high,
coloured flags in their hands,
   where candles are stuck in apples.
From the candle in the flag that each one holds
their figures are lit up,
   and their cheeks turn red [?].

The cantor lets out his voice,
   the "helpers" back him up:
the gabbai with the whole congregation
   join in quite merrily.
From the back and from above as well,
the tailor, the shoemaker in one tone,
   even the "rabiner" [the government rabbi] too.

With Torah scrolls in their hands,
   paupers just like rich men,
decked out in beautiful mantles
   of different colours,
and from the gold-covered crown
the little bell-pomegranates
   ring out splendidly [?] and fine.

The bearers float through the congregation
   in the glow of the lamps,
the "crowd" rushes with fervour
   to kiss the Torah scrolls.
— "I wish you joy of luck
   this year!"
— "And may you never
   know trouble!"

A New Novel by Yehuda Varshaviak.

[Literature — a new book.] The "Mekor" publishing house (Warsaw) will shortly bring out a new novel by Yehuda Varshaviak [Jehuda Warszawiak], entitled "Orot me-Ofel" (Lights out of Darkness). The novel depicts the life of a young Jewish man in Poland in the year 1920 who is transformed from a leader in the PPS [Polish Socialist Party] movement into a simple chalutz [pioneer], who actually leaves the Diaspora and emigrates to the Land of Israel.

The original novel, in which the life of a Jewish socialist in the ranks of the PPS is depicted for the first time in our literature, and in which Polish reality immediately after the World War finds a sharp echo, has aroused great interest in literary circles.
Off I Go to „Yoshev Beseter" [Kgey iz yoshev beseter]

[Humour — satirical feuilleton; the Polish Sejm.] By J. Oberżanek.
Told by a Jew who has a deputy (member of the Sejm) for a neighbour.
Hefz[?] — what do you say to my troubles? Not enough that I have a wife who lives on a diet and eats „pshe-pisars"[?]; not enough that I have a landlord who is a „stały agitator"[?] (permanent agitator) of the „Sana"[?] [Sanacja?] and constantly feeds me „hpozagies"[?] and evictions — as if all that were not enough, I need a deputy on my head as well: a neighbour who is a deputy.
Oh, you will surely ask: is it a bad thing to have a deputy for a neighbour? On the contrary: from such a neighbour one can sometimes get some benefit — now a little protection[?], now a wink[?], running an errand where a plain flesh-and-blood mortal has no „foothold"... who knows what one can get from a neighbour who is a deputy.
True, a deputy for a neighbour really is a good thing; the trouble is that my neighbour the deputy has my name: I am called Pulka and he, the deputy, is called Pulka; the only difference is that I am called Nosn Note Pulka, and he, my neighbour the deputy, is called Wojciech Pulka. He, Wojciech Pulka, took 1300 złoty a month for three years for sitting at home, and I for three years ate suffering and drank fever with „zsiadłe mleko" (sour milk)...
I would have forgiven him all that: take your 1300 złoty, sit at home — whom does it bother, does it cost my money? What do you say? If the state likes it, I don't mind. I would have forgiven him everything, if only he did not have my name.
It's no small matter, the troubles I have from my neighbour the deputy, who chose my name of all names, Pulka. He takes the pension, and they drive me mad[?] all day long with knocking and ringing. At dawn I am woken: in bursts a whole camp of peasants with the sołtys (village head) at their head; I go dazed[?], my ears start ringing[?], my wife faints, the children raise a hue and cry, and they shout: „Pantse-boyemi[?] da pana posła" [garbled Polish: „...to the honourable deputy"]...
I would have put up with that too — as you say, one gets used to troubles. If not for the latest misfortune — ah, listen, Jews, did I have a week! I would not wish it on my enemies. And because of whom? — again because of my neighbour, the „poseł" (deputy) Wojtek Pulka. Listen to this:
It was this very week. I am lying in my own troubles: the household is crying for holiday money, I have to redeem my wife's fur coat[?] from the pawnshop (lombard), and where is a cartload of coal for the winter; the school fees and two quarters' rent — have they converted and run off? And the bills of exchange falling due — they are bastards, eh?
As I lie there thinking about my bundle of troubles, I hear whispering behind the door and right after it a ringing on the bell-pull[?]...
— „Kto tam?" (Who's there?) — I ask.
— „Otworzyć!" (Open up!) — comes a voice in a commanding tone — „Policja."
On hearing „police" my teeth began chattering. How does the police come to me? What business do I have with the police? A „garvar"[?] I don't have, an „upadłość"[?] (bankruptcy?) certainly not — what can it be, what? Should I say that they don't mean me but my neighbour the „poseł", who has the same name as I do? But that cannot be: a „poseł", as is well known, is „nietykalny" (immune); over a „poseł" the police, according to the constitutional Shulchan Arukh, has no authority. It can only be that they mean my own honour...
— „Czy tu mieszka pan Pulka?" (Does Mr Pulka live here?) — asks a young fellow with a briefcase in his hand and a stiff moustache.
— „Tutaj" (here) — I say — „tu mieszka Pulka, ale..." (Pulka lives here, but...)
— „Bez ale" (no buts) — replies the fellow with the stiff moustache — „proszę się wylegitymować" (show your papers, please).
— „Ale panie naczelniku" (but, sir) — I try to argue — „ja przecież nie jestem. Prawdziwy Pulka tu nie mieszka" (I am not... the real Pulka doesn't live here)!
— „Na, na" — says the fellow with the stiff moustache — „znamy się; a kto," he says, „dostał diety?" (we know your sort; and who got the per-diem allowances?)
— Chane Beyle — I say to my wife — if so, he means you. The gentleman is talking about „diet" — you are the one on a diet.
— „Tak, tak" (yes, yes) — I explain to him.
— „Teraz ta[?] historia już jest jasna" (now the story is clear): „moja żona Chane Bejle cierpi, lo aleykhem, na żołądek" (my wife Chane Beyle suffers — may it never befall you — from her stomach)...
— „Czy pan udaje Greka?" (are you playing dumb?) — the fellow with the stiff moustache flew off the handle — „Ubrać się!" (get dressed!) — he shouted.
Well, I think to myself, „ubrać się" is „ubrać się", and I start getting dressed.
What went on in the house you can imagine for yourselves. A trifle! In the middle of everything — a business with diets and with „ubrać się". Why does this happen to me? What sin have I committed, what? Meanwhile I again try to argue with the fellow with the stiff moustache: „Gdzie jest yosher?" (where is justice?) I ask him. „Może pan ma a toes?" (maybe you, sir, are making a mistake?) „Przecież tu jest jeszcze jeden Pulka" (there is another Pulka here, after all).
„Czy mi pan tyle Pulków?" (how many Pulkas have you got for me?) — the fellow flares up like a havdalah candle. „Na Wiejskiej[?]," he says, „pan był[?]" (you were on Wiejska Street — i.e. in the Sejm?).
When my Jewish wife heard the word „wiejskie" (rural), she started to talk language — and in Polish my Chane Beyle is at home. „Byłam," says my wife, „byłam na wsi, w lesku, ...[?] letnisko" (I was in the country, in the woods, ...a summer resort). „Jadłam wiejski ser, wiejska śmietana, wiejski chleb też[?] jadłam" (I ate country cheese, country cream, country bread I ate too).
„Nie rozumiem!" (I don't understand) — the fellow jumped up as if scalded. You hear that? „Nie rozumiem" — what is there to „rozumieć"? My Chane Beyle spoke clear words, it seems, and in Polish to boot — what is there not to understand, what?
My wife talked, and he kept shouting: „Nie rozumiem". Once he had got really angry, he asks me again: „A ślubowanie spodnie[?] gdzie pan ma?" (and where do you have your ... ?)
„Co to znaczy?" (what does that mean?) I ask him once more.
Fool, my Chane Beyle cut in: what don't you understand here? „Ślubowanie spodnie" — wedding trousers. He is asking you whether you still have your wedding trousers.
So I say: „Panie naczelniku, już jestem bez złego oka (kein ayin-hore) dwadzieścia[?], do stu lat, po ślubie, skąd teraz ślubowanie spodnie?" (Sir, I am already — no evil eye — twenty [years], may it be to a hundred, after the wedding; where would I have wedding trousers now?)..
Clear words, it seems — even a child would have understood — and he boiled over again and again started shouting and stamping his feet: „Nie rozumiem".
„A marszałka pan zna?" (and do you know the Marshal?) he asks me again.
He is asking you, my Chane Beyle translates for me again, whether you had a „marshalik" (wedding master of ceremonies) at the wedding.
„Ja" (yes), I say, „jeszcze jakiego marszałka! On już jest na świat prawdy[?]" (and what a marshalik! he is already in the world of truth) (he has already passed into the World of Truth).
Who would not understand a few such Polish words? He gets angry again and shouts again: „Nie rozumiem". „Mów pan," he shouts, „po polsku!" (speak Polish!)
And what am I speaking — Turkish? It seems to me I'm speaking, and my Chane Beyle is speaking — we both speak „prawdziwy" (genuine) Polish.
Finally he asks me: „A serdelki pan lubi?" (and do you like sausages?)
What is that? Chane Beyle, what is the meaning of „serdelki"? Even such a „polit-chke"[?] as my Chane Beyle didn't understand that one..
When he saw that both of us, my Chane Beyle and I, were shrugging our shoulders, he gave a shout: „Panie Pulka — ariazu[?]" (arrest?)
When I went out with the fellow with the stiff moustache, my wife fainted, the children wailed, and I myself? I didn't understand what he wanted from me, that stiff-moustached fellow. He talks such foreign („zagraniczne") words: „ślubowanie spodnie", whether I like sausages; whether I had a marshalik[?] at the wedding, whether my wife ate country bread — what kind of plague is this, what?
You want to know the end? The end was that only there, at the „komisariat" (police station), did the mistake come out: all those „zagraniczne wyrazy" (foreign expressions) were not meant for me but for my neighbour the deputy, Wojtek Pulka.
Jews, how does one get rid of this neighbour? He took the pension — and I sat in „yoshev beseter" [i.e. in custody; after Psalm 91:1]...
What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: From the First Days of Sukkot

[Page header:] Friday, P״Ḥ [sic; probably Ḥol ha-Moʿed], 18 Tishrei 5691 — Piątek 10 października 1930 [Friday, 10 October 1930].
Będzin
From the first days of Sukkot.
The first days of Sukkot were cold and rainy, and this greatly disturbed the "Season of our Rejoicing"; above all, the unfavourable weather harmed the young people, who could not show themselves in the street in their new holiday clothes.
In the town synagogue ("Shtot-shul") a "terrible cold" also prevailed: the choir went on strike in the very middle of the holiday and refused to go up to the cantor's desk; only after many interventions and promises by the synagogue worshippers that its pay ["pension"] would be paid out did the choir finally agree to sing..
Besides that, the synagogue worshippers had a second "sensation". In honour of the holiday the kehilla board had fenced off 12 places with wire (corresponding to the twelve tribes..). The fence, however, was taken down on the first day of the holiday in such a way that a warden ["dozor"?] came with his Christian servant, who "liberated" the places...
— In short, the first days passed very gloomily, cold, brr.. brr.. brr..
Annual General Meeting of the “Hakoach” Gymnastics Association

In the hall on "Górna Zamkowa" Street the annual general meeting of the "Hakoach" gymnastics and sports association took place on Tuesday afternoon.
The meeting, as had been foreseen, aroused great interest among the members of the society. It is very rare to find such a large number of members as at this meeting. The hall was almost full. Besides, many members who were "in arrears" [with their dues] had gathered in the "corridors", not having had the privilege of entering the hall where the meeting took place.
The president, Dr. Rechtman, opens the meeting and proposes Mr. M. Gold as chairman, to which those assembled agree. The chairman invites Messrs. M. L. Koziłowski and Schlesinger as assessors, and A. Ehrlich as secretary.
After the reading of the minutes of the last general meeting, Mr. S. Rozenblum gives a report, from which it can be seen that the board was very active in all fields during its term. For example, the number of members grew from 240 to nearly 700. An orchestra of its own was created, and fine places were achieved on the excursions that took place during the year.
The reports of the technical commission and the state of the treasury are given by Mr. Montag.
The member of the audit commission, Mr. Jakub Ehrlich, declares that the commission was unable to establish the exact state of the society because the books are not kept formally, but he stresses that all expenditures and income are in the best of order.
After the reports a discussion develops, in which Messrs. Sobkowski, Langnus, Cygnaman, Podliński, Prener and Wajgtraub take part.
Dr. Rechtman replies to the various reproaches, and on the motion of Mr. Melach confidence is expressed in the outgoing board.
After Dr. Rechtman's address on future activity, the following board is elected by acclamation: Dr. Rechtman, P. Borgiblat[?], Mrs. Sara Lasker, Abraham Kromołowski, S. Rozenblum, Yechezkel Brzykowski, Z. Lichtenstein, A. Wajner, Y. Montag, Moshe Lasker, A. Ehrlich, P. Goldhar[?]. Deputies: M. Plesner, Ch. Krakowski, Yitzchak Tencer.
Audit commission: Jakub Ehrlich, Salek Trojb, Ss.[?] Sztajer.
In conclusion thanks are expressed to the editorial office of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung", to editor S. Lewkowicz, S. Rotenberg, Dr. Weinzieher, S. Fürstenberg and son, Dr. Rechtszaft[?], the Red Cross [and] the Magistrate for helping in the work for the benefit of "Hakoach".
To Messrs. Salomon Gutman and Naftali Ulert — thanks for handing over the sports ground.
Learned the “Laws of Ritual Slaughter” at the Wedding...

On Małachowskiego [?] Street a wedding celebration took place at the home of one of the underworld. Among the guests at the wedding there also came a member of the family, a certain "Felek", who was "popular" in the town.
During the dancing a quarrel broke out between Felek and one of his friends, and the latter did not think long: he pulled out a bayonet and with it "slaughtered" his friend Felek at the wedding.
After carrying out the bestial deed he drank down a hefty portion of vodka and then went off to the police station, where on entering he declared: "I have just killed a man".
Mayor Michel on the State List

In 16th place on the state list there figures, from the N.D. [National Democracy, the "Endeks"], the local town president [mayor] Michel.
On the same list there figures, from the B.B. [Non-Party Bloc for Cooperation with the Government], the president [mayor] of Dąbrowa, Dr. Mazejski[?].
On the Celebrations of 18 October and 11 November

On Friday a meeting was held at the Będzin starostwo [district office] of representatives of all political and economic organisations, representatives of the surrounding gminas [communes] and representatives of the press. On the agenda was the question of organising celebrations for the 10th anniversary of the great victory of the Polish army over the onslaught of Soviet Russia. A committee was elected, which Rabbi Lewin joined on behalf of the Jewish population. The festivities will be organised with a full parade and will at the same time be a demonstration against Minister Treviranus's speech.
At the session it was also resolved that on 11 November [listopad] the monument on 3 Maja Square in Będzin is to be unveiled.
Meetings

This coming Saturday night [motzei Shabbat] a parents' meeting will take place at Public School No. 4 (in "Piast"). Current questions of concern to Jewish parents will be discussed.
———
On Sunday[?] at 4 in the afternoon the annual general meeting of the leather guild will take place in the premises of the Artisans' Association.
At the meeting, besides the reports, important points for Jewish craftsmen of the leather and shoe trade will be discussed.
Zionist-Revisionist movement.
This Sabbath the annual general meeting will take place in the Zionist premises with the participation of the well-known youth leader Dr. Feldschuh (Ben-Shem).
The agenda comprises very rich content, which promises to be very substantial and instructive.
The general meeting has aroused great interest because at the meeting Mgr. Gutkowski will deliver a lecture on the topic: "The situation in the movement".
Sosnowiec — The Election Campaign Has Already Flared Up

Sosnowiec
The election campaign has already flared up.
Brawls between the Endeks and the Sanacja.
On Tuesday the Endek election committee held a pre-election meeting, at which the Będzin town president [mayor] Michel came forward with a speech. During the speeches a group burst in, which was out to disrupt the meeting. Having no grounds to disrupt the speaker, the group began to sing "The First Brigade".
In reply the Endeks began to sing the "Rota"; sticks from both sides also provided accompaniment. The police appeared in the hall and dissolved the meeting.
The Endeks' pre-election meeting in Dąbrowa had the same result.
Session of the Kehilla Board
On Sunday a session of the kehilla board took place. At the session several commissions connected with the activity of the kehilla board were elected.
Dr. Pawełek has left the P.P.S. party.

[Zagłębie — politics, Sejm elections.] These days the Central Committee of the PPS [Polish Socialist Party] in Zagłębie allocated its candidates for the Sejm elections. In first place figures the ex-deputy Bień [?], in second place the director of the mine workers, Bielik [?]; but in connection with the ordering [of the list] a split has occurred in the PPS committee in Zagłębie. As is reported, the lawyer Dr. Pawełek, whose candidacy was not taken into consideration, has left the PPS party.
Large conference of all Jewish artisans' associations

[Sosnowiec — artisans.] Owing to the situation that has arisen in the Central Committee and Executive of the Central Union of Jewish Artisans in Poland, by which the general and most painful interests of Jewish artisanry in Poland directly suffer — the Supreme Council of the Union of Jewish Artisans in Zagłębie, at its plenary session on Sunday the 5th of this month in Sosnowiec, resolved to call the representatives of all Jewish artisans' organisations in the territory of the whole Kielce voivodeship to a larger conference, which will take place on Sunday the 12th of this month at 10 o'clock in the morning in Sosnowiec.
Each organisation numbering up to 100 members delegates 1 representative; from 100 to 500 members — 2 representatives; and from 500 members and more — 3 representatives. All delegates must bring written authorisations from their local organisations.
The agenda of the gathering is: the guild law and the Jewish craftsman (on postponing the examination deadline for artisans by 3 years); long-term cheap credits for artisans; the situation in the Central Union of Jewish Artisans in Poland; our position on the Sejm and Senate elections.
A sukkah burned down.
[Czeladź — fire.] Avrom Epsztajn in Czeladź went out of the sukkah on Monday evening and left candles there, from which a fire broke out, and the sukkah went up in smoke.
Rockefeller subsidies for Zagłębie.

[Będzin district — health.] Of the Rockefeller subsidies received for the health institutions in the Będzin county (powiat), the "Sejmik" [county council] has allotted 3 thousand zł. to Sosnowiec, 2 thousand zł. to Będzin, 1,500 zł. to Dąbrowa and 2,500 zł. to Czeladź.
—o—
A resident of Bydgoszcz shot himself in Niwka
[Niwka — suicide.] The 35-year-old Knopf [?], a resident of Bydgoszcz, came to visit his brother-in-law in Niwka; on Sunday the guest went out into the street and did not come back.
After much searching the police found him shot dead in the nearby forest.
He had shot himself with his brother-in-law's revolver.
—o—
From Zionist life in Sosnowiec
[Sosnowiec — Zionism.] A short time ago, with the help of the Zionist Organisation, a Zionist youth organisation "Hashachar" was founded. The provisional committee has so far been conducting intensive work, and tomorrow at 6 in the evening, in the premises of the Zionist Organisation, the reorganisation of "Hashachar" will take place with the participation of the members of the Będzin and Olkusz "Hashachar".
Dąbrowa

[Dąbrowa — Zionism and youth movements.] Dąbrowa
From "Hechalutz".
In the premises of "Poalei Zion" (Right) the annual general meeting of "Hechalutz" took place. The meeting is opened by Mr. Frylich. Mr. Landner (Hashomer) is elected chairman. Reports are then given: on the secretariat — Mr. Magierkiewicz, on the treasury — Mr. Lustiger, on the KKL [Jewish National Fund] — Szojmer [?]. From the reports it emerges that "Hechalutz" numbers over 100 members and that the board was active in a range of fields.
After Mr. Lustiger's lecture on future work, discussions follow, in which take part: Bornsztajn, Wajswalk [?], Magierkiewicz, Grosfeld, Blicki and Lemkowicz. Then the following board is elected: Lustiger, Borgsztajn [as printed], Magierkiewicz and Gliksztajn, and one seat was reserved for "Poalei Zion". The meeting is closed with "Hatikvah".
From "Hashomer Hatzair".
To the convention of "Hashomer Hatzair", which opens on Sunday of Chol HaMoed, comrade A. Lemkowicz has been delegated from Dąbrowa.
Annual general meeting of the League for Labour Palestine.
Tomorrow afternoon the annual general meeting of the League for Labour Eretz Israel will take place in the premises of the Right "Poalei Zion".
Jabotinsky's Greeting to the Revisionist Conference in Sosnowiec

[Sosnowiec — Zionism, Revisionists; Zagłębie and Upper Silesia — short news.]
Preparations for the conference are in full swing. Over 200 guests and 70 delegates from the surrounding area are coming to the conference.
A letter of greeting has also been received from Jabotinsky, who writes, among other things:
"I wish success to your conference and to our movement; I ask you to convey a special wish to my friends of Brit HaTzohar in Sosnowiec — one of those fields in which it is worth sowing the Revisionist seed"...
—o—
Ministerial commission in Zagłębie.
Yesterday a commission on behalf of the Ministry of Commerce came to Zagłębie with the purpose of carrying out an inspection of the coal mines.
The commission's task is to establish whether the work in the mines is carried on within the framework of the regulations and whether the workers are protected from accidents.
—o—
Secretary of the trade union arrested.
On Wednesday, by order of the public prosecutor's office, the secretary of the trade union of textile workers, Mr. Karcher, was arrested.
The arrested man was taken to the Mysłowice prison.
—o—
Towards a split in the PPS?
In today's issue we report elsewhere the news that Dr. Pawlak[?] has left the PPS. The same example was followed by the well-known PPS activist[?] Radek and Szumański[?], who have also left the PPS party.
—o—
Working days in the coal mines are increasing.
In connection with the considerable improvement of the situation on the coal market, the normal working time has been reintroduced in almost all the coal mines of Upper Silesia.
Terrible Storm Winds in Upper Silesia

[Upper Silesia — short news; Zagłębie — crime.]
On Tuesday a terrible storm wind swept across Upper Silesia, tearing off roofs and breaking the telephone and telegraph wires, as a result of which there is great damage.
In Nowy Bytom the hurricane tore off the roof of a hospital building, as a result of which a woman was injured.
In Katowice the storm broke the electric wires on Krasińskiego Street.
A cart drove over the torn wires and the horse was killed.
—o—
Director of the "Klucze" paper factory robbed.
In the night from Wednesday to Thursday armed bandits broke into the flat of the director of the "Klucze" paper factory and, terrorizing [the household], the bandits robbed all the valuables that were in the flat.

Revisionist and Jewish Artisans' District Conferences Disrupted

On Sunday conferences of the Jewish artisans' associations, and of the Revisionists of the Kielce voivodeship, were to have taken place here. To the artisans' conference, at which the artisans' position on the Sejm and Senate elections was to be discussed, dozens of delegates had come[?] from the various towns and townlets, and members of the Central Union in Warsaw had also come.
The district conferences, however, did not take place. Right[?] before the opening the local police authority did not permit the artisans' gathering. A police guard stood in front of the building and did not allow anyone to enter the premises of the artisans' association.
———
The same fate befell the district conference of the Revisionists. Only the „academy“ (festive assembly) took place, in the theatre, chaired by Mr. Klarman. After greetings from a number of delegates, lectures were given by Dr. Wdowiński, Magister Gutkowski and others, who did not spare the honour of personalities in the Zionist world.
Trade Unions Closed in Upper Silesia

All the professional class unions in Upper Silesia have now been closed in Upper Silesia.
In the course of the day searches were carried out in the closed unions and at the homes of trade-union activists.
The reason for the closure, according to the official communiqué, is that the unions were dominated by revolutionary organisations which were preparing high treason.

Dynamite Explosion in the Flats of 2 Doctors in Beuthen
In Beuthen [Bytom] Doctor Spiker received a parcel by post. When he took the parcel in his hand an explosion occurred. The window panes were blown out, the walls cracked, and the doctor was injured.
At the same time Doctor Wilhelm also received [one]; he managed to run away. The room was completely wrecked.
The investigation established that the parcels had been sent from Zabrze[?]. They were tin cans filled with dynamite. Inside there was a device such that as soon as one opens the parcel the fuse ignites, and this sets off the explosion.

From the Latter Days [of the Festival].

[Będzin and Sosnowiec — Community life; Sukkot and Simchat Torah.]
The latter days of Sukkot "paid off" the "debt" of the first days. The sun was as warm as in summer, and thanks to that the streets were full of strollers.
In the Będzin city synagogue it was boiling as in a kettle — one sensation after another, and the public had plenty to talk about.
On the first days the conductor did not want to sing with the choir, and in honour of the latter days cantor Żupowicz[?] declared to the worshippers that he would not lead the prayers. Why? Quite simple: "if there is no flour there is no Torah" — since the gmina [the kehilla] pays no salary and there is nothing with which to prepare for the festival, — says the cantor — I will not lead the prayers...
And he kept his word: he indeed did not lead the prayers, and only at the request of the Chevra Kadisha gabbaim did he lead the morning service of Shemini Atzeret alone.
For the hakafot the Będzin synagogue this year had very "distinguished" guests. The "Pirster Zwad"[?], who in honour of Simchat Torah had been making merry at the "Rebbe's" in the apartment, came into the synagogue very drunk, brought along "good brothers" (non-Jews too) and by force took over control of the hakafot.
When the Chevra Kadisha gabbaim, who already hold the established right to honour people with hakafot, saw that they might get "real hakafot" [i.e. a beating], they left the synagogue.
As it turns out, the kehilla leaders were not entirely sure that the hakafot would pass off peacefully, for in the middle of the hakafot police appeared in front of the synagogue entrance.
———
In the Sosnowiec city synagogue, on Simchat Torah night, a fight took place between father and son. The fight was waged over a hakafa "transaction". Both of them, father and son, waged a competitive battle. In the end the father remained with the "merchandise".
In general the public made merry a little, tried to forget the prevailing crisis and allowed themselves to enjoy a drop of liquor.

A Bloc or a Bluff?

[Będzin — Sejm elections 1930; a united Jewish bloc.]
On Tuesday a meeting was held in the premises of the Zionist Organisation in Będzin, attended by representatives of all national and social movements (except the "Agudah").
On the agenda was the question of uniting all Jewish groupings in Zagłębie and of putting up a Sejm candidate specifically from Zagłębie Jewry.
After a lengthy discussion the initiative was handed over to the vice-president Mr. Rubinlicht: he is to prevail upon the "Agudah" to join the "united" Jewish election committee in Zagłębie.

Your Management. A Reply to the Municipal Public Figure

[Będzin — City council; polemic.] By Councillor Adv. Dr. Rechtman.
In the issue before last of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung", Mr. Rubinlicht took the floor in order to justify himself for the constant injustices that the Jewish population of Będzin suffers thanks to his specific methods.
His article consists first and foremost of personal attacks, to which I shall not reply. I would not have answered at all, so as not to stir up what [?] lies in the self-government mud.
But the matter must be cleared up.
Mr. Rubinlicht writes that an opposition of 3 persons formed "immediately after the elections". Yet a few lines further on he has already forgotten this and gives reasons (the ławnik [alderman] elections, a commission, etc.) that could only have arisen some weeks or months later.
Is that consistency? What connection do such "arguments" have with the truth?
After all, everyone in Będzin without exception knows that I — as the representative of the "Hitachdut" — have been in opposition in the present city council since the first sessions, when you, Mr. R., forcibly created a bloc against the will and interests of the Jewish population. Since then I have been fighting the methods and the "work" of the present ringleaders and politicians, with you at their head.
With your means, suspicions and politicking you have dazzled no one; your management is one great scandal, which I shall soon prove with figures.
You sing your own praises, saying that you "work with blood and sweat, one [...] [?] after another".
Which ones [i.e. which fruits] — we ask? Perhaps you mean the affair of the old market? Perhaps the ławnik elections? Perhaps the investment tax of 100,000 zł., which you with your own hands laid upon the impoverished Jewish population? Perhaps you mean the million-złoty budgets with tens of thousands of złoty in "per diems" and "pensions" for your hangers-on?
Perhaps you have in mind the "numerus clausus" against Jewish officials and workers that you introduced? Perhaps — the roughly 7 million in debts and heavy thousands in interest that the poor taxpayer will pay for your management?
Perhaps you mean the running bills of exchange and protests for about 400 thousand zł.? The deficits of the concrete works, etc.
You surely mean the banquets at the city's expense — thousands of zł. — with brawls of drunken councillors! Truly fine "customs" [?]...
With bought souls from right and left ("mshteygs gezunt" [?]) you have bolted yourself in, and that is your victory. What the city treasury says about it is superfluous to write.
You further write about "your" merits on account of certain subsidies. It is truly a disgrace! With a budget in 1929/30 of about 2 million — barely a few tens of thousands of zł. for institutions that cost Jewish society hundreds of thousands and that ought in fact to be maintained entirely by a city in which we pay 80 percent of the taxes.
And finally, the modest subsidies are not your merit either. The items you list have been in the Będzin budget for 2—3 terms already!
It was, after all, the previous city council that decided on building 2 schools and buying 2 [summer] colonies. Can you deny it?
You boast of 20 Jewish municipal officials!
Where are they?
In the summer colonies, which are run "derekh oyv" [?] by Dąbrowski-Gaszcz [?] for barely 2 months a year, you, Mr. R., find "his" 8 Jewish municipal "officials".
Can you mean that seriously?
Of the 20, then, 12 remain.
Subtract 3 members of the city council, de facto parliamentary representatives: myself, the Jewish ławnik, and the director, vice-president E—ch — 9 remain, of whom 3 have long been practising doctors. Of the 20 there remain barely 6 low-ranking officials, 3 in the magistrate and 3 in the electricity office.
6 out of about 130 officials.
A whole 4 percent — your joy..
And above all, the 6 officials were engaged (except for 1 [...] [?]) already during the previous term, and some of them after a hard fight with you, Mr. Rubinlicht!!
Where are your merits? What do you come to Jewish society with after 2 years of autocracy?
You criticise the opposition for working little.
Who fought over the old-market question? Do you know that the opposition travelled around at its own expense and intervened, lost time and money, and in the end suffered a defeat because of the intrigues of your false friends?
Who fought against your investment tax? Who demanded that the million-złoty budgets be reduced? Who fought your water-tax project with its fantastic water norms and a price of 60 groszy?
For 2 years we have been calling: give the population back the rebates on the electricity price that are due to the subscribers under the concession.
It is a matter of tens of thousands of zł. of public money.
We know that you are looking for excuses just so as not to pay out the money.
It is impossible to enumerate here our hard work, although our voice is stifled by the well-paid "communal workers".
You, Mr. R., write that the opposition works little. Should it, under such conditions, brawl with you?
In connection with the recent elections in the main electoral commission, where until now you held a monopoly, you criticise the Mr. President S. and are ironic about my "allies".
Let the Jewish public therefore know that in the recent elections almost all the Jewish councillors, after a prior understanding, voted for the candidate of the B.B. [?] [Non-Party Bloc, BBWR], Dr. Barylski [?], who failed because of 1 traitor, and therefore the B.B. [?] councillors — quite rightly and reasonably — wanted to have at least one representative and [?] consistently voted for their man.
Is that a sin?
Thank you for the intervention with the whole 2 N.D. [National Democrat] councillors to have them vote for me; if it is true, it is a... bear's favour [i.e. a disservice].

Only not on paper. II (What is happening with the control over our economic institutions — do they exist or not?)

Not long ago a Supreme Council of the Zagłębie Jewish artisans' organisations was created in Sosnowiec. What, then, is a supreme council? How do we picture this institution? What is it needed for, and what is its task?
It is not hard to understand that such an institution must have the task of seeing to it that the existing boards are active as they should be and bring benefit to the members. The Supreme Council must be the supervising authority, which should take pains to investigate and to supervise everything, to create what has not yet been created and to see to it that what is not being used is put to use.
The Supreme Council must therefore not allow the branch institutions to "sleep"; it must not forget that it was created only for the purpose of seeing to it that the institutions under it prosper intensively and that it should use everything in order to bring help and support to their members. It is high time that the members derived benefit from their institutions.
In the first chapter of this article we emphasised "only not on paper", i.e. if the institution does not occupy itself more or less with the work indicated above, does not see to progressing, does not see to unifying and concentrating the necessary economic activity, it will mean that the Supreme Council exists only on paper, and such "activity" not only brings no benefit, but on the contrary, it brings enormous damage, because people are sure that the institutions are under some supervision, and since in that case no faults are held against them, the members think that everything is in perfect order; and therefore we say that the Supreme Council is responsible for its activity both when it brings benefit, and all the more so when it exists only on paper.
That is what the Supreme Council must remember, and on every occasion it must render an account of the purpose for which it was created.
The necessity of creating the supreme institution cannot be overestimated. Firstly, great importance attaches to the concentration, the unified activity and the supervision of the activity of each institution in its town separately; this very awareness, that the institution is subject to a higher control, no longer allows the board of this or that institution to be paralysed; and secondly, it is in itself of great importance that every institution is subject to a certain control, which every board must reckon with, willy-nilly.
But, again the same thing — "only not on paper", because in that case the Supreme Council sins both against the institutions over which it has authority and against their members.
A higher authority of this kind has in fact already existed among us for about a year: a Central of the merchants' and small traders' associations in Zagłębie was created at the time, with its seat in Będzin.
It goes without saying that this institution is no less important than the Supreme Council that has been created, for who among us Jews is not a merchant or a small trader, and who among them is not wronged at every step? And that ninety percent of the wrongs are kept silent and swallowed with bitten lips is also a certainty; and that the existing trade associations are on the one hand weak and small and on the other hand helpless and powerless — that is not known only since today.
And therefore the value that the creation of such a trade Central would have had for us cannot be overestimated — a Central which in fact exists no more than on paper, for otherwise one would have heard of its activity, of its representation, of its board.
It would therefore be important to know what has become of this Central: does it still exist, and what does it do, what does its activity consist of, what has it created and accomplished in the course of the time since it was created? Which institutions has it improved and which have received reproaches from it? Which have been recognised by it as capable and useful and which — as incapable and harmful?
We have heard nothing at all from it, and therefore we do not know what its activity consists of.
If it no longer exists, we should have been told that too. If it has liquidated itself, it should have proclaimed this to the public, so that people should not live in error and should not think that the existing merchants' and small traders' associations have to submit to someone and be subject to the control of a higher authority.
It is a crime, an unheard-of crime, when such an institution exists only on paper; it does enormous damage to the people's interests, and such unheard-of frivolity must not be allowed.
The merchants' organisations in Zagłębie must at any price be concentrated and must be subject to some higher control, and only then can one hope for fruitful and unified activity; otherwise everything goes to waste and [—] not what is indeed being done [—] what is not, what can be done, and [—] cannot be achieved.
Just as the newly created Supreme Council must not exist [only] on paper, so too the Central of the merchants' and small traders' associations in Zagłębie must not exist only on paper, for if the artisans need a higher authority to show them what is useful and what is harmful, all the more do the merchants' and small traders' associations need it, because among them there are still [—] splits and [—] [?], still more unknown [?] and complicating things, which bring poverty into the ranks of the broad strata of the trading population.
Such a Central has many tasks on its life's path, and with diligent work it has a broad field of fruitful activity; therefore one must see to it that in this field fruits are produced [?] which can bring much benefit to the elements that need the fruits.
Let the Central, then, begin to demonstrate its useful activity.
E. S.
Napoleon and the Young Polish Countess Walewska

[History — Napoleon and Countess Maria Walewska; part 3.]
By M. Osherowitch.
3.
Not for nothing did Dmitri Merezhkovsky say in his book "Napoleon the Man" that although forty thousand books have already been written about him, about Napoleon, he has still remained the "unknown soldier"; that no one has yet penetrated the deepest depths of his soul — and that this is because Napoleon's soul is so great, so many-sided and so singular that it cannot be held captive on the pages of books.
Countess Walewska again did not answer Napoleon's second letter. Then he wrote her a third letter, again begging her not to reject him, to come to him. And in this third letter — having no other choice — he slipped in a hint that if she did not spurn his love, he would do something for her country.
"Your country," he wrote to her in that letter, "will become dearer to me if you take pity on your heart" [so printed].
By the same messenger he also sent her precious diamonds and a beautiful bouquet of flowers. But she was so delicate and refined that she sent the diamonds back to him. Let it not be said that if she did come to him after all, she had sold herself for diamonds...
—
The hint the great emperor had given in his letter about liberating Poland gave the whole affair a different direction. Instead of what had been a private matter between two people, it suddenly became an important national question.
The Polish noblemen [Yiddish "pritsim"], who were close to the young countess and knew what the emperor demanded of her, held a special consultation about it and resolved that she must sacrifice herself on the altar of the country...
Her own brother, Count Łączyński, expressed the same opinion. All the aunts and uncles sided with him too; none of them wanted to hear the young countess's arguments that she did not want to go to Napoleon, that it was a disgrace for her to become his mistress for a short time when she had not the slightest feeling of love for him...
And when they saw that she was so obstinate, they read out to her an address from the most distinguished Polish aristocrats and patriots. The address is very characteristic, and I shall therefore render it here word for word. It reads:
"Do you think that Esther gave herself to Ahasuerus because she loved him? Did not a shudder run through Esther's body when Ahasuerus looked at her? Did she not faint? And does this not prove that she felt nothing for him? She sacrificed herself to save her people and won [?] fame as her people's redeemer."
The address was read to the young countess by none other than the famous Polish patriot Madame Abramowicz; the countess's brother also argued at length, and when Walewska saw that she could no longer help herself at all, that the whole affair was no longer her private one but a national one, she bent her own dignity aside and went to Napoleon...
She came to him at night, between ten and eleven o'clock — tearful, dejected and ashamed.
She was disgusted by the fact that she knew, that she knew what she was going for...
She thought that when she entered Napoleon's presence and remained with him face to face, she would surely see before her a stern man with cold looks; she imagined how victory would gaze out of his grey, steely eyes and how he would take her without unnecessary ceremony, just as if she were a sacrifice thrown to him. And this plunged her into such a depressed mood that she sobbed hard and her legs seemed to give way under her.
Marshal Duroc [printed "Dura"], who brought her to Napoleon, later related that on the stairs she had to be carried [printed "she had to carry"], because she was so weak and so nervous that she could not walk.
It was one of the most terrible moments in the life of a tender, sensitive young woman whom circumstances had entangled in the net of a great task, which seemed to her not only small but also petty and ugly...
Her bad impression, however, was soon wiped away when she saw the emperor before her.
Quiet, gentle, with a soft look in his eyes, he stood before her; quietly and courteously he took her by the hand and seated her on a soft chair; he let her cry her fill, and then he began to talk with her in such a tone that she suddenly came to trust him, and when he asked her to tell him something about her married life, she told him, just as if he were an old friend of hers.
Her bearing aroused in him sympathy and fine, warm feelings.
Around two o'clock before dawn the young countess went home.
Just as innocent and just as pure as she had come...
She, the small, pretty, blonde countess, conquered the great conqueror with her refinement...
This can be seen from the little letter he sent her the next morning.
"Maria," he writes to her in the little letter, "my sweet Maria, my first thought is of you, my first desire is to see you again. If you do not come, the eagle will fly to you. I shall see you at dinner. I give you my word. I beg you, wear the bouquet of flowers I am sending you; it will be a silent messenger between the two of us while we are among people... In this way we shall understand one another: when you see that I lay my hand on my heart, you shall know that my heart is wholly yours; and in answer you shall press the flowers to your breast. Love me, my dear, charming Maria; do not take your hand away from the flowers!"
Three days later Countess Maria Walewska again came to Napoleon at night...
This time no one forced her any more; she came of her own free will...
No longer thinking that her coming here was a national duty...
And one must admit that it was the noble attitude of the mighty man and his great and earnest love that [—] the young countess [—] [the last lines are lost in a tear in the page]

Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings and remarks on this week's portion (Bereshit)

[Oneg Shabbat — weekly Torah portion.] Torah sayings and remarks on this week's portion.
Collected and adapted by Y. L.
Parshat Bereshit
—o—
a) Bereshit (1:1).
[—] The Torah begins with a bet, because the bet is [closed o]n three sides and open on only one side — the [n]orth side. „North“ (tsafon) signifies money („Gold comes out of the north“). [—] that only money makes a breach in the Torah, that [—] the north (money) — there the bet is open... Kli Yakar.
—o—
b) God created (ibid.).
The Midrash says that when God wished to create the [wo]rld, He took counsel with Truth, which said: „Do not create“ — no, it is not worth creating the world, for „it is all falsehood“. Peace, too, did not agree to the creation of the [wo]rld, „for it is all strife“ — for it will be full of quarrels. Well[?], [what] did God do? „The Holy One, blessed be He, cast Truth to the ground“ — God threw Truth [down] and created the world (Parasha 8).
[—] asks: and if Truth was removed, what [—] did Peace say? Peace, after all, was just as much an opponent as Truth, and yet it was not thrown away. [This] is the answer: if one throws away Truth, there can [no longer] be Peace either... Rabbi Mendel of Kotsk.
• • •
That is why Truth was the one thrown away: because, as the above Midrash says, the defenders of the world's creation were Lovingkindness and Righteousness. Righteousness argued: let the world be created, because people will give charity. [—] Lovingkindness likewise: the world will do acts of lovingkindness. But when Truth came and said that „it is all falsehood“, it means that all those charities will come from false, stolen[?] money. Well, such charity is already worth nothing at all. Righteousness is always mentioned together with justice, because charity given with dishonest money is hateful to God. Therefore the opposition of Truth is more dangerous than that of Peace, because with Truth's argument the defence pleas of Righteousness and Lovingkindness fall away — charity with dishonest money has no value.
Ohel Yaakov.
• • •
„When disorder is repaid in Israel, when the heads of the people volunteer“ — this is aimed at those who go bankrupt, do not pay their creditors, and hand out charity with a generous hand. To them one says: „bi-fro'a pera'ot be-Yisrael“ (pira'on — payment): when you have paid your debts, only then „when the people volunteer“ — only then may you distribute donations. Hida (Devash le-Fi).
—o—
c) And behold, it was very good (1:31).
A Yalkut says about this: „Good — this is the Angel of Life; very — this is the Angel of Death.“
„Good“ — he who is content with the little good that life gives him — „this is the Angel of Life“: he has a taste for life. „Very“ — he who wants everything „very, very much“, who chases after the superfluous, after luxuries — „this is the Angel of Death“: that is man's angel of death. R' Yaakov Krantz [the Dubno Maggid].
—o—
d) And man became a living soul (2:7).
Onkelos renders the verse „And man became a living soul“ as „and man became a speaking spirit“. It follows, then, that speech — man's speaking — is his vitality, his soul, and so from a person's words one can discover what he is in his inner essence.
Rabbi Israel Baal Shem Tov.
—o—
e) A help meet for him (2:20).
Rabbi Yeshayale of Prague[?] had a wife who was known as a shrew, and on top of that she was pious. When R' Yeshayale wanted[?] something to eat she would be saying Psalms. Thereupon R' Yeshayale said that now he understood the Gemara's interpretation: „If he is worthy — she becomes a help to him; if not worthy — against him.“ „If he is worthy“ — if one is fortunate — „she becomes a help to him“: she helps her husband; he sits and studies and she sees to it that he has something to eat and drink meanwhile. „If not worthy“ — if one has bad luck — „against him“: she, his wife, becomes his[?] competitor; he sits over the Gemara and she over the tkhine (women's prayer book).. Well, such a competitor is no luck at all for a husband...
—o—
f) And the Lord God caused a deep sleep to fall upon Adam (2:21).
That is why woman was created while Adam slept: because sleep is one sixtieth of death, and woman has in her a share, a root of death („a bad wife is more bitter than death“); the word mar means a drop, a small part — „as a drop of a bucket“..
—o—
g) She gave me of the tree, and I did eat (3:12).
Characteristic is the Baal ha-Turim's interpretation of this verse: „She gave me of the tree“ — she gave it to me with a stick over the head — „and I did eat“ — I had to eat...
—o—
h) And dust shalt thou eat all the days of thy life (3:14).
What sort of curse did the serpent receive here? To eat earth — on the contrary, that is a blessing! Earth is found everywhere, one need not toil for it, it never runs out; the serpent is surely the luckiest of all with it — all living people must toil so hard for their food, and he has it so easy.
But it is precisely in this ease — in the fact that it never runs short for him, that he need not seek his livelihood, that he need not ask God to send him sustenance — that the greatness of the curse lies: a creature that need not seek at all, nor ask — — —
Rabbi Simcha Bunem of Przysucha.
—o—
i) And Cain spoke to Abel his brother (4:8).
The Midrash says: Cain said to Abel: let us divide the world between us. Abel answers: good. Then Cain wanted precisely the place where Abel's offering had been accepted before God, and because of this their quarrel broke out.
Those public activists who, though they have enough room and honour in the world, find it all too little; they want to push into Abel's poor territory as well, they want to dominate the synagogue too, to become parnasim (community wardens) — everything is too little for them; even that small piece of the Temple's place they will not let Abel have — these Cains.
Yalkut ha-Drush.
—o—
j) This is the book of the generations of Adam (5:1).
Once an author came to a rabbi with a book and asked for an approbation. The rabbi leafed through the book and saw that it was worthless, so he said to him: „This is the book — this book — the generations of Adam“ — it has the same history as man. Man is created from earth and returns to earth after death. The paper of this book comes from rags; a machine made it into paper, and you have turned it back into a rag...
In Honour of the Sabbath.

By Leonidas.

The festival has ended with a crack
and been concluded with "Ḥazak",
now Bereshit comes back
in Moses' beloved Torah.

At the table stands the Torah reader
and he reads from the Torah:
"Bereshit bara" — through God's will
something was made from nothing.

It was waste and void,
without joy and without desire,
without form, without a shore,
without goal and without purpose.

Black chaos seethed
over bottomless abysses.
Deadness reigned all around,
cold darkness, still and mute.

And the spirit that creates and lives
hovered in calm
above this realm of death
like a swan above a river.

But suddenly, strong and bold,
the creative spirit
raised its face
and said: "Let there be light!"

"Still and cold is eternity.
Let us create light and t i m e!
Eternity is rest without motion —
let there be unrest and movement!

"Eternal rest is not good,
it cools the blood of creation.
Let there be dying, let there be becoming,
day and night and sun and stars!

"Let there be a beginning, let there be an end,
let there be reward and let there be punishment,
let there be life, which changes,
forever dying and renewing itself.

"Bereshit bara — forever comes into being
what has come to be on the earth.
What was and has passed
comes back and is made anew.

"Life is a tohu-va-vohu
filled with raw materials,
yet the creative power
forever shapes there and creates.
