On Monday, Hoshana Rabba, a sequestrator (tax bailiff) came to the flat of Mrs. Gelbard at Mandzhejer [Modrzejowska?] Street 11 and wanted to take away a sewing machine for a tax debt. Because the sewing machine is the only source of livelihood of the woman and her 17-year-old son, the young men Kamiński and Ha-gigman [?] began negotiating with the sequestrator that he should release the sewing machine and the tax debt be paid in instalments.
The negotiations did not bring the desired result, and the machine was taken out of the cellar [?] room.
While the machine was being carried out there arose, as we are told, an incident between the sequestrator and the owners of the machine, by which the sequestrator felt insulted, and he called a policeman, who, according to the sequestrator's statements, drew up a report against Messrs. Poslaniek [?], Abraham Kamiński and Alter Hagigman [?], who were accused of having thrown themselves at the sequestrator and of having thereby insulted the Polish state.
On the basis of this accusation the young men were arrested and sent to the investigating judge.
The arrested were released only the next day, but they are under police supervision.
When Will the New Station Building Be Opened?

[Będzin — railway, construction.]
The work on the building of the local railway station is already almost entirely finished, both outside [?] and inside, but the station will probably be opened in the first months of next year.
Preparations to Celebrate 11 November in Zagłębie

[Zagłębie — state holidays.]
Under the chairmanship of the starosta, Mr. Baksa [?], a meeting was held of the executive committee which is occupied with arranging the celebrations of the 10th anniversary of the Bolshevik invasion and the celebration of 11 November [Polish Independence Day].
After the discussion it was decided that the celebration should take place not on the 11th (Tuesday) but on Sunday, 9 November.
“And They Shall All Form One Band…”

[Będzin — municipality, water and sewerage.]
At the local magistrate [municipality] a conference took place with the participation of representatives of the Sosnowiec and Dąbrowa magistrates, with the aim of drawing up general regulations concerning water supply and sewerage in Zagłębie.
It was decided to prepare the appropriate material so that the question may be decided at the next conference, which will take place.
Minister Kwiatkowski Is Coming to Zagłębie

[Zagłębie — industry, government.]
On the 26th of this month Minister Kwiatkowski will be in Zagłębie, where he will take part in the 30th jubilee of the “Saturn” coal group.
The minister will also hold a series of conferences with representatives of industry in Zagłębie and Upper Silesia.
Wanted to Get “Lucky” in the Mikveh…

[Będzin — theft.]
On Sunday morning a visitor to Zylberberg's mikveh handed Zylberberg a wallet in which there were a few hundred zł. and bills of exchange.
Z. laid the wallet down on a bench for a while and later completely forgot about the deposit.
When the owner demanded his wallet back, only then did Z. notice that the deposit had vanished…
Because of this Zylberberg and the victim stationed themselves at the exit and began, without regard to anyone, to search the guests. The search was successful, and the one on whom suspicion fell threw away the “find”…
Tried to Steal Leather

[Będzin — theft, Jewish–Polish relations.]
On Monday afternoon 2 Christian thieves came into Fiszer's leather shop on Kołłątaja Street “to buy leather”.
While looking over the goods one of them tried to steal a soft hide; this was noticed by Fiszer's son, who detained the thieves, but the thieves put up resistance, and because of this a tumult arose in the street.
At the cries of Mr. Fiszer, who called the police, a benighted mob gathered, which began to incite that “the Zhids [?] are beating Christians”.
Amid the tumult one thief escaped through Erlich's house, and the second was brought [?] to the police station by the carter [?] (przewoźnik?) Sa-gacka [?].
For Insulting the Veterinary Doctor

[Będzin — trade, police.]
On the order of the starosta the veterinary doctor carried out an inspection (lustracja) of the food-product stalls in the market halls on Modrzejowska Street.
During the inspection the doctor was insulted by Jan Widawski, who was punished for it with two weeks' prison.
Poisoned by a stove.
At Modrzejowska[?] 68 a Christian couple was poisoned at night by fumes from a stove. A doctor was called at once, who brought the poisoned couple back to consciousness.
A daring burglary in Ząbkowice.

During the night from Wednesday to Thursday the apartment of Director Jaszarski[?] in Ząbkowice was broken into.
The thieves took several household articles and a fur coat worth 12 thousand zł.
Meeting of the Jewish leather guild.

On Sunday the annual general meeting of the local Jewish leather guild ("tsekh") took place in the premises of the Artisans' Association. The meeting was opened by Mr. Y. Tuchsznajder, and the chair was handed over to Mr. D. Kilsztok.
After the reports of Messrs. Klajnman and Fajgenblat a discussion developed on the activity of the board, which in the end received continued confidence.
The new board includes: Klajnman (starszy — guild master), Tuchsznajder, Abragik[?] and Messinger (podstarszy — deputy masters), Ickowicz, Fridman, Szwarc, Markowicz, Rozenberg, Zeliger, Blacharusz[?], Kahan and Berner.
The meeting was informed that two delegates of the guild had been delegated to the examination commission in Kielce.
A worker falls and is killed.

By the gymnasium building on Premis[?] Street the following unfortunate accident occurred the day before yesterday[?].
While unloading boards from a cart, the 49-year-old worker Maciąg[?] slipped and fell face down onto the pavement. The fall, however, was so fatal that the worker received a severe wound[?] to the head and died a few hours later in the local hospital.
An unsuccessful theft.

During the night from Monday to Tuesday a certain thief tried to get into a provisions store on Kościuszki Street.
While the thief was busy with his "work", the storekeeper welcomed him with a revolver shot.
After receiving first aid the thief was taken to the local jail.
Suicide.

On Tuesday the 25-year-old Kosowska drank a small bottle of vinegar essence with the aim of committing suicide. The would-be suicide was taken to hospital in a serious condition.
—o—
"From the Hitachdut"
Tomorrow afternoon there will be a lecture by Mr. Yaakov Białopolski (Warsaw) on the topic "The paths of working Eretz Israel after the congress in Berlin". Afterwards the annual general meeting will take place with the participation of Mr. Białopolski.
—o—
At the Revisionists.
Today, Sabbath, the continuation of the general meeting takes place in their own premises. On the agenda: discussion of the reports submitted and election of a new board.
The meeting takes place at 2 in the afternoon regardless of the number of those present.
Sosnowiec — a double suicide.

Vice-President Jarży[?] shoots himself and his wife.
Yesterday at 10 in the morning the former vice-president [of the city] Jarży was walking with his wife on Teatralna Street.
Suddenly several revolver shots were heard, and the above-mentioned persons lay on the pavement in a pool of blood.
First Jarży shot at his wife, who was wounded, and then he shot himself and fell dead on the spot.
The cause of the incident is so far unknown.
The murder and suicide caused a great sensation in the town.
The candidate list submitted.

Today, Friday, the district list will be submitted, on which the following figure as candidates in our electoral district: Messrs. Gen[?], Deputy Hartglas, Adolf Trusker, Engineer Czerniaków and others.
The Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce in Radom.

The local Chamber of Commerce [of Sosnowiec] has taken the initiative to organise, from time to time, regular meetings of industrialists and merchants in other towns outside Zagłębie.
The first meeting took place on Sunday the 12th of this month in Radom. Taking part in the meeting were delegates of the voivodeship [województwo; doubtful reading], representatives of the local authorities, councillors of the Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce and a large number of Radom merchants.
The meeting was opened by the president of the local Chamber of Commerce, Mr. Gadamski [?], who explained the aim of the regular meetings.
Then papers were read by Director Czernichowski and others.
PPS leaders in Zagłębie.

In connection with the split in the ranks of the PPS [Polish Socialist Party] in Zagłębie, the well-known PPS leaders Pużak and Niedziałkowski stayed here this week and held a series of consultations with the local party leaders.
It is conjectured that a list of candidates of the Independents will be formed, headed by Dr. Patelek [?].
An interesting trial at the District Court.

In September [wrzesień] 1928 the well-known trial took place at the local District Court against several Jewish merchants and forwarding agents, the inspector [rewident] Chomczyk [?] and the head [kierownik] of the local customs office, who were accused of illegally importing colonial goods from abroad.
At the time the accused were acquitted by the local District Court.
The prosecutor, however, lodged an appeal with the Supreme Court in Warsaw, which quashed the first verdict and ruled that on 6 November [listopad] the trial is to take place for the second time at the local District Court.
Winter air-travel timetable.

As of yesterday the winter timetable of Polish air transport has been introduced.
According to the new timetable, planes leave Katowice for Vienna via (Brno) every Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday at 11:15 in the morning.
Direct from Katowice to Vienna they leave at 11:15 on the days: Monday, Wednesday and Friday.
The new timetable is valid until 15 March 1931.
—o—
From "Hashomer Hatzair".
The local "Hashomer Hatzair" has decided "to renew the former Jewish tradition of 'kinyan sefarim' [acquiring books]".
For this purpose a badge sale was held on Hoshana Rabbah, which brought in 342 zł. 97 gr.
— Tomorrow a members' meeting will take place in its own premises, at which current important matters will be discussed.
Bloody brawl in the Czeladź beit midrash

For a long time now there have been sharp quarrels between M. Gragrin [?] and his son-in-law Hamburger. As a suitable moment to take "revenge" both sides used the night of Shemini Atzeret, when in the beit midrash a bloody brawl with knives broke out between them.
The family "war" was liquidated only by the police, and the epilogue will take place in court.
Items forgotten on the tram

During the month of September [wrzesień] various passengers, while riding the tram, forgot the following items: 1 booklet entitled "Z minionych dni" ["From days gone by"], 1 bag, a work suit, bicycle parts, several pairs of old stockings, a small suitcase [preceding word unclear], a pair of leather gloves, a lady's umbrella, a man's umbrella, a walking stick, 2 Yiddish booklets, 2 men's shirts, 1 man's hat, a lady's shawl.
—o—
A "treasure" found in the sand.
In Piaski, boys of local workers were playing in the sand; while digging they came upon a "treasure".
The boys ran to their parents to announce the good news; soon a large crowd gathered and jostled [?] around the "treasure", but instead of money, mining tools and "black diamonds" were found.
Dąbrowa

From the League for Labour Palestine.
On Saturday, the 3rd day of Chol Hamoed [Sukkot], a general annual meeting of the "League for Labour Eretz Israel" took place in the premises of the P.Z. [Poalei Zion] (Right).
Reports were given: general report on the activity — Sh. Grossfeld; secretariat — Y. D. Szywek; treasury — Chana Spielberg; press — Sh. Kożuch [?].
From the reports it emerges that in the year 5690 up to a thousand zł. were collected for the P.A.S. [?].
Elected to the new committee were the following members: P.Z. (united with Z.S. [Tzeirei Zion]) Y. D. Szywek, Shimon Grossfeld, Shlomo Kożuch [?]; "Hashomer Hatzair" Chana Spielberg; "Gordonia", "Hitachdut" (bloc) Avraham Frydman.

Sunday matinee: The Tales of Hoffmann,
Sunday evening: "Der Franka" [?],
Tuesday: "Palestragt" [?].

Detailed report on the district conference of the Revisionists in Sosnowiec

[Detailed report on the district conference of the Revisionists in Sosnowiec]
The Sosnowiec Revisionists made great preparations for the conference of the Zionist Revisionists of the Kielce voivodeship, but on the day [?] of the conference the starost gave them a surprise: he revoked the permit for the sessions, and they had to content themselves with the first part only — the opening, which bore a festive character.
Early in the morning "new faces" were noticed in the streets of Sosnowiec: these were delegates from the whole voivodeship and Betar members from the surrounding towns, who wanted to march through the streets, but the starost did not permit this either.
The conference began with an Eretz Israel academy (gala meeting) in the municipal theatre. After the orchestra played the Polish and the Jewish anthems, Mr. Klarman delivered the opening address, in which he dwelt on the idea of the "Judenstaat". At the end of his speech he read out a letter of greeting from Jabotinsky, which was received by the assembly with stormy applause.
Greetings were then delivered: on behalf of the Sosnowiec kehilla — Mr. Levi Jungster; the Zionist Organization in Będzin — Mr. Marek Szajn; the Zionist Org. in Sosnowiec — Mr. Wolf Gitler; "Mizrachi" — Mr. Chaim Kupermintz; the Betar command in Poland — deputy commander Gold; WIZO — Mrs. Rosman; the directorate of Keren Tel Chai — Mr. Unger; Betar Sosnowiec — commander Glidman; Betar Będzin — Pinchas Szajnerman; "Tze'irei Mizrachi" — Mr. Meir Tzvi Jungster; "Keren Hayesod" — Mr. Tencer; "Keren Kayemet" — Mr. Feinreich; the artisans — Mr. Gachtman [?]; the small traders — Mr. Feldman [?]; the Revisionists of Katowice — Mr. Karalnik [?]. Of the written greetings the following deserve mention: the Revisionist Executive in London, the Revisionists and Betar in Eretz Israel, the Zionist Central Committee in Poland, Keren Hayesod and Keren Kayemet in Poland, the chairman of the Va'ad HaRabbanim Rabbi Hager, "Masada", and others.
Dr. Feldszua [?] discussed the present critical political situation in Zionism, which Weizmann has brought about with his "all-right" policy.
Dr. Wrachinski [?] spoke about the Zionist youth, which has moved away from the pure Zionist ideal and serves the socialist appetites [?]; he holds that the only youth that has remained faithful to Herzl's ideal is Brit Trumpeldor.
Mgr. [?] Wtkowski [?] sharply criticised the present Central Committee. Among other things he mentioned the agreement that the C.C. concluded with "HeChalutz", although this is not in accordance with the resolutions of the national convention.
Dr. Lipman gave an overview of the convention of the Radicals in Lwów, the last session of the Zionist Actions Committee in Berlin and the Revisionist convention in Prague. Analysing the three conventions, the speaker demonstrated the justice of the Revisionists' demands over [?] the last years.
With the strains of "Hatikvah" the academy was closed.
On behalf of the conference the following telegram in Hebrew was sent to Jabotinsky, who is celebrating his 50th jubilee: "Wherever you go — we shall go; your victory is the victory of pure Zionism; go forth and prosper."
How the Former Vice-President of Sosnowiec „Settled Accounts“ with His Wife.

[Sosnowiec — crime; family tragedy.]
The bloody family tragedy that took place in Sosnowiec last Thursday is still veiled in a fog of mystery.
As the investigation shows, Kazimierz Jarosz, after his removal from the Magistrat [city council executive], found himself in material difficulties. Life between the couple, however, remained undisturbed until the split in the ranks of the PPS. Only then did the first frictions occur, and they grew sharper after Mrs. Jarosz took up [work] in the office of Dr. Pawałek [?].
Mrs. Jarosz, who had joined the „Fraks“ [the PPS-Frakcja faction], decided to divorce her husband. On the critical day the couple left the apartment; Mrs. Jarosz went to Dr. Pawałek's office, and Jarosz, after taking leave of his wife, rode off on the tram.
A few minutes before 10 Mrs. Jarosz left the office with Mrs. Wanda S., intending to go to the court.
At the corner of Teatralna and Sienkiewicza streets she was stopped by her husband, to whom she put the question in surprise: „What are you doing here?“
The husband, instead of answering, asked:
— Is Dr. Pawałek at home?
— He is not — the woman answered.
— Really not? — asked the husband.
— He is not, he has gone to Zawiercie, to the court.
At that moment Jarosz took the Browning out of his upper pocket and fired 3 shots.
The first bullet singed the face of Mrs. Wanda S. The second bullet pierced the neck of Mrs. Jarosz, and the third bullet he turned into his own heart, falling dead on the spot.
The police, who arrived at once, made a search, finding on the deceased a number of documents and one złoty and 19 groszy.
On Sunday the doctors removed the bullet from Mrs. Jarosz. The patient's condition is satisfactory. If no complications arise, she will soon recover.

Weapons Confiscated from Members of the PPS.

[Zagłębie — police; politics.]
The security authorities had for some time been receiving confidential information that the PPS militia possessed arms, guns and ammunition.
In this connection, on the night from Sunday to Monday the police carried out searches at the homes of PPS members in Sosnowiec, Będzin, Dąbrowa and Czeladź, where several dozen Brownings of the newest model and several thousand bullets were found.
The weapons were confiscated and handed over to the investigation office in Sosnowiec.

„Hakoach“—„Zagłębie“ 0:2 (0:2)

„Policja“ K.S. (Katowice) — „Hakoach“ 2:3 (2:0)
Once again the Będzin players have shown that they are now in very good form. The exchange with fresh players turned out to the team's advantage. In the first half „Hakoach“ had more of the game; splendid combinations quickly lead to the Katowice goal. In the 13th minute Szymek 3 shoots at goal, the ball rebounds [?] off Gutman [?] and goes into the goal. A few minutes later Gutman shoots the second goal from Richter's „centre“. After the change of ends the guests come to life and, thanks to their hard play, manage not only to equalise but also to score the winning point, with the help of the „Hakoach“ goalkeeper Neuberg [?]. The Rozen brothers [?] distinguished themselves, again having no luck in the second half, since they were injured. Jankielewicz 2 and Gutman also played well. Referee Mr. Mazur good.

Anything but abstention!

So the lists have been submitted, and the Jewish front is broken.
And the voter stands confused and does not know what to do, for whom to vote.
And this very confusion [?] spreads among the masses the poison of abstention — of standing aside and simply not voting.
That would be the worst thing of all.
There is nothing more harmful than the citizen's evading [?] the use of his right to determine the fate of his country.
The practice of parliamentarism has shown masses of cases in which mandates were lost because of single votes.
One must remember that although the Zagłębie Jewish mandate is in great danger, as the calculations of the previous elections show [?] — all that was with a turnout of 50–60 percent of the voters; but there are moments that demand a maximum exertion of the social forces, and if our masses are permeated with a sense of responsibility and go to the ballot box in double the usual numbers, then the picture becomes quite different and the impossible becomes possible.
We understand the disappointment and apathy that seized the voter when he learned, at the last moment, how the Jewish leaders haggled like shopkeepers over the mandates, how their stubborn [?] ambition broke and disrupted all our hopes.
Let the voter then consider who is most to blame for this, and which of the candidates put forward deserves more trust.
There is still time for that. The election campaign, which will surely be conducted at the proper pace, will help the man in the crowd to find his way both in the political problems and in the tactics of all the contending parties.
There is still time to decide for oneself for whom to vote. But one must not let the interest fall asleep; abstention would be a crime.
Let the voter know that vote he must, for his social duty will call him to the ballot box; and let him, by his interest and his search for the truth, bring it about that the election campaign now beginning leads the Jewish street to complete clarity.
Let us not forget for one minute that both contending Jewish parties are, after all, together only one front with respect to the other side. This thought must spur us to the strongest interest in the elections.
P. K.
A letter from Kraków

(The beginning of the school year. — The nationality question [?].)
The academic year has already begun, and with it the specifically academic life. Masses of students from various towns and shtetls all over Poland have arrived in Kraków. The streets, bookshops, libraries, etc. are full of them.
At the university the youth bustles — a large generation [?]. Despite all the voices that have lately appeared in the press about the surplus among the working intelligentsia and in the free professions, despite all the opinions about the pointlessness [?] of the studies, the influx has not become smaller.
The number of Ukrainian students has grown this year because the doors of the Lwów university were closed to them, as a response to the recent uncivilised acts through which Ukrainian nationalism expressed itself.
At the same time the academic associations began their work. A whole series of general meetings took place. At the meeting of "Ha-Shachar", which is the strongest Zionist association in the academic field in Kraków, Dr. Schwarzbart spoke with tears in his eyes about the question of the nationality which the Jewish students declare. It is truly sad that now, after so many years of struggle and work, one still has to clarify the question of Jewish versus Polish nationality. The statistics show that more than half of the Jewish student youth do not declare themselves of Jewish nationality. There was a time when the Polish universities did not want to recognise and grant equal rights to "the Jewish nationality". The Jewish youth waged a struggle. It was after the World War, in which Poland came forward with democratic and national demands and realised them; the Jewish academics came forward with the same slogans. But those who on one side preached and fought in the name of various ideals and demanded their realisation for themselves, on the other side violated those same ideals with regard to the Jews. But after a long time victory came. Jewish nationality was recognised — and the larger part did not declare Jewish nationality! Laconically ring the reports: wyznanie mojżeszowe [Mosaic faith] — 30 per cent; narodowość żydowska [Jewish nationality] — 11 per cent. The figures speak for themselves.
It brings a material loss, because the university distributes the subsidies in proportion to the number of members. And so the size of the subsidy which the Jewish institutions receive depends on the number of academics who are included in the Jewish nationality; and those who do not declare themselves of Jewish nationality reduce the income of the Jewish self-help institutions — yet come themselves and benefit from them.
But the most important thing — where is the human dignity, where is the national pride of those who are supposed to lead the people and be an example to it?!
A. Gertner.
An important collection campaign

(On the sale of stickers for the benefit of the "Talmud Torah".)
For several months now the "Chinese walls" that fenced in the Będzin "Talmud Torah" have been broken down. The "finance gabbaim" [?] have managed to raise the institution to such a level that, besides the sacred studies, which are conducted according to a certain system, secular subjects are also taught to the poorest children, and all the preparations for the Talmud Torah to be licensed within the framework of a public elementary school are in full swing.
But the main nerve, so that everything should function properly, has been weakened. The financial situation, owing to the present colossal expenses, is critical, and the deficit grows from day to day.
For this reason, for the "first" time since the Talmud Torah has existed, a sale of stickers is being organised, which begins this coming Sunday and is carried out by specially delegated women and men.
Let everyone who buys the sticker bear in mind the saying "Take heed of the children of the poor" [for from them Torah will come forth]: that in the present bitter time the Talmud Torah is the only place where poor children are taught; let him not get off with paltry groschen, but give for the sticker according to his means, for — "the study of Torah outweighs them all"...
Sh. L. [?]
He Took the Last of His Wife's Possessions and Abandoned Her.

[Będzin — desertion case.] Mrs. Regina Oszerowska, living in Będzin at Kołłątaja 41, came to the editorial office and told the following story of her tragic fate.
Eight months ago she married a certain Jakub Lichtensztajn, who lived with his parents in Pogoń[?]. Soon after the wedding Lichtensztajn took a fancy to going to Paris. (He had been there before the wedding.) At first the young wife had no wish to emigrate, but when her husband kept pressing her and did not stop persuading her that in France "they would be happy," she finally agreed to her husband's plan to go to Paris.
Lichtensztajn set about completing all the formalities, such as passports and visas, and when everything was almost ready the couple sold their furniture and came to Będzin for the holiday, to her mother. The departure for Paris was to take place 8 days after Sukkot.
Now it turns out that the husband had all along been working out a cunning[?] plan against his wife. Without his wife's knowledge he had prepared himself a passport with a visa for Paris, and on Wednesday, at the close of the holiday, he said that "he was going to Warsaw, where through string-pulling with military people he knew he would obtain reduced prices for the passports and visas"...
The naive woman believed everything the "faithful" husband uttered, gave him the 1,500 zł. she had from the sale of the furniture — and he vanished...
When the young wife realised that she had fallen victim to her own husband, she came to the editorial office so that we should announce "to the whole world" that Jakub Lichtensztajn has left behind in Będzin a pregnant wife without any means of support.
All Jewish newspapers are asked to reprint this report.

What I Heard, What I Saw.

[Będzin — local feuilleton.] By Ben Amotz.
The "Będzin Ghetto"...
That Będzin is a mother-city in Israel, a town with rare antiquities — that was clear to me; but that in this distinguished town there is also a "ghetto" — that I only learned this week.
A few town activists were standing and debating (pilpul-style) about municipal matters until the conversation "came down" to the eruv — more precisely, to the lamentable eruv, which was broken no less than thirty weeks in the course of one year...
And one of them says: Do you know, gentlemen, that on Małachowskiego Street there is a "ghetto"?
— What?
— Yes, he says, up to Trapojer's[?] house one may carry on the Sabbath, beyond it — not...
— But a whole community of Jews lives there?...
— Well, so what, who cares that Jews desecrate the Sabbath.
— Where are the "Shomrei Shabbat" society, the Eruvin society and in general the whole holy gang?
— It's all on paper. What then — he says — if they don't repair the eruv, which should cost no more than ten gulden, will anyone take care that the Jewish residents on "that side" don't desecrate the Sabbath unwittingly?...
Grünbaum knows them..
He grew up with respectable householder parents; his father owned a house on Kołłątaja Street; he himself — a quiet man, only unfortunate by nature.
— A cripple, he has only one hand...
He stands in the street selling Jewish newspapers, and from that he supports himself and his household...
So he, the Jewish cripple, came into the Agudah bank; the clerks buy newspapers from him, but a Hasidic Jew met him (one known, of all things, as a solid, quiet man), who shouted:
— "Out of here with the goyish newspapers, this is a Jewish bank!"...
The newspaper-seller left the bank embittered and ashamed, and before us, with tears in his eyes, poured out his bitter heart...
We listened and kept silent; only the bystander who had witnessed the scene said:
"Apparently Grünbaum knows the Agudah crowd well, if such a quiet man should suddenly become such a zealot and take revenge in so low a way — that never entered his mind."
— Yes, Grünbaum knows them...
Let us unite.
A Jewish woman comes into the editorial office, middle-aged, with Jewish grace and modesty, and demands of the editors too that we do something in this field.
The woman argues thus:
— You don't know anything, Mr. Ben-Amotz, about what goes on in Jewish homes today. The modest Jewish daughter has become a ruin. No woman is safe with her husband; go ahead and find yourself a house where no young women neighbours live — even that doesn't help: they creep into the neighbouring houses, into strange streets, and talk strange men round. That's what they do — one snatches from the other; "there is no house where there is not one dead." The men are not to blame at all... And why should it be so, why shouldn't the wives make an agreement among themselves that one shall not take away the other's husband, not talk him round, not carry on[?] with strange men, not flirt with anyone — that would be good for all and look decent before the world.
Let us unite, the woman appeals — to all her sisters — let us be loyal to one another, and if a man attaches himself to a strange woman, the lawful wife must be told about it, and such a woman must be boycotted, put under a ban; one woman should help the other guard her husband, for today — me, tomorrow — you; no one knows who is walking behind his back...
We did the woman's bidding and have published her appeal.
A request from a community
The communities of Zagłębie are known as places of generous charity. When any community needs support, one immediately turns to the Jewish communities in Będzin and in Sosnowiec.
Such an appeal for help we have also received from the community of Olpiny near Biecz.
Its content is as follows:
"Behold — it is known to everyone that the community of Olpiny near Biecz has existed for 150 years already, and in all that time the community has not turned to anyone for support; only now, after the war, the town has been burnt down and impoverished.
50 per cent have emigrated and everything has been ruined[?]; and now the peasants come and destroy the cemetery, in which holy rabbis and Torah scholars lie — they plough it over and cut the grass.
Therefore we ask you very much, Jews, merciful sons of merciful fathers, that you be of help to us to fence the 'house' [the cemetery], and by this merit the Blessed Name will help you with all kinds of salvation, and 'He will swallow up death forever.'
The Holy Community of Olpiny near Biecz."
A very important matter. Perhaps this appeal will at the same time remind the Będzin and Sosnowiec communities that they too should think about it, that "the Zagłębie peasants shall not plough over the graves"...

The Dead Machine...

[Essay — the machine and unemployment; sound film and the musicians.]
By Dr. A. Mukdoni.
The man who works and creates was frightened to death of the first machine. [A machine] which merely mimics the doings of the living man, which imitates him more cheaply[?], dully, and with a cold and dull impetus.
The man who works and creates sensed in the dead machine a dangerous, cruel and rapacious[?] competitor.
A dead, cold machine advances upon living people; it comes to darken and embitter his life.
So cried, in great despair, the simple working[?] and creating people.
People laughed at these benighted folk who were frightened of the great, important and heroic deeds of awakening mankind; the savages who fell upon the first useful shoots of civilization were harshly punished.
Every new machine was celebrated in song by the educated, and every new machine cast terror upon those who work with their living hands.
And the singers of the machine's praises and the wardens of civilization won.
The machine became the idol, and the further it went, the greater and greater grew its power over people.
Now the machine is the new but almighty idol, to which people bow, before which millions upon millions of people kneel.
— Almighty machine.
A fervent faith — accompanied, as is the way of things, by a dark superstition — in the machine has seized the world; people wait for wonders, for miracles and for the redemption of the world from it, from the dead, cold and dully-impetuous[?] machine.
And in this fervent faith and superstition in the almightiness of the machine, the fattened capitalist and the dried-up communist meet. Both pray in one minyan to the machine. Both hop together at the "Kadosh" before the almighty machine.
And the working man keeps silent; he has been shouted down, but he is still, deep in his heart, the enemy of the cold and dead machine.
He, the worker, has indeed not died of hunger; his fear that the machine would tear the morsel of bread out of his mouth was exaggerated — the piece of bread [it left him]; [but] the dead machine has taken from him the blessing of labour, it has robbed him of the creativity of his work, it has plundered from him the freedom, the little bit of independence and joy in his work.
The dead machine has made the living, creating man its mute slave. The living man has become the servant, the accursed Canaanite slave of dead wheels, steel teeth, leather belts and boiling cauldrons.
Poets sing songs and praises to it, and great minds stand before the machine with the greatest reverence — so the simple working man is ashamed to voice his hatred of the almighty idol — of the machine.
———
And the machine watches people, what they do, and imitates everything: human hands are already almost superfluous. The wondrous, mysterious and creative human hands have almost nothing left to do. They can only tend the machine with a few counted mechanical movements.
And dead objects the machine casts out of itself; these objects possess no living breath of any human warmth.
So the world is now full of dead objects.
Dead creations of the dead machine.
When people look for a living object, something that human hands have made, they pay large sums for it. Let it be old, let it be hundreds of years old — as long as living hands made it, as long as human breath can be felt from it, as long as one senses life in it.
And the dead machine does not stop; day by day it makes man ever more superfluous in the world. It becomes the great mistress of life, and the exalted king of all creatures, the deposed[?] majesty — man — has become the servant of the machine.
And no one is safe, no one.
Who, for instance, imagined that one fine morning tens of thousands of musicians would get up and discover that they are superfluous in the world, and that the machine is already an artist too, that it can sing and play all instruments?
It never occurred to the musicians that some machine would come along that would sing and play like an instrument.
So one fine morning tens of thousands of musicians were left without work; tens of thousands of people face the very near danger of dying of hunger.
Now the machine plays in thousands of cinemas; it plays instead of the tens of thousands of living players. And hardly anyone gets anything out of it. The cinema-goers who enjoy music get, for the same money, dead machine-music, music without a soul, invalid music, desecrated music; they pay the same price as for living human music — the dead machine simply swindles them, the machine that came and, before our eyes, brought misfortune on thousands of musicians' families, and no one took fright, no one raised a voice.
Hush — the almighty machine is allowed everything.
When a river overflows its banks and brings disaster on a district, or on a settlement of a few tens of thousands of inhabitants, there is at once a great panic.
A flood.
And here a machine has done far worse than a flood.
A flood does subside after all: the water recedes and people return to their places, eat the same bread, go on leading the same life; but a little music-machine has come for a long time, perhaps for ever, and those who suffered no longer have any hope at all of getting back to their piece of bread.
And about such a catastrophe, about such a slaughter at the hands of the dead machine, nobody speaks.
The machine, the almighty machine.
A fervent superstition has seized us.
The almighty machine, the redeemer of the world.
Here go about pious, God-fearing citizens, anguished[?] with worry for our poor morality; they are constantly afraid lest it, God forbid, be harmed. Why are there no such good and pious citizens who would go looking for harmful machines, which bring no benefit to the public at large and take away the morsel of bread from tens of thousands of people?
There is, after all, a censorship of harmful books — why should there not be a censorship of harmful and senseless machines?
When an individual takes away someone's property, or his ability to make a living, he is a criminal: he is tried and convicted. Why may this be done behind the shoulders of a machine?
Why may he, with the help of a machine, throw tens of thousands of musicians out into the street?
Who needs this machine? Whom does it benefit? What does it create?
And who knows what kind of machine will come tomorrow?
Tomorrow other tens of thousands of people who work and create may be thrown out.
Is the machine already the devil to whom mankind has sold its soul?
Thousands, tens of thousands of destroyer-machines stand and wait to be let loose upon working and creating people.
Someone acquainted with the flood of inventions has said that if all the inventions were released, a real catastrophe would befall the world.
Everything, absolutely everything the machine will do; people will become entirely superfluous in their own world.
There will remain only a small handful of busy[?] people who tend the machines.
And later the tenders too will become superfluous: one machine will be left to tend the others.
Something horrible is creeping up on this poor world of ours.
Why not a censorship of the rampaging machine?...
Down with the Men!

[Sosnowiec — satirical feuilleton; Sejm elections, women in politics.] By J. Oberżanek [„אבערזשאנעק“].
Feigele [“little bird”].
That is her name, my wife's “koleżanka” [friend].
Why is she called Feigele and not “łabędź” [swan], or even “sosna”[?] [pine]? To my mind she ought to have been called “Skyscraper”, not Feigele. If you could only see this “Feigele”!... In short, she is tall and thin, with a neck stretched out like a swan's. I am no runt myself, after all — in the army I was a “cavalryman” — and yet next to her I look like a teakettle next to a samovar...
Until a few years ago this “Feigele” was a Jewish wife like all Jewish wives: she baked kugel, cooked and nagged[?] [„געפיאדעט“] her husband... But ever since the new “wynalazki” [inventions] appeared, ever since gramophones and radios appeared, the Feigele has turned into a “ptaszek” [little bird]. Every day she studies the radio programme and searches for “fale” [waves]. She “connects” [„פאלאנטשעט זיך“ — łączy się] to Mussolini's speeches — Rome; she knows exactly when to “catch” the Roman opera and when to “catch” Paris. A complete master at tuning the “lines”[?] [„ליניעס“], she knows what “krótka fala” [short wave] means and what “długa fala” [long wave] is. And needless to say, with the gramophone she is right at home; since she has been cranking the “music machine” she has become “strasznie” [terribly] musical... She sings the Ninth Symphony as easily as water, and she is crazy about our townsman Jan Kiepura... All day long she sings hit songs; she goes to bed with “Zapomnisz o mnie” [You'll forget me], gets up with “Szkoda twoich łez” [Pity your tears], and stands at the stove with “Już nigdy” [Never again]. Besides that, she likes to smoke “ladies'” cigarettes and plays “dziewiątka”[?] [„דזשעוויאנטקע“]...
We would forgive Feigele all of that — after all, why should she be a “wyjątek” [exception] among the other Feigelekh, Chayelekh, Treinelekh and Yentelekh? We would forgive her all of it if she did not want to meddle in politics.
But she has become a politician too, and is stirring up the women — and against whom is she stirring up the women? Against the men, of course...
This past Saturday night Feigele convened the first “poufna narada” [confidential meeting] of a number of female activists, well-known Sosnowiec “działaczki” [activists]; a “przewodnicząca” [chairwoman], a “zastępczyni” [deputy] and a “presidium” were elected.
At first the other “działaczki” “took offence” [„אבראזשעט“ — obrażały się]: why should the “beauty Nela” [„נעלע קראסאוויצע“ — Nela krasawica] get to be “przewodnicząca”, and why of all people the painted-up doll [lalka] as “zastępczyni”? And just because one can make eyes [„שנעבעלעך“, lit. “little beaks”] at “married men” [„זשאנאטע מענטשיזנעס“ — żonaci mężczyźni], must one be “przewodnicząca”?..
And indeed at first the “działaczki” were very “zazdrosne” [jealous] of the “przewodnicząca” and the “zastępczyni”, but after Feigele had “explained” [„וויאשניעט“ — wyjaśniła] to them that all those “present” [„אבעצנע“ — obecne] would figure on the list and would sit in the “gminy” [communities], the “działaczki” “calmed down” [„אוספאקאיעט“ — uspokoiły się] and the “poufna narada” got under way...
The “przewodnicząca” rings the bell and declares: “Koleżanka Felicja ma głos” [Colleague Felicja has the floor].
Feigele takes the puderniczka [powder compact] out of her purse[?] [„סא-קעווקע“ — sakiewka?], rubs her nose and forehead with the “poduszka” [powder puff], smears her lips with the pomadka [lipstick], checks in the mirror whether her hairdo is “w porządku” [in order], stands up and begins her “election agitation”:
“Szanowne koleżanki [Esteemed colleagues], we have gathered here today for a ‘poufna narada’ in order to establish ‘raz na zawsze’ [once and for all] who we are, the ‘kobiety’ [women], and who they are, the ‘mężczyźni’ [men]? Are we still merely wives and mothers and nothing more, or are we, besides being wives and mothers — also human beings?!
All the women cry out: We are human beings!
— Yes, Feigele goes on — pardon, ‘koleżanka Felicja’ — ‘koleżanki’! Just take a look at what is going on now here on the Jewish street around the ‘wybory’ [elections]: people are tearing each other apart over blocs. Congress Poland is negotiating with Galicia, the Folkists are ‘pertraktują’ [negotiating] with the Agudists, the ‘pious’[?] [„נאבאזשנע“] have ‘oficjalnie oświadczyli’ [officially declared] to the Sanacja who they are. All the ‘Kongresowcy’ [Congress-Poland men] and ‘Galicians’[?] [„גאליליאושעס“]! All the Folkists and Hasidim! — men!... What is Adolf Truskier — a male?!.. What is Elazar Rubinlicht? ‘Urodzony mężczyzna’ [a born man]!.. A ‘stuprocentowy mężczyzna’ [hundred-percent man]!.. And what are the Galicians — not men?!... Yes, they are all men. And they, these masculine anti-feminists, are waging a ‘wojna’ [war] among themselves. They haggle over mandates: so many for me, so many for you. They quarrel and make up... They conclude blocs and break up the blocs, a ‘rupowisko’[?] [„רופאוויסקא“ — perhaps a battlefield/shambles] arises on the Jewish street...
I ask you, ‘koleżanki’: did they ask you much for your opinion? Did they offer us women, who make up 70 percent of the ‘głosy’ [votes] on the Jewish street, even a single mandate? Did they invite [„זאפראשעט“ — zaprosili] us ‘kobiety’ even once ‘na herbatkę’ [for a cup of tea]? Did any of the ladies present have even one ‘randka’ [date, meeting] with the men about the ‘wybory’?
All the women from their seats: No, not a single randka!...
So they, the men, perhaps think that we women are still just wives — then they are greatly mistaken! Enough carrying [children] and baking kugel! Under the constitution we have full and equal rights. We have 70 percent of the ‘głosy’, and over our women's votes we are the mistresses of the house — are we the mistresses of the house or not?
All the women jump up with a shout: We are the mistresses of the house!..
‘Koleżanki’, Feigele gets more and more carried away — what is this Sejm anyway? What ‘qualifications’ must a ‘poseł’ [deputy] have? Do you know? A ‘poseł’ must be able to talk a lot, take money, ‘obiecywać’ [promise] golden fortunes and ‘nabierać’ [dupe] the voters. A ‘poseł’ must be able to pay little compliments, sometimes ‘na prawo’ [to the right] and sometimes ‘na lewo’ [to the left], ‘i tak dalej’ [and so on]...
Well, I ask you, koleżanki, who can ‘nabierać’ and talk about fire and water? Who has nine measures of talk?
All the women from their seats: We women!
Who can promise golden fortunes and take money?
We, the women!
‘Koleżanki’! Feigele cries out heatedly: who can pay little compliments ‘na lewo i na prawo’ [left and right]?
All the women from their seats: We women!..
So who, I ask you — Feigele cries — should sit in the Sejm: they, the men, or we, the women?
All the women from their seats: We, the women!...
And Feigele ends her ‘mowa’ [speech] with a squealing shout: Precz [down] with the men! Long live women's solidarity!...”
All the women shout along: “Precz with the men”, “Precz”, “Niech żyje” [long live]! Feigele once more ‘poprawia’ [fixes] her hairdo, once more rubs her nose with the ‘poduszka’ and the ‘pomadka’, and the following resolution is adopted:
“The ‘poufna narada’ establishes: 1) that the trading in mandates without the women is ‘skandaliczne’ [scandalous], 2) that the ‘female sex’, which accounts for 70 percent on the Jewish street, must have its own ‘przedstawicielki’ [women representatives] in order to ‘bronić’ [defend] women's interests in the Sejm, 3) that women have all the necessary ‘qualifications’ that a poseł must have, 4) that the men ‘zdradzają’ [betray] the women behind their backs.
Proceeding from the above-mentioned standpoints, the ‘poufna narada’ resolves to break away from the men and not to go with the men in any bloc whatsoever. The women go to the elections independently, with their own, women's platform”...
Who knows how much longer the ‘poufna narada’ would have dragged on, had the ‘przewodnicząca’ not glanced at her wristwatch and remembered that she had a ‘randka’ right now on the ‘Główna’ [main street] — and because of that the ‘poufna narada’ was broken off.
So, as we see, we must expect yet another bloc: a purely women's bloc, with a purely women's ‘platform’...
A Sanacja Organ Demands Freedom for Trade

[Poland — trade; Sunday rest.] Lately the press in Poland has repeatedly carried reports about permitting Jewish merchants to trade on Sunday for a few hours. These reports struck the Endeks [National Democrats] and the "Rozwój" people [?] [probably members of the antisemitic Rozwój society; printed "ראזוואציקעס"] like thunder. In their press organs they came out strongly against desecrating Sunday and, it seems [?], their outcry was soon heard, because the official Polish Telegraph Agency (P.A.T.) reported that the government has no intention whatsoever of easing the law on Sunday rest. In contrast to the above-mentioned report, however, the "sanatorial" [mock name for the Sanacja camp] "Il. Kurier Krakowski" [so printed] comes out with a sharp article demanding that trade in Poland be given F-R-E-E-D-O-M. What will that freedom consist of? Here is what the Sanacja organ writes about it:
"For a number of years now trade in Poland has been oppressed by a law that stems from socialist tendencies and which severely restricts the freedom to earn a living in Poland. Under this law shops may be open only from 9 to 1 and from 3 to 7 in the evening. The amendment to the law, which appeared a few years ago, permits keeping shops open between 1 and 3, provided, however, that the worker's eight-hour working day is not violated. At exactly 7 o'clock in the evening the inhabitants of the city can observe a scene that evokes no cheerful reflexes at all: there go policemen from shop to shop, watch in hand, to fine the firms that served their customers a few minutes after 7. Sometimes it happens in our cities that an assault or some other incident occurs — then you cannot find a single policeman; but when the shop-closing hour has to be enforced, the policeman is always 'at his post' [posterunek]."
The author of the article goes on to discuss the question of protecting the worker. For this purpose there are labour inspectors throughout the country whose task is to safeguard the eight-hour working day. But neither the labour inspectorate nor the police exist [?] in order to kill off trade, restricting the freedom to earn and thereby ruining the taxpayer, who with his hard work sustains the state treasury.
"The present — we read further — police system of opening and closing shops is a grave injustice to the broad masses of state and private employees. For when is such an employee to do his shopping, if in the morning he sits in the office and in the afternoon he is also occupied [?] in the office? It follows that the employee must go shopping during the lunch hours — and he, after all, is also a human being who needs to eat lunch and rest a little so as to be able to go on working. As a result many people give up shopping, harming the various branches [?]; the merchant loses by it, trade limps along, and the strength of the taxpayer grows ever weaker.
Before the war freedom to earn prevailed throughout the world. The writer of these lines once arrived in Berlin at 2 o'clock at night and lost his travel kit at the station; he immediately bought tooth powder ['proszek'], a toothbrush and a piece of soap at a special kiosk on Friedrichstraße. Some clever person had realised that in a city of millions many people may suddenly find themselves in such a situation, so he set himself up in a kiosk and sold toilet sundries all night long, and nobody disturbed him in this."
"In France or Italy — writes 'Sz. L. K. K.' further — there is to this day no police system regarding trading hours. Even after midnight one can get a pair of shoes or a necktie in those countries. Only in countries that have gone through socialist governments has trade been encircled with a chain of police ordinances," and therefore the author arrives at the conclusion:
"Society must demand of the government, which now — at a time when there is no Sejm — has broad powers to issue laws, that the question of freedom of trade and freedom to earn be settled in principle. Every state must have order [printed 'ארגונג', misprint for 'ארדנונג'], but not a calculated police order that makes a ruin of all economic workshops and is a ruin for the state."
Clear words, it would seem. Our deputies have always — at every opportunity — pointed out that Sunday rest destroys the merchant class in general and the Jewish merchant class in particular. But who listened to them? Who cared [?] that the Jewish merchant must rest 2 days — one [?] more in the week? Perhaps now — after reading the article in the Sanacja organ — government circles will come to realise that the Sunday-rest law must after all be changed.
Or perhaps the Kraków "Kurier"'s article is an election manoeuvre? After all, we are somewhat close to the Sejm and Senate elections.
A question about a story?..
S. Szach.
Summer Is Gone

[Poem — seasonal humour.] Leonidas [pen name].
The holiday together with the summer —
how quickly it has gone!
And now comes autumn
crawling like a snail,
and behind it drag
the wintry days.

Joy runs past quickly,
only sorrow drags on long,
insults — those come cheap,
yet rarely does one get thanks.
It is hard to get well,
yet easy to fall ill.

The leaves turn yellow-red,
the skies turn grey.
The season begins
of [—] [?] and of straw.
And oh! for a fur coat
my wife has taken a fancy.

The children need little shoes,
the mother-in-law needs a shawl,
and you must also manage
to eat out your gall,
and at midnight fall asleep
in the concert hall.

The night goes through your bones,
you feel as if frozen stiff.
You must get a charitable loan [gemilut ḥesed]
(though getting one is hard)
to redeem the coat
that still lies in the pawnshop ["Lombard"].

People still kiss in the parks,
but no longer with ardour.
You can already get there
a seat somewhere or other.
The love of summer
in autumn becomes a joke.

The bear in the forest is already starting
his long winter sleep.
Now they feel safe,
the donkeys and the sheep.
They come to meetings
and [bray?] without end.

I don't know how it is with you.
You are, after all, quite "normal",
but for me, I beg your pardon,
my gall simply turns over
when I see donkeys
as "saviours" of the community...

Yes, yes, my dear friends,
the summer is gone.
To light linen and love affairs
an end has come.
Don't forget to cover yourselves
with a woollen blanket.

Now begins the series
of cards and of tea,
of babblers and crude jokes,
of lectures and of woe [?]
and the plague of making a living!
And ah and woe...
Summer, Autumn and Winter.

By Eliash.

Although as a feuilletonist I am obliged to be in a humorous mood, I will confess that when a holiday passes I feel a little sad at heart. Especially [when it is] such a joyful holiday as Sukkot and Simchat Torah.

True, before Sukkot we have the Days of Awe, which are not joyful at all; but if you like, Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur are also quite joyful holidays — after all, they give us the "opportunity" to cleanse ourselves of the sins we commit in the course of the whole year — and when can a person be as joyful as at the moment he feels he has been rid of a bundle of sins?

Therefore, when the holiday passes, a sadness, as I said, falls on the heart. Life is so grey and humdrum, especially in Zagłębie, where one is always toiling[?], and the holiday refreshes the spirit a little, so that one really does not want to part with the holiday.

After Passover, true, the dear summer comes — the world turns green like a fresh shop sign after a bankruptcy... and the heart grows bright seeing how nature puts on[?] her many-coloured clothes: and nature, as you know, although she is feminine in grammar, does not hold with the new women's fashions of short hair and short little dresses,

Nature, on the contrary, wears long hair — in the form of grasses and flowers, and her clothes, in the form of the various growths, of the plantings, are long, so that it is a delight to look at. If I were now in a mood to sing, I would sing such a song about nature:

Nature is
almighty[?] strong.
That is clear to everyone:
she wears no short
little dresses
and does not dye her hair.
Nor does she use
powder or rouge,
never any make-up;
naturally
beautifully coloured
are her mountain and her valley too.

That is how I would sing, I tell you, if I were now in a better mood. But, as I have already explained, my mood is not an elevated one, because the holiday is gone and now winter comes with its frosts and blizzards, with its snows and mud, with its long, tedious[?] nights and dark days.

But if you like, one can find a consolation, a comfort; if one wishes, one can even establish that after Sukkot is better than after Passover and after Shavuot.

How so?

Here you have it — I will go here point by point, and take it well to heart, and you will feel better.

Number one:
After Passover, Sukkot approaches — and what comes after Sukkot you already know; whereas after Sukkot, Passover approaches, and with every day the joyful, dear Passover draws nearer.

Number two.
After Passover comes the season of dachas [summer cottages], of mountains and of the sea, when you, poor thing, become a "straw widower" and are left stranded all alone; you squander money on the dachas and you yourself must every Friday get blackened[?] [with travel soot], dragging yourself to "nature", or rather: to your wife.

After Sukkot, on the other hand, you have no such burden on your head; your home is home and you truly rest.

Number three.
After Passover, when the so-called dear summer comes, there descends upon you — and upon all mankind — the calamity of congresses. Every day another congress with resolutions and votes and programmes and a tumult to high heaven.

In winter you know nothing of such things. Winter is the time when none of the resolutions of all the congresses are carried out.

You might as well lie down and sleep!

Winter is the time when resolutions are broken. Whereas summer is the time when resolutions are made...

Understood?

That, my dear readers, is the difference between summer and winter.

As for hearts, however, the story is reversed: in summer hearts are broken, and in winter — they become whole.

How many hearts of young men and girls are broken in summer at the "spas" — broken from great love!

But when winter comes, a miracle happens: the hearts become whole again, as if they had never been broken. And as soon as a heart becomes whole — love is over!

Which means that in winter hearts simply freeze up.

The trouble, however, is that in winter the heart freezes not only with regard to that love which has wedding-canopy urges in mind[?], but also with regard to love for the people and for mankind.

So... yes, where were we? We are at the question of which is better after all: winter or summer?

We have given the readers all the arguments for and against summer and for and against winter — and so it remains for you yourselves to decide which is better...

Which is better,
winter, summer?
Always better,
if without worries!
Comes the winter,
come the snows:
let the heart
always rejoice!
If the heart is
good and willing[?] —
the weather makes
no difference.
Beautiful is summer
with its colours,
with its flowers,
with its sheaves,
beautiful is autumn[?],
beautiful too is winter's
frosty-white
flowers; it mirrors[?],
[—]
