Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings and remarks on this week's portion (Noach)

[Oneg Shabbat — weekly Torah portion.] Torah sayings and remarks on this week's portion.
Collected and adapted by Y. L.
Parashat Noach
—o—
a) "Noah was perfect in his generations; Noah walked with God" (6:9).
1.
"Noah walked with God" — Noah went his way with God alone; it did not concern him that his generation was sinful; he did not rebuke them or call on them to mend their ways, and therefore "he was perfect in his generations" — that is why his generations loved him: because he did not preach morals to them and did not tell them his opinion.. "A rabbi whom the townspeople love — it is because he does not rebuke them in matters of Heaven" (the rabbi whom the town loves — that is because he does not rebuke it.. Tiferet Uziel.
2.
There are those who at home are pious and observant Jews, but when they come among people, into society, they are ashamed of their piety; and there are, on the other hand, those who at home commit every evil and only among people pass themselves off as pious and put on a God-fearing face. The true, whole Jew, however, is: "perfect in his generations" — pious among people, and also "with God" — when they are alone with God they are honest as well. Yalkut HaDerush.
—o—
b) "Make thee an ark of gopher wood" (6:14).
Noah shut himself up in his little study-house, learned and prayed, and did not want to go out into the street to improve the people and rebuke them; therefore his punishment came — to shut himself up in an ark and thus [terribly?] have to be cut off from the whole world. And because he did not want to be a leader, a "shepherd", a guide, he had to become a shepherd in the plain sense of the word: a herdsman — he had to take wild beasts and cattle into the ark and tend them.. Torat Moshe.
—o—
c) "The earth was corrupt before God, and the earth was filled with violence" (6:11)
The world stands on three things: justice, truth and peace. If everything had become violence, and the world was full of robbery, plunder and robbery — on what could the world stand? "And the earth was corrupt" — the legs of the world were broken, so the world [?] tottered and threatened to collapse. Tiferet Yehonatan.
—o—
d) "And Noah began to be a husbandman, and he planted a vineyard" (9:20).
Once a Jew meets a great tzaddik and asks him to wish him something. The tzaddik blesses him that the first business he does on coming home now shall be blessed. The Jew reasons: since he has at home a "knippl" (a little bundle) of money, as soon as he comes in he will start counting the money, and so the blessing will enter into it.
He comes home in a rush and cries out, breathless, to his wife: Give me the bundle of money, quick — faster! She thinks that he has, God save us, gone mad, and starts cursing him with fierce curses. He doesn't let it pass in silence, and a quarrel breaks out until tables and benches are being thrown.
In any case the tzaddik's blessing was fulfilled: the first business the Jew did on coming home — the quarrel with his wife — received the blessing.. yes, the curses multiplied with a blessing.. Instead of a blessing in money, as the Jew had [?] wanted, he had a blessing in curses...
The same happened with Noah.
When the Flood had ceased and God again showed His mercy to the world — had Noah set about repairing the world (tikkun ha-olam), rebuilding the world, God's blessing would have rested on it and he would have succeeded; but he set about a vineyard, and so the blessing was fulfilled in that: on the very same day — as the Sages say — that he planted, the grapes grew; on that same day he made wine from them, drank and got thoroughly drunk, until his sons did with him what they did.. Instead of a blessing in rebuilding the world, he had a blessing in drunkenness..
R. Yaakov Kranz (the Dubno Maggid).
—o—
e) "And he drank of the wine and was drunken" (9:21).
To R. Abele Pastiler [= Posvoler?] came a poor man begging for pity: since he had two daughters to marry off, would the rabbi give him a letter of recommendation to the Jews of Vilna, that they should take pity on him and give him alms. Afterwards people came and told R. Abele that the poor man was drinking away all the money he collected. He had him called and said to him:
— Now I understand why one says "drunk as Lot" and not "drunk as Noah". After all, Noah came before Lot, and he too got drunk not a little. The answer is: Noah had sons — so he was allowed to get drunk; but Lot had two grown girls, two daughters whom he could not marry off — why did he get drunk?...
—o—
f) "God shall enlarge Japheth, and he shall dwell in the tents of Shem" (9:27).
"Shem" is, as is known, the symbol of Jewishness, and "Japheth" — of worldliness. If it is "the tents of Shem", if the home is Jewish in its spirit, one may bring in something of Japheth's treasures; there is no harm in taking in the best of the worldly. It is bad only when one wants to build "tents of Japheth", worldly homes, and [?] merely to discharge an obligation bring in a remnant of "Shem", of Jewishness, simply for decoration.. Yalkut Derush.
—o—
g) "Wherefore it is said: Even as Nimrod the mighty hunter before the Lord" (10:9).
Nimrod and all his followers commit every evil, and always with the excuse "before the Lord" — they supposedly mean it only for God's sake. Orach Chaim.
—o—
h) "Let us make bricks and burn them thoroughly .. and let us make us a name"
We want to quote here a characteristic passage from "Degel Machaneh Efraim", which we translate here word for word:
"The Torah hints here at a sect of liars who want to pass themselves off as the faithful of Israel, who in the end will have no endurance, for falsehood has no endurance.. And that is what the verse hints: earlier, "And the whole earth was of one language (safah)" — all were cleaving to the Shechinah ("Shechinah" in the sense of "safah"), "and of one speech" — because they cleaved to God, great unity reigned among them and they did not say one thing with the mouth and another in the heart. Later, "As they journeyed from the east (mi-kedem)" — when they went away from the Primeval One of the world, "they found a plain (bik'ah)" — and sank into a dark, deep pit, and they make themselves out to be tzaddikim and say "let us make bricks (nilbenah levenim)" — let us put on white kapotes like the true tzaddikim; "and burn them thoroughly" — let us clap our hands with fervour, and all this "let us make us a name" — to make a name for ourselves and buy up towns and townlets into our domain"...
"The end will be: and they had brick for stone" — the white kapotes will become for them a stone [of stumbling?]; "and slime (chemar) (an acronym: chacham mufla [?] rabbanan — 'wondrous sage, rabbi') — those who passed themselves off as sages and rabbis — had they for mortar" — it will turn into a plain swamp of clay, in which they will sink. "Because there [the Lord] did confound" — because through them came quarrels and gratuitous hatred, "and confound their language" — so that no one understands the other's speech".
An Official Converts to Judaism and Causes a Great Sensation

[Białystok — conversion to Judaism; sensation.] All of Białystok is now in an uproar over a sensation that could have held its own [?] even in Warsaw.
There is in Białystok a Jewish girl, no longer quite young, from a simple working-class family, very decent [?] and clever, but, poor thing, crippled in both legs. In the street she walks on two artificial (machine) legs, leaning besides on a stick on one side and on a person on the other. At home she must take off the mechanical legs and drag herself about on her knees. Yet, as everyone [?] reports, she is a great "briye" (a capable, energetic woman): her tidying and cleaning and her handiwork of all kinds [?] are truly a marvel. In the face she is actually quite pretty.
Some time ago a young Christian began visiting the girl at home, a man of about 22, an official in the Finance Office, an able and very likeable young man.
As time went on the young Christian became an ever more frequent visitor in the Jewish home, where he used to spend whole evenings with the unfortunate girl, until.. a few weeks ago he informed her Jewish parents that he was in love with their daughter and wanted to marry her.
The parents, of course, were overjoyed, and their joy was greater still when the young admirer told them that he did not demand that their daughter convert, but that he was ready to accept Judaism...
Soon the news was known in town, and people became convinced that the young man was serious, for he went to the rabbi, told him the story and asked him to perform the ceremony. The rabbi explained to him that here this was a difficult matter. Besides, one may not convert someone for the sake of love, but only out of conviction.
The young man, however, did not stop before the difficulty. Having obtained leave from his office, he went to Danzig, underwent the operation (circumcision) and all the formalities there, and then came back to Białystok already a full-fledged Jew.
His state post he lost at once. But he was not frightened, married his beloved and went to live with her parents.
This past Yom Kippur he was already in the Jewish synagogue, where he did not pray himself, but listened to how others pray.
A true righteous proselyte.
It is only a pity that Białystok's Jewish youngsters cannot restrain themselves in the face of the sensation. They keep running after the "little householder" in crowds and peer into his eyes, as if to convince themselves whether it is really true.
Coming out of the synagogue on Yom Kippur and seeing a group of curious youngsters around him, the young man said:
— I love the Jewish people, the Jewish religion, but the Jewish youngsters are great hooligans [?] ("łobuzy")...
Napoleon and the Young Polish Countess Walewska — by M. Oszerowicz

[Historical serial — Napoleon and Maria Walewska; chapter 4.] By M. Oszerowicz.
4.
From then on the countess began coming to the Emperor ever more often; not infrequently she would stay with him until morning; between them arose one of the most beautiful and strongest loves that ever were. And it would perhaps be no exaggeration to say that, had Napoleon not been so strongly interested in leaving after him precisely a dynasty with genuine royal blood in it, he would have married Maria Walewska and not the Austrian princess Marie-Louise.
He himself thought about it quite seriously. But he held that the interests of the country were more important than his own interests.
———
In her love for Napoleon Maria Walewska sought no personal advantages; she literally worshipped him, he was everything in the world to her.
In a conversation with a faithful servant she indeed once said:
"All my thoughts come from him and go back to him. He is everything in the world to me, my future, my life!"
But she was not sure that he would always love her, so she once gave him as a present a little ring with this inscription: "When you no longer love me, remember that I still love you".
Just when the love between the two was at its very height, the war on the battlefields flared up fiercely and the Emperor could no longer remain in Warsaw. He had to leave his beloved and set up his headquarters in Osterode.
On the battlefield thousands of people fell like flies, the roar of the cannons deafened the ears, blood flowed like water, and the Emperor was busy day and night with the strategic plans he drew up. But at the same time he did not stop thinking about his beloved. He longed for her greatly, wanted her to be beside him, for without her life was hard for him. But he spared her, and later, at the beginning of April, when he managed to move his headquarters to a palace at Finckenstein, West Prussia, farther from the battlefield, he immediately began making all the necessary preparations to bring his beloved there.
He did not have to wait long; a few weeks later she was already with him, and then Napoleon had still more occasions to convince himself how faithful and devoted she was to him.
In the three weeks she was with him in the palace she never went out anywhere by day; even when she wanted to catch a little fresh air, she went outside at night, not by day.
Nothing concerned her. Nothing interested her. Body and soul she was absorbed in one person only — in Napoleon. And quite often, when she quietly looked out through the window and saw him review the soldiers and them shouting with enthusiasm "Long live the Emperor"!, her heart bathed in delight — the Emperor is hers! Her beloved, her life.
To that time belongs the letter Napoleon sent to Josephine in reply to her writing to him that she had heard he was corresponding with other women.
"I do not know what you are talking about," he wrote to her, "I love only one woman in the world, and that is my little, good, naughty and capricious Josephine, who is graceful even when she quarrels, just as she is graceful in everything she does, for she is always lovely — except when she is jealous; at such a moment she is a little devil".
Napoleon, however, was no liar by nature; to deceive someone — be it even his own wife — he could not. So in the same letter he added this:
"But let us return to those women of yours whom you mention in his [?] (your) letter. If I really were interested in one of them, she would have to be as lovely and as fresh as a flower".
This was meanwhile a hint [?], because the young Countess Walewska was to him truly "as lovely and as fresh as a flower".
After the war against the Russians and the Prussians had ended, Napoleon went to Tilsit, where he made the acquaintance of the Prussian Queen Louise and also turned her head a little.
From Tilsit he came back to Paris as the great victor and, it seems, had somewhat forgotten the Polish countess, or simply had no time to think about her too much.
At the beginning of 1808 Maria Walewska came to Paris.
It is hard to establish whether Napoleon asked her to come, or whether she did it on her own responsibility. The fact, however, is that when she came Napoleon was very glad of her and at once arranged a fine apartment for her in the street "Rue la Victoire" number 48, and came to her very often.
(To be continued).
Kehilla board decides to open a cheap kitchen. New board member rescues the financial situation

[Będzin — kehilla; finances and welfare. Followed by a short item: the Ministry of Religious Affairs and the budget.]
On Monday a meeting of the kehilla board took place. The meeting dealt with the critical financial situation of the kehilla treasury. From the report delivered by the secretary Mr. Frajlich it emerges that the arrears [?] of kehilla taxes for the year 1930 amount to nearly 200,000 zł. The encumbered [?] kehilla owes 49 thousand zł. for pensions, and the unpaid subsidies for the year 1929 amount to 38 thousand zł.
At the same time it was also reported that the sick fund (Kasa Chorych) has placed a distraint on the office furniture, machines, the safe etc., and in the coming days the items will be sold at auction.
In order to avert the auction, the new board member (dozór) Mr. Avraham Liwer [?] announced that he is lending a sum of 1000 zł. to pay the debt to the sick fund.
Also adopted was the urgent proposal of Mr. Avraham Liwer that, in order to raise the moral prestige of the kehilla board, a cheap kitchen be opened for the winter for the needy population.
—o—
The mouth that forbade is the mouth that permitted...
This week the Ministry of Religious Affairs informed the kehilla board that the expenditures in the budget for the mikveh, repairs in the synagogue etc. are being withdrawn.
The subsidy for the gemilut chesed (free-loan) fund is struck out entirely.
City council meeting.

[Będzin — city council; municipal finances, "Hakoach".]
At the Monday [?] meeting of the city council, before the agenda, Councillor Lewin turned to the presidium of the city administration asking for an explanation of the following charges made by Dr. Rechtman in the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" no. 42, where it is said that 1) the debts of the magistrate amount to 7 million zł.; 2) protested bills and bills of exchange for 400 thousand zł. are in circulation; 3) the pension of the vice-president amounts to 1500 zł.; 4) banquets are held with municipal money, etc.
President Michel [?] gives a reply in which he refutes with figures every charge addressed to the city administration.
Then a series of tax statutes and the magistrate's loan of 250 thousand zł. are adopted in the third reading.
A longer discussion takes place over the magistrate's proposal to annul the resolution adopted at the time that the premises of "Hakoach" be renovated at the magistrate's expense; instead, this should be arranged by the landlord, Mr. Zmigród.
Speaking against the resolution: Jakubowicz, Rzechnik [?], Lewin and Hampel [?]. For: the president, the vice-president, councillor(s) [?], Błaupowicz [?] and Fajner [?].
By 12 votes to 8 the magistrate's proposal is adopted.
They carried out the 'verdict' before the din Torah took place

[Będzin — a brawl at a rabbinical arbitration.]
On Sunday Messrs. G. Briger and Seliger came to the Rabinow [?] house to hold a din Torah (rabbinical arbitration). Before the proceedings both "parties" "settled accounts", whereupon Mr. Briger snatched the [?] box from the table and threw it at Seliger, who was left covered in blood. First aid was given to Z—n [Seliger] by the feldsher Mr. Hartman.
Caught in the heat of the moment...

[Będzin — gossip; an affair.]
In Grynbaum's house on Czeladzka Street there is an office for writing petitions. The owner of the office lives in a neighbouring house.
Last Sunday late in the evening, the wife of the office owner, seeing that her husband was not coming home, went to look for him, and in the office premises she indeed found her husband "amusing himself" with Perl, who works in the office...
On seeing such a scene, the "little wife" snatched up his and her clothes and ran off... A short while later she came back, opened the door of the office and loudly "blessed" the enamoured, half-naked couple...
In the lane the sensation spread quickly, and the local residents had a bit of a merry time.
Must a father pay his son's debts?

[Będzin — taxes; distraint.]
On Tuesday a bailiff (executor), accompanied by police, came to Mr. Szymon Fiszel on Małachowskiego Street to carry out a distraint for the tax debt of his son Nachum, who lives in his father's apartment.
Mrs. Fiszel became very agitated and began smashing window panes, but the bailiff was not impressed by it; only when he received an instalment did he leave.
A crowd of people gathered in the street.
Conference of Jewish sports clubs in the Kielce voivodeship.

[Zagłębie — sport; Maccabi, Hakoach.]
Next Sunday a conference of all Jewish sports clubs of the Kielce voivodeship belonging to the "Maccabi" World Union will take place in Kielce.
The above-mentioned clubs are requested to delegate their representatives to the conference.
In this connection a preliminary conference took place last Sunday, attended by the vice-chairman of the local "Hakoach", B. Barenblat, who proposed that the Jewish sports clubs of Class A [?] be released from the championship matches of the P.Z.P.N. (Polish Football Association) so that they can take part in the Maccabiah in the Land of Israel.
Tax appeals on the green table...

[Zagłębie — taxes; appeals.]
On the 27th, 28th, 29th and 30th of this month [?] the appeals against turnover and income tax will be examined by the appeals commission at the "Izba Skarbowa" (Treasury Chamber) in Kielce.
Those concerned should apply for exact information at the merchants' institutions.
Minister Kwiatkowski in Zagłębie.

[Zagłębie — ministerial visit.]
Next Sunday, the 26th, the Minister of Commerce Kwiatkowski will be in Zagłębie. The minister will take part in the jubilee celebration of the "Saturn" coal mine.
Shoes Stolen at School.

[Będzin — Education.]
In the building of Public School No. 2 it has been introduced that the children may not enter the classrooms in shoes, only in slippers.
This “reform”, however, causes damage to the parents, especially to those who are not well-off, because there are cases in which shoes disappear...
“Means” — How to Take Revenge...

[Będzin — Crime.]
On Wednesday morning, when Mr. Moshe Gezundheit was going to pray at the tanners' shtibl, he was attacked on the way by the young Zajdeman and a Christian, who cruelly beat Gezundheit with sticks and blunt objects.
As we are told, this is an act of revenge. Gezundheit had carried out a “zajęcie” [distraint] at Zajdeman's father's, also a tanners' Hasid[?].
Young Communist Punished

[Sosnowiec — Courts.]
The Sosnowiec district court sentenced the 21-year-old Shlomo Ferstba[?] of Mandoszew[?] to 6 months' imprisonment.
F. was accused of distributing leaflets with revolutionary content.
—o—
Activity of “Sinai”.
[Będzin — Youth movements.]
The youth organization “Sinai” has been reorganized and is setting about cultural work. Tonight, Friday evening, Mr. Yitzchak P[e]lc[?] will teach Chumash with Rashi; on Monday evening a question-box evening takes place, and on Thursday evening — a lecture by Mr. Zider.
—o—
Programme of Activities of the “Muza” Society.
[Będzin — Culture.]
Today, Friday, second lesson by Guchimow[?] on the history of Yiddish literature (Sholem Aleichem); tomorrow, Saturday, first choir lesson by Kaner-Manszejn[?]; Sunday, third lesson by Guchimow on the history of Yiddish literature; Tuesday, first lesson by M. Kaner on “splaeds”[?]; Wednesday, first lesson by Y. Tojman[?] on the history of Yiddish theatre; Thursday, discussion exercises led by Guchimow.
David Damb, of Blessed Memory

[Będzin — Obituary.]
The news that the 38-year-old David Damb, very much beloved by everyone, had died made a heavy impression in the whole town.
Hundreds of people from all strata of the local Jewish population took part in the funeral.
In the Aleksander shtibl the deceased was eulogized by the moreh tzedek R' Dan and by the director of the yeshiva “Beit Yisrael”. The director's eulogy brought rivers of tears from the mourners.
On the way to the cemetery the rabbi delivered a eulogy, and at the grave — the uncle of the deceased, R' Hershel Rapaport of Zawiercie. May his soul be bound in the bond of life.
The Funeral of Vice-President Jaroszy.

[Sosnowiec — Politics.]
On Saturday the funeral took place in Sosnowiec of the city's vice-president Jaroszy[?], who shot himself on Sienkiewicza Street.
Besides thousands of PPS members, a large number of Jews also took part in the funeral.
At the open grave “Czerwony Sztandar” [The Red Flag] was sung.
Premises for the Kehilla.

[Sosnowiec — Kehilla.]
At Monday's meeting of the kehilla board it was decided, among other things, to look for suitable premises for the kehilla.
It is to be hoped that this decision will not share the fate of all the decisions — to remain on paper. It is simply a disgrace that such a Jewish community should have premises like the ones it has had until today.
Meeting of Polish Women Dissolved.

[Sosnowiec — Politics.]
The organization “Union of National Polish Women” called a meeting. Police appeared in the hall and dispersed the meeting of the “righteous women”.
Shot at a Hare and Killed His Friend.

[Sosnowiec — Accidents.]
Two Christian friends from the village of Okradzionów[?] went off[?] hunting in the neighbouring wood.
At a certain moment a hare came out of the bushes, and the one holding the gun fired at the running hare. The bullet, however, went astray and hit his friend, who was severely wounded and died the next day in the local hospital.
Well-known safe-crackers arrested on the train.

On Sunday at 5 in the afternoon, on the Warsaw—Vienna express (courier) train, a secret agent of the local police recognised in the second-class corridor 3 well-known bandits, who had tickets only as far as Będzin.
The agent handed the arrested men over to the local chief commissioner, who was travelling on the same train. A few minutes later the agent Ch. P.[?] arrested 2 bandits in a first-class compartment, accomplices of the well[?]-known safe-cracker „Szpic-Brudka“, who had escaped not long ago from the Częstochowa prison.
The arrested pickpockets are: Aharon Dimant, Shmuel Ferncter[?] and Yechiel Trush[?], all from Łódź.
A month in prison for selling sequestered goods

At the local district court the trial took place of Mr. Ch. Garbash, who was charged by the prosecutor with selling goods sequestered for tax debts. Garbarsh was sentenced to a month in prison.
—o—
Trial of former deputy Kwapiński — on the 27th of this month.
Next Monday, the 27th of this month, the trial of former deputy Kwapiński will take place at the local district court; K. is accused of criminal acts against the authorities.
The defence will be conducted by advocate Rudziński[?], who has received permission from the prosecutor to meet the arrested man in the Mysłowice prison.
—o—
Sudden death of the former komornik.
In the night from Sunday to Monday the former komornik (court bailiff) Michalis died in his own flat at the age of 56.
—o—
An arsonist arrested.
In Małobądz a fire broke out in a peasant's cottage, which burned down together with a grain barn.
In connection with this a local resident was arrested, who is suspected of having set fire to the cottage.
—o—
She wanted revenge.
On Tuesday a Christian woman ran up to her husband, a trader, in the street and doused him with vitriol. Luckily only his jacket was splashed.
The reason for the revenge is that the husband is on bad terms with her and avoids her..
Dąbrowa

He fancied the bicycle.
On Monday a Christian baker came riding here on a bicycle and stopped at Grabowski's shop in Walber's house on 3 Maja Street. The Christian went into the shop and left the bicycle in front of the store.
At that very moment a known thief got on the bicycle and set off. The victim chased him and, with the help of bystanders, caught the thief and handed him over to the police.
—o—
Suicides.
At Konopnickiej 24 the 18-year-old Pietrasówna drank a small bottle of acid essence with the aim of committing suicide. She was taken in a hopeless condition to the Henryger[?] hospital.
The 49-year-old worker Ganiewicz[?] drank the same „drink“. The reason for the suicide is family quarrels.
—o—
Theatre and cinema.
In the Polish theatre, in Kampanic[?], the following repertoire is given:
This Saturday evening „Ferlibte“[?] (The Beloved?).
Tuesday 〃 „Palestrant“[?].
In the German theatre:
Today, Friday, Klau r-Kagbers[?] by M. Rosental[?]. Sunday „Die neue Sachlichkeit“, Monday „Amnestie“.
Monday the 3rd of listopad [November] a performance by Paul Wegener in Strindberg's „The Father“.
In the Sosnowiec municipal theatre:
Today, Friday, „Artists“.
Tomorrow, Saturday, M-l. Flute[?].
—o—
The Jazz-Band Singer.
In the „Gweszczy“[?] cinema the sound film „The Jazz Singer“ is being shown. The film displays great technique and very many song numbers. Among others one will also hear „Kol Nidre“ by the cantor[—] and the well-kn[own —] [—]blatt[?].

Week's Notes

[Week's Notes — short world news.]
In almost all Jewish communities throughout the world protest meetings have taken place against the English government for its betrayal[?] regarding Eretz Israel.
—o—
In Austria, Czechoslovakia and France there have been tremendous snowstorms and floods. The damage is very great.
—o—
The Turkish military carried out a terrible slaughter of the Kurds. They slaughtered 15 thousand people.
—o—
In Tel Aviv the Revisionists organised a huge demonstration against the government. It came to a clash with the police.
—o—
In Radom 5 Torah scrolls were burned. Several thousand people took part in the funeral.
—o—
The Main Electoral Commission in Warsaw has invalidated, in a number of districts, the lists of the „Centrolew“ and of other opposition parties.
—o—
In a coal mine in the Saar region (Germany) a catastrophe has again occurred. 94 workers perished.
—o—
In Berlin there were clashes between Hitlerites and Communists. Many persons were wounded.
—o—
In India[?] there were protest demonstrations against England. The police fired on the demonstrators; there are 154 dead.
What's New in Upper Silesia?

[Upper Silesia — Katowice: Zionism, elections, municipal and court news; ten items.]
Protest Resolutions Against the Labour Party
On Saturday the Katowice Brit HaTzohar organised an evening devoted to the 50th jubilee of the leader Jabotinsky, with the participation of an important speaker, the instructor of „Keren Tel Hai“ in Poland, Mr. Unger of Warsaw.
The speaker, criticising very sharply the Labour government for its false tactics towards the Jewish people and for its latest betrayal, then passed on to the subject proper, to the man celebrating the jubilee, and stressed that only Jabotinsky, with his great abilities, could have saved the situation.
After the lecture the following resolutions were adopted unanimously:
1) The meeting, having heard the lecture of Mr. Unger, expresses its sharpest protest against the new decrees of the Labour government and resolves to remain faithful to the idea of the Jewish State and to fight for its realisation.
2) The meeting protests most sharply against the Executive, which with its policy has led to the present situation, and calls on it to convene the Zionist Congress immediately; also, until a new Executive is elected, an emergency-aid committee must be created to conduct Zionist affairs.
—o—
The Zionist List Confirmed
At Monday's session of the main electoral committee in Katowice the Zionist list, which bears the number 14, was confirmed among others.
At the session it was taken note that the arrested Korfanty has declared that he agrees to put forward his candidacy for the present Sejm.
—o—
Shop Hours — Tomorrow
At the proposal of the Katowice Merchants' Association, the local authority has permitted all shops to be open tomorrow, Saturday 1 November (listopad), from 2 in the afternoon until 7 in the evening.
—o—
On the Holidays One Must Be Serious...
The police directorate has ordered that on Saturday the 1st and Sunday the 2nd of November no performances whatsoever, dance evenings, balls, theatre performances of a light genre and the like may be organised.
—o—
A Year in Prison for Swindling Merchants
Moshe Wajnsztajn and Fishel Kaushitek[?] opened a ready-made clothing (konfekcja) shop in Katowice in 1927. As Łódź people[?] they made their purchases in Łódź and, as is the custom, on bills of exchange — partly their own, and partly with their[?] endorsements (giros). They used to seek out unemployed people and home workers who, for a couple of złoty, would sign blank bill forms. In finding such willing persons to issue bills they were helped by a certain Erhard[?] Szwarc. When the bills fell due and neither their own nor the endorsed ones were paid, the Łódź people reported the „enterprise“ to the Katowice investigation office, but there it turned out that the merchants had already liquidated and vanished.
This week the trial took place; Szwarc defended himself by saying that he had believed the „merchants“ would redeem their bills.
The court sentenced Mr. Szwarc to one year in prison.
—o—
Protest Meeting
This evening, Motzei Shabbat, all Jewish societies and associations are holding a protest meeting in the hall of the „Merchants' Association“ against the new English decree concerning Eretz Israel.
—o—
Murderous Deed of a Woman
In Königshütte a Christian landlady struck the 60-year-old subtenant Szymon Brander a blow with a sharp axe while he was asleep. B. was taken to hospital in a most serious condition.
—o—
Telephone Calls with Hungary
From the 20th of this month one can telephone from Katowice to Hungary. A „word“[?] (call unit) costs 5 fr[ancs] and 40 cent[imes].
—o—
Campaign Against Rats
The days from the 4th to the 11th of November have been fixed as the days for exterminating rats and mice. Every house owner must buy the necessary poison at the magistrate (municipal office).
—o—
Meeting of Post Officials
On Sunday meetings of post officials took place in a number of localities; they resolved to vote for Marshal Piłsudski.
Former PPS Activist, Sejm Deputy Kwapiński, Sentenced to 1 Year in Prison

[Sosnowiec — political trial.]
On Monday the trial of former Sejm deputy Kwapiński took place at the Sosnowiec district court. The trial aroused great interest throughout Poland; all the Warsaw newspapers were represented at the press tables.
The indictment states that on 1 December 1929 Kwapiński appeared at a meeting in Olkusz with a speech in which he called for hatred against the government; he demanded that the members of the government be removed by force and their places[?] be filled by others. He also called for a general strike, for organising demonstrations in the villages and marching on the towns, for bloody struggles and for a civil war, so as to overthrow the government even by means of terror.
16 witnesses were summoned to the trial, 10 for the prosecution and 6 for the defence.
As defence counsel: Berenson and Rudzinski[?] (Warsaw) and the Sosnowiec advocate Krzyżowski[?].
After the reading of the indictment the accused declared that he does not admit guilt for the crimes he is charged with; he only — he says — gave the listeners at the meeting instructions that, if such a moment should come when adventurism triumphs over political reason and it comes to an overturn of the state, then his party would call a general strike with the aim of overthrowing the government.
The most important witness at the trial is the police commandant of Olkusz, who supports the charge. The witness states that Kwapiński called for a general strike and a bloody revolution.
After the hearing of witnesses and the speeches of the lawyers, the verdict was delivered on Tuesday at 4 before dawn, according to which Kwapiński is sentenced to 1 year in a fortress.
The defence's request to release Kwapiński on bail was rejected. Kwapiński remains in custody in the Mysłowice prison.
Sports News.

K.S. 06 Katowice — “Hakoach” 2:2 (0:1)
The match between the above-mentioned teams brought the Będzin club a fine success [?]. It achieved a draw against the vice-champion of the Silesian League, which took the field with only 3 substitutes, and “Hakoach” with six players [sic]. The game itself was, despite difficult ground conditions, very interesting. In the first half the visitors had more of the match; several sure chances were foiled by the excellent defenders Rotenberg and Yankelevitch 2. Only in the 31st minute does Zambek score the first goal. Several favourable scoring chances are not taken. After the change of ends the centre-half Mrazek raises the score to 0:2. “Hakoach” gets down to work; in the fifth minute Rotenberg converts an awarded penalty (“Elfer”). [—] arise in front of both teams’ goals, but without success. In the 25th minute Turner breaks through nicely and shoots the equaliser. Outstanding for “Hakoach”: Gutenberg [?], the defence and Rozen 2. Referee Mr. Miner [?] very good.
“Wiktorja” of Sosnowiec into the Cup final.

The Czeladź team took the field without its best player Stanisicki [?], and this had a fatal effect on the whole side (drużyna). The visitors’ only bright spot was the defender Czapla [?], who was the best man on the field. “Sosnowiec” played its best match of the season and won deservedly.

Perhaps We Ought to Give It Some Thought?

(We could master the serious situation if we knew how to respond to it.)
The beautiful, bright summer is over, and the gloomy autumn has arrived, filling us with longing when we see the yellow, dried-up leaves on the trees, which leave sorrow in our hearts as soon as they fall from the tree.
But after autumn comes winter — the hard, ice-cold winter that sets like lead upon the hearts. Somehow people have always been afraid of winter; somehow it has been a great burden since olden times.
When winter comes, people grow sad and worried: how does one undertake to bring the winter into the householder's home? How does one manage it so as not to be shamed before others? How does one prepare clothing, food and heating for these hard days?
A feverish crisis is raging throughout the country; today one does not know what tomorrow will bring; whoever is today considered "prima" [first-rate] is right to fear that tomorrow his outstanding debts will be lost. Of course such a situation is very, very nasty, and under these conditions it is impossible to lead a normal, quiet life; under such conditions it is very easy, unwillingly, to be shaken off the rails and to cease to exist in the economic sense — for nowadays the slightest flood current sweeps along boulders and in this way makes it impossible to continue existing trade relations.
Owing to the unheard-of, economically difficult conditions in which the country finds itself, the smallest change threatens both manufacturing and commerce — not to speak of small manufacturing, the artisans and the small traders!
These middle strata of the population, the small people, upon whom every snapping of a string has an immediately catastrophic effect — they are simply not taken into account at all. When there is talk in the high windows about crisis, about catastrophe, it is only about the big ones, about those who ride on horses; the small ones, the broad mass, the middle strata of the population — nobody has them in mind; it never occurs to anyone to drop a word about them.
Yes, one appeals to the popular masses only when one needs their votes, as at various elections; if no elections were held in the country, people would have entirely forgotten that such people exist in the Polish Republic. That is how they are forgotten at every step, how they are not reckoned with at all; they do not count when they are unemployed, nobody takes an interest in them when they go hungry and when they are going through the most severe crisis. On the contrary — in certain circles one tries to forget completely that such people exist; one does not want them to be seen in the country at all, and so indeed they are never reckoned with.
True, we ourselves are much to blame; true, these categories are helpless at every step and remain forlorn when no one leads them; and worse still, on the one hand they do not let themselves be led, and on the other hand there are none of the experienced people who would be capable of this responsible work.
More than once we have had the opportunity in this very place to point out the shortcomings. We have shown that the whole ruin lies in this: that everything, from beginning to end, is rotten through and through; that we Jews do not want to earn and do not understand how to organize our sources of livelihood; we fool ourselves and think we are fooling the other — there lies the crux, that is how we are unable to steer ourselves onto the right, straight and safe road.
There are many, many ways, many and many means of improving the situation of the middle class and of the lower elements. It would be quite good if, first, people set about it intensively, calmly and sincerely, and second, if these elements were not so venomously stubborn; if they did not want to fool one another — which ends in everyone fooling himself, thinking it will not touch him; and if one did not want to trip up the other with "little feet" steeped in so much poison, so much hatred, so as to wipe out the other, to destroy the competitor, to get rid of the neighbour across the way, whom he can no more look at than a Jew can look at a piece of pork.
Jews could make a living, only they do not want to. True, people want to tear the bite out of the middle class's mouth, and it is left to fight bitterly for its existence; true, outside elements want to destroy it — but one must not forget that the Jew has such qualities that he can be sure no one will be able to get the better of him, and from whatever side stones may be thrown at him, he will still remain standing on his feet.
We must be alert once and for all; we must remember that we, like all nations, now live under entirely different conditions, and therefore we should not be ashamed to admit openly and clearly that we do not know how to adapt to the emerging conditions, which actually bring an entirely different adjustment[?], an entirely different outlook into our life; and so it seems to us that everything comes unexpectedly, whereas in reality, had we understood calculation and modern reckoning, we would have known in advance that these catastrophes of the small businesses come upon us in an entirely normal way.
It does not matter — once people here begin to understand and begin to analyse all this, they will come to realize that, just like a small child, we cannot allow ourselves to walk the road alone, because in that case one may stumble; and just like the small child who cannot yet walk by itself, we must learn to start walking with firm, sure steps. But as long as we laugh at all this, as long as everyone here is petty and wants to be sharper than the next man, we will not free ourselves of the shortcomings that drive us off the right, straight road on which we could so easily walk with sure, firm steps, and one could attain secure livelihoods, and we would rise onto better economic foundations.
These same categories of people, with the very same occupations, exist all over the world, and they do not have to fight nearly so hard for their existence as is the case with us. On the contrary, they are not badly situated at all and lead a normal, quiet life, just as God commanded from the six days of Creation on...
And here, as winter now approaches, one's hair stands on end at the great worries people have: here the children have nothing warm to wear, and there there will be nothing to heat with in winter. It is no small matter for us — when winter comes, this burden takes up one's whole head, leaving no mind for running the businesses and the workshop.
Could it have been otherwise? Could we have arranged a better and more systematic life for ourselves?
Yes, with full awareness this could have happened, if only we had thought about it seriously and sincerely, if only we had set about it with all our strength, just as people set about — let us say — competing with one another.
And perhaps we really ought to give it some thought?
R. Let.
Former cantor Sherman on the cantorial question in Będzin

The cantorial affair in Będzin, and especially the "sensational" Din Torah [rabbinical court case] on the question, has found an echo with the former Będzin cantor R' Avraham Yitzchak Szerman, who is now a cantor in America.
In a letter to a friend of his in Będzin he writes, among other things, the following opinion, which we believe will arouse interest among a certain part of our readers.
"I was simply astonished — writes Mr Szerman — reading in the 'Zaglembier Tsaytung' the ruling of the Beth Din; I could not make sense of it and believe that a Beth Din could be so one-sided, for example: 1) that the cantor should have no precedence to the 'RḤSh' [the rabbi-cantor-sexton fee] that is paid in at the rabbi's — why so? Why should the cantor stand like a beggar at the door of the in-laws? And how one feels at such a moment is very well known to me. 2) The cantor is disqualified as a witness to a marriage — the question arises: may a cantor who is disqualified from testimony lead the service [the Avodah]? 3) If a Beth Din has no sufficient[?] evidence to remove him, how can he be disqualified as a witness to a marriage? 4) The Beth Din writes that it has a hidden secret, on account of which it wants to introduce this throughout the Jewish diaspora — that we understand: since it is a secret, it is a... but to do this to just one person and to shame him in public!
The ruling of the Beth Din is very complicated; I shall raise the[?] question at a meeting-session of the local Agudat HaChazanim [Cantors' Union], and their resolution will be published in the entire Jewish press.
Dear friend! Now you can understand my mental and physical suffering in Będzin, where I spent my young strength. I always set aside my own will before the will of others; I killed in myself every desire for life and held back from being present even at a se'udat mitzvah [religious feast], just so as not to be counted among the recipients [of gifts]; I suffered a great deal, but swallowed everything, in order to avoid a bad odour[?] [i.e. ill repute], which disturbs more than other sufferings. 'Your deeds will bring you near and your deeds will drive you away': when I made a Mi Sheberakh for Reuven I looked towards Shimon, so that Reuven should not think that I was casting an eye on his few groszy. But He who knows all thoughts helped me, and I have come out from darkness to light and from bondage to redemption — for I am no longer in the town of cantorial brawls[?], with dairy and meat cantors"...
Minister Kwiatkowski's visit to Zagłębie

On Sunday the Minister of Commerce, Kwiatkowski, stayed in Zagłębie; he took part in the 20th jubilee of the "Saturn" coal mine.
In the afternoon hours the minister was at the Chamber of Commerce in Sosnowiec, where he received the delegation of big industry and of the merchants.
The merchants' delegations handed the minister a memorandum, in which a series of demands concerning tax relief and commercial questions was set out.
In the Chamber of Commerce the minister gave a speech, in which he stressed the important activities of the chambers of commerce in Poland and declared that all demands put forward by the chambers of commerce will be realised by the government, according to its possibilities.
Then the minister left for Katowice, where he held a conference with the Upper Silesian industrialists.
After the conference the minister, together with Voivode Paczerkowski[?], drove to Dąbrowa, where he visited the premises of "Kuźnica"[?] and gave a speech. Among other things the minister said that the Polish szlachta [gentry] and the present-day deputies, who in the name of so-called democracy want to "arrange" all of Poland for themselves, as in the times of the November Uprising.
"There was a time — says the minister — when such kinds of figures circulated in the corridors and ministerial offices that all officials were afraid of them. When I asked who these 'M.A.'[?] were, it turned out that they were deputies. Under such conditions it is impossible to run the state economy, when the actual government was divided among 444 deputies."
At 1 a.m. the minister left for Warsaw.
I'm happy, I'm fine, I'm a voter... (A kopeck philosophy)

Hush, Jews[?]! It's happening, people are going to the elections — a brand-new word has been added.
Once people knew: one goes to Selichot, or one goes to the Hakafot, one goes to elect a rabbi, a cantor. But today, in the twentieth century, when the whole world is going forward — civilisation, progress, parliamentarism and the like — people go quite differently, oh, how they go! One goes on chopped troubles... another goes "keri'a and gli'a"[?]...
And therefore, when such a "delight" as elections happens to come along — it is "let us rejoice and be glad", as in "Shash arayn"[?].
One's heart gets a little lighter, almost as when one is rid of a tooth abscess or of the bailiff... for it always seems — who knows, perhaps something will turn round for the better... As they sing in "Pintele Yid": oh, I'm happy, oh, I'm "dobrze" [fine], it's a delight to be a... voter!
For imagine: all at once you are rid of a whole series of "kłopoty" [worries] on your head, and you are provided with everything of the finest and best...
And I, Yankel Glas the shoemaker, who am blackened and darkened day and night and nobody so much as looks at me, suddenly begin to acquire importance...
For some time now, since the elections have been approaching, people have been fussing over me as over a member of a tax commission... And what's more, there's talk that I should agree to accept from someone a "guterl"[?] [little favour?], and if the adversary sees it, then the opponent really gets the "gkhpe"[?].
Well, so what then, I ask you, do I need more honour? A kapore [scapegoat] for Hindenburg, Wiślicki, Melech Ravitch — oh, what good will that do me? Rent money — taking the landlord a few złoty so he won't file for eviction, you say? A thousand times over [lit. "a thousand shok"]! When I'll have my own big, bright room — and if I want, a whole house... A livelihood? Comes "dear Friday", [unclear][?], a few złoty to prepare for Shabbat — what do you want to say? — a "sukkah" [i.e. a curse] on my enemies! I shall lack nothing, not even bird's milk... Taxes? What, the bailiff is going to take away the rotten cupboard with the last few odds and ends for the turnover tax ["obrotowe"]? I have a ruling: I laugh at his grab; let Yankel Glas just give a "peep" to his chosen deputy — that very moment he is here beside me and protects me with all his "immunity" and makes ruins of everyone...
You see, gentlemen, only one more thing is bad — with bridegrooms for my daughters — that I still have to rack my brains myself over where to get them...
But I think that in this too I'll find a way. In the present elections I'll really try to dig in my heels: bridegrooms for my maidens I shall have! What's the matter? They're not too ill to take care of that... Few[?] young men hang around them in the parties! Lads like oak trees! My eldest would capture her heart with such a one... And there's a chance I'll achieve it, because 5 votes, you must know, there are at my place, no evil eye, and if not — I won't go to the elections.
Oh, gentlemen, you will surely ask: what good are the philosophies to you, Yankel Glas, the heated fantasies with the foolish promises, when all this is no more than mouth-work; the proof: how many times have there already been elections, and parties and little parties promised mountains and hills, and from all of them came out in total an attic [i.e. nothing], a bluff, and indeed [unclear][?] one acted as if there had never been any elections in the world... That's what you'll ask me.
The answer — it really is bitter, but what choice do I have?
Would that it seemed to me just a dream: and, getting back to the point — what do I get out of it if there are no more elections? I ask you — is it something bad if you have almost a good dream? And perhaps, I think... eh? When God wills, even a broom shoots; who knows, maybe yes... And meanwhile, I beg you, don't confuse me and don't disturb my joy.. I'm happy, I'm fine, I'm a voter!...

The International Spa in the "Ne'ila" Season

[Travel sketch — Karlsbad.] By L. Szpigelman.
Whom does one not see in Karlsbad [Karlovy Vary]? — A little statistics on the spa, which has existed for more than 600 years. — The "Ne'ila" season and the Polish, Czech and Russian spa guests — Prof. Durov and other Russian personalities. — Greetings from Russia.
Karlsbad can rightly, and in the full sense of the word, be called the international spa, for which of the world's rulers, princes, kings, billionaires, philosophers, eunuchs [?] has not trodden Karlsbad soil? Which of the peoples of all parts of the world has not stood there, gathered together in the queues at the Mühlbrunn and the Sprudel springs? Which of the greatest personalities in the world does not stroll, to this very day, year after year, drinking the waters in the colonnades of the springs?
All this is in itself no news, since Karlsbad is the most popular spa in the world, and it has been written about in various periods. What is interesting is only how Karlsbad looks at the end of the tenth month [October], when people have already dispersed from all the spas.
Now, before the beginning of the winter cure, it stands at the end of the summer season, and it is in this very "Ne'ila" season that we want to take a stroll through the oldest international spa in the world.
Of course the splendour is already over; it is no longer what it is in the high [?] season, when nature blooms and everything calls to life. Thus, for example, the very large hotels such as the Pupp, the Imperial etc. are already closed; the very large shops too are already shut, because their appetites are only for American dollars, English pounds, ministers, world rulers, magnates.
The spa administration, too, is systematically reducing its colossal expenses: not all the baths are open any more, the library and reading rooms are already closed, and the springs are now open only until 7 in the evening. It is interesting in this connection that on the evening after Yom Kippur the springs were open until 8, so that Jews would have the opportunity to drink the waters after the fast — and our brethren the Children of Israel did indeed drink and enjoyed the privilege.
Instead of live orchestras the spa administration has economised and uses the radio; only at the Sprudel is there still an orchestra twice a day for a short time. The rest of the time is filled with the radio, and it makes the impression of the cinematograph replacing the living art theatre.
On this occasion it will be interesting for the readers to give a historical overview of Karlsbad. The spa has existed for more than 600 years and was founded by the Austrian Emperor Charles IV, which is why it bears his name. Today there are 16 springs, and the waters range from 40 to 72 degrees of heat. There are 6 bathing establishments.
The most interesting thing is to watch with what force the Sprudel's outpouring is thrown up: it pours out 2000 litres in a single minute and about 2½ million litres a day. During the high season 23,000 glasses of thermal water are drunk daily. Every year, through the well-known Jewish firm Löbel Schottländer [?] [printed "Schot-Sender"], 4 million bottles of mineral water and 90,000 kilos of Sprudel salt are exported to all parts of the world.
In the high season 6 to 7 thousand baths are used daily.
The owners of the boarding houses and hotels complain bitterly that this year attendance was considerably smaller, which is explained by the world crisis; nevertheless [?], up to the 11th of this month 62,578 guests were registered with the spa administration. Now, in the so-called "Ne'ila" season, there are still some 3000 guests, the greatest number of whom are from Czechoslovakia and Poland. This is explained by the fact that for the Czechs the spa prices are now especially cheap, and having served spa guests in various places, they now come to Karlsbad to recuperate themselves.
Guests from Poland, too, came so late for reasons of economy, since everything is cheaper here now. This also shows that those who come from Poland to take the cure in Karlsbad are people who really need the Karlsbad cure.
We now also meet here a fair number of patients from Soviet Russia, so that the sound of the Russian language is heard in the colonnades.
Of course it is not so easy to get out of Russia abroad, and so one must suppose that those who are here are people from the "high windows" [?] [i.e. the upper circles] or simply privileged persons; and therefore the writer of these lines very much wished to have a chat with the Russian guests.
And here is the interesting part: my first conversation I had — together with, and thanks to, my friend the dentist Mrs. Grinberg-Lekowska [?] — with the old Russian professor Durov, who, by the way, had already been declared dead by the foreign press a year ago.
Many of our readers surely do not know who Prof. Vladimir Durov is, so it is interesting to explain briefly that Prof. Durov has occupied himself all his life with the psychology of various animals, in which he has distinguished himself not only in Russia but also abroad.
Prof. Durov carries out astonishing experiments not only with dogs, lions, bears, cats and the like, but also with rats; and with mice he runs trains [?], and under his supervision they are employed just like people.
Before the war Prof. Durov played an important role in Russia; for his liberalism he was arrested more than once by the Tsarist government, notwithstanding the fact that in the "high windows" they had to reckon with him, so that at the Imperial court he achieved everything he wanted.
An interesting episode is told about Prof. D. In Tsarist times there was in Odessa a city governor (gradonachalnik) Zelenoi, who persecuted Jews without limit. Once Prof. D. arrives in Odessa with his "troops"; he then performed his experiments in one of Odessa's largest theatres, where scholars and the Russian intelligentsia were present, and among them also the gradonachalnik Zelenoi. Prof. Durov doesn't think twice and leads out before the public a pig that had been decorated green from head to foot, and says: "Here's [?] a green pig" [Russian "zelyonaya svinya" — a pun on the governor's name]. The political joke was so sharp that in its time it made an impression throughout Russia. The gradonachalnik had his eye on the professor and sought to settle accounts with him.
Prof. D. conducts a discussion [?] with the writer of these lines, and among other things he says: "Well, so with you I have already died — and no other way than of hunger." And here he shows his walking stick with the golden handle, made like the foot of an animal; in the foot is set a precious sapphire, and around it [?] various silver and golden animals are mounted. Then he shows, in his tie, his large tiepin — a rat set with diamonds. "That means," he says with a smile on his lips, "that as long as I still have all this, together with the gold watch, I could not die of hunger."
And further Prof. Durov says: "I am 68 years old now, and nobody disturbs me in my scientific studies; my priceless treasure now belongs to the Russian state, which maintains [?] the large menagerie. Ah —" suddenly his heart grows heavy — "what a great spender I am on my animals at a time when so many people are starving!"
Prof. D. relates that his scientific researches are now appearing in German and French as well; and then the writer of these lines, together with the dentist Grinberg-Lekowska, proposes that he permit his works to be translated into Yiddish and Hebrew too. To which he replies: "I permit the translation, and I would be most happy if my lectures were read [?] at the Jerusalem University. But I have one condition: I do not want any fee [?]; therefore I want the translations to be professionally competent [?] and good."
Prof. D. is here with his wife, who watches over him and comes every moment to take a look so that he should not exert himself too much and not talk too much... Prof. D. takes his leave and says: "Pass on to your readers, pass on to your Jews the most heartfelt greetings from Prof. Durov, and tell them that I always felt their suffering in Tsarist Russia and their thirst for education."
We also had an interview with another Russian personality, whose name we cannot mention for understandable reasons.
To our question how the actual situation in Russia looks now, the interviewee answers: "With us it is bad, with us it is bitter and dreary [?] — it couldn't be worse. It keeps getting uglier and uglier. The great Russian land has been turned into parties, into factions, into sects. No one has any right to think and believe as he understands, as his logical mind dictates to him; for such 'sins' one pays with one's life.
A dog, a cat, a horse may think according to its notion, according to its understanding, but a human being in Russia is not entitled to it. A human being with us in Russia is just like a machine: it must move as its master, the machinist, dictates to it."

England, You Will Not Defeat Us... (On the English government’s fresh decree)

[Poem — Palestine; the Passfield White Paper.]
Darkness reigns among [?] Israel
from the new British betrayal;
upon the holiest thing that Balfour once said
a shameful assault has been made.
But we will not turn pessimistic —
whoever believes in the survival of the nation
need not debate about it,
and above all — must not lose courage.
We have no soldiers,
no warships and no cannons,
no rifles and no bombs —
our only weapon
is — to make a racket and to shout!
Our method — regrettably —
cannot break down walls,
but it can bore holes in ears...
We are too weak to punish you, England,
for your present bluffs;
with our “appeal to the world’s conscience”
one cannot shoot at you;
our strongest phrases
are no match for your chemical gases.
Our strength lies only in the tongue,
and for your bluffs
we can punish you only
by not letting you sleep in peace...

Shattered is the harmony we kept for years —
but no one can play the hero
when the Jew employs his power of speech;
that is more terrible than spear and knife —
the land of Spain knows that best...
When Israel opens his sharp tongue
and his voice rings out across the world
with protest and with wailing,
with storm and with a curse —
then even the cleverest diplomats begin
to search for good advice
against our cries and clamour,
which grow ever wilder
and no longer seek to drown
in the sea of shed Jewish tears...
————

not by force and not by lies;
with declarations and “White Paper” debates

you and your war-cannons.

our wailing will wake you,
