The Arab Problem in Eretz Israel

V. Jabotinsky.

Editorial note: We are beginning to print a series of articles which we have received for our newspaper, written by the master of the pen V. Jabotinsky. Although the articles were written before the latest events in Zionism, they do not lose their topicality.

1.
The Iron Wall.

A.
Contrary to the rule — to begin a treatise with the very most important part of its content — I consider it necessary to begin this essay with an introduction, and moreover with a personal introduction.

The author of these lines is regarded as an enemy of the Arabs, as a supporter of their expulsion from Eretz Israel, etc. That is not correct. My emotional attitude to the Arabs is the same as to all other peoples, i.e. — polite indifference. My political attitude is determined by two principles: first — I consider the expulsion of the Arabs from Eretz Israel, in whatever form, to be impossible. Eretz Israel will always be a state of nationalities (not to be confused with a bi-national state — Ed.). That is entirely sufficient for me, on condition that the Jews become the majority there. Second — I belong to the group which once formulated the Helsingfors Programme. We formulated it not only for the benefit of the Jews, but for the benefit of all peoples. The basis of that programme is: equal rights for all nationalities. Like all the others, I am ready to take an oath on this basis for myself and for our coming generations. It seems to me that this is a quite peaceful "credo" ("Ani ma'amin").

But quite different is the question whether peaceful intentions can be realised in a peaceful way. The answer to this question has nothing to do with our attitude to the Arabs, because the answer is expressly determined by the Arab attitude to Zionism.

After this introduction we can proceed to the actual subject.

B.
There can be no talk of a voluntary peace between the Arabs of Eretz Israel and us, neither now nor in the near future. I express this conviction in such sharp form not because I enjoy hurting good-hearted people. Besides, I do not believe that they will take it much to heart, because everyone — except the blind from birth — has long since realised that it is impossible to obtain the voluntary consent of the Arabs to turning this very Eretz Israel from an Arab country into a country with a Jewish majority.

Every reader surely has a general idea of the history of colonisation in other countries. I recommend that the reader recall all the known examples and try — going through the whole of history — to find even one single case where colonisation was carried out with the consent of the natives. Such a case has never occurred anywhere.

Natives, no matter whether civilised or uncivilised, have always fought stubbornly against colonisation. It made no difference whether the colonisers were civilised or not. Moreover, the conduct of the colonisers had no influence whatever on the attitude of the inhabitants.

The companions of Cortés [printed "Kartel"?] and Pizarro, or (as one might perhaps remark) also our forefathers in the days of Joshua son of Nun, behaved like robbers; but the English-Scottish Pilgrim Fathers, the first true pioneers of North America, were exceptional people with a lofty ethical pathos. People who did not touch [?] [anyone], people [who] sincerely believed that on the prairies there was enough room for whites and for reds — and nevertheless the natives fought with the same murderous ferocity against the good colonisers as against the bad ones.

In this respect the question whether there is a lot of room in the country or not plays no role at all. In 1921 there were 340,000 Indians counted on the territory of the United States, but even in their best times their number reached 314 [?; probably meant ¾] million, over the whole huge area from Labrador to the Rio Grande. At that time there was not one person in the world with such a rich imagination as to picture a danger of real "expulsion" of the natives by strangers. The natives fought not because they [printed: "we"] consciously feared being driven out of their land, but quite simply because colonisation will never appear to the native as a welcome [?] matter. Every settled people, whether civilised or savage, regards its land as its national home, where it is the sole master, and as such it also wants to remain. A people will not voluntarily admit not only new masters, but even partners or associates in the economy — and this applies to the Arabs too.

C.
The peacemakers in our ranks try to convince us that the Arabs are either fools, who can be deceived with a "moderate" formulation of our true aims, or "a bribe-taking gang", who for the price of cultural and economic concessions will let us gain the upper hand over Eretz Israel.

I am quite decidedly against such an assessment of the Arabs of Eretz Israel. Culturally they lag some 500 years behind us; spiritually they possess neither our power of endurance nor our will-power; but with that the entire inner difference between them and us is exhausted. They are exactly as sharp-witted psychologists as we are, and, like us, they have been educated for centuries in incisive pilpul. We can tell them whatever we like, but they understand the depths of our soul just as we grasp the depths of theirs. And they feel towards Eretz Israel at least the same love and the same organic jealousy as the Aztecs felt towards their old Mexico and the Sioux towards their prairies. The illusion of the Arabophiles that this people will voluntarily consent to the realisation of Zionism, in exchange [?] for the moral and material comforts which the Jewish coloniser will bring it — this childish fantasy stems from an exaggerated disdain for the Arab people, from a kind of notion [?] of the Arab race as a rabble of bribe-takers, ready to give up its fatherland for a good railway network.

D.
This notion has no foundation whatsoever. It is said that individual Arabs take bribes. But it does not follow from this that the Arabs of Eretz Israel as a whole would be capable of selling their jealous patriotism — something that even the Papuans have not sold.

Every people fights against colonisation as long as it has even the slightest hope of freeing itself from the danger of colonisation. That is how the Arabs of Eretz Israel act, and that is how they will go on acting as long as they still have a spark of such hope.
Friedrich Nietzsche

[Essay — philosophy; 30th anniversary of Friedrich Nietzsche's death.] Shimon Rotenberg.
(On his 30th yahrzeit)
From time immemorial the human mind has been tormented by the problems of spirit, of life and death, of free will and the iron laws of nature. From time immemorial there has stood before us, like a terrible gigantic spectre, the eternally old-new Hamletian problem of "to be or not to be". What is the meaning of human life? What must be man's chief striving? What must he do in order to attain the highest happiness?
Various are the teachings and paths shown to us by the philosophers who have lived from humanity's childhood to the present day. Deep abysses very often divide the thinkers in their conclusions about the meaning of human life.
If Tolstoy, for example, sees the whole meaning of human existence in love of one's neighbour, and to that end sacrifices art, science and culture on the altar of this love; if Kant teaches us that in our breast is hidden a mystical voice, "a categorical imperative", which commands us to seek the good and avoid the evil — Nietzsche teaches that "the others" exist only so that we may trample on them and exploit them for our own satisfaction. Nothing worse can happen to a man than when he listens to all the phrases of morality, to all the swindle-talk of "good" and "evil", love of the other and self-sacrifice. His motto is "everything is permitted, nothing is true". Strive for your own power and guard yourself against the greatest misfortune that can befall you — against loving the other.
At first Nietzsche stood under the influence of Hellenism, of Wagner's music and of Schopenhauer's pessimism and metaphysics of the will, which sees the highest stage of worldly being in art in general and in music in particular. Wagner was therefore for Nietzsche the idol in whom the world-substance revealed itself. Music is the sphere in which man escapes from life and from the will to be. Music is the one and only art capable of throwing a person into a mystical trance and compelling him to ponder the problems of God, man and the world. But later, in his book "The Gay Science", Nietzsche combats everything romantic and regards art, religion and philosophy as illusions which man created for himself as necessities in the struggle for his existence.
Nietzsche's aim is consciously to breed the higher type, the "Übermensch". This type, Nietzsche holds, has already appeared often enough, but only as a lucky accident, as an exception; he was never consciously reared and cultivated — on the contrary, every means was used to hinder his life and creation. Now, after the revaluation of all values, one must see to it that all forces are applied so that the brilliant natures of power can develop as well as possible. No new god can help — says Nietzsche — only a new man, the "Übermensch", who grasps the meaning of the earth.
To get an idea of what demands Nietzsche places on his new, higher human type, we will let Zarathustra himself speak.
"You want to go the way of your sorrow, which is the way to yourself? Then prove to me that you have the right and the strength for it. Are the new strength and the new right hidden in you? The first movement! The wheel rolling of itself! How many ambitious ones strain toward the heights — prove that you do not belong to them!"
Thus spoke Zarathustra, and in his words lies the deep meaning of this new, free personality.
According to Nietzsche it is the will that decides what shall be true and good, and not reason, for all our actions arise from the mysterious world of drives and instincts which are inaccessible to reason. There are, however, no drives toward the true and the good; all drives can be traced back to one single primal drive, the will to power, to a stronger, richer and higher existence.
Nietzsche divides morality into a master-morality and a slave-morality. The comparison of the various moral codes of the peoples teaches us that there are two basic types of morality: master-morality and slave-morality; the Greek, Roman and Germanic cultures arose through the subjugation of peaceful tribes by warlike master-peoples.
The ideal of humanity, democracy and socialism are, according to Nietzsche, nothing other than modern variants of the Christian-Jewish slave-morality. If Christianity demands the equality of all men before God, democracy in turn demands the equality of all men before the law. Both, however, Christianity as well as democracy, are united in the faith in the herd and in the fear of the master-nature. The consciousness of sinfulness, man's constant bad conscience, is nothing other than the great, most important trait of the slave, who always feels guilty — not only toward his master but toward his God as well.
Nietzsche feels a deep contempt for woman. He is against her emancipation; she is at bottom a slave-nature. Her real purpose in life should be, according to Nietzsche, to help bring forth strong-willed men. If a woman feels an inclination toward science, she surely suffers from some abnormal deviation in the sexual sphere. The expectations with which woman is filled regarding sexual love represent for her all broad perspectives. Too long have the slave and the tyrant been hidden in woman; therefore she is incapable of friendship; she knows only love, and the love of woman is bound up with injustice and blindness toward everything she does not love.
With the same contempt as toward woman, Nietzsche also regards the masses. He is an outspoken individualist; he hates the masses and despises them. "The happiness of the rabble is the happiness of laziness and dullness. Life is a well of delight, but this well is poisoned when the unclean lips of the rabble touch it." (Thus Spoke Zarathustra.)
Yet for all his great genius Nietzsche overlooked the fact established by Marx, that not the genius and not the deeds of an individual, but the masses and the economic relations determine the course of all events. Precisely those masses which stand outside Nietzsche's teaching give ideas the strength to live and grow, and only blood-kinship with the masses can ensure a thinker spiritual immortality.
These, in brief (as far as it is possible to fit into the frame of a newspaper article), are the basic ideas of Nietzsche's philosophy, which run like a red thread through all his works with their contradictions and paradoxes.
Thus the human spirit eternally torments itself over the various problems of its existence, and remains standing helpless, as thousands of years ago, before the great phenomenon, before the great tragedy "man and world".
Nature, in creating primeval man, surely did not reckon that she was creating her own greatest enemy. She surely did not foresee that in the course of millions of years the brain of the "ape-man" would develop so far, and his spirit reach such a level, that he would turn into a restless, ever-active, thousand-footed creature which crawls everywhere that still remains dark and incomprehensible to his feeling, and bites with his sharp teeth into the depths of nature in order to tear from her the unconscious that lies deeply hidden behind her stage-wings. It seems that it has become the passion of the human spirit to spy out all the secrets of nature and life, and to that end it creeps after them like a shadow, so as constantly to thin the thick fog in which nature disguises herself.
In the gallery of the great spirits Nietzsche occupies a very important place. His thinking is like a mighty storm, thundering and bloody; like a suddenly erupting volcano he spews fire in order to destroy everything with the watchword of his incomparable language, with the style of "Thus Spoke Zarathustra",
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings and remarks on today's Torah portion (Lech Lecha)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings and remarks on today's Torah portion.
Collected and adapted by Y. L.[?]
Parashat Lech Lecha
—o—
a) "And I will make of thee a great nation" (Gen. 12:2).
1.
Rashi says on this verse that travel has a bad effect on a person in three respects, namely: on children, on money and on reputation; therefore Abraham had to be blessed with these three things when he set out on his journey.
How does travel harm a person's good name?
— The Maggid of Dubno once said: every clever man also says foolish things at times. But one retells his wise sayings and keeps silent about the follies. So it turns out that those close to him sometimes hear a folly from the sage too, while far away people know only of his wisdom..
But when the sage sets out on the road, strangers come to know his weak sides as well, and that is why travel harms a good name. Divrei Shaul.
2.
Yes, the road — our long road of exile — harms three things: children, money and name.
Children — at the time of the destruction of the Second Temple the Jewish people numbered six million souls, and now, after so many tens of hundreds of years, and given the pure family life that Jews lead, we ought by the natural growth[?] process to number at least a hundred and fifty million souls. But the savage pogroms and the cruel decrees swallow them up.
Money — how much capital has been amassed through Jewish energy and diligence and has come to nothing, melted away[?]. In every age the Jews had great magnates, great capitalists — and where is Jewish wealth?
Name — a name far too loud[?] is what we have earned in exile... There is one single rescue: "Go forth to the land that I will show thee" — go and build the Land of Israel. Derashot RYG.
—o—
b) "And thou shalt be a blessing" (ibid.).
1.
Rashi:
The verse refers to what is said in the Shemoneh Esreh prayer: "God of Abraham, God of Isaac and God of Jacob", while the closing blessing ends only with "Shield of Abraham" — with Abraham alone.
How did Abraham merit this?
— The Gemara says that Abraham instituted the morning prayer, that is, Abraham prayed right early in the morning, at dawn, so that he could receive guests the whole day. Isaac instituted the afternoon prayer, meaning that he prayed the whole day until the time of Minchah. Well[?], hospitality — that was done by his people, the servants. And because Abraham did not want to entrust the commandment of hospitality to anyone, but performed it himself, God Himself is his protector ("Shield of Abraham"). Isaac, who could rely on an agent in receiving guests, is protected by God also through an agent — through Abraham. Rabbi Meir'l of Przemyślany.
2.
A priest once asked the Maharal: You Jews glorify Moses so much — why do you not say "God of Moses" in the Shemoneh Esreh prayer, just as you say "God of Abraham"?
The Maharal answered him on the spot: because Moses had a blemish in the family: he had a priest for a father-in-law (Jethro).
—o—
c) "And I will bless them that bless thee, and him that curseth thee will I curse" (Gen. 12:3).
The verse is somewhat inverted: of blessing it says "I will bless those who bless you", that is: before they bless you I will bless them. Of cursing, however, the verse says "him that curses you I will curse" — that is: only when they curse you will I curse them. Why this inversion of language?
— When a poor man wishes something it is worth nothing, for what notion, so to speak[?], does a poor man have? To him even bread alone can be called a blessing.. Therefore God says: those who will want to bless you I will bless first; they will become rich, and so they will have the means with which to bless you. But those who will want to curse you I will make into poor people only after the curse, because a poor man curses better than a rich one... From[?] the Vilna Gaon.
—o—
d) "And Abraham was very rich in cattle, in silver and in gold. And he went on his journeys"
Although Abraham had become a newly rich man and was suddenly laden "with silver and gold" — still: "he went on his journeys", he went his former way, did not put on airs; he went his way as if nothing had ever happened. R' Yosef Shaul Nathanson.
* * *
Money should lie in a pocket, in a purse or a cash box; there it lies quietly and makes no noise. But when it is "istara b'lagina" [a coin in a jug], when money lies not in its proper place but in an earthen[?] vessel, it rattles and makes a noise. Thus we see that before the war money was held by many families of good lineage who made no noise with their money. Now, however, it has fallen into the hands of newly rich magnates — and see how the money jingles and clatters with them. The true messianic times will come when "the penny is gone from the purse", when money will be taken out of the purse, its proper place, and put into the jug, where it will rattle and clatter... Milei de-Rabbanan.
—o—
e) "And there was a strife... and the Canaanite and the Perizzite dwelled then in the land" (Gen. 13:7)
The verse tells how intolerable the quarrel was, because "the Canaanite and the Perizzite dwelled then in the land": when the foreign enemy is here in the country, all internal frictions must be silenced. Divrei Emet.
—o—
f) "But the men of Sodom were wicked and sinners — before the Lord exceedingly" (Gen. 13:13).
So wicked and sinful were they, the people of Sodom — they did no one any kindness; but "before the Lord" — in heavenly matters, there "exceedingly": they were extraordinarily pious; at "Forgive us" they beat their breasts hard with their fists, at "Aleinu" they spat a lot — there they spared nothing... Alei Zayit.
—o—
g) "Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim" (Gen. 14:8).
In Berlin the community resolved no longer to let poor people go begging from door to door; instead the community fund would pay each a fixed donation. When the resolution was handed to the local rabbi for approval, he said: Well, this is an old resolution of the Council of Four Lands — what is new about it?
The community administrators heard this and were amazed: did the Council of Four Lands once decide such a thing too?
— Yes — says R' Hershele — such a resolution was probably adopted by the council of the four lands: Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim...
—o—
h) "And he believed in the Lord, and He counted it to him for righteousness" (Gen. 15:6).
The Apter Rav (Rabbi Avraham Yehoshua Heschel) related: Rabbi Elimelech of Leżajsk was once my guest, and I gave him a separate little room. Once I came in and heard him reckoning with himself whether he was worthy of the World to Come or not.. And he said to himself: "Oh my soul, my soul is not fit for the World to Come", and he said every bad thing about himself. Then he reconsidered: although you truly do not deserve the World to Come, you will have it nevertheless, for the Gemara says that God fulfils the whole Torah; He fulfils the commandments of comforting mourners, charity etc.[?] — and what charity can God do in the other world? Distribute money, perhaps? Rather this is the meaning: He will hand out the World to Come freely[?], even to those who are not worthy — He will hand it out as charity..
"And He counted it to him for righteousness [tzedakah = charity]" — Abraham too reckoned this way: that if he would have anything good, it would come to him only as charity.. Siftei Tzaddikim.
—o—
i) "And a deep sleep fell upon Abram" (Gen. 15:12).
This vision now shown to Abraham signified the later exile: "thy seed shall be a stranger in a land that is not theirs". The exile with all its cruelties was shown to him, and this came through a deep sleep, a heavy slumber, to symbolise that one of the tragic sorrows of exile would be the torpor — that Jews would sleep and do nothing; they would be tormented and sit with folded hands in a deep sleep... Ohel Yaakov.
—o—
j) "In a land that is not theirs" (Gen. 15:13).
They will be tormented by those foreign nations too; even the minorities who are themselves strangers will also torment the Jews... Midrash Shmuel.
Napoleon and the Young Polish Countess Walewska

[Serialized historical story — Napoleon and Maria Walewska; installment 5.]
M. Osherowitch.

5.

As the beloved of the great emperor, Maria Walewska could have lived in wealth and honour and literally bathed in pleasures; at that time she could have amassed a great deal of money. But she was not one of those women who seek material favours [?] in love, and at the time when she sacrificed her whole life to him, she demanded one thing of him — love.

In Paris she went almost nowhere; the charm of the French capital did not interest her; the box that Napoleon had prepared for her at the theatre almost always stood empty; the young countess mostly sat at home and waited for her beloved emperor, or for the carriage he would send for her so that she might come to him...

So a stretch of time passed. And later, when the war with Austria broke out and Napoleon again went off to battle, he took the young countess with him..

Not far from Vienna he rented a palace for her, and every evening he sent a carriage for her so that she would come to him..

At that time she confided to him the great secret that in a few months she would bear a child, and to Napoleon this was such glad tidings that he felt like the happiest man in the world..

A child from the woman whom he loved so much. "If only it were a boy!" — he expressed the wish, and began to show the young countess still more love, still more tenderness, and there is reason to believe that he then thought quite seriously about finding a way to make the son heir to his throne...

But fate had marked out something else for Napoleon. He, the man of destiny, was often not master of himself; though he displayed such a strong, such an iron will, he was nevertheless often tossed like a chip by the waves that he himself had stirred into a storm. "He was a stranger in the world, everything was a mystery to him" — so the Russian poet Lermontov once said of Napoleon.

Perhaps a stranger, too, in the world that he himself had created with his genius [printed "noygus"]...

When the peace agreement with Austria was concluded, Napoleon went back to Paris, and his beloved travelled to Poland, and there she bore a son.

This was on the 4th of May in the year 1810. The son was given the name Florian Aleksander Józef [?], and it fell to his lot later to play an important role in the Second Empire. He was minister of foreign affairs under Napoleon III, and he died in Strasbourg in 1868.

Meanwhile everything had turned in another direction, and into the great love, which had held so much joy, the tragic side was brought, which brought both parties so much sorrow..

As is usually the end of all loves.. both when they end in marriage and when they end in a separation...

When Maria Walewska came to Paris a few months later and brought there the child she had borne to Napoleon, circumstances were already entirely different, and "the man of destiny" was already being carried along by new politics [?]. Within a short time Napoleon managed to divorce [lit. "give a get"] his wife Josephine and to marry the Austrian princess Marie Louise, the daughter of King [sic; i.e. Emperor] Francis..

For Countess Maria Walewska this was a great blow. To lose Napoleon's love meant to her losing everything in the world...

And Napoleon no longer wished to continue his relations with her..

Wholly absorbed in the thought that he had a duty to leave an heir after him, in whose veins true royal blood would flow, he cast [?] an eye on his second wife, who was a true princess, and just as he wanted her to be faithful to him, so he too wanted to remain faithful to her...

Whether he remained faithful to her later as well — that is very doubtful. But at first he was very faithful and devoted to her...

Then Maria Walewska felt terribly lonely in Paris. She met Napoleon very rarely. Their relations were very friendly. And here it must be added that Napoleon could be a truly good friend. For a good friend he could always do even the hardest things. He showed special attention to the women he had once loved and who had conducted themselves so as to be worthy of that love. He provided for all of them and saw to it that they should want for nothing.

And he did the same for Countess Walewska.

At that time Walewska became close friends with Josephine, Napoleon's first wife. The two women, who earlier had had reason to hate each other, now grew fond of each other, and they would sit for hours talking about the man whom they had both loved so much...

And later, when Napoleon's star began to fade: when he was forced to give up the throne and the crown — in April 1814 — Maria Walewska was the only woman who came to console him. A whole night she waited in the antechamber for him to call her in, so that she might soothe his sorrowful spirit in her arms. But he did not call her in, because that night he was so distraught that he even wanted to commit suicide.

In her eyes he was not the emperor, the conqueror, the ruler of the world: to her he was and remained — t h e  m a n whom she truly loved.. him and no other...

When he was exiled to the island of Elba, she immediately wrote him a warm letter, which he soon answered, and afterwards she came to him on the island and spent several days there with him ..

She wanted to stay there with him. Just as Ruth said to Naomi, she too told him that his fate was her fate and that wherever he was, there she would be too; but he did not want her to sacrifice herself so much for him, and told her to go back...

In the Hundred Days, when Napoleon again seized power after he had managed to escape from the island of Elba, Maria Walewska was again by his side.

At every opportunity she showed her true love, her true devotion to him...

A rare woman,
a remarkable woman.
There are not many like her ..

Napoleon, however, did not fully appreciate this. At the time when Maria Walewska showed him so much love and loyalty, he was thinking rather of his wife Marie Louise, who had already exchanged him for another.

And when he had already been exiled to the island of Saint Helena, where he later died an outcast of the whole world: when he learned there that Maria Walewska had married his cousin Count Philippe Antoine d'Ornano, he felt deeply hurt by it. It vexed him terribly, and he regarded it as a betrayal..

And this was natural for him, because like most men of egoistic disposition, Napoleon too understood that in love he may betray a woman, but no woman may betray him...

(On Napoleon's romance with the widow Josephine — in the next issue).
Inspection of the Municipality.

[Będzin — municipality.] On Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday a special delegate of the Kielce Voivodeship carried out an inspection (lustracja) of the activity of the local town administration.
At the present moment the inspection has naturally aroused a certain interest, and various conjectures are being voiced, among them that the inspection is connected with the town administration as well as the town council being about to be dissolved.
In this connection we turned to the authoritative quarters, which explained that although the activity of the Będzin magistrate (municipality) is recognised as exemplary, it may nevertheless happen that today or tomorrow the magistrate will be dissolved.
As we write these lines no change whatsoever has yet taken place.
The General Meeting of the Zionist Revisionist Organisation.

[Będzin — Zionism; Revisionists.] On Saturday the annual general meeting of the Zionist Revisionist Organisation took place in the premises of the Zionist Organisation.
After the opening by Mr. Hofer, Mr. A. Tenenbaum was elected chairman, Mr. Zweigenhaft secretary, and Messrs. Turiner and Zylberberg as members of the presidium.
The representative of the Central Committee, Mgr. Gutkowski [?], delivers a lecture in which the most topical Zionist-Revisionist problems are illuminated, and passes on to the present situation of Polish Revisionism, where he notes a growth of the branches.
After the reading of the minutes of the last general meeting the reports follow. The general report and the Keren Tel Hai report are given by Mr. Hofer; Mr. Zuckerman gives the treasury report, according to which the organisation has operated from 8 March of this year until today with a budget of about 1500 zł.
The press report is given by Mr. Frajman, and after the other reports the general meeting is adjourned because of the late hour.
The continuation was conducted by Mr. Diament.
A discussion develops on the reports given, in which Turner [?], Alter, Stuszewski, Danziger and Cygan [?] take part. On behalf of the board Messrs. Langnojs and Frajman reply.
In connection with the 50th jubilee of the Revisionist leader Ze'ev Jabotinsky it is resolved to send a greeting telegram and to inscribe him in the Golden Book (Sefer ha-Barzel) of „Keren Tel-Hai".
The elections gave the following result: to the board: Hofer (president), Diament (vice-president), Zweigenhaft (secretary), Langnojs and Alter. As candidates (deputies): Jaskrowicz, Tenenbaum and Stuszewski (treasurer); to the audit committee: Jakubowicz, Szojmer and Danziger.
District Conference of the Jewish Communities.

[Będzin — kehilla; Palestine.] In connection with the latest events in Palestine (Eretz Israel), a meeting of the kehilla board was held on Sunday morning, which adopted a resolution to convene a conference of all Jewish communities in the Kielce Voivodeship.
At the conference a position will be adopted on the above-mentioned question.
On behalf of the local kehilla protest telegrams were also sent to the English consul in Warsaw, to the Warsaw kehilla and to the Central Committee of the Zionist Organisation.
He Got the „Dowry" for the Engagement..

[Będzin — daily life; matchmaking.] In our town there is a young man who has a weakness for writing tna'im (engagement contracts). The young man had apparently already forgotten his failure in Zawiercie and got matched with a young girl, the daughter of the tinsmith [?] Z. on Zawale Street.
For the girl's parents the match was a stroke of luck — imagine, in these present times, that a young man comes into the house, and a handsome fellow at that, a skilled tradesman, and above all one who wants no dowry...
As the devil would have it, the „groom" is unmasked by his friend, who reveals the secret that he already has 2 wives.
When the girl's parents heard this, they began to count out to him (not a dowry) — one by one...
Today Is Judgement Day for the Candidate Lists.

[Będzin — elections.] Today, Friday, at 7 in the evening a meeting of the Main Electoral Commission will take place. At the meeting the fate of the candidate lists that have been submitted will be considered.
The „Przemsza" Has Burst Its Banks.

[Będzin — weather; flood.] Because of the rains the „Przemsza" „ran wild" [?] on Wednesday and burst its banks.
The surrounding lanes were flooded; in particular the Zawodzie lane, the so-called „Bukowina", was inundated, where the inhabitants were „cut off" from the town.
From the Artisans' Supreme Council in Zagłębie.

[Będzin — artisans; taxes.] A delegation consisting of the president of the local Artisans' Association A. Apatowski [?], Dr. Rotsztajn and town councillor Efraim Klajnman presented itself to the Będzin starost, Mr. Baksen [?], and handed him a detailed memorandum on the difficult economic situation of the Jewish artisans in Zagłębie in connection with a series of topical questions of taxes and (trade) examinations.
The starost listened attentively to all the wishes expressed and promised to meet all the just demands of the Supreme Council.
Lidia Potocka in Zagłębie.

[Zagłębie — theatre; followed by two short Będzin items: WIZO, Tze'irei Mizrachi.] The famous Jewish actress Mrs. Lidia Potocka, who is making a tour of the larger Jewish towns in Poland, is also coming to Zagłębie for a few guest performances.
The repertoire: „Mirele Efros", „Ghosts", „The Woman Who Is Talked About", etc.
The first performance is to take place on Friday, 7 November.
—o—
Practical Courses of „WIZO".
The board of the local women's association „WIZO" has resolved to organise practical courses for its members.
The first courses, in hand-sewing, begin in the middle of the present month.
—o—
A Collective Lecture on Eretz Israel.
The board of „Tze'irei Mizrachi" has resolved to renew its activity in all areas of the organisation.
In connection with the present serious situation in Zionism, the board is conducting broad educational work among the members. The first collective lecture on the political situation in Zionism, with the participation of the members Openheim, Lewin, Manela [?] and others, takes place on Saturday night in the premises of „Mizrachi".
Sosnowiec — Meeting of the Chamber of Commerce

On Tuesday evening the members of the local Chamber of Commerce in Sosnowiec held a meeting. After the report on its activities, given by the chairman, Mr. Krysztak [?] raised the question that the Chamber of Commerce should react to the fact that the Ministry of Finance has not taken into consideration the Chamber's wish that a taxpayer, before the sequestrator (bailiff) comes, should first receive a notice that he must pay the tax instalment by that date.
The budget for the year 1931, in the amount of 405 thousand zł., was adopted without discussion.
Under the item 'free motions' it was decided to apply to the railway directorate that the morning train to Kielce should leave Sosnowiec at 8.20 a.m.
A Ministerial Commission in Sosnowiec

In connection with the water-supply and sewerage installations, which are to be opened on the 10th of next month, a ministerial commission stayed here this week and acquainted itself with the above-mentioned installations.
Founding of a Jewish Watchmakers' Guild

Last Sunday, with the participation of the speaker Y. Lechowski [?], the founding meeting of the Jewish watchmakers', jewellers' and engravers' guild (cech) in Zagłębie took place.
Because only a small number of members from the surrounding area were present, only a 'starszy' (guild master — Mr. Max Goldkorn) and three deputy masters ('podstarsi'), Messrs. Bimka [?], Liberman and Hampel, were elected.
The continuation of the meeting will take place next Sunday at 4 p.m. in the premises of the local Craftsmen's Association. At that meeting a board, a supervisory council and a court of honour will be elected.
Mass Meeting of Craftsmen

On Sunday a large mass meeting of the local Jewish Craftsmen's Association took place in its own premises, devoted to the question of examinations and master's diplomas.
The meeting was opened by the chairman A. Opatowski, who pointed to the present critical time for Jewish craftsmen.
After Mr. Gancwajch had reported at length on the regulations and procedure of the examinations, those assembled, numbering more than 200 men, resolved to sit the master's examination immediately.
Chairman Opatowski made a declaration that the board disclaims responsibility for the further consequences of not presenting oneself for the examinations, since the board is already convening the 10th meeting on the said matter.
Craftsmen's Meetings in Modrzejów and Czeladź

Next Sunday evening craftsmen's meetings will take place in Modrzejów and in Czeladź on important current questions.
The meeting in Modrzejów will also be attended by the craftsmen of Niwka [?], Dańdówka and Klimontów.
In Honour of Jabotinsky's Jubilee

In connection with the 50th jubilee of the Zionist leader and writer Vl. Jabotinsky, a large meeting devoted to Jabotinsky's jubilee took place on Saturday in the premises of the Zionist Organisation. Mr. Klarman spoke about Jabotinsky the thinker and Zionist spokesman. Messrs. Rajzman, Glidman, Fajnrajch, Priger [?] and Jasny also spoke.
The meeting sent Jabotinsky a telegram of greetings.
—o—
From 'HaShachar'.
In the premises of the 'Ziog. Org.' [Zionist youth organisation?], under the chairmanship of Dov Tenenberg, the organising meeting of 'HaShachar' took place. After hearing the greetings of the 'Ziog. Org.', Betar, 'HaShachar' Będzin and Olkusz, Y. Szydłowski gave a report on the activity so far; a lecture on the further activity was given by Mr. Birman of 'HaShachar' (Będzin). Then a board was elected consisting of the following persons: Szydłowski, Mulsztajn, Tenenberg, Kołopać [?], Miadowna [?].
—o—
A Postman — a Swindler.
The postman Pak has been arrested; he embezzled a sum of 1200 zł.
—o—
Leader of a Gang of Thieves Caught
This week the police finally caught the well-known thief Suchecki, leader of a gang of robbers in Zagłębie.
During the search of Suchecki's flat stolen goods were found, together with part of the loot stolen from the merchant Rozenblum in Wojkowice.
Zawiercie

Founding Meeting of 'Bruria'.
On Sunday, in the premises of the 'Gemilut Chasadim' (free-loan) fund, the founding meeting of the women's organisation 'Bruria' took place with the participation of a member of the Central Committee in Poland, Mr. Gajsler [?]. The meeting was opened by Miss Rivka Framan [?], and the chair was handed over to Mr. Zvi Landau, who invited to the presidium Mr. Gajsler (Warsaw), Baster (Kraków), Miss Jungster (Będzin), Miss Wajnryb (Będzin), and as secretary Mr. Baster. Then came greetings: on behalf of 'Bruria' (Będzin) Miss Jungster; the regional committee of 'Bruria' Miss Wajnryb; 'HaShomer HaDati' (Kraków) Mr. Baster; 'Tse'irei Mizrachi' (Będzin) B. Lajchfer [?]; 'Tse'irei Mizrachi' (Zaw.) Mr. Israel Herman; 'HaShomer HaDati' Zvi Rubinsztajn; 'Gedud Kfurim' [sic, perhaps 'Gedud Kfirim']; 'HaShomer HaDati' Shalom Granek; 'Chug Ivri' David Wajcman. Then Mr. Gajsler gave a very successful lecture, which at the end was rewarded with loud applause. Then the board was elected: Rivka Framan, Wajl [?], Liberman, Najman, Danger [?], Gampligska [?], Malka Framan, Grynbaum.
—o—
From 'Frayhayt'.
On Tuesday, in the premises of 'HeChalutz', the organising meeting of 'Frayhayt' took place with the participation of Mr. Kraśniewski (Będzin); but as the latter began his lecture, a group burst into the hall and disrupted the meeting. P.A.Z. [?]
—o—
8 Years' Hard Prison for Murdering a PPS Activist.
Last week the Sosnowiec District Court held a session here, before which the trial of Bronisław Misa [?], 'Srak', also took place; he murdered the PPS activist Jan Klekocki [?].
The political murder was committed on 31 December 1929 in Zawiercie. After committing the murder the murderer fled; only a few weeks ago did he fall into the hands of the police in a village not far from Pilica, where he was staying with his lover, who was also connected with the murder.
At first the murderer claimed that he had committed the murder because he had to defend his life, but all the witnesses showed that the murderer was lying and that he had declared even earlier that he would 'put an end to the red ties', i.e. to the PPS activists, to whom the murdered man belonged and among whom he was an active worker.
The court sentenced the murderer Misa to 8 years of hard imprisonment,

Celebrations of 11 November (Listopad) in Będzin

Next Tuesday, the 11th of this month, the day of Poland's liberation, celebrations will take place in Będzin according to the following programme:
In the morning there will be religious services with the participation of the military, the police, the schools, the guilds, etc.
In the afternoon hours a film will be shown at the „Gm-Kheshtshi“[?] for the school youth and afterwards for the military.
At 4 in the afternoon a festive „academy“ (ceremonial assembly) will take place at the „Kapitol“ cinema.
Besides this, the committee [is organising?] the following events:
Sunday, the 9th of this month, a sale of badges for the benefit of the Marshal Piłsudski orphanage.
Monday, at 6 in the evening, a march through the town with the participation of the military, the fire brigade, etc.

Merchants and industrialists worried about the patents for 1931

The question of the patents [business licences, a tax] for the year 1931 is already becoming topical.
Because of the shortage of cash, a project is being put forward in merchant and industrial circles to grant facilities for the purchase of the new patents. The facilities should above all consist in allowing trading enterprises of the 3rd and 4th category and industrial categories 6, 7 and 8 to pay for the patents in two instalments: on 15 January and on 15 April 1931.
An important facility should be that the financial authorities accept payment of the first instalment of the patent fee until 14 January 1931, and that until that date no patent inspections be carried out, or — that those who do not hold patents by that date not be fined.
As an important concession it is demanded that trading enterprises of the 3rd category be permitted in individual cases (on the basis of applications) to buy patents of the fourth category, if their turnover for 1930 did not exceed 30 000 zł.

An Open Letter to Dr. Rechtman*)

[Będzin — Merchants' Association; municipality.] In the columns of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" no. 42 of the 17th of this month there appeared a letter of yours under the heading "On Economy", full of attacks addressed to the vice-president [of the town] Mr. Rubinlicht, who is at the same time also president of the Będzin Merchants' Association.
The Merchants' Association, as an economic institution interested solely in the economy of the municipality (Magistrat), and in whose name A. Rubinlicht was elected councillor (Ratman) and later vice-president, took an interest in your article and, on the basis of a resolution of the board meeting of the 27th of this month, turned to you with the following letter:
"To Dr. Rechtman in Będzin.
In no. 42 of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" of the 17th of this month, in the article by the Doctor, accusations were made regarding the president of our association, Mr. Rubinlicht. The board of the Merchants' Association, at a meeting on the 26th of this month, resolved to turn to you, Doctor, so that you prove the accusations you made by Wednesday the 29th of this month, 6 p.m. Otherwise the board will regard your accusations as false and will [—][?] draw the further consequences from it."
Respectfully,
Będzin Merchants' Association.
To this letter you, Doctor, replied on the 29th of this month with the following letter:
"To the board of the Merchants' Association in Będzin. In reply to your letter of the 27th of this month I declare that in my article, printed in the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" of the 17th of this month, there are no accusations addressed to the president of the Będzin Merchants' Association; therefore I consider that you have no grounds to intervene on behalf of the association.
Respectfully,
R. Rechtman."
Your answer may be formally in order, since your accusations were directed against Mr. Rubinlicht as vice-president and not as president of our association; but you, Doctor, know very well (as former secretary of the association) that the same person is also president of the Merchants' Association, and to cover oneself with such an evasive excuse can only mean lacking the civil courage to face a civil court.
As said, the Merchants' Association, as an economic institution, is most interested in the whole municipal economy — for who pays most of all the taxes, if not the Jewish merchant? And if the money were managed the way you present it in your article, it would truly be the greatest disgrace for the whole merchant community, whose representatives also sit in the municipality and do not fulfil their obligations. We therefore call on you once again publicly not to cover yourself with any formal excuses, but for the good of the town: prove factually your accusations concerning our representation in the municipality by Tuesday the 11th of November (Listopad), and if things are really managed the way you have shown, we shall be compelled to recall our representatives from the municipality and the town council and draw the proper consequences; but should you fail to prove it by the above-mentioned date, we shall take it as gossip and a personal attack, and the Merchants' Association will be compelled to regard your action as a disgraceful deed.
With respect,
The Board of the Będzin Merchants' Association.
*) For technical reasons the letter did not get into last Friday's issue.

A Jewish woman from Pińczów married a Chinese man and murdered him

For 8 years the Jewish woman Feige Dubrowski[?], a widow from among the homeless of the World War, from Pińczów in the Kielce district, has been languishing in the Harbin prison.
The poor[?] widow married in Harbin a Chinese man, Wan-Fun[?], who converted to Judaism for her sake and received the name Abraham. The life together of two people utterly alien to each other soon opened an abyss between the couple. Quarrels began, which turned into beatings; the husband applied "Asiatic methods", and one dark night, when the battered[?] and tormented[?] Jewish woman could bear it no longer, she seized an axe and brought it down on the head of her enraged[?] husband. The husband fell dead on the spot in a pool of blood. The woman did not try to hide; she took the little baby[?] in her arms, went to the nearest police station and asked to be arrested.
"Take me, I have just killed my husband!"
The Chinese higher[?] court in Harbin sentenced the woman to life imprisonment.
Under an amnesty, Feige Dubrowski's[?] life sentence was commuted to 5 years of special supervision, and the term of her imprisonment ends on 2 July 1932.
But since the quiet, downcast and broken woman has behaved well all along under the extraordinary conditions of prison, the great heavy gates of the Harbin prison will open for her in a few months' time.
The horrifying fact that a poor widow from Pińczów, who knows no language other than Yiddish, a pious Jewish woman who used to bless the candles and say tkhines, the widow of a poor Jewish tailor from the Polish provinces with two small orphans, married a Chinese man and was driven to the fatal moment of committing a murder — is extraordinary, and unrolls in all its magnitude one of the dark pages of the recent past.
All the railway stations were then packed with expelled Jews. At one of these stations they took off and buried the consumptive tailor who had died in the railway car — Feige Dubrowski's husband. The widow and the two children travelled on with many more driven-out Jews.
The Harbin Jewish community set up barracks for the homeless. One of the overseers and keepers of order was the Chinese man Wan-Fun.
Wan-Fun did not remain indifferent to the quiet and modest 35-year-old widow Feige Dubrowski, who had arrived with one of the last transports from Western Siberia with two children. A declaration of love began. At first the widow rejected every such thought. But the Chinese man began a stubborn struggle, promised happiness, pledged to convert, to keep all the commandments and to become a kosher Jew. In the end the quiet, downcast woman consented; she entered into the match for the sake of a livelihood and a bit of a roof over her head — to be rid of the barracks.
The convert, Abraham Wan Fun, was sure that after he had been circumcised and shed his blood for Judaism, the Jews of Harbin would take him under their protection, settle him and give him a better position. It turned out the opposite. All the women shook themselves free of the Jewish woman who had joined up with a Chinese man; people kept their distance from her and from him as well. He lost his position in the barracks.
On the other side, the Chinese — his acquaintances and friends — mocked him, took revenge on him, did not help him and reproached him for his ill-considered deed. Bread began to run short at home; meanwhile a child was born, he was circumcised, and the expenses grew.
Disappointed and embittered at his fate, the Chinese husband began to leave home, smoke opium and use morphine in the Chinese tea-houses; he would pawn the last belongings and torment his wife, until… the tragedy came…
In broken, mangled Russian the unfortunate woman tried to tell the Chinese court of her hard, painful life, the suffering she had endured, the details of the murder and the state she was in at the time of the act. Her poor Russian was hard for the Chinese interpreter to understand and made no impression.
The trial lasted one hour in all, and the verdict, which under other circumstances could have been much milder, was very sad for the unfortunate woman: life imprisonment at hard labour (katorga).
During the eight years in prison Feige Dubrowska has changed so much that she is quite unrecognisable. The middle-aged woman has turned into a broken, sick old woman. She counts the days, weeks and months and does not stop weeping and lamenting: what will happen afterwards, when she comes back out into the bright world.
Upper Silesian “Yahudim” and Polish Jews — (Some clarifications ahead of the kehilla elections in Katowice)

[Article — Upper Silesia, Katowice kehilla elections.]
(Some clarifications ahead of the kehilla elections in Katowice.)
For a long time now, not very friendly relations have been noticeable in Upper Silesia between the Upper Silesian, i.e. German, Jews and those who immigrated there since after the war, i.e. our Polish Jews. And to tell the truth, this is no wonder either: German "Yahudim" and our Polish Jews — these are, after all, two separate categories, two types set apart from one another; these are two outlooks; in a word, these are two peculiar, separate worlds, where one cannot understand the other; each looks at life differently, each of them has a different view and entirely different outlooks; between the one and the other there is thus a great distance.
And this very fact, that one does not understand the other and each lives separately, has led to quarrels and to estrangement, which certainly brings no good to the Jewish community as a whole.
But one must take this question seriously; one ought to try by every possible means to bring a little harmony into this field, because after all one must bear in mind that something does unite all Upper Silesian Jews, that they do have common interests — regardless of their envy and hatred and of the fragmentation that prevails in their ranks.
One must point out [?] and not forget that these Jews do live together and that all of them have one and the same interests, however much they may want to be apart and separate; and therefore it is necessary to bind together a united front among all Upper Silesian Jews.
For example, kehilla elections will very soon take place in Katowice, in which all strata of the Jewish population will certainly be represented. It would be desirable, however, that no fire flare up between the German and Polish Jews, from which no one will gain anything good; on the contrary, it could lead to various intrigues that will give no one any pleasure, and such [?] doings must absolutely be avoided, because all this certainly brings no public benefit.
The Polish Jews must therefore approach the elections according to a definite system and with calculation, for one must not forget that here one is dealing with a shrewd [lit. "twisted"], conscious element, which is more parliamentary than our Jews and finds its bearings in the given moment incomparably better and faster than the Polish Jews.
We must not want to fool ourselves; we must be conscious and look at the truth as it looks, as it is in reality.
The German Jews, the "Yahudim", are after all assimilated from head to toe. They cannot bear the Polish Jew at all, they do not understand him, and the worst thing is really that they do not want to understand him at all; they do not want to penetrate his world, they do not take the trouble to want to understand his sufferings and the heavy yoke that they draw upon themselves with the tormented, abnormal [?] life that binds him on all sides.
The German Jews were in the fortunate position of having been brought up under the German government, where culture, progress and the economy held first place, at a time when we here were Russian subjects; and besides the fact that in the Russian Empire everything was neglected and rotten and nothing was done according to any system, the Jew as such was hunted and tormented so much that he could not raise his head at all, for here he was not allowed to budge [?] and there he was not permitted to take a stand; all this led to a level of helplessness and abnormality. And therefore it is no wonder that with such [?] an "upbringing" the Polish Jews find themselves in such abnormal conditions, and the contrast between the two categories of Jews is enormous — only we can understand that this is indeed so; the German Jews will by no means be able to understand it, even if they wanted to, let alone [?] when the German Jews do not even give themselves an account of all this.
Our Jews must therefore take all this well into consideration, since they have common interests and live together.
That does not mean, however, that they must go on remaining so helpless and so abnormal. One must not forget that we now live in entirely different conditions, that the whole of public life today rests on parliamentary foundations, and this must absolutely be reckoned with.
As we have already shown above, the German and the Polish Jews are two completely separate worlds, and it stands to reason that it is hard to merge [?] them; but that does not mean that one cannot conduct fruitful public activity.
And since Katowice is now on the eve of kehilla elections, one must prepare for them properly and see to it that one is well and comprehensively represented.
The Polish Jews must approach the elections consciously and with a settled mind; they must see to it that their parnasim understand the tasks they take upon themselves in becoming public representatives. All possible means must be applied to bring in as many representatives as possible; at the same time, however, one must remember one thing, namely that the representatives be worthy of filling the offices entrusted to them.
And when the German Jews see that the Polish have so-and-so many representatives of their own, they will have to reckon with it, because then they will be facing an accomplished fact and will not be able to deny the real situation; then the German Jews will see that they must reckon with the established number of members.
Only in that case can there be an understanding and a common, useful public activity.
It is therefore important, first of all, to prepare consciously for the kehilla elections; these are the first steps, which must be taken with understanding, and this will bring much benefit for the further work.
Dr. Papuri.
The Agudah-Style „Honour of the Torah“

[Będzin — kehilla; polemic against Agudat Israel.]
An old story — when the Agudah wants to push something through, it always has an old, well-tried [?] means: it speaks in the name of the honour of the Torah.
It does not matter whether large undertakings are at stake or only petty matters are under consideration — as soon as it comes from the side of the „Agudah“, the „Agudah's“ monopoly article is always right here on the table.
A simple thing: at the last kehilla meeting the „Agudah“ dozór [member of the kehilla board] wanted to push through that the rabbinate should have a permanent secretary, who would record everything that goes on there. A natural matter, it would seem, the matter of an official; but Mr. Rigski [?] argued with fervour that the honour of the Torah demands it, and that „whoever will not agree to such an official is simply nothing more and nothing less than against the honour of the Torah“.
No arguments helped — that the rabbinate ought to provide itself with such an official, simply because, apart from its kehilla salaries [„pensions“], the rabbinate also has side incomes, over which the kehilla has no control whatsoever and consequently nothing at all to say about them.
The explanation did not help that at the present moment, when the financial crisis in the Jewish kehilla of Będzin is catastrophic — the „Agudah“ dozór keeps on shouting: either an official, or else the honour of the Torah is in danger..
Had the „Agudah“ dozór not been after other hidden intentions with his proposal, but truly had the honour of the Torah in mind, he could surely have guarded the honour of the Torah in a better way: first of all he would have seen to it that a member of the rabbinate should not have to stand like a beggar at the door of the kehilla and plead for a few złoty on account of his salary; he ought to have concerned himself that a moreh tzedek [rabbinical judge], who is owed 9 months' salary, should not have to knock on the doors of the dozors [board members] so that they take pity on him and pay him part of his salary, simply because he has very important family matters at hand..
It would seem that what is mentioned here has more to do with the honour of the Torah than some young man from Stryków or Wieluń who has wandered [?] here into the Będzin rabbinate.
And in general, how does a kehilla dozór at the present moment have the nerve to demand that the kehilla hire new officials and burden itself with new expenses? How does the „Agudah“ dozór not understand that at a time when the kehilla owes its officials and clergy nearly 50 thousand zł. in salaries, at such a time one must think only of how to obtain income and not of hiring new officials.
Is it not more important to see to it that the „orphanage“, which is being built with so much toil and sweat, should receive from the kehilla treasury its subsidies, or at least a part of them, so that the poor little orphans may at last have a place of rest, rather than create a post for an outside young man who can find his livelihood in another town as well.
And perhaps the honourable „Agudah“ dozór might have given a thought to the fact that it is more important that the Będzin mikveh, which has been under construction for a number of years already, should at last be completed, rather than to fight for the Stryków „guest“ to grab himself a post as an official in the kehilla. And this the „Agudah“ dozór has surely forgotten: that it is a moral crime when poor officials, families of small children, who are employed by the kehilla, have not been paid their salaries for months, and winter is approaching.
And if the „Agudah“ dozór has forgotten all this or does not understand it, one must tell him: this is not the way [lo zu ha-derekh]!
Make an effort, first of all, to drag the kehilla out of the great tangle and crisis, in which you, Mr. Rigski, bear a large share, since you have been sitting there in the kehilla office for some 2–3 years already. You allow yourself not to come to a meeting for months on end, and when you do deign to appear for once, then let your first concern not be to burden the kehilla with new expenses, and do not spin us a „spodik“ [i.e. do not pull the wool over our eyes; a spodik is a fur hat] that hiring a new official has anything to do with the honour of the Torah.
———
Call the child by its name — say openly that what you care about is „Agudah“ politics, prestige — this we understand, and that is why we cannot agree with you.
Urgent, important kehilla matters beg to be settled, and there is a possibility of settling them — but when? When one wants to work, but not when one wants to play politics with demagogic tricks.
Therefore we tell you: plain party combinations must by no means be wrapped in a mantle of „the honour of the Torah“.
A Liwer [?].
