Kehilla Representatives at Work

[Article — Będzin, kehilla and welfare.]
(Do our communal leaders really mean to renew their activity? — Is this an attempt for the good?)
Should one talk about the kehilla representation or keep silent about it? Take an interest in its affairs or leave it in peace, as if it did not exist, as if it found no echo in our little Jewish world? This thought comes to mind whenever one has to speak about our parnassim — about the kehilla representatives of whom we once spoke with so much respect, with so much reverence, and who, unfortunately, most unfortunately, made themselves so sorry [?], so ridiculous, that it is not worth taking pen in hand to argue with their "problems", over which they mostly made themselves so ridiculous that conscious, intelligent people blushed for shame, and this led to the level of abstention, to the level of unheard-of indifference.
Their deeds led to the sad situation in which all strata of the population, without exception, kept crying out: what are they sitting there on the kehilla benches for? What need is there of these people who, not content with doing nothing for us themselves, also make things harder for what is specifically Jewish and bring still more mould into the sad muck [?] that had to be cleared out with so much energy, courage and awareness?
The dissatisfaction was understandable and well-founded, and the whole Jewish public demanded, and indeed still demands, the dissolution of the Jewish kehillot; but the demands are not met, regardless of the fact that their term of office ended long ago.
And as the Jewish folk saying goes: if you can't get under, you must go over. Here we see that not only is there no move to dissolve our kehillot, but new representatives are actually being appointed, and about these new ones — or, more precisely, about the old-new ones — we would like to say a few words.
A few fresh members have just joined the Będzin kehilla in whom one senses a will to accomplish something for the Jewish community, and in this case we must dwell on them and give them attention and a sympathetic attitude.
We have seen that as soon as these people met, they began to deal with questions seriously and sincerely and to try to bring order into the [?] (unclear word), and they want to root out what is bad and remove what is undesirable; this must be welcomed unconditionally in the present sad Jewish economic situation in which we find ourselves.
Here we see that one representative borrowed a certain sum so that the office furniture would not be put up for auction [licytacja]; and another thing that has a very important meaning for us is the decision adopted by the kehilla representatives that they will set up a cheap kitchen. So here we see initiative, here good will is noticeable.
A cheap kitchen for the Jewish population over the winter — can we imagine how important this institution is, all the more so at a time when the crisis rages so; and therefore we want to hold the representatives to their word: we want the decision not to remain merely on paper, but to have real substance and to be realised in life.
The initiative is an important one, and the creation of such an institution is exceptionally necessary, so that the deed will be received by the population with the greatest satisfaction, and it will see that something is being done for the welfare of the hungry and the suffering.
So let the kehilla representatives take the question seriously and see to it that the cheap kitchen is created and enters everyday life.
If our kehilla representation is really out to improve the forms of our everyday life, we would have one more bit of work for them, which would bring much honour both to them and to us.
Normally we really should not need to give them any new work as long as they have not carried out what they have undertaken. But this, too, is important — indeed no less so than creating the cheap kitchen — so that here, too, one cannot wait.
It is a matter of rooting out the ugly, disgusting system of professional beggary, which brings so much disgrace and shame to our horizon, sad enough as it is.
We have grown so used to beggary that we no longer notice its shameful forms, which penetrate ever deeper into our most varied circles; we no longer notice how we are viewed by outside circles when they see what kind of elements we allow ourselves to raise.
But even if we did not want to reckon with the outside world at all, even if what others say did not interest us — although that is very, very wrong — we must surely give an account to ourselves. We must surely look around ourselves and see the fruits that have constantly grown out of beggary. For today we possess, for example, an enormous repertoire of beggary; we have three categories: professionals; the boundlessly "respectable", under whose mask all sorts of orgies are carried out; and then come various specialists in the field from whom even wise and sharp people will not wriggle free. And it is interesting that this "genre" is making huge progress among us — and what is the end? It goes without saying that the best business here is done by the specialists in this field, whereas those who must not be allowed to fall, the truly needy [?], those who must be supported with all our strength, in fact fall through on all fronts, because they are the real shlimazls and remain unhelped in their unfortunate situation.
So the end is that those who truly need support are not even noticed; among the great army of beggars the few honest ones, who have poor things come down to a hard crust of bread, get lost. So the question arises: whom are we supporting and whom are we maintaining? What do we aim at by maintaining and constantly raising such a staff of beggars? What does the Jewish people get from them, and what does the beggar-squad get from it? To this there is an easy answer: we bear the badge of shame, and they become cripples [?] for ever and ever, and they raise their children on the same system.
Must one still argue how necessary it is to bring a radical change into this field? Must one still prove how shameful and dangerous this is, both for ourselves and in the eyes of the outside world?
We hope that as soon as our kehilla representatives seriously reflect on this painful question, and there is also good will, they will have every possibility of solving the problem radically.
R. Let.
It Didn't Work Out for Her...

[Będzin — feuilleton; local tale.] (From the local stories).

"If you have no luck — people say — you shouldn't go mushroom-picking at all"; and when a "deal" sometimes fails, no ancestral merit helps, and it comes up like oil on water...
The story with a moral that I want to tell you here happened last week with the good wife of a local kehilla "cooking-ladle" [a busybody who stirs every pot] — a town "adviser" and "head-of-the-table sitter", and altogether a respected "personality" among the "popular" masses.
So this good wife fancied a fine dinner. She went out to the market, snatched the finest hen from a peasant woman and, without even asking how much it cost, "vanished" among the crowd of women with her bargain, "forgetting" for the time being to pay.
The peasant woman soon realized that the "Żydówka" [Jewess] had not paid her, and began shouting and making a racket. How could such a thing happen? Right under her hands? — If at least it had been a poor woman. But this was — she shouted — a rich "pani" [lady] with gold teeth and a respectable coat; who would have expected it?!
This really angered the women standing by, and they advised the peasant woman to go to the slaughterhouse and keep an eye out there — perhaps someone would come to have the bird slaughtered.
The peasant woman did not dawdle and indeed went to the slaughterhouse, and before long a shikse [gentile maid] arrived there to have the bird slaughtered. The peasant woman raised a hue and cry and threw herself at the shikse, demanding that she give back the stolen goods; the latter, however, declared that she knew nothing, but that she should come with her to the "gospodyni" [lady of the house].
Coming to the "gospodyni", the peasant woman did indeed recognize in her the "Żydówka" with the gold teeth, and demanded of her the few gulden [złoty] she had not paid. The "pani" at first denied it flatly ["stone and bone"], but when the peasant woman threatened to go to the "rabin" [rabbi] and tell the whole story, the husband took fright at the compromising scandal that could come of it and, to his shame, poor man, had to pay the peasant woman the money for his wife's "taken" "bargain".
No luck for her, poor thing: after so much practice from her husband's communal activity she still hasn't properly learned his "Torah"...
X.
Our Panorama

[Zagłębie and district — weekly feuilleton; communities, rabbinate and cantors.] (The election apathy. — New times, old songs. — "And there was a shochet in the land", and 3 shochtim grew out of him. — A town without a cantor and without a synagogue gabbai. — A lost hoshana. — "Second room" abolished. — "National" deeds).

With special satisfaction I turned to the local post. I was more than sure that elsewhere, in the smallest little towns, the apathy is not as great as here — that there things are bustling and boiling around the elections; but I was mistaken: no sign, not a rustle of elections — hush, quiet, as if nothing had happened, the world goes its usual way, and the post again "tells" of

— "New times, old songs".
Once again they are fighting each other over a moreh hora'ah [rabbinic decisor], a shochet [ritual slaughterer], a cantor and the like.
Let us begin in order.
In Szczekociny a shochet died. Well, so what? Died and buried. But the trouble is that in Szczekociny the opposite happened of what happened to our father Jacob, peace be upon him: back then "of many stones there became one stone", and in Szczekociny out of one shochet there became no fewer than 3 shochtim...
— How so? Very simple. The rabbi's son-in-law wants to be a shochet, the moreh hora'ah's son-in-law also wants to be one, and the old shochet's son-in-law surely wants to be one too?..
As is known, 3 sides arose: every shochet has a side, and every side has its own butcher's stall with its own cattle...
———
Olkusz is in a worse position: it has nothing — no cantor, no gabbai, literally — nothing...
Ever since Sosnowiec took the "Leichter" [lamp] from the Olkusz kehilla, that is, Cantor Leichter, the Olkusz kehilla has had no rest.
Instead of a cantor Olkusz "took on" a prayer leader, an everyday Jew — and that's that.
And to tell the truth, what does one need cantorial trills for? The main thing is an honest Jew; so what if "he bangs it out like a baker"? That's no disaster either — the main thing is the heart...
— So argues the old generation; the young generation in Olkusz, on the other hand, the "civilized" synagogue worshippers, are not impressed by the prayer leader, and they demand
— a cantor with all the jingles.
So two "trends" are fighting: "darkness" against "light" [a pun: Leichter = lamp], "backwardness" against "civilization", and "screeching" against "music"...
The final battle fell, "symbolically", right on Shabbat Bereshit. The deeds were fitted to the Torah portion: "And the earth — on the ground — in the Olkusz synagogue was without form and void, and dozens of overcoats hovered, left lying on the reader's stand"...
The local mara de-atra [rabbi] came and closed the synagogue, and when the synagogue was closed, the gabbai handed in his resignation.
So the Olkusz kehilla is without a cantor and without a gabbai.
— Będzin communal workers! Seize the opportunity...
———
Of the same "ailment" the holy congregation of Katarzyna [?], near Sosnowiec, has also "fallen ill".
And this is how it happened.
On Hoshana Rabbah, during prayers, the Torah reader in the Katarzyna beit midrash suddenly saw that his slender, decorated hoshana had vanished.
Naturally there was an "uproar" — such an incident! No small matter: the hoshana that the Torah reader had bound himself was lost!
The youngsters even assured him that the hoshana had been lost on the way into the beit midrash and that all efforts to find it were hopeless; but the words of the youth had no effect on the Torah reader, who issued an ultimatum:
— "If the hoshana is not found, he resigns as Torah reader".
And he indeed kept his word and read no more, only at the end he "treated" the worshippers to a "surprise", on account of which the Sosnowiec district court too will become acquainted with the story, which is called
— "A Lost Hoshana"...
———
In the Gerer shtibl in Będzin a "reading" [Torah reading] has "got lost" for the "winter season".
For several years now the Torah has been read twice in this shtibl, in the "first room" and in the "second room".
When the present election period drew near, they realized "up above" that the feeling of unity must be strengthened, even among our own people.
And an order came: 1) not to read any other newspaper but the "Tagblat" [the Agudah daily], which is kosher to the most scrupulous standard, and in order to spread Torah in Israel such a paper costs no more than 10 gr. [groszy], so that every cheder boy who gets 10 gr. from his mother for sweets should buy himself the paper, which strengthens religion.
2) The reading in 2 rooms shall from this day on be abolished; it shall be read only in one room, so that the threefold cord — Hasidism, politics and our own "newspaper" — be strengthened.
———
And so that this should have happened thus — "may the hands of the Będzin Betar be strengthened too".
From the Będzin "HaShachar" — a little letter:
"Our club premises are shared with the premises of 'Betar' — our own flesh and blood. Once we left them alone in the premises, and they — so it is told — started holding 'military manoeuvres' according to the well-known formula: they turned the tables and benches upside down as on Tisha B'Av, tore the pictures off the walls, did not spare even Herzl's picture, and at the end strewed the floor with flowers, curtains[?] — rubbish..."
So writes "HaShachar" to us.
As we have already stressed once: if it is true, you Betar boys deserve
— a "big yasher koach"...
Ben Amotz.
The Arab Problem in Palestine (Eretz Israel)

[Article — Zionism, Palestine and the Arab question.]
V. Jabotinsky [Ze'ev (Vladimir) Jabotinsky].
2.
The "Misunderstanding" Between Arabs and Jews.
A.
Many of us still believed [?] that it was a matter of a misunderstanding: the Arabs do not understand us, and that is why they are against us; and if we could only explain to them how modest our intentions are, they would hold out their hand to us in peace.
This is an error that has been proven. I want to recall here only one case out of many: some years ago Mr. Sokolow [Nahum Sokolow] — during his stay in Palestine (Eretz Israel) — gave a big speech about this very "misunderstanding". He clearly demonstrated what a great error the Arabs are making in thinking that we Jews want to take away their property, force them to emigrate, and generally oppress them.
— "We do not even want a Jewish government; we only want a government as Mandatory of the League of Nations."
To this speech the Arab newspaper "Al-Karmil" [Haifa] replied at the time in a leading article. I give the gist of the article from memory, but accurately: "The Zionists get worked up in vain: there is no misunderstanding whatsoever. Mr. Sokolow is telling the truth. But the Arabs themselves understand it quite well too. Certainly the Zionists are not dreaming now of any Jewish government. For the time being they only want the Arabs to let them immigrate undisturbed. The Zionists assure us that they want to immigrate only in such quotas as will be appropriate to the economic absorptive capacity of Palestine. The Arabs have never doubted this: after all, it is self-evident; otherwise it is not logical to immigrate." The Arab editor even fully agrees that the potential absorptive capacity of Palestine is very great, i.e. that one can settle countless Jews in the country without pushing out a single Arab.
Precisely "this" is what the Zionists want, and precisely "this" is what the Arabs do not want, because then the Jews will obtain a majority, and from that a Jewish government will automatically arise. And then the fate of the Arab minority will depend on the goodwill of the Jews. And that the situation of a minority is not an especially good one — about that the Jews themselves can tell.
B.
So there are no misunderstandings at all; the Jews want only one thing: a majority and immigration. But the Arabs do not want precisely this immigration.
This argument of the Arab editor is so clear and so impossible to refute that one ought to learn it by heart, and in all further excursions into the Arab question it should serve us as a guiding principle.
It is not a question of which words we use for explanation in the course of our colonizing efforts; let them be the words of Theodor Herzl or of Herbert Samuel — that does not change the essence of the matter. Colonization carries within itself its own single, unchangeable explanation, which is comprehensible to every normal Jew and every normal Arab. Colonization can have only one aim. For the Arabs of Palestine this aim is unacceptable; that lies in the nature of the matter, and unfortunately nature cannot be changed.
C.
Others, again, favour the following plan: to obtain consent to Zionism not from the Arabs of Palestine, because that is impossible, but from the rest of the Arab world, such as Syria, Mesopotamia, the Hejaz and even Egypt. Even if this were conceivable, it would, in essence, have changed nothing. In Palestine itself the attitude of the Arabs towards us would have remained the same.
In his time, as the price [?] for the unification of Italy, Trento and Trieste remained under Austrian rule; but the Italian inhabitants of Trento and Trieste were not satisfied with that; on the contrary, they carried on their struggle against Austria with even greater energy.
Should we succeed (which I strongly doubt) in persuading the Arabs in Baghdad and Mecca that for them Palestine is only a small, insignificant border territory — even then Palestine would remain for the Arabs of Palestine not a border territory, but their only fatherland, the centre and mainstay of their own national existence. Therefore even then one would be compelled to carry out colonization against the will of the Arabs of Palestine, i.e. under the same conditions as now. But an agreement with the Arabs outside Palestine is also an unrealizable fantasy. For a concession of such a kind as renouncing the Arab character of Palestine (a country lying right in the centre of the "Federation") we would have to offer the nationalists of Baghdad, Mecca and Damascus a very large equivalent. Obviously only two forms of equivalent are possible here: money, or political support, or both together. But we are in a position to offer neither the first nor the second. As for money, it is downright ridiculous to think that we are capable of financing Mesopotamia and the Hejaz when we do not have enough even for Palestine. Even a child understands that those countries, with their cheap labour forces, will obtain the necessary capital on the commodity market far more easily than we can for Palestine.
All the chatter about material support is either a childish delusion or unconscionable frivolity. And it would be especially unconscionable on our part to talk about political support for Arab nationalism, which strives for the same thing that Italian nationalism strove for until 1870, namely: unity and political independence. Put simply, this means expelling England from Mesopotamia and Egypt, driving France out of Syria and later perhaps also out of Tunis, Algiers and Morocco. To help in this on our part would mean suicide and treason.
D.
We rely on the English Mandate; France too signed the San Remo declaration; we must not take part in any political intrigue whose purpose is to drive England out of the Suez Canal and the Persian Gulf and to destroy France completely as a colonial power in the East. Such a double game is not only impermissible — it is not even fitting to think about it. We would be literally crushed — and with deserved disgrace — before we made even the slightest move in that direction. The conclusion: neither the Arabs of Palestine nor the other Arabs can we give such compensation for Palestine as they would consider satisfactory. Therefore a voluntary agreement is unthinkable. And therefore those who consider such an agreement a "conditio sine qua non" of Zionism can already now say "non" and renounce Zionism.
Zionist colonization must either be stopped or else carried on against the will of the native population. Therefore it can be carried on only under the protection of a power that is independent of the local population — under the protection of an iron wall which the local population will be unable to break through. That is what our entire Arab policy consists of — not merely should consist of, but explicitly does consist of, however much we may wrap it up in as many clever interpretations as you like.
What, then, is the Balfour Declaration for? What is the Mandate for? Their meaning and significance consist [printed "for:"] in creating for us in Palestine such conditions as would deprive the native population, regardless of its wishes, of every possibility of hindering Jewish colonization, both administratively and politically. And all of us, without exception, urge this external power on day after day to carry out the task it took upon itself without any indulgence [?]. In this respect there is truly no difference between our "militarists" and our "vegetarians". Some prefer an iron wall of Jewish [bayonets], others — of English bayonets; the third group, the supporters of an agreement with Baghdad, are content with Baghdadi bayonets (a strange and dangerous taste!). But all of us strive day in, day out to obtain an iron wall. With our declarations about an agreement we ourselves spoil our cause, because by them we give the Mandatory power to understand that it is not a question of an iron wall but of sermons threshed over anew each time. These are declarations that bring our cause to ruin; to discredit them, to prove that they are just as fantastic as they are objectively dishonest, is therefore not only a pleasure but also a duty: to demand an iron wall!
Napoleon's Romance with the Young Widow Josephine

[Serialized historical story — Napoleon and Josephine.]
M. Osherowitch.

Among all the women whom Napoleon had known before he was appointed chief commander of the army in the country, to defend the Republic against its enemies within, there was not one who took so strong an interest in him that she would use any means whatever to make him really fall in love with her.
To bring Napoleon to the point of truly falling in love, and of being ready not only for the pleasures but also for the sufferings [?] one usually endures when one is deeply in love — that was something not every woman could do.
For that one needed a skilled coquette, a great specialist in love, and on top of that one who would sense by instinct and understand that this short-statured general would in the end attain such a position that it would one day [?] pay off in every respect to be his mistress, or his wife...
Just as it is hard to change the laws of nature, so it was hard to tear Napoleon away from the important tasks in which he was absorbed. Every task had to be closely bound up with his enormous ambition; if not, it did not concern him at all and he soon cast it aside.
And history relates the following case:
Once, while leading the army against the enemy, Napoleon noticed that the picture of his beloved woman, which he kept in his pocket, had broken. This greatly upset him, and, halting the whole army, he reined in the horse he was riding and, turning to one of his generals, said:
"The picture of the woman I love so much has broken, and that is a bad sign. It means one of two things: either she is ill now, or she is now giving herself to another..."
Having said this, he did not even pause, but in a firm voice gave the soldiers the command:
"Forward!"
Not every woman could take such a man into her hands. For that one needed a woman who had enough experience in love; one for whom love is not a rare accident but a really well-studied profession...
And such a woman was found.
It was the young and beautiful widow Josephine, who at that time was a respected figure in the finest Paris salons, where people who had power and means allowed themselves to live it up in grand style...
Napoleon became acquainted with Josephine by chance. When he was appointed commander of the army of the interior, he issued an order that the civilian citizens be deprived of the weapons they had.
The order was carried out; searches were made in all the houses, and wherever a civilian had any piece of weaponry, it was confiscated. And then a little boy of twelve came to Napoleon and asked that his father's sword be returned to him, because it was the only keepsake left to him of his father.
Such things always moved Napoleon deeply, and he ordered the sword to be returned.
From the details he learned from the boy, he even found out that his father, a general of the old French army, had been an ardent monarchist and had fought against the Revolution, for which his head had indeed been cut off on the guillotine; but this still did not prevent Napoleon from ordering the sword to be given back.
Napoleon Bonaparte's deed made a very good impression on the boy's mother. She had not expected him to show such kind-heartedness, so she later came herself to thank him for it; and when Napoleon saw her, he immediately fell in love with her.
That was Josephine — the woman who afterwards became famous in history thanks to fate having brought her together with Napoleon.
Josephine was a born coquette; besides, she thought very highly of herself and never for a minute forgot that she was very beautiful.
Even before she was left a widow, she did not live in peace with her husband and constantly gave him one reason or another to be jealous. She could not do otherwise, because she loved having as many gallant cavaliers as possible revolve around her, and all of them pining after her every step.
At the time when she carried on her love affair with Napoleon, she was in fact the mistress of Paul Barras, who was then the head of the Directory, which was the French government after [printed "in"] Robespierre's fall. In general she was one of those ladies who are great artists at arranging their lives well [?] at a time when an upheaval takes place in a country — they carry on a love affair with power.. Whoever holds power in his hand — with him they are in love...
Here she had only just been sitting in prison as an adherent of the king, and here she already is the "respected lady" in the circles that run the Republic...
Her position is never a secure one, and yet she feels secure everywhere, because her best weapon is — her beauty..
With it she makes herself a free path among those who are for a monarchy and also among those who are for a republic...
With her sharp mind and her sound instinct, Josephine realised that the relations between her and Napoleon must not end as a passing episode that is later forgotten. Apart from believing that Napoleon would not stop in one place and would surely rise higher and higher, she thought a great deal about the fact that she had long since passed her first youth, and that in a few years' time she would surely no longer be the lady who so strongly arouses the lust of men who chase after pleasure...
That she thought a great deal about this can be seen from the letter she wrote to a friend of hers:
"Now," she writes in the letter, "when my first youth is already gone, can I really hope that I will still be able to keep in him such a stormy love, one that borders on madness?"
A stormy love that borders on madness! No other love did Josephine understand.
And in Napoleon she found such a love for herself, although she had already passed her first youth. Of all the women he had known before, she was for him the first specialist in love.

Oneg Shabbat — Torah Sayings, Remarks and Anecdotes on This Week's Sidra

[Oneg Shabbat — weekly Torah portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes around this week's sidra.
Collected and styled by Y. Y.
Parashat Vayera
—o—
a) "And he sat in the tent door" (18:1).
The Midrash cites, and Rashi too explains the verse, that Abraham sat by the door of the tent to see whether there was an "over vashav" (a passer-by and returner), in order to take guests into his house. What is meant by the term "over vashav"?
— There are guests who, if they have eaten once at someone's, are already ashamed to go to the same person a second time. These very [?] "passers-by and returners" (who have already been once and come a second time) Abraham, the great host of guests, looked out for, in order to bring them in to himself, because on their own they would have been ashamed. Shir Yedidut.
* * *
An old Hebrew aphorism:
When one comes to someone the first time one is an oreach (a guest), the second time — a toreach (a nuisance), the third time — a soreach (a stinker)...
* * *
Rabbi Gershon Henech of Radzyń said:
All hunchbacks ("hoykers") are crooked, after all; only one "hoker" is straight: "hoker raglekha mi-beit re'ekha" (Withdraw your foot from your neighbour's house — visit your friend rarely, don't be a frequent guest at his place)... [Pun on Yiddish hoyker, "hunchback".]
—o—
b) "Make ready quickly three measures of fine meal" (18:6).
The Gemara (Bava Metzia 87) expounds on this: "It is written 'meal' and it is written 'fine flour' — from here, that a woman begrudges guests." Rashi explains there: Abraham ordered fine flour (roll flour) to be brought. From this [?] it is deduced that a woman begrudges guests. In truth, according to the order of the verse it appears that Abraham ordered meal to be brought and Sarah — fine flour; and if so — people ask — where is it deduced that a woman begrudges guests? On the contrary, Sarah was more hospitable than Abraham.
The answer is: this time Sarah was clever [?] and ordered the finest and best to be brought for the guests, so that Abraham would no longer feel like inviting guests a second time.. Sichat Chullin.
—o—
c) "Whether they have done altogether according to the cry of it, which is come unto me" (18:21).
That is how they were, the Sodomites: they cried out against those who had plundered and robbed them, and straight away the robbed in turn robbed the next man. "Ha-ketza'akatah" — the very thing they had cried and shouted about — "asu": they straight away did it to others. Kehal Yaakov.
—o—
d) "Peradventure there be fifty righteous within the city" (18:24).
Abraham said thus to God: why do You need to destroy Sodom? If fifty tzaddikim are found in the town — they will destroy it themselves soon enough.. An old Misnagdic quip.
—o—
e) "Righteous within the city" (ibid.).
If there are true tzaddikim in a town, they drag the evil inclination into the beit midrash ("If this scoundrel meets you — drag him to the beit midrash"); and where the tzaddikim are found "within the city", in the street — but there are no such [true ones] — the evil inclination stays in the street and strolls about free and easy... Toldot Yaakov Yosef.
—o—
f) "And there came two angels to Sodom" (19:1).
To Abraham the angels appeared in the form of men, and to Lot actually in the true form of angels. Why?
Abraham was a sincere host of guests and took everyone into his house; Lot, on the other hand, already needed angels — ordinary people he would not have taken in..
Divrei Shaul.
—o—
g) "This one fellow came in to sojourn, and he will needs be a judge?" (19:9).
R' Avraham Turkower [?], rabbi of Dobromil, was renowned for his honesty and frankness; he showed favour to no one. Once a head of the community was offended during a din Torah, and on leaving [the rabbi's] house he wrote on the door: "This one came to sojourn, and he will needs be a judge?"..
On learning of it R' Avraham said this: in truth, why were the Sodomites so angry at Lot over his bad (in their terms) judgment? They, who knew nothing of justice and fairness, of all things got angry: "and he will needs judge"?
— They got angry at him because he had judged a just judgment, that was their outcry: "and he will needs judge"? An honest judgment, in Sodom of all places? Such murder! — so they clamoured.
— Well then, it is quite right — R' Avraham concludes — that what that head of the community wrote on my door: he too is shocked by an honest judgment. Asifat Geonim.
—o—
h) "But his wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt" (19:26).
Why did Lot's wife become a lump of salt?
— Because when the angels came to Lot, she ran around to all the neighbour women: "Lend me a little salt, I have guests" — she so [?] wanted, in womanly fashion, to blab to everyone that she had guests, and she ran around borrowing salt everywhere.. Therefore her punishment was that she was turned into a lump of salt. Midrash Rabbah.
—o—
i) "And they two made a covenant" (21:27).
Although they made a covenant, Abimelech with Abraham, they nevertheless remained "the two of them". Even a covenant, a friendly union, cannot mix together an Abimelech with an Abraham — they still remain separate. R' Simcha Bunem of Przysucha, "Far tsvey nistarim" [?].
—o—
j) "And Abraham said unto his young men: Abide ye here" (22:5).
Abraham had taken along two young men, gabbaim. He wanted to conduct himself in lordly style. At once — "and he saw the place afar off": he saw how God (Makom — God) was far from him, angry with him, because God hates pride. So Abraham said to them: "Abide ye here", sit here, I will go alone, without a parade of servants. At once — "and they came to the place" — he drew near to God. R' Shlomo Kluger.
Theatre Notes

[Sosnowiec — theatre.] "The Cry of Conscience", a play in 3 acts by L. Mergi, staged by Ida Kamińska and Zygmunt Turkow at the "Pałac" cinema-theatre in Sosnowiec.

Stronger than death is love, and mightier than love is the feeling of jealousy. Woe to love and to the beloved when jealousy is their companion. The eye of the jealous breaks through the strongest walls, sees in the blackest darkness, and like a beast in the field the jealous one senses danger while the hunter is still dozens of kilometres away from it. The sound of footsteps, the tone, half a glance of an eye, the ring of a telephone, a hidden smile — every slightest movement reveals the secret to the jealous eye; jealousy makes a person a prophet, able to know and sense danger in advance.

The young painter, Maurice, fell in love with and married a woman, knowing that before him she had had a lover, and knowing too that she now belongs to him with all her soul, and happy is their wedding day. But already on the first night after the wedding the serpent of jealousy steals into Maurice's heart; it comes through a telephone ring late at night.
— Who rang so late just now?
— My godfather, Lambertie.
— Why then did you, with your very first words, make him aware, as if innocently, that "my husband is standing by the telephone" — you thereby warned him to be careful with his words.

Germaine lies, justifies herself, has no courage to confess and reveal to her beloved and husband the whole truth: that she is held captive by her godfather, the millionaire Lambertie, an older man, and that she is unable to wriggle out of his claws. She does not tell, because she fears that her beloved husband will judge her harshly, that she will lose him, and she falls into a double game; one sin leads to another, through one lie she comes to a second lie, she wants to put out the fire with the help of fire — the husband's suspicion grows, her heart aches from it, she wants to calm him, to heal his pain, but she is unable to, because she has no courage to tell her husband the bitter truth, nor to break with the old Mr. Lambertie, to whom she feels great gratitude. And so the tragedy grows from day to day, the catastrophe approaches with hurried steps, and when Maurice meets Lambertie face to face and the latter's glance confirms his suspicion — he strangles him. Germaine suffers over the death of her friend, but she is content that she has finally been freed and that her husband will suffer no more. She denies everything during the investigation and helps the investigating authorities accuse an innocent person, so that no suspicion should fall on the real murderer — her husband. But Maurice cannot quiet his conscience, and he gives himself up into the hands of the police.

A theme — an eternal one: love, jealousy and betrayal — the theme is new only in its stage form. The author, L. Mergi, himself an actor, knows the secret of the stage; it is new also in its staging: on stage one sees only the two main characters, Germaine and Maurice. Even Lambertie does not appear on stage; this makes it possible to concentrate all attention on the two main characters, their suffering and pain, suspicions and doubts, love and jealousy, hatred and remorse.

For 3 hours we saw Ida Kamińska and Zygmunt Turkow on stage. The spectator had his fill of them. With bated breath one sat the whole time and listened to the splendid duet of Ida and Zygmunt, the incomparable masters of dialogue. One was not only carried away, but also drew much delight, and looking at the stage one was proud that the Yiddish stage possesses such artists as Ida and Zygmunt.
Y. G.

Będzin: City Council and Administration Dissolved.

[Będzin — municipality.] The rumours that the local council and the city administration would be dissolved have finally been confirmed.
On Tuesday at 10 o'clock in the morning the representative of the self-government department of the Kielce voivodeship, Mr. Strzyzicki [?], came to the magistrate [city hall], bringing with him a decree of the Ministry of the Interior that the city council as well as the members of the city administration are dissolved. At the same time the engineer Rzepeszkowski [?] of Sosnowiec has been appointed temporary manager of the municipal economy.
Why did this happen?
The reasons — are political.
The grounds for the dissolution, which were handed to each member of the administration, state the following:
The city council, elected in 1928, has no secure majority, and the consequence is that the city administration must secure for itself a majority whose members are political enemies of one another.
Such a situation creates an atmosphere of uncertainty and causes abnormal activity in the city administration.
In connection with this one must at the same time recognise that it is not in the city's interest that, in the period until new elections, the present politically partisan magistrate should carry out its functions.
For this reason the Minister of the Interior has ordered the dissolution of the council and the administration. And from 4 November [Listopad] Mr. Rzepeszkowski takes over the office.
How did the takeover proceed?
On Tuesday at 10 in the morning the delegate of the voivodeship, Mr. Strze[?]necki [?], handed the president [mayor], Mr. Michał, and the vice-president, Mr. Rubinlicht, the decree that they are suspended from their offices.
Mr. Michał, after handing over the state of the treasury to the commissioner, called together all the magistrate's officials and took leave of them.
The ushers became "nervous" and began to cry.
In the evening the city administration, both ex-presidents and the aldermen [ławnicy] had themselves photographed and then went off to supper at the "Warszawska" confectionery.
When will the council be convened?
In a conversation with the commissioner, Eng. Rzepeszkowski, the latter explained to us that the financial situation of the magistrate is worse than he had imagined; for this reason he is of the opinion that the convening of the so-called "Rada Komisaryczna" [appointed commissarial council] will probably come about only in the last days of next week.
Who is the commissioner?
The municipal commissioner nominated by the ministry, Eng. Rzepeszkowski, is the officer (referent) for the trade and industry department at the Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce.
The Confusion over a Fifth Shochet.

[Będzin — kehilla.] For months now a candidate for a fifth shochet [ritual slaughterer] has been "floating" around the kehilla premises [?]. A series of resolutions has already been adopted on the question, agreements and combinations have already been concluded, but the matter has brought no positive result.
On Tuesday evening a meeting of the kehilla board took place.
The shochet question was also on the agenda. But a few hours before the meeting began, the butchers' guild sent in a letter stating that the fifth shochet is not needed if the kehilla leaders will put the shochtim question on the proper footing.
Decision to Engage a Secretary for the Rabbinate.

[Będzin — kehilla.] On Sunday the kehilla board held a meeting, at which this time the rabbi and all the morei hora'ah [rabbinical judges] were present.
At the meeting the question of engaging a secretary for the rabbinate was raised. The proposal was presented by board member [dozor] Mr. Rygski, who declared that "whoever seeks the honour of the Torah will surely not be against the proposal".
Against was Mr. Liwer [?], who argued that the secretary's expenses should be borne by the rabbinate.
By a majority of votes it was resolved to engage a secretary.
Protest Meeting — Not Permitted.

[Będzin — Zionism.] The local Zionist groups called a protest meeting against the new English decree [the Passfield White Paper].
Before the public had assembled, the permit for the meeting was revoked.
Political Murder in Koziegłowy. Endek Kills a Member of the B.B.

[Koziegłowy — politics.] On Sunday a young Christian, a member of the B.B. [the pro-government Nonpartisan Bloc, BBWR], was killed by a political opponent, an Endek [National Democrat].
The funeral of the murdered man took place with great pomp.
He Who Strikes His Father and Mother — 2 Weeks' Arrest.

[Będzin — court.] Before the Sosnowiec district court stood a 17-year-old Christian from Będzin, who was accused that, when his father and mother rebuked him for coming home late at night, he "honoured" them with blows.
The "gem" was sentenced to 2 weeks' arrest.
City Treasury Receives a Large Sum from the Katowice Magistrate.

[Będzin — municipality.] Throughout the whole period of tram service the local magistrate did not receive the turnover tax from the tram directorate; instead the directorate paid the tax to the magistrate in Katowice.
For this reason the former city administration of Będzin turned with this claim to the Ministry of Finance, which recognised that the local magistrate's claim is correct, and the whole sum, amounting to seventy-odd thousand złoty, the Katowice magistrate will have to pay back.
Congress of Kehillot Called Off.

[Będzin — kehilla.] On Sunday a congress of the kehillot of the Kielce voivodeship was to have taken place in our town.
On Friday morning the starosty [district office] notified the local kehilla board that the congress is not permitted and can take place only after the Sejm elections.
Election Meetings of the B.B.

[Będzin — elections.] In the hall of “Gmatshtshi” [?], an election meeting organised by the B.B. [the Nonpartisan Bloc for Cooperation with the Government, BBWR] took place on Sunday morning. Those assembled, after hearing the speeches, resolved to vote for List 1.
A Drunkard's Resistance

[Będzin — crime.] On Monday evening a policeman tried to arrest a drunkard on Kołłątaja Street. The drunkard tried to put up resistance, and with the help of a friend of his he tried to tear himself out of the policeman's hand.
After quite a long time a second policeman finally came, and the “heroes” were led off to the police station.
A Brawl Between a Son-in-Law and His Mother-in-Law

[Będzin — local news.] On Tuesday the residents of the Old Market had something to talk about. A brawl took place there between Mrs. S. and her son-in-law. The cause of the brawl is that the son-in-law wants to remove his mother-in-law, Mrs. S., entirely from the business, which until now they had held in partnership.
Election Meetings in a Number of Towns

[Zagłębie — elections.] The Supreme Council of the Artisans' Organisation in Zagłębie is convening election meetings this coming Saturday night (Motzei Shabbat) in the following places: Będzin, Sosnowiec, Dąbrowa, Czeladź and Strzemieszyce.
District Conference of List 17

[Będzin — elections.] On Sunday a district conference of List 17 took place here, with the participation of delegates from Sosnowiec, Zawiercie, Dąbrowa, Strzemieszyce, Żarki and Ząbkowice.
Mr. A. Liwer [?] opens the conference in the name of the district election conference and invites to the presidium Messrs. Turner [?] (Zawiercie), Tenenbaum (Dąbrowa) and Lancman (Sosnowiec); he also greets the delegate on behalf of the Centre, Mr. Igusz [?] Landsztok, who gives a report on the course of the election campaign and appeals to all present to agitate energetically for List 17.
From the reports which the delegates give about their towns it emerges that election committees have been founded everywhere with the participation of small traders, artisans and merchants.
With the adoption of various resolutions concerning an energetic election campaign for List 17 in our electoral district, the conference is closed.
Lessons at “Sinai”

[Będzin — societies.] The committee of “Sinai” announces that in the course of the coming week the following lessons will take place:
Friday evening — Chumash with Rashi, by H. Goldberg. Sunday — Zionist history; Tuesday — Palestinography (geography of Palestine), by S. Magla [?]. Thursday — a members' meeting.
Protest of the Jewish Community Against the English Government

[Sosnowiec — community; Palestine.] The kehilla board held a meeting at which it was resolved to send protest telegrams to the English Parliament, to the Labour Party, to Baldwin and to the League of Nations concerning the decree of the English government in the Land of Israel.
A Plan to Build a “German” Synagogue

[Sosnowiec — community.] Several wealthy Jews have taken the initiative to build a “German” synagogue [a 'Deitsche shul' — a modern-style synagogue of the acculturated]. For this purpose a committee has been created, which is occupied with buying a suitable plot.
Petition Against England

[Sosnowiec — Zionism; protest against Britain.] From Sunday on, specially delegated pairs will visit the homes of the local Jewish population, among whom signatures will be collected for a petition against the English government for its betrayal.
Meeting of Jewish Small Traders and Artisans

[Sosnowiec — Sejm elections; small traders and artisans.] In the „Momus“[?] cinema in Pogoń a pre-election meeting organised by the artisans and small traders took place on Monday evening. After the speeches of the dentist Rotsztejn, of the chairman of the Small Traders' Association Mr. Oliner and others, those assembled resolved to vote for List 1.
It was also resolved to send greetings in honour of the President of the State and Marshal Piłsudski.
The local „Agudah“ [Agudat Yisrael] had intended to organise this meeting, but the above-mentioned got ahead of it; for that reason the second meeting took place on Sunday.
Meeting of „Hashomer Hatzair“ / Search at Mr. Szczelecki's / Serious Car Accident / Arrested and Released / Lida Potocka in Zagłębie

[Sosnowiec — Zionism; „Hashomer Hatzair“; followed by four short items: police, accidents, theatre.] In the premises of „Hashomer Hatzair“, under the chairmanship of engineer Mr. Mangel, a large meeting of former senior Shomrim took place in order to create a circle of sympathisers at the local „Hashomer Hatzair“. After a detailed lecture by Mr. Avraham Chlewicki on the present situation in the world movement of „Hashomer Hatzair“, a discussion developed in which comrades[?] engineer Mangel, the student Gelbard, Asher Klajnberg, Tsvi Fergricht[?] and others took part.
A provisional committee is elected, which is to organise all former Shomrim in Sosnowiec. The committee consists of: Wolf Stański, engineer Mangel, Asher Klajnberg, Naftali Abramowicz, Ada Fajner.
—o—
Search at Mr. Szczelecki's
On Tuesday a search was carried out in the flat of the former senior commissioner (nadkomisarz) Szczelecki. During the search Szczelecki's brother-in-law, the ex-president [mayor] of Będzin Mr. Mipel[?], was present in the flat; he was detained until after the search.
In the search Endek [National Democrat] proclamations and Szczelecki's revolver were seized.
A search was also carried out in the premises of the Endek association at Kołłątaja[?] 3, where [—] were confiscated [—], [—][?] and other [—] documents.
—o—
Serious Car Accident
On Tuesday at midday an unfortunate car accident occurred on 3 Maja Street.
When the usher (woźny) of the local magistrate's office, Mr. Chochulski, wanted to cross the street, a car ran into him and severely injured Chochulski.
— A second car accident occurred the same day in Piaski, where 12-year-old Szewczyk fell under the wheels of a car; she was badly battered[?] and was taken to hospital in a dangerous condition.
—o—
Arrested and Released
On Sunday several local Endeks were arrested; they were taken to Zawiercie, where they were released after the investigation.
—o—
Lida Potocka in Zagłębie
The famous Jewish actress Lida Potocka is coming for three guest performances. The repertoire includes, among others, „Mirele Efros“, which was the crowning role and stage jewel of the late, unforgettable Ester Rachel Kamińska. It is therefore interesting to see Potocka perform the same work; one wants to believe that the gifted actress will display her artistic talent in this role too.
The ensemble accompanying Potocka counts significant artistic forces among its members.
Lida Potocka's performances take place: tonight, Friday evening, in Sosnowiec, tomorrow evening in Dąbrowa, and on Sunday in Sosnowiec.

[Sosnowiec — notices; religious and Zionist youth groups; KKL.] The religious-national youth organisation „Sinai“ announces that Hebrew courses are being opened, conducted by a specially engaged teacher. For members of „Sinai“ the lessons will be free. Members can register every evening from 9 to 10 at the premises of „Mizrachi“, Potocka 5.
The Committee.

The „Ha-Atid“ Circle
of the Zionist youth organisation named after Theodor Herzl in Sosnowiec donates 20 złoty to the KKL [Jewish National Fund] instead of flowers on the grave of the late father of our comrades Yitzchak and Shlomo Grajcer.
The trial against the customs officials — postponed.

As we have already written, the prosecutor lodged an appeal against the verdict of the Sosnowiec district court concerning the charges against a number of officials of the customs office and merchants, who had been accused of bringing goods from abroad illegally.
The trial was to take place yesterday for the second time in the same court.
Because several important witnesses did not appear, the trial was postponed.
—o—
Former Będzin president on his activity.
In the latest number of "K. Z." the former city president of Będzin, Artur Michał, published an article about his activity during his 5-year term.
After the introduction, in which he condemns the act of [dissolving?] the city council and the city administration, he passes to the matter itself, where he lists his great merits for a number of economic institutions in Będzin.
—o—
Threw herself down from a height of 311 metres.
At the "Juliusz" coal mine, 21-year-old Glik worked as a "rigerin" [?]. She had more than once stressed to her acquaintances that she was weary of life and would commit suicide.
She carried out the terrible deed this week, throwing herself into the abyss of the mine shaft, to a depth of 311 metres.
—o—
Loans for building purposes.
Today, Friday, at 9 a.m., a meeting will take place at the Dąbrowa municipality about the 200 thousand zł. which the municipality has obtained [permission] to borrow for building purposes.
—o—
Brawls at election meetings.
The "Left Socialist Bloc", the "Bund" and the "Independents" held election meetings on Saturday in Sosnowiec and in Dąbrowa.
During the speech of Mr. Siebert [?] the hall was quiet, but when a representative of the "Independents" was given the floor, other left-wing elements began an obstruction, from which a brawl arose.
The police, who were present, dispersed the meetings.
—o—
Trial over the municipal hospital
For a long time now the Będzin municipality has been taking appropriate steps to have the hospital in Będzin belong to the municipality.
The matter has already been heard for the second time by the courts, which handed down the verdict in favour of the municipality. The Sejmik [county council], which regards itself as the owner of the hospital, has turned with the question to the Supreme Tribunal, where the trial will take place on 28 November [Listopad].
—o—

The 11th of November Celebrations in Zagłębie

[Będzin and Sosnowiec — Independence Day celebrations.]
In Będzin the celebration began on Monday evening with a torchlight procession through the town. Already decorated were the buildings of the Starostwo, the Magistrat, the post office, the premises of the Jewish kehilla and a number of balconies of private persons.
On Tuesday morning a divine service took place in the synagogue; the rabbi spoke about Piłsudski's merits for Poland and called on people to vote for List 1.
A lecture in Polish on the November Uprising was given by the director of Fürstenberg's gymnasium, and the school orchestra played the Polish and the Jewish anthems.
In Sosnowiec the Jewish kehilla issued an appeal to the Jewish population to come to the festive divine service.
———
The synagogue was packed. After cantor Mr. Leichter sang the appropriate prayer, Rabbi Hager delivered a speech that left a powerful impression on the listeners.
Dr. Meladysta[?] appeared with a speech in Polish, talking about the significance of the celebration.
A Bloody Political Discussion in Łódź / 1 Killed — 3 Wounded

[Łódź — crime and politics.]
In the restaurant of Chruszansza[?] several Christians were sitting who, after a few glasses, conducted a discussion about political matters.
The discussion was a heated one, and from words they passed to deeds — to shooting with revolvers.
The result was that a certain Saligowski[?] from Zawiercie received a bullet in the stomach, from which he died.
Three more persons were also wounded in the shooting.
A Boarding House for Out-of-Town Pupils / At the Jewish Crafts School in Piotrków

[Piotrków — vocational education.]
We are written to from Piotrków:
The Piotrków crafts school has 2 departments: mechanical locksmithing and furniture joinery.
The course in each trade lasts 3 years. Boys not younger than 14 who have completed 5 grades of elementary school or 2 classes of secondary school are admitted to the 1st class.
Pupils younger than 14 who have completed 4 grades of elementary school are admitted to the preparatory class.
The crafts school in Piotrków has already existed for 10 years and is licensed by the Ministry of Education.
The pupils enjoy various discounts. Among others they also enjoy railway discounts — they receive train tickets 50 per cent cheaper.
Because of the extremely important significance of modern vocational training for the growing Jewish generation, the management has set about organising at the crafts school a boarding house for 25 out-of-town pupils.
In the boarding house the pupils will receive lodging and full daily board for a modest payment in the amount of the cost price itself.
Special discounts will also be made for poor pupils.
The opening of the boarding house will take place at the end of November of this year. Candidates are already being registered.
Applications should be sent to the following address: Crafts School, Piotrków Tryb., Legionów[?] Street 12.
Aeroplane Campaign of the "Keren Tel Hai" in Honour of Z. Jabotinsky's 50th Jubilee

[Zionism — Revisionists.]
To celebrate the 50th jubilee of Zeev Jabotinsky, the creator of the Keren Tel Hai idea, the Directorate of Keren Tel Hai in Poland has resolved to present to the Jewish sport-avionette club and to the Keren Tel Hai in Eretz Israel a squadron of five sport avionettes, which shall bear the name of Zeev Jabotinsky.
The avionettes will be "made in the Land", i.e. they will be built in Eretz Israel itself by the members of the club and the students of the Jewish Technikum in Haifa.
The Directorate undertakes to raise the necessary funds for this purpose still this year (5691, Jabotinsky's jubilee year).
Our Reply to the Management of the "Merchants' Association" in Będzin

[Będzin — municipality and taxes; polemic.]
We publicly declare that we fully identify with the position of our representative Dr. Rechtman towards the activity of the last town council, and also towards the individuals whom you are now trying, after the fact, to defend.
Because of the unheard-of form of your "open letter" we will not polemicise with you, and as our only reply we say: all those who bear the burdens of the economy run until now — such as the market tax, the small traders, the poor taxpayer — condemn the tactics and economic methods of such representatives of yours, who increased the tax burden and loaded the town with debts.
The reproaches addressed to your representatives are clear and plain. Further explanations are superfluous. Let them defend themselves for the deeds concerning the old market, the investment granary, the large budgets and the like.
Therefore do not threaten our representative with consequences, of which we are not afraid. Our hands are clean, [?] whatever you may be covering up.
We will know how to defend our representative and our position.
The Committee of the "Hitachdut" in Będzin.

The Rabbi of Będzin on the Sejm Elections

[Będzin — rabbinate; the Sejm elections.] In the Agudah organ of last Wednesday the following letter of the Rabbi of Będzin was printed; we bring the letter, on account of its "importance", word for word.
To the honourable, dear brethren, children of Israel, in the State of Poland, in all their places of residence, may the Rock guard them and keep them alive.
Although who am I that I should come with a letter, yet I cannot hold myself back, out of love for you, dear Jews, for whom I hope that it may go well with you in both worlds. Have pity on yourselves, and do not, God forbid, let yourselves be lured into the nets of those whose striving is only to make a separation between Jews and the dear Father in Heaven, blessed be His name, between Jews and the holy Torah, and between Jews themselves. They are the inciters and destroyers of all holiness, of unity; and you — see to it that you are together without exception, you with your wives and children, as one man, on number 18; in this way you will save Judaism and the honour of the Jews. And it is written in the Gemara: "'That which is crooked cannot be made straight' — this is one who neglected the reading of the Shema; 'and that which is lacking cannot be numbered' — one whose companions were counted for a commandment and he was not counted with them", that is: as though he had, God forbid, not read the Shema. So know that it depends on you to save yourselves in both worlds, and may the Blessed Name grant you all blessing, success and all good.
Hanoch Tzvi HaKohen [Levin], head of the rabbinical court of the holy community of Będzin.
With Us and With Others

[Będzin — the post office; a sketch.] A well-known Będzin merchant relates the following fact, which characterises how an official abroad treats a Polish citizen — and how he is treated at the Będzin post office.
I — he relates — was not long ago at a spa abroad. Coming once to the post office to send off a telegram, I was short of the local currency, so I offered the official to leave a Polish banknote with him as a guarantee.
The post official was offended by the offer and cried out:
— What! You will pay me the rest later anyway — do I need a guarantee?!
With us:
I came to the post office to collect a parcel from abroad.
Because the parcel had been damaged on its way here, the customs office put the parcel into a sack. On collection the (woman) official would not let me take the sack home, although I wanted to leave with her as a pledge a sum amounting to more than 10 zł.
With this "difficult" request the official went off to the controller, who did not allow the "object" to be lent to me even against a special guarantee..
