A Fitting Monument (On the 17th yahrzeit of Rabbi R' Yissachar Berish Graubart, of blessed memory)

[Będzin — Rabbinate; memorial article.] Year after year, when the yahrzeit of Rabbi R' Yissachar Berish [Graubart], of blessed memory, comes round, we remember him; we then recall his greatness, his beauty; others remind us of his virtues, his genius in learning, his sharp wit, his good qualities, his fine manners and his aristocratic appearance. Everyone who knew the personality of Rabbi Graubart of blessed memory at all closely can repeat on his yahrzeit some sharp-witted saying of his, a witticism, a characterisation aimed at some communal "cooking ladle" [a meddling busybody of the kehilla]. All his pupils still remember with what enthusiasm they sat over the Gemaras under the direction of that luminous figure.
More than once we have happened to hear great men talk, who envied us, saying: after all, a great man occupied the rabbinical seat in your town, an important personality; after all, you had R' Yissachar Berish as your rabbi. Yes, we had R' Yissachar Berish as our rabbi, but did people know at the time what a personality we had as our spiritual leader? Did we know how to appreciate his greatness, his lofty ideal thoughts, which he carried about with him and with which he wanted to illuminate the little Jewish world? He always strove to unite in one strong organisation all the religious elements, which in those years were not only splintered and petty but still raw: they had as yet no system at all and did not know how to appear in the public arena. At the rabbinical assembly that took place in those years in Petersburg [St. Petersburg], Rabbi Graubart played a significant role among the great Russian rabbis.
In those days the religious parties had not yet crystallised, nor did they play such a role as in today's parliamentary era; in those days new parties were not born and did not die every Monday and Thursday at the hands of people who have no merits in any direction whatsoever — and yet people looked differently at the creators, at the spokesmen; people knew something: that here they were dealing with personalities for whom the ideal and the truth stand higher than anything in the world. And it may be that this was precisely the reason why people had full trust in these men, why they held them to be called to stand at the height on which they then found themselves. Oh, those were quite different times then; people could not even imagine that party politics must be approached in a small-minded way and that the main nerve of this or that party is falsehood and hypocrisy; and this has unfortunately penetrated so deeply, into the marrow of the bones, that people no longer understand that it can be otherwise, that one can get by with the innocent, naked truth, just as it is.
In those days the world was not yet so refined and had not even begun to walk the paths of "modern party-ism"; in those days everything was still so primitive and innocent that one can hardly imagine it today. Today both social-party life and private-egoistic life have changed fundamentally; the whole system of life has been completely transformed, so that mankind in general and we Jews in particular have entered a quite different phase, and the conditions in which we now find ourselves are quite different. Thus a completely new world-outlook has arisen. The European war introduced a quite different system into the conditions of our way of life, so that the outlook and the train of thought are quite different and rest on other foundations in our present-day life.
It therefore happens quite often that we would gladly take a stroll through the corners of that life, when before the war we were so closely bound together; we would gladly pay a visit there and draw from the spring of memories that breathed into us so much hope for the future. With all the shortcomings of those days and the mouldy junk, we would know how to appreciate the simplicity and naivety of those days, of which we have, unfortunately, so little in our present time.
And here is what is interesting: we notice that although mankind hoped so much for new times and therefore forgot the world of before the war, at a certain point a longing for the past began, and people began to study the beautiful sides that we lost in the bygone world of before the war. This is thus a sign that mankind is now not much more contented — and possibly even less than once.
This is apparently also the reason why we here in Będzin had forgotten to honour the memory of the late Gaon; it went so far that the town even forgot the yahrzeit of the deceased. And it is interesting that, as if by instinct, Jewish Będzin roused itself and with great enthusiasm began to long for the spirit of the great religious leader, and only then did it awaken and begin to take part in his yahrzeit in such masses[?], so that every year the number of participants grows and the memorial becomes more impressive.
Only now, years later, do people begin to appreciate the greatness of the late rabbi. It is an old rule with us: "after the death of the holy ones" — after death one begins to enumerate the virtues; in life we see nothing. When our great men are among us we do not appreciate their greatness, and not only do we not know how to appreciate their greatness and beauty, but people pay no attention at all to the personality that lives and works among us.
The same happened with Rabbi Graubart too: however much reverence and respect people may have had for him, they were far from knowing how to appreciate what a Gaon then occupied the Będzin rabbinical seat. Only now do people begin to understand him; only now does the great spirit hover before[?] our eyes.
Yes, now people are beginning to grasp whom and what we had in Będzin as a spiritual leader, and therefore it would be only just to perpetuate the memory of the great Gaon and leader, who was rabbi in Będzin for 20 years; he has earned that a fitting institution be created in his name, through which his spirit would be sanctified, and thereby religious Jewry would show that it knows how to appreciate its personalities, its great men.
On the 17th yahrzeit one ought to speak seriously about this, so that the aim is achieved and the proposal becomes a reality.
In any case, Rabbi Graubart had enough merits towards the town that he has rightly earned a fitting monument. This we see on the day of the yahrzeit, when various strata of the population gather to honour the memory of the great spiritual leader. Let the question therefore become topical, and let it be treated with the full seriousness and sincerity that such a matter must carry.
R. Let.
A Fortress of Yiddish

[Canada — Montreal; the Yiddish language.]
There is a city in the world which is in itself a true fortress of Yiddish.
If you happen into this city, in the first minute it is simply hard to orient yourself as to where you are. Eretz Israel? But there they speak Hebrew. Soviet Russia, or Ukraine? But you see no Bolsheviks. "Mandushever"[?] streets? Then where are the Jews in kapotes? New York's East Side, or London's Whitechapel? Then where are the English signs on the shops?
In short: you are in Montreal.
Montreal is the true capital of the Yiddish language.
You walk through whole streets and quarters and you do not find on any shop any sign other than a Yiddish one; you hear no other language than our mother tongue.
Of course, only in the Jewish quarters, because of the million and 200 thousand inhabitants that Montreal has, only 60 thousand Jews live here in all.
But these 60 thousand Jews are the most active element, and even when the city administration has to turn to them with some appeal or announcement, it does not disdain Yiddish either.
The journalist Mr. Firsht [Fürst?], describing Montreal, asks himself the question: where did Yiddish draw such strength to spread in the largest Canadian city more than in any other city in the world?
And he himself finds an answer:
Montreal is a city of Frenchmen and Englishmen, who have for years been waging a quiet war between them over stamping their cultural mark on the city.
Both groups have equal strength here — although the French are more numerous, they stand on a lower cultural level (the Canadian French descend from peasants), and[?] England is, after all, the ruler of the country.
Meanwhile, to this day neither group has managed to defeat the other, and in the meantime the Jew profits from it — he does not let himself be enlisted by either side and goes his own way — Yiddish!
He speaks Yiddish at home and in the street, and a pure, juicy Yiddish. The sign on his shop is in Yiddish, and he also keeps the books of the business itself in Yiddish. He reads a Yiddish newspaper and a Yiddish book — so the older generation, and so the younger.
One can only pity the Jewish young people and women from Poland, Romania and other countries, who back in the old home did not want to speak a word of Yiddish, and here, poor things, they have to break their tongues...
The Bloody Farce

[Eretz Israel — opinion piece; the Passfield White Paper.]
The bloody farce called "English betrayal" has been performed with Messrs. Passfield and MacDonald as the leading heroes.
But the curtain has not yet come down. We Jews must still play the last scene, the epilogue, and play it so that the whole world, Great Britain with it, will be shaken up.
Our stage is broad and great: the whole globe. In this lies our power, our power of exile, which brought us to the Balfour Declaration, to San Remo, to the splendid work in the Emek, to the holy stones and the kvutzot and moshavot.
If the Passfields and MacDonalds lock the doors of Eretz Israel to us, if they drown in pioneers' blood the holy stones of pioneers' sweat, we will play the epilogue in all corners of the world with that Bar Kochba fire which once already cost six hundred thousand Jewish souls and was the herald of the downfall of the Roman Empire.
That epilogue was played on the mountains of Judea, with Rome by no means the victor — Rome is dead and Jerusalem lives — we will play the epilogue beginning at Bar Kochba's headquarters and ending in the most distant corners of the British Empire.
And we will show the world that the bloody farce of the Passfields and MacDonalds, with the scenes entitled "Pogroms in Eretz Israel", "Shaw Report", "Simpson Report", "White Paper" and "Brazen Promises", is not only a betrayal of the English people, of the British Empire.
If England wants to build a secure road to India across Eretz Israel, it will not happen through betrayal of the Jewish people, which has won from the world [the right] to build its home! It will not happen over an English colony "Palestine"! The British Empire will sooner crack in all its corners before it comes to that!
Our power? If Jewish history has not proved enough that Jews have emerged as the victors from all bloodbaths and betrayals, the blind Passfields and MacDonalds will quickly regain their sight when the Maccabean spirit of the Jewish people takes into its hands every possible weapon of defence — and against betrayal all weapons are kosher, as the whole world knows.
We Jews are not frightened of betrayal, even when it comes from the socialist camp, from which we least expected it. We can also survive the mockery of this or that antisemite or hooligan. But betrayal together with mockery from a great power that signed and approved the Balfour Declaration and the Eretz Israel Mandate, before the eyes of the whole world and over the signatures of dozens of nations — such a bloody farce cannot be played over our heads!
That is too much even for such a long-suffering[?] and believing people as we Jews are, and too brutal for all times, and all the more so for the post-war period.
The dark English colonial politicians, with Passfield and MacDonald as holy priests, may have learned nothing and forgotten nothing from the World War. But the world has learned a great deal, and so have we Jews.
And what we have learned is that nations which were oppressed for hundreds of years came out of the bloodbath liberated, with recognised rights to build their own destiny, and that among these nations is the Jewish people too. And we remember, and the whole world with us, how solemnly our right to Eretz Israel was recognised by the English statesmen from 1917 to San Remo and by the League of Nations with its several dozen nations. This is the history of our own days. Millions of people in the world know the text of the Balfour Declaration and the Mandate by heart. And the memory of the world, and all the more so of us Jews, is not yet so weak that the text of such documents should be forgotten overnight.
The audacity of the MacDonald and Passfield government in coming before the world with a "White Paper" and manipulating the text of the Mandate with the slyness and dexterity of the back alleys is the most brazen politics that has been played out in the last fifteen years in the whole swamp of world politics.
It is not hard for anyone to catch MacDonald and Passfield by the hand stealing[?] from the pocket of the Jewish people its recognised right to Eretz Israel. We are by no means so helpless that we could not rap the nimble socialist-colonial hands and bring the pickpockets to court before the world tribunal, before the League of Nations.
We have an agreement with England as the Mandatory power that it should help us build up our national home, but an English government that pursues a pogrom policy — with such a government we will no longer sit down at the table!
We have lost our trust in it, and our request to the world through the League of Nations can now be only one: England out of Eretz Israel: it has deceived us and the League of Nations. The Mandate must pass to another government that is truly willing to help us build our homeland. And victory will have to be with us, when the League of Nations, like us, will not want to be so cynically deceived.
And that it does not want that, it has already shown once.
The bloody farce "English betrayal" will have to stop at this point, at the scene where we Jews begin to play with the full force of a tragic people that stands robbed and mocked by diplomatic swindlers — and together with us the League of Nations, the finest child of the World War.
L. Kosman.
The Economy of Self-Government

(On the dissolution of the city councils in the Zagłębie districts.)
Of the city councils in Zagłębie, practically only Dąbrowa is left. After the dissolution in Sosnowiec and Zawiercie, the Będzin city council has now been dissolved as well.
It is common knowledge that when one completes a building or finishes some undertaking or other, one draws up a summary and renders an account, as is the custom in the world; and here too we would have understood that it ought to be so: since the city councils were dissolved in Sosnowiec, Zawiercie and now in Będzin, the councillors and the city administration should have come and given an account to the voters. They ought to have told them what was done for them and what was not, where obstacles arose and what they managed to carry out and realise.
Unfortunately we do not see anyone from the three dissolved city councils finding it necessary to call a meeting at which one could hear what has been accomplished for the local citizens. Yet one must nevertheless reckon with the voters; one must not forget that in the end the voter's vote will be needed once again, so one must come to him and say: thus and thus, this and this we did, this we wanted to do and could not, because such-and-such elements obstructed the work. And so, when nothing is done, when no report meeting is called, nobody knows anything — one does not know what was done and what, for whatever reasons, could not be done.
Granted, Sosnowiec and Zawiercie will apparently no longer give any public account, since they could have done so until now; Będzin, by contrast, is still fresh, and perhaps some faction will yet come forward and show what its activity consisted of.
It is interesting, however, that the former mayor (president) of Będzin, Mr. Michel [?], has already found it necessary to tell the readers of "Kurier Zachodni" what he accomplished during his term as mayor of Będzin. So the question arises: if one is giving a report anyway, why not to the voters who elected him? Surely it is more fitting to come directly to the voter and render him an account.
The Będzin councillors, both of the right and of the left, should take the trouble to say what their activity consisted of. They must explain it publicly if only because the last self-government did not work harmoniously at all; and then the opposition too must show itself, and let clear and open words be heard.
No doubt it is not easy to run the municipal economy; nowadays it is very responsible work, both for the authorities and for the citizens. The municipal economy costs the citizens a great deal of money; many millions are now being administered, so one must see to it that these millions are spent properly and bring benefit to the population. Thus we know, for example, that many mistakes were made — so why should we not hear what the good consisted of and what the bad? After all, that is a lesson for the future.
Thus we know that at every city-council session one sought revenge on the other, satisfaction. Normal, systematic, definite activity was either not carried out or was not allowed to be carried out in concrete form. And so the reports of the sessions can tell only of outbursts and of tripping one another up; it reached the point where the representatives quite often forgot that they were fulfilling a public mission; it seemed to them that they had come together simply to chatter or to settle scores with whoever it might be. To such a level, to such a low state, no city council in Będzin had ever sunk before. Often one blushed with shame watching how public municipal affairs were being handled; it cost serious, honest people their health, and they withdrew from watching such unseemly conduct.
Many of the councillors never asked themselves why they had entered the city council at all; they forgot that the millions taken from the citizens must be spent with more deliberation; they did not remember at all that public problems must stand considerably higher than private, disgusting intrigues.
And now that the Będzin city council has been dissolved, one must come to the voters and give them an account of who brought benefit and who did not, who accomplished something and who did harm. First of all the party councillors must come and present their reports to their voters. Then we ought to hear a word from the city administration as such, and let it tell us what its activity consisted of in the course of its term.
To dissolve a city council while its members have nothing to say to the local citizens would mean that they have no connection whatsoever with the voters and consequently no responsibility towards them either.
The voters therefore have the right to demand an account from the people who were sent to administer the municipal economy; and just as the voters have the right to demand it, so a duty lies upon the representatives to tell the voters everything they did as city fathers, as local representatives.
Selekt.
The Arab Problem in Eretz Israel

[Article — Palestine, the Arab question; series, part 3.] By V. Jabotinsky [Vladimir (Ze'ev) Jabotinsky].

3.
The foundation of a mutual agreement.
Editorial note: this article is an introduction to the forthcoming detailed article.

A.
Two brief remarks: a) To the hackneyed reproach that the [above?]-mentioned standpoint is not ethical, I answer: not true! One of the two: is Zionism moral, or immoral? It was our sacred duty to decide this question for ourselves even before we bought the first shekel, and we answered the question in the affirmative — which means, then, that Zionism is morally just. Then this justice must be put into practice, without reckoning with whether A, B or C agree to it or not. And if A, B or C want to obstruct the realisation of this justice by force because they feel wronged[?] by it, then they must be deprived by force of the possibility of obstructing — that is ethics. There is no other ethics!
b) As long as the Arabs have the hope of getting rid of us, they will not sell us this hope — not for sweet words and not for tasty bread and butter — precisely because they are not a wild rabble but a living, albeit backward, people. A living people yields on such fateful, heavy questions only when it can no longer find any crack in the iron wall. Only then do the radical groups, whose watchword runs „Never“, lose their prestige; only then do the most moderate groups begin to gain greater influence; only then will the most moderate groups come to us with proposals for mutual concessions; only then will they begin to bargain with us over practical questions, such as: a guarantee against „expulsion“, equal rights, or national self-rule.
The only way to agreement is[!] the iron wall, i.e. the consolidation in Eretz Israel of a power that shall be inaccessible to Arab influences — which is precisely what the Arabs are fighting against. In other words: the only way for us to arrive at an agreement in the future consists in the absolute renunciation of any attempt whatsoever to reach an agreement at present.

B.
Let us pause for a while on the Helsingfors programme, which we mentioned in one of the previous chapters.
I, as one of its authors, certainly have no intention of doubting the justice of the principles laid down in it: it guarantees civic equality and national self-government. I am firmly convinced that every impartial judge will recognise this programme as an ideal foundation for a peaceful, good-neighbourly coexistence of 2 peoples. And nevertheless it is foolish to demand of those very Arabs the psychology of an impartial judge, because in this conflict they are not judges but a party. First of all there still remains the first and most important question: even if the Arabs could believe in a peaceful coexistence — do they want at all to tolerate[?] „neighbours“, even good ones, in the country which they regard as their own?
Even those who want to soothe and quiet us with fine-sounding[?] words will not have the „courage“ to deny that national homogeneity is more convenient[?] than a mixture of nations; on what ground, then, should a people that is fully content with its isolation let in good neighbours in such a considerable[?] number? „Neither your honey nor your sting“ — that is its, the people's, natural answer.
But even setting aside this fundamental difficulty, one cannot demand that precisely the Arabs should believe in the Helsingfors programme — or in any programme at all of a state form with a nationally mixed population. Such a demand means demanding something impossible.

C.
Springer's [printed „Spriger“; Rudolf Springer, pen-name of Karl Renner] theory is barely 35 years old; until now, however, no people, however civilised it may be, has yet been ready to apply this theory honestly in practice. Even the Czechs under Masaryk's leadership, the teacher of all autonomists — they too could not or would not realise
As for the Arabs, even their intelligentsia has perhaps not yet heard of this theory; but this the intelligentsia knows excellently: that minorities have everywhere and always suffered very much — the Christians in Turkey, the Mohammedans in India, the Irish under the rule of the English, the Poles and the Czechs under German rule, and vice versa, and so on without end.
One would have to get drunk on all sorts of sermons to the point of stupefaction in order, after all this, to demand that the Arabs should believe that precisely the Jews are capable (or at least have the good will) to realise such a plan, which other nations with greater authority did not manage to carry out.
I insist on this not so that we too should renounce the Helsingfors programme as a basic foundation for the future modus vivendi. On the contrary, we — at least the writer of these lines — believe in this programme and also in our ability, regardless of doubts[?] and precedents, to carry it out in political life; but it would be pointless to praise it now in the eyes of the Arabs: they will not understand it, will have no trust in its foundations and will not appreciate it properly.

Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Chayei Sarah)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion
Collected and styled by Y. Y.
Parashat Chayei Sarah
—o—
a) "The years of Sarah's life" (23:1).
Ordinary, average people are reckoned according to time: "in such-and-such a year So-and-so son of So-and-so was born" — that is how one usually speaks. People are thus reckoned to the years. It is different with great people: time is reckoned to them; one says and speaks of "the year in which that personality[?] was born" — the years are thus attributed to them. "The years of Sarah's life" — the years were designated as those in which Sarah lived and worked.
Divrei Shaul, by[?] R' Yosef n"z[?].
—o—
b) "Four hundred shekels of silver, between me and thee" (23:15).
From the words "I will give the price of the field" (verse 13) Rashi infers that Abraham said to Ephron: "would that I had already given it to you" — would that I had given you the money earlier. What is this "would that"?
Ephron demanded four hundred shekels from Abraham, because, not knowing what sum to take from Abraham, it occurred to him to set the payment by a play on words, and he said to Abraham: "between me and thee" — the middle letters of my name and of yours are, after all, two reshes (Ab-r-aham, Eph-r-on); resh is two hundred, so for our two reshes give four hundred shekels. Abraham then said to himself: would that I had given it to you earlier — earlier, when I was called Abram, I would have had[?] to give only two hundred shekels, for my name then had no middle letter at all...
Pitgamei Orayta.
—o—
c) "And the Lord had blessed Abraham in all things" (24:1).
1.
With what did God bless Abraham so? With what was he so blessed?
Says R' Nechemiah (Midrash Rabbah 59): in that he had no daughters...
2.
In another homily the Midrash says: "Abraham had a daughter and her name was Bakol."
"Bat" (daughter) also means a measure (as in Ezekiel 45: "a just bath"). Abraham had the quality of "bakol" — he was content with everything, and therefore he was so blessed.
Similarly:
"They that seek the Lord shall not want any good thing" (Psalms 34) — those who seek the Lord shall not want; they never lack anything. Why? — because "all" — of everything that happens to them they say "good": it is good this way, it has to be this way... R' Moshe of Kobrin.
* * *
Rabbi Shmelke of Nikolsburg [Mikulov] and his brother Rabbi Pinchas once asked their rebbe, the Maggid of Mezeritch, how it is possible to fulfil the saying in the Talmud (Berakhot): "A man must bless God for the bad just as he blesses Him for the good" — a person must thank God for the bad exactly as for the good. How is that possible?
The Maggid told them to go to the study house: there sits someone called Zusha (Rabbi Zusha of Hanipol, a brother of Rabbi Elimelech of Leżajsk), and he will answer them.
They come into the study house; there sits Rabbi Zusha smoking a pipe, but he is ragged and threadbare; poverty, one can see, is his constant companion. They[?] tell him that the Maggid sent them to ask him the question mentioned.
— Wha-at? — Rabbi Zusha opens his eyes wide — me you ask such a question? Such a question you can ask someone who has already suffered something bad, but not me, who since I was born have not yet had a single bad minute — — —
Looking at this pauper, who had already suffered every kind of trouble, and hearing such an answer from his mouth, they understood the saying..
* * *
King David in the Book of Psalms so disdains — good riddance to them[?] — all kinds of worldly pleasures, and even exclaims: "The troubles have enlarged[?] my heart" — troubles actually give him breadth of mind, troubles actually give him pleasure. But sometimes — Rabbi Nachum of Horodna [Grodno] said — when rich men indulge too much in a life of pleasure, their income does not cover their expenses and they suffer, because they allow themselves too much pleasure; this pleasure from troubles, too, is not good in excess... Aggadat Ezov.
—o—
d) "And the Lord had blessed Abraham in all things.."
"That thou shalt not take a wife unto my son of the daughters of the Canaanites" (24:3)
Earlier Abraham was not afraid that the Canaanites, the gentiles, would want to make a match with him; but when he became rich, then he was afraid: now they would want to marry even into a Jew's family, for the sake of his money..
Peh Kadosh.
—o—
e) "At the time of evening, the time that women go out to draw water" (24:11).
In the Midrash there is the following obscure passage on this verse: "Rav Huna says: when someone goes to take a wife and hears dogs barking, he understands what they are saying. And this happens towards evening."
???
We shall quote two interpretations:
a) King Solomon says: "A bad wife is more bitter than death" (Proverbs) — a bad woman thus has in her an aspect of death, and, as is known, the Gemara says: "When the Angel of Death is in the town, the dogs howl" — when dogs sense death, they bark. This is what the Midrash says: whoever wants to discover the nature of his intended should go out towards evening, when dogs roam the street and girls go to draw water; if the dogs bark, it is a sign that this girl has in her the aspect of death, that she is a bad wife..
Agra de-Kallah.
b) When someone comes to a town to make inquiries about a match, he should not go to stay at a respectable inn but precisely to simple people — right there, where everyone is talked about and one says things about everyone that are forbidden to say. And therefore Eliezer went straight to the well, where the shepherds, water-carriers and all sorts of chatterers gather — there he had the best way to inform himself. Ohel Yaakov.
—o—
f) "Perhaps the woman will not follow me" (24:39).
1.
Rashi: "Ulai" (perhaps) is written without a vav [so it can be read "elai", "to me"], because Eliezer had a daughter and wanted Abraham to agree to marry her off to Isaac; Abraham answered him: you are a slave, and "the cursed does not cleave to the blessed" —
But it should have been written the other way round: "the blessed does not cleave to the cursed"; only it often happens that when a "blessed" one — a refined person from a distinguished family — wants to make a match with a rich man of low stock, it is the "cursed" one, the rich man, who puts on airs. Nothing is good enough for him: "the cursed does not cleave to the blessed" — it is the "cursed" one who actually does not want... Butzina de-Nehora.
2.
Why in fact did Eliezer tell Bethuel that he had asked Abraham: "Perhaps the woman will not follow me?" — what for?
A provincial merchant had an employee[?], a very honest man, whom he used to send to the capital to buy goods; he traded on credit. Suddenly he orders the employee to bring a larger quantity of goods — he intended, this last time, to take on credit and say... (the second verse of the Song of Songs..). The employee's conscience, however, did not let him help with such a crime, and on the other hand it was his duty to carry out his master's order; so he said to the chief merchant (so that the latter would guess for himself): "My master sent me for a lot of goods, and I answered: perhaps the merchant will not want to give so much?" — — —
The merchant was clever enough to understand what the honest employee was hinting to him, and he gave no goods.
Eliezer, who had a daughter whom he very much wanted to marry off to Isaac, but had to carry out Abraham's order to go to Bethuel to seek a match, took counsel like that employee and said to Bethuel: "I said to Abraham: what if she will not want to?"... He wanted them to work out for themselves that if Eliezer had asked Abraham such a question, there was probably something to it; probably she really ought not to want... With this seemingly innocent talk he wanted to prompt them to that.
Rav Yaakov Krantz (the Dubno Maggid).
—o—
g) "And I came this day" (24:42)
Rashi:
"Today I set out and today I arrived." Eliezer told them that the road had miraculously shortened for him.
The question is: why should they believe him? Was he such a fool as to boast of something they would not believe? — how would he prove when he had left home?
— On the verse "all the goods of his master [printed: ארניו] were in his hand" (24:10) Rashi says that Abraham gave Eliezer a deed of gift in which he had written all his property over to Isaac. And if such a deed was written as he set out on the road, then by the date of the deed one could tell when Eliezer left home..
Drush Shmuel, by the Rebbe R' Heshel.
—o—
h) "Our sister, be thou the mother of thousands of ten thousands" (24:60)
Laban the Aramean (knowing that "most sons [printed: הנגים] take after the mother's brothers" — that children take after their mother's brothers, so her children would take after him..) blessed his sister: may you have tens of thousands of children — so there would be, as said, tens of thousands of Arameans in the world..
Rav Yitzchak of Volozhin [Wołożyn].
—o—
i) "Then Abraham expired and died in a good old age, an old man, and full" (25:8)
"Full" — sated did Abraham depart from the world. Of the wicked it is said that they die "with half their desire in their hand" — they never have enough, they always lack something..
Rabbeinu Bachya.
—o—
"And Mishma, and Dumah, and Massa" (25:14).
"Mishma" — hear it out; "and Dumah" — and be silent; "and Massa" — and bear it.
Rabbi Simcha Bunem of Przysucha.
The Inexhaustible Spring

[Heritage — in memory of a Będzin rabbi.] (For the 17th yahrzeit of the great Rabbi R' Yissachar Berish Graubart, of blessed memory)
Collected and retold by Sz. Lewkowicz.

Like scattered pearls lie strewn the ever-refreshing Torah sayings and the sharp-witted quips of the Będzin rabbi, Rabbi Graubart, of blessed memory.

A.
From a neighbouring rabbi the Rabbi, of blessed memory, often suffered troubles, insults and even deeds unbecoming a rabbi.
Intimates advised the Rabbi how he could rid himself once and for all of that man's doings...
The Rabbi shook off this "good advice", would not hear of it, and said:
— God forbid! Of the sons of Jacob it is written "and so it ought not to be done" [Genesis 34:7]; they, the sons of Jacob, also could not take revenge on Shechem son of Hamor with the same weapon as he...
— Had he, that rabbi, wanted to win favour with his community through finer deeds than I do, with a better sermon than I preach, I would have had a counter-weapon: I would have had to strive with still finer deeds, with a still finer sermon. But with ugly deeds I cannot take revenge on him. —
And so it ought not to be done.

B.
The Rabbi, of blessed memory, gave his last sermon on Shabbat Shuva 5674 [1913]. At that time — as Będzin Jews probably remember — props ["slupes", Pol. słupy] had been standing in the synagogue for quite a long time because of the renovation.
At the same time the gabbaim of the Chevra Kadisha asked the Rabbi to mention during the sermon that the wall around the old cemetery needed repairing.
To this the Rabbi said:
It is written: "For the stone shall cry out of the wall, and the beam out of the timber shall answer it" [Habakkuk 2:11].
— What is the meaning of the word "shall answer it" — the beam answers it back?
But the plain meaning is this — said the Rabbi: "the stone shall cry out of the wall" — the cemetery wall cries out to be repaired; "and the beam out of the timber", the wooden props, "shall answer it", reply to it:
— What are you crying about, cemetery wall? You, whom people see so rarely — no wonder they forget you; but I, the wooden prop in the synagogue, whom people see every day, and in spite of that they leave me in such a state — how much more should I cry out!

C.
An author came to the Rabbi, of blessed memory, wanting the Rabbi to buy his work, titled "Avraham Yagel" ["Abraham shall rejoice"].
When the Rabbi took the book in his hand, he remarked:
— "Abraham shall rejoice" is out of print [lit. "out of the press"], "Isaac shall sing" is also already out of the press, only "Jacob and his sons" — Jacob and his sons are still "in druk"...
[A pun on the Sabbath afternoon hymn "Avraham yagel, Yitzchak yeranen, Yaakov u-vanav yanuchu vo": Yiddish "in druk" means both "in print" and "under pressure, in distress".]

D.
Once — it was on the eve of Sukkot — there was a great glut of etrogim in Będzin; prices dropped from hour to hour, so that by evening one could get a complete "set" for half a rouble.
A market trader who had bought himself such a "bargain" came rushing in with the "set" to the Rabbi to ask whether the etrog was kosher.
When the man left happily, since his "merchandise" was kosher, the Rabbi burst out laughing and said to those present:
— People come to me with all sorts of questions, but it has never yet happened that anyone asked me the law of "a just ephah and a just hin" [Leviticus 19:36]...

E.
About a well-known, "respected" Będzin magnate, who was reputed to be an honest man, but about whom people told far from nice stories concerning his former conduct —
When the Rabbi, of blessed memory, heard this, he said ironically:
— How much must a poor man rob, plunder and murder in the course of his life in order to remain a bit of an honest man...

F.
One day before the eve of Passover a grave question concerning a lung [the kashrut of a slaughtered animal] arose in Sławków, which could have caused great financial loss, besides the town being in "danger" of remaining without meat.
So the then halachic authority there, a great scholar, sent his son to Będzin to the deceased [i.e. Rabbi Graubart] with the question.
The Rabbi, of blessed memory, studied the question at length and then told the messenger these words:
— There is only one decisor who permits it, and I and your father will also say kosher...

G.
The verse in Psalms "For this let every pious one pray unto Thee in a time when Thou mayest be found; surely, when the great waters overflow, they shall not reach unto him" [Psalms 32:6] the Rabbi, of blessed memory, interpreted with this legend:
In the days of the Destruction the enemy took captive 400 children, boys and girls, to convert them. As they sailed on the ship, first the girls jumped into the sea and then the boys. Because the girls sanctified the Name first, it was proclaimed in Heaven that the souls of the girls would descend to the world once more, and their reward would be "and she shall rule over him" — they would dominate the men.
That is the meaning — said the Rabbi — "for this let every pious one pray": for this a pious man prays, that "at the time of finding", when he takes a wife, "the great waters shall not reach": that he not get such a wife from among those who perished in the water, so that he will not have the true "woman more bitter than death" [cf. Ecclesiastes 7:26]...
As a rule — the Rabbi, of blessed memory, added — ideal men get the worst shrews...
A Difficult Beginning.

[Poland — Jews and legislation; article.]
For years people have been talking about the various painful Jewish questions that must be changed by way of legislation. All these questions are burning ones, of the greatest importance for Polish Jewry, which stands before an abyss.

From time to time notices appear in the newspapers that any moment now a decree will be issued that will ease, if only to a small degree, the heavy burdens weighing on Jewish life.

Of all these announcements, a regulation on the Jewish kehillot (communities) has finally appeared. It regulates two matters: first, the term of office of the kehillot is set at 4 years; second, the manner of electing rabbis is laid down. In small towns a rabbi will be elected by the entire Jewish population, and in the large towns — by the kehilla councils.

We will not now enter into a discussion of how far these provisions satisfy our wishes. But we cannot refrain from expressing our astonishment that precisely at the present time, when Polish Jewry is almost completely ruined by the heavy[?] tax system, by the Sunday rest, by a system of etatism[?] and monopolies that push the Jew out of all economic positions and threaten his means of livelihood and his very existence — precisely at this moment such reforms are begun as have no influence whatsoever on the grave situation of the Jewish population and are not likely to ease the desperate Jewish plight.

There is an economic crisis in Poland, but the same crisis also reigns over the whole world, and one cannot make any complaints about that. When the crisis weakens everywhere, we hope that the economic situation will improve here too.

But apart from the general national calamity, there exists in Poland a chronic, specifically Jewish crisis that can be alleviated only by radical means.

Whoever deals seriously with this chronic illness understands that it can be helped only by reforms of the tax system and of the Sunday rest, by abolishing etatism, and by admitting the Jew, equally with the other parts of the population, to the various means of earning a living.

These questions concern equally all strata of the Jewish population — the merchant, the small trader, the artisan and the worker alike.

We deliberately do not touch on the national-cultural questions; we mention only those points that can today be solved by decree.

Were we to go into the matter of the Jewish kehillot, we would first of all have to point out that the questions of how a rabbi is to be elected and how long a kehilla's term should last play a very small role compared with the general kehilla problem, which consists in this: that the kehilla must be a Jewish autonomous body dealing with the whole complex of national-Jewish problems.

No more than a few more weeks — and the questions[?] pointed out could be changed by way of decrees.

It is the ardent wish of the entire Jewish population that this should finally happen.

We have been waiting for it for 10 years already.

Will the answer come now?

Dr. Y. Rozenblat.
Napoleon's Romance with the Young Widow Josephine

M. Aszerowicz.
2.
She knew how to take him into her hands: she knew how to stir his passion [?] and how to arouse jealousy in him, so that his love for her should truly border on madness; and therefore it is no wonder at all that he fell in love with her.
She kindled in him a fire that kept on burning, and since he could not always be together with her, he wrote her such letters in which every word breathed [?] love and fiery passion.
"I wait for you," he writes to her in his letter, "I am entirely full of you; your image and the intoxicating evening we spent together give me no rest. Dear, sweet Josephine, I can find no one to equal you. What have you done to my heart? Are you perhaps angry with me? Are you perhaps sad? Do you perhaps not feel at your best?... I console myself that at least in thought I surrender to the power of my passion for you, and I think of how on your lips and on your breast the flames of love that burn in me will blaze up even more. Last night I gazed at your picture for a long time. And then it became clearer to me than ever that the picture cannot take the place of you yourself. This afternoon you will set out to me; in three hours I will see you. And meanwhile, my darling, I send you thousands of kisses. But I beg you not to give me a single kiss, because every kiss of yours sets my blood on fire"...
Such were the letters Napoleon wrote to Josephine. And after he married her (on 6 March 1396 [sic; read 1796]) his love for her grew stronger still, and when he was later on [?] the battlefield and had to be far from her for a longer time, he longed for her so much that he nearly lost his mind. And whenever he could snatch a free hour, he wrote her a letter full of love and passion.
Although Josephine was six years older than Napoleon, she trembled for him less than he did for her. At the time when he was leading the battles on the Italian front and marching with his army from victory to victory, driving the enemies of the newly founded Republic ever further and further back and spreading the borders of France ever wider and wider — at that very time Josephine was living it up in Paris as only the world allows, surrounding herself with gallant cavaliers who followed her every step and were jealous of one another.
The great victories in Italy made Napoleon famous throughout the world and much beloved in France. All the newspapers wrote about her [sic; read "him"]; in all the houses, in all the salons and in all the streets people talked about him; his name was on everyone's lips; he was the pride of the Republic, the hero of the whole nation; everywhere people told what wonders he worked on the battlefield and how many treasures he sent into the camp [?] after taking a town or a region. And precisely then, when Napoleon's name was so great and so beloved in France, Josephine began, on the strength of it, to play the role of the great victor's wife. And she greatly enjoyed being shown great honour everywhere and being given ovations in all the theatres she came to.
Hardly a single day passed without Napoleon sending her a love letter to Paris. In every letter he begged her to come to him.
"You must come to me," he wrote to her, "I want to feel your head on my breast, I want to feel your body in my arms! Faster! Fly, fly to me, my dearest."
But she seldom answered his letters, and as for coming to him in the camp, where the thunder of cannons and rifles is heard, she did not think of it at all, because it paid her better to be in merry Paris, where she could bathe in honour on the strength of her husband's great heroic deeds, and in love — on the strength of her beauty...
Jealousy burned in Napoleon like a hellish fire; all the great victories he had won on the Italian front did him no good; his longing for her grew so strong that he, the proud Napoleon Bonaparte, who never forgot for a single minute that when speaking with a person he must stress his importance and his greatness with every word — he still often behaved like a boy, and when showing Josephine's picture to the staff officers he wanted them to express their enthusiasm over how beautiful she was.
However hard it was for him to feel that she was unfaithful to him, that she had intimate relations with another man, he still had to think about it, and in one of the letters he sent her from the battlefield he wrote thus:
"Do you perhaps have a lover? Have you perhaps got tangled up in a romance with some nineteen-year-old [printed "gayntsn", a misprint for "nayntsn"] whippersnapper? If so, I shall let you feel the taste of my strong fist."
Josephine, however, was not frightened of his strong fist. When she had read the letter through she burst out laughing, and since she happened to be spending time with Tallien, the former secretary of the Paris municipal administration, she showed him the letter and said with a smile:
"An odd man, this Bonaparte!"
Indeed, precisely such a man, with such an iron will and such tremendous ambition as Napoleon, could suffer so much from jealousy and yet not neglect the smallest detail on the battlefield.
It gave him no rest, and yet he went on with his wars and his plans.
Writing to his friend Carnot, the war minister of the French government, about some matters that were very important for the state and the army, he suddenly switched in the middle of it to personal matters. "I am in great despair," he suddenly began to complain to the war minister, "my wife does not want to come to me here. It can only be that she has a lover, and that is why she does not want to leave Paris. I hate all women."
These last words were no more than an expression of anger, as happens quite often at such a moment, when one is angry with a woman one loves very much. And later, when he heard that Josephine was somehow not feeling well [?] and that there was a supposition that she was pregnant, a new sea of feelings stormed up in his heart. On the one hand he was very pleased, because he very much wanted an heir, and on the other hand he was very displeased, because he was not sure whether she was pregnant by him or by someone else altogether.

Będzin
4-year-old girl under tram wheels.
A tragic victim on the Old Market
On Friday at midday, as 4-year-old Chanele Erlich was crossing the tram line at Old Market [Stary Rynek] 6, the „red angel of death“ [the red tram] came rushing at speed from Jana[?] Street and dragged the little girl under its wheels.

Premises for the Cheap Kitchen

[Będzin — kehilla, welfare.]
As we have already reported, the kehilla administration has decided to open a cheap kitchen. All preparations have already been made, but the hold-up is that it is hard to obtain the necessary premises for the kitchen.
Anyone who wishes to give premises for such a purpose should notify the gmina [the Jewish community office] about it.
Intervention Concerning the Eruv

[Będzin — religion and municipality.]
On Wednesday a delegation, accompanied by the electrical technician Mr. Retman, called on the municipal commissioner concerning the eruv fence in the town.
After Mr. Retman's explanation of what it was about, the commissioner promised not to make any difficulties.
The Debts Will Be Paid Off Bit by Bit

[Będzin — municipality, finances.]
The town commissioner informs us that next week the magistrate [municipality] will receive 50.000 zł. as part of the loan that was allotted to the previous town administration. From this sum — he says — the creditors will receive partial coverage.
In Honour of the Yahrzeit of Rabbi Graubart, of Blessed Memory

[Będzin — rabbinate and charity.]
Next Sunday falls the 17th yahrzeit of the Rabbi of Będzin, the great Rabbi R' Yissachar Berish Graubart, of blessed memory.
As every year, on this day too a large number of Jewish children from the „Talmud Torah“ will be clothed by the local „Malbish Arumim“ [clothing-the-naked society].
With this clothing the name of the deceased is honoured, who stood at the head of the Malbish Arumim.
Annual General Meeting of „Hitachdut“

[Będzin — Zionism, parties.]
The annual general meeting of „Hitachdut“ [the Zionist labour party] took place in its own premises. Taking part in the meeting on behalf of the Central Committee was Mr. Yaakov Białopolski of Warsaw. The meeting was opened by Dr. Rechtman with a short introduction on the situation that has arisen in Zionism. Then a presidium was elected, into which entered: Dor Liwer, Białopolski, Gutbinder[?], Sanela[?]. The report on the activity to date was given by Mr. Dr. Rechtman, who pointed out that the activity to date had been satisfactory. The treasury report was given by Mr. Gertler. From the report it emerges that the turnover for the last year reached up to 4000 zł. Further reports were given by: cultural commission — Mr. Zygrajch, secretariat — Mr. Goldminc, regional committee (Va'ad ha-Glili) — Mr. Gertner, Keren Kayemet — Mr. Ginsberg, youth section — Miss Holender, press — Mr. Openhajm. A larger number of members took part in the discussions on the reports. Then Mr. Białopolski was given the floor and spoke on the situation in Labour Zionism and also on the world conference of „Hitachdut“ in Berlin.
The continuation of the general meeting took place under the chairmanship of Mr. Dor Liwer.
On future activity Messrs. Gertler and Zygrajch reported. A report from the town council was given by Dr. Rechtman. The report aroused great interest; many members took part in the discussion, expressing their dissatisfaction with the municipal economy. Then a resolution was adopted unanimously expressing recognition to Mr. Dr. Rechtman for his activity to date in the Będzin town council.
Protest resolutions were then adopted against English policy regarding Eretz Israel.
After the outgoing committee was granted a discharge (absolutorium), elections were held with the following result: Dr. Rechtman (chairman), Gertler (vice), Gertner (secretary), Holender (treasurer), Goldminc (press), Ginsberg, Zygrajch, Z.B.[?] Liwer. Members' court: Rozenker, D. Liwer, Snicer. Audit commission: Granecki, Balimowski, Richter.

On Tuesday a Jewish woman, a Litvak, came into the local beis-medresh, where she wanted to abandon her own child, a little boy 2 years old, „to God's mercy“[?].
Several Jewish porters thwarted the plan.
Kiddushin Declared Invalid After the Wedding

[Będzin — rabbinate, weddings.]
On Sunday something happened in Warpie[?] that resembles the tales of „A Thousand and One Nights“.
A wedding took place there at Mr. Gliksman's. At the chuppah a scandal broke out because of shouting by the cantor Mr. Żubowicz against the synagogue beadle Mr. Kapłan, that „the latter may not be a witness at a kiddushin“.
The incident was settled by having 2 other witnesses stand at the „Harei at“ [the betrothal formula], and not those authorised by the rabbinate.
Later, when the wedding meal was almost over, a messenger from the rabbinate came, following Mr. Kapłan's intervention, and announced that the kiddushin that had taken place were invalid.
On hearing such a thing, several wedding guests went off to the Rabbi, but they were not let into the Rabbi's apartment; for a long time they knocked and pleaded with the Rabbi's beadle to open the door, but nothing helped. They went back to the wedding, where the company made merry until broad daylight...
A Jewish Trade Is Going Under

[Będzin — crafts and employment.]
Years ago — as our attention is drawn — the hairdressing trade was entirely in Jewish hands; not to speak of the small shtetls, but even in the larger towns the number of non-Jewish barbershops [„rezuras“] was minimal.
Lately the following phenomenon is noticeable: the [Jewish] element in the trade is constantly shrinking. In almost all barbershops (Jewish ones too) non-Jewish workers are employed, and at best a Jewish barbershop has 3 non-Jews and 1 Jew.
As we are informed, no Jewish apprentices are coming forward, and the barbershop owners have to engage non-Jews in their place.
This is happening at a time when Jewish parents are looking for employment for their children.

[Będzin — police.]
On Sunday the young people Rapaport and Golbard were arrested because they were suspected of conducting agitation for an “election action” [campaign].
In the evening the young people were released.

Sosnowiec — Hooligan Attack on the Dozór Member Mr. Saks

[Sosnowiec — violence.]
On Saturday night, as the dozór member [kehilla board member] Mr. Itshke Saks was about to enter the building where he lives, he was attacked by the young man Mordechai Gitler, who dealt Saks cruel blows with a stick and knocked him down, so that Mr. Saks was left lying unconscious.
By chance a neighbour passing by noticed Mr. Saks lying there and raised the alarm; a doctor came and gave first aid, and afterwards S. was taken to the hospital on Wawel, where it was established that S.'s right arm was broken in 2 places.
Later S.'s sons took up the wrong done to their father and “settled accounts” with G. as befits.
He Took Deposits from His Employees — A Cunning Swindler Arrested

[Sosnowiec — crime.]
In the month of September a certain Józef Szymkiewicz came to Zagłębie; he rented premises in Sosnowiec at Warszawska 18, where he opened a trading office for the sale of foodstuffs.
Szymkiewicz advertised in a number of newspapers that he was looking for male and female employees for his trading office against a deposit (kaucja).
Very many male and female clerks answered the advertisements, but Szymkiewicz engaged only women, from whom he took deposits of 200 and 300 zł.
From those who had no cash S. took bills of exchange, which he forged to larger sums.
When the “employees” finally realised that their “breadgiver” was a plain swindler, they handed the matter over to the police, which after an investigation arrested the “office owner”.

On Saturday night several windowpanes were smashed at the premises of the administration of the Endek [National Democratic] organ “Kurier Zachodni”.
Kwapiński's Trial Before the Court of Appeal

[Sosnowiec — courts, politics.]
This week the local district court sent to Warsaw, to the defence counsel of the former deputy Kwapiński, the grounds of the verdict.
Next week the defence counsel will lodge an appeal with the Court of Appeal, where the trial is to take place next month.
As Head of the Hospital He “Made Himself Healthy”

[Dąbrowa (?) — crime.]
The security authorities received confidential information that the intendant [steward] of the hospital in Pekin, Domagała, was taking home various products and articles belonging to the hospital.
In this connection a search was carried out this week in Domagała's flat, where a considerable number of quilts, bedsheets and other hospital articles were found.
“Sentence Me to Death” — A Murderer Cries Out in the District Court

[Sosnowiec — courts, murder.]
In the Sosnowiec District Court a scene took place these days which made a shattering impression even on the judges.
Some weeks ago, not far from Mysłowice, near the colony “Wygara” [?; perhaps Wygoda], the 23-year-old Palchis was found killed.
The first suspicion was that he had fallen victim to a bandit, but afterwards it was established that Palchis had been murdered by his friend Gala, with whom he had personal scores to settle.
This week Gala stood before the local District Court. The course of the trial and the statements of the witnesses weakened the charge, and it was evident that the accused would receive a milder punishment.
But when the prosecutor delivered his speech for the prosecution, the murderer became so agitated that he ran up to the judges' table and said:
— “I ask you to pass a just sentence: you should sentence me to death, because I killed him.”
After an hour-long deliberation the murderer was sentenced to 8 years of heavy prison.

A Letter to the Editor

[Będzin — kehilla; kashrut; poultry dealers.]
Dear Mr. Editor!
Allow us to print the following letter in your esteemed newspaper.
Whereas the Będzin gmina [Jewish community] demands from us poultry dealers a levy on poultry brought in from outside, and we can by no means meet it because of today's competitive prices [?];
The Będzin gmina demands something that does not exist anywhere in the whole of Poland. This measure may lead to the livelihood of dozens of Jewish families being taken away, especially in a town like Będzin, which needs and must have poultry from outside.
We therefore turn to the kehilla administration through the newspaper, asking it to withdraw this unheard-of [?] project and to avoid catastrophic consequences.
Let the Jewish public know that the fact that the poultry is now not provided with any labels [“kvitlekh” — kashrut tags] is, God forbid, not because of the kashrut, but because the levy cannot be met; for every dealer is provided with certificates of kashrut [hekhsherim] just as until now, but the rabbinate does not allow the labels to be attached until we settle the new levy at the gmina.
Respectfully,
The Poultry Dealers' Section, Będzin.

Reasons of the Sosnowiec District Court why Kwapiński was sentenced to a year of fortress
As is known, the Sosnowiec District Court handed down a verdict under which former deputy Kwapiński (PPS) was sentenced to a year's imprisonment. The reasons for the verdict have now been published. From the reasons it can be seen: first, the court relies on the representatives [?] of the police and on witnesses. Besides that, Kwapiński's guilt is proven by the fact that he has no other occupation except as a 'public activist' and received a salary for his public work.
Secondly [?], the court saw Kwapiński's guilt in his having spoken before a crowd of unschooled workers in Olkusz about a large number of cars at the Belweder, about ministers' trips abroad, about 8 million zł. spent by former minister Czechowicz, and about the visit of officers in the Sejm".
Former deputy Kwapiński's appeal to his past, full of suffering for the interests of Poland, is in the court's opinion a play on feelings and not an argument against the charge. The court therefore found Kwapiński guilty and sentenced him to a year's imprisonment.
As mitigating circumstances regarding the accused the court recognized:
1) his services to the independence of Poland.
2) the unimportant consequences of his offence, and
3) partisanship [?] in the struggle with the government of the day.
Because of these reasons the court applied the lowest penalty: a year's imprisonment. The court could not apply a smaller penalty because 1) the accused showed too much [?] ill will, 2) Kwapiński is in constant opposition to the government, as he declared in his final word, and as such he deserves no pardon.

A Jewish Boy Run Over in Sosnowiec

[Local.] On Wednesday, 7-year-old Moshe Buszezszotski [?] was walking, and as he was crossing „First of May" street in Sosnowiec a car [—] ran over the boy and injured him severely. — A child swallows a pin. On Wednesday evening the 1½-year-old child Piekarski [?] in Będzin swallowed a pin it had been playing with. At the hospital the pin was removed, and the child was saved from danger.
To Save the Traders [?] on Będzin's Old Market
[Local.] All the way from Vilna, Rabbi R. Yitzchok Sztejn travelled to Kielce; he figures on list 17 of the Kielce Jewry [?].
A False Accusation against a Hasidic Young Man

[Local.] On Wednesday evening, as the Hasidic young man Sh. was walking [—] along Sosnowiecka street in Będzin, he was accosted by an unknown woman who clung to him and shouted that „he should give her another 10 zlotys"... Hearing the slander, the young man [ran] into the new shtibl on Małachowski street; but at the woman's cries a policeman came up and took the young man to the commissariat, where it emerged that the woman was mentally ill. A report (protocol) was nonetheless drawn up. — A break-in at a mill. On Jasna street in Będzin unknown persons broke into the mill of Mr. L. Hercberg, [taking?] the leather belts and a large number of sacks; the damage amounts to about 2,000 zł.
Concert by the „HaPoach" Orchestra

[Local/culture.] On the 19th of this month a concert will take place in Będzin, performed by the orchestra's own ensemble, founded some months ago [?] at the „HaPoach" sports club. On the programme — interesting musical works, well worth hearing performed by the Jewish school youth. — Neighbours tear at each other's noses... At Kołłątaja 9 in Będzin two Jewish neighbours quarrelled over an attic beam. From words they turned to deeds, and the „war" ended with [one] neighbour [biting off] the other's tongue and half his nose...
Sosnowiec Already Has a Nominated Council
[Local.] Last night we received word from Sosnowiec that the Kielce voivode has already appointed the „Rada Komisaryczna" (commissarial council). Among those nominated is also Mr. L. Zedl.
Jabotinsky Is Coming to Będzin
[Local.] Last night the Revisionist organization in Będzin received a telegraphic report that on December 24th Jabotinsky will give a lecture in Będzin at the „Kapitol".

The Election Fight for the Senate. Vile Attacks on the Candidate Rabbi Rubinstein

[Political/local.] As is known, Senate elections take place this coming Sunday. In 1928 the Kielce voivodeship elected[?] Rabbi Rubinstein, who is again a candidate in the present Senate elections on List 17. But the 'Aguda' [Agudat Israel] set itself the task [—] of disrupting the move; simply put, the 'Aguda's' aim is to break the only Jewish mandate in the Kielce voivodeship. On Tuesday the Będzin 'Aguda' summoned the representatives of all the shtiblekh to a conference at the 'Aguda' hall. Only 18 [men][?] came, mostly younger Hasidim.
With 'speeches' there came forward orators from the well-known clique who had made a 'name' for themselves in the last Sejm elections. In the 'speeches' the 'anshei shlomenu' were called upon to agitate [the public/the regions?], to go out to the fight so as to break Rabbi Rubinstein's mandate; in doing so they debased the rabbinic authority with the vilest words…
The same day the Sosnowiec 'Aguda' called a meeting, but when Mr. Rigski[?] uttered the first word, 'Gentlemen!', an uproar broke out, thanks to which the meeting was dispersed.
A Clarification

[Local/community.] From the Jewish Butchers' Section in Będzin to the Community Board, regarding the question whether a fifth shoykhet is needed.
In connection with the action we undertook concerning the appointment[?] of a fifth[?] shu"b (shoykhet-u-bodek, ritual slaughterer-and-examiner), we have the honor to state the following:
Taking into account that recently slaughtering has significantly decreased, and also the [—] situation of the Community Board, we convened a meeting of all the butchers to consider the question of appointing a fifth shoykhet. After a long, serious debate we reached agreement that, with good will and with the help of the Community Board and the rabbinate, the 4 shu"b can fully carry out their task. For our part we will take the trouble to adapt to the conditions so as to [complete] the work. We set out the work plan thus: every Thursday and Friday, when there is [much][?] slaughter, all the shoykhtim shall [work]. Through the rest of the week, when poultry slaughter is minimal, R' Yisroel Moyshe shu"b will handle that [work], while the remaining 3 shoykhtim shall be [—] through the week. In such a case it must be established that the shoykhtim come to the slaughter punctually according to the regulations. We are confident that with such a distribution even a larger slaughter will be [—] handled. We are ready, should it eventually be needed, to come in person to carry the matter out. Bringing the above to your knowledge, we remain
with respect,
the Butchers' Section in Będzin.
How to Guard Against Angina (Sore Throat)

[Health.] The damp season [of our days][?] has brought on many illnesses, such as grip(pe), angina, influenza and hysteria[?]. Trifles, Defects

[Feuilleton/op-ed.] (What sort of attitude do the officials have toward the citizens? — In Poland, and how does it look in other countries?)
It often happens that a citizen comes to some institution or office and is not treated properly, then leaves in frustration, convinced that 'we are very far from the cultured world' — even though Poland lies in the center of Europe and strives by every means to stand at a proper cultural level. Instead of informing and instructing the citizen how to fulfill his civic duty, the official snaps at him or ignores him, and the citizen must stand and 'knock' (klapn) before him so he will deign to grant a word. Such an attitude is not seen in the cultured countries of Europe, and in Poland it is not official policy — government circles insist that officials treat citizens courteously and provide the needed information. Things sometimes reach quarrels and formal protocols, and the offended citizen must then prove he meant no harm. After such an 'operation' the official grows even more arrogant and acts as an 'autocrat.'
The writer gives examples: the telephone operator (telefonistke) who fails to connect the right number, deliberately delays, or answers that she is 'busy,' and if you reproach her does it 'out of spite'; and another: a citizen asks at the post office how many stamps an express letter abroad needs, is told, affixes and mails them — and the next day the letter returns as insufficiently franked, so he must pay a surcharge. To the official this is a 'trifle' not worth discussing.
Abroad, says the writer, such a wrong would be treated with more respect, and an official who gave wrong, damage-causing information would be punished and perhaps even dismissed; there every official is responsible for his department and serves the public by clear regulations.
Another fact he read in the 'Zaglembier Tsaytung': a respected merchant from Będzin recounts that abroad he could not pay for a telegram in the local currency and offered the official a Polish banknote as a pledge until he could exchange his money — and the official took offense; and at home too, at the post, they refused to accept a pledge from him. The difference: abroad, where he is not known, he felt ashamed before the official; while at home, where he is known, he was shamed — because even on a pledge they will not trust him.
It is no wonder, then, that the heart aches at such disorders, which the Polish government surely does not condone, but which meanwhile stifle the development of commerce and hold back cultural progress. 'These are perhaps trifles, defects — but with such trifles a country must reckon.' R. Lem.
One Year of Agricultural Work in Zaglembie

[Local/agriculture.] At the beginning of the month the general meeting of the Jewish Society for Agriculture (Yidishe Gezelshaft far Landvirtshaft), Zaglembie branch, was held in Będzin in the hall of the Merchants' Association. The society has existed in Zaglembie only one year. It began its activity in a very small circle of devotees of tourism and agriculture; twenty persons [—] were the participants in its founding meeting. They set themselves the aim of bringing the Jewish public something new [—].
With agriculture, the writer adds, we did not long occupy ourselves, although we Jews have already wandered a great deal [—]. The first Jewish agricultural society in Poland arose three years ago in Warszawa; today it already counts hundreds of members, and from year to year the number of members grows, for whom the society arranges summer and winter colonies and excursions throughout Poland and Europe.
Here in Zaglembie we have far better conditions for agricultural work than in Warszawa: here, where in Upper Silesia (Oybershlezyen) lie the largest factories and mines in the country. [—] they are not accessible to visit, but once we founded the agricultural society we first gained the possibility to become acquainted up close with the industrial works of Zaglembie and Upper Silesia.
Within a few hours by train we can reach a beautiful mountain region, yet it is very rare that Jewish tourists from Zaglembie are met in the Beskidy. This is not about the individual, but about creating a mass movement — as has existed for decades in Western Europe. [—] Berlin alone is left by three million people on a holiday. The cultured person today has a real need to go outside the city to calm his nerves and strengthen his body and spirit with fresh powers [—] in nature, in the mountains [—]. [Signed] W—n.

After Five Years (To the Jewish Population of Będzin), by L. Rubinlicht

[Article — end-of-term accounting.] Five years ago the Jewish population of Będzin entrusted to me the hard office of vice-president, to represent and protect Jewish interests in the Będzin magistrate. At that time a Jewish vice-president was something new, not only among us but in all of Poland; the whole Jewish press in Poland, regardless of its line, then reported the news that in Będzin, in the center of antisemitic Zagłębie, a Jewish vice-president had [been elected]. [...] In my first months in the magistrate, rivals broke their teeth when they had to address a 'Mrs. Vice-President,' but slowly I secured my position and earned [trust] among all the officials, especially the non-Jewish ones, since at that time there was not a single Jewish official in the magistrate. Over the 5 years I had to work with allies of every sort, from Communists to rabid antisemites, yet I always managed to carry through all my demands on behalf of the Jewish population. I must also express my appreciation to the Jewish councilmen (with the exception of 2–3) who gave much time and work and helped realize the economic program, which fundamentally changed the city's outward appearance and its municipal economy. Our program was to create useful public municipal institutions that would give the city treasury revenues, so that within a few years part of the present taxes could be reduced. In a short time we managed to create a municipal electric plant yielding about 300,000 zł a year, which is why the price is cheaper than in all of Poland; the municipal slaughterhouse about 80,000 zł; water pipes were laid in streets that had had no water. We levied certain taxes (e.g. on a [—] bridge) bringing up to 50 thousand zł a year, and other taxes lower than in other towns — 25% from the houses (instead of 50 groszy as in Sosnowiec, Dąbrowa, Częstochowa, Kielce and others). Especially for the Jewish population: the magistrate today employs 20 Jewish officials, 3 Jewish doctors, 1 Jewish hygienist, 1 Jewish sequestrator, 2 Jewish clerks, 1 Jewish manager at the slaughterhouse, 2 collectors at the electric plant, the deputy director of the plant, 8–10 officials at the Jewish colonies, and up to 30 Jewish workers in public works. In recent years the magistrate paid subsidies to Jewish (cultural, social and other) institutions totaling about 150 thousand zł: the Jewish 'orphanage' 35 thousand, [—] 25 thousand, the Jewish colony 27 thousand, the 'old-age home' 15 thousand, etc. — such a sum for Jewish institutions was not granted in any magistrate's budget. Comparing today's figures with those in the budget 5 years ago, one sees how much the Jewish councilmen and representatives did over the 5 years for the Jewish population of Będzin. How do the streets used only by the Jewish [population] look now — such as Modrzejowska, [—], Czeladzka[?], the Old Market, the Fish Market! — where for 20 years not a stone was moved and nothing was lit? Broad sidewalks, squares, good lighting (Będzin now has 110 electric lamps instead of 52 six years ago). For Jewish children the magistrate built a magnificent school building for 400,000 zł, and a modern outpatient clinic from which the Jewish population greatly benefits (80%); and thanks to the improved sanitary conditions, Jewish mortality in Będzin decreases each year. One must also acknowledge that in the last 6 years Będzin has changed greatly for the better, thanks to the city administration: a modern railway station was built in the city center for 2 million złotys, a magnificent post-office building, and a [—] insurance company is building a 4,000,000 zł structure on the magistrate's sale-plots. We managed [matters] carefully, perhaps even frugally, yet everyone who needed the magistrate's help always received it. The present magistrate was the first to allow taxes (padatkes) to be paid over 3 months without interest or penalties. Every citizen, poor and rich, could always consult me. Throughout our term we had no friction with the supervisory council, and the Będzin population showed great confidence. Now that the supervisory authority has dissolved us on purely political grounds, we are proud that the delegate who inspected our activity in the magistrate over 5 days found nothing with which to reproach us. I step down from the city administration with a clear conscience, having honestly fulfilled the office entrusted to me as a Jewish vice-president in Będzin, and I hope my successors will continue the work that remains to be done for the Jewish population in the Będzin magistrate, and will not let go to waste what has, with great effort, been achieved until now.
Cards

[Satirical feuilleton.] 'Cards.' Among us cards were always a sought-after commodity; people played in the big cities and in the little towns — in the towns even more than in the cities, for what better pleasure could one afford in a shtetl on the long winter evenings? Even yeshiva boys in the yeshivas and study-houses used to 'steal' the 'little Shas' more than the big one. But card-playing as it has gone on among us these last years has never been seen, and the chief [players] are the women — they trail after the card-table more, than, lehavdil, at a Christian funeral... One starts playing in autumn; in summer people go off to the dachas and start there too; in autumn they return to town and start with even more zest, for the head is rested and, thanks to acquaintances made at the dacha, fresh [partners] come along... And once one plunges into the cards one forgets how one stands in the world; for we Jews are made either with measure and limit, or not at all. Today, for example, the 'poker fashion' — the whole Jewish conversation revolves around it: 'there is no house that has no poker'... What is more: people play not only in the evenings but also by day, in the morning and the afternoon; for the balebosteh has no time at all, and, thank God, she lacks for nothing — what is she to do? Run the household? There is a maid. Think about a match? She will not meddle in her husband's affairs, and he in hers — he thanks God she does not pester him, and her head is in the cards and his head is calmer... It even has an advantage for him: at cards she may lose, but she may also win; but if she goes about idle and [bored], the 'vexation' will cost him dearer... [The writer] recalls not only her, her husband and her children, but much else: the whole of Jewish communal life — besides women who now give themselves to poker, did any once occupy themselves with philanthropy and public work? He recalls Jewish [letters], Jewish literature and the whole of Jewish culture. Ask me whether she ever reads a newspaper (apart from the serialized novel she skims with her eyes before she sits down at the card-table), and what she knows about the elections? More than one Jewish woman did not go to the ballot-box because she could not tear herself from the card-table, and more than one Jewish vote was lost for the sake of poker... Interestingly, in America too the Jewish women have lately spread the 'card epidemic,' and the newspapers storm against them. But there, such as it is, at least the sum is apportioned to a sacred purpose — the money won is given to charity, used to maintain Talmud Torahs, or even to write a Torah scroll. [One consoles] oneself that it is a 'law' — good deeds through demoralization; yet by all opinions one feels there that there is something ugly about it, that it is not in order — and among us... Women! Women! After reading these few lines, take a look in the mirror — have you not turned red with shame?... Onkeles.
