Hanukkah.

[Hanukkah feuilleton — childhood memories]
"Kindle, kindle, little candles, / and light up my black walls[?], / you alone, you only, / can tell me, can recount, / and we'll speak from the heart..." (M. Bar-Kohen).
Tell me, do you not remember now, as you stand before your Hanukkah lamp, the Hanukkah of long, long ago? Tell me, how often[?] does it happen that a longing[?] kindles in you to live once more a Hanukkah evening of the not-distant past that lives on in memory — when nature was so hard, so wild and yet so beautiful, so genuine?...
You recall a Hanukkah evening during a fiery, breath-taking frost or a great dusty snowstorm...
Hanukkah of old..
It always came on time, always full of mood, always its own self...
Already several weeks before, when the snow began to fall and fall, as though strewn by an invisible hand over the earth, over houses and trees, until it grew into a thick white featherbed; or when snow-mountains piled up[?], sculpted[?] by the wind, sparkling at night in the moonlight with crystal brilliance — then one felt the arrival of Hanukkah...
Then it came.
Everyone's anticipation was wonderful: it seemed as if we were awaiting a quiet, distinguished guest. A great aristocrat whom each wants to receive ever more beautifully, more splendidly and more warmly — everyone awaited him, the children, with all the Jews of the shtetl; each prepared with something different:
Mother — with rendered fat, with "ganzn"[?] latkes; Father — with a pack of cards. Father, an ardent kehilla man, something of an Orthodox, whose life ran so calmly, so orderly, became another man on Hanukkah. All year no card was allowed into the house; he did not hold with it, since it is not a Jewish thing — but Hanukkah, that is something else. It was an old custom of his to play "oke" [twenty-one] on Hanukkah. Then he allowed himself and played with his father-in-law. But he never forgot to take off from every "pot" a share for the "Talmud Torah", which he cared for so much and supported by every means. The "stakes" had to be considerable, and so the game was lively, burning.
And Hanukkah?... Meanwhile it crept up quietly, like a breath, like a song.
Right after Minhah the wind stopped; the frost began to take everything under its power; the further it went, the harder it bit[?] and burned with its cold fire... Wherever you looked, everywhere you saw its power, but that power was already in harmony with the "mood-filled Hanukkah"...
Up onto the window[?] was brought everything needed to light the candles. Soon Father drew us children to him and showed us how to bless the Hanukkah candles. The candles burned and their bright glow poured over the whole room. Later Grandfather came, and we children hung about him:
— Grandpa, give Hanukkah gelt.
— Yes, yes, children, you'll get it; but do you know what Hanukkah is?
— Of course we know.
Then Grandfather stroked us, sat down with us and began telling us all the beautiful stories and miracles and the heroic deeds of the Hasmoneans.
Ah, how warmly everyone's hearts beat then.
Yes, yes — frost reigned in nature. But in the human heart there swayed a sea of light, a sea of gentleness.
The Hanukkah candles burned, smiled[?], flickered and went out again, pouring forth joy, homeliness and memories, lived-through and not lived-through.
Today there are no longer those burning frosts at Hanukkah. Nature has become softer, milder; only the human heart has changed: it has taken over the hardness of the old winter Hanukkah-time.
G. Perlzon.
Who Bears the Kehilla Burden?

[Polemical article — the Będzin kehilla and Agudah]
Several years have passed since the Polish state favored the Jewish population of Poland with a democratic Jewish kehilla. Naturally, as soon as today's kehillot came into being, no one — apart from the Agudah — was satisfied with the form they took, simply because the kehillot were created mainly to deal with religious and klei-kodesh [religious functionaries'] matters. And as soon as anyone once made an attempt[?] to take up a Jewish matter that was not klei-kodesh — such as schools, subsidies for cultural institutions, Eretz-Israel questions — it was promptly struck out, and it became clear that the dissatisfaction with the kehilla "gift" is justified, because the nationally minded Jew wants to see the kehilla as the institution that deals with the whole of Jewish life — creating something positive in the Jewish street — for Jewish culture, and not merely a little kloyz that deals with ritual slaughterers, mikvehs, etc.
Several years have already passed since today's "modern[?] democratic" kehillot were born, and unfortunately we see that the kehilla is the same old "dead shtibl", nothing else; the only difference is that the old dead shtiblekh had just 2–3 balebatim, while today's has in all 31 "opinion-givers".
If we want to convince ourselves of all this, it suffices to take as an example the kehilla in Będzin, and the whole sad picture of kehilla life will stand plainly before our eyes.
Throughout its "life" our kehilla truly has nothing positive to credit to its account. There were several capable and welcome members in the gmina, people whose work could have been useful, but they had no possibility of working because of the obstruction methods of the Agudah people and their hangers-on.
Dr. Weinzieher, Director Fürstenberg or Mr. Winiadzki[?] wanted to work in the gmina — work that would consist not only of klei-kodesh matters but the work Jewish life demands, work embracing all the concerns of the Jewish population; but they realized that the Agudah clique would not allow such work — on the contrary, everything was done to obstruct them — so they slammed the kehilla door and left.
Other people remained who run the work to this day; the term of office has ended, but there is plenty of sitting and standing — "work" goes on. —
And what does the work there look like now? —
Suffice it to point out that when the writer of these lines re-entered[?] the administration 2–3 months ago, the situation there was catastrophic. A large part of the duty-members [dyżury] had long since forgotten that they were on duty and for a long time did not come even to a single meeting. Consequently 1 or 2 persons ran kehilla life in Będzin — and one can say that the kehilla is a sheer ruin: 8–10 months[?] of pensions unpaid, living off the few złotys a collector brought in or when a wealthy man died. The situation today is not much better — only let it be said that as soon as several members showed good will to do something and drag the kehilla out of its plight, the "Torah-loyal" at once appeared and began to be "active": their activity, of course, consists of "dealings", tripping people up, and above all creating new expenses such as slaughterers, secretaries for the rabbinate and the like; and amid this famous activity, under these "fine"[?] working conditions, the Agudah people have got a brand-new joy:
— they have lived to take revenge on the Zionists and the "sinners" (poshim).
The state has given the Agudah people a sweet: "those who can openly [act] against religion may neither vote nor be elected in the kehillot"; and although the matter is still pending[?], the Agudah people are already dancing in the air that they will now settle comfortably in the kehilla shtibl.
But they, the Agudah people, have forgotten that with this "candy" they will, on top of everything, shatter Jewish kehilla life.
Will national Jewry in Poland calmly watch as it is robbed of its Jewish civic rights? Will these "sinners", the beardless citizens, be the money-givers for the privileged "bearded citizens"?
And do the Agudah people not know that the klei-kodesh get their salaries only thanks to the "sinners", who are for the most part the money-givers? Does one not know, for instance here in Będzin, who the big city taxpayers are? Are they perhaps the fine bearded Jews? Has a fine bearded Jew ever given such a large donation for the mikveh as was given precisely by a Zionist, a "sinner"? And the orphanage in Będzin — who has been building it until now? Are not 95 percent of the donors precisely "sinners"?
And who in general the money-givers in Będzin are — in the next article.
A. Liwer.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion: Parshat Miketz

[Column — Torah sayings and anecdotes for Miketz and Hanukkah]
Collected and styled by Y. Y.
a) "Can we find such a man, in whom is the spirit of God?" (Gen. 41:38)
Joseph, as is known, dressed modern and elegant, adorned and decked himself out, "curling his hair and touching up his eyes to look handsome". Pharaoh wondered at this: "can we find such" — is there really such an elegantly dressed man, who knows many languages, in whom "is the spirit of God" — that he should be godly? Pharaoh marveled that one can look elegant and modern, be educated, and still be godly. (Rabbi Bunem of Przysucha)
The Chortkov Rebbe once spoke about dress — that one is compelled[?] to dress in a worldly way — and expressed himself thus: "God tests the Jews each time with something different: once with this kind of dress and once with that kind, but the pintele yid [the Jewish spark] always remains." (Divrei David)
b) "And the famine was over all the face of the earth" (41:56)
"The face of the earth" means the rich, for with them the hunger began. Why are the rich called "the face of the earth"? Because he who is well off shows everyone his smiling face, while the poor man hides his face — he has no face... (Bereshit Rabbah 91:5)
c) "Why do you look at one another" (42:1)
Jacob said to his sons: "Why do you show yourselves?" — do not display yourselves before Esau when you are sated, lest they envy you... (Tractate Ta'anit 10)
d) "When he besought us, and we would not hear" (42:21)
"When he besought us" — where is it mentioned anywhere in the verse that Joseph pleaded with his brothers? Where?
— One who is dragged[?] off to be flogged still has strength and courage to scream; but one condemned to death stays motionless[?], without a sign of life; he is dazed, and if he weeps it is a dazed, confused, incomprehensible weeping.
"When he besought us" — he wept before us so quietly, so incomprehensibly, that "we would not hear" — it could not be heard... (Ohel Yitzhak, R. [?] of Amshinov)
e) "And Benjamin's portion was greater" (43:34)
The sale of Joseph came about through the brothers' envy of Joseph. Now Joseph wanted to test whether they had already corrected the bad trait of foolish envy; so he gave Benjamin more, to see whether they would envy him. (Nifla'ot Hadashot)
Hanukkah.
a) Hanukkah and charity. The "Magen Avraham" (§672) records a custom that on Hanukkah young men go collecting donations. What is the sense of it? — The Hanukkah miracle, as is known, was that only one jug of oil was found and instead of one day it burned eight days. The "Beit Yosef" asks: if so, the miracle was only for seven days, since for one day [oil] had been found. The "Turei Zahav" answers: the Zohar says that a blessing does not rest upon an empty thing. How then did the miracle happen on the first day, when the jug was empty? It must be that although the jug held only enough to burn for one day, a miracle occurred in that something remained for the second day as well, on which the blessing could already rest; thus on the first day too a miracle occurred, in that something remained... There are rich men who, if one comes to them for a donation, give not a penny, but do not stint on blessings: "Trust in God, Reb Jew, He will help you, better than in people"... Therefore one comes to them on Hanukkah, when it is clear that no blessing rests when the pocket is empty, and one tells them: you bless, you give blessings — see to it that there is something in the pocket for the blessing to rest upon... (Yerah la-Mo'adim)
b) The shammashim. The beit-din beadle of Białystok was a very bad man, a thorough villain, and caused much grief to the rabbi R. Velvele (author of "Agudat Ezov"). Once, when R. Velvele was in a good mood, he said to him: you know that Jews have three shammashim: the "shammash" of the Hanukkah lamp, the "shammash" of the tzitzit and the "shammash" of the beit din. The Hanukkah-lamp shammash gets burned up, the tzitzit shammash gets wound around — only the beit-din shammash will neither be burned nor wound, so one can never get rid of him...
c) The "Kedushat Levi" on card-playing. "For our many sins a breach has opened among our brethren the Children of Israel to play cards, and the matter is light in their eyes. But they should know that every card surely has a great kelipah [impure shell] that is not fit to mention. Heaven is my witness that I do not mean merely to preach, only to make people take heed." (Kedushat Levi, Miketz)
d) Hanukkah and the Torah. Antiochus was the worst villain, who wanted to fight the Torah; all the Jews' enemies before him contended only for the Jewish land or wealth, whereas he wanted only to undermine Jewish culture. His methods of struggle against the Jewish spirit [serve] his successors to this day. He, the worst of all, invented a libel that in the Temple a Greek was sacrificed on the altar — and his successors use this libel, saying that Jews need blood for ritual purposes. He spread a lie that in the Holy of Holies there is a "donkey's head", and our opponents decry us as "the people of matter", a people sunk only in materialism, whose soul is nothing but the coin — — — (Derashot RY"N)
Hanukkah Motifs

[Satirical Hanukkah poem opening the humour supplement "Der Kokh-Lefl" (The Cooking Ladle), "appearing in honour of Hanukkah, by Ben Amotz".]

When the day's takings are no takings
and not a customer is seen,
and the paupers [?] say
"nieszczęście" [? Polish: misfortune] and weep;

and the "urząd" [tax office] assesses [?] him,
one must carry fat sums —
and if one still stays on one's feet,
one may say "Al ha-nissim" ["For the miracles"]...
* * *
When the crisis is almighty,
bills of exchange and taxes must be paid,
and six mouths want to eat —
you can well picture it.

And imagine, surely,
such a picture in your thoughts [?]:
that like little candles
we go out and flicker...
* * *
Today we marvel at the heroic deeds
of the Hasmonean heroes,
how they [beat out?] the Greeks —
wonder of wonders!

But when one gets through a day
without seeing the face of a groszy —
that too, dear Jews,
is surely no small heroic deed..
D. Fletter.
Today's Miracles

[Humorous parody of the "Al ha-nissim" ("For the miracles") prayer.] Miracles and wonders: a blessing came into a jug of oil. Well, well, some miracles!) The real miracles happen today:
When one comes home from the Będzin synagogue with whole bones — for the miracles.
When the Talmud Torah teachers did not [smash] the windowpanes at the gmina [community/municipal office] — for the miracles.
When Shlomo Yitzchak and Avremel Liver [?] sit at one table and both have whole noses — for the miracles.
When one sees the Jewish posters with their "inspired orthography" and can bear such a disgrace — for the miracles.
"Fine Jews" [notables] sit at election meetings with... and see no desecration of God's name — for the miracles.
When one gets out safely from [?] the premises of the Sosnowiec gmina, one really must say — for the miracles.
When the Będzin Revisionists could not manage to get Jabotinsky to come to Będzin — for the miracles.
When one sends for a doctor on Sunday and he comes only on Tuesday — for the miracles.
And when the tenants get out "in peace" from the new housing decree, they will have to say every day — for the miracles.

Between Merchants.
[Joke.] — Tell me, Reb Notl, what is the difference between the Hanukkah miracle and a merchant?
— I'll tell you: at Hanukkah a candle is added every day and it gets brighter, while with a merchant something is taken away every day, and things get darker for him..
Leib Stabinski.
Show Your Shoulders!

[Satire/Hanukkah humour — three short pieces in one column: "Show Your Shoulders!", "Always Hanukkah", "Once and Today".]
(A little scene from the present day)
In one house there are several patients of various "qualities", such as flu, nerves, old-age "weakness", asthma and the like. In comes the feldsher [barber-surgeon/medic], panting, barely gets a word out, and orders:
— "Show me your shoulders, your shoulders!
— What do you mean? We came for an examination.
— No time, — answers the feldsher, — show me your shoulders, yes, yes, flu, flu, flu, compresses, cupping glasses, hand over the couple of gulden, because there's no time.
Going out the door you can still hear the feldsher mutter: flu, flu, compresses, cupping glasses, aspirin...

Always Hanukkah.
For merchants it is Hanukkah all year round:
1) Their heads are "spun" [like a dreidel] all year.
2) Their shoes and clothes are full of latkes (pun: pancakes / patches).
3) When they receive a promissory note (veksl) they say "Al ha-nisim" [for the miracles].
4) After signing a promissory note they light a candle.
5) Over a "nakaz" [?] [court payment order] on a promissory note they say "Shehecheyanu".
Leyb Shtshabinski [?].

Once and Today.
Once you got latkes only at Hanukkah. Today there are latkes [patches] everywhere: in your trousers — patches, in your shoes — patches, on the seats by the eastern wall [of the synagogue] — patches, you walk into any institution whatsoever — patches, and young men who want a three-thousand-dollar dowry — nothing more than patches.

Armed...

We are asked to announce that all members (członkowie), flu patients, who come to the outpatient clinics of the Sick Fund (Kasa Chorych) should bring along suitcases with food...
Hanukkah Latkes

[Hanukkah feuilleton in three parts: "Ha-nerot halalu", "The Jewish Dreidel", "Hannah and Her Seven Sons".]
Pini Bal-Loshn [pen name, "Pini the Wordsmith"].
1.
"Ha-nerot halalu" [These lights]...
These lights — these little candles! — Once again the candles, once more the candles! The same thing every time! Nothing new at all!
— No, no, gentlemen, nothing! And we have nothing to be ashamed of in the old candles!
One should be ashamed of darkness, but not of light.
And when we see the darkness in the great world, our own candles ought to become even dearer and more beloved to us.
"Ha-nerot halalu" — these little candles which we do see [?] twinkling here and there, "anu madlikin" — we kindle them for the world.
We are the lighters of the light from eternity until this very day.
Without us there would be even more darkness in the world.
For truly, in what does the great world now stand higher than in the past? What has the world itself ever put right without our help?
Nothing whatsoever.
The world has not yet brought forth any new prophets; the world has not yet created any new luminous ideals.
Apart from the old ones, which we gave it.
The old hatred between nation and nation is now even stronger than before.
Falsehood rules the world now more than ever.
The greatest outcasts still stand at the world's helm today — they are the power-holders and world leaders.
If, for example, Pharaoh were alive today, he would probably be a dictator in Italy.
If Haman were alive he would surely have become premier in Hungary.
If Titus and Antiochus were alive, they would surely have become the chief leaders somewhere in black, yellow and even red parties.
And our candles are still of great use to the world to this day.
The only trouble is that "we have no permission to make use of them" — we are given no right to use them!
The world does not want to use our candles itself, and it doesn't let us either!...
But be ashamed of our old candles — that we certainly need not.
Only what do we gain from our complaints, if we merely stand "by the lamp"?!
2.
The Jewish Dreidel.
Look at the Hanukkah dreidel and see in it the eternal Jew.
A true symbol of the Jewish people. Jews are, as it were, a "dreidel" in all generations and in all countries.
The world spins us and we spin around in the world.
We get dreidel-spun and we spin ourselves.
It has been so from time immemorial: when someone just wants to play a game, they grab us by our little heads and play dreidel with us.
Where is there a people that has not spun us by the head?
And where on the globe is there a country where we have not spun about?
Nowhere, nowhere! We are the only dreidel in the world; everywhere they spin us and everywhere we spin.
They promise us equal rights — at once they spin us.
They even give us a Land of Israel — again they spin us.
And from all this spinning our heads are so dizzy that we keep on spinning without pause.
We spin ourselves into all sorts of foreign interests, we rack our heads for everybody's benefit — and ourselves we forget.
We spin so long until we fall, and every time we fall on another side:
Here — we fall on the socialist side.
There — we fall on the communist side.
Somewhere else — we fall on the capitalist side.
And everywhere it is all only for others, for strangers — and when it comes to ourselves we are left with no side at all!..
Our heads spin only for others — and for ourselves we no longer have a head left!...
And looking at the dreidel every Hanukkah I think:
— When will we finally stop being a dreidel-game for the world?!
3.
"Hannah and Her Seven Sons".
There is a Jewish woman Hannah who has seven sons.
Handsome are the seven sons, no evil eye, like seven suns.
Tall, grown-up, with strong muscles, with plump, rosy cheeks — a delight to behold.
Real Jewish heroes.
Their names are: Józek, Bolek, Stefek, Janek, Adolek, Antek, Salek [?].
All ending in "-ek" — a blessing of a beloved name.
And mother Hannah devotes herself body and soul to her children: she dresses them up early in the morning, gives them the best sweets and sends them off to school.
When they come home she gives them the best dinners and sends them off to learn to play.
One plays the fiddle, the second — the clarinet, the third — the saxophone, the fourth — jazz band, the fifth — the flute, the sixth — the trumpet and the seventh — the drum.
And after this playing they go off to play again: handball, football and just plain ball.
Up comes the old grandfather, plays with the grandchildren, kisses them, strokes them and asks lovingly and faithfully:
— Beniekl [little Ben], are you learning a Yiddish/Jewish word too?
He answers him: "Nie rozumiem" [Polish: I don't understand].
The grandfather sadly lowers his head, tears fall on his grey beard, and he begins telling the children a little story:
"Once upon a time in the Land of Israel there was also a mother Hannah; she too had seven sons; they were all called by Jewish names and good Jewish children they were.
The king called all seven of them to him and ordered them to become gentiles, to forget the God of Israel, to leave the Jewish people.
He made a fire, set up soldiers with swords and told the seven Jewish children that if they did not obey he would kill and burn them all...
Do you know, children, what the seven sons answered? They answered that they would rather die than become gentiles!...
And all seven indeed died for Jewishness"...
His daughter gets angry and shouts at him:
— Why are you frightening the children, father?
— I'm frightening them?! — says the old grandfather — I'm merely telling them how Jewish children must sacrifice themselves for Jewishness, and they don't even want to know a single Yiddish word!
— Oh, don't be such a fanatic! They have so much work already — should I torment them with Yiddish too? It's a pity on them, a real pity!...
The old grandfather sighs:
— Oy-oy-oy, my daughter. That Hannah of the Land of Israel was a "cruel one", and this Hannah of Poland is a "merciful one" — woe and alas for these times!...
Strike of the Talmud Torah Teachers — Ended.

[Local.] On Saturday night a large meeting took place in the Talmud Torah premises, to which representatives of all the "shtiblekh" and minyanim(?) were delegated (except the Agudah and the Ger shtibl). The meeting dealt with the strike of the melamdim, brought about by the improper conduct of the kehilla board regarding the subsidy for the Talmud Torah.
Following the promise of councillor(?) Mr. Rygiski(?) that the subsidy for the Talmud Torah would be paid out, it was resolved to end the strike.
Shop Hours before Hanukkah.

[Local.] This coming Sunday all shops may be open from 1 p.m. until 6 in the evening.
Every day until Hanukkah the shops may stay open until 9 o'clock in the evening.
Protest Meeting against Raising the Rent.

[Local.] In its own premises the Tenants' Association held a protest meeting on Sunday against the bill to raise rents. Messrs. Lewin(?) and Fryde(?) spoke on the question. A protest resolution was adopted and sent to all the Sejm clubs.
On Help for the Poorest Children.

[Local.] At the Starostwo (district office) the organizing meeting took place to found a committee that will concern itself with supporting children of unemployed families. Besides food, the children are also to receive warm clothing.
A board was elected, headed by the Starosta, Mr. Beksa(?).
Large Sums Approved for Building Purposes

[Local news – Będzin.] This week, under the chairmanship of the temporary commissioner, a meeting of the building committee at the Magistrat (town council) took place. The meeting considered the building programme, which is to be carried out over 5 years. According to the programme, a sum of nearly 13 million zł. is needed for building purposes over 5 years. For the coming year 1 million 939 thousand zł. has been allocated for building purposes. This sum includes, on the motion of Mr. Goldsztajn, 50 thousand zł. for the Jewish 'Orphans' Home' (Yesomim-hoyz) and 75 thousand zł. to build a building for teachers.
The Little Watch Saved Him

[Local news – incident.] On Wednesday a sharp quarrel broke out in the local slaughterhouse between Shimon Hersh Szajer and Szwarcberg. It went so far that Szajer struck at Szwarcberg with a knife. The knife hit Szwarcberg's (pocket) watch, which was broken, but thanks to it Sz. was saved from a serious wound.
Policeman Shoots at a Bandit

[Regional news – Strzemieszyce.] At daybreak the policeman on duty in Strzemieszyce noticed a person carrying a hefty load. When the policeman ordered the person to stop, he only began to run faster; the policeman then fired at the suspect, who was wounded.
As it turned out, the wounded man is a well-known bandit who had carried out a theft at Garecki's drugstore warehouse in Strzemieszyce.
On the bandit were found 1,345 zł. and cosmetic goods.
Echoes of an Accident at the Local Hospital. Dr. Jarzębowski Found Not Guilty

[Local news – courts.] Two years ago the following case occurred at the local municipal hospital: the 8-year-old Katalicki, who was in the hospital for treatment, while walking in the garden fell into a sewage pit 4 metres deep.
The boy suffered a serious head wound from the fall and one of his eyes was damaged.
The police drew up a report, and the matter later came before the local court, which sentenced Dr. Jarzębowski, as chief director of the hospital, to 10 days' arrest or a fine of 155 zł.
This week the case was heard by the Sosnowiec District Court, which annulled the verdict of the first instance, on the grounds that the director of the local hospital is not Dr. Jarzębowski but Dr. Kaszybowicz [?], and above all that the accident happened not because the safety measures were not in order, but because the boy himself is temperamental and, being left unsupervised for a while, went off to dangerous places. Sz.
—o—
Tragic Death of an Alcoholic.
On the road to Małobądz a certain Pucek, a worker at the Będzin Magistrat, was found dead. It turned out that Pucek had got drunk on vodka, then threw off his clothes and lay down to sleep in the field...
A Bandit Attack in Strzemieszyce. The Attackers Arrested.

[Local.] On Szosowa(?) Street in Strzemieszyce three bandits attacked several workers who were coming from the "Hiplage"(?) [apparently a workplace; reading doubtful]. Threatening them with knives, the bandits robbed the workers of everything they had on them; even their clothes were taken from them.
The police promptly carried out a round-up (obława) and arrested the attackers.
"Hitachdut" and the Zionist Congress.

[Local.] In connection with the forthcoming 17th Congress, the Zionist labour party "Hitachdut" in Zagłębie has actively joined the shekel campaign, for which all party members have been mobilised.
On Tuesday a consultation about the Congress took place in Będzin with the participation of all the surrounding "Hitachdut" branches. The chairman of the Będzin "Hitachdut", Dr. Rechtman, reported that at the conference of the party council the wish was expressed to go to the Congress independently, without uniting with the Right Poale Zion, because of their conduct during the last Sejm elections.
Today and tomorrow comrade Dr. Rechtman will give reports in Będzin, Dąbrowa and Sosnowiec on the last session of the "Hitachdut" party council.
An Income of 400 Złoty.

[Local.] This winter the "Malbish Arumim" (Clothing the Naked) society did not confine itself to the clothing campaign, but(?) gave out garments beyond the set quota. Because of this the society, to cover(?) the deficit, arranged a theatre performance, which was a success.
The net income was 400 zł.
From "Tarbut".
For several weeks now the "Tarbut" society has introduced systematic Tanakh (Bible) courses, conducted by comrade Bergsztajn. The courses, held on Friday evenings, are very well attended because they are free of any charge.
Suicide of a Schoolgirl.
The 16-year-old schoolgirl Pierczalk(?) was to have been removed from school; because of this she threw herself under a train, which crushed her.
Again 330 Workers Laid Off.
In the mechanical factories in Poręba another 330 workers have been laid off.
Sosnowiec. Meeting of the Chamber of Commerce.

[Local — Sosnowiec.] On Monday the communications committee of the Chamber of Commerce held a meeting at which the question of improving postal, telegraph and telephone communications was discussed.
After the report by Mr. Gadomski a discussion developed in which Messrs. Rojbiglicht(?), Dr. Patak(?) and Kukarski took part.
The committee resolved to approach the proper authorities so that parcels arriving in Sosnowiec be delivered to the addressees' homes, that the post-office building be built as quickly as possible, that a post-office branch be opened in Pogoń, and that the office hours for registered letters at the Będzin post office be extended.
The proposal to intervene with the Kielce voivode for the improvement of the Olkusz–Sosnowiec highway was also supported.
Intervention by the Artisans' Supreme Council.

[Local — Sosnowiec.] Some time ago many Jewish craftsmen paid for diplomas (craft certificates) at the Chamber of Crafts in Kielce. To this day the Chamber of Crafts has not sent any commission to qualify the craftsmen who run independent workshops.
Because the police fine craftsmen who do not possess diplomas, the Supreme Council of the artisans' associations in Zagłębie submitted a memorandum to the starosta requesting that craftsmen who have paid for diplomas not be fined for the time being.
The starosta promised to settle the matter favourably.
Sensational 'favour' (protection) trial. G., a starostwo official, sentenced to one year in prison.

On Monday and Tuesday the [—] district court heard the trial of Górnicki, a former official (referent) in the Olkusz starostwo, a referent of the P.K.U. [district recruitment command] in Miechów(?), and of the owner and an employee of the firm 'Vesten'(?) in Olkusz, who were accused of helping to free a certain employee, Misel(?), from military service.
The defendants were defended by the well-known advocates Magilicki(?) and Glenbocki(?) of Warsaw and the Sosnowiec advocates Krzemuski(?), König and Pawełek(?).
The court delivered its verdict: Górnicki was sentenced to one year in prison. The others were acquitted.
On extending the deadline for buying trade patents (licences).

As is known, the deadline for buying trade patents is the 31st of this month. On 2 January (styczeń) inspections (lustrations) are already to take place.
In this connection the merchants' associations have turned to the Finance Ministry with a request that, because of the severe crisis, the deadline for buying patents be extended to 15 January, and that no patent inspections take place until then.
Whether the request will be granted is not yet known.
Several schools closed because of the influenza epidemic.

With the participation of the local school authorities, representatives of the Kraków [school] curatorium and doctors, a conference was held because 25 percent of the pupils, boys and girls, are sick with influenza.
It was decided to close the boys' gymnasium named after Staszic ('a. n. Staszic'), the technical railway school, the teachers' seminary and several public (elementary) schools.
Intervention by Sejm deputies concerning the unemployed in Zagłębie.

The [several?] deputies from Zagłębie, headed by the Zawiercie commissioner, presented themselves to the Minister of Labour, to whom they described the grave situation of the unemployed in Zagłębie.
The minister promised to fulfil all the demands (postulates) put forward by the delegation.
Instead of strolling in the mountains, he took up smuggling goods.

The local police arrested Mr Fürst of Cieszyn at the 'Hotel Warszawski'. F. had received from the Tourist Society a permit to walk in the mountains lying on the Czech-Polish border. Mr F., however, used the permit to bring in foreign goods illegally. Together with large quantities of goods, Mr F. was handed over to the customs office.

Took away 'the horse and(?) the whip'.
Piter Radek came here with a cart of coal. Having sold part of the coal, Radek went into a shop on Modrzejowska(?) street to buy goods. Coming out, he found nothing at all — neither the wagon nor the horses. After searching a whole day he finally found his 'outfit' in a side alley, but the cart was empty and instead of his horses he found an old nag (szkapa).
The police began a search and discovered the thief, a resident of Zagórze, who was arrested.

A 'test' of the firemen.
The local town commissioner, Mr Kuszniak(?), organised a fire alarm in order to check the speed of the local firemen. The firemen arrived within 4 minutes.

Terrible accident at the tunnel construction.
During work at the tunnel a board(?) collapsed and 3 workers fell into a pit and were seriously injured.

Short-term loans from the 'Joint'.
The 'Gemilut Hasadim' (free-loan) funds in Sosnowiec and Będzin received loans of up to 4000 zł from the 'Joint'. The funds must repay the sums within 4 months.

Number of doctors increased.
Because of the prevailing illnesses, the sickness fund (Kasa Chorych) has engaged at its disposal almost all the doctors in Zagłębie. In addition, a number of doctors from the nearest towns outside Zagłębie have been engaged.

An old lecher punished.
The 64-year-old Feliks Kuc stood before the district court; he had seduced young girls and [?] them. The lecher was sentenced to one year in prison and loss of all rights.
The trial was held behind closed doors.
Announcement.

Attention 'Hitachdut' branches in Będzin, Dąbrowa and Sosnowiec!
Today, Friday, at 8 in the evening an urgent members' meeting will take place in [our] own premises, at which Comrade Dr Rechtman will report on the last session of the Party Council.
The same report will be given tomorrow, Saturday, at 2 p.m. in Dąbrowa, and in Sosnowiec at 4 p.m.

The cultural activity of the Zionist Organisation in Strzemieszyce

(R.) Recently the Strzemieszyce Zionist Organisation has been conducting broad cultural activity: every Friday evening there are interesting question-box evenings, every week there are lectures by invited speakers, and a reading room has also been set up, where daily and periodical newspapers are available.
Last Sunday the festive opening of its own library took place, attended by the representative of the Central Committee, Mr. Pinchas Fegelman[?], who gave a rich and instructive lecture and wished, in the name of the C.C., fruitful activity.
The impressive celebration was closed with the singing of „Hatikvah".
From the Keren Kayemet.

On a mission from the Central Office of the KKL [Jewish National Fund], Mr. Pinchas Fegelman[?] stayed in Strzemieszyce; in his presence the committee was reorganised, and with new forces it will be intensively active.
The Union of Zionist Revisionists in Będzin.

Last Sabbath Mr. Bialobrat[?] of Warsaw lectured on the situation in the Zionist movement.
Last Wednesday Mr. Bialobrat lectured on the state of the Zionist camp, which he brands as harmful both from the right and from the left.
Both lectures were a great success and were delivered before a large number of people.
This Friday evening at 8 o'clock there will be discussions on the topics mentioned.
A flat emptied in Strzemieszyce.

(R.) Last Thursday at 5 o'clock thieves got into the flat of Mr. Yechiel Szpigelman in Strzemieszyce by removing a pane from the window, and robbed everything from there. The police carried out several searches and arrests, and the entire loot was found in Jaworzno. It is interesting that the technical „surgeon" of the theft is a local Jew, a convert[?] K., who has been arrested together with his whole family. The court will now judge what he has earned for the operation he carried out.

A Ministry Circular on the Road Tax

[Będzin — municipality and taxes.] A few weeks ago we reported on the question of the road tax, which is being demanded unlawfully by our magistrate [town council].
Now the matter has already been settled finally and favourably by the ministry.
It is worth giving our readers in brief the vicissitudes the road-tax matter has gone through.
In point 9 of the circular of 19 February 1927 (number FS 824/27) the Ministry of the Interior explained that road levies may be introduced only for the benefit of communal district associations, and only in exceptional cases also for the benefit of the towns that are separated from the communal district associations.
The Supreme Administrative Tribunal, however, in its judgment of 19 November 1929 (No. 4642/28), took the position that under Art. 19 of the Roads Act of 10 December 1920 („Dz. Ustaw” R. P. of the year 1921, number 6, item 32) only voivodeship and communal district associations may, by resolutions, impose special levies; gminas [communes], on the other hand [?], both urban and rural, may not impose such special levies — which means, of course, also the separated towns. And they must cover the costs of building and maintaining the gmina roads from the general sources of revenue.
Because of all this, and also because of the provisions of Art. 5 of the Act of 3 August 1922 on the Supreme Administrative Tribunal, in the wording of the annex to the Prime Minister's circular of 26 June 1926 („Dz. Ust.” R. P. 89, item 400), the Ministry of the Interior, by a circular of 10 November of this year, number 202/SF 224/3, amended point 9 of the above-mentioned circular, giving it the following wording:
„Road levies may be fixed only for the benefit of powiat [county] communal associations.
„Urban and rural gminas have no right to collect special road levies, which are spoken of in the said circular, because the collection of such levies rests on Art. 19 of the Act on the construction and maintenance of public roads in the Polish Republic of 10 December 1920 (Dz. Ust. R. P. number 6/1921, item 32), which expressly grants the appropriate powers only to the powiat and voivodeship communal associations.
In accordance with the ministry's circular, the road tax will no longer be included in the new municipal budget.
As for the sums already paid in, it may be possible that the magistrate will refund them.
Bandits Strip Peasants Stark Naked and Rob Them

[Poland — crime.] In Częstochowa the following bestial assault was carried out: on Saturday evening the 2 young peasants Ignacy Michalski [?] and Stanisław Kalusza [?] set out in a cart. When they were on the highway near the forest, several armed bandits in masks sprang out of the forest thicket. They stopped the cart, threatening to shoot the passengers. The peasants stopped. Then the bandits demanded „money” of them. Kalusza and Michalski declared that they did not have a single grosz on them. The bandits did not believe them and took the trouble to strip the peasants stark naked, and beat them on their naked bodies with thick [?] sticks. „We will beat you until you tell us where you have the money” — the bandits shouted; the peasants then told where the money was hidden: it was lying under the hay. The bandits took „the money together with the clothes and vanished. Naked, the peasants went back into the village.
Improved Rail Connection of Zagłębie with the Beskids, Kielce, Radom and Lublin

[Zagłębie — railways and transport.] At the conference of the railway directorate with representatives of the Chamber of Commerce, which took place a few weeks ago in Sosnowiec, a series of postulates was put forward concerning the improvement of the rail connection to Kielce, Radom, Lublin, and that there should be a direct connection with the Beskids.
The postulates were considered by the Minister of Railways, who decided that from 15 January (styczeń) to 15 February (luty) 1931 a direct connection from Warsaw to Katowice is to be introduced by means of special carriages of 1st, 2nd and 3rd class.
The carriages will be attached to the Kraków Courier, which leaves Warsaw at 10.53 in the evening and arrives at Ząbkowice at 4 before dawn.
From Ząbkowice the carriages will be attached to the local train, which leaves Ząbkowice at 4.20 in the morning and arrives at Katowice at 5.30.
From Katowice a special train will depart at 5.50, which will run via Oshnesh [?], Skoczów [?] (not via Dziedzice [?] as until now).
Independently of the new Warsaw—Beskids connection, the proposal of the Chamber of Commerce was accepted: from 1 [?] May 1931 several trains to Kielce and Radom will run at a greater speed, which will shorten the travel time from Katowice to Kielce by 113 minutes.

The Wife Comes Back from America...

A fine fellow he was, at any rate, so the Zagłębie girls said of Isaac. Always elegantly dressed, neatly shaved, perfumed, a few złoty in his pocket, and one could[?] go out[?] with him to a cinema, a theatre, a confectioner's, etc.
Isaac „lived off“ his father, who ran a large business. But when the business began to go downhill and Isaac had nothing to cover his needs, he decided: he would get married.
Barely a year ago an „American woman“ came to Sosnowiec on a visit; she had emigrated from here to America a number of years before. No great beauty is she, but the neighbours knew „exactly“ that she owned thousands of dollars, ran „important“ [ważne] businesses in America, and that her husband would not lack even bird's milk with her. Just a wedding canopy, a visa and off we go — into the golden land.
And Isaac at once signed the engagement contract (tenoim) with her. Isaac received a big thick ring. Soon the wedding was celebrated, and the young wife left for America to prepare the business for her „boy“ from „Europe“.
Isaac began preparing for the journey. As the husband of an American citizen he could easily obtain a visa. He already had a ship's ticket ready, 300 dollars of pocket money too, and all happiness then awaited him only in America...
Suddenly the American consul in Warsaw decided to stop issuing visas to young men who had married American girls in Poland, and Isaac was told for the time being to sit at home.
But the American so-and-so had no patience to wait so long for her „boy“, and these days Isaac received a little letter from her saying that, since business in America is going very badly and she has lost all the money she had on the stock exchange, she is therefore coming over to her husband, and she asks him, her husband, to prepare some nice flat...
A Letter to the Editor

To the editors of the „Zaglembier Tsaytung“.
Dear Mr. Editor.
In connection with the „letter to the editor“ by the kehilla board members (dozors) A. Liwer, L. Diamant and H.[?] Goldsztajn, which was printed in the last issue of your paper, we ask you to publish the following statement:
1) The putting through of the secretary (for the rabbinate) was not done „in a hurry“, as the authors of the „letter“ assert, but took two negotiating sessions. The first session, with the participation of the Rabbi (may he live long and well), both Liwers, Boruszykowski[?], Plessner, Prawer and Ryński[?], decided — against the vote of Mr. A. Liwer — to engage the rabbinate secretary. At the second session Messrs. Goldsztajn and A. Liwer did not protest at all against the „hurried putting through“, but together with us set for the secretary „a salary“ [pensye].
2) The resolution to announce a competition for the post of a second shochet (ritual slaughterer) was adopted by the kehilla administration on 14 August of this year with the votes of the dozors Prawer, Plessner and Goldsztajn against the vote of Mr. Boruszykowski. At the last session the matter of the shochet was dealt with once again. Although the majority was in favour of the shochet being engaged at once, it was nevertheless decided — on the motion of A. Liwer — first to deal with the matter at a narrower consultation of the dozors Prawer, Ryński, Goldsztajn, Liwer and Buchweitz[?], in order to find a way out that would satisfy both sides. To the narrower consultation came the dozors Prawer, Ryński, Goldsztajn and Liwer, and they unanimously decided to admit the shochet to the slaughterhouse without any obligations. On this basis the vice-president Mr. Prawer issued an order to admit the shochet to the slaughterhouse.
This is the truth, and now the public may judge.
M. J. Prawer,
Sz. J. Ryński.

We Must Give It Some Thought. (The World Crisis and Our Serious Situation. Can We Tolerate This?)

[Poland and Zagłębie — economy; opinion piece.]
It seems that the crisis, which rages in so severe a form across the whole country, was still not enough to fill the cup with bitter drops — on top of it came illnesses, which torment great and small, old and young. These illnesses spare not a single house; everywhere we meet either the after-effects of the illness or people preparing to become candidates for this "pleasant profession"; in any case, one is at that stage.
Lately the illnesses have decreased thanks to the fact that the climate has changed and wintry weather has set in, but for that, God forbid, nobody is "to blame": it was not our self-government bodies that helped, it was not they who took any interest in seeing the illnesses eased, nor did anyone think about how to come to the aid of the population here. The municipal authority took no interest whatsoever in all this, as if nothing had happened, as if everything were in the best of order and the citizens were living in the most comfortable conditions.
But let us say that it is all behind us, that the exhausted citizens are already healthy and strong and can once more take up everyday life, each occupied with his trade, each with his profession — even then this is no easy matter, for nowadays the crisis plays first fiddle, so that there is nothing to do and nothing to be occupied with. Among decent people, in such a case, one considers what to do, how to remedy the dreadful critical situation; here, however, one sadly does not dwell on such questions, which one would like to forget as quickly as possible, reckoning that in this way salvation will come. That is exactly as if one wanted not to see the bright light by closing one's eyes; in reality, though, indifference of this kind causes a great deal of harm.
The situation would look quite different, however, if the serious problem were approached with more awareness and composure, with more responsibility and intensity; then the good will to meet the citizens halfway in their need, in their critical moment, would show itself. In that way people could help one another, one would hold out a hand to the other, and rays of hope would appear.
But what comes of it? There is no talk at all of help or of meeting people halfway, and so it turns out that it is getting ever worse and harder to pull the yoke of life, the yoke of existence. Especially now, when the business classes have to buy their patents [trade and craft licences], and the season has been anything but favourable [?], so that the bills of exchange issued, which are now falling due, cannot be paid. Taking all this into account and considering the prevailing situation, the prospects are not at all encouraging.
Thus, for example, we see that in recent years fewer and fewer patents are being bought, and that is certainly no good sign and no gratifying phenomenon for a country. True, the crisis prevails not only here in Poland but also throughout Europe and even across the ocean; but one must not forget one thing: elsewhere the unemployed and the fallen are provided for in such a way that they do not become a burden on the state, whereas here nobody wants to know about anything, and the support and help that is given is a drop in the ocean compared with the need and hunger, which seek out ever more respectable houses and spread themselves freely both in the poor cellars and in the rich palaces.
One ought, surely, to react properly to such tragic phenomena, which bring ruin upon a country, and to think up counsels and stratagems for remedying them and coming to the aid of those who need help. Instead, thanks to the extraordinary indifference and apathy, it is becoming ever more entrenched [?], to the point of losing one's balance, so that it is a crime to stand by at a distance as if it were a question for individuals, as if it did not touch the whole community.
And if the crisis prevails throughout the country for all citizens of the Republic, it is self-evident that for us Jews it is considerably stronger, and here we are, as usual, the ones who suffer more, who risk more, who are more abandoned.
It would therefore be only right that we Jews should think more seriously about this painful matter, which brings us more damage and ruins us more than all other citizens of the country — if only because the slightest wind is able to overturn us and the smallest change ruins our livelihoods and leaves us in a helpless, serious situation in which we can go neither here nor there.
In the present situation in which we now find ourselves, one must think seriously about the near future, and then we will come to the conviction that if we leave everything as it is, as if it were not us who are meant, as if our living conditions were none of our concern, the consequences may be very serious, very sad. That is what we must fear; that is why we must dwell on all this more seriously.
We must not forget for a single minute the saying "If I am not for myself, who will be for me": if we do not help ourselves, nobody will help us. Only we must not deceive ourselves and go about with the thoughts: what do I know, it will be all right, it must be all right, He in heaven will surely send salvation. One must not be frightened or afraid to look reality in the face — then it will not be as terrible and invincible as it would be if we chose to close our eyes to the sad truth.
We have professional associations — of artisans, merchants and small traders — which must always carry with them the thoughts: only do not deceive yourselves, only tell the members the truth, the pure, true truth, without regard to anything at all, for only in this way will they learn to trade and calculate and compete on sound foundations and become accustomed not to fear the slightest breeze.
The same holds now, when we, together with the whole country, find ourselves in a critical time that spares almost no one: the institutions also have the task of not letting the members be deceived and comforting them that things are not as bad as people think, and, of course, also of not letting them remain in a desperate state, which brings just as little use as self-deception. Both are equally dangerous, both are equally unhealthy and inconsistent, and can bring no benefit.
The truth must be told at all times, however terrible it may be, and then one can adopt forms and means of guarding against the danger, for one can always [?] guard against a catastrophe when one has foreseen [?] in advance that we must guard against it. Our watchword must be always and at all times: only do not deceive ourselves, only do not be frightened, only do not remain helpless and despairing — for these can bring no benefit whatsoever in our hard life and teach us nothing. It will be better, bolder [?] and more useful for us when we learn to be steadfast and to run our businesses on sound foundations that are correctly calculated. When we have learned that, we will know how to keep control of ourselves when a critical time comes; it will be a lesson for the future, and in this way we will learn not to fall on a slippery road in a time of crisis.
Ah, a great deal. Our professional associations have a great deal of work for their members, for whom they do [—] nothing [?], notwithstanding that almost all of them have to be drilled from the elementary ABC; but still it cannot stay this way, because at this stage the situation, under the prevailing conditions, is becoming ever more serious and dangerous.
— That is why [?] the highest time has come to give it some thought!
R. Les.
The Year 1930 Gets Ready for the Road

[Satire — year's end; Dąbrowa.] The old man named 1930 is hastily packing his belongings into a big suitcase and getting ready for the express train, which leaves next Wednesday at 12 midnight. The old man is being helped by a young, cheerful lad named "1931".
— Well, grandpa dear, everything packed already? Forgotten nothing?
— It seems, everything.
— And the high cost of living — did you take it with you?
— What should I do that for?.. I left it for you, dear 1931.. After all, while the high prices hold, one might have thought that it is really true what the Sanacja papers write about the luck and blessing that has reigned in the country since May 1926..
— Dear grandpa, drop in at Dąbrowa and take along from the Dąbrowa city council the Jewish councillors; take along the kehilla president too — upon my life, the town would become a little quieter and calmer..
— I'm afraid to pack them into the suitcase; they hold on so tightly [?] that they keep their hands hooked together [?].
— Then take in their place the handful of "dakiares" [?], who are after all toy mannikins; most of them have not said a single word in 4 years. They won't even look around to see what is going on in the suitcase, for such is their nature [?] — they don't see what is going on under their nose..
— I did indeed think of taking them along; I waited for months for a meeting of the kehilla council and could not wait it out. So I'll leave them to you, and I believe that with younger strength you, 1931, will manage them.
— Grandpa dear, at least stay for my birthday party! We'll drink a l'chaim!..
The old man agreed, and when on Wednesday at 12 midnight you hear glasses clinking, know that it is grandpa "1930" taking leave of his newborn little boy "1931".
Yankele.
Napoleon's Last Years of His Life

[History — Napoleon; part 2.] M. Oszerowicz [?].
2.
The wheel had turned.
He no longer suffered from jealousy, but she...
And then Joséphine began spending treasures of money on clothes and jewellery; on her wardrobe she squandered more than the hated French queen Marie Antoinette; she kept dressing up incessantly in order to preserve her youth, her beauty, but nothing helped her — Napoleon kept carrying on love affairs with other women, and this grieved her so much that she, the clever Joséphine, often lost her good sense, and when she did once have the luck that he spent a night with her, she would afterwards boast of it noisily [?] before the servants..
More than one of Napoleon's mistresses tried to secure her influence over him so that he would take her opinion into account in political and also in military affairs, but they did not succeed. With no woman — however dear she might be to him — did Napoleon talk about his plans, and he was certain that more than one ruler had lost his head because a beloved woman had had too great an influence over him.
———
In the year 1810 Napoleon divorced Joséphine, and the only reason for it was that she had no children.
Never could Napoleon so easily forgive wrongs done to him as [he did] the woman from whom he was divorced. He truly forgave Joséphine all the wrongs she had committed against him. He treated her very well, not only when she was his wife but also when she was no longer his wife. He was a frequent guest at her palace, provided every comfort for her, and wrote her the warmest and friendliest letters.
The question of securing his dynasty was very important to Napoleon. He knew that all the other crowned rulers of the world, the "born monarchs", as he called them, looked askance at him; that they still could not make peace with the thought that a simple man, a child of the people, had attained a crown thanks to his own abilities; that it was clear to them that the example Napoleon had set by his rise was a great danger to the belief that a king is anointed by God Himself; that they still regarded him as a child of the Revolution, which was a thorn in their eyes — so he decided to "buy himself into pedigree" and marry a real princess, the daughter of a "born monarch", so that the son she would bear him would in every respect be fit for a throne.
He himself hated the "born monarchs" with utter hatred, and whenever he had an opportunity to show his bloody hatred of them, he did so. He could — sitting in Dresden at table with several crowned rulers — suddenly, in the middle of it [?], begin telling a story that would start like this: When I was a simple lieutenant; and when he noticed how all the "born monarchs" had bowed their heads in great embarrassment so as not to meet his gaze, he began the same story [?] differently and said thus: "When I had the honour of being a simple lieutenant"...
With whatever he could, he hurt them. But he held to the rule that even when one has an enemy of one's own, one must know how to use him for oneself; so he acted also when he was First Consul of the country, even before he was crowned as Emperor. He then greatly disliked the Jacobins, the extreme left party of the French Revolution; he said of them that "with their phrases they can kill off not just one state but twenty whole states", and nevertheless he negotiated with them and used them as far as he possibly could.
He did the same with the "born monarchs", whom he did not like. He used them as far as he possibly could; through them he wanted to secure the future of his dynasty...
And so, accordingly, after he had divorced Joséphine, he began negotiating with the Russian Tsar Alexander I that he should give him his sister Ekaterina as a wife.
In everything, both on the battlefield and in his private life, Napoleon never contented himself with a single plan; he always prepared two plans, so that should he fail with the first he would have a second one ready.
And so he did also when he began "looking for a new wife". At the same time as he sent envoys to negotiate with the Russian Tsar about his sister Ekaterina, he also sent envoys to negotiate with the Austrian king [sic] Franz I about his daughter Marie Louise.
Nothing came of the negotiations with the Russian court, because the old Russian Tsarina, the wife of Paul I, who went down in history as the "mad Tsar", was against the match. She did not want her daughter to marry the French emperor, in whose veins no imperial blood flows, although she actually thought very highly of Napoleon and said that she would wish her sons to be as able as he and as brilliant as he...

Downhill.

There are also people in the Jewish street who, perhaps more for subjective than objective, psychological than logical reasons, are ready to say amen to everything that is happening now, and are also ready to search out all kinds of arguments to justify this or that action, so that you should have no doubts at all and accept that everything is going as it should[?] — a truly ideal time, the Messiah has all but come, and we may simply rejoice that things happen this way and not otherwise.
And when these people sometimes get into a tight spot and sense that the public in the street shrugs its shoulders and does not understand what sort of greatness[?] this is for Jewish heads, they grab at this excuse:
— It could have been even worse.
The "this too is for the best" (gam zu le-tova) feeling is a very fine and ideal one, but only in philosophy; in life, however, if one breaks one leg, one does not actually rejoice that the other leg has remained whole — rather the heart aches strongly and deeply over the misfortune.
Talking us into believing that we must rejoice in the present reality in Poland because it could have been even worse is quite incapable of convincing anyone, if only his own interests and demands are wronged by the present reality. And such people number 999 out of a thousand.
In fact everything is now going downhill.
What significance can protests against high taxes have today — who takes account of protesting today? And if one is strong, why indeed not put an end, once and for all, to the possibility that in the sick fund (Kasa Chorych) the insured person should have a say, and that there should loom the danger that instead of commissioner X with his staff a "civilian" member of society might come to power and make the main point of the sick fund's work that first of all the interests of the sick be safeguarded and best cared for — because he is elected directly by the insured.
And if one doesn't give a hoot about the world, why indeed not solve the housing question in such a way that the tenant should, with[?] a 100-percent surcharge, help build new houses, and in some 22 years we will find out how many houses have been built...
The newspapers tell us that in Warsaw self-government is being liquidated. Instead of an elected city council and an elected magistrat (city executive), some kind of communal association will be created with a council of 48 persons, who will have the same significance as the advisory council (bei-rat) that the first government commissioner in Sosnowiec put together for himself. Put short and clear, it means we are on the eve of the complete liquidation of self-government. The magistrats are being bureaucratized and brought under the rule of the administrative authority. Instead of a councilman we will have a policeman, and instead of a city president — a starosta (appointed district head).
Could there be a brighter perspective...
The rest of it is already clear today even to someone who has only a faint notion of what is meant by such a democratic form of state life.
The practice of commissarial rule has taught the Jewish street particularly well to understand the difference between a democratic city council and a nominated administrator. Public life, the role and significance of the ordinary citizen, is degraded to zero[?]. This is the downhill slide of public, social life in Poland. A handful of officials will do everything for us, and we will have a delightful life — do what we are told and pay as much as is fixed.
Afterwards[?] they will be spared knocking at the door of the simple Jew and canvassing him to vote for this or that list; there will no longer be any need of the simple man. In return, however, the simple Jew and Jewess will have to knock at other doors, and once again types of "machers" (fixers) will hatch[?] — strongmen who persuade people that the "nachalstvo" (Russian: the authorities) is theirs; in a word — those types whom we had already brought to a Jewish burial will rise from the dead.
Such a perspective smiles upon us.
We know that history cannot be turned backwards. One can try, and indeed people are trying, to turn back the wheel of history. But the strongest individuals grow tired, and life goes forward.
What is happening now is merely an episode.
An episode with which Jewish society certainly has no reason to be satisfied.
Y. N—m.
The Will of the People.

Thirteen years have passed since the moment when we celebrated a great victory because the British Empire, with the well-known Balfour Declaration, recognized the justice of the Jewish postulates and made it possible to begin practical work in Eretz Israel.
Herzl's dream of international recognition of our rights to our Old-New Land (Altneuland) was realized.
But after thirteen years England has issued the "White Paper" [the Passfield White Paper, October 1930], an antithesis of the Balfour Declaration, which rests on the false Simpson report [the Hope Simpson report]. The glorified England has shown itself to us in its true form, with its imperialist face, ready — for its own interests — to break its given word, to withdraw from the given and San Remo obligation.
We must give a worthy answer; our work must be strengthened and conducted in two directions. Just as the Balfour Declaration signified the victory of political Zionism, so now — in case the "White Paper" is not withdrawn — we must return to political work, to the struggle in the international arena.
At this moment the Jewish people must document its unbreakable will even more strongly. We have already lived through more than paper declarations, greater enemies than Messrs. Simpson and Passfield; peoples [printed "melker", misprint for "felker"] have perished, kingdoms have long lain in ruins, and we live and will live forever. Would the Roman Emperor Titus have believed, when he looked from Mount Scopus with his triumphant gaze and a smile on his face at Jerusalem burning — would he then have believed that this weak people would outlive the Roman "gens humanum"?
With "Shema" on their lips the Jews died in the flames of the heaps of burning Jewish sacred objects. Today too we may not disgrace the tradition of our forefathers, who died for a bright future.
Here stands the will of an entire people; a national popular idea cannot be broken by this or that declaration, this or that government. We will not give up Eretz Israel. To all the rights we have to Eretz Israel one more has been added: the fresh[?] number of those who sacrificed themselves and defended the positions won by labour.
We are now conducting a shekel campaign — the outward symbol of our inner aspirations; it is the Zionist legitimation. Every Jew who buys the shekel joins the ranks of those who have resolved, despite all difficulties, to fight for a bright future for the most unfortunate people. We must show the whole non-Jewish world that our cry[?] is the cry of millions, that our call is the call of all who believe in justice.
England!
Our long martyrology has strengthened us. We are used to everything and prepared for anything.
Over the heads of your statesmen, against the will of your imperialist interests, the ideal dreamed of for generations in the tormented Jewish soul, dreamed in the dark alleys of the ghetto — will be realized!
Eliyahu Gertner.

What I Heard, What I Saw.

[Będzin and district — weekly feuilleton.] Related by Ben Amotz.

A "Grippe Hanukkah".
This year's Hanukkah passed quietly, without leaving the slightest impression on the Jewish street. Once, even in recent years, the season of Hanukkah events was a rich one; every organisation considered it a duty to arrange something in honour of Hanukkah; even our "powszechniczki" [girls of the state primary schools] worked for weeks on end so that the "wieczór chanukowy" [Hanukkah evening] would come out "doskonale" [perfect]...
This year the Maccabees[?] were received coldly. The balls that were held were "as if forced by a demon", as the saying goes: pinch your cheeks so they stay red"... The Sosnowiec Betar members "invited" the Hasmoneans to a dance, and the Będzin "Hakoah" only intends to celebrate Hanukkah — on New Year's Eve (Sylvester)...
The upshot is that this year's Hanukkah was no "welcome" guest, much like the grippe: heat and chills, high temperature and cold compresses.
— A "Grippe Hanukkah"...

According to the American Version.
The beit midrash — packed full; the large crowd stands agape, swallowing the words of the preacher. This was when the doors of the Będzin Talmud Torah were shut. The melamdim [teachers] had gone on strike and hundreds of poor children had become "free". So the preacher in his sermon rebuked the Będzin kehilla: why is the neglect of Torah study of hundreds of children allowed, how can it be?...
In a corner of the beit midrash sits a Będzin householder, who says: "Yes, it's all very fine [lit. 'it's a wedding'], but what business has a stranger lecturing us on morals? Don't we have in Będzin a staff of Torah monopolists who should rouse and admonish the public to support the Talmud Torah? Ha, where are they?"
— Excuse me, Reb Yid, it won't be long before the American system is introduced here; there will grow up among us the "Reverend" types, who will be at the disposal of the kehilla. The "Reverends" will have various "qualifications": eulogy-makers, supervisors of "kosher", eruv-masters and "speechers" for when some institution needs support...
— We are Americanising...

A Just Complaint.
On the Tram.
My neighbour is a well-known Jewish teacher at the state primary schools (szkoły powszechne) in Będzin. The conductor asks him: "Dokąd?" [Where to?]
— "Będzin!"
I see my neighbour's face suddenly turn red, an expression of anger.
— What's the matter with you?
— Nothing — he answers — it vexes me with you people: why do you keep silent about such a scandal? A company whose main income in Zagłębie comes from Jews should so ignore them and not hire even one single Jew as a conductor! I ride the tram very rarely, but every time I boil over with anger because of it...
— Don't get upset, sir [Panie]... You surely know that they don't even admit us to the post of night watchmen. It is truly a great injustice on the part of the tram company, which to this day has not understood that the tens of thousands of Jewish passengers in Zagłębie have the right to demand that among the great number of non-Jews there should also be a few Jewish conductors — but the tram company has a "heter" [dispensation] for itself: at a time when among a hundred Magistrat [municipal] officials there is one Jew, and when in a town such as Będzin there is not even one Jewish postman — so how could Jews become conductors?...

"The Goy Is Right"...
In the columns of our paper it was mentioned, in a mild form, that at the moment when "a new king arose" several Jewish officials were dismissed from the Będzin Magistrat.
A few hours passed after the paper appeared, and already in all the departments it was known that the "impudent" "Zaglembier Tsaytung" had dared to offend the dignity of the sovereignty of the Będzin Magistrat.
— Panie! — I ask one of the Magistrat officials — who has already brought you the news that we are waging a hate campaign against the Magistrat? Which Moszek has already passed you the little denunciation?
— Panie redaktorze! You yourself don't know your pious little Jews (nabożne żydki); we know them — one wants to sell the other, to swallow him alive...
— — — — — — —

A "Miracle" Not on Hanukkah..
By nature — an acquaintance of mine tells me — I am a Jew who is a "looker": when I stroll down the street I stop at every theatre poster, at announcements of the Magistrat, the Skarb [tax office] and the like; I stand and read every line; above all I "swallow" the Yiddish texts — a delight, I tell you, to read the new "orthography" of the Jewish printing shops; heaven forbid, if the publishers of the Moscow "Emes" have such "geniuses"...
— Why am I telling you this? — Well, have a little patience and hear me out to the end. The other day, it was about two weeks ago, during my daily stroll I catch sight of a poster in letters as big as for Kiddush Levanah: "The Wedding Dress"...
The name alone — I tell you — "bewitched" me. No small thing, "a story with a wedding dress"; surely, I think to myself, this play will show a great tragedy of a wedding dress belonging to an unhappy princess...
With great curiosity I read on and... what do I see? They will show what "a wedding among Jews" looks like? And where am I? Somewhere in Africa, or in Będzin, on the New Market? Have I — and all of you — seen few Jewish weddings? And what does it come to teach us?...
Who knows where my thoughts would have sunk, were it not for the "panic". Thanks to the "panic" on the market I came back to my first ideas, and only then convinced myself that I am indeed in Będzin, in the town where there is a rich gallery of types, among them also such Jewish "artists" who advertise themselves by promising to show the Jewish visitors what "a wedding among Jews" looks like...

On the Strict Inspection of the Craftsmen's Workshops.

[Zagłębie — craftsmen; article.]
On the 15th of this month the Polish guild law officially came into force, under which — as we already reported at the time — every craftsman who does not hold a craftsman's card will have no right to work independently or to run a workshop on his own account. Besides this, and this is especially important at the present moment, every craftsman who wishes to hold the title "master" and to have the right to employ "terminants" (apprentices) is obliged (under Arts. 149 and 150 of the law) to hold a master's diploma.
The matter of employing terminants (apprentices) occupies on the whole a prominent place in the guild law. [?] The whole attention of its authors was directed at what are the foundations of the future body of craftsmen — skilled, properly prepared [?] and for that very reason truly creative — which should in no respect lag behind our Western European neighbours.
Yet [?] incomprehensible is the indifferent attitude of the greater part of the Jewish craftsmen (who after all hold no diploma) to the severity of the guild regulations.
Last week all magistrates, gminas (rural communes) and police precincts received exact instructions concerning craftsmen's workshops in connection with "15 December 1930". By 28 February (luty) 1931 the police authorities must carry out a strict inspection of all workshops in the Będzin powiat (district), and if workshops are closed, or even only heavy fines are written (up to 100 zł. and 14 days' arrest) for keeping apprentices — it will in more than 90 cases out of a hundred certainly hit the Jewish craftsman.
With an apprentice (terminant) the employer is obliged to write a contract (umowa). If the employer holds no master's diploma, the "umowa" makes no difference anyway [sic], since this is stated [?] explicitly in the wording of the law (Art. 149 of the Industrial Law and § 36 of the decree of the President of the State of 7 December [?] 1927, Dz. Ust. No. 111, item 942). From this it also follows of itself that for all craftsmen who made "umowas" with their apprentices, the "umowas" lost their force as of 15 December 1930, and the apprentices themselves lost their term — since [?] the craftsman (employer) holds no diploma or does not try to obtain one.
All those who received master's diplomas from the respective guilds by 15 Dec. 1927 have the right to the title "master". All the others, i.e. those who hold no diplomas (on 15 Dec. 1927 all guilds were dissolved), must sit a master's examination before a special commission of the Chamber of Crafts. In this connection a special reduced examination applies to those who ran a workshop (the craft) independently before the decree on the new [printed "גייעם", a misprint] compulsory guild law came out, i.e. before 15 Dec. 1927.
According to the regulations of the Kielce Chamber of Crafts, the examination fee (the tax) for such a kind of craftsman amounts to 140 zł.; if he holds a journeyman's diploma — 100 zł. But because of the difficult material situation, the Jewish craftsmen throughout the country turned with duly reasoned memoranda to the Minister of Commerce Kwiatkowski, asking to reduce the examination fee to 50 zł. On 7 October (październik) of this year Min. Kwiatkowski turned with a letter to the Kielce Chamber of Crafts, in which, for the same reasons, he proposes to lower the fee to 50 zł. On the 26th of the same month the letter was considered at the plenary session of the "Izba" (Chamber) (by the way — where were the [?] Jewish councillors?), and by a majority of votes (16 members were present, Christians and Jews...) it was resolved that in principle the fee indeed remains 140 zł., but the president of the "Izba", Mr. Smuga (a man from Częstochowa), is given the competence to set smaller payments, minimum 50 zł. To this end the candidate must attach to the application a certificate of poverty (świadectwo ubóstwa) or a proper confirmation from a guild or craftsmen's organisation (a nice [?] favour...).
The examination regulations of the Kielce Chamber of Crafts were approved on 16 April of this year by the voivode. The Chamber of Crafts as such is the only public-law institution empowered to issue diplomas. But — one asks — how is one to understand the decree sent to the police commissariats and "posterunki" (police posts) about the strict inspection (the deadline given to the police is 28 February 1931) at a time when the public-law institution (the Kielce Chamber of Crafts), which alone and exclusively is empowered to issue the diplomas — has to this day not yet begun to set up the examination commissions, although from Zagłębie alone several hundred applications from Jewish candidates alone have already been sent in for the examinations.
On whom, then, will the blame fall when a police agent writes up a fine for keeping an apprentice, while the craftsman concerned already a year ago turned with an application to the "Izba" to be admitted to the examination!
The same question is also raised regarding the "dispensations", which have been lying for over 2 years at the voivodeship office, without which (under Art. 146 of the law) the craftsman concerned cannot obtain a craftsman's card from the district authority (starostwo).
The only fair solution would therefore be that for all authorities, but especially for the police inspection, a confirmation from the local craftsmen's association or guild board should fully suffice that the craftsman concerned began in good time his efforts to obtain a craftsman's card and especially a diploma — from the moment the application was sent and the fee paid he should be given [?] the full right to employ terminants, just as if he held an actual diploma.
In this sense, indeed, last week the supreme body of the Jewish craftsmen's associations in Zagłębie handed corresponding memoranda to the starostas.
If this just demand is not accepted, a wrong will thereby be done to hundreds of craftsmen in our region. We wish to believe, however, that the voivode, whom all these appeals will reach, will recognise that the guilty party in this case is precisely the "Chamber of Crafts" (in Sławków and in Mushinluach [?] "diplomas" can no longer be fabricated for nothing...) and will revoke, or else properly correct, the latest decree on the strict inspection of workshops.
A. Gancwajch,
Secretary of the Craftsmen's Supreme Union [?] in Zagłębie.
